identification.summary: 1937CN is a China-linked group that Bkav, a Vietnamese security firm, believed was behind a wave of spyware intrusions into Vietnamese organizations from mid-2016, including the 29 July 2016 compromise of Vietnam Airlines' website and airport display and speaker systems [S4][S6]. Trend Micro (2023) assesses that its cluster Earth Zhulong is likely related to 1937CN, based on similar shellcode-loader code and overlapping victims [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: Bkav reported detecting the spyware in Vietnamese networks in mid-2012 [S7]. The earliest dated 1937CN-attributed event in the sources gathered is the late-June 2016 wave of intrusions [S4]. The imported record's claim of activity since 2013 is not confirmed by the sources gathered.
identification.notes: The 1937CN name comes from a self-styled Chinese group; press reports say it neither confirmed nor denied the 2016 airport attack, and one headline says it denied involvement [S5]. Trend Micro tracks Earth Zhulong as a separate vendor cluster that is only 'likely related' to 1937CN [S1]. Do not merge the 2016 Bkav-attributed activity with Earth Zhulong activity. No Microsoft actor name was found for this group.

attribution.confidence: Bkav stated the 2016 hackers were 'believed to be' members of 1937cn [S4]. Trend Micro describes Earth Zhulong as 'likely related' to 1937CN [S1]. No government attribution to a state sponsor was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Bkav: stolen data was sent to a lookalike domain of the Communist Party of Vietnam website (xxx.dcsvn.org) [S4]. Trend Micro: similar shellcode-loader code and overlapping victimology [S1][S2]. Vietnamese authorities and media blamed the group for the airport incident [S5][S6].

sectors: Telecommunications, technology and media (Earth Zhulong, 2020 onward)
regions: Southeast Asia (Trend Micro revised its Earth Zhulong report title to Southeast Asian firms) [S2]
targeting.notes: Bkav said the spyware compromised Vietnam Airlines and many other state organizations, businesses, banks, research institutes and universities [S4]. The July 2016 airport and airline incident carried messages about the South China Sea dispute [S6]. Telecom, technology and media targeting since 2020 is Trend Micro's finding for Earth Zhulong, not directly for 1937CN [S1][S3].

capabilities.summary: 2016 activity: Bkav described spyware that disguised itself as antivirus software, collected accounts and passwords, and received remote commands from the attacker; stolen data went to victim-specific subdomains of a spoofed Communist Party of Vietnam domain [S4]. Earth Zhulong (likely related): lure documents with malicious macros injecting Cobalt Strike shellcode, a custom ShellFang loader (three variants, 2020 to 2022, the latest with exception-based execution obfuscation and API hashing), and in early 2022 Group Policy Object abuse to deploy loaders and Cobalt Strike [S2][S3]. Cymulate also lists SharpHound, EarthWorm and Macamax among its tools [S3].

campaigns.name: Spyware first detected in Vietnamese networks
campaigns.summary: Bkav said it first detected the spyware in Vietnam's computer networks in mid-2012 and warned agencies, banks, institutes and universities several times afterward. Bkav's later link of this malware to 1937CN is its own assessment [S7][S4].

campaigns.name: Spyware wave against Vietnamese organizations
campaigns.summary: Bkav traced attacks on Vietnamese websites from late June 2016 to a spoofed Communist Party domain and said the hackers were believed to be 1937cn members [S4].

campaigns.name: Vietnam Airlines and airport compromise
campaigns.summary: Flight information screens and speakers at Noi Bai and Tan Son Nhat airports displayed or broadcast South China Sea messages, and the Vietnam Airlines website was compromised. Reports put leaked frequent-flyer records at more than 400,000 [S4][S6]. Flights were delayed as staff used manual check-in [S6].

campaigns.name: Group response to attribution (reports conflict)
campaigns.summary: A Cyware headline republishing VnExpress says the group denied involvement; other reports say it first claimed the attack and then declined to confirm or deny. The article text was not verified [S5].

campaigns.name: Bkav publishes spyware and fake-domain findings
campaigns.summary: Bkav said the malware stolen data went to xxx.dcsvn.org, a copy of the Communist Party of Vietnam website, and released a free scan tool [S4].

campaigns.name: Earth Zhulong ShellFang activity (likely related cluster)
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro verified three ShellFang loader variants used between 2020 and 2022 against telecom, technology and media targets, with GPO abuse for deployment in early 2022 [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: Trend Micro publishes Earth Zhulong report
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro assessed Earth Zhulong as likely related to 1937CN; the report was first titled for Vietnam and later revised to Southeast Asian firms [S1][S2].

diamond.adversary: A China-linked group using the 1937CN name; Bkav believed it was behind the 2016 intrusions [S4]. Sponsorship is not established in the sources gathered.
diamond.capability: Antivirus-disguised spyware with credential theft and remote control (2016) [S4]; macro lures, ShellFang loader and Cobalt Strike (Earth Zhulong, likely related) [S2][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Lookalike domain dcsvn.org of the Communist Party of Vietnam site with per-victim subdomains [S4].
diamond.victim: Vietnam Airlines, Vietnamese airports, state bodies, banks, businesses, research institutes and universities [S4][S6]; telecom, technology and media firms (Earth Zhulong) [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: The 2016 airport messages concerned the South China Sea dispute [S6].
diamond.technology: Vietnamese airport public-information systems, airline web and loyalty systems, and Windows enterprise networks with Group Policy [S6][S3].

gaps: Trend Micro's Earth Zhulong report (www.trendmicro.com) could not be opened by fetch; details come from search-result summaries and secondary coverage [S1][S2][S3].

The imported leads (Recorded Future hacktivism analysis, Securityaffairs, Votiro or Sebdraven malicious-document reporting) could not be retrieved or confirmed in this pass; Votiro linkage to 1937CN and shared infrastructure is reported only second-hand.
No state sponsor, government attribution, or technical indicators (hashes, IPs) for the 1937CN-named activity were found.
Imported record says active since 2013 and mentions 2015 defacements; these were not confirmed by the sources gathered.
A secondary summary ties Earth Zhulong to the name Goblin Panda; this is unverified here and is not added as an alias.
Press reports conflict on whether the group denied or neither confirmed nor denied the airport attack [S5].
Vendor-cluster boundary: Earth Zhulong is only 'likely related' to 1937CN [S1]; no Microsoft name or MITRE group ID was found.

provenance.importedSummary: 1937CN is a Chinese hacking group that has been active since at least 2013. The group is known for targeting Vietnamese organizations, including government agencies, businesses, and media outlets. 1937CN has been linked to a number of high-profile cyberattacks, including the hacking of Vietnam Airlines in 2016 and the defacement of Vietnamese government websites in 2015.

identification.summary: Ababil of Minab is a pro-Iran persona that claimed a March 2026 cyberattack on the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (LA Metro), including administrative access to its VMware vCenter environment and a related attack on GPS service provider Vyncs [S1]. Israeli firm Gambit Security assesses it is not a standalone hacktivist crew but is tied to Black Shadow and Iran's MOIS [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: 2026-03: LA Metro detected the intrusion around 16 March 2026, and the persona claimed it online about two weeks later [S2][S1]. Public reporting before this incident was not found.
identification.notes: The name refers to a US strike on a girls' school in Minab, Iran [S1][S2]. Dataminr cautioned that a definitive capability or intent assessment was premature [S1]. Gambit's MOIS/Black Shadow linkage is a vendor assessment; see attribution and gaps [S2][S3]. No Microsoft name or MITRE group ID was found for this persona.

attribution.sponsor: Gambit Security (Israel) assesses the group is tied to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) via Black Shadow infrastructure [S2][S3]. No government attribution of this specific incident was found.
attribution.confidence: Contested. Gambit states the group is not a new standalone hacktivist crew as it claims [S2]. ClearSky and Israel's National Cyber Directorate are cited as linking the infrastructure to Black Shadow, which Israel attributes to MOIS [S3]. LA Metro said attribution is part of the investigation and it would not speculate [S2]. Dataminr called definitive assessment premature [S1].
attribution.basis: Gambit forensic analysis of the intrusion and infrastructure overlap with Black Shadow [S2][S3]; ClearSky separate work [S3]. These are vendor findings, not government attribution.

actors.objectives: The persona's messaging is pro-Iran and framed around retaliation for the Minab school strike [S1]. Gambit assesses the activity is state-directed with a hacktivist cover, combining data theft and destruction [S2][S3]. Specific operator intent is not confirmed.

sectors: Regional transit (South Florida Regional Transportation Authority)
regions: Israel, Saudi Arabia and Turkey (victims identified by Gambit)
targeting.notes: Gambit reports the wider campaign hit SFRTA, UNIMAC and Vyncs besides LA Metro, with victims also in Israel, Saudi Arabia and Turkey [S3]. LA Metro said train and bus circulation was not interrupted; internal systems were taken down, affecting fare reloads and arrival signs [S1][S2].

capabilities.summary: The persona claimed administrative access to LA Metro's VMware vCenter environment [S1]. Gambit reports attackers deleted virtual machines, used backup software to wipe disks, and stole at least 700 GB of emails, backups and other files [S3][S2]. Gambit also reports the group used ChatGPT to refine a Python script that enumerated and dropped databases in the Vyncs environment [S3]. The group claimed 500 TB wiped and 1 TB exfiltrated; LA Metro confirmed partial access but did not validate those volumes [S2][S5].

campaigns.name: LA Metro intrusion
campaigns.summary: LA Metro detected a breach around mid-March 2026; internal systems were taken down, with delays to fare-card reloads and non-operational arrival signs, but no interruption to rail or bus service [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: Public claim of LA Metro and Vyncs attacks
campaigns.summary: Ababil of Minab claimed the LA Metro attack (vCenter admin access) and an attack on Vyncs, and alleged 500 TB wiped and 1 TB exfiltrated [S1][S5].

campaigns.name: LA Metro confirms breach
campaigns.summary: Reporting states LA Metro confirmed the breach on 2 April 2026; one report says it had not confirmed as of 15 April, so reporting is inconsistent [S3][S1].

campaigns.name: Gambit Security attribution report
campaigns.summary: Gambit publishes findings tying the activity to Black Shadow/MOIS and identifying further victims including SFRTA, UNIMAC and Vyncs [S2][S3][S4].

diamond.adversary: Pro-Iran persona; Gambit assesses MOIS-linked operators behind it [S2][S3].
diamond.capability: vCenter-level access, VM deletion, disk wiping via backup software, bulk data theft, AI-assisted database-dropping script [S1][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Overlap with Black Shadow infrastructure per Gambit and ClearSky; specific indicators not obtained [S3].
diamond.victim: LA Metro, SFRTA, UNIMAC, Vyncs; further victims in Israel, Saudi Arabia, Turkey [S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Persona branding invokes the Minab school strike as a grievance narrative [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Virtualization management (VMware vCenter), backup systems and database environments at transit and tracking-service providers [S1][S3].

gaps: Primary Gambit Security report and ClearSky report were not opened; findings rely on press coverage (TechCrunch, Security Boulevard, Route Fifty, Reuters via i24).
WebFetch failed (host resolution) for TechCrunch, SecurityAffairs, Dataminr and The Record, so article details come from search-result summaries only.
Initial access vector and specific malware are not public in the sources gathered.
Some search summaries describe Black Shadow as also tracked as Static Kitten/MuddyWater; this was not verified and may conflate vendor clusters. Do not merge until confirmed in a primary source.
Claimed volumes (500 TB wiped) are unverified; reported dates conflict (confirmation 2 April vs not confirmed as of 15 April).
No Microsoft actor name, MITRE group ID or government attribution located.
Security Affairs piece is opinion-style analysis; treat as commentary.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Virtualization management (vCenter), backup platforms and database servers at transit and logistics providers are key terrain; public transit is a visible, non-DoD civilian target [S1][S3]. STEP 2: The persona gives plausible deniability and a grievance narrative, which may lower the threshold for destructive action against US civil infrastructure [S2]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is administrative access to virtualization, deletion of VMs, wiping via backup tooling, and bulk theft, followed by a public Telegram-style claim [S1][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is further wiper/theft intrusions against US and regional civil operators of modest hardening, with inflated claims. MDCOA is destructive access to a provider with DoD or installation transport/logistics ties timed to US-Iran escalation. Candidate indicators: unusual vCenter admin logins, mass VM deletions, backup software issuing disk-wipe jobs, large mail/backup exfiltration, and database-drop scripts [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track claims by Iran-aligned personas but separate claims from verified impact, since volume claims were unverified [S5]. (2) Authorities: incidents at civilian operators sit outside DoD networks, so coordination runs through CISA/FBI and DC3 for DIB-linked suppliers; Gambit's attribution is not government attribution [S2]. (3) Mission assurance: harden and back up offline virtualization management and backup systems for installation-supporting services, and plan for loss of internal systems with continued physical operations, as LA Metro experienced [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with commercial providers and partners in Israel, Saudi Arabia and Turkey where victims were identified [S3].

provenance.importedSummary: Ababil of Minab is an emerging pro-Iranian hacktivist group with a limited public profile and little verifiable prior activity in threat intelligence reporting. The group claims responsibility for a cyberattack and allegedly possesses administrative access to targeted systems. Their pro-Iran messaging and targeting of a major US public transit authority align with known patterns of Iranian-aligned actors targeting US critical infrastructure. The use of escalatory language suggests potential for further activity.

identification.summary: admin@338 is a China-based cyber espionage group. FireEye says it has used newsworthy events as lures and has mostly targeted organizations involved in financial, economic and trade policy, usually with publicly available RATs such as Poison Ivy plus some non-public backdoors [S1][S6]. The name comes from a password the operators used with Poison Ivy [S3]. In March 2014 the group sent spear-phishing lures themed on Malaysian Airlines MH370 to an Asia-Pacific government and a US-based think tank [S4][S5]. In August 2015 FireEye linked it, with hedging, to spear phishing against Hong Kong media using the Dropbox-abusing LOWBALL backdoor [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Coverage of FireEye's 2013 Poison Ivy report says the group used Poison Ivy from about January 2008 [S3]. FireEye's 2015 post says FireEye had tracked the group since 2013 [S1][S7].
identification.notes: FireEye treated admin@338 as an uncategorized APT group with no APT number, saying it lacked enough information to assign one [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as admin@338 (G0018) [S6]. MISP-derived aliases TEMPER PANDA (CrowdStrike), Team338 and MAGNESIUM are already on the record. None of the sources opened for this profile give a current Microsoft Typhoon name for MAGNESIUM. Some low-quality secondary blogs equate admin@338 with APT18, Dynamite Panda, TigerMilk or Poseidon Group. Those are separately tracked clusters, and no primary source reviewed supports the merge, so they are not added.

attribution.sponsor: Not formally attributed by any government in the sources reviewed. FireEye describes the group as China-based [S1][S4].
attribution.confidence: FireEye said only that admin@338 'may have conducted' the 2015 Hong Kong media activity. It explicitly declined to attribute a second, related Dropbox-based operation to the group [S1]. The China-based assessment comes from FireEye, not from a government [S1].
attribution.basis: FireEye malware and infrastructure analysis. A BUBBLEWRAP sample in the 2015 campaign connected to a domain that resolved to an IP address the group had used before [S1]. Poison Ivy connection passwords linked the 2014 MH370 lures to the group [S4][S5]. FireEye also judged that the targets matched Beijing's likely intelligence interests [S1].

actors.objectives: Espionage. Earlier collection focused on financial, economic and trade-policy information [S1][S2]. FireEye assessed that the 2015 targeting of Hong Kong media was probably a response to political and economic challenges in Hong Kong and China. It said that access could give the government advance warning of protests, information on pro-democracy leaders, and insight needed to disrupt activity on the Internet [S1].

sectors: Financial services and financial, economic and trade-policy organizations [S1][S2]
ISP/telecommunications, government and defense (secondary per FireEye 2013) [S3]
targeting.notes: FireEye noted that the August 2015 campaign was the first it had seen from this group aimed at readers of traditional Chinese script. Earlier lures were in English and aimed at Western audiences [S1]. The campaign coincided with criminal charges against democracy activists and followed the late-2014 Umbrella Movement protests [S1].

capabilities.summary: Spear phishing with topical, news-cycle lure documents [S1][S4]. These included Word documents exploiting the old Office vulnerability CVE-2012-0158 [S1] and an executable disguised as a Flash video by binding a Flash icon to it [S4]. Malware includes the Poison Ivy RAT [S2][S4], WinHTTPHelper [S5], and the first-stage LOWBALL backdoor. LOWBALL uses the Dropbox API with a hard-coded bearer token over HTTPS port 443 for command and control, and runs operator-supplied batch files to gather directory, network, user/group, service and netstat information [S1]. The second-stage BUBBLEWRAP backdoor (Backdoor.APT.FakeWinHTTPHelper) persists at boot, communicates over HTTP, HTTPS or SOCKS, and supports plugins [S1]. Dropbox revoked the access token LOWBALL used after FireEye notified it [S1][S7].

attack.name: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location

campaigns.name: Poison Ivy espionage against finance and policy targets
campaigns.summary: In its 2013 Poison Ivy report, FireEye identified admin@338 as one of three groups (with th3bug and menuPass) using Poison Ivy in targeted attacks. It said admin@338 mainly targeted financial services, with significant activity against the ISP/telecom, government and defense sectors [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: MH370-themed spear phishing
campaigns.summary: On 10 March 2014, two days after the flight disappeared, the group sent a 'Malaysian Airlines MH370.doc' lure that dropped Poison Ivy to a government in the Asia-Pacific region. On 14 March it sent MH370-themed lures to a US-based think tank [S4][S5].

campaigns.name: Hong Kong media spear phishing (LOWBALL / Dropbox C2)
campaigns.summary: Traditional-Chinese lures about an Umbrella Movement anniversary and a Hong Kong University referendum carried CVE-2012-0158 Word exploits. They targeted Hong Kong newspapers, radio and TV, delivering LOWBALL with Dropbox command and control and the BUBBLEWRAP second stage. FireEye said admin@338 'may have' conducted the activity. It also found a possibly related second operation with up to 50 targets that it did not attribute [S1][S7].

diamond.adversary: China-based espionage group that FireEye tracks as an uncategorized APT. No government attribution has been made [S1].
diamond.capability: Topical spear-phishing lures, CVE-2012-0158 Office exploits, Poison Ivy, WinHTTPHelper, LOWBALL and BUBBLEWRAP [S1][S4][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Legitimate cloud storage (a Dropbox account and API token) used as command and control. Dynamic-DNS-style domains such as accounts.serveftp[.]com resolving to IPs the group had used before [S1].
diamond.victim: Financial, economic and trade-policy organizations; Asia-Pacific government officials; a US think tank; Hong Kong media [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection aligned with Beijing's interest in economic policy and, per FireEye, in monitoring Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement and the press that covers it [S1].
diamond.technology: Unpatched Microsoft Office (CVE-2012-0158), user trust in news-related attachments, and trusted cloud services that mix C2 traffic into normal HTTPS [S1][S4].

gaps: No admin@338 activity after 2015 was found in the sources reviewed. Whether the group is still active, has been renamed or has been merged into another vendor cluster is unknown.
Microsoft's current name for MAGNESIUM, if any, was not confirmed. No Microsoft source was found.

The primary FireEye 2013 reports ('Poison Ivy: Assessing Damage and Extracting Intelligence' and 'Know Your Enemy: Tracking a Rapidly Evolving APT Actor') could not be opened. Their content here relies on press coverage [S2][S3].
The FireEye MH370 blog was seen only through a mirror and coverage. The MITRE ATT&CK, CFR Cyber Operations Tracker, Security Affairs and Dark Reading pages could not be fetched (DNS failures).
FireEye's attribution of the 2015 campaign is hedged ('may have'). The second Dropbox operation (up to 50 targets) is explicitly unattributed [S1].
Secondary blogs claim links to APT18, Dynamite Panda, TigerMilk, Poseidon Group and the MSS. None of these is supported by a primary source reviewed, so they are excluded.
Claims of a separate 2014 theft of classified MH370 investigation documents were not tied to admin@338 by any source reviewed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): User email clients and Office document handling are key terrain, as are outbound HTTPS channels to sanctioned cloud storage, which this actor used for command and control [S1]. STEP 2 (effects): News-cycle lures (MH370, protests, political events) reach targets within days of an event, so lure risk rises during any high-profile crisis involving US or allied forces [S1][S4]. STEP 3 (adversary model): Topical spear phish, then an Office exploit or disguised executable, then a first-stage backdoor running discovery commands (directory, ipconfig, net user/group, services, netstat), then a second-stage persistent backdoor [S1]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is email-borne collection against policy, finance and think-tank-adjacent staff using topical lures and cloud-storage C2. MDCOA is persistent, low-visibility access to planning or liaison networks through trusted-cloud C2 that blends with normal traffic. Candidate indicators: Office documents exploiting CVE-2012-0158; executables with Flash icons; Dropbox API calls from non-browser processes with bearer tokens; files named [COMPUTER_NAME]_upload.bat or _download; connections to accounts.serveftp[.]com [S1][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Track news-event lure activity and cloud-service API use from unusual processes. FireEye's case shows that defender-provider coordination (Dropbox revoking the token) can sever C2 [S1]. Authorities: Disrupting actor use of a commercial cloud account depends on the provider and on law-enforcement or industry channels, not DoD action. Mission assurance: Patch legacy Office vulnerabilities and restrict executable attachments, because the documented access vectors are old exploits and disguised executables [S1][S4]. Coordination: Share indicators with cloud providers, and with partners whose staff (think tanks, policy and finance liaisons) were historically targeted [S1][S4].

provenance.importedSummary: China-based cyber threat group. It has previously used newsworthy events as lures to deliver malware and has primarily targeted organizations involved in financial, economic, and trade policy, typically using publicly available RATs such as PoisonIvy, as well as some non-public backdoors. This threat actor targets prodemocratic activists and organizations in Hong Kong, European and international financial institutions, and a U.S.-based think tank.

identification.summary: Iran-based group that MITRE says has been active since at least 2010 and moved from website defacement to malware-based cyber espionage by 2014, targeting the US defense industrial base and Iranian users of anti-censorship tools [S1]. FireEye's Operation Saffron Rose report described the group using fake conference lures, spoofed login pages and 'Stealer' malware that exfiltrated data over FTP [S4]. CrowdStrike tracks the same activity as FLYING KITTEN [S3]. MITRE also associates the Rocket Kitten / Operation Woolen-Goldfish reporting with this group as a potential relationship [S1].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least 2010 (defacement era) [S1]. CrowdStrike: tracking as FLYING KITTEN since mid-January 2014 [S3]. Rocket Kitten reporting: operating since at least mid-2014 [S8].
identification.notes: No Microsoft threat-actor name was found for this cluster in the sources gathered. MITRE G0130 groups Ajax Security Team, Flying Kitten, Operation Saffron Rose, AjaxTM, Operation Woolen-Goldfish and Rocket Kitten, but describes the Rocket Kitten link only as a 'potential relationship' based on infrastructure, tools and modes of operation [S1]. Ajax/Saffron Rose/Flying Kitten reporting comes from FireEye and CrowdStrike (2014) [S3]; Rocket Kitten, Woolen-Goldfish and Thamar Reservoir reporting comes from Trend Micro, ClearSky and Check Point (2015) [S5][S6][S8][S9]. Facts are kept attributed to the reporting vendor.

attribution.sponsor: Iran (suspected). FireEye assessed the Ajax Security Team was likely backed by the Iranian government but could not say whether it operated alone or within a larger coordinated effort [S4]. Press coverage of Check Point's Rocket Kitten report linked the group to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, though Check Point's own wording was more cautious [S9].
attribution.confidence: Vendor assessments only. FireEye: suspected Iranian-government backing; press coverage is inconsistent, with some quoting the report as calling the government relationship inconclusive [S4]. Trend Micro: Woolen-Goldfish 'possibly state-sponsored' [S5]. ClearSky: evidence points to Iranian hackers [S6]. Check Point: suggested an official body may have recruited local hackers; press coverage linked the group to the IRGC [S9]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Persian-language and Iran time-zone settings on most victim machines found on one C2 server [S4]; Iranian forum origins and defacement history [S1][S4]; Persian-language references in code (Rocket Kitten, per researchers Anderson and Guarnieri) [S10]; operational-security failures exposing a developer persona 'Wool3n.H4T' [S9].

actors.objectives: Espionage supporting Iranian state interests: collecting information from US defense contractors and monitoring Iranian dissidents and users of anti-censorship tools [S4]. Trend Micro and ClearSky judged Rocket Kitten was not after monetary gain but was keeping tabs on individuals affiliated with foreign-policy and defense actors [S8]. ClearSky assessed Thamar Reservoir access was sought for espionage or other nation-state interests [S6].

sectors: Diplomacy, defense and security, journalism, human rights [S6]
targeting.notes: FireEye identified 77 victims on one C2 server, most with Persian-language and Iran time-zone settings [S4]. ClearSky counted about 550 targets, mostly in the Middle East, in the Thamar Reservoir / Rocket Kitten activity [S6][S8]. Citizen Lab's 2015 diaspora 2FA-phishing report shares infrastructure and tactics with earlier Iranian campaigns but does not name this group [S7].

capabilities.summary: Low-to-moderate sophistication social engineering and credential theft. Spearphishing with fake conference (IEEE) lures and spoofed credential pages such as Outlook Web Access, followed by prompts to install a fake 'browser patch' [S3][S4]. Custom 'Stealer' malware exfiltrating data over FTP [S4]. Trojanized anti-censorship software [S4]. Rocket Kitten used GHOLE malware, a modified version of a Core Security penetration-testing tool, and later OneDrive links to files posing as PowerPoint presentations [S5]. Thamar Reservoir activity combined compromised trusted websites hosting fake pages, multi-stage malware, phone calls and social-media messages [S6]. Real-time phishing designed to defeat Gmail two-factor authentication was documented against Iranian diaspora targets (not attributed by name) [S7]. Telegram account takeover via intercepted SMS codes and abuse of Telegram's API to enumerate 15 million Iranian phone numbers was attributed to Rocket Kitten by outside researchers [S10]. ClearSky judged the operators technically unsophisticated and prone to mistakes [S6].

diamond.adversary: Iran-based operators who emerged from Iranian hacker forums and defacement activity; developer persona 'Wool3n.H4T' exposed by Check Point [S1][S4][S9].
diamond.capability: Spearphishing, spoofed login pages, Stealer malware, GHOLE malware, trojanized anti-censorship tools, real-time 2FA phishing, SMS-code interception [S3][S4][S5][S10].
diamond.infrastructure: Typosquat domains spoofing target organizations, FTP exfiltration servers, compromised trusted websites hosting fake pages, OneDrive-hosted lures [S3][S5][S6].
diamond.victim: US defense contractors; Iranian dissidents, activists and anti-censorship users; Israeli and European researchers, diplomats, journalists and defense personnel [S3][S5][S6][S10].
diamond.socioPolitical: Monitoring of regime opponents and collection on foreign-policy and defense communities of interest to Iran [S4][S8].
diamond.technology: Webmail and OWA credential flows, SMS-based authentication, consumer messaging apps (Telegram) and personal accounts that bridge into corporate networks [S3][S8][S10].

gaps: Cluster boundary: MITRE treats Rocket Kitten as only a potential relationship to Ajax Security Team; FireEye/CrowdStrike (Ajax/Flying Kitten) and Trend Micro/ClearSky/Check Point (Rocket Kitten) reporting may describe distinct but related clusters [S1].
No Microsoft threat-actor name, and no US government attribution or indictment, was found for this cluster.

Primary documents not opened directly: FireEye Saffron Rose PDF, Check Point 'Campaign With 9 Lives' report, Trend Micro white papers, ClearSky Thamar Reservoir PDF and the MITRE G0130 page (WebFetch failed); details rely on search-result summaries and press coverage.
The FireEye PDF is labeled 2013 while coverage dates publication to May 2014; exact publication date unverified.
Citizen Lab's 2015 2FA phishing report does not attribute the activity to a named group; inclusion here reflects shared Iranian infrastructure only [S7].
Imported aliases Group 26, Sayad, Timberworm, TEMP.Beanie and Thamar Reservoir were not confirmed by a source gathered in this pass.
No reporting on activity after 2016 was found; current status (dissolved, renamed or absorbed into other Iranian clusters) is unknown.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): key terrain is identity rather than networks: personal webmail, OWA portals, SMS-based 2FA and messaging accounts of defense staff, analysts and dissident contacts [S3][S7][S10]. STEP 2 (effects): personal-account compromise lets the actor bridge from weakly defended home networks into corporate accounts [S8]. STEP 3 (threat evaluation): template is spoofed domain or lure (fake conference, OneDrive document), credential capture, then a stealer or GHOLE implant with FTP exfiltration [S4][S5]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is persistent credential phishing of defense-industry and policy personnel and their personal accounts for espionage [S3][S8]. MDCOA is real-time 2FA bypass or SMS interception against personnel with access to mission systems, enabling account takeover and contact-network mapping [S7][S10]. Candidate indicators: lookalike domains of the unit or contractor, unsolicited conference invitations, 'browser patch' download prompts after login, unexpected 2FA codes or calls from foreign numbers, outbound FTP from user endpoints [S3][S4][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: fuse phishing reports from personal and official accounts, since this actor targets both [S8]. Authorities: personal and diaspora-contact accounts fall outside DODIN defensive authority; coordinate with counterintelligence and law enforcement. Mission assurance: phishing-resistant MFA instead of SMS codes and awareness training for staff targeted via conference and Iran-studies lures [S4][S7][S10]. Coordination: share lookalike-domain and C2 indicators with DIB partners, who were primary 2014 victims [S3].

identification.summary: Amaranth-Dragon is a name used by Check Point Research for a previously undocumented activity cluster that it says shares links to the China-affiliated APT41 ecosystem [S1]. Check Point reported campaigns in 2025 against government and law enforcement organizations in Cambodia, Thailand, Laos, Indonesia, Singapore and the Philippines, typically focused on one or two countries at a time [S1][S4]. The cluster rapidly weaponized WinRAR CVE-2025-8088, with exploitation reported from 18 August 2025, four days after a working exploit became public [S5].
identification.firstObserved: Check Point reports tracking the activity since March 2025 [S5].
identification.notes: The name is Check Point's; no Microsoft name or MITRE group ID was found in the sources gathered. Check Point describes the link to APT41 as overlap in tooling and operational patterns, not a confirmed merger of clusters [S1][S4]. Keep Amaranth-Dragon distinct from APT41 (Microsoft: Brass Typhoon) when citing.

attribution.confidence: Check Point Research assesses the actor is closely linked to, or part of, the APT41 ecosystem, based on shared tooling and operational patterns [S1][S4]. No government attribution to a specific PRC organization was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Check Point cites similarities between the custom Amaranth Loader and tools associated with APT41 (DodgeBox, Dustpan, Dusttrap) [S4]. Analysis of file compilation times and campaign timelines suggests the operators work in UTC+8 (China Standard Time) [S4].

actors.objectives: Espionage against ASEAN-region government and law enforcement organizations, based on the victim set and event-themed lures reported by Check Point [S1][S5]. Specific collection requirements are not stated in the sources gathered.

targeting.notes: Campaigns were each restricted to one or two countries [S1]. One secondary report adds further Southeast Asian states (Brunei, Malaysia, Myanmar, Timor-Leste, Vietnam); this is not confirmed by the Check Point summary and should be treated as unverified [S7]. Lures were themed around geopolitical or local events [S5].

capabilities.summary: Early campaigns used ZIP archives containing LNK and BAT files that decrypt and run the Amaranth Loader via DLL side-loading . Later campaigns exploited WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 (path traversal) to place a script in the Startup folder and create a Registry Run key, launching the loader [S5]. The loader is a custom 64-bit DLL that fetches an AES key and decrypts a payload in memory; the final payload was usually the open-source Havoc C2 framework [S4]. TGAmaranth RAT, a Telegram-bot-controlled RAT with anti-debugging and anti-AV features, was used in some intrusions [S5]. C2 servers sat behind Cloudflare and answered only to IP addresses from the targeted country, returning HTTP 403 otherwise [S4].

diamond.adversary: Unnamed cluster assessed as linked to the APT41 ecosystem; operators apparently work in UTC+8 [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: Amaranth Loader (DLL side-loading), Havoc C2, TGAmaranth RAT, WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 exploit, LNK/BAT droppers [S5].
diamond.infrastructure: C2 behind Cloudflare with country-level geofencing (HTTP 403 for non-target IPs); malicious archives hosted on cloud services; Telegram bot C2 for the RAT [S5].
diamond.victim: Government and law enforcement organizations in six ASEAN countries [S1][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Lures tied to real geopolitical and local events suggest regional political and security intelligence interest; sponsor intent is not stated in sources [S5].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints with unpatched WinRAR (fixed in 7.13) and users who open archive attachments; cloud-hosted payload delivery [S5].

gaps: Primary Check Point Research report (research.checkpoint.com) could not be opened; details rest on Check Point's blog summary as returned by search and on secondary coverage.

A secondary aggregator gave specific 2025 campaign dates (19 March Cambodia, 28 April Cambodia, 3 July Thailand/Laos, 18 August Indonesia) that were not verified against the primary report and are not used as fact here.
One aggregator said the October Philippines campaign did not use CVE-2025-8088; unverified.
No government attribution, sponsor organization, Microsoft name or MITRE ID found.
Extent of overlap with APT41 (Brass Typhoon) infrastructure or personnel is unknown; the link is assessed from tooling similarity.
Victim names, data stolen and any post-Havoc activity are not public in the sources gathered.
No activity after the late-2025 campaigns is documented in the sources gathered.

Two secondary news sources (The Hacker News and Infosecurity Magazine) were dropped during fact-checking because their URLs could not be confirmed in search results; claims resting only on them were removed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is end-user Windows workstations in partner-nation government and law-enforcement networks, and the cloud file-hosting services used to deliver archives. STEP 2: The actor operationalizes newly disclosed archive-tool vulnerabilities within days and geofences C2, so researchers and defenders outside the target country may see nothing [S5]. STEP 3: The template is an event-themed lure, a RAR/ZIP archive, Startup-folder or Run-key persistence, a side-loaded loader, then Havoc or a Telegram RAT [S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against ASEAN government and law-enforcement targets, one or two countries per campaign. MDCOA is retargeting to defense or maritime organizations, or US/coalition personnel working with partners, using lures on regional security events (the Philippines Coast Guard lure is an indicator of maritime interest) . Candidate indicators: WinRAR versions below 7.13 on endpoints, scripts written to Startup folders from archives, new Run keys, side-loaded DLLs, Telegram API traffic from servers, and unexpected Havoc beacons [S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: partner-nation ASEAN networks are the observed victims, so shared-indicator exchange with partners matters; geofenced C2 means local telemetry from the victim country is required to see the infrastructure . (2) Authorities: monitoring or hunting on partner networks requires partner consent and the appropriate agreements; US-network action follows normal DODIN and DCO authorities. (3) Mission assurance: enforce WinRAR 7.13 or later and restrict archive handling on mission systems, since exploitation began days after exploit release [S5]. (4) Coordination: coordinate with allied cyber centers and the vendor (Check Point) for indicators, and with DC3 where contractors are exposed.

provenance.importedSummary: Amaranth-Dragon is a previously untracked threat actor assessed to be closely linked to the China-affiliated APT 41 ecosystem, exhibiting similar tooling and operational patterns. The group demonstrated technical maturity by rapidly operationalizing CVE-2025-8088, a vulnerability in WinRAR, shortly after its public disclosure. Check Point Research has identified multiple campaigns targeting Cambodia, Thailand, Laos, Indonesia, Singapore, and the Philippines, with operations typically focused on one or two countries at a time. The overlaps in technical and operational indicators strongly suggest that Amaranth-Dragon is either affiliated with or part of the broader APT-41 ecosystem.

identification.summary: Kaspersky describes Angry Likho (called Sticky Werewolf by some vendors) as an APT group it has monitored since 2023, which it placed in its Likho cluster because it strongly resembles Awaken Likho [S1]. BI.ZONE first documented Sticky Werewolf in October 2023 and said it had been active since April 2023 with at least 30 attacks on government organizations in Russia and Belarus [S4][S5]. Kaspersky reports its 2025 attacks deliver the Lumma Stealer via spear-phishing with archives containing shortcut (LNK) files and a lure document [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: April 2023 (BI.ZONE and Morphisec: active since April 2023); first publicly documented October 2023 [S4][S3][S5].
identification.notes: Kaspersky name: Angry Likho; Sticky Werewolf is the name used by other vendors (BI.ZONE, Morphisec) [S1][S3]. Kaspersky treats it as a separate cluster from Awaken Likho while noting strong resemblance [S1]. Whether the 2023-2024 Sticky Werewolf reporting and the 2025 Angry Likho reporting describe exactly the same operator is stated by Kaspersky and press coverage but the vendors' own cluster boundaries were not verified against primary documents [S1][S2].

attribution.confidence: Not attributed to a state by any source gathered. Morphisec says the group's origin is unclear and no definitive evidence points to a specific national origin, noting only a possible but unconfirmed link to a pro-Ukrainian cyberespionage group or hacktivists [S3][S6].
attribution.basis: Targeting concentrated in Russia and Belarus [S1][S4]. Kaspersky reportedly judged the operators likely native Russian speakers based on the fluent Russian of the bait files (as relayed in search-result summaries of the Securelist report) [S1]. These are vendor assessments, not government attribution.

actors.objectives: Kaspersky says attacks focus on employees of large organizations, including government agencies and their contractors, and Lumma harvests browser data, banking details, credentials and cryptowallet files [S1][S2]. Morphisec assessed that recent techniques suggest espionage and data exfiltration intent [S3]. Coverage also emphasizes a financial-theft dimension, so the objective mix is unresolved [S2].

targeting.notes: BI.ZONE: government organizations in Russia and Belarus in 2023 [S4][S5]. Morphisec (June 2024): a pharmaceutical company, a Russian microbiology and vaccine institute, and the aviation sector, with email lures impersonating an executive at a Moscow aircraft and spacecraft firm [S3][S6]. Kaspersky (Feb 2025): hundreds of victims in Russia, several in Belarus, additional incidents elsewhere assessed as likely incidental; main targets are in Russia and Belarus [S1].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing with RAR or password-protected archives containing LNK files and decoy documents; LNKs fetch payloads from WebDAV servers, an earlier chain used gofile.io download links [S3][S6]. Kaspersky reports Lumma Stealer delivered in 2025, including via an NSIS self-extracting archive named FrameworkSurvivor.exe, with sandbox/emulator checks that exit or wait 10,000 ms, a technique also seen in Awaken Likho implants [S1][S2]. Kaspersky describes a compact infrastructure, a limited range of implants and reliance on readily available malicious utilities from darknet forums [S1]. Earlier Sticky Werewolf payloads reported by BI.ZONE and Morphisec: NetWire (2023), DarkTrack, MetaStealer, Rhadamanthys Stealer and Ozone RAT, with a variant of the CypherIT cryptor [S5][S3][S6].

campaigns.summary: Standardized spear-phishing with RAR archives and LNK files delivering Lumma Stealer; new FrameworkSurvivor.exe NSIS delivery; hundreds of victims in Russia and several in Belarus.

diamond.adversary: Unattributed cluster tracked as Angry Likho (Kaspersky) and Sticky Werewolf (BI.ZONE, Morphisec); origin disputed or unknown [S1][S3][S6].
diamond.capability: Archive and LNK phishing chains, WebDAV payload hosting, commodity stealers and RATs (Lumma, Rhadamanthys, Ozone RAT, NetWire, DarkTrack) and NSIS packaging [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Compact infrastructure per Kaspersky [S1]; WebDAV servers and gofile.io links used for payload delivery [S3][S6]. Specific indicators not gathered.
diamond.victim: Government agencies and contractors, aviation, pharmaceutical and vaccine research organizations in Russia and Belarus [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Targets sit inside Russia and Belarus; Morphisec notes a possible but unconfirmed pro-Ukrainian link, which remains uncertain [S6][S3].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints reached by email attachments; Windows shortcut (LNK) files, WebDAV and self-extracting archives abused; browser-stored credentials and cryptowallet files targeted [S1][S3].

gaps: Could not open the primary Securelist, Morphisec, BI.ZONE or The Hacker News pages (fetch failed); statements rely on search-result excerpts of those documents and should be verified against them.

Sponsor, nationality and motive are unresolved: Morphisec cites only a possible, unconfirmed pro-Ukrainian link and says no definitive origin evidence exists; Kaspersky's Russian-speaker judgment is only indirect evidence. An earlier F6 'pro-Ukrainian' characterization was not verified.
Exact relationship to Awaken Likho (shared tooling or single operator) is raised by Kaspersky but not resolved [S1].
Records from this encyclopedia list country RU; no cited source supports Russian state origin, so that field should be reviewed.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID or Microsoft name located; no IOCs, C2 domains or hashes gathered.
Activity after February 2025 not found in searches.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Email gateways and user endpoints at government, defense-industrial, aviation and pharmaceutical organizations are the exposed terrain, but the cited victims are Russian and Belarusian, so direct US exposure is not shown in sources [S1][S3]. STEP 2: Capability is commodity: purchased stealers and RATs, LNK/archive lures, compact infrastructure [S1]. STEP 3: Template is spear-phish with archive, then LNK, then WebDAV or NSIS payload, then Lumma or RAT, then credential and wallet theft [S1][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued phishing waves against Russia and Belarus government and industry. MDCOA is retargeting at other aviation or pharmaceutical organizations using the same lures. Candidate indicators: LNK files inside RAR archives launching executables from WebDAV paths, FrameworkSurvivor.exe, sandbox sleep of 10,000 ms [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat this as a low-sophistication commodity-malware cluster; track vendor reporting for spread beyond Russia and Belarus [S1]. (2) Authorities: no US-relevant victimization shown; any defensive action stays within owned networks. (3) Mission assurance: block or alert on LNK-in-archive attachments and outbound WebDAV from user endpoints; protect browser-stored credentials [S3]. (4) Coordination: share indicators through standard CTI channels if observed; attribution is unresolved, so avoid naming a sponsor.

provenance.importedSummary: Angry Likho is an APT group that has been active since 2023, primarily targeting large organizations and government agencies in Russia and Belarus. Their attacks typically involve spear-phishing emails with malicious attachments, such as RAR archives, and utilize a known payload, the Lumma stealer, for data exfiltration. The group employs a compact infrastructure and has been linked to espionage activities, particularly in sectors like aviation and pharmaceuticals. Their operations have shown a focus on collecting sensitive information, including cryptowallet files and user credentials.

identification.summary: Antique Typhoon (formerly tracked as Storm-0558) is a China-based threat actor that Microsoft says has espionage objectives and mainly seeks unauthorized access to employee email accounts at targeted organizations [S1][S8]. In 2023 it used an acquired Microsoft account (MSA) consumer signing key to forge authentication tokens and read Exchange Online and Outlook.com email at about 25 organizations, including government agencies [S1]. The US Cyber Safety Review Board (CSRB) later found the intrusion was preventable and resulted from 'a cascade of security failures at Microsoft' [S6][S7].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: interest in OAuth applications, token theft and token replay since at least August 2021 [S1]. Forged-token email access began 2023-05-15 [S1]. CSRB Acting Deputy Chair Dmitri Alperovitch said industry has tracked the actor for over two decades (reporting) [S6].
identification.notes: Microsoft renamed Storm-0558 to Antique Typhoon in an August 2024 update to its July 2023 analysis [S1]; Microsoft's naming map lists Storm-0558 as the other name [S8]. Microsoft reports minor overlaps with Violet Typhoon (ZIRCONIUM, APT31) but holds high confidence that this is a distinct group [S1]. No MITRE ATT&CK group ID was found.

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (assessed). Microsoft calls the actor China-based with espionage objectives [S1]. Press coverage of the CSRB report describes the group as affiliated with the PRC; China has denied involvement [S5][S6].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft assesses with moderate confidence that the actor is China-based, and with high confidence that it is distinct from Violet Typhoon [S1]. The CSRB report characterizes the actor as PRC-affiliated (per press coverage; the report text was not opened) [S6]. No indictment or sanctions naming this actor were found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and incident response, including activity hours matching China Standard Time, Monday to Friday [S1]; CSRB review of the 2023 intrusion (via press coverage) [S6][S7].

actors.objectives: Espionage through collection of email from government, diplomatic, economic and legislative targets, with particular focus on US and European bodies and on individuals tied to Taiwan and Uyghur geopolitical interests [S1]. In the 2023 campaign, nine of ten compromised State Department accounts reportedly belonged to people working on East Asia and the Pacific [S5].

sectors: Individuals tied to Taiwan and Uyghur interests [S1]
targeting.notes: The 2023 campaign hit about 25 organizations per Microsoft [S1]; CSRB coverage cites 22 organizations and over 500 individuals, including Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo, US Ambassador to China R. Nicholas Burns and Congressman Don Bacon [S7]. About 60,000 unclassified emails were taken from 10 State Department accounts, along with a list of the department's email accounts (reporting a Senate briefing and State Department confirmation) [S5].

capabilities.summary: Cloud identity abuse is the signature capability. The actor forged Azure AD and MSA tokens with an acquired MSA consumer signing key, which Microsoft code accepted for enterprise tokens because of a validation error, and abused a flaw in the GetAccessTokenForResource API to mint new tokens from issued ones [S1]. It ran a custom web panel for token replay, used dedicated SoftEther proxy infrastructure, and used PowerShell and Python scripts with hardcoded bearer tokens to call the OWA Exchange Store REST service, optionally over Tor or SOCKS5 [S1]. Wiz assessed the key could have signed OpenID v2.0 tokens for other Azure AD applications such as SharePoint, Teams and OneDrive, though no exploitation of those services was confirmed [S3][S9]. Historically Microsoft has seen phishing, credential harvesting, exploitation of public-facing applications leading to China Chopper web shells, the Cigril malware launched via DLL search-order hijacking, and credential theft from LSASS memory and the SAM hive [S1]. Microsoft's September 2023 account of key theft (crash dump moved to a corporate debugging environment, then a compromised engineer account) was later revised: in March 2024 Microsoft said it had not found a crash dump containing the key [S2].

A federal agency detected anomalous MailItemsAccessed events and reported them; Microsoft began its investigation on 2023-06-16 and blocked the key [S1][S4]. About 60,000 State Department emails were stolen [S5].

diamond.adversary: China-based espionage actor (Microsoft, moderate confidence), active on China Standard Time working hours [S1]; described as PRC-affiliated in CSRB coverage [S6].
diamond.capability: Forged MSA/Azure AD tokens, token replay panel, PowerShell and Python OWA scripts, China Chopper web shells, Cigril malware, credential dumping [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Dedicated token-replay servers with a web panel at /#/login, SoftEther proxy hosts fingerprinted by JARM, Tor and SOCKS5 routing [S1].
diamond.victim: About 25 organizations incl. US government agencies and associated consumer accounts [S1]; State Department, Commerce Secretary and other officials [S5][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on US and European diplomacy and East Asia policy, plus Taiwan- and Uyghur-related individuals [S1][S5].
diamond.technology: Microsoft cloud identity: MSA consumer signing keys, Azure AD token validation, Exchange Online/OWA, Outlook.com [S1][S3].

gaps: How the actor actually obtained the MSA signing key is unresolved; Microsoft withdrew its crash-dump explanation in March 2024 [S2].
CSRB report (cisa.gov PDF) and CISA advisory AA23-193A could not be opened; details are from press coverage and search summaries [S4][S6][S7].
Victim count differs: Microsoft about 25 organizations vs CSRB coverage 22 organizations and over 500 individuals [S1][S7].

The reported link to Operation Aurora (2009) and RSA SecurID (2011) comes from a CSRB official's quoted remark in press coverage, not a verified primary attribution; vendor cluster boundaries for those older intrusions are not established here [S6].
Microsoft's July 11, 2023 blog and MSRC posts on blogs.microsoft.com and msrc.microsoft.com, and Wiz's original post, could not be fetched.
No public reporting on Antique Typhoon activity after 2023 was found; current operations are unknown.
Whether the key was used against Azure AD applications beyond Exchange Online (Wiz scenario) is unconfirmed [S3][S9].
No MITRE ATT&CK group entry was found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The operational environment includes commercial cloud identity providers and hosted email (Exchange Online/M365). Key terrain sits in the provider's token-signing infrastructure, outside DoD control [S1][S3]. STEP 2: A provider-side key compromise lets the actor bypass tenant authentication and MFA entirely, so tenant hardening alone does not close the gap. Detection depends on audit logs such as MailItemsAccessed [S1][S4]. STEP 3: Doctrinal template: acquire signing material or credentials, forge or replay tokens through dedicated proxy infrastructure, then run scripted bulk mailbox collection of selected officials, with no on-host malware in the victim tenant [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet, targeted email collection against officials working East Asia and Pacific policy, especially around diplomatic events [S1][S5]. MDCOA is undetected forged-token access to DoD or coalition M365 tenants during a Taiwan crisis, exposing planning traffic and enabling follow-on targeting [S1][S3]. Candidate indicators: MailItemsAccessed from unusual AppIDs, tokens with unexpected issuers or key IDs, mailbox access from SoftEther/JARM-fingerprinted or Tor egress, and REST calls to OWA from unknown clients [S1][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: the intrusion was found by a customer agency's logs, not the provider, so JCC2 views must ingest cloud audit telemetry (premium logging) from mission-relevant tenants [S1][S4][S7]. (2) Authorities: response to a cloud-provider-side compromise relies on the provider and on CISA/FBI channels; define in advance who requests provider forensics and log access [S4][S7]. (3) Mission assurance: treat unclassified commercial email as exposed to collection for East Asia operations and keep sensitive planning on DoD-controlled systems [S5]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with CISA, the FBI and cloud providers quickly, as AA23-193A did; plan for vendor root-cause findings to change over time [S2][S4].

identification.summary: Antlion is the Symantec Threat Hunter Team name for a China-linked, state-backed espionage group that ran a persistent campaign against Taiwanese financial institutions and a manufacturer over at least 18 months in 2020-2021, using a custom backdoor Symantec named xPack [S1][S2][S4].
identification.firstObserved: SecurityWeek reports the group is believed active since at least 2011 [S3]. The campaign Symantec described ran about 2020-2021 and was published in February 2022 [S1][S4].
identification.notes: No Microsoft Typhoon name is recorded in this encyclopedia for Antlion, and no source gathered links Antlion to a Microsoft name. Dark Reading says Antlion is also tracked as Pirate Panda and Tropic Trooper [S5]; those are separate vendor clusters, so the overlap is flagged in gaps rather than merged. MITRE group ID is not recorded.

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (assessed by Symantec as state-backed) [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: Symantec describes Antlion as a Chinese state-backed APT group and assesses the aim as espionage based on observed data theft [S1][S2]. SecurityWeek words it as 'likely backed by the Chinese government' [S3]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Vendor assessment from Symantec's analysis of tooling, targeting of Taiwanese organizations and data exfiltration [S1][S2]; secondary coverage repeats it [S3][S4].

actors.objectives: Espionage: Symantec assessed the goal as intelligence collection because the attackers exfiltrated data from victim networks [S1][S2].

targeting.notes: Symantec reports at least three Taiwanese organizations compromised: two financial entities and a manufacturing company [S1][S2]. Dark Reading's summary of the report cites at least six Taiwanese financial institutions [S5]; the discrepancy is unresolved. Dark Reading also says earlier espionage by the tracked group focused on South China Sea neighbors such as India, Vietnam and the Philippines [S5].

capabilities.summary: Custom backdoor xPack: a .NET loader that decrypts AES-encrypted payloads, passed a Base64-encoded password on the command line, and can run standalone or as a service [S2]. It lets operators run WMI commands remotely, use SMB-mounted shares to move data to C2, and act as a web proxy to mask attacker IPs; EternalBlue exploitation was also observed [S1][S2][S4]. The actor relied heavily on living-off-the-land tools such as WMIC, PowerShell, ProcDump (LSASS dumping) and PsExec [S4]. Initial access was not confirmed; use of MSSQL to run system commands suggests exploitation of a web application or service, and spear-phishing has been associated with the group before [S2][S4].

campaigns.name: Taiwan financial-sector espionage campaign
campaigns.summary: Symantec reports a persistent campaign of at least 18 months against Taiwanese financial institutions and a manufacturer using xPack and living-off-the-land tools; one financial victim network was occupied about 250 days and the manufacturer about 175 days [S1][S4].

campaigns.name: Symantec public disclosure
campaigns.summary: Symantec publishes 'Antlion: Chinese APT Uses Custom Backdoor to Target Financial Institutions in Taiwan'; BleepingComputer, The Hacker News, SecurityWeek and Dark Reading follow within days [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5].

diamond.adversary: China-linked, assessed state-backed espionage group tracked by Symantec as Antlion [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: xPack .NET loader/backdoor with WMI execution, SMB file transfer and proxying; EternalBlue; living-off-the-land tools (WMIC, PowerShell, ProcDump, PsExec) [S1][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Attacker C2 servers received data via SMB-mounted shares and xPack proxying [S4]; specific infrastructure was not captured in the sources gathered.
diamond.victim: Taiwanese financial institutions and a manufacturing company [S1][S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection against Taiwan's financial sector consistent with PRC state espionage interests, as assessed by Symantec [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Windows enterprise networks, MSSQL and other exposed services as probable entry points, and SMB (EternalBlue) for lateral movement [S2][S4].

gaps: Primary Symantec blog could not be opened directly in this session (host unreachable); details rely on search-result summaries and secondary coverage [S1][S4].

Victim count conflict: Symantec-based coverage says three organizations; Dark Reading says at least six financial institutions [S2][S5]. Dwell times also differ (250/175 days vs. roughly eight/six months).

Name overlap: Dark Reading states Antlion is also Pirate Panda and Tropic Trooper [S5]; these are tracked by other vendors as separate clusters and were not merged. Verify against Symantec and Trend Micro primary reports.
Initial access vector unconfirmed.
No Microsoft actor name, MITRE ATT&CK group ID or government attribution found.
No activity reporting after February 2022 was found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is Taiwanese financial and manufacturing networks, especially internet-facing MSSQL and web services and internal SMB. STEP 2: Long dwell times (about 175-250 days) with living-off-the-land tools mean intrusions can persist undetected [S1][S4]. STEP 3: Likely template is an exposed-service foothold, then xPack, credential dumping via ProcDump, WMI/PsExec lateral movement, SMB-staged exfiltration [S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued quiet espionage against Taiwan's financial and industrial base. MDCOA is leveraging the same footholds for financial-system disruption in a Taiwan crisis (assessment, not sourced). Candidate indicators: xPack-style .NET loaders with encrypted .bin payloads, MSSQL spawning command shells, remote WMI execution, LSASS dumps, unexpected SMB share mounts to external hosts [S2][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Taiwan financial-sector and supply-chain compromise reporting as a warning indicator for regional cyber posture. (2) Authorities: partner-nation networks fall under host-nation authorities; share indicators via established intelligence-sharing channels. (3) Mission assurance: DoD-adjacent suppliers or partners with Taiwan manufacturing exposure should be hunted for the listed behaviors and kept patched against EternalBlue. (4) Coordination: align with DC3/DIB CS and combatant command J2/J6 for sharing living-off-the-land detection logic, since signature-based detection missed the actor for months [S1][S4].

identification.summary: Aoqin Dragon is a China-linked cyberespionage cluster that SentinelLabs disclosed in June 2022. SentinelLabs says it has been active since at least 2013 and mainly targets organizations in Southeast Asia and Australia [S1][S5]. Its main focus is espionage against targets in Australia, Cambodia, Hong Kong, Singapore and Vietnam [S1]. Targeted sectors are government, education and telecommunications [S3][S7]. The group uses document lures, some on regional political affairs and some pornographic, and relies heavily on USB shortcut techniques and fake removable devices. Intrusions usually drop one of two backdoors: Mongall or a modified version of the open-source Heyoka project [S1][S3][S7].
identification.firstObserved: SentinelLabs: active since at least 2013 [S1]. Coverage of the report describes exploit-document campaigns running from 2012 to 2015 [S8][S9].
identification.notes: There is no Microsoft name for this cluster in the sources gathered. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as Aoqin Dragon (G1007) [S2]. SentinelLabs assesses with moderate confidence a possible link to the cluster Mandiant tracks as UNC94 [S1][S4], and reports some tactical association with Naikon [S8]. These are possible overlaps, not merges.

attribution.sponsor: No government or vendor source gathered names a sponsoring state organization. SentinelLabs describes the actor as a small Chinese-speaking team whose targeting closely aligns with the Chinese government's political interests [S1][S7].
attribution.confidence: SentinelLabs assesses with moderate confidence that Aoqin Dragon is a small Chinese-speaking team with possible ties to Naikon and UNC94 [S1][S4][S8]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: The assessment rests on SentinelLabs' malware, infrastructure and victimology analysis [S1], on Chinese-government-aligned targeting [S7], and on tooling and tactical overlaps with UNC94 and Naikon [S4][S8]. Vietnam's Authority of Information Security (AIS/NCSC) named Aoqin Dragon among APT groups expanding command-and-control infrastructure in the first half of 2022, but did not attribute it to a state [S6].

actors.objectives: Long-term espionage against government, education and telecommunications organizations in the Asia-Pacific region [S1][S3]. SentinelLabs says the targeting closely aligns with Chinese government political interests [S7]. Decoy content mostly targets readers interested in APAC political affairs [S7].

targeting.notes: Country list per SentinelLabs [S1]. Vietnam's AIS/NCSC told agencies to monitor for and block connections to listed Aoqin Dragon infrastructure in mid-2022 [S6].

capabilities.summary: Initial access, per SentinelLabs reporting: (1) weaponized documents exploiting the old, already-patched Office flaws CVE-2012-0158 and CVE-2010-3333, mainly in 2012-2015 [S8][S9]; (2) fake antivirus executables; and (3) forged removable-device folders, used since at least 2018, that trick users into opening the wrong folder and running the malware [S4][S7][S9]. The malware copies itself to real removable devices attached to the host, which spreads it through USB shortcut techniques [S3][S10]. For defense evasion it uses DLL hijacking, Themida-packed files and DNS tunneling [S8][S2]. Mongall, in use since about 2013, is a simple implant that provides a remote shell and file upload and download [S9]. The modified Heyoka is more capable: it can kill processes, manipulate files and collect process information [S9]. The original Heyoka project exfiltrates data over spoofed DNS requests, and the actor loads its version through DLL injection [S3].

campaigns.summary: From 2018 the actor adds fake removable devices and fake antivirus lures alongside document exploits, and spreads through USB shortcuts.

campaigns.summary: SentinelLabs publishes the Aoqin Dragon report, covering about ten years of espionage against Southeast Asia and Australia and a moderate-confidence possible link to UNC94.

campaigns.summary: Vietnam's Authority of Information Security says several APT groups, including Aoqin Dragon, expanded C2 infrastructure in the first half of 2022. It orders agencies to monitor for and block the listed IPs and domains.

diamond.adversary: SentinelLabs assesses with moderate confidence a small Chinese-speaking team with possible ties to UNC94 and Naikon [S1][S8].
diamond.capability: Exploit documents (CVE-2012-0158, CVE-2010-3333), fake antivirus lures, fake removable devices and USB propagation, DLL hijacking, Themida packing, and the Mongall and modified Heyoka backdoors with DNS-based C2 and exfiltration [S3][S8][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-controlled C2 IPs and domains. Vietnam's AIS reported this infrastructure expanding in the first half of 2022 and published blocking indicators [S6]. DNS tunneling is used for C2 and exfiltration [S3][S8].
diamond.victim: Government, education and telecommunications organizations in Australia, Cambodia, Hong Kong, Singapore and Vietnam [S1][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection aligned with Chinese government political interests in the Asia-Pacific region, including regional political affairs [S7].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints running unpatched Microsoft Office, plus environments where removable media is shared, which the USB propagation exploits [S3][S8][S10].

gaps: The SentinelLabs primary report, MITRE G1007 page, Avertium and Security Affairs pages could not be fetched directly (DNS resolution blocked). Their content is taken from search-result summaries and secondary coverage.
The khonggianmang.vn PDF (CB_941) in the imported record was not opened. The dispatch is cited through a provincial republication, and its IOC appendix was not reviewed.
No public reporting on Aoqin Dragon activity after mid-2022 was found. Current operational status is unknown.

The UNC94 and Naikon links are only SentinelLabs assessments (moderate confidence or 'possible'). Mandiant's own UNC94 reporting was not located. Microsoft and other vendor naming for the cluster is unknown.
The start date is inconsistent across sources: 'at least 2013' in SentinelLabs versus exploit campaigns dated 2012-2015 in secondary coverage.
Specific victim organizations, dwell times and data stolen are not public in the sources gathered.
No government (US, Australian or other Five Eyes) attribution or advisory naming Aoqin Dragon was found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain is government, education and telecom networks in Australia and Southeast Asia, including partner-nation networks that coalition operations depend on. Removable-media transfer paths across air gaps or between enclaves are a relevant avenue [S1][S3]. STEP 2 (effects): The actor's reliance on old Office exploits and USB propagation means poorly patched systems and ones with weak media control are the most exposed. DNS tunneling can carry C2 through networks that only lightly inspect DNS [S3][S8][S9]. STEP 3 (adversary model): The template is a political or pornographic decoy document, fake antivirus or fake removable-device folder, followed by DLL-hijacked or Themida-packed Mongall or Heyoka, DNS-based C2, and spread to attached USB devices [S7][S8][S9][S10]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is quiet, long-duration espionage against regional government and telecom targets aligned with PRC political interests [S1][S7]. MDCOA is USB-borne spread into partner or coalition mission networks that share removable media with targeted regional agencies, enabling persistent collection on combined planning; this is an extrapolation, not reported activity. Candidate indicators: Office processes exploiting CVE-2012-0158 or CVE-2010-3333; executables masquerading as antivirus tools or as removable-drive folders; DLL side-loading from removable media; Themida-packed binaries; anomalous high-volume or encoded DNS queries; and hits on the Vietnamese AIS IOC list [S2][S6][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: fuse the Vietnamese AIS IOC list and SentinelLabs indicators into DNS and endpoint monitoring for Indo-Pacific mission partner networks [S1][S6]. Authorities: activity is espionage against foreign partner-nation and civilian networks. Response on partner networks depends on partner consent and information-sharing agreements, and any action beyond DoDIN defense needs separate authorities. Mission assurance: enforce removable-media controls, patch legacy Office and inspect DNS for tunneling on systems exchanging data with regional partners, because the actor relies on USB propagation and DNS C2 [S3][S8][S10]. Coordination: share detections with partner CERTs (for example Vietnam's AIS/NCSC, which already tracks the cluster [S6]) and with vendor reporting on the UNC94 and Naikon overlaps, keeping vendor confidence levels distinct from government attribution [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: SentinelLabs has uncovered a cluster of activity beginning at least as far back as 2013 and continuing to the present day, primarily targeting organizations in Southeast Asia and Australia. They assess that the threat actor's primary focus is espionage and relates to targets in Australia, Cambodia, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Vietnam. We track this activity as 'Aoqin Dragon'. identification.summary: AppMilad is described by Zimperium as an Iranian-based hacker group that used social media and Telegram to push users to sideload a fake app [S3]. Zimperium assesses that the actors behind the RatMilad Android spyware acquired the code from the AppMilad group and integrated it into a fake app [S2]. Coverage presents this as a hypothesis, and all sources found re-report one October 2022 Zimperium disclosure [S2].
identification.notes: AppMilad (a code source/ group) and the RatMilad operators (who used the code) are not established as the same entity; the link is Zimperium's belief .

attribution.confidence: Low. Zimperium states a belief, presented in coverage as a hypothesis; no government attribution found .
attribution.basis: Zimperium believes the RatMilad operators acquired code from AppMilad [S2]. No state sponsor is stated in the sources reviewed.

targeting.notes: Zimperium first saw RatMilad after a failed infection of a Middle East enterprise Android device protected by its software [S2]. Zimperium later assessed the RatMilad operators use a random-target approach, not a targeted campaign . Infection scale is unknown [S2].

capabilities.summary: RatMilad is Android spyware distributed outside app stores through links on social media and Telegram, tricking users into sideloading it and granting extensive permissions [S2][S3]. It was hidden in a VPN/phone-number spoofing app called Text Me, and a later live sample in NumRent, a renamed and graphically updated Text Me [S2][S3]. It can use the camera for pictures and video, record audio, get GPS location, view pictures, and collect SMS, call logs, contacts, SIM information and clipboard data, and read/write files [S2][S3][S4].

campaigns.name: RatMilad spyware disclosure (Text Me / NumRent)
campaigns.summary: Zimperium zLabs reported RatMilad after it failed to infect a Middle East enterprise device [S2]. Samples were found in Text Me and later NumRent, spread via Telegram and social media; a Telegram post had over 4,700 views and over 200 shares [S2][S4].

diamond.adversary: AppMilad, an Iranian-based group per Zimperium, supplier of code later used by the RatMilad operators, whose identity is unknown .
diamond.capability: RatMilad Android spyware (camera, audio, GPS, SMS, call logs, contacts, files) [S2][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Telegram channels/posts and social media links for distribution; sideloaded APKs, not app stores [S2][S3].
diamond.victim: Enterprise Android users in the Middle East; random-target approach per Zimperium [S2].
diamond.technology: Android devices; sideloaded apps masquerading as VPN/phone-number spoofing utilities [S2][S3].

gaps: Zimperium's original blog could not be opened in this research; findings rely on secondary coverage of it [S2].
No evidence found of a state sponsor, tasking, or relationship between AppMilad and the RatMilad operators beyond Zimperium's belief.
Infection count, victim identities, C2 infrastructure and IOCs not captured.
No reporting found on AppMilad activity after October 2022.
Vendor naming overlaps with other Iranian clusters were not found; none should be assumed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Battlespace: personal and enterprise Android devices in the Middle East reachable via Telegram and social media [S2]. Threat: low-sophistication, random-target spyware distribution through sideloading [S2]. MLCOA: continued social-engineered distribution of repackaged utility apps (VPN, number spoofing) with data collection from camera, microphone, GPS and messages [S2][S3]. MDCOA: reuse of the code against selected enterprise or government personnel, which sources do not show. Candidate indicators: sideloaded apps named Text Me or NumRent, Telegram links promoting VPN/number apps, apps requesting camera, microphone, SMS and location permissions [S2][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: brief personnel deployed to the Middle East on sideloading risk and Telegram-delivered apps [S2][S3]. Authorities: mobile device management and BYOD restrictions fall to the owning command or enterprise; no cited source addresses authorities. Mission assurance: enforce app-store-only installation and mobile threat defense on devices handling mission data [S2]. Coordination: report suspected samples to the local cyber security service provider and share indicators with the mobile security vendor community.
