provenance.importedSummary: APT41 is a threat group that researchers have assessed as Chinese state-sponsored espionage group that also conducts financially-motivated operations. Active since at least 2012, APT41 has been observed targeting various industries, including but not limited to healthcare, telecom, technology, finance, education, retail and video game industries in 14 countries. Notable behaviors include using a wide range of malware and tools to complete mission objectives. APT41 overlaps at least partially with public reporting on groups including BARIUM and Winnti Group.

identification.summary: BrazenBamboo is the name Volexity uses for a suspected Chinese state-affiliated threat actor that Volexity credits with developing the DEEPDATA, DEEPPOST and LIGHTSPY malware families [S1][S2]. Volexity describes the group as the developer of the tools, not necessarily the operator of every deployment [S1]. While analyzing a DEEPDATA sample, Volexity found a zero-day credential-disclosure flaw in Fortinet's FortiClient for Windows (v7.4.0) that a DEEPDATA plugin used to pull VPN credentials from process memory [S1][S3]. Volexity also documented a previously unreported Windows variant of LIGHTSPY [S1][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Volexity identified zero-day exploitation of the FortiClient flaw in July 2024 and published on 2024-11-15 [S1][S2]. LIGHTSPY itself was first reported in 2020 (iOS watering-hole campaign) [S6]. The first date BrazenBamboo's own activity began is not established in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: Microsoft has no mapped name in this record. Vendor overlap: BlackBerry attributes the same DeepData/LightSpy Windows tooling to APT41 [S5]; ThreatFabric linked LightSpy Android code to DragonEgg, which Lookout attributed to APT41 [S6]. Volexity's BrazenBamboo is a separate vendor cluster name; do not merge facts across these without the primary reports. The Volexity primary page could not be opened in this session (host unreachable); Volexity details are from search-result summaries of that page and secondary coverage [S1][S2].

attribution.sponsor: Volexity describes BrazenBamboo as suspected Chinese state-affiliated [S2][S3]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Volexity characterizes the actor as a suspected China-linked, state-affiliated developer [S2]. BlackBerry states it believes with high confidence that the LightSpy actor is associated with APT41 [S5]. These are vendor assessments only.
attribution.basis: Volexity: malware development lineage across DEEPDATA, DEEPPOST and LIGHTSPY, and C2/operator-panel analysis [S1][S8]. ThreatFabric: location plugin recalculating coordinates with a China-specific system [S6]. BlackBerry: DeepData framework layout matching LightSpy and APT41 association [S5].

actors.objectives: Surveillance and data theft: DEEPDATA harvests credentials and sensitive data from Windows hosts, and LIGHTSPY collects messaging, location, audio and other data from devices [S3][S5][S6]. Specific tasking or end customer is not established. One database summary of the Volexity report says the operator panel references domestic law enforcement and supports multiple users, which would suggest tools built for government clients; this is unverified here [S8].

regions: Southern Asia / Asia-Pacific (BlackBerry reporting on DeepData victims) [S5]
targeting.notes: BlackBerry describes DeepData campaign victims in Southern Asia. Volexity's own victim sectors could not be confirmed from accessible sources. Earlier LightSpy activity targeted Hong Kong iPhone users via watering holes [S6].

capabilities.summary: DEEPDATA is a modular Windows post-exploitation framework: a DLL loader decrypts and launches 12 plugins through an orchestrator module (frame.dll) [S2]. One plugin exploits the FortiClient 7.4.0 flaw to read usernames, passwords, gateways and ports from process memory [S3]. Other plugins target messaging apps (WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, WeChat), browsers, password managers and system/network data, and can record audio [S5]. DEEPPOST exfiltrates files to a remote endpoint [S2]. Volexity reported the flaw to Fortinet on 2024-07-18 and Fortinet acknowledged it on 2024-07-24; Volexity's update says Fortinet publicly acknowledged the flaw on 2024-12-18; no CVE or patch was confirmed [S1][S3]. The Windows LIGHTSPY variant runs shellcode in memory, uses WebSocket and HTTPS for C2, and has an orchestrator-plus-plugins design [S4]. ThreatFabric's iOS LightSpy analysis (core 7.9.0) found 28 plugins including seven with destructive boot-interference functions, Safari-based initial access and jailbreak privilege escalation [S6]. Hunt.io (Feb 2025) reported LightSpy command support for over 100 functions across Android, iOS, Windows, macOS, routers and Linux, and Facebook/Instagram database targeting on Android [S10].

gaps: Volexity primary report, BlackBerry blog and ThreatFabric blog could not be opened in this session (host unreachable); details rely on search-result summaries and secondary coverage.

Volexity's victim sectors and geography for BrazenBamboo are not confirmed; the existing record's claim of a focus on domestic targets and custom analyst software is unverified here, and one secondary summary of the C2 panel referencing domestic law enforcement is unconfirmed [S8].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the VPN client and its stored credentials on Windows endpoints, plus personal messaging apps on mobile devices used by personnel [S3][S5]. STEP 2: The actor has a developer-grade toolset with a zero-day, so defenders should assume patches lag exploitation (July 2024 exploitation, December 2024 public acknowledgement) [S1]. STEP 3: Template is an unknown initial foothold, DEEPDATA plugin execution, credential theft from FortiClient memory, exfiltration via DEEPPOST, then possible VPN reuse [S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued credential and messaging-data theft against regional targets in Asia [S5]. MDCOA is use of stolen VPN credentials for access into defense or partner networks, or destructive mobile functions as seen in LightSpy iOS [S6]. Candidate indicators: unexpected frame.dll orchestrator loading, access to FortiClient process memory, outbound transfers to unfamiliar endpoints, and FortiClient 7.4.0 installs without vendor mitigations [S1][S2][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track endpoint FortiClient versions and apply any Fortinet guidance; include vendor reporting on DEEPDATA and LightSpy in hunt planning [S1]. (2) Authorities: remediation of personally owned mobile devices running LightSpy-targeted messaging apps needs policy coverage beyond managed networks [S5][S6]. (3) Mission assurance: rotate VPN credentials after any suspected compromise since credentials were read from memory [S3]. (4) Coordination: attribution is vendor-only and overlaps with APT41 reporting, so share indicators through established channels without asserting a single actor name [S5].

provenance.importedSummary: BrazenBamboo is a Chinese state-affiliated threat actor known for developing the LIGHTSPY, DEEPDATA, and DEEPPOST malware families. Their infrastructure includes capabilities for zero-day exploitation, specifically targeting vulnerabilities like FortiClient, and employs a command-and-control architecture that supports multi-platform operations. Volexity's analysis indicates that BrazenBamboo is a well-resourced entity with a focus on domestic targets, utilizing custom analyst software to manage data collected from their malware. The ongoing development of their malware families is evidenced by the timestamps associated with their latest payloads.

identification.summary: China-based cyberespionage group that Microsoft tracks as Brocade Typhoon (formerly BORON) and that other vendors call APT3, Gothic Panda, UPS, Buckeye and TG-0110 [S1][S4]. FireEye/Mandiant tied it to browser and Flash zero-day campaigns in 2014-2015 (Operation Clandestine Fox, Operation Clandestine Wolf) [S2][S9]. Symantec reported a targeting shift from the US to Hong Kong political entities starting in June 2015 [S4]. Security researchers linked the group to the Guangzhou firm Boyusec, three of whose personnel were indicted by the US in November 2017 [S6][S7]. Symantec reported that known Buckeye tool activity ceased in mid-2017 [S5].
identification.firstObserved: Symantec (2016) assessed the group had been operating for 'well over half a decade' [S4]; the 2017 US indictment alleges intrusions from 2011 to May 2017 (reporting DOJ indictment) [S7]. Earliest named public campaign: Operation Clandestine Fox, April 2014 [S9].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Brocade Typhoon. Microsoft's public mapping lists BORON, GOTHIC PANDA, UPS, APT3, OLDCARP, TG-0110, Red Sylvan and CYBRAN as other names [S1]. Symantec calls it Buckeye and equates it with APT3, Gothic Panda, UPS Team and TG-0110 [S4]. Palo Alto Unit 42 tracks the same activity as UPS and associates it with the Pirpi backdoor [S10]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the group as APT3 (G0022) [S11]. Boyusec is a company the researchers link to the group; whether Boyusec is all of APT3 or only one component was unresolved in 2017 reporting [S8].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China, Ministry of State Security (MSS), per Recorded Future's assessment that Boyusec worked on behalf of the MSS [S6]. The US indictment does not name the Chinese government [S7][S8].
attribution.confidence: Recorded Future assessed with high confidence (May 2017) that APT3 is attributable to the MSS through the contractor Boyusec [S6]. FireEye's Ben Read said FireEye believed the indicted individuals and Boyusec are linked to APT3 [S7]. The November 2017 US indictment charged three Boyusec personnel (Wu Yingzhuo, Dong Hao, Xia Lei) but, per press reporting, made no reference to Chinese state links [S7][S8]. Microsoft's mapping lists the origin as China [S1].
attribution.basis: Domain-registration analysis by the anonymous 'intrusiontruth' blog tied Pirpi C2 domains to Boyusec shareholders, which Recorded Future corroborated and linked to Guangdong ITSEC, which it describes as subordinate to the MSS-run CNITSEC [S6][S8]. Charges against Boyusec personnel cited use of 'UPS'/'exeproxy' malware (reporting DOJ indictment) [S7]. Vendor malware and campaign reporting from FireEye/Mandiant, Symantec and Unit 42 [S2][S3][S4][S5][S10].

actors.objectives: Espionage and theft of commercial and technical intellectual property: the indictment alleges theft of Siemens energy, technology and transportation business data, Trimble satellite-navigation (GNSS) development data and Moody's Analytics economist email (reporting DOJ indictment) [S7]. From 2015 it also collected against political entities in Hong Kong [S4].

sectors: Industrial and engineering (Siemens energy, technology, transportation businesses) [S7]
regions: Vietnam and the Philippines (later use of the Bemstour/DoublePulsar package; Symantec did not tie that later use to Buckeye's known tools) [S12]
targeting.notes: Symantec counted 13 Hong Kong, 3 US and 1 UK victim organizations in its 2016 reporting, and said US and UK targeting stopped from March 2016 (reported by SecurityWeek) [S4]. The Vietnam and Philippines intrusions used the Bemstour exploit tool with different malware after Buckeye's known tools went quiet in mid-2017, so they may not belong to this cluster [S5][S12].

capabilities.summary: Early access to browser and plugin zero-days: Internet Explorer CVE-2014-1776 (Clandestine Fox, April 2014) [S9] and Adobe Flash CVE-2015-3113 delivered by phishing links to compromised servers, followed by the SHOTPUT backdoor (Clandestine Wolf, June 2015) [S2]. Rapid use of newly disclosed exploits such as CVE-2014-6332 and CVE-2014-4113 within days of disclosure (Operation Double Tap, November 2014), with PlugX/Kaba C2 noted [S3]. Custom backdoors including Pirpi/UPS [S10] and 'exeproxy' [S7]. From March 2016 the group used a DoublePulsar variant, newer than the Shadow Brokers version, delivered by the custom Bemstour exploit tool, which chained Windows vulnerabilities including the zero-day CVE-2019-0703 for remote kernel code execution; this was over a year before the Shadow Brokers leak [S5]. Spearphishing with malicious attachments or links is alleged in the indictment [S7]. MITRE lists software including PlugX, SHOTPUT, OSInfo, RemoteCMD and LaZagne [S11].

diamond.adversary: PRC-based operators linked by researchers to Guangzhou Boyu Information Technology (Boyusec), assessed by Recorded Future as working for the MSS; three Boyusec personnel indicted by the US [S6][S7].
diamond.capability: Browser and Flash zero-days (CVE-2014-1776, CVE-2015-3113), fast use of new n-days, SHOTPUT, Pirpi/UPS, exeproxy, PlugX, and a pre-leak DoublePulsar variant with Bemstour (CVE-2019-0703) [S2][S3][S5][S7][S9][S10].
diamond.infrastructure: Phishing links to compromised servers hosting exploits [S2]; actor-registered C2 domains, including Pirpi domains registered to a Boyusec shareholder [S6][S8]; domains such as securitywap.com and walterclean.com in Double Tap [S3]; email forwarding rules on a victim mail server [S7].
diamond.victim: US aerospace, defense and industrial firms (Siemens, Trimble, Moody's Analytics); Hong Kong political entities; targets in the UK and Belgium [S2][S4][S7][S12].
diamond.socioPolitical: Commercial and technical IP theft benefiting PRC industrial priorities, plus political intelligence on Hong Kong from 2015 [S4][S7].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints running Internet Explorer and Adobe Flash; Windows SMB and kernel vulnerabilities exploited by Bemstour; enterprise email servers [S5][S7][S9].

gaps: No Microsoft Threat Intelligence report specific to Brocade Typhoon/BORON was found; Microsoft coverage is limited to its naming map [S1].
The DOJ press release and indictment (justice.gov) could not be opened; indictment details come from Security Affairs and Foreign Policy coverage [S7][S8].

The original FireEye/Mandiant, Symantec, Recorded Future, Unit 42 and Secureworks (BRONZE MAYFAIR) pages could not be fetched (network blocks); details come from search-result summaries and press coverage.
MITRE ATT&CK G0022 could not be fetched in this session; the software list is taken from the imported actor record [S11].

Activity after mid-2017 is not publicly attributed to this cluster. Bemstour/DoublePulsar use into late 2018 (Vietnam, Philippines) was with different malware, and Symantec did not attribute it to Buckeye [S5][S12].
It is unresolved whether Boyusec is the whole of APT3 or one part of it, and how Buckeye obtained Equation Group tools [S5][S8].
Aliases Boyusec, Group 6, Pirpi, Threat Group-0110 and UPS Team in the imported record come from MISP/other mappings; only those in cited sources are added below.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is user endpoints running browsers and plugins, enterprise mail servers and Windows SMB-exposed hosts at defense, aerospace, industrial and navigation-technology firms, including DIB contractors whose engineering data has value (Siemens, Trimble precedent) [S2][S5][S7]. STEP 2 (effects): Zero-day and fast n-day use (exploits within about a week of disclosure) shortens the defender's patch window; stealthy mail-forwarding rules allow long-term, low-noise collection [S3][S7]. STEP 3 (adversary template): phishing link or attachment, then browser/Flash exploit, then SHOTPUT/Pirpi/PlugX backdoor, then credential theft and lateral movement, possibly with a kernel-level implant such as DoublePulsar, then data staging and exfiltration [S2][S3][S5][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet theft of engineering and program data (for example GNSS and energy technology) from DIB and partner networks. MDCOA is use of an unpublished exploit chain that gives kernel-level implants across many hosts. Candidate indicators: unexpected mailbox forwarding rules to external accounts, anomalous SMB traffic consistent with DoublePulsar, browser processes spawning shells, and connections to newly registered domains [S5][S7]. Note: no public activity has been attributed since mid-2017 [S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track emergency browser, plugin and Windows patches alongside exposure of mission-relevant enclaves, since this actor used exploits within days of disclosure [S3]. (2) Authorities: activity against contractors such as Siemens and Trimble falls under law enforcement and DIB channels; the US addressed it by indictment, not military response [S7]. (3) Mission assurance: PNT-related development data (Trimble GNSS) was a target, so protect PNT program and supplier data as mission-critical [S7]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3/DIB CS partners and commercial vendors, since public attribution came from vendor and researcher reporting (Recorded Future, Symantec, FireEye) [S5][S6][S7].

identification.summary: BRONZE EDGEWOOD is the Secureworks Counter Threat Unit (CTU) name for a suspected China-based espionage group active since at least 2018 that targets government and private enterprises across Southeast Asia [S1]. In early 2021 CTU observed it exploiting Microsoft Exchange Server at a Southeast Asian organization, deploying a China Chopper webshell and a Nishang PowerShell script to reach C2 [S1]. It is publicly linked to the Chinoxy, PCShare and FunnyDream malware families and also uses Cobalt Strike [S1]. Bitdefender's November 2020 report on the Chinoxy/PCShare/FunnyDream chain, which Recorded Future associates with its own cluster TAG-16, reports more than 200 systems affected over roughly two years [S3][S5].
identification.firstObserved: Active since at least 2018 per Secureworks CTU [S1]. Bitdefender dates the FunnyDream actor to about 2018 [S3].
identification.notes: Secureworks name; no Microsoft name is mapped in this record. Red Hariasa is the PwC name given as an alias [S1][S5]. Recorded Future's TAG-16 is a separate vendor cluster that reporting associates with the same Chinoxy/FunnyDream tooling; whether BRONZE EDGEWOOD, Red Hariasa and TAG-16 are identical is not established by the sources gathered, so facts from Bitdefender and Recorded Future are attributed to those vendors and not asserted as CTU findings [S3][S5].

attribution.sponsor: Secureworks CTU assesses the group operates on behalf of the Chinese government [S1].
attribution.confidence: Secureworks CTU: moderate confidence [S1]. Recorded Future judged TAG-16 highly likely to be a state actor, with targeting consistent with Chinese political and economic goals [S5]. Bitdefender said evidence points to a Chinese-speaking group but cautioned that attribution is difficult [S3]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: CTU states a remit covering political espionage based on its observed targeting [S1]. Recorded Future cites targeting alignment with South China Sea and Belt and Road interests and shared custom capabilities with RedFoxtrot [S5]. Bitdefender cites the tooling and infrastructure largely in Hong Kong, with some in mainland China and Vietnam [S3].

actors.objectives: Political espionage against Southeast Asian governments and enterprises [S1]. Bitdefender describes the FunnyDream activity as long-term persistence with collection and exfiltration of sensitive documents [S3]. Recorded Future links TAG-16 targeting to regional territorial disputes and Belt and Road objectives [S5].

provenance.importedSummary: In early 2021 CTU researchers observed BRONZE EDGEWOOD exploiting the Microsoft Exchange Server of an organization in Southeast Asia. The threat group deployed a China Chopper webshell and ran the Nishang Invoke-PowerShellTcp.ps1 script to connect back to C2 infrastructure. The threat group is publicly linked to malware families Chinoxy, PCShare and FunnyDream. CTU researchers have discovered that BRONZE EDGEWOOD also leverages Cobalt Strike in its intrusion activity. identification.summary: BRONZE SPIRAL is the Secureworks Counter Threat Unit name for the actor Secureworks earlier called SPIRAL, which Secureworks linked to deployment of the SUPERNOVA web shell on an internet-facing SolarWinds Orion server in late 2020[S2]. Secureworks assessed the group appears to be based in China, and reporting did not say whether it is state-affiliated or criminal[S2]. Secureworks said the SUPERNOVA intrusion is unrelated to the broader SolarWinds supply-chain compromise[S2], and CISA likewise assessed the SUPERNOVA actor in its own incident as separate from the supply-chain APT [S5].

capabilities.summary: The SUPERNOVA web shell is a .NET implant hidden in a modified Orion module, app_web_logoimagehandler.ashx.b6031896.dll, that receives remote code and runs it in memory without writing artifacts to disk [S3]. The DLL was unsigned, unlike the SUNBURST DLL of the supply-chain operation [S3]. Secureworks said the exploited flaw was CVE-2020-10148, an Orion API authentication bypass, used before the 23 Dec 2020 SolarWinds patch[S2]. CISA's separate incident analysis described SUPERNOVA as a webshell that lets an operator inject C# code, placed directly on Orion hosts rather than delivered by a trojanized update [S5].

provenance.importedSummary: In December 2020, the IT management software provider SolarWinds announced that an unidentified threat actor had exploited a vulnerability in their Orion Platform software to deploy a web shell dubbed SUPERNOVA. CTU researchers track the operators of the SUPERNOVA web shell as BRONZE SPIRAL and assess with low confidence that the group is of Chinese origin. SUPERNOVA was likely deployed through exploitation of CVE-2020-10148, and CTU researchers observed post-exploitation reconnaissance commands roughly 30 minutes before the web shell was deployed. This may have been indicative of the threat actor conducting scan-and-exploit activity and then triaging for victims of particular interest, before deploying SUPERNOVA and attempting to dump credentials and move laterally. BRONZE SPIRAL has been associated with previous intrusions involving the targeting of ManageEngine servers, maintenance of long-term access to periodically harvest credentials and exfiltrate data, and espionage or theft of intellectual property. The threat group makes extensive use of native system tools and 'living off the land' techniques.

identification.summary: BRONZE SPRING is Secureworks' Counter Threat Unit (CTU) name for a China-linked group that CTU assesses with high confidence operates on behalf of China, stealing intellectual property from defense, engineering, pharmaceutical and technology companies; the same text lists UNC302 as a synonym [S1]. CTU assesses that two Chinese nationals indicted by the US DOJ in July 2020 (Li Xiaoyu and Dong Jiazhi) are members of the group [S1]. The DOJ alleged the pair ran an intrusion campaign of more than ten years against companies in the US and about ten other countries [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: The DOJ indictment alleges the pair's campaign began in 2009 [S1]. No vendor first-observed date for the BRONZE SPRING cluster itself was verified.
identification.notes: Secureworks names for other China-linked groups that also use China Chopper (BRONZE PRESIDENT, BRONZE UNION) are separate clusters and are not merged here [S1]. Wikipedia reportedly links the Guangdong State Security Department to BRONZE SPRING/UNC302, which was not verified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing web servers and collaboration software at defense contractors, engineering and technology firms (DIB) are key terrain [S1][S3]. STEP 2: The actor rewards rapid exploitation of known vulnerabilities, so patch latency is the main defender weakness [S3]. provenance.importedSummary: BRONZE SPRING is a threat group that CTU researchers assess with high confidence operates on behalf of China in the theft of intellectual property from defense, engineering, pharmaceutical and technology companies. The threat group typically uses scan-and-exploit for initial access, deploys the China Chopper webshell for remote execution and persistence, and creates RAR archives with a '.jpg' file extension for data exfiltration. In July 2020 the U.S. Department of Justice indicted two Chinese hackers CTU researchers assess are members of the BRONZE SPRING threat group. The Department of Justice allege these hackers were responsible for compromising networks of hundreds of organisations and individuals in the U.S. and abroad since 2009, and that exfiltrated data would be passed to the Chinese Ministry of State Security or sold for financial gain.

identification.summary: BRONZE VAPOR is a targeted threat group assessed with moderate confidence to be of Chinese origin. Artefacts from tools associated with this group and open source reporting on related incidents indicate that BRONZE VAPOR have operated since at least 2017. The group conducts espionage against multiple industries including semiconductors, aviation and telecommunications. CTU researchers assess BRONZE VAPOR's intent to be information theft, with operations focused on intellectual property (semiconductors) and personally identifiable information such as traveller records (aviation). Compromise of telecommunications companies can yield personally identifiable information and meta data on client communications such as Call Data Records (CDR). Prior to 2019 their operational focus, with some exceptions, revolved around targets in East Asia particularity Taiwan with it's thriving semiconductor industry. In 2021 details emerged in open source of attacks on at least one European semiconductor company believed to date back to 2017. In 2019 BRONZE VAPOR attacked one of more entities in the European airlines sector. The group gains initial access via VPN services, may use spearphishing with 'Letter of Appointment' themed lures, and deploys Cobalt Strike along with custom data exfiltration tools to target organizations. Post-intrusion activity involves living-of-the-land using legitimate tools and commands available within victim environment as well as using AceHash for credential harvesting, WATERCYCLE for data exfiltration and STOCKPIPE for proxying information through Microsoft Exchange servers over email. BRONZE VAPOR uses a set of tactics that, although not individually unique, when viewed in aggregate create a relatively distinct playbook. Intrusions begin with credential based attacks against an existing remote access solution (Citrix, VPN etc.) or B2B network access. Cobalt Strike is deployed into the environment and further access is then conducted via Cobalt Strike Beacon and other features of the platform. Sharphound is deployed to map out the victim's Active Directory infrastructure and and collect critical information about the domain including important account names. Command and control infrastructure is hosted on subdomains of Azure and Appspot services to blend in with legitimate traffic. The threat actor also registers their own domains for command and control, often with a "sync" or "update" related theme. WinRAR is commonly used for compressing data prior to exfiltration. Filenames for these archives often involve a string of numbers and variations of the word "update". Data is exfiltrated using WATERCYCLE to cloud based platforms such as OneDrive and GoogleDrive.

Budminer is Symantec's name for a cyberespionage group that Symantec said used the Taidoor backdoor until 2014 and, in March 2016, linked to a new custom backdoor, Backdoor.Dripion, mainly because the Blugger downloader that delivered Dripion had been used only by Budminer [S1][S2]. Symantec said it had not seen new Taidoor campaigns since 2014 and believed the group changed tactics to avoid detection after public exposure [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro's data shows the earliest Taidoor campaign-related activity in October 2010 [S4]. US agencies describe the Taidoor malware family as first discovered in 2008 [S5]. Trade coverage of Symantec's reporting says Budminer has been active since 2009 [S2].
identification.notes: Trend Micro's 'Taidoor' is a campaign and malware name, and the 2020 US agency report describes the Taidoor malware, not a group named Budminer [S4][S5]. Whether vendor clusters fully overlap is not established in the sources gathered.

attribution.confidence: No source gathered names a government sponsor for Budminer. Symantec linked Dripion to Budminer on the strength of the shared Blugger downloader and a shared root domain in earlier Taidoor-related activity, and noted there are no code similarities between Dripion and Taidoor [S1][S2]. Separately, CISA, FBI and DoD stated that the Taidoor malware is used by Chinese government cyber actors, and the FBI stated high confidence that such actors use malware variants with proxy servers to maintain presence on victim networks [S5]. That statement concerns the Taidoor malware and is not a government attribution of Budminer by name.
attribution.basis: Symantec infrastructure and tool overlap (Blugger downloader, shared root domain) [S1][S2]. US agency malware analysis report on Taidoor (AR20-216A), seen here only through search-result text and press coverage [S5][S6].

actors.objectives: Collection of information from targets with an interest in Taiwan and US-Taiwan affairs: Symantec said Taidoor-era targets were mainly private industry and influential international think tanks involved in US and Taiwanese affairs, and Dripion was built to steal files [S2][S3]. Trend Micro found Taidoor victims it identified were in Taiwan and mostly government organizations [S4].

Japan and South Korea (reported in later trade coverage of Dripion) [S2]

capabilities.summary: Taidoor-era delivery relied on emails with attachments that exploited known document vulnerabilities, including CVE-2012-0158; Symantec said PDF was the most common exploited document type, followed closely by Word, and that the exploited flaws were generally already patched [S3][S4]. Trend Micro tracks the malware as BKDR_SIMBOT variants with remote-access-trojan features [S4]. After 2014, Symantec linked a custom backdoor, Backdoor.Dripion, installed by the Blugger downloader, which pulled it from English-language blogs that may have been compromised or attacker-created [S1][S2]. Dripion could steal files and upload and run new files, and its C&C used domain names disguised as antivirus vendor sites [S2]. Blugger encrypts its communications [S2]. The US agency report describes Taidoor as a service DLL with a loader that decrypts a second file run in memory as the main RAT [S5].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Email gateways, document readers and the Taiwan and US-Taiwan policy community (think tanks, industry, government) are the relevant terrain [S3][S4]. STEP 2: The actor relied on already-patched document vulnerabilities, so slow patching widens exposure [S3]. STEP 3: Template is spear-phishing with exploit-laden PDF or Word attachments, then a RAT; later, a downloader fetching a backdoor from blogs, with C&C on domains imitating AV vendors [S1][S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-volume collection against Taiwan-focused organizations with changed tooling to evade detection [S1]. MDCOA, an assessment not stated in sources, is reuse of the same infrastructure patterns against US defense-adjacent policy contacts. Candidate indicators: downloads from unfamiliar English-language blogs by non-browser processes, DNS lookups to look-alike AV vendor domains, and service-DLL persistence with in-memory second stage [S2][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Taiwan-related phishing against partners and contractors; detection coverage for Taidoor samples was weak in 2020 [S6]. (2) Authorities: reporting of PRC-linked intrusions on contractor or partner networks should go through DC3 and FBI channels, as the US report asks recipients to report to CISA or FBI [S5]. (3) Mission assurance: enforce patching and attachment handling on staff who engage with Taiwan policy. (4) Coordination: share Symantec and US agency indicators with partners; treat vendor cluster names as separate until overlap is confirmed [S1][S5].

identification.summary: Buhtrap is a Russian-speaking financially motivated cybercrime group that ESET named 'Operation Buhtrap' (from the Russian word for accountant plus 'trap') after first spotting the campaign in April 2015; secondary reporting says activity dates to 2014 and that attacks on financial institutions were first detected in August 2015 [S1][S4]. Group-IB reported 13 successful attacks on Russian banks between August 2015 and February 2016 [S1][S4]. ESET reported in 2019 that, since late 2015, the same actors' toolset had expanded to espionage against government targets in Eastern Europe and Central Asia [S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: Activity dating to 2014; first attacks on financial institutions detected August 2015; ESET first spotted the campaign April 2015 [S1][S4].
identification.notes: Other names reported: Ratopak/Ratpak Spider (CrowdStrike) and UAC-0008 [S4][S7]. ESET notes that ransomware first tagged Win32/Filecoder.Buhtrap was renamed Win32/Filecoder.Buran because it is not linked to the original Buhtrap group; the 2018-2019 Yandex.Direct malvertising campaign mixed Buhtrap with other unrelated families [S3]. Malpedia says the Buhtrap source code has leaked, so later use of Buhtrap tooling does not by itself prove the original operators [S7][S8].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor is identified in the sources gathered. Sources describe a Russian-speaking criminal group that later conducted espionage-style operations [S4][S5].
attribution.confidence: ESET assessed with high confidence that the same people were behind both the earlier attacks on banks and businesses and the later government-targeting campaigns, reasoning that the change in targets preceded the public availability of the source code. ESET researcher Jean-Ian Boutin said it is unclear whether one or several members decided to change focus, or why [S6].
attribution.basis: ESET malware and infrastructure analysis [S2][S3][S5][S6]; Group-IB incident reporting on the bank thefts [S1]. Whether any state tasking exists is not established.

actors.objectives: Financial theft from Russian and Ukrainian banks and business customers (fraudulent payment orders) [S1][S4]. ESET (reporting in 2019) observed, since late 2015, espionage-oriented tooling used against government institutions in Eastern Europe and Central Asia; motive for that shift is unknown [S5][S6].

targeting.notes: Group-IB reported most bank victims in Russia with about ten percent in Ukraine, per secondary coverage [S4]. The October 2015 Ammyy Admin website compromise affected mostly Russian companies (88% per a Russian news write-up) [S2]. The 2018-2019 malvertising campaign aimed ads at accountants searching for invoice and contract templates [S3]. Group-IB reported 2022-2023 activity using sites posing as resources for accountants and lawyers [S9].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing impersonating the Russian Central Bank and FinCERT, malware that scans for the Central Bank of Russia automated bank-customer system, and, per Group-IB as relayed by the actor record, a network worm to spread across bank infrastructure [S1][S4]. Moved to strategic web compromise in October 2015 by bundling malware with Ammyy Admin downloads [S2]. In 2018-2019 used malicious Yandex.Direct ads and GitHub-hosted payloads [S3]. In June 2019 used a Windows win32k zero-day (CVE-2019-1132) for local privilege escalation, the first zero-day ESET saw the group use; the exploit relied on popup menu objects and was patched in July 2019 [S5][S6]. Decoy documents delivered a password stealer for email clients and browsers plus full remote access [S6].

diamond.adversary: Russian-speaking criminal group; ESET judges with high confidence the same people moved from bank theft to government-targeted operations [S4][S6].
diamond.capability: Phishing, worm-assisted spread in bank networks, trojanized software downloads, malvertising, and a win32k zero-day (CVE-2019-1132) [S1][S2][S3][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised legitimate website (ammyy.com), Yandex.Direct ads, lure template sites and GitHub-hosted payloads, plus actor C2 servers [S2][S3].
diamond.victim: Russian and Ukrainian banks, Russian businesses and accountants, and a government institution in Eastern Europe [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Financial crime in the Russian-speaking space; the 2019 government targeting suggests intelligence interest, but motive is not established [S5][S6].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints, the Central Bank of Russia bank-customer software, remote administration tools, and unpatched Windows 7 / Server 2008 era systems exposed to CVE-2019-1132 [S1][S2][S5].

gaps: WebFetch could not open any host in this session, so all content comes from search-result summaries; the primary ESET and Group-IB documents were not opened directly. Group-IB report publication month is unverified.
Group-IB's claim that Buhtrap was the first group to use a network worm in bank networks is taken from the actor record's imported text and was not independently re-verified.
The identity and exact number of operators, and whether the 2019 espionage activity involved state tasking, are unknown.
The date and manner of the source code leak is not established in the gathered sources; Malpedia cites DCSO and Gelos analyses that were not opened.
Post-2019 activity: Group-IB reporting on 2022-2023 campaigns was only seen via Habr reposts, and it is unclear whether those operators are the original group or copycats using leaked code.
Dollar totals vary between sources ($25.7 million to about $27.4 million) and Ukrainian losses are unknown.
No Microsoft (Storm-/Typhoon-style) name was found; MITRE group id absent in the record.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is financial-sector and accounting workstations running bank-customer software, remote-administration tool download sites, and older unpatched Windows hosts. STEP 2: The group adapts delivery between phishing, web compromise, and malvertising, and tooling may be reused by others after the source leak [S2][S3][S7]. STEP 3: Template is lure or trojanized download, then backdoor and credential theft, then privilege escalation and fraud or collection [S1][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued financially motivated intrusions against Russian-speaking-region businesses. MDCOA is use of a fresh exploit or trojanized download channel against government networks in Eastern Europe or Central Asia, as seen in 2019 [S5][S6]. Candidate indicators: unexpected installers bundled with remote-admin tools, malvertising to template sites, GitHub-hosted payloads that go dormant, and win32k popup-menu exploitation on legacy Windows [S2][S3][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat Buhtrap-family detections cautiously, since leaked code means tooling presence does not confirm the original actors [S7]. (2) Authorities: relevance to US forces is limited by the sources, which show regional criminal and government targeting in Eastern Europe and Central Asia; any partner-network support needs to follow existing agreements. (3) Mission assurance: enforce patching of legacy Windows and restrict unapproved remote-administration software on mission systems [S2][S5]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partner CERTs through established channels and track ESET and Group-IB reporting for updates.

provenance.importedSummary: Buhtrap has been active since 2014, however their first attacks against financial institutions were only detected in August 2015. Earlier, the group had only focused on targeting banking clients. At the moment, the group is known to target Russian and Ukrainian banks. From August 2015 to February 2016 Buhtrap managed to conduct 13 successful attacks against Russian banks for a total amount of 1.8 billion rubles ($25.7 mln). The number of successful attacks against Ukrainian banks has not been identified. Buhtrap is the first hacker group using a network worm to infect the overall bank infrastructure that significantly increases the difficulty of removing all malicious functions from the network. As a result, banks have to shut down the whole infrastructure which provokes delay in servicing customers and additional losses. Malicious programs intentionally scan for machines with an automated Bank-Customer system of the Central Bank of Russia (further referred to as BCS CBR). We have not identified incidents of attacks involving online money transfer systems, ATM machines or payment gates which are known to be of interest for other criminal groups.

identification.summary: Iran-based cyber espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Burgundy Sandstorm and maps to REMIX KITTEN, Cadelle and Chafer [S1]. Mandiant defined APT39 to consolidate this activity and says it largely aligns with 'Chafer', though vendors report it differently [S2]. The group concentrates on collecting personal information and tracking individuals of interest. It has prioritized telecommunications, travel and the IT firms that support travel [S2]. In September 2020 the US government named Rana Intelligence Computing Company as an MOIS front company for APT39 [S3][S9].
identification.firstObserved: Symantec observed Cadelle/Chafer activity from at least July 2014, with C2 registration data hinting at activity possibly as early as 2011 [S4]. Mandiant has tracked APT39 activity since November 2014 [S2]. US government reporting describes APT39 activity since 2014 [S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Burgundy Sandstorm. Microsoft maps REMIX KITTEN, Cadelle and Chafer to it [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as APT39 (G0087) [S10]. Symantec originally described Cadelle and Chafer as two separate teams using different backdoors (Cadelspy and Remexi) [S4]. Microsoft and MITRE fold both into one actor, but that merge rests on vendor judgment [S1][S10]. Unit 42 noted code overlap with OilRig but tracks Chafer and OilRig separately [S6]. Mandiant judges APT39 distinct from APT34 while noting the groups may share resources [S2].

attribution.sponsor: Iran, Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). The US Treasury and FBI stated in September 2020 that APT39 and its front company Rana Intelligence Computing Company are owned and controlled by MOIS [S3][S9].
attribution.confidence: US government: Treasury sanctioned APT39, 45 associated individuals and Rana under E.O. 13553, and the FBI issued a FLASH alert based on a long-term FBI Boston investigation (as reported by press) [S3][S9]. Mandiant states 'moderate confidence' that APT39 operations support Iranian national interests [S2]. Symantec assessed that Cadelle and Chafer victims are most likely of interest to an Iranian entity [S4]. Kaspersky did not directly attribute its 2018 Remexi activity to a specific Iranian group or individual [S7].
attribution.basis: Mandiant cited regional targeting, infrastructure, timing and similarities to APT34 [S2]. The US government action identified Rana personnel by role (managers, programmers, hacking experts) [S3][S9]. Microsoft's naming feed lists Iran as origin [S1].

actors.objectives: Mandiant assesses the main mission is to track or monitor targets of interest and to collect personal information, including travel itineraries and telecom customer data. A possible secondary goal is geopolitical data for government decision-making [S2]. The FBI and Treasury describe monitoring of Iranian citizens, dissidents and journalists as well as neighboring governments' networks [S3][S9]. Symantec assessed that compromising airlines and telecoms was possibly meant to monitor targets' movements and communications [S4].

sectors: Travel, airlines, aircraft services and air transportation [S2][S4][S5][S8]
IT and software firms supporting air and sea transport [S2][S5]
regions: Global scope, concentrated in the Middle East [S2]
Israel, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and UAE (2017 activity) [S5]
Kuwait and Saudi Arabia (2018-2020 activity reported by Bitdefender) [S8]
targeting.notes: Targeting combines domestic surveillance of Iranians with access to regional telecom, travel and government data stores. Those holdings let the group track individuals at scale [S2][S4][S9].

capabilities.summary: Initial access through spearphishing with malicious attachments or links (typically POWBAT), lookalike domains impersonating services relevant to targets, web-server exploitation to plant web shells (ANTAK, ASPXSPY), and stolen credentials against exposed Outlook Web Access [S2]. Custom backdoors include SEAWEED, CACHEMONEY and a POWBAT variant [S2]. Other tooling includes Remexi, which captures keystrokes, screenshots, credentials and browser data and uses Windows BITS for C2 and exfiltration [S4][S7], and Cadelspy [S4]. MechaFlounder is a PyInstaller-compiled Python backdoor seen in 2018 [S6]. Post-exploitation relies on Mimikatz (including repacked builds), Windows Credential Editor, ProcDump, Ncrack, the BLUETORCH port scanner, the REDTRIP/PINKTRIP/BLUETRIP SOCKS5 proxies, RDP, SSH, PsExec, RemCom and xCmdSvc. Data is staged with WinRAR or 7-Zip [S2]. Bitdefender reported living-off-the-land techniques and Metasploit-related PowerShell in 2018-2020 Gulf intrusions [S8]. The FBI FLASH described eight malware sets, including VBS, AutoIt, BITS-based executables, a Python script and a malicious Android APK [S3][S9].

diamond.adversary: Iranian MOIS cyber espionage operators working through the front company Rana Intelligence Computing Company. 45 associated individuals were sanctioned in 2020 [S3][S9].
diamond.capability: Spearphishing, web shells, OWA credential abuse, custom backdoors (SEAWEED, CACHEMONEY, POWBAT, Remexi, MechaFlounder), public credential-dumping tools and SOCKS proxies, plus Android malware [S2][S6][S7][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Lookalike domains impersonating services relevant to targets [S2]. Reused C2 such as win10-update[.]com and 185.177.59[.]70 [S6]. BITS-based C2 channels [S7].
diamond.victim: Telecom and travel companies, governments in the Middle East, foreign diplomatic entities in Iran, academia, and Iranian dissidents and journalists [S2][S5][S7][S9].
diamond.socioPolitical: Regime security and surveillance: monitoring dissidents, journalists and persons of interest, and supporting Iranian intelligence on neighboring states [S2][S3][S9].
diamond.technology: Large personal-data stores at telecom and travel providers (customer records, itineraries) and exposed email and web services [S2][S4].

gaps: No Microsoft blog post or Microsoft Threat Intelligence profile describing Burgundy Sandstorm operations was found. Microsoft coverage here rests only on the naming mapping feed [S1].
Primary US government documents (Treasury press release sm1127, FBI FLASH on Rana malware) could not be opened from this environment. Details rely on press coverage [S3][S9].
Original Kaspersky (Securelist) and Bitdefender whitepaper texts could not be fetched. Those campaign details rely on press coverage and search excerpts [S7][S8].
Cadelle vs. Chafer: Symantec described two teams. Microsoft and MITRE consolidate them, and the exact cluster boundaries are not public [S1][S4].
No publicly documented Burgundy Sandstorm/APT39 campaign after 2020 was found in the sources gathered. Current activity level is unverified.
The precise publication days of the 2015 Symantec, 2018 Symantec and 2019 Unit 42 reports were not confirmed. Dates are given to month precision.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is the regional telecom and travel providers that hold subscriber records and itineraries, plus Middle East government networks [S2][S5]. Host-nation and commercial providers supporting deployed forces in the Gulf fall within this terrain [S5][S8]. STEP 2 (effects): Compromise of telecom or airline data could expose personnel movements and communications patterns without touching DoD networks [S2][S4]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Spearphish or web-server exploit, then web shell or POWBAT/Remexi foothold, then Mimikatz credential theft and SOCKS proxy or RDP lateral movement, then archive and exfiltrate [S2][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent collection of personal and travel data from regional telecom, aviation and government victims [S2][S8]. MDCOA is using that data to track specific individuals of interest, including personnel in the region [S2][S9]. Candidate indicators: lookalike domains spoofing services relevant to targets, ASPX web shells on public servers, bitsadmin-driven transfers, PyInstaller binaries named lsass.exe, and newly created local accounts [S2][S6][S7][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Exposure through third-party telecom and travel providers is outside DoDIN visibility, so JCC2 pictures should flag partner and commercial dependencies in the Gulf [S2][S8]. (2) Authorities: Activity against host-nation and commercial networks needs coordination with partner nations and interagency rather than unilateral DCO [S3][S9]. (3) Mission assurance: Treat personnel travel data and OWA credentials as protected assets. Mandiant documents OWA credential abuse [S2]. (4) Coordination: Use the FBI FLASH malware sets and MITRE G0087 for hunt content, and share with partner CERTs in states named as targets [S9][S10].

provenance.importedSummary: APT39 was created to bring together previous activities and methods used by this actor, and its activities largely align with a group publicly referred to as "Chafer." However, there are differences in what has been publicly reported due to the variances in how organizations track activity. APT39 primarily leverages the SEAWEED and CACHEMONEY backdoors along with a specific variant of the POWBAT backdoor. While APT39's targeting scope is global, its activities are concentrated in the Middle East. APT39 has prioritized the telecommunications sector, with additional targeting of the travel industry and IT firms that support it and the high-tech industry.

identification.summary: Cadet Blizzard is a Russian state actor that Microsoft associates with the GRU. Microsoft began tracking it as DEV-0586 in January 2022, after the WhisperGate destructive malware and defacements of Ukrainian government websites [S1][S2]. Microsoft says its goals are disruption, destruction, information collection and possibly intimidation. Its main targets are Ukrainian government organizations and IT service providers, with further targets in Europe, Central Asia and Latin America [S1]. US government agencies attribute WhisperGate and later operations against NATO members to GRU Unit 29155 [S3][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft assesses the group has been operational in some capacity since at least 2020, with historical compromises of Eastern European entities as early as April 2021 [S1]. WhisperGate first appeared on victim systems on 2022-01-13 [S2]. The US joint advisory says Unit 29155 has conducted offensive cyber operations since at least 2020 [S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Cadet Blizzard (formerly DEV-0586; renamed in April 2023) [S1][S2]. Microsoft describes it as distinct from the other GRU-affiliated groups Forest Blizzard (STRONTIUM) and Seashell Blizzard (IRIDIUM) [S1]. MITRE tracks it as Ember Bear (G1003) with aliases UNC2589, Bleeding Bear, DEV-0586, Cadet Blizzard, Frozenvista and UAC-0056 [S7]. The joint advisory maps Cadet Blizzard, Ember Bear, Frozenvista, UNC2589 and UAC-0056 to Unit 29155 activity, and cautions that these may not exactly match US government attribution [S3]. CLUSTER BOUNDARY: MITRE tracks Saint Bear (G1031; Storm-0587, TA471, UAC-0056, Lorec53) separately. It is the Saint Bot/OutSteel phishing cluster, and MITRE says it is distinct from Ember Bear despite past confusion [S7][S8]. Microsoft reports that Cadet Blizzard has intersected with Storm-0587, a phishing and document-stealer cluster active since April 2021, but tracks it separately [S1]. This profile therefore does not merge Saint Bot or OutSteel campaign facts into Cadet Blizzard.

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation: the GRU (Main Directorate of the General Staff). Microsoft assesses the actor is associated with the GRU [S1]. The FBI, NSA and CISA attribute the corresponding cyber activity to GRU Unit 29155 [S3], and a US indictment names a Unit 29155 cyber commander and officers [S4].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft says it has 'gained high confidence in our analysis and knowledge of the actor's tooling, victimology, and motivation' and assesses that Cadet Blizzard is associated with the GRU [S1]. The September 2024 joint advisory makes a US and allied government attribution to GRU Unit 29155. It also notes that vendor alias mappings may not exactly match US government attribution [S3]. US federal indictments (June 2024 and September 2024) charge a civilian and five GRU officers over WhisperGate. These charges are allegations, not convictions [S4][S5].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and incident response [S1][S2]; FBI/NSA/CISA joint advisory AA24-249A [S3]; DOJ indictments of Amin Stigal (June 2024) and of Col. Yuriy Denisov and four Unit 29155 lieutenants (September 2024) [S4][S5]. Microsoft also assesses that at least one Russian private-sector organization materially supported the WhisperGate operation [S1]. The FBI assesses that the cyber operators are junior active-duty GRU officers working under experienced unit leadership, and that they rely in part on non-GRU cybercriminals [S3].

actors.objectives: Microsoft lists disruption, destruction, information collection and possibly intimidation, and notes that some operations appear designed as public signals [S1]. The US advisory says Unit 29155 conducts computer network operations against global targets for espionage, sabotage and reputational harm [S3][S4]. It exposes stolen data through hack-and-leak fronts such as 'Free Civilian' [S1].

regions: Europe and NATO member states, especially those providing military aid to Ukraine [S1][S3]
targeting.notes: Microsoft describes a 'compromise one, compromise many' approach through IT providers [S1]. The FBI observed more than 14,000 instances of domain scanning across 26 NATO members and several other EU countries (reported via secondary coverage of the advisory) [S3]. The Stigal indictment says later targets included systems in countries supporting Ukraine, including the United States [S5].

capabilities.summary: Destructive capability: WhisperGate is a two-stage wiper disguised as ransomware. It overwrites the Master Boot Record with a fake ransom note, then downloads a file corrupter from Discord that overwrites targeted files, and it has no recovery mechanism [S2]. Initial access comes mainly through exploitation of internet-facing web servers and of known Confluence and Exchange vulnerabilities, including CVE-2021-26084, CVE-2022-41040 and ProxyShell [S1]. Post-exploitation relies on web shells, renamed open-source and living-off-the-land tools (Impacket, netcat, GOST, procdump), and anonymization through commercial VPNs and Tor. Microsoft also reports anti-forensics and disabling of Microsoft Defender [S1][S2]. Operations are paired with website defacement and hack-and-leak information operations [S1]. Microsoft judges the group less prolific than Seashell Blizzard and its operational security weaker than that of Forest Blizzard or Seashell Blizzard [S1].

Cluster boundary unresolved: UAC-0056 is listed under both MITRE Ember Bear and Saint Bear. MITRE's Saint Bot software entry associates the tool with Ember Bear, while its Saint Bear group entry calls the two clusters distinct [S7][S8]. Unit 42 attributes Saint Bot and OutSteel phishing (for example against a Ukrainian energy organization on 2022-02-01) to UAC-0056, which other vendors call TA471, SaintBear and Lorec53 [S6]. The imported record's aliases (Saint Bear, SaintBear, Lorec53, TA471, Nodaria, Storm-0587, DEV-0587) may belong to the Saint Bear/Storm-0587 phishing cluster rather than to Cadet Blizzard and should be reviewed.
The imported record's software list includes Saint Bot, which may belong to Saint Bear/Storm-0587 rather than Cadet Blizzard [S8].
No public Microsoft reporting on Cadet Blizzard after 2023 was found in this research pass, so current activity levels are unverified.

The full list of CVEs and initial-access techniques in AA24-249A was not reviewed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key cyber terrain is internet-facing web servers and Confluence and Exchange instances on perimeters and in DMZs, plus IT service providers whose access reaches many government customers [S1]. The operating environment covers Ukraine and the NATO states that support it, including US systems [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 2 (effects): Destructive wipers can make government and NGO endpoints inoperable without recovery [S2]. Hack-and-leak and defacement add information effects aimed at intimidation and reputational harm [S1][S3]. STEP 3 (adversary template): exploit a public-facing service, then plant a web shell, dump credentials (LSASS, registry hives), move laterally with Impacket, and either exfiltrate data and leak it or deploy a wiper; anonymization runs through VPNs and Tor [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage and hack-and-leak against Ukrainian and allied government and IT-provider networks, preceded by broad scanning of NATO domains [S1][S3]. MDCOA is coordinated destructive wiper deployment through compromised IT providers against allied government or critical-infrastructure networks during a crisis [S1][S2][S3]. Candidate indicators: scanning spikes against exposed Confluence and Exchange servers; new web shells on DMZ servers; renamed procdump, netcat or GOST binaries; reg save of SAM or SYSTEM hives; Impacket remote execution over ADMIN$; payloads retrieved from Discord; disabled Defender; new Free Civilian-style leak channels [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track Cadet Blizzard, Ember Bear and Unit 29155 reporting together, but keep the Saint Bear/Storm-0587 phishing cluster separate to avoid mis-cueing defenders [S1][S3][S7][S8]. Authorities: US attribution rests on the joint advisory and indictments. Vendor alias mappings are flagged as inexact, so planners should cite the government attribution for actions and vendor reporting for TTPs [S3][S4]. Mission assurance: give priority to patching and monitoring internet-facing collaboration and mail servers, and to backups and MBR protection for mission systems that depend on IT service providers, given the 'compromise one, compromise many' approach and the destructive intent [S1][S2]. Coordination: because targeting includes allies that support Ukraine and the US, coordinate with CISA, FBI and allied CERTs (for example CERT-UA) on indicators and on hack-and-leak responses [S1][S3][S5].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-exposed Exchange servers, SMB services and telecom mail infrastructure are key terrain. STEP 2: The actor weaponizes freshly disclosed Exchange flaws within days and reuses long-lived PlugX infrastructure [S4][S5]. STEP 3: Template is SMB or credential access or Exchange exploit, then web shell, PlugX/Whitebird, credential dumping, lateral movement with RemCom and FRP [S2][S6]. identification.summary: China-linked cyber espionage group that Microsoft tracks as Canary Typhoon and maps to BlackTech, Palmerworm, CIRCUIT PANDA and APT24 [S1]. Trend Micro first described BlackTech in 2017, linking the PLEAD, Shrouded Crossbow and Waterbear campaigns to one group operating against East Asia, particularly Taiwan, and occasionally Japan and Hong Kong [S2]. A September 2023 US-Japan joint advisory warned that BlackTech modifies router firmware and abuses trust between subsidiary and headquarters networks to pivot into targets in Japan and the US [S7][S8]. Trend Micro reported in 2024 that the group (tracked as Earth Hundun) continued to develop Waterbear and its successor Deuterbear against technology and government organizations in Asia-Pacific [S9][S10].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro (2017): PLEAD active since 2012, with secondary reporting placing Shrouded Crossbow activity as early as 2010 [S2]. Symantec states the group has been active since at least 2013 [S5]. Trend Micro reports Waterbear versions dating back to 2009 [S9].

Microsoft's public mapping lists CIRCUIT PANDA, APT24, Palmerworm and BlackTech for Canary Typhoon and gives no former DEV/element name; no Microsoft blog post describing Canary Typhoon activity was found [S1]. The joint advisory lists Palmerworm, Temp.Overboard, Circuit Panda and Radio Panda as BlackTech aliases [S7].

Trend Micro assessed from C2 mutexes and domain names that the campaigns are likely designed to steal targets' technology, and PLEAD shows a penchant for confidential documents [S2]. targeting.notes: The 2023 advisory describes BlackTech compromising branch or overseas-subsidiary routers to pivot into headquarters networks in Japan and the US, so multinational corporations with East Asian subsidiaries are exposed even when the parent is outside the region [S7][S8]. Sector lists differ slightly between the advisory text (government, industrial, technology, media, electronics, telecommunications, entities supporting US and Japanese militaries) and the CISA press release (which cites the defense industrial base); this wording comes from secondary reporting [S7].

capabilities.summary: Custom, regularly retooled malware: PLEAD backdoor and DRIGO exfiltration tool, KIVARS and Waterbear (secondary backdoor installed after privilege is gained) [S2]; Consock, Waship, Dalwit and Nomri backdoors plus dual-use and living-off-the-land tools in 2019-2020 [S5]; Flagpro downloader, SelfMake Loader and Spider RAT from 2020-2021 [S6]; BendyBear and FakeDead cited in the 2023 advisory [S7]; and Deuterbear, a Waterbear successor first seen in October 2022 with anti-memory-scanning, shellcode plugins and HTTPS C2 [S9][S10]. Waterbear is described by Trend Micro as having more than ten versions since 2009 with extensive anti-debug and anti-sandbox features [S9]. Code signing with stolen certificates from D-Link and Changing Information Technology to sign PLEAD and a password stealer (2018) [S3]. Probable router-level man-in-the-middle abuse of the ASUS WebStorage update process to deliver PLEAD (2019) [S4]. Spear-phishing with password-protected archives containing macro documents impersonating business partners [S6]. Network-device tradecraft: after gaining admin access (typically stolen credentials), modifying Cisco router firmware with an SSH backdoor that hides connections from logs, disabling logging, and exploiting router domain-trust relationships to move from subsidiaries to headquarters; the agencies note the technique is not limited to Cisco [S7][S8]. PLEAD operators were also reported to scan for vulnerable routers and enable their VPN feature to stage C2 or delivery servers [S2].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key cyber terrain includes edge and branch routers connecting East Asian subsidiaries, partner sites and contractors to US and Japanese headquarters networks, since BlackTech pivots along those trust paths [S7]. Defense-supporting organizations in Japan and Taiwan sit inside this environment [S7]. STEP 2 (effects): Firmware-level router persistence with log suppression degrades defenders' visibility and survives host-level remediation; stolen code-signing certificates and hijacked update channels undermine software-trust assumptions [S3][S4][S7]. STEP 3 (adversary template): spear-phishing or stolen credentials, then first-stage downloader (Flagpro/PLEAD), then secondary backdoor (Waterbear/Deuterbear), then document theft; in parallel, admin access to routers, firmware replacement, and lateral movement from subsidiary to headquarters [S2][S6][S7][S9]. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent technology and document theft from government, technology and defense-supporting entities in Taiwan, Japan and the US [S2][S5][S7]. MDCOA is covert firmware-level control of routers on paths serving US and Japanese military-support networks, positioning the actor to collect or disrupt traffic during a Taiwan Strait crisis (analyst extrapolation; no disruptive activity reported). Candidate indicators: router firmware image hash mismatches, unexpected reboots or image changes, SSH sessions not reflected in logs, outbound VTY connections, logging disabled on network devices, and executables signed with revoked Taiwanese vendor certificates [S3][S7][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: network-device integrity (firmware hashes, configuration drift, logging status) should be a reported data feed, because host EDR alone will not see this actor's router persistence [S7]. (2) Authorities: many affected routers belong to coalition partners, contractors or overseas subsidiaries outside DoDIN control; responses depend on partner and private-sector coordination rather than unilateral action [S7]. (3) Mission assurance: map mission dependencies on links that traverse East Asian partner or subsidiary networks and treat them as potentially compromised; apply zero-trust controls and review subsidiary connections as the advisory recommends [S7]. (4) Coordination: the advisory was co-authored by US and Japanese agencies, so information sharing with Japan's NPA and NISC and with DC3/DIB partners is the natural channel for indicators and remediation status [S7].

provenance.importedSummary: BlackTech is a cyber espionage group operating against targets in East Asia, particularly Taiwan, and occasionally, Japan and Hong Kong. Based on the mutexes and domain names of some of their C&C servers, BlackTech’s campaigns are likely designed to steal their target’s technology. Following their activities and evolving tactics and techniques helped us uncover the proverbial red string of fate that connected three seemingly disparate campaigns: PLEAD, Shrouded Crossbow, and of late, Waterbear. PLEAD is an information theft campaign with a penchant for confidential documents. Active since 2012, it has so far targeted Taiwanese government agencies and private organizations. PLEAD’s toolset includes the self-named PLEAD backdoor and the DRIGO exfiltration tool. PLEAD uses spear-phishing emails to deliver and install their backdoor, either as an attachment or through links to cloud storage services. Some of the cloud storage accounts used to deliver PLEAD are also used as drop off points for exfiltrated documents stolen by DRIGO. PLEAD actors use a router scanner tool to scan for vulnerable routers, after which the attackers will enable the router’s VPN feature then register a machine as virtual server. This virtual server will be used either as a C&C server or an HTTP server that delivers PLEAD malware to their targets.

identification.summary: APT32 is a suspected Vietnam-based threat group that has been active since at least 2014. They have extensively used strategic web compromises to compromise victims.

identification.summary: CeranaKeeper is a China-aligned APT group that ESET named in October 2024 [S1][S2]. ESET says it has been active since at least early 2022 and mainly targets government institutions in Southeast Asia, with Thailand the primary focus [S2][S4]. The name is wordplay on 'beekeeper' and Apis cerana (the Asian honeybee), based on a recurring string in the group's tools [S2]. It uses custom backdoors and abuses cloud and file-sharing services such as Dropbox, OneDrive, GitHub and PixelDrain for command and control and exfiltration [S2][S6].
identification.firstObserved: ESET: active since at least early 2022; campaigns against Thai government institutions observed from 2023 [S2][S4]. ESET white paper published 2024-10-02 [S6].
identification.notes: ESET separates CeranaKeeper from Mustang Panda: some of its activity was earlier attributed to Mustang Panda, but ESET concluded it operates independently, while possibly sharing information or third-party resources with it [S2][S4]. In Feb 2025 Trend Micro published on 'Earth Preta' activity using a TONESHELL variant; ESET said it tracks that threat as CeranaKeeper [S8][S9]. Trend Micro and ESET names are not interchangeable without the primary reports; see gaps.

attribution.confidence: ESET describes CeranaKeeper as 'China-aligned' [S2]. The sources gathered do not name a specific Chinese government agency or contractor.
attribution.basis: ESET assessment of tooling and targeting; the group shares some tooling or resources with Mustang Panda but ESET tracks it as a separate cluster [S2][S4].

actors.objectives: Large-scale data theft from government institutions. ESET reported extensive wildcard expressions that sometimes traversed entire drives, which it said showed an aim of massive data siphoning [S4].

regions: Myanmar, Philippines, Japan, Taiwan (listed in one ESET press release; Thailand is the only country confirmed in ESET's own campaign findings) [S2]
targeting.notes: Sector and regional focus from ESET press materials and press coverage [S2][S3][S4]. Initial access routes were reported as unknown [S4].

capabilities.summary: Custom backdoors including TONESHELL, DropboxFlop (Python backdoor using Dropbox C2, apparently based on the public Dropflop project), OneDoor (C/C++ backdoor abusing OneDrive) and BingoShell (uses GitHub pull requests as covert C2, named for the string 'bingo#') [S2][S3][S4]. In a mid-2023 intrusion a compromised machine brute-forced a domain controller in a Thai government network, giving privileged access; the group then deployed TONESHELL and a credential-dumping tool and abused a legitimate Avast driver to disable security protections [S2]. Archived files were exfiltrated via cloud services, with a newer version using PixelDrain [S6]. In 2025 a TONESHELL variant was reported sideloaded through a legitimate Electronic Arts application and using MAVInject.exe to inject into waitfor.exe when ESET software was present [S7][S9].

diamond.adversary: China-aligned APT tracked by ESET as CeranaKeeper, distinct from Mustang Panda per ESET [S2][S4].
diamond.capability: TONESHELL, DropboxFlop, OneDoor, BingoShell; LAN brute force; credential dumping; driver abuse; cloud-service exfiltration [S2][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Legitimate cloud and code-hosting services (Dropbox, OneDrive, GitHub, PixelDrain) used for C2 and exfiltration [S2][S6].
diamond.victim: Government institutions, mainly in Thailand, with other Asian countries listed in one press release [S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection of government data in Southeast Asia consistent with a China-aligned espionage mission, per ESET's 'China-aligned' characterization [S2][S4].
diamond.technology: Windows domain environments with weak credential controls and tolerance for outbound traffic to mainstream cloud services [S2].

gaps: I could not open the ESET WeLiveSecurity article, ESET white paper, or press releases directly (fetch failed); details come from search-result summaries of those documents and secondary coverage [S1][S2][S6]. Validate against the white paper.
Initial access vector is reported as unknown [S4].
No government attribution or named sponsoring agency found.
Overlap with Mustang Panda, Earth Preta (Trend Micro) and Stately Taurus (Palo Alto) is not resolved; Trend Micro and ESET cluster boundaries differ and should not be merged [S2][S8][S9].
Listed non-Thai victim countries (Myanmar, Philippines, Japan, Taiwan) rest on one press release and were not independently confirmed [S2].
Press sources disagree on which file-sharing services were used (Pastebin appears in one secondary source only); not included here.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID known for this record.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is Windows domain controllers and file servers in government networks, plus outbound paths to cloud and code-hosting services [S2]. STEP 2: The actor blends C2 and exfiltration into Dropbox, OneDrive, GitHub and PixelDrain traffic and abuses signed drivers to disable security tools, which degrades detection built on network reputation [S2][S6]. STEP 3: Observed template is a foothold, LAN brute force against a domain controller, privileged access, TONESHELL and credential dumping, then wildcard sweeps and cloud exfiltration [S2][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued bulk collection from Southeast Asian government networks. MDCOA is use of the same cloud-abuse tradecraft against coalition or partner-nation government networks in a regional crisis. Candidate indicators: repeated failed logons against domain controllers from internal hosts, loading of an unexpected Avast driver, unusual GitHub pull requests containing 'bingo#', and bulk archive uploads to PixelDrain, Dropbox or OneDrive from servers [S2][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track partner-nation government networks in Southeast Asia as likely collection targets and share vendor indicators with partners. (2) Authorities: monitoring cloud-service egress on DoD networks and blocking driver loads need clear owners and approvals before an incident. (3) Mission assurance: protect domain controllers and mission file shares through credential hygiene and lockout alerting. (4) Coordination: because cluster boundaries (CeranaKeeper vs. Mustang Panda or Earth Preta) are unsettled, coordinate through DC3 and partner CERTs on indicators rather than waiting for name resolution [S2][S8].
