implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Relevant terrain includes public-facing information platforms (news CMS, streaming/IPTV, digital displays, SMS gateways and IoT cameras) and personal data on servicemembers and citizens, because the actor turns access to these into influence effects [S3][S6][S9][S10]. STEP 2: The actor's goal is psychological and reputational effect, not long-term espionage; a modest intrusion paired with a persona claim and sockpuppet amplification creates outsized perceived impact [S2][S3][S7]. STEP 3: The pattern runs intrusion or data theft, then a persona claim (Holy Souls, Al-Toufan, Savior Pro), then a leak on Telegram or forums, bulk SMS/email intimidation and AI-enhanced media, then amplification [S2][S3][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is opportunistic hack-and-leak and intimidation messaging against Israel-aligned and Western audiences, timed to geopolitical triggers such as elections, insults to Iranian leadership or major events [S2][S3][S4][S9]. MDCOA is a compromise of media, display or SMS infrastructure used to deliver threatening messages to US personnel or families during a US-Iran crisis, possibly combined with destructive encryption malware as reported against a US organization [S3][S7]. Candidate indicators: new hacktivist personas claiming breaches of US or allied entities; bulk SMS or email threats referencing recipients' personal data; unauthorized content on displays or streams; and reconnaissance scans of election or media websites [S3][S4][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: fuse cyber intrusion reporting with information-environment monitoring, because this actor's effects appear first as persona claims and leaks [S2][S3]. (2) Authorities: activity mixes cyber intrusion with influence operations against civilians and elections, so response may cross DoD, FBI, CISA and DHS lanes; FBI has already acted against the group's media-CMS access [S6]. (3) Mission assurance: protect installation and family-facing communications channels (mass notification, base media, displays) against hijacking and spoofed threats [S3][S9]. (4) Coordination: partner with allies already engaged against the actor, including Israel's INCD (co-author of the 2024 advisory) and France and Sweden as victims, and with platform companies that suspend persona accounts [S2][S8][S10].

provenance.importedSummary: In May 2018, we discovered a campaign targeting dozens of mobile Android devices belonging to Israeli citizens. Kaspersky spyware sensors caught the signal of an attack from the device of one of the victims; and a hash of the APK involved (Android application) was tagged in our sample feed for inspection. Once we looked into the file, we quickly found out that the inner-workings of the APK included a malicious payload, embedded in the original code of the application. This was an original spyware program, designed to exfiltrate almost all accessible information. During the course of our research, we noticed that we were not the only ones to have found the operation. Researchers from Bitdefender also released an analysis of one of the samples in a blogpost. Although something had already been published, we decided to do something different with the data we acquired. The following month, we released a private report on our Threat Intelligence Portal to alert our clients about this newly discovered operation and began writing YARA rules in order to catch more samples. We decided to call the operation “ViceLeaker”, because of strings and variables in its code.

identification.summary: Crimson Sandstorm (formerly CURIUM) is an Iran-based espionage actor [S1][S2]. Microsoft says it uses a network of fictitious social media accounts to build trust with targets and then delivers malware to exfiltrate data [S1]. Microsoft says it has targeted the defense, maritime shipping, transportation, healthcare and technology sectors, often using watering-hole attacks and social engineering to deliver custom .NET malware. Microsoft also notes earlier research on its malware that used email for command and control [S2]. Microsoft's 2021 CyberWarCon presentation describes CURIUM spending months posing as an attractive woman on LinkedIn or Facebook before sending a malicious document [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: active since at least 2017 [S2]. Symantec (as Tortoiseshell): active since at least July 2018 (summary of Symantec report via Malpedia) [S4].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Crimson Sandstorm (formerly CURIUM) [S1][S3]. Microsoft states other researchers track it as Tortoiseshell, Imperial Kitten and Yellow Liderc [S2]. Microsoft's profile also lists Houseblend and Tortoise Shell [S1]. PwC tracks it as Yellow Liderc and lists Imperial Kitten, Tortoiseshell, TA456 and Crimson Sandstorm as overlapping names (reported via press) [S8]. Proofpoint tracks TA456 and says it overlaps with Tortoiseshell and Imperial Kitten (reported via press) [S7]. Press coverage of Meta's 2021 takedown says researchers linked much of the activity to Mandiant's UNC1833, with some infrastructure overlap with APT35 [S6]. This is a press claim and is not used to merge clusters. CrowdStrike's IMPERIAL KITTEN is also mapped by Microsoft to Cuboid Sandstorm and Smoke Sandstorm, which Microsoft tracks separately. Facts from CrowdStrike IMPERIAL KITTEN reporting [S9] should therefore be read as the CrowdStrike cluster, not Microsoft's boundary.

attribution.sponsor: Iran. Microsoft assesses Crimson Sandstorm to be connected to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) [S2]. Meta (Facebook) said the malware used in the 2021 Tortoiseshell campaign was developed by Mahak Rayan Afraz, a Tehran IT company with ties to the IRGC (reported via press) [S6]. CrowdStrike assesses that IMPERIAL KITTEN likely fulfills Iranian strategic intelligence requirements associated with IRGC operations (reported via press) [S9].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft describes the actor as 'assessed to be connected to' the IRGC and gives no numeric confidence level [S2]. Its public profile names Iran as country of origin without naming a sponsor [S1]. CrowdStrike uses 'likely' [S9]. In 2019, Symantec and Cisco Talos declined to tie Tortoiseshell to a specific nation-state [S5]. No government attribution of this cluster was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and its 2024 OpenAI collaboration, which disabled Crimson Sandstorm accounts and assets [S2]. Meta platform investigation and malware-developer attribution [S6]. Vendor victimology and malware analysis from PwC, Proofpoint and CrowdStrike [S7][S8][S9].

actors.objectives: Strategic intelligence collection in support of Iranian (IRGC-associated) requirements [S2][S9]. Targets include US military and defense contractors, IT services firms, and Middle Eastern governments [S1]. The actor uses supply-chain access through IT, engineering and contractor firms to reach their downstream defense and intelligence customers [S1][S4][S7]. Since 2023 it has collected against Israeli and Mediterranean maritime, logistics and technology entities [S8][S9].

sectors: US military personnel and defense contractors [S1][S6]
Aerospace and defense, including smaller subsidiaries of contractors [S6][S7]
IT services and engineering providers to US defense and intelligence agencies [S1]
IT providers in Saudi Arabia (supply chain) [S4]
targeting.notes: Microsoft says that in 2021 the actor spear-phished companies providing IT and engineering services to US defense and intelligence agencies, probably to reach their customers [S1]. Focus shifted from Middle East IT firms (2018-2019) to US military and defense personnel (2019-2021) [S4][S5][S6]. It shifted again to Israeli and Mediterranean shipping, logistics and technology targets (2022-2023) [S8][S9].

capabilities.summary: The actor's signature is long-duration social engineering through fictitious personas on LinkedIn, Facebook and other platforms. It builds trust over months, sends benign media, and then sends a look-alike malicious file [S1][S3][S6][S7]. Lures include fake recruiting and job sites: 'Hire Military Heroes' (2019) delivered a reconnaissance downloader [S5], and a site spoofing a US Labor Department job site was used in 2021 [S6]. The actor runs watering-hole (strategic web compromise) operations that use JavaScript to fingerprint visitors and selectively serve malware [S2][S8][S9]. It also uses macro-laced Excel phishing, credential theft for VPN access, and one-day vulnerability exploitation [S9]. Custom .NET malware includes IMAPLoader, which uses email as C2 and AppDomain Manager Injection [S8], and StandardKeyboard, which uses email C2 and installs as a Windows service [S9]. LEMPO (an updated Liderc) handles persistence, reconnaissance, exfiltration to actor email accounts and artifact deletion [S7]. A Python reverse shell has also been observed [S9]. In 2023 Microsoft observed the actor using LLMs for phishing content, scripting, and defense-evasion code [S2]. In the Symantec-reported Saudi supply-chain intrusions it gained domain-admin access in at least two organizations [S4].

diamond.adversary: Iran-based operators that Microsoft assesses to be IRGC-connected [S2]. Meta tied malware development to Mahak Rayan Afraz (reported) [S6].
diamond.capability: Fictitious social-media personas, fake job sites, watering holes with visitor fingerprinting, and macro Excel phishing. Custom .NET malware with email C2 (IMAPLoader, StandardKeyboard, LEMPO/Liderc) [S1][S5][S7][S8][S9].

Primary vendor reports (Symantec 2019, Cisco Talos 2019, Proofpoint 2021, Meta 2021, PwC 2023, CrowdStrike 2023) could not be fetched; content is from press coverage and search-result summaries.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): The human and persona layer of cyberspace is key terrain. This includes LinkedIn and Facebook profiles of service members, recruiters and contractor staff, plus third-party IT and engineering providers with access into DoD and intelligence networks [S1][S3][S6]. STEP 2 (effects): Months-long trust building defeats one-time phishing awareness. Email-based C2 blends with normal mail traffic, and watering holes on sector websites let the actor select victims passively [S3][S7][S8][S9]. STEP 3 (adversary template): The template is a fake recruiter or attractive persona, or a compromised sector website with JavaScript fingerprinting. That leads to a lure file or fake job app, then a .NET implant with IMAP/SMTP C2, then reconnaissance and exfiltration to actor email [S5][S7][S8][S9]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against US defense personnel, contractor subsidiaries, and Israeli and Mediterranean logistics targets through persona-driven social engineering. MDCOA is leveraging compromised IT and engineering providers for supply-chain access into defense or intelligence customer networks, as seen in 2018-2021 [S1][S4]. Candidate indicators: unsolicited recruiter or persona contacts with Airmen or contractors that move to off-platform chat or file sharing [S6][S7]; downloads of 'job' applications [S5]; outbound IMAP from non-mail hosts [S8][S9]; AppDomain Manager Injection artifacts [S8]; and a new 'Keyboard Service' Windows service [S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: fuse platform-takedown reporting (Meta, LinkedIn), vendor IOCs for IMAPLoader and StandardKeyboard, and DIB partner reporting into the common operational picture, since the actor's entry points sit outside DoDIN boundaries [S6][S8][S9]. Authorities: persona engagement with personnel on commercial platforms and compromises of contractor networks fall to counterintelligence, the DC3/DIB program and platform providers rather than DODIN defenders alone. Coordinate early [S1][S6]. Mission assurance: prioritize hunting for email-protocol C2 egress and macro and Excel execution on mission systems. Identify contractor and IT service accounts with privileged access as supply-chain risk [S1][S4][S8][S9]. Coordination: share persona and fake-job-site indicators with force protection and OPSEC offices for awareness training on long-duration social engineering [S3][S5][S6].

identification.summary: Iran-based cyber-espionage cluster that Microsoft tracked as DEV-0228 and now calls Cuboid Sandstorm [S1][S2]. In July 2021 it compromised a single Israel-based IT company that provides business management software. It then used that company's credentials and access to reach downstream customers in Israel's defense, energy and legal sectors [S1][S3]. Microsoft says the group compromised at least a dozen other organizations and assesses that at least four were reached with the stolen IT-provider access [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: July 2021 (credential dumping at the Israeli IT provider in early July 2021) [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Cuboid Sandstorm (formerly DEV-0228) [S2]. When Microsoft published its 2021 report, a DEV designation marked a cluster whose origin or identity was not yet established with high confidence [S1]. Microsoft's mapping also lists IMPERIAL KITTEN (CrowdStrike) for Cuboid Sandstorm, but the same file lists IMPERIAL KITTEN under Crimson Sandstorm and Smoke Sandstorm as well, so that alias is a many-to-one overlap rather than an equivalence [S2]. Cybereason's MalKamak / ShellClient reporting has tooling similarities but is a separate vendor cluster (see gaps) [S4][S8]. No MITRE ATT&CK group ID is recorded.

attribution.sponsor: Iran. Microsoft assesses the cluster as based in Iran and treats the activity as part of a broader Iranian espionage effort against organizations of interest to the Iranian regime [S1]. No specific Iranian organization is named for Cuboid Sandstorm in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft (MSTIC) assessment: based in Iran [S1]. In 2021 the DEV label meant Microsoft had not yet reached high confidence on origin or identity. No government attribution was found for this cluster. Microsoft maps the CrowdStrike name IMPERIAL KITTEN to three Sandstorm actors [S2], so CrowdStrike assessments of that cluster should not be applied to Cuboid Sandstorm specifically.
attribution.basis: Microsoft incident telemetry, nation-state notifications and tool hashes [S1]; Microsoft naming mapping [S2].

actors.objectives: Espionage against Israeli organizations of interest to the Iranian regime, achieved by compromising a trusted IT service provider and pivoting to its customers [S1]. Microsoft frames the wider 2021 Iranian IT-sector targeting as an effort to gain indirect access to IT providers' clients and subsidiaries [S1].

sectors: IT services / business management software providers [S1]
targeting.notes: All victims named for DEV-0228 are in Israel [S1]. Microsoft's report also covers wider Iranian activity against IT companies in India and the UAE, and covers DEV-0056 in Bahrain. Those findings belong to the broader Iranian set or to DEV-0056 (now Smoke Sandstorm), not to Cuboid Sandstorm specifically [S1].

capabilities.summary: Microsoft describes a supply-chain style pivot. The group dumped credentials on the IT provider's on-premises network, then reused the provider's accounts to reach customers. It used PAExec for remote execution against a law firm, and an email account the IT provider had in a defense company's Office 365 tenant [S1]. Its custom .NET remote access trojan used Dropbox for command and control and was disguised as RuntimeBroker.exe or svchost.exe. Microsoft Defender detects it as Backdoor:MSIL/ShellClient.A [S1]. After gaining persistence, the operators dumped LSASS memory. They staged lsa.exe, PAExec (pa.exe), ProcDump (pc.exe) and Rar.exe in C:\Windows\TAPI. Mimikatz-related detections were also reported [S1]. Microsoft did not publish C2 IP addresses or domains [S1].

campaigns.name: Israeli IT provider compromise
campaigns.summary: DEV-0228 compromised an Israel-based business-management software provider and dumped credentials from its on-premises network in early July 2021.

campaigns.name: Downstream customer intrusions
campaigns.summary: Using the provider's access, the group compromised at least a dozen other organizations. These included an Israeli law firm in August, reached via PAExec, and an Israeli defense company reached through the provider's Office 365 account. Defense, energy and legal sectors were affected.

campaigns.name: Microsoft public disclosure
campaigns.summary: Microsoft published DEV-0228 activity, tool hashes, Defender detections and hunting queries as part of its report on rising Iranian targeting of the IT sector.

diamond.adversary: An Iran-based espionage cluster (Microsoft assessment). No named organization or individuals are given [S1].
diamond.capability: Credential dumping (LSASS, ProcDump, a custom lsa.exe); PAExec lateral movement; a custom .NET RAT detected as ShellClient that uses Dropbox C2; RAR staging [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: The Dropbox cloud service used as C2; reused IT-provider accounts and an Office 365 tenant account as access paths. No dedicated C2 domains or IPs were published [S1].
diamond.victim: An Israeli business-management software/IT provider and its downstream customers in Israeli defense, energy and legal sectors [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Iranian regime intelligence interest in Israeli defense, energy and legal organizations, pursued through trusted third parties [S1].
diamond.technology: Trusted IT-provider relationships: shared credentials, provider-managed accounts, and provider accounts inside customer Office 365 tenants. Also abuse of legitimate cloud storage for C2 [S1].

gaps: Alias ambiguity: Microsoft's mapping lists IMPERIAL KITTEN under Cuboid, Crimson and Smoke Sandstorm, so CrowdStrike's IMPERIAL KITTEN reporting cannot be assigned to Cuboid Sandstorm from the sources gathered [S2].

Possible overlap with Cybereason's MalKamak (Operation GhostShell). Cybereason's ShellClient RAT also used Dropbox C2 and ran as svchost.exe with the internal name RuntimeBroker.exe. It was first found in a July 2021 incident, and reporting also mentions an lsa.exe credential dumper. Microsoft's DEV-0228 detection is named ShellClient. However, no source gathered explicitly equates DEV-0228/Cuboid Sandstorm with MalKamak. MalKamak victims were aerospace and telecom firms, mainly in the Middle East with others in the US, Russia and Europe [S1][S4][S8].
No public Cuboid Sandstorm activity after the November 2021 disclosure was found. Current operational status is unknown.
The sponsoring Iranian organization (MOIS, IRGC or a contractor) is not stated by Microsoft.
The identities of the Israeli IT provider and the downstream victims are not public.

Could not open Microsoft Learn's threat actor naming page, the Cybereason primary report, Malpedia or ETDA cards (fetch blocked or DNS failure); relied on the Microsoft blog, the Microsoft GitHub mapping and press coverage.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain includes IT and managed-service providers with standing credentials or tenant accounts in defense and energy customers [S1]. STEP 2 (effects): Trusted-provider access can bypass perimeter controls on the end target. Abuse of Dropbox C2 blends with sanctioned cloud traffic [S1]. STEP 3 (threat model): Compromise a provider, dump credentials (LSASS/ProcDump), reuse provider accounts, move laterally with PAExec, plant a Dropbox-C2 RAT disguised as svchost.exe or RuntimeBroker.exe, and stage data with RAR [S1]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is espionage against Israeli or partner defense and energy organizations through a shared IT vendor. MDCOA is the same pivot technique applied to a vendor that supports US or coalition defense contractors, giving broad covert access across multiple customers. Candidate indicators: files created in C:\Windows\TAPI; PAExec execution; Defender detections Backdoor:MSIL/ShellClient.A or Mimikatz; LSASS access by unusual processes; svchost.exe or RuntimeBroker.exe running from non-standard paths and calling Dropbox APIs; provider-provisioned O365 accounts logging in from anonymizing services [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Track third-party and MSP accounts that hold access into DoD-adjacent and DIB tenants. Cuboid Sandstorm's documented path ran through a provider's O365 account in a defense company [S1]. (2) Authorities: Defending contractor and provider networks generally falls to the owners plus DC3 and DIB coordination rather than DoD cyber forces directly. Pre-coordinate information sharing. (3) Mission assurance: Enforce MFA and conditional access on vendor accounts, block ActiveSync bypass, and enable the ASR rule against LSASS credential theft, following Microsoft's mitigations [S1]. (4) Coordination: Share IOCs with coalition partners, especially Israel. Alias overlap (IMPERIAL KITTEN mapped to three Microsoft actors) means cross-vendor reporting must be deconflicted before it drives attribution-based decisions [S2].

STEP 1: Government, defense-industrial, logistics and manufacturing networks in Russia, Ukraine and Central Asia are the observed terrain [S2][S3]. STEP 2: The actor operates against a nominal partner state, showing PRC collection is not limited to adversaries [S2]. STEP 3: Tradecraft is not documented in the sources; templating is not possible. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against regional government, military and logistics targets [S2]. MDCOA (speculative) is extension of the same access to logistics and manufacturing networks supporting regional military supply chains. Candidate indicators: the IP addresses in TAG's March 2022 post [S1] (not retrieved here).
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor reporting on PRC activity in Eurasia as indicator of PRC regional collection priorities. (2) Authorities and mission assurance: no US-targeted activity is evidenced in the sources, so treat as a regional intelligence-gap item rather than a defended-network threat. identification.summary: Curly COMrades is a cluster Bitdefender first described in August 2025 as a previously unknown, Russia-aligned espionage group targeting Georgia and Moldova [S1][S3]. Bitdefender says the name comes from heavy use of the curl utility for command and control and data transfer and from hijacking of COM objects [S3]. A November 2025 Bitdefender report described the group hiding malware in a Hyper-V virtual machine on Windows hosts [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Bitdefender has tracked the activity since mid-2024; the earliest confirmed MucorAgent use is November 2023 [S3]. Reporting on the Hyper-V activity describes the cluster as active since late 2023 [S5].
identification.notes: Name is Bitdefender's. No Microsoft name or MITRE group ID is established in the sources gathered. Amazon reports infrastructure overlap with APT44/Sandworm-linked activity but frames the clusters as possibly complementary, not identical [S7][S8]. One aggregator lists Curly COMrades as an alias of APT44; that conflicts with Amazon's framing and was not adopted.

attribution.sponsor: Bitdefender describes the group as Russia-aligned, operating in support of Russian interests [S1][S3]. Amazon assesses that the broader activity it tracked is associated with Russia's GRU and says Curly COMrades infrastructure overlaps with it [S7][S8]. No government has attributed Curly COMrades by name in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Bitdefender stresses there are no strong overlaps with known Russian APT groups [S3]. Security Affairs labels the Russia link as alleged [S5]. Amazon states high confidence for GRU association of its own activity cluster (via Sandworm/APT44 infrastructure overlap), and hedges that the two clusters may be complementary operations within a broader GRU campaign [S7][S8]. That is Amazon's assessment and is not a confirmed merger of clusters.
attribution.basis: Bitdefender technical analysis and victimology (Georgia, Moldova) [S1][S3]; Amazon infrastructure overlap, including IP 91.99.25[.]54 per secondary coverage [S7][S8].

actors.objectives: Bitdefender states the group's main aim is persistent access to networks and stolen credentials, in support of Russian interests [S1][S3].

targeting.notes: Bitdefender observed focused attacks against judicial and government bodies in Georgia and an energy distribution company in Moldova [S1][S3]. Victims in the Hyper-V report were not named; Georgia's CERT-GE assisted the investigation [S2]. Amazon's wider cluster targeted energy, telecom and technology providers [S7]; that is a separate cluster and is not merged here.

capabilities.summary: Bitdefender reports repeated attempts to extract the NTDS database from domain controllers and to dump LSASS memory, with Mimikatz and DCSync cited in coverage [S1][S3]. Proxy and tunnel tools (Resocks, SSH, Stunnel) provide multiple entry points, and remote commands were often run with Atexec [S1][S3]. MucorAgent is a custom three-stage .NET backdoor that runs AES-encrypted PowerShell, bypasses AMSI, and persists by hijacking CLSIDs tied to the NGEN component via an apparently inactive scheduled task [S3]. The initial access vector was not determined [S3]. In the later campaign the group enabled Hyper-V on selected Windows 10 hosts to run a minimal Alpine Linux VM (about 120MB disk, 256MB memory) named to resemble WSL, hosting CurlyShell (libcurl reverse shell) and CurlCat (reverse proxy tunneling SSH as HTTP), which let activity largely evade host-based EDR [S2][S5]. Attackers used a compromised website as a proxy for their real infrastructure [S5].

campaigns.name: Amazon reports infrastructure overlap
campaigns.summary: Amazon Threat Intelligence reports a GRU-associated campaign against energy and other sectors and notes infrastructure overlap with Curly COMrades, possibly complementary operations.

diamond.adversary: Russia-aligned cluster per Bitdefender; possible complementary relationship with a GRU-associated cluster per Amazon [S3][S7].
diamond.capability: MucorAgent, CurlyShell, CurlCat, Resocks/SSH/Stunnel tunnels, Atexec, NTDS and LSASS credential theft, NGEN COM hijacking, Hyper-V VM abuse [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: A compromised website used as proxy for actor infrastructure; curl-based C2; IP 91.99.25[.]54 overlaps with Amazon's cluster [S5][S8].
diamond.victim: Georgian judicial and government bodies; Moldovan energy distribution company [S1][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Targets sit in countries facing major geopolitical shifts, consistent with collection supporting Russian interests per Bitdefender [S1].
diamond.technology: Windows domain controllers and Windows 10 hosts with Hyper-V available; EDR products that do not see inside guest VMs [S2].

gaps: Initial access vector is not determined in Bitdefender's August 2025 report [S3].
Relationship to Sandworm/APT44: Amazon suggests complementary operations; Bitdefender sees no strong overlap with known Russian groups. Unresolved [S3][S7].
No Microsoft actor name, MITRE group ID, or government attribution found.
Victims of the November 2025 campaign are unnamed [S2].
No campaign activity after December 2025 found in searches.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is Windows domain controllers (NTDS), hosts that can enable Hyper-V, and government or energy networks in Georgia and Moldova; coalition partner networks in the region share this exposure [S1][S3]. STEP 2: Host-level virtualization hides implants from EDR, and the initial access vector is unknown, narrowing defender visibility [S2][S3]. STEP 3: Template is initial access (unknown), proxy/tunnel tools, credential theft from domain controllers, COM-hijack persistence, then a hidden VM with reverse shell and proxy [S1][S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued credential-focused espionage against regional government, judicial and energy targets. MDCOA is use of the same persistence on partner or US-supported energy and government networks, or coordinated use with GRU-associated access operations as Amazon speculates [S7]. Candidate indicators: Hyper-V role newly enabled on workstations, unexpected VMs named like WSL, NGEN-related CLSID changes and disabled-looking scheduled tasks, NTDS/LSASS access, outbound curl-style traffic to compromised sites [S2][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: add hypervisor and VM-inventory telemetry on Windows endpoints to hunt plans, since EDR may not see guest activity [S2]. (2) Authorities: partner-network hunting in Georgia or Moldova depends on host-nation consent; Bitdefender's work relied on CERT-GE cooperation [S2]. (3) Mission assurance: protect domain controller credentials for energy and government mission systems against NTDS/LSASS theft [S1]. (4) Coordination: attribution is contested between Bitdefender and Amazon, so share indicators with partners and vendors rather than waiting on naming [S3][S7].

provenance.importedSummary: Curly COMrades is a threat actor identified by Amazon Threat Intelligence and Bitdefender, believed to operate in support of Russian interests. They employ techniques such as Hyper-V abuse for EDR evasion and utilize proxy tools like Resocks, SSH, and Stunnel to gain access to internal networks. Their activities include repeated attempts to extract the NTDS database from domain controllers and establishing covert access through virtualization features on compromised Windows 10 machines.

identification.summary: CFR lists Cutting Kitten as an alias of Operation Cleaver, also known as Group 41, a suspected Iranian-sponsored group targeting governments and private-sector entities for espionage and sabotage; CFR says it is believed responsible for compromising US Navy computers on the Navy Marine Corps Intranet and energy and airline firms in several countries [S1]. Cylance's December 2014 report tracked the actor as Tarh Andishan and said it had compromised more than 50 victims since at least 2012 [S2][S3]. Dell SecureWorks' TG-2889 is reported to appear to be the same Iranian-sponsored activity Cylance documented as Operation Cleaver [S4].
identification.firstObserved: Cylance said victims had been targeted and compromised since at least 2012 [S3].
identification.notes: This record's imported text (DoS attacks on US banks in 2012-2013; three individuals indicted in 2016) describes a different CFR entry and does not match the cited coverage of the 2016-03-24 DOJ action, which reports seven defendants employed by ITSecTeam and Mersad Company [S6][S7]. The sources gathered do not state that the Cleaver/Tarh Andishan cluster and the ITSecTeam bank-DDoS defendants are the same organization. The ITsecTeam alias appears on this record from MISP/aggregator data only (not verified in a primary vendor source here). Do not merge facts across these clusters without primary documents.

attribution.sponsor: Suspected Iran. CFR names Iran as the suspected state sponsor of Operation Cleaver / Cutting Kitten [S1]. The 2016 DOJ indictment (as reported) states the ITSecTeam and Mersad Company employees had ties to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps [S6].
attribution.confidence: Contested. Cylance linked activity to Tarh Andishan, with some operations traced to IP blocks registered to that entity in Tehran, but reporting notes that strong connections to Iranian state backing were difficult to prove and a senior Iranian official dismissed the report [S3]. SecureWorks assessed with high confidence that the fake LinkedIn network was built for social engineering; its link of TG-2889 to Cleaver is stated as an apparent match [S4].
attribution.basis: Cylance technical reporting and IP registration [S2][S3]; SecureWorks CTU research on TG-2889 [S4]; CFR profile [S1]. DOJ attribution applies to the ITSecTeam/Mersad defendants, reported via press [S6][S7].

actors.objectives: Espionage and sabotage against governments and private-sector entities, per CFR [S1]. Cylance said the group exfiltrated extremely sensitive data from critical infrastructure companies but had no direct evidence of successful compromise of specific ICS/SCADA networks [S3].

sectors: Telecommunications, government and defense (LinkedIn social-engineering targets)
regions: Global; more than 50 victims, about 10 headquartered in the United States [S3]
Middle East (most real LinkedIn accounts in the TG-2889 network belonged to people in the Middle East) [S4]
targeting.notes: Cylance counted nine oil and gas firms among victims [S3].

capabilities.summary: Cylance reported initial access by SQL injection, spear phishing or watering-hole attacks, no zero-days observed, and a proprietary botnet called TinyZbot [S2][S3]. SecureWorks documented a network of at least 25 fake LinkedIn personas (17 of them supporter personas), used for social engineering [S4].

diamond.adversary: Suspected Iran-based operators; Cylance named Tarh Andishan [S1][S3].
diamond.capability: SQL injection, spear phishing, watering holes, TinyZbot botnet, fake social-media personas [S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: IP blocks registered to Tarh Andishan in Tehran for some operations [S3].
diamond.victim: Airlines, airports, oil and gas, manufacturers, government and universities worldwide [S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Suspected Iranian state espionage and sabotage interest [S1]; specifics beyond this are not established in gathered sources.
diamond.technology: Internet-facing web applications vulnerable to SQL injection, user trust in professional social networks and email [S3][S4].

gaps: Primary documents not opened: Cylance Operation Cleaver report (a FOIA-released copy exists, S8), SecureWorks original report, DOJ indictment text. WebFetch could not reach any host; findings rely on search-result summaries.
Unclear whether ITsecTeam (DOJ-charged bank-DDoS defendants) and Cleaver/Cutting Kitten are the same organization; imported record merges them.
Imported summary says three individuals were indicted; press reports say seven.

Claimed evolution of the group into Charming Kitten / APT35 appears only in an aggregator and is unverified.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID or Microsoft name mapping confirmed for this record.
Full victim and country list and the complete malware inventory were not verified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing web applications, airline and airport networks, energy and oil and gas firms, and personnel on professional social networks are key terrain [S3][S4]. STEP 2: The actor used commodity initial access with no zero-days, so basic web hygiene shifts defender advantage [S3]. STEP 3: Template is SQL injection or spear phishing or watering hole, then botnet implant and data exfiltration, supported by social-engineering personas [S3][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against energy, aviation and defense-linked targets. MDCOA is movement from data theft toward disruption of critical infrastructure, which CFR's espionage-and-sabotage description allows but Cylance did not observe [S1][S3]. Candidate indicators: SQL injection against public web apps, unsolicited recruiter contacts from new LinkedIn profiles with mutual-endorsement networks, and anomalous outbound beaconing.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Iran-linked activity against DIB, energy and aviation partners, keeping separate the Cleaver and ITSecTeam DDoS clusters [S3][S6]. (2) Authorities: activity against non-DoD critical infrastructure routes through DHS/FBI and DC3 partnerships rather than DoD action. (3) Mission assurance: NMCI compromise reported by CFR suggests prioritizing web-facing application hardening and phishing awareness [S1]. (4) Coordination: share social-engineering persona indicators with security and counterintelligence personnel [S4].

identification.summary: Cyber Av3ngers (CyberAv3ngers) is an Iranian persona that CISA and partner agencies describe as IRGC-affiliated and that has claimed many attacks on critical infrastructure [S1]. It is best known for compromising internet-exposed Israeli-made Unitronics Vision Series PLCs in late 2023 [S1], for the IOCONTROL IoT/OT malware reported by Claroty Team82 in December 2024 [S3], and for a 2026 campaign against Rockwell Automation PLCs described in advisory AA26-097A [S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: Cyble reports that the group claims to be behind power outages in parts of Israel since 2020 (a claim, not verified) [S7]. Government-documented activity: Unitronics PLC compromises from about 22 November 2023 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name per coverage of AA26-097A: Storm-0784 (Microsoft's own page was not retrieved). Other names listed in that coverage: Shahid Kaveh Group, Hydro Kitten, UNC5691 [S5]. Treat vendor cluster names as the vendors' own tracking until mapped; do not merge vendor facts without the primary reports.

attribution.sponsor: Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Cyber-Electronic Command (IRGC-CEC). CISA, FBI, NSA, EPA and Israel's National Cyber Directorate called the actors IRGC-affiliated in AA23-335A [S1]. The 2026 advisory (AA26-097A) links the activity to the IRGC-CEC [S5].
attribution.confidence: Stated by government agencies in joint advisories [S1][S5]. Treasury sanctioned six IRGC-CEC officials on 2 February 2024 over IRGC-affiliated actors' Unitronics PLC intrusions; a State Department reward offer of up to $10 million explicitly named the CyberAv3ngers group [S4]. Claroty describes the group as believed to be part of the IRGC-CEC [S3].
attribution.basis: Joint government advisories [S1][S5]; US sanctions on IRGC-CEC officials and a later reward offer (per press coverage, not primary documents) [S4]; Claroty's attribution of the IOCONTROL sample source to the group [S3].

actors.objectives: Disruption and psychological/propaganda effect against Israel-linked and US critical infrastructure. In 2023 the actors said they chose Unitronics PLCs because of their Israeli manufacturer, and displayed anti-Israel messages on compromised HMIs [S2]. In 2026 reporting, operators tampered with PLC project files and manipulated HMI/SCADA displays, causing operational disruption and financial loss [S5][S6].

targeting.notes: 2023 Unitronics targeting spanned water/wastewater, energy, food and beverage, and healthcare [S1]; the Aliquippa, Pennsylvania water authority was among the victims [S2]. IOCONTROL affected Orpak and Gasboy fuel management systems in Israel and the US [S3]. The 2026 campaign hit Rockwell/Allen-Bradley devices across US government services, water and wastewater, and energy; victims were not named [S5][S6]. Some Israeli claims (for example power outages and water stations) were not independently confirmed [S7].

capabilities.summary: 2023: access to internet-exposed Unitronics PLCs/HMIs using default credentials, then defacement of HMI screens, in some cases rendering devices inoperable [S1][S2]. Dec 2024: IOCONTROL, a custom modular Linux-based IoT/OT malware reported to run on devices from multiple vendors (including Baicells, D-Link, Hikvision, Red Lion, Orpak, Phoenix Contact, Teltonika, Unitronics); it allows remote OS command execution and self-deletion, and the deployment method was not determined [S3]. 2026: direct connection to internet-exposed Rockwell PLCs using legitimate engineering software (Studio 5000 Logix Designer), Dropbear SSH for persistence, extraction, modification and redeployment of project files, and HMI/SCADA display manipulation, per advisory coverage [S5]. A secondary report states CVE-2021-22681 was used and sources disagree on its CVSS score [S6]. The July 2026 advisory update reportedly broadened vendor scope to include Schneider Electric and Siemens PLCs [S5]. Tradecraft is largely opportunistic use of exposed, weakly protected devices rather than demonstrated zero-days [S1][S6].

campaigns.name: Claimed attacks on Israeli power and water
campaigns.summary: Cyble reports the group claimed compromise of Israeli electricity and water infrastructure (including Nahariyya and Yavne electricity facilities and water stations) and published video evidence; Cyble found some screenshots did not support the claims, and independent confirmation was absent.

campaigns.name: Unitronics PLC compromises
campaigns.summary: From about 22 November 2023 the actors compromised internet-exposed, default-password Unitronics Vision Series PLCs in multiple sectors, including the Aliquippa, Pennsylvania water authority, and defaced HMIs.

campaigns.name: US sanctions on IRGC-CEC officials
campaigns.summary: Treasury sanctioned six IRGC-CEC officials on 2 February 2024 over Unitronics PLC intrusions; a related State Department reward offer of up to $10 million named the CyberAv3ngers group.

campaigns.name: IOCONTROL reported
campaigns.summary: Claroty Team82 published analysis of IOCONTROL extracted from a fuel management system allegedly compromised by the group; a wave hit several hundred Orpak and Gasboy systems in Israel and the US.

campaigns.name: Rockwell PLC campaign (AA26-097A)
campaigns.summary: Joint advisory of 7 April 2026 describes IRGC-CEC-aligned activity against Rockwell Automation PLCs across US government services, water and energy, with operational disruption; updated 22 July 2026 with wider vendor scope (Schneider Electric and Siemens) and new indicators.

diamond.adversary: IRGC-CEC-affiliated operators using the Cyber Av3ngers persona [S1][S5].
diamond.capability: Default-credential exploitation of exposed PLCs/HMIs, IOCONTROL, legitimate vendor engineering software, Dropbear SSH [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Per secondary reporting, leased VPS infrastructure and EtherNet/IP (port 44818) access to internet-exposed PLCs [S6]; IOCONTROL command-and-control details not captured here [S3].
diamond.victim: Water/wastewater, energy, fuel management, healthcare, food and beverage, and municipal operators in the US and Israel [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Anti-Israel messaging and targeting of Israeli-made equipment, with IRGC-CEC sponsorship per government advisories [S1][S2][S5].
diamond.technology: Internet-exposed OT devices with default or weak credentials and direct remote engineering access [S1][S5].

gaps: Primary documents (CISA AA23-335A, AA26-097A and its July 2026 update, MITRE G1027, Treasury and State releases, Microsoft and Dragos pages) could not be opened; this record relies on search-result summaries and secondary reporting [S1][S5].

Microsoft's Storm-0784 mapping and the Dragos (Bauxite) and Mandiant (UNC5691) cluster definitions were not verified from the vendors' own pages; one search summary attributed such mappings to a Tenable FAQ whose date was not captured.
Initial access method and deployment of IOCONTROL were not determined by Claroty [S3].
Credibility of many Israel-focused claims (power outages, water stations) is unconfirmed [S7].
2026 victim identities, exact CVE use (CVE-2021-22681 reported only by secondary sources) and the Siemens/Schneider scope are unverified [S6].
Exact date of the State Department reward announcement was not captured [S4].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-reachable PLCs, HMIs and fuel management systems at installations, utilities and supporting commercial infrastructure are key terrain [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 2: The environment favors the actor because exposed devices often retain default credentials and open engineering ports [S1][S6]. STEP 3: Template is scan and access exposed OT, use default credentials or legitimate engineering software, alter project files or HMI displays, and publicize the result [S1][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued opportunistic defacement and disruption of exposed US and Israeli water, energy and fuel systems, timed to regional events [S1][S5]. MDCOA is use of IOCONTROL-class malware or project-file manipulation for lasting physical disruption of supporting utilities [S3][S5]. Candidate indicators: PLC/HMI defacement, unexpected Studio 5000 or EtherNet/IP (44818) sessions from unfamiliar hosts, new Dropbear SSH services on OT devices, changed PLC project files [S5][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track CISA/FBI advisory updates and OT exposure of base and contractor utilities. (2) Authorities: remediation of non-DoD utilities lies with owners and civil agencies; coordinate through established channels rather than act directly [S5]. (3) Mission assurance: identify OT dependencies (water, power, fuel) of critical missions, remove PLCs from direct internet exposure, change default passwords and add access controls [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partner agencies and sector ISACs; separate persona claims from verified effects before reporting [S7].

provenance.importedSummary: Cyber Av3ngers is an Iranian IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command-affiliated threat actor that targets internet-exposed operational technology and industrial control systems. Public reporting documents disruptive targeting of Israeli-made Unitronics PLCs and HMIs, broader critical-infrastructure targeting, and use of the IOCONTROL malware against IoT and OT devices.

identification.summary: CyberBerkut (also written Cyber Berkut) is a pro-Russian hacktivist persona that emerged during the 2014 Russia-Ukraine conflict and is named after the Berkut riot-police unit associated with the Kyiv Maidan crackdown [S1]. Its public activity has been DDoS attacks, website disruption, and publication of stolen or altered data against Ukrainian, NATO and Western government and corporate targets [S1][S2][S4].
identification.firstObserved: March 2014 (DDoS claims against NATO sites) [S2].
identification.notes: Reporting uses the spelling Kiberberkut for the same persona [S1]. Vendor and press reporting treats it as a self-described independent group whose independence is disputed; see attribution and gaps [S5][S7].

attribution.sponsor: Not formally attributed in the sources gathered. Citizen Lab (2017) reported digital links between CyberBerkut and the APT28/Fancy Bear cluster, which is widely described as Russian military intelligence (GRU)-affiliated, but did not conclusively attribute the technical elements to a sponsor [S7].
attribution.confidence: Low to moderate and analytic, not governmental. Citizen Lab said many elements overlapped with activity publicly linked to Russia without conclusive sponsor attribution [S7]. Fortune reported that conclusively tying CyberBerkut to the Russian government is difficult [S5]. Ukraine's prime minister publicly blamed Russian secret services for the January 2015 German DDoS; this is a political statement, not a technical finding [S4].
attribution.basis: Citizen Lab found a shared URL-shortening (tiny.cc) account used in phishing against Bellingcat journalists and linked to both APT28 and CyberBerkut, and found stolen material from phishing victims published on the CyberBerkut site [S7]. ThreatConnect (2016) described CyberBerkut action against Bellingcat alongside a separate spear-phishing campaign it assessed as Fancy Bear activity [S5][S6].

actors.objectives: Disrupt and embarrass Ukrainian government institutions and Western governments and alliances perceived as supporting Kyiv, and shape political narratives through leaks and defacement. Examples are the group's call for Germany to stop financial and political support for Kyiv [S4], disruption of the May 2014 Ukrainian election [S3], and publication of stolen material to discredit targets [S7].

sectors: Journalists and investigative researchers (Bellingcat, David Satter)
Civil society (Open Society Foundations material appeared on CyberBerkut site)
regions: United States and international media (leak and phishing victims) [S7]
targeting.notes: Targets track Russian-aligned political themes. Victim selection for the 2016-2017 journalist and civil-society cases comes from Citizen Lab and ThreatConnect [S6][S7].

capabilities.summary: Publicly observed capabilities are DDoS against government and NATO websites [S2][S4]; data theft and public posting of customer records (PrivatBank, July 2014, including passport and account data) [S1]; intrusion into and defacement of election-reporting systems, with Ukrainian officials reporting that a CEC administrator-planted virus gave access [S3]; and publication of stolen, sometimes forged, documents as 'tainted leaks' following phishing [S7]. Technical sophistication cannot be assessed from the sources gathered; the more advanced malware and phishing seen in related cases is tied by analysts to APT28 rather than shown as CyberBerkut tooling [S3][S7].

campaigns.name: DDoS against NATO websites
campaigns.summary: CyberBerkut claimed DDoS attacks on NATO web servers, including the NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence site; a NATO spokeswoman said operational capabilities were not affected [S2].

campaigns.name: Ukrainian Central Election Commission intrusion
campaigns.summary: Ahead of the 25 May 2014 presidential vote, CEC systems were disrupted and a false image announcing a Right Sector leader as winner was posted; Ukrainian security service said an administrator-planted virus provided access. Outcome was unaffected because ballots are verified manually. Responsibility for the false graphic is not certain in all reporting [S3].

campaigns.name: PrivatBank customer data leak
campaigns.summary: On 4 July 2014 the group posted PrivatBank customer data (passport, account, phone details) and announced it on VKontakte; the bank's co-owner Igor Kolomoisky had become governor of Dnipropetrovsk region [S1].

campaigns.name: DDoS against German government websites
campaigns.summary: On 7 January 2015 sites of the Bundestag, the Chancellery and the Foreign Ministry were taken down; CyberBerkut claimed responsibility and urged Germany to stop supporting Kyiv. The claim could not be verified, and the German government did not name a perpetrator [S4].

campaigns.name: Bellingcat targeting reported by ThreatConnect
campaigns.summary: ThreatConnect described CyberBerkut activity against Bellingcat, including use of a compromised contributor account to post criticism, alongside a spear-phishing campaign it attributed to Fancy Bear [S5][S6].

campaigns.name: Tainted Leaks (Citizen Lab)
campaigns.summary: Citizen Lab traced phishing of journalist David Satter (October 2016) to stolen and altered documents published on the CyberBerkut site, and found a shared tiny.cc account linking the persona to APT28-related phishing. It did not conclusively attribute the technical elements to a sponsor [S7].

diamond.adversary: Self-described pro-Russian hacktivist persona; independence disputed, with analytic links to APT28 but no conclusive sponsor attribution [S5][S7].
diamond.capability: DDoS, data theft and leaks, defacement/election-site manipulation, publication of altered documents [S1][S2][S3][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: Public-facing CyberBerkut website and social media (VKontakte) used to announce and publish material [S1][S7]; shared URL-shortener account with APT28-linked phishing [S7]. Other infrastructure not established.
diamond.victim: Ukrainian government and election bodies, PrivatBank, NATO, German government, journalists and civil-society organizations [S1][S2][S3][S4][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Pro-Russian narrative operations during the Ukraine conflict, framed around opposition to the post-Maidan government and Western support for Kyiv [S1][S4].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing government and NATO web servers vulnerable to DDoS, election-results reporting systems, and personal email accounts susceptible to credential phishing [S2][S3][S7].

gaps: Primary documents not opened: ThreatConnect report, Citizen Lab Tainted Leaks report, WSJ reporting, NATO and Ukrainian security service statements. Findings rely on secondary coverage.

Several searches returned a claim that the Wall Street Journal and Citizen Lab linked CyberBerkut to APT28; the original WSJ text was not reviewed, so only the Citizen Lab finding via university coverage is used [S7].
No government attribution statement for CyberBerkut was found. A claim that the UK NCSC linked it to the GRU appeared in a Wikipedia mirror only and is unverified.
Membership, organizational structure, and tasking are unknown.
Activity after mid-2017 is not documented in the sources gathered; a 2017 report of CyberBerkut allegations about Hillary Clinton was seen only as a headline.
Attribution of the false election graphic in May 2014 to CyberBerkut specifically is uncertain in some reporting [S3].
MITRE ATT&CK group ID and Microsoft naming are not established for this persona; relationship to APT28 (Forest Blizzard) should not be treated as identity.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes public-facing government and alliance websites, election-results systems, and personal accounts of journalists and civil-society figures [S2][S3][S7]. STEP 2: The persona offers plausible deniability and narrative amplification, blending low-sophistication DDoS with leaks that may be altered [S7]. STEP 3: Pattern is political-event-timed disruption (elections, summits, aid decisions) followed by claimed responsibility online [S3][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is DDoS and defacement of allied government and alliance sites timed to Ukraine-related political events, with leak-and-claim messaging. MDCOA is a tainted leak of altered coalition or partner documents following phishing, used to undermine alliance cohesion. Candidate indicators: pre-event hacktivist claims on VKontakte or similar, volumetric traffic against allied sites, credential-phishing of staff using URL shorteners [S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: monitor claimed-responsibility posts around Ukraine-related events and election or summit calendars [S3][S4]. (2) Authorities: attribution of the persona is unsettled, so response options should be framed for the effects observed, not for a named state sponsor [S5][S7]. (3) Mission assurance: ensure public information sites and results-reporting have DDoS mitigation and manual or out-of-band verification paths, as manual vote verification limited impact in 2014 [S3]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with allied and host-nation CERTs and public affairs, since leaks may mix forged and genuine content and need rapid verification [S7].

actors.primaryName: Cyber fighters of Izz Ad-Din Al Qassam

identification.summary: Self-styled hacktivist persona (Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Cyber Fighters, QCF) that claimed Operation Ababil, a 2012-2013 campaign of distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks against US financial institutions, presenting it as protest against the film 'Innocence of Muslims' [S1][S4]. The group announced its plans on Pastebin on 18 September 2012 [S5].
identification.firstObserved: 2012-09-18 (Pastebin announcement) [S5]. The 2016 US indictment describes the related DDoS campaign as beginning in approximately December 2011 [S2].
identification.notes: Malpedia lists Fraternal Jackal as an alternate name and gives the aliases Qassam Cyber Fighters and QCF [S6]. Do not confuse with other Palestine-linked 'Jackal' clusters or with the Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Brigades (Hamas military wing); this record covers only the Operation Ababil persona. Dates of the campaign differ between reports (see gaps) [S2].

attribution.sponsor: Disputed. The US Justice Department 2016 indictment, as reported by Help Net Security, charged seven Iranians employed by ITSecTeam and Mersad Company, which it alleged were sponsored by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), for the DDoS campaign [S2]. The persona itself denied ties to the Iranian government [S1].
attribution.confidence: Attributed by whoever made the claim: unnamed US officials and Sen. Joe Lieberman suggested Iran and the Quds Force in 2012 [S1]; the DOJ (as reported) alleged IRGC sponsorship of the two firms in 2016 [S2]; Treasury (as reported) designated ITSec Team and Mersad-linked individuals in September 2017 [S3]. Some 2012 analysts questioned a single-actor or state explanation, and Prolexic argued multiple groups using varied tools were involved [S1]. This record does not itself assign confidence beyond those statements.
attribution.basis: Press coverage of the DOJ indictment [S2] and of Treasury OFAC designations [S3]; 2012 news reporting of US official statements and analyst dissent [S1]. The primary DOJ and Treasury documents were not opened.

actors.objectives: Publicly stated: force removal of the film 'Innocence of Muslims' from the internet, with attacks suspended when a copy was removed from YouTube and threatened to continue until the film was gone [S1][S4]. Alleged underlying objective, per the indictment as reported: disruption of US financial-sector websites by IRGC-sponsored firms [S2].

sectors: Dam control systems (separate charge against one defendant, not attributed to the persona)
targeting.notes: Named victims included Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank, PNC, Citibank, Regions Financial, SunTrust and BB&T [S1][S4]. The indictment as reported cites 46 companies, primarily financial, and hundreds of thousands of customers cut off from online access; no customer account data was stolen [S2]. Treasury, as reported, said ITSec Team attacked at least nine large US financial institutions including stock exchanges between December 2011 and December 2012 [S3].

capabilities.summary: Volumetric DDoS, reported as up to 100 Gbps in 2012 and up to 140 Gbps per the indictment as reported [S1][S2]. Prolexic and Arbor Networks tied the attacks to the PHP-based 'itsoknoproblembro' (Brobot) toolkit and also to KamiKaze and AMOS botnets; the toolkit was publicly available before the campaign [S1]. One defendant allegedly helped build the botnet and another obtained and managed servers used to coordinate the attacks [S2][S3]. Some analysts (for example Akamai's Michael Smith) judged the scale inconsistent with ordinary hacktivists [S1].

campaigns.name: Alleged start of DDoS campaign (per indictment)
campaigns.summary: The 2016 indictment, as reported, describes the DDoS campaign against US financial targets as beginning around December 2011, with sporadic attacks into September 2012 and near-weekly attacks through May 2013.

campaigns.name: Operation Ababil announced
campaigns.summary: The persona announced Operation Ababil on Pastebin as protest against the film 'Innocence of Muslims'.

campaigns.name: Resumption of attacks after pause
campaigns.summary: After a pause of roughly three months in the main wave per the cited report, the persona resumed attacks around 11 December 2012; officials publicly suggested Iranian involvement and the group denied it.

campaigns.name: Phase 4 announcement
campaigns.summary: On 23 July 2013 the persona announced a new phase described as different from earlier ones, again naming major US banks and demanding removal of the film.

campaigns.name: DOJ indictment of seven Iranians
campaigns.summary: DOJ unsealed charges against seven Iranians employed by ITSecTeam and Mersad, alleged IRGC-sponsored firms, for DDoS attacks on 46 companies; one defendant also charged over the Bowman Dam SCADA intrusion.

campaigns.name: Treasury designations
campaigns.summary: OFAC designated ITSec Team and associated individuals, and Mersad-linked individuals, in connection with the DDoS attacks, as reported.

diamond.adversary: Hacktivist persona 'Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Cyber Fighters'; alleged operators are seven Iranian employees of ITSecTeam and Mersad, said by the DOJ (as reported) to be IRGC-sponsored [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Volumetric DDoS using the itsoknoproblembro/Brobot toolkit and other botnets, in phased weekly waves [S1][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Servers obtained and managed to coordinate the attacks and a botnet, per the indictment as reported; Pastebin used to announce phases and targets [S2][S3][S5].
diamond.victim: Major US banks and stock exchanges; websites knocked offline though no customer data was stolen [S2][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Public framing as religious protest against 'Innocence of Muslims'; alleged state sponsorship by the IRGC per US charges [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing bank web services dependent on upstream DDoS mitigation capacity [S1][S2].

gaps: Primary DOJ indictment and Treasury OFAC press release were not opened; they are known here only through press coverage [S2][S3].
Whether the persona was a front for the indicted firms, a separate hacktivist group, or a mix is unresolved; 2012 analysts disagreed [S1].
Reports disagree on the campaign timeline (December 2011 vs December 2012 start); not reconciled here [S2].
Fraternal Jackal alias is taken from an aggregator (Malpedia); no vendor primary report was found, and its basis is unverified [S6].
No post-2017 activity by the persona was found in these searches.
Several useful sources (Recorded Future, CFR, Brookings, Dark Reading) could not be fetched or dated and are not cited.
The existing Dancho Danchev blog and Pastebin leads in the record were not opened.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Public-facing web portals and the DDoS-mitigation providers that front them are key terrain; the campaign targeted customer-facing bank sites rather than internal data [S2]. STEP 2: Adversary used announced, scheduled weekly waves, and peak volume of 100-140 Gbps exceeded typical single-hacktivist capacity [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Template is a Pastebin announcement of targets and dates, then botnet-driven volumetric DDoS in phases [S4][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is a recurring, grievance-triggered DDoS wave on financial-sector sites under a hacktivist persona. MDCOA is the same persona structure used as deniable cover for state-directed disruption timed to a crisis, which the indictment's IRGC sponsorship allegation makes plausible [S2]. Candidate indicators: public posts naming targets and dates, a new persona claiming a grievance, and sudden multi-gigabit floods against financial sites.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: monitor public paste and social channels for announced target lists and dates, since this campaign pre-announced waves [S4][S5]. (2) Authorities: attribution shifted from persona to state-sponsored firms over four years, so response authorities should not wait on attribution [S1][S2]. (3) Mission assurance: ensure upstream DDoS scrubbing capacity for mission-critical public-facing services exceeds the 100-140 Gbps seen here [S1][S2]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with commercial mitigation providers and financial-sector partners, who held most of the visibility [S1].

identification.summary: Cyber Islamic Resistance (CIR) is a Telegram-based hacktivist persona described by Malpedia as ideologically aligned with Iran, engaged in website defacement, DDoS and data exfiltration claims against Israeli and Western entities, and as having claimed access to industrial control systems [S2]. Vendors describe it as an umbrella identity for smaller hacktivist groups that share resources and synchronize campaigns [S7], and CSIS argues more generally that Iran's hacktivist personas can mask state-coordinated activity [S3]. Reporting concentrates on the February-March 2026 Iran-Israel-US conflict [S4][S5][S8].
identification.notes: No source gathered gives a founding date; all retrieved reporting is from 2026. Name overlaps: Recorded Future's 2013 'Islamic Cyber Resistance' reporting concerns a different, earlier period and is not used as evidence here. A search summary also used 'Islamic Cyber Resistance' for the 313 Team; do not merge the two without primary evidence. Cyber Jihad Movement (al-Qaeda-affiliated) is a separate actor [S5].

attribution.confidence: No government attribution located. CSIS argues generally that Iranian hacktivist personas can front state operations and that hacktivist TTPs increasingly resemble state APTs [S3]; the search summary seen did not confirm that CSIS names CIR specifically. This is an analyst assessment, not an official finding.
attribution.basis: Self-presentation as Iran-aligned [S2]; analyst assessments of coordination [S3][S7][S10]. A joint claim signed by CIR, 313 Team, FAD Team, Cyber Fatteh Team and others was reported in March 2026 [S9]. No technical forensics tying CIR to IRGC or MOIS were found.

actors.objectives: Disruption, psychological and reputational impact against Israeli and Western targets, framed as retaliation and 'mobilization' during the 2026 conflict [S2][S8]. Rapid7 treats such visible activity as possible signaling, pressure and preparatory shaping rather than isolated nuisance [S1].

sectors: Israeli defense industry (Rafael air-defense and drone-detection claims) [S6]
Civil alerting (Home Front Command app claim) [S8]
regions: Gulf states, including a Qatari company website in a joint claim [S4][S9]
targeting.notes: Target lists come from the group's own claims relayed by trackers and press; most are unverified [S2][S4][S6].

capabilities.summary: Primary activity is DDoS, defacement, claimed intrusion and information operations [S2][S4]. Rapid7 characterizes the wider Iran-linked ecosystem as relying on established techniques (phishing, credential access, DDoS, edge-device compromise) rather than novel exploits [S1]. CIR reportedly participated in an Electronic Operations Room, a Telegram coordination hub set up 2026-02-28 that coordinated more than 50 hacktivist cells [S4]. OT/ICS access claims (PLC controllers, energy dashboards, 2026-03-02) were treated as unverified by analysts [S4].

campaigns.name: Electronic Operations Room formation
campaigns.summary: Cyble reports a Telegram umbrella coordinating more than 50 hacktivist cells was established as US and Israeli strikes began; CIR is reported as part of it.

campaigns.name: Claimed attacks on Rafael systems and ICS/OT access
campaigns.summary: Euronews reports a group it calls the 'Islamic Cyber Resistance Axis' (reported here as CIR) claimed attacks on Israeli defense firm Rafael's air defense systems and the VigilAir drone-detection service; Cyble reports claims of access to PLC controllers and energy dashboards, treated as unverified.

campaigns.name: Home Front Command app 'general mobilization' claim
campaigns.summary: FalconFeeds reports the CIR Telegram channel announced a 'general mobilization' and cited reports of a malfunction in Israel's Home Front Command alert app; link between the malfunction and CIR is unverified.

campaigns.name: Joint claim against Qatari company website
campaigns.summary: A claim signed by CIR, 313 Team, FAD Team, Cyber Fatteh Team and others was reported; one Kurdish member later withdrew from the coalition.

campaigns.name: Claimed breach of Israeli cybersecurity firm
campaigns.summary: CIR is reported to have published batches of allegedly exfiltrated files and database exports; claim unverified.

diamond.adversary: Self-described Iran-aligned hacktivist persona; sponsor unproven, with analyst assessments of coordination [S2][S3].
diamond.capability: DDoS with downtime proofs, defacement, claimed data theft, claimed ICS/OT access, information operations [S2][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Telegram channels and coalition hubs (Electronic Operations Room) for command, claims and propaganda [S4][S8]; DDoS-for-hire style tooling reported but not verified.
diamond.victim: Israeli security firms, defense industry, academia and civil alerting; Gulf government and commercial sites [S2][S4][S6][S9].
diamond.socioPolitical: Wartime retaliation narrative during the 2026 Iran-Israel-US conflict; coalition messaging amplifies psychological effect [S1][S8].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing web services, exposed OT/ICS and mobile alerting apps are the claimed exposure points [S4][S8].

gaps: No WebFetch access was available (host resolution failed), so all sources were read through search-result summaries only; Rapid7, SOCRadar, Malpedia, CSIS, Outpost24, Sophos and FalconFeeds pages were not opened in full.
No founding date, leadership, or state sponsor is established; the IRGC/MOIS link is analyst inference for the ecosystem, not for CIR specifically [S3].
ICS/OT, breach and Home Front Command app claims are unverified self-claims; no victim confirmation or technical indicators found.
Boundaries with 313 Team, FAD Team, Cyber Fattah and the Electronic Operations Room are blurred; an 'Islamic Cyber Resistance' label is also used elsewhere.
Exact publication dates for the CSIS, LevelBlue and Outpost24 items were not seen.
Activity after the April 2026 provisional ceasefire is not documented in gathered sources [S4].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes internet-facing web portals, civil alerting apps and exposed OT/ICS devices in Israel and the Gulf, plus the Telegram channels used for coordination [S4][S8]. STEP 2: The actor operates as a loose coalition persona whose claims outrun verified effect; its signal is mostly psychological [S1][S7]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is DDoS and defacement with downtime proof, breach-claim leaks, and OT access claims posted on Telegram [S2][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-impact DDoS, defacement and exaggerated claims timed to kinetic events. MDCOA is that a real state-directed access to OT is fronted by the persona, as CSIS notes for other Iranian personas [S3]. Candidate indicators: Telegram mobilization posts, coalition-signed joint claims, check-host downtime proofs, and spikes in DDoS against Gulf government sites [S4][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: monitor Telegram claims but triage them as unverified until victims or telemetry confirm [S4]. (2) Authorities: persona activity may be state-directed, so coordinate with intelligence and law enforcement partners before response decisions [S3]. (3) Mission assurance: verify exposure of internet-facing OT and web services at supported installations and partner nations, and plan DDoS mitigation [S4]. (4) Coordination: share claims with regional partners and the information-operations community to counter inflated narratives [S8].

provenance.importedSummary: Cyber Islamic Resistance is a hacktivist collective ideologically aligned with Iran, engaging in operations such as website defacements, DDoS attacks, and data exfiltration targeting Israeli and Western entities. They have claimed breaches of Israeli cybersecurity firms and academic platforms, framing their actions as part of a broader narrative of retaliation. The group has also targeted critical infrastructure, asserting access to industrial control systems and operational technology environments. Their activities are often presented as part of a coordinated cyber mobilization campaign, emphasizing psychological and reputational impacts.

identification.summary: Cyber Serp (CyberSerp) is a Telegram-based group that claimed responsibility for a March 2026 phishing campaign impersonating CERT-UA to deliver the Go-based AGEWHEEZE remote access trojan to Ukrainian recipients; CERT-UA tracks the activity as UAC-0255 under CERT-UA#21075 [S1][S2][S3][S4]. CERT-UA linked UAC-0255 to the CyberSerp Telegram channel, which publicly claimed the attack on 2026-03-28 [S1][S2]. The group presents itself as a Ukrainian collective, while a Russian-language comment was reportedly found in the fake site's HTML [S5].
identification.notes: Only one campaign is publicly documented in the sources reviewed [S1][S4]. Name variants: Cyber Serp, CyberSerp, UAC-0255 (CERT-UA identifier) [S1][S2]. No Microsoft name identified.

attribution.basis: CERT-UA tied UAC-0255 to the CyberSerp Telegram channel, and the fake domain's HTML contained a Russian-language comment naming CYBER SERP, per Bitdefender [S1][S4]. The group describes itself as Ukrainian, but the Russian-language comment is cited as the main reason to suspect otherwise [S5][S4]. No source reviewed states state sponsorship or a government attribution.

actors.objectives: Stated or implied objective is remote access to victim endpoints in Ukraine via the AGEWHEEZE RAT; the underlying motive (espionage, disruption, notoriety) is not established in the sources reviewed [S1][S3]. Public Telegram claim of the attack suggests a notoriety element [S2][S4].

targeting.notes: Targeted victims included Ukrainian government agencies, healthcare, financial and educational organizations [S3]. CERT-UA reported only a few infections, mainly personal devices of educational institution employees [S4][S2]. A claim of about 1 million recipients circulated via Telegram and one vendor blog; treat as unverified [S4][S6].

capabilities.summary: Delivery was by emails impersonating CERT-UA (e.g., from incidents@cert-ua.tech) sent 2026-03-26 and 2026-03-27, with a password-protected ZIP (CERT_UA_protection_tool.zip) hosted on Files.fm presented as security software [S4][S3]. The payload, AGEWHEEZE, is a Go RAT communicating over WebSockets (reported C2 at an OVH-hosted IP on port 8443 with a self-signed certificate) that supports command execution, file operations, clipboard monitoring, keyboard and mouse emulation, screenshots, and process/service management [S3][S4]. Persistence is via scheduled tasks (reported names SvcHelper and CoreService), registry Run keys, or Startup entries [S3][S4]. The lookalike site was likely AI-generated [S4].

campaigns.name: CERT-UA impersonation / AGEWHEEZE phishing (CERT-UA#21075)
campaigns.summary: Phishing emails impersonating CERT-UA were sent 2026-03-26 and 2026-03-27 delivering a password-protected ZIP with the AGEWHEEZE RAT [S4][S3]. The CyberSerp Telegram channel claimed the attack on 2026-03-28 [S2]. CERT-UA assessed few infections, mostly personal devices of education-sector staff [S4][S2].

diamond.adversary: Cyber Serp / UAC-0255, a Telegram-fronted group of unknown composition and location [S1][S5].
diamond.capability: Phishing with brand impersonation, Go-based AGEWHEEZE RAT with persistence mechanisms [S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Lookalike domain cert-ua.tech, Files.fm file hosting, OVH-hosted WebSocket C2 on port 8443, Telegram channel for claims [S3][S4][S2].
diamond.victim: Ukrainian public and private sector organizations; confirmed infections mainly education-sector personal devices [S3][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Activity occurs in the context of the Russia-Ukraine conflict and a trend of impersonating trusted Ukrainian entities (earlier UAC-0190, UAC-0252) [S2]; ideological alignment of the group is unconfirmed [S5].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints, email, and file-sharing services; Go malware over WebSockets [S3][S4].

gaps: Primary CERT-UA#21075 advisory could not be opened (fetch blocked); details rely on secondary coverage.
Group origin, membership, and any state link are unknown; self-described Ukrainian identity versus Russian-language artifact is unresolved.
Actual victim count and recipient volume unverified (1 million figure is unconfirmed).
Motive and prior or subsequent activity not found in sources reviewed.
Malpedia and MITRE entries not opened; no MITRE group ID known.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: the relevant environment is Ukrainian government, health, finance, and education email and endpoint space, where trusted-entity impersonation of CERT-UA erodes defender credibility [S3][S2]. Step 3: the actor shows low-to-moderate sophistication, with AI-assisted lure infrastructure and a commodity-style Go RAT [S4]. Step 4 MLCOA: further impersonation phishing with file-sharing-hosted archives against Ukrainian entities; MDCOA: broader volume campaigns or use of the access for follow-on operations (not evidenced). Candidate indicators: emails from lookalike cert-ua domains, Files.fm password-protected ZIPs, scheduled tasks SvcHelper/CoreService, outbound WebSocket to port 8443 on a self-signed host [S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track CERT-UA advisories and Telegram claims, treating actor claims of scale as unverified [S4]. Authorities: for non-Ukrainian partners, sharing and defensive actions fall under existing network defense authorities; no offensive implication drawn from sources. Mission assurance: verify the authenticity of any CERT or government security-tool email via out-of-band channels and block execution of password-protected archives. Coordination: relay IOCs to Ukrainian partners and CERT-UA via established channels [S2][S3].
