provenance.importedSummary: UAC-0255 is a threat actor that conducted a phishing campaign impersonating CERT-UA to distribute the AGEWHEEZE RAT, targeting organizations in Ukraine's public and private sectors. The campaign is part of a broader trend of using trusted identities to enhance victim engagement, as seen in previous activities like UAC-0190 and UAC-0252. CERT-UA identified UAC-0255 after discovering links to the CyberSerp Telegram channel, which claimed responsibility for the attack. The activity is documented under the identifier CERT-UA#21075, with detection rules available for cybersecurity analysts.

identification.summary: Cyber Toufan (also written Cyber Toufan Al-Aqsa) is a hacktivist-branded group that emerged in November 2023 and has primarily targeted Israeli organizations with hack-and-leak and destructive (wiping) operations [S1][S4]. Press reporting says it claimed more than 100 victims [S1][S4]. Check Point researchers, quoted in press, called it an Iranian threat actor, while the group presents itself as independent [S1][S4].
identification.firstObserved: 2023-11 (Dark Reading reports the Signature-IT hosting compromise on 16 November 2023) [S1][S4].
identification.notes: No Microsoft name is known to this research pass; none is asserted. Do not merge with Handala or CyberAv3ngers: Check Point is quoted as listing CyberAv3ngers and Cyber Toufan as separate Iran-affiliated groups [S1]. The source dates below are approximate (see gaps).

attribution.confidence: Disputed and unconfirmed. Check Point is quoted by Dark Reading as calling the group an Iranian threat actor [S1]. A threat-intelligence executive quoted by SAN said its patterns, timing and focus mirror Iranian state-aligned activity, while SAN notes the evidence does not conclusively establish state ties [S4]. Other firms were more hedged and the group has not stated its origin [S1][S3].
attribution.basis: Vendor and expert assessments of targeting, timing and operational patterns as quoted in press [S1][S4]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.

actors.objectives: Disruption, data exposure and psychological pressure against Israeli public and private organizations, aligned with the Gaza conflict; the group's 2025 defense-sector leaks were stated to follow Israeli actions in Gaza [S1][S4].

regions: International firms doing business in Israel [S1]
targeting.notes: In late 2025 the group leaked data attributed to defense contractor Maya Engineering and said it targeted 17 defense-linked companies [S4][S5]. These are largely the group's own claims and early reporting [S4].

capabilities.summary: The group compromised Signature-IT, an Israeli hosting company, on 16 November 2023, which gave access to dozens of Israeli companies and government bodies and to international firms doing business there [S1]. It wiped servers, leaked data on Telegram, and later ran follow-on email attacks against victims' employees and customers [S1][S4]. Kevin Beaumont called the group well organized and disruptive [S1]. The group claimed destruction of over 1,000 servers, which is unverified [S1]. In the Maya Engineering case it claimed 1.5 years of network access, enabling access to other contractors; this is a claim [S5]. No malware families or exploit details were found in the sources gathered.

campaigns.name: Signature-IT hosting compromise
campaigns.summary: Compromise of Israeli hosting firm Signature-IT gave access to dozens of Israeli companies and government organizations plus international firms. The group denied that all leaks stemmed from it, contrary to Check Point's view [S1].

campaigns.name: Mass hack-and-leak against Israeli organizations
campaigns.summary: More than 100 organizations were hit in about a month, with data leaks and wiping; victims included government bodies and technology vendors. Check Point noted leaks paused during a cease-fire [S1][S6].

campaigns.name: Follow-on email attacks
campaigns.summary: As leaks slowed the group sent follow-on emails to victims' employees and customers [S1].

campaigns.name: Maya Engineering defense-contractor leak
campaigns.summary: The group leaked CCTV footage and technical documents attributed to Maya Engineering, claiming 17 defense-linked targets and 1.5 years of access. Reported dates vary (late October 2025 per SOCRadar and BreachSense listings via search results); claims are unverified [S4][S5].

diamond.adversary: Hacktivist persona assessed by some vendors as Iran-linked; unconfirmed [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: Supply-chain compromise of a hosting provider, data exfiltration and leaking, destructive wiping, follow-on phishing emails [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Telegram channel used to publish leaks [S4]. Other infrastructure not found in sources.
diamond.victim: Israeli government, technology, retail, academic and defense organizations, and foreign firms using Israeli hosting [S1][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Gaza conflict and Israel-Iran tension; leaks timed to events and paused during a cease-fire [S1][S4].
diamond.technology: Reliance on a single hosting/MSP provider created a single point of compromise for many tenants [S1].

gaps: WebFetch could not reach any publisher host in this run, so all content comes from search-result summaries, not full articles; verify each source before use.
Publication dates for S1-S6 were not visible in results and are approximate, inferred from event timing; confirm them.
The Check Point primary report (listed in the existing record as research.checkpoint.com 2023 11th December threat intelligence report) and Kevin Beaumont's original post were not opened.
Initial access method, malware, wiper names and infrastructure are not stated in the sources gathered.
Iranian state sponsorship is not established; no government attribution was found.
Relationship to Handala and other Iran-aligned personas is not established.
Date of the Maya Engineering leak differs across listings (about 30-31 October 2025); the 2025 campaign and victim claims are unverified.
The SecurityWeek source was removed: its URL was not seen in verification searches; the named 2023 victim list and 'one-third unrecovered' detail were dropped.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Third-party hosting and managed IT providers serving Israeli and allied organizations are key cyber terrain; defense contractors are secondary terrain [S1][S5]. STEP 2: A single provider compromise exposed dozens of tenants, and wiping degraded recovery [S1]. STEP 3: Template: provider compromise, data theft, Telegram leak, wiping, then follow-on phishing [S1][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA: continued hack-and-leak and wiping against Israeli entities timed to conflict events. MDCOA: leaks of allied defense-contractor data or supply-chain compromise of a provider serving US or coalition partners. Candidate indicators: new Telegram leak posts naming defense firms, sudden mass wiping at tenants of one hosting provider, and employee-targeted phishing after a leak [S1][S4][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track hacktivist leak channels and third-party provider incidents affecting partner and DIB organizations [S1][S4]. (2) Authorities: attribution is unconfirmed, so avoid treating it as state action in planning documents [S4]. (3) Mission assurance: verify offline backups and provider-dependency mapping for contractors, since wiping left victims struggling to recover [S1]. (4) Coordination: share leaked-data exposure with affected contractors via DC3 and the DIB program, and with partner nation CERTs [S5].

provenance.importedSummary: Cyber Toufan is a threat actor group that has gained prominence for its cyberattacks targeting Israeli organizations. The group's tactics suggest potential nation-state backing, possibly from Iran. They have been involved in hack-and-leak operations, data breaches, and data destruction, impacting over 100 organizations. Cyber Toufan's activities align with geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and their attacks are characterized by a combination of technical breaches and psychological warfare.

identification.summary: DAGGER PANDA is CrowdStrike's name for the activity Kaspersky publicly reported as Icefog; RedFoxtrot and UAT-7290 are related by vendor overlap statements [S3][S4], but those mappings rest on third-party statements, not on CrowdStrike text I could open [S1][S5]. Kaspersky announced Icefog in September 2013 as a small group, active since 2011, focused on South Korea and Japan and on supply-chain attacks against defense contractors, shipbuilders, telecom and satellite operators and media companies [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Kaspersky: operation began in 2011 [S1]. Recorded Future dates RedFoxtrot activity to 2014 [S3]. Talos has tracked UAT-7290 since at least 2022 [S4].
identification.notes: Three vendor clusters are in play and must not be merged: Icefog (Kaspersky, 2013-2014) [S1][S2]; RedFoxtrot (Recorded Future, 2021), which Recorded Future says overlaps Temp.Trident and Nomad Panda [S3]; and UAT-7290 (Cisco Talos, 2026), which Talos says shares significant victimology, infrastructure and tooling overlap with Red Foxtrot [S4]. The Icefog-to-RedFoxtrot-to-UAT-7290 chain is therefore inferred through the encyclopedia's imported alias list and an aggregator page, not through a single primary document [S5]. Microsoft has no mapped name for this actor in this record.

attribution.sponsor: Recorded Future ties RedFoxtrot to PLA Unit 69010 in Urumqi, Xinjiang, assessed as likely a cover designator for a Technical Reconnaissance Bureau within the PLA Strategic Support Force Network Systems Department [S3]. No source I opened attributes Icefog itself to a state.
attribution.confidence: Recorded Future assessed with high confidence that RedFoxtrot is Chinese state-sponsored [S3]. Talos assessed with high confidence that UAT-7290 is China-nexus [S4]. Kaspersky described Icefog operators as likely based in China, South Korea and Japan and as a small mercenary-style team, an inference from behavior rather than confirmed tasking [S1][S2].
attribution.basis: Recorded Future: operator OPSEC lapse exposing the unit's headquarters address, plus procurement and court documents, and shared custom capabilities (as summarized in search results, not the full report) [S3]. Talos: victimology, infrastructure and tooling overlap with Red Foxtrot [S4]. Kaspersky: infrastructure IP lists [S1].

actors.objectives: Espionage. Kaspersky said Icefog operators quickly took the information they wanted and left [S1]. Recorded Future reports RedFoxtrot collection against aerospace and defense, government, telecommunications, mining and research organizations [S3]. Talos describes UAT-7290 as espionage-motivated and also an initial-access provider building relay infrastructure other China-nexus actors can reuse [S4].

regions: United States oil and gas companies (Javafog, Jan 2014) [S2]
Afghanistan, India, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan (RedFoxtrot) [S3]
South Asia and Southeastern Europe telecoms (UAT-7290) [S4]
targeting.notes: Targeting differs by vendor cluster: East Asia and supply chain in 2013 [S1], Central/South Asia in 2021 [S3], South Asian and European telecoms in 2026 [S4].

capabilities.summary: Icefog: spear-phishing with exploits for known vulnerabilities (CVE-2012-0158, CVE-2013-0422 per search coverage of the Kaspersky report), backdoors for Windows and Mac OS X, and the Java-based Javafog; Kaspersky counted more than 4,000 unique infected IPs, including a few dozen Windows and over 350 Mac OS X victims [S1][S2][S5]. RedFoxtrot: custom and publicly available malware [S3]. UAT-7290: exploitation of one-day vulnerabilities in public-facing edge devices, target-specific SSH brute-forcing, public PoC code, Linux implants RushDrop (ChronosRAT), DriveSwitch and SilentRaid (MystRodX), and Windows RedLeaves and ShadowPad [S4].

campaigns.name: Icefog operation begins
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky dates the operation to 2011, focused on South Korea and Japan and supply-chain targets [S1].

campaigns.name: Kaspersky discloses Icefog
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky publishes the Icefog report describing hit-and-run espionage with Windows and Mac OS X backdoors [S1].

campaigns.name: Javafog against US energy companies
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky reports a Java backdoor variant targeting at least three US oil and gas companies [S2].

campaigns.name: Recorded Future reports RedFoxtrot
campaigns.summary: Insikt Group links RedFoxtrot to PLA Unit 69010 and reports targeting across Central and South Asia since 2014 [S3].

campaigns.name: Talos reports UAT-7290
campaigns.summary: Talos describes edge-device exploitation against South Asian and Southeastern European telecoms and notes overlap with Red Foxtrot [S4].

diamond.adversary: Small China-linked operator group (Icefog) [S1]; RedFoxtrot linked by Recorded Future to PLA Unit 69010 [S3]; UAT-7290 assessed China-nexus by Talos [S4].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing, known-vulnerability exploits, cross-platform backdoors [S1][S5]; edge-device one-day exploitation and Linux implants in the 2026 cluster [S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Icefog C&C infrastructure with IP lists suggesting China, South Korea and Japan [S1]; UAT-7290 builds relay box infrastructure reusable by other actors [S4].
diamond.victim: East Asian defense, maritime, telecom and media firms [S1]; US oil and gas [S2]; Central and South Asian government, defense and telecom [S3]; South Asian and European telecoms [S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection supporting PRC defense and regional interests, with RedFoxtrot focus on bordering Asian countries per Recorded Future [S3].
diamond.technology: Windows, Mac OS X and Java hosts for Icefog [S1][S2]; internet-facing edge networking devices and Linux systems in telecom networks for UAT-7290 [S4].

gaps: Primary documents (Kaspersky Securelist reports, Talos UAT-7290 blog, Recorded Future RedFoxtrot report, CrowdStrike DAGGER PANDA profile) could not be fetched in this session; details rely on search-result summaries and the Kaspersky press release.
No CrowdStrike source mapping DAGGER PANDA to Icefog was opened; the mapping rests on the encyclopedia's imported MISP/Malpedia data.
The Icefog to RedFoxtrot to UAT-7290 lineage is inferred from vendor overlap statements; whether one organization operates all three is unconfirmed.
Icefog activity after 2014 and any direct state attribution of the original Icefog cluster are not established in sources gathered.
No Microsoft name or MITRE group ID is mapped.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Telecom networks, edge devices and defense-industrial supply chains in Asia are key terrain [S1][S4]. STEP 2: Operators exploit known vulnerabilities rather than zero-days, so patch latency is the adversary advantage [S1][S4]. STEP 3: Template is spear-phish or one-day edge exploit, then backdoor, targeted collection, rapid exit or relay-box use [S1][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection against regional telecom and defense targets. MDCOA is use of compromised telecom or edge infrastructure as relays for other China-nexus actors against allied networks [S4]. Candidate indicators: unpatched edge devices showing SSH brute-force, unexpected Linux implants on network appliances, and Mac OS X backdoors on staff of defense suppliers [S1][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track edge-device advisories and telecom-sector reporting for partner nations [S4]. (2) Authorities: partner and contractor networks sit outside DoDIN authorities; coordinate through DC3 and DIB cybersecurity channels. (3) Mission assurance: telecom and logistics suppliers in the Indo-Pacific are candidate dependencies to map [S1][S4]. (4) Coordination: because vendor names diverge, share indicators by technique and infrastructure rather than by group name.

provenance.importedSummary: Operate since at least 2011, from several locations in China, with members in Korea and Japan as well. Possibly linked to Onion Dog. identification.summary: Daggerfly is Symantec's name for a China-linked espionage group, also tracked as Evasive Panda and BRONZE HIGHLAND [S1][S5]. The group's signature tool is the modular MgBot framework, which Kaspersky says Evasive Panda has used for cyber espionage since at least 2012 [S9]. It has repeatedly delivered malware through hijacked or trojanized software updates, watering holes and supply-chain compromises [S3][S4][S7][S9]. Symantec judges the group 'capable of responding to exposure by quickly updating its toolset to continue its espionage activities with minimal disruption' [S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: Kaspersky: MgBot in use by Evasive Panda since at least 2012 [S9]. Malwarebytes linked 2020 activity to earlier attacks in 2014 and 2018 that used MgBot variants [S2].
identification.notes: Vendor names: Daggerfly (Symantec), Evasive Panda (ESET, Kaspersky; also listed for CrowdStrike in the imported record), BRONZE HIGHLAND (Secureworks), StormBamboo (Volexity) [S3][S4][S5][S8]. MITRE lists Evasive Panda and BRONZE HIGHLAND as associated groups under Daggerfly G1034 [S10]. A check of Microsoft's public naming-mapping file (2026-10-15) found no Microsoft name for this actor, so none is assigned here. Volexity's StormBamboo reporting is treated as an overlapping vendor cluster [S8].

attribution.sponsor: China-linked per vendor reporting; no government attribution found in the sources gathered [S1][S4][S5].
attribution.confidence: ESET attributed its 2023-2024 Tibetan watering-hole and supply-chain campaign to Evasive Panda with high confidence [S4]. Malwarebytes attributed its 2020 India and Hong Kong campaign to a Chinese APT group with moderate confidence [S2]. The imported Secureworks profile assesses with moderate confidence that BRONZE HIGHLAND operates on behalf of China. That assessment comes from the encyclopedia's existing record and was not re-verified here.
attribution.basis: Symantec links its 2023 Africa telecom campaign to Daggerfly partly through a renamed Rundll32.exe and the loader DLL pMsrvd.dll, both seen in a 2020 Evasive Panda campaign [S1]. Symantec tied the macOS backdoor Macma to Daggerfly through code overlaps with MgBot and a shared C2 server [S5][S6]. ESET linked IPs in its Tencent QQ campaign to the earlier LuoYu APT campaign [S3].

actors.objectives: Espionage, including what Symantec calls internal espionage. Its 2024 targets included a US NGO operating in China [S5][S6]. The group has watched the Tibetan diaspora and Buddhist community [S4] and pro-democracy-linked Hong Kong website visitors [S6]. It has also collected intelligence on regional governments and telecoms around China's periphery and in Africa [S1][S2].

sectors: International NGOs operating in mainland China [S3][S5]
Academic networks (Georgia Tech network named among ESET targets) [S4]
Users of Chinese consumer software (Tencent QQ, iQIYI, SohuVA) [S3][S9]
regions: Australia and United States (watering-hole target networks) [S4]
targeting.notes: Targeting combines regional government and telecom espionage with surveillance of groups the PRC treats as domestic security concerns: NGOs in China, Tibetans and Hong Kong activists [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5]. The DNS-poisoning delivery Kaspersky reported was selective and aimed at specific victims [S9].

capabilities.summary: MgBot is the core of the toolkit. It is a modular Windows framework with plugins for keylogging, file theft, credential theft and command execution. Symantec documented previously unseen MgBot plugins in 2023 [S1][S9]. The group runs a cross-platform arsenal. Symantec says MgBot, Macma and other Daggerfly tools share code from one library used to build Windows, macOS, Linux and Android threats. Symantec also reports evidence that the group can trojanize Android APKs, intercept SMS and DNS requests, and target Solaris [S5][S6][S7]. Nightdoor (also tracked as Suzafk/NetMM) is a newer Windows backdoor that uses the Google Drive API for C2 [S4][S6]. Delivery methods: spear-phishing with template-injection documents carrying Cobalt Strike and MgBot [S2]; trojanized software updates [S3][S9]; watering holes on compromised sites; and trojanized installers from a compromised Indian software vendor [S4]. Volexity reports DNS poisoning at a compromised ISP that redirected insecure HTTP update requests to MACMA and POCOSTICK (MgBot) payloads [S8]. Kaspersky reports DNS poisoning that served encrypted payload parts, a new loader, and hybrid encryption that makes implants unique per victim [S9]. After intrusion, the group has used BITSAdmin and PowerShell to fetch AnyDesk. It has run GetCredManCreds to dump Windows Credential Manager, created local accounts for persistence, and used a PlugX loader [S1]. It also exploited an Apache HTTP server vulnerability for initial access [S5][S6]. Malwarebytes reported Android apps that collect call logs, contacts and SMS and record audio and the screen [S2].

campaigns.name: India and Hong Kong spear-phishing (MgBot/Cobalt Strike)
campaigns.summary: Malwarebytes reported spear-phishing against Indian and Hong Kong government targets from 2 July 2020. Lures included a fake gov.in security check. Payloads were Cobalt Strike and MgBot, alongside malicious Android apps. Timing coincided with Hong Kong's new security law and India's app ban [S2].

campaigns.name: Tencent QQ malicious updates against an NGO in China
campaigns.summary: ESET found MgBot delivered through Tencent QQ automatic updates to individuals in Gansu, Guangdong and Jiangsu, mostly members of an international NGO. ESET could not decide between supply-chain compromise and adversary-in-the-middle; reported in April 2023 [S3].

campaigns.name: African telecom operator intrusion
campaigns.summary: Symantec tracked activity against an African telecom from November 2022 using new MgBot plugins, a PlugX loader, AnyDesk and GetCredManCreds; reported April 2023 [S1][S7].

campaigns.name: Fake-update / DNS-poisoning MgBot campaign
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky reported lures posing as updates for SohuVA, iQIYI Video, IObit Smart Defrag and Tencent QQ, delivered with DNS poisoning, against systems in Türkiye, China and India; reported December 2025 [S9].

campaigns.name: ISP DNS poisoning of software updates (StormBamboo)
campaigns.summary: Volexity traced infections back to DNS poisoning at a compromised ISP. Update traffic for several software vendors was redirected to install MACMA and POCOSTICK (MgBot); reported August 2024 [S8].

campaigns.name: Monlam festival watering hole and Tibetan software supply chain
campaigns.summary: ESET found the Kagyu International Monlam Trust website compromised for watering-hole attacks. The actor also trojanized Tibetan-language software from an Indian developer, delivering MgBot and Nightdoor to networks in India, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Australia and the US; reported March 2024 [S4].

campaigns.name: Major toolset update (Taiwan and US NGO in China)
campaigns.summary: Symantec reported a new MgBot-based malware family, a new Macma version and Nightdoor. They were used against Taiwanese organizations and a US NGO in China, with an Apache HTTP server exploit used for access [S5][S6].

diamond.adversary: China-linked espionage group named by several vendors (Daggerfly, Evasive Panda, BRONZE HIGHLAND, StormBamboo). It has been active since at least 2012 and changes its tools quickly after exposure [S5][S8][S9].
diamond.capability: MgBot modular framework, Nightdoor, Macma (macOS) and Android implants; PlugX and Cobalt Strike; trojanized installers and updates; DNS poisoning; credential theft with GetCredManCreds [S1][S2][S4][S5][S8][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised legitimate websites used as watering holes; a compromised software vendor's distribution site [S4]; DNS poisoning at a compromised ISP [S8]; Google Drive API C2 for Nightdoor [S6]; multiple redundant MgBot C2 servers [S9]; and C2 shared between MgBot and Macma [S6].
diamond.victim: Tibetan communities, NGOs in China, Hong Kong and Indian government targets, Taiwanese organizations, an African telecom, and users in Türkiye, China and India [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5][S9].
diamond.socioPolitical: Surveillance of groups Beijing treats as internal security concerns (Tibetans, Hong Kong pro-democracy circles, foreign NGOs in China), plus regional and strategic intelligence collection [S2][S3][S4][S5][S6].
diamond.technology: Exploits insecure HTTP update mechanisms that do not verify installer signatures [S8], trust in software vendors' update channels [S3][S4][S9], and internet-facing Apache servers [S5].

gaps: Primary vendor reports (Symantec 2023 and 2024, Kaspersky Securelist 2025, Volexity 2024) could not be fetched (DNS failure); details come from search-result summaries and secondary coverage.
Microsoft has no public name for this actor in its naming-mapping file as of 2026-10-15.
No US or allied government attribution or indictment specific to Daggerfly/Evasive Panda was found.

Cluster boundaries are not settled. Volexity's StormBamboo is equated with Evasive Panda in press coverage [S8]. ESET noted IP overlap with LuoYu [S3]. Third-party alias lists (TAG-112, Digging Taurus, Storm Cloud) were not confirmed by primary vendors and were excluded.

Whether Tencent QQ updates were compromised at the vendor or in transit (AiTM) remains unresolved [S3]. Kaspersky's DNS-poisoning findings and Volexity's ISP finding may describe the same mechanism, but this is unconfirmed [S8][S9].
The role of KsRemote (Android RAT, from the imported Secureworks summary) was not confirmed in the sources gathered.
Symantec's Solaris and Linux capability claims come from secondhand coverage, without analyzed samples in the sources seen [S7].
The imported Secureworks moderate-confidence assessment was not re-verified against a live Secureworks page.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Software update channels, upstream ISP DNS resolution, and websites trusted by target communities are key cyber terrain. Theater networks in the Indo-Pacific, India, Taiwan and Africa that rely on regional ISPs and consumer software count as relevant terrain [S4][S8][S9]. STEP 2 (effects): Any application that updates over unauthenticated HTTP can be turned into a delivery vector, and the group retools quickly after public exposure, so signature-based defenses lose value fast [S5][S8]. STEP 3 (threat model): Typical chain is a hijacked update, watering hole or spear-phish; then the MgBot or Nightdoor loader; then plugin-based keylogging, file and credential theft; with C2 over actor servers or the Google Drive API [S1][S2][S4][S6][S9]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued selective surveillance of NGOs, diaspora and activist communities and regional government and telecom networks using poisoned updates and watering holes [S1][S3][S4][S9]. MDCOA is ISP-level DNS poisoning that pushes malicious updates to Windows and macOS hosts of personnel or partners in the region during a Taiwan-related crisis [S5][S8]. Candidate indicators: update binaries fetched over HTTP whose hashes do not match the vendor's; DNS answers for update domains that point to unexpected IPs; renamed Rundll32.exe or a pMsrvd.dll loader; GetCredManCreds; unexpected AnyDesk installs via BITSAdmin/PowerShell; new local accounts; Google Drive API traffic from non-browser processes [S1][S6][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track software inventories with insecure update channels and DNS integrity alerts for forward-deployed and partner networks that rely on host-nation ISPs [S8]. (2) Authorities: the ISP and third-party software vendors sit outside DoD control, so remediation needs coordination with host-nation, vendor and interagency partners rather than unilateral action [S3][S8]. (3) Mission assurance: enforce signed-update verification and DNS over trusted resolvers for mission systems and mobile devices, given Macma and Android capabilities [S5][S6]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3, CISA and allied CERTs, especially those of Taiwan and India, and keep in mind that vendors track overlapping clusters (StormBamboo, Evasive Panda, Daggerfly) under different names [S4][S5][S8].

provenance.importedSummary: BRONZE HIGHLAND has been observed using spearphishing as an initial infection vector to deploy the MgBot remote access trojan against targets in Hong Kong. Third party reporting suggests the threat group also targets India, Malaysia and Taiwan and leverages Cobalt Strike and KsRemote Android Rat. CTU researchers assess with moderate confidence that BRONZE HIGHLAND operates on behalf of China and has a remit covering espionage against domestic human rights and pro-democracy advocates and nations neighbouring China

identification.summary: Dalbit (also reported as m00nlight) is a threat group named by AhnLab's ASEC after the Korean word for moonlight, because it moved to a hosting server under "*.m00nlight.top" as C2 and download server after some Korean company servers it had abused were blocked [S1][S2]. ASEC counted more than 50 confirmed attack attempts against Korean companies since 2022, most against small and mid-size firms and some against major companies [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: ASEC reports attacks since 2022; the report was published in February 2023 [S1][S3].
identification.notes: Name and cluster boundary are ASEC's (AhnLab). Dalbit has no Microsoft name or MITRE group ID in the encyclopedia record. The imported record text (poorly patched Windows servers, email servers, MS-SQL servers) comes from the MISP Galaxy entry citing ASEC reports; the cited ASEC report pages beyond the Feb 2023 report could not be opened, so MS-SQL and email-server claims are not independently verified here.

attribution.confidence: ASEC assessed the group as having at least a partial connection with China, based on tooling [S1][S2]. This is a vendor inference, not government attribution, and no state sponsor is identified in the sources gathered [S1].
attribution.basis: ASEC cited a proxy tool assumed to have been obtained from a Chinese-language community and a tool with Chinese documentation; the group relied on open-source tools and left little distinctive profiling data (no PDB information) [S1][S2].

actors.objectives: ASEC describes data theft (credentials and emails collected, with extortion implied) and, in some cases, drive encryption with BitLocker for impact; exact motivation is not established [S1][S2][S3].

targeting.notes: Most victims were small and mid-size companies, with some major companies; ASEC said about 30% of infected companies used a certain Korean groupware product, with no vulnerability in it confirmed [S1][S2]. The true victim count may be higher than the 50 identified [S1].

capabilities.summary: Initial access through web and SQL vulnerabilities (one example cited: WebLogic CVE-2017-10271), then webshells including Godzilla, ASPXSpy, AntSword and China Chopper [S1][S3]. Tools were downloaded with certutil and Bitsadmin, privilege escalation used Potato-family exploits, and FRP and LCX were used as proxy tools, including FRP registered in Task Scheduler for persistence [S1][S3]. Compromised victims were left as proxy and download servers to relay communications for later intrusions [S1][S2]. Evasion included VMProtect packing and log and firewall tampering, and BitLocker was used for encryption [S3]. The group relies largely on public and open-source tooling [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: Korean company intrusions begin
campaigns.summary: ASEC reports attack activity against Korean companies from 2022, with server infrastructure in abused Korean company hosts, later moved to a m00nlight.top domain after blocking.

campaigns.name: ASEC publication of Dalbit (m00nlight) campaign
campaigns.summary: ASEC publicly named the group and reported 50+ confirmed attacks on Korean companies using webshells, FRP/LCX proxies and, in some cases, BitLocker encryption.

diamond.adversary: Unattributed group with an assessed partial China connection by ASEC [S1].
diamond.capability: Public webshells (Godzilla, ASPXSpy, AntSword, China Chopper), FRP and LCX proxies, certutil/Bitsadmin download, Potato privilege escalation, BitLocker for impact [S1][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: m00nlight.top hosting for C2 and downloads; compromised Korean company servers reused as proxy and download nodes [S1][S2].
diamond.victim: Korean small, mid-size and some large companies, about 30% of them running a particular Korean groupware product [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing, poorly patched web, SQL and groupware servers on Windows [S1][S2].

gaps: The primary ASEC reports (asec.ahnlab.com/en/47455, /56236, /56941) could not be opened (host unreachable from the research environment); details come from search summaries and secondary coverage. Content of /56236 and /56941 is unverified.
Sponsor, operator identity and motive are unknown; the China link is a tooling-based vendor inference.
The groupware product is not named in sources gathered and no vulnerability in it is confirmed.
A 2023-09 Sekoia report (BlueShell used against Korean and Thai targets) was tagged with Dalbit in an aggregator listing, but the report was not opened and linkage is unverified.
Claims about email-server and MS-SQL targeting come from the MISP Galaxy description only.
Activity after February 2023 is not covered by sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing Windows web, SQL and groupware servers are key terrain, and compromised servers double as relay nodes [S1][S2]. STEP 2: The actor uses public tools and old vulnerabilities, so patch gaps matter more than novel capability [S1][S3]. STEP 3: The template is vulnerable server, webshell, certutil/Bitsadmin tool download, Potato escalation, FRP/LCX tunnel, credential and email theft, optional BitLocker [S1][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued opportunistic intrusion of poorly managed Korean servers. MDCOA is use of relay nodes in allied networks to stage intrusions against higher-value targets. Candidate indicators: FRP scheduled tasks named debug, a new admin account named main, certutil/Bitsadmin downloads from web server processes, and m00nlight.top domains [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track exposed Windows web and groupware servers on partner and contractor networks in Korea. (2) Authorities: remediation on non-DoD partner systems requires host-nation or owner action. (3) Mission assurance: BitLocker misuse can cause availability loss, so maintain offline backups and recovery procedures. (4) Coordination: share indicators with ROK counterparts and the vendor community [S1][S2].

identification.summary: DEV-0147 is Microsoft's emerging-threat designation for a China-based cyber espionage actor. On 2023-02-13 Microsoft Security Intelligence said it observed the actor compromising diplomatic entities in South America, which it called a notable expansion of data-exfiltration operations that traditionally targeted government agencies and think tanks in Asia and Europe [S2][S4]. Microsoft said the actor uses ShadowPad (also called PoisonPlug) for persistence and QuasarLoader, a webpack loader, to download and run further malware [S2][S4]. Post-exploitation included abuse of on-premises identity infrastructure for reconnaissance and lateral movement, and Cobalt Strike for command and control and exfiltration [S2][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Public naming: 2023-02-13 (Microsoft Security Intelligence post, per press coverage) [S4]. Earlier activity against Asia and Europe is described only generically [S4].
identification.notes: DEV-0147 is a Microsoft 'development' designation, meaning an unfinalized cluster; no Microsoft final (weather-based) name was found in the sources gathered. The primary post is a short social-media thread; most detail here comes from news coverage of it [S2][S3][S4]. One vendor blog title links DEV-0147 to 'Naplistener' [S7]; NAPLISTENER was not mentioned in the other coverage of Microsoft's post, so this link is unverified.

attribution.confidence: Microsoft describes DEV-0147 as 'China-based' [S4]. No state sponsor, agency or unit is named in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Microsoft's own telemetry-based statement (as relayed by press) [S4]. Press notes ShadowPad is used by several China-linked groups, and Secureworks CTU linked ShadowPad use to MSS-affiliated and PLA-affiliated groups; this is context about the tool, not attribution of DEV-0147 [S2].

actors.objectives: Data exfiltration from government agencies, think tanks and, as newly observed in 2023, diplomatic entities, consistent with espionage [S4].

targeting.notes: South America is the new area as of 2023-02; Asia and Europe are described as the group's traditional focus [S4]. Number, countries and names of South American victims were not published in the sources gathered [S2][S4].

capabilities.summary: ShadowPad RAT for persistent access [S4]; QuasarLoader webpack loader to download and execute additional malware [S2][S4]; Cobalt Strike for C2 and exfiltration [S4]; abuse of on-premises identity infrastructure for recon and lateral movement [S4]. ShadowPad is a modular RAT described as a successor to PlugX, used by multiple China-linked groups, so the tool alone does not identify DEV-0147 [S2][S4]. Microsoft did not disclose the initial-access method; phishing and unpatched applications were commentators' speculation only [S4]. Microsoft said Defender for Identity and Defender for Endpoint detect the activity and urged enforcement of MFA [S2][S4].

campaigns.name: South American diplomatic entity compromises
campaigns.summary: Microsoft Security Intelligence reported DEV-0147 intrusions at diplomatic entities in South America using ShadowPad, QuasarLoader and Cobalt Strike, with identity-infrastructure abuse for lateral movement. Disclosed 2023-02-13 [S2][S4].

diamond.adversary: China-based espionage actor tracked by Microsoft as DEV-0147; sponsor not named [S4].
diamond.capability: ShadowPad, QuasarLoader, Cobalt Strike, identity-infrastructure abuse [S2][S4].
diamond.victim: Diplomatic entities in South America; historically government agencies and think tanks in Asia and Europe [S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection of diplomatic and policy information, inferred from victim set; Microsoft describes the activity as data exfiltration [S4].
diamond.technology: On-premises identity infrastructure in victim networks was abused; the specific product (for example AD FS) was not named in the sources gathered [S2][S4].

gaps: Primary Microsoft post could not be opened or verified in search results and was removed as a source; details rely on press coverage.
No Microsoft blog or technical report with IOCs, victim count or timeline was found.
Initial access vector is undisclosed.
Which identity infrastructure was abused (AD FS, Active Directory, Entra Connect) is not stated in the sources gathered.
No state sponsor, MITRE group ID or other-vendor cluster mapping was found; overlap with other ShadowPad users (APT41, REF2924 and others) is unestablished and must not be assumed.
Unverified vendor claim linking DEV-0147 to NAPLISTENER [S7].
No activity after 2023-02 was identified in the searches run; possible later renaming by Microsoft not checked.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Diplomatic networks and their on-premises identity infrastructure are key terrain [S4]. STEP 2: The actor has broadened from Asia/Europe government and think-tank targets to South American diplomatic entities, indicating regional collection interest beyond its earlier footprint [S4]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is persistent RAT (ShadowPad), loader (QuasarLoader), Cobalt Strike C2/exfiltration, and identity-system abuse for lateral movement [S2][S4]; initial access is unknown. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued data exfiltration from diplomatic and government networks using these tools. MDCOA (not sourced; planning hypothesis) is expansion to additional regions' foreign ministries. Candidate indicators: ShadowPad and Cobalt Strike detections, anomalous identity-server queries and authentications, and webpack-loader-style payload downloads [S2][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track Microsoft naming updates for DEV-0147 and ShadowPad reporting; treat the tool as shared across China-linked groups [S2]. Authorities: any partner-network defensive support needs the appropriate legal and policy authority; this record supports none by itself. Mission assurance: harden and monitor on-premises identity servers, enforce MFA, and use endpoint and identity detections Microsoft cited [S2][S4]. Coordination: share indicators with Microsoft, allied diplomatic and CERT partners; verify claims against the primary post .

provenance.importedSummary: DEV-0147 is a China-based cyber espionage actor was observed compromising diplomatic targets in South America, a notable expansion of the group's data exfiltration operations that traditionally targeted gov't agencies and think tanks in Asia and Europe. DEV-0147 is known to use tools like ShadowPad, a remote access trojan associated with other China-based actors, to maintain persistent access, and QuasarLoader, a webpack loader, to deploy additional malware. DEV-0147's attacks in South America included post-exploitation activity involving the abuse of on-premises identity infrastructure for recon and lateral movement, and the use of Cobalt Strike for command and control and data exfiltration.

identification.summary: Microsoft tracked DEV-0270, also known as Nemesis Kitten, as a sub-group of the Iranian activity group PHOSPHORUS and tied multiple ransomware campaigns to it [S1]. In an April 2023 update Microsoft renamed PHOSPHORUS to Mint Sandstorm and DEV-0270 to Storm-0270 [S1][S2]. Microsoft says the group scans the internet for vulnerable servers and devices and then encrypts victims with BitLocker or DiskCryptor [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft's profile was published 2022-09-07 [S1]; Secureworks reporting on the overlapping Cobalt Mirage cluster dates to May 2022 [S7][S8]. Earliest DEV-0270 activity is not stated in the sources reviewed.
identification.notes: Microsoft does not describe DEV-0270 as a front company in the profile, but says infrastructure overlaps tie it to two public aliases, Secnerd (secnerd[.]ir) and Lifeweb (lifeweb[.]ir), linked to Najee Technology Hooshmand in Karaj, Iran [S1]. Press coverage reports that Microsoft, Secureworks and Mandiant independently linked the activity to Najee Technology and Afkar System [S4]. Secureworks tracks Cobalt Mirage with two clusters; Cluster A (opportunistic BitLocker/DiskCryptor ransomware) corresponds in press coverage to the Nemesis Kitten/DEV-0270 activity, while Cluster B is a more targeted intelligence-gathering set [S7][S8]. Vendor cluster boundaries may not match exactly [S7].

attribution.sponsor: Iran. Microsoft assesses DEV-0270 operates on behalf of the Iranian government [S1]. Treasury (as reported) described Najee Technology and Afkar System as affiliated with the IRGC [S4].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft: moderate confidence that DEV-0270 conducts network operations, including widespread vulnerability scanning, on behalf of the Iranian government; low confidence that some ransomware attacks are 'moonlighting' for personal or company revenue, based on targeting that often lacked strategic value to the regime [S1].
attribution.basis: Microsoft infrastructure overlaps to Secnerd, Lifeweb and Najee Technology Hooshmand [S1]. Press coverage reports that OFAC sanctioned ten individuals and two entities in September 2022 [S4]. The Treasury release and the joint CISA/FBI/NSA advisory were not opened by this analyst.

actors.objectives: Mixed or unclear. Microsoft describes opportunistic ransomware and data-extortion activity, including ransom demands (about USD 8,000 for decryption keys in one case) and offering a victim's stolen SQL database for sale after a refusal to pay [S1]. Microsoft assesses with low confidence that part of this is revenue-seeking moonlighting, while network operations such as vulnerability scanning are assessed as done for the Iranian government [S1].

targeting.notes: Microsoft describes targeting as opportunistic and often of little strategic value, driven by what vulnerable servers the actor finds [S1]. Secureworks coverage places Cobalt Mirage victims in Israel, the US, Europe and Australia [S8]. Parent group Mint Sandstorm is described by Microsoft as espionage-focused against dissidents, activists, defense industrial base, journalists, think tanks, universities and governments [S2].

capabilities.summary: Initial access through exploitation of internet-facing systems: Exchange (ProxyLogon CVEs 2021-26855, -26858, -26857, -27065) and Fortinet SSL VPN (CVE-2018-13379); Log4j exploitation was attempted but ransomware deployment was not observed from it; newly disclosed vulnerabilities are adopted quickly [S1]. Post-exploitation includes WDigest cleartext credential enablement, LSASS dumping via comsvcs.dll MiniDump (output named ssasl.dmp), a 'DefaultAccount' admin account for RDP, scheduled tasks pulling a renamed dllhost.exe reverse proxy, web shells, Defender real-time protection disabled, a spoofed root certificate, and Impacket WMIExec for lateral movement [S1]. Impact: a setup.bat script enables BitLocker, and DiskCryptor is dropped over RDP on workstations for full-drive encryption; ransom text is placed in the registry [S1]. Time to ransom was about two days in some cases [S1].

campaigns.name: Secureworks Cobalt Mirage ransomware reporting
campaigns.summary: Secureworks reported Cobalt Mirage ransomware operations using BitLocker and DiskCryptor, split into an opportunistic financially motivated Cluster A and a more targeted intelligence-oriented Cluster B; cited here as coverage of the Secureworks report.

campaigns.name: Microsoft profile of DEV-0270 ransomware operations
campaigns.summary: Microsoft publishes its profile tying ransomware campaigns to DEV-0270, a PHOSPHORUS sub-group, detailing Exchange and Fortinet exploitation, BitLocker and DiskCryptor use and links to Secnerd, Lifeweb and Najee Technology Hooshmand.

campaigns.name: US sanctions and joint advisory
campaigns.summary: As reported by The Record, OFAC sanctioned ten individuals and two entities (Najee Technology, Afkar System) tied to Iranian ransomware and malicious cyber activity, and the DOJ charged three individuals. The primary Treasury and DOJ documents were not opened.

campaigns.name: Microsoft renames actor
campaigns.summary: Microsoft updates its naming: PHOSPHORUS becomes Mint Sandstorm and DEV-0270 becomes Storm-0270.

diamond.adversary: Iran-linked operators; Microsoft assesses with moderate confidence they act on behalf of the Iranian government, with low-confidence possible moonlighting; infrastructure links to Najee Technology Hooshmand (Karaj) via Secnerd and Lifeweb [S1].
diamond.capability: Exploitation of Exchange and Fortinet SSL VPN flaws, LSASS credential dumping, Impacket WMIExec, RDP, web shells, BitLocker and DiskCryptor encryption [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Secnerd (secnerd[.]ir) and Lifeweb (lifeweb[.]ir) public aliases; reverse proxy masquerading as dllhost.exe; web shells on compromised servers. File hashes and IPs were not published in the Microsoft page [S1].
diamond.victim: Opportunistically selected organizations running vulnerable internet-facing Exchange or Fortinet systems [S1]; Secureworks coverage lists Israel, US, Europe and Australia [S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Unresolved mix of state tasking (vulnerability scanning for Iran) and possible private-company profit seeking, per Microsoft's moderate and low confidence assessments [S1]. US government actions treated the entities as IRGC-affiliated (as reported) [S4].
diamond.technology: Unpatched internet-facing Exchange and Fortinet SSL VPN appliances, weak local admin practices, and unprotected LSASS; built-in BitLocker and open-source DiskCryptor are abused for impact [S1].

gaps: Microsoft's profile lists no file hashes or IP indicators; IOCs are said to be in Microsoft products only [S1].

The joint CISA/FBI/NSA advisory and the Treasury press release were not reviewed; US government actions are known only via press coverage [S4], and whether the advisory names DEV-0270/Nemesis Kitten was not confirmed.

The original Secureworks Cobalt Mirage blog posts, Mandiant reporting and CrowdStrike reporting were not opened; vendor cluster mapping (Cobalt Mirage Cluster A vs B vs DEV-0270) rests on secondary coverage [S7][S8] and is inconsistent across outlets (some coverage equates Cluster B with Nemesis Kitten). No source reviewed stated CrowdStrike as the origin of the name Nemesis Kitten.
Sector-level victim data and total victim counts are not given in Microsoft's profile.
Activity after 2022 specific to Storm-0270 is not documented in the sources reviewed; the Mint Sandstorm page only notes the sub-group relationship [S2].
The alias UNC2448 and TunnelVision appear only in secondary coverage and are not firmly assigned to a vendor in the sources reviewed [S4].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (battlespace): internet-facing Exchange servers, Fortinet SSL VPN appliances and RDP-reachable hosts on defended networks are the relevant key cyber terrain [S1]. STEP 2 (effects): ransomware via BitLocker/DiskCryptor can render hosts inoperable within roughly two days of access, and data may be offered for sale [S1]. STEP 3 (adversary evaluation): the actor scans broadly, adopts newly disclosed CVEs quickly, and uses living-off-the-land tools, Impacket WMIExec and RDP [S1]; its tasking mix is uncertain [S1]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is opportunistic exploitation of unpatched internet-facing services followed by credential dumping, lateral movement and disk encryption or extortion [S1]. MDCOA, labeled as analytic extrapolation, is that the same access is used for deliberate disruption of a defended mission network rather than for ransom; this is not demonstrated in the sources. Candidate indicators: new 'DefaultAccount' admin accounts, WDigest UseLogonCredential changes, comsvcs.dll MiniDump of LSASS, Defender real-time protection disabled, setup.bat enabling BitLocker, DiskCryptor drops, registry ransom text 'Your drives are Encrypted!' [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track patch status of Exchange and Fortinet systems and monitor for the Microsoft-listed behaviors above; ASR rules for LSASS theft and WMI/PsExec process creation are Microsoft-recommended mitigations [S1]. Authorities: response on DoD networks versus defense-industrial-base partners follows different authorities; this note does not resolve them. Mission assurance: offline backups, LAPS for local admin passwords, and restricting SMB/RPC and outbound connections from SSL VPN appliances limit blast radius [S1]. Coordination: share indicators with network defenders and the relevant government cyber agencies.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The OE includes software vendors and CI/CD infrastructure that supply DoD and DIB networks; supply-chain paths are key terrain. STEP 2: A validly signed installer defeats allow-listing based on signer trust, so terrain analysis must include update channels. STEP 3: The template is n-day exploitation of developer infrastructure or trojanized signed software, then credential theft (ForestTiger) and hijack-based persistence (RollSling), then espionage or destruction. STEP 4: MLCOA is espionage against defense and IT targets with opportunistic financial theft. MDCOA is a destructive attack, Sony-style, against a high-profile target during a Korean Peninsula crisis. Candidate indicators: unexpected child processes from vendor updaters, DLL search-order hijacks in IT tools, and newly exploited CI/CD CVEs [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Supply-chain visibility: JCC2 data should flag vendor-signed binaries behaving abnormally, not just unsigned code. (2) Coordinate with INDOPACOM and USFK on Korean Peninsula crisis I&W, since DPRK cyber activity can precede or accompany provocations. (3) Revenue-focused operations (crypto theft) are a Treasury, FBI and law-enforcement lead, but they finance regime programs and so are relevant to campaign-level assessment. (4) Naming discipline: reporting chains should carry the specific cluster (Diamond, Onyx, Jade, Sapphire Sleet), because 'Lazarus' aggregates distinct actors with different targets.

identification.summary: DiceyF is the name Kaspersky uses for an APT cluster that has targeted online casinos and other victims in Southeast Asia, reportedly for years [S1]. Kaspersky's October 2022 write-up describes an intrusion at an online casino development studio in which the actor deployed a malware framework it named GamePlayerFramework [S1]. Secondary coverage describes GamePlayerFramework as a C# rewrite of the C++ PuppetLoader malware, with Tifa and Yuna branches (Yuna being the more complex), and with functions such as cookie and clipboard theft, keylogging, screenshots and virtual desktop sessions [S3][S4]. Kaspersky reports overlap with LuckyStar PlugX and with Earth Berberoka/GamblingPuppet activity documented by Trend Micro [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Secondary reporting says the activity dates to at least November 2021, when Kaspersky's investigation began and found PlugX loaders and other payloads delivered through an employee monitoring service and a security package deployment service [S3].
identification.notes: Kaspersky's full two-part report with IoCs and YARA is stated to be available only to private report subscribers; only part of the technical analysis is public [S1]. The Earth Berberoka link is an overlap reported by Kaspersky, not a statement that the clusters are identical [S1]. Trend Micro tracks Earth Berberoka (also GamblingPuppet) as its own cluster and lists PlugX, Gh0st RAT, PuppetLoader, Xnote and HelloBot among its tooling [S2]. Keep Kaspersky DiceyF and Trend Micro Earth Berberoka facts separate [S1][S2]. Microsoft has no mapped name in the record; none was found in sources.

attribution.confidence: Kaspersky says the motive is unclear and that it saw no evidence of immediate financial gain; it suggests possible espionage and IP theft [S1]. Secondary outlets report Kaspersky and Trend Micro findings as pointing to Chinese-speaking/Chinese-origin actors, but no source reviewed names a state sponsor [S4][S2].
attribution.basis: Overlap with Earth Berberoka, which Trend Micro attributes to Chinese-speaking actors based on tooling such as PlugX and Gh0st RAT [S2][S4]. No government attribution to DiceyF was found.

actors.objectives: Kaspersky assessed the motives as unclear, possibly a mix of espionage and intellectual property theft rather than immediate financial gain [S1]. Targeting of a casino game development studio is consistent with interest in source code or development assets, but sources do not state this explicitly.

targeting.notes: Kaspersky reports DiceyF targeting online casinos and other victims in Southeast Asia, with a specific intrusion at an online casino development studio [S1]. Trend Micro's related Earth Berberoka reporting describes gambling sites, mainly in China, as targets [S2]. Specific victim names and countries were not given in the sources reviewed.

capabilities.summary: GamePlayerFramework is a modular framework that secondary reports describe as a C# variant of PuppetLoader, offered in Tifa and Yuna branches, with remote access, keylogging, clipboard and browser cookie theft, screenshots and virtual desktop sessions [S3][S4]. Kaspersky states the actor continuously evolved its codebase and added encryption [S1]. Secondary reporting says the actor delivered PlugX loaders and other payloads through an employee monitoring service and a security package deployment service, and used a fake employee data synchronization app lure that dropped Yuna downloaders inside the network [S3][S4]. Kaspersky's public text notes that lack of obfuscation in GamePlayerFramework eases YARA-based detection [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: DiceyF is an advanced persistent threat group that has been targeting online casinos and other victims in Southeast Asia for an extended period. They have exhibited overlapping activity with LuckyStar PlugX and Earth Berberoka/GamblingPuppet, as reported by various cybersecurity vendors. identification.summary: Domestic Kitten is the name Check Point gave to a mobile surveillance operation using malicious Android apps against Iranian citizens; reporting links it to APT-C-50 [S1][S3][S5]. Check Point's 2018 report described targets as Kurdish and Turkish natives and ISIS supporters, all Iranian citizens [S1][S2]. A February 2021 Check Point update described 10 unique campaigns since 2017, over 1,200 targeted individuals and more than 600 successful infections [S3][S4]. ESET in 2022 described a new variant of the Android malware FurBall used in a Domestic Kitten campaign by APT-C-50 [S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: Check Point (2018): attack ongoing since 2016 [S1]. Check Point (2021): campaign series beginning in 2017 as reported by press [S3][S4]. ESET: active since at least 2016 per press summaries [S6].
identification.notes: No Microsoft name is known to this record. Aliases per cited sources: APT-C-50 (ESET, via press) [S5][S6] and Bouncing Golf, which Trend Micro described as possibly tied to Domestic Kitten based on similar code string structure and data format [S7]. The Bouncing Golf link is tentative and Trend Micro's campaign (GolfSpy) targeted Middle Eastern countries with mostly military-related data, a different victim profile, so the clusters should not be merged [S7].

attribution.sponsor: Iranian government, as assessed by Check Point [S1][S3].
attribution.confidence: Check Point's 2018 report said researchers had not identified the exact actors but judged from the nature of the apps and the infrastructure that Iranian actors were behind them [S1][S2]. The 2021 report linked the operation to the Iranian government [S3][S4]. No government attribution located.
attribution.basis: Targeting of groups Check Point says Iranian bodies such as the IRGC and Ministry of Intelligence routinely surveil, plus app content and attack infrastructure [S1][S2].

actors.objectives: Domestic surveillance of individuals the regime views as threats, including dissidents, the Kurdish minority, opposition forces and ISIS supporters [S1][S3][S4].

regions: Victims also reported in the US, UK, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Turkey and Uzbekistan [S3][S4]
targeting.notes: Targeting is of individuals, not organizations or infrastructure [S1][S3]. Lures observed: ISIS-themed wallpaper changer, fake ANF Kurdistan News update app, fake Videogram messaging app (2018) [S1][S2]; VIPRE Mobile Security, Exotic Flowers, Iranian Woman Ninja and a fake restaurant app (2021) [S3][S4]; a translation app hosted on a copycat of an Iranian website since June 2021 (ESET) [S5][S6].

capabilities.summary: Android spyware delivered as trojanized or fake apps outside official stores. Data collected includes contacts, call logs, SMS, photos, browser history and bookmarks, geolocation and surrounding audio, sent to C2 over HTTP POST with AES encryption (2018) [S1][S2]. The later FurBall malware collects device identifiers, SMS, call logs, media, location and microphone audio [S3][S4]. Delivery channels included SMS links, an Iranian blog and Telegram channels [S3][S4], and copycat websites reached via messages, social media, email, SMS and SEO poisoning [S6]. ESET says FurBall is based on the commercial stalkerware KidLogger and that the 2022 version mainly added obfuscation to evade detection, requesting only a contacts permission in the analyzed sample [S5][S6].

diamond.capability: Android spyware (FurBall, built on KidLogger) with audio, SMS, call, location and media collection [S3][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Fake or copycat websites, Iranian blog, Telegram channels, SMS links and HTTP POST C2 [S1][S3][S6].
diamond.victim: Iranian dissidents, Kurdish minority, opposition and ISIS supporters, with some victims abroad [S1][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Regime internal security and surveillance of perceived threats [S1][S3].
diamond.technology: Sideloaded Android apps and unmanaged personal devices; users lured via messaging and social platforms [S3][S6].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The relevant environment is personal mobile devices and the messaging channels (SMS, Telegram, social media, copycat websites) used by Iranian dissident and minority communities [S3][S6]. STEP 2: Adversary strength is moderate technically (stalkerware-derived malware, obfuscation) but persistent over years [S1][S5][S6]. STEP 3: The template is a lure app or copycat site, sideloaded install, then continuous collection of audio, SMS, calls and location to C2 [S1][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued domestic surveillance with rotating lure themes [S3][S6]. MDCOA is extension of the same tooling against diaspora, coalition-partner or foreign government personnel in the region, since victims were found in several countries [S3]. Candidate indicators: sideloaded apps imitating local news, security, translation or lifestyle apps, and HTTP POST traffic carrying encrypted device data [S1][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat this as low direct threat to DoD networks but a counterintelligence and force-protection concern for personnel and partners operating in or near Iran, Iraq and Turkey. (2) Authorities: monitoring of personal devices is a policy and legal matter; coordinate with command security and counterintelligence rather than assuming network-defense authorities. (3) Mission assurance: reinforce no-sideloading guidance and mobile device management for deployed personnel. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partner nations and mobile security vendors [S3][S6].

identification.summary: DragonSpark is the name SentinelLABS (SentinelOne) gave to an activity cluster that used the open-source, Go-based SparkRAT against organizations in East Asia, staging tools from compromised servers in China and Taiwan [S1][S2][S3]. SentinelLABS described it as the first activity cluster in which SparkRAT was consistently used in attacks, while noting other adversaries also appear to use the tool [S3].
identification.notes: First-observed month (September 2022) comes from secondary coverage of the SentinelLABS report [S4]. Microsoft reported SparkRAT misuse in December 2022; SentinelLABS found no concrete link between that activity and DragonSpark, so the two should not be merged [S3]. One secondary source reports a shared C2 IP with Zegost infostealer activity; this is single-sourced and not a cluster merge [S2].

attribution.confidence: SentinelLABS assessed it as highly likely that a Chinese-speaking actor is behind the DragonSpark attacks [S1][S3].
attribution.basis: SentinelLABS based its assessment on the actor's tooling, including Chinese-developed open-source tools and use of the China Chopper webshell, and on compromised infrastructure in China and Taiwan [S3]. No state sponsor or government attribution was found in the sources reviewed; the sources describe the actor as Chinese-speaking only.

targeting.notes: Sources describe organizations in East Asia, with compromised networks in Taiwan, Hong Kong, China and Singapore belonging to gambling-related companies, art galleries, travel agencies and schools [S2][S4]. It is not clear from the sources whether these were end victims or only infrastructure used for staging; some staging servers belonged to legitimate businesses [S2]. Initial indicators were compromised web servers and internet-exposed MySQL database servers [S2].

capabilities.summary: SparkRAT is an open-source, multi-platform remote access tool written in Go that runs on Windows, Linux and macOS, communicates with its C2 over WebSocket and can update itself via the C2 [S1][S2][S3]. DragonSpark also used a custom loader (m6699.exe) that uses the Yaegi framework to interpret Go source code embedded in the binary at runtime, which hinders static analysis [S3][S4]. The actor used the China Chopper webshell and other Chinese-developed open-source tools including SharpToken and BadPotato (privilege escalation) and GoToHTTP (remote access) [S4]. Coverage also lists XZB-1248 and a shellcode loader among tools [S4].

identification.summary: DriftingCloud is the name Volexity uses for a Chinese APT actor it observed exploiting a then-unpatched Sophos Firewall authentication-bypass/remote-code-execution flaw (CVE-2022-1040) from early March 2022, about three weeks before the fix [S1][S2][S3]. The imported MISP Galaxy description characterizes it as a persistent actor that targets many industries and locations, develops or acquires zero-days, and commonly compromises gateway devices [S7].
identification.firstObserved: 2022-03 (Volexity-reported first exploitation of CVE-2022-1040, reported as 5 March 2022 by The Hacker News coverage) [S3].
identification.notes: No Microsoft name is mapped to DriftingCloud in the sources gathered. Trend Micro's 2023 ShadowPad research on Pakistani targets references 'DriftingCloud malware' in conference slides, but the sources reviewed do not state that Trend Micro attributes that intrusion to the Volexity DriftingCloud cluster; keep the two vendor contexts separate [S5][S6]. Volexity's primary blog post was not opened (host unreachable from this environment); details come from press coverage of it.

attribution.confidence: Volexity is reported to describe DriftingCloud as a Chinese APT group [S1][S3]. The sources gathered do not state a Volexity confidence level or tie the actor to a specific PRC agency or contractor.
attribution.basis: Press coverage of Volexity's June 2022 report; use of the Behinder web-shell framework, which coverage notes other Chinese groups also used against Confluence CVE-2022-26134, is cited as context, not as attribution proof [S2]. MISP Galaxy lists country CN [S7].

actors.objectives: Volexity-reported activity indicates the firewall was an initial foothold; the actor aimed to breach cloud-hosted web servers hosting the victim's public websites and to intercept administrator CMS credentials and session cookies through DNS manipulation [S1][S2]. Broader strategic objectives are not stated in the sources gathered.

regions: South Asia (Sophos stated CVE-2022-1040 exploitation targeted a small set of specific organizations primarily in South Asia; this is a Sophos observation, not an attribution to DriftingCloud) [S4]
targeting.notes: Volexity's report described a single unnamed victim organization whose web properties were targeted [S1][S2]. Sector for that victim is not given in the coverage reviewed. The MISP Galaxy text says 'various industries and locations' without detail [S7].

capabilities.summary: Exploitation of Sophos Firewall CVE-2022-1040 (CVSS 9.8, affecting v18.5 MR3 and earlier) as a zero-day before the fix, with hotfixes starting 23 March 2022 [S1][S4]. Reported post-exploitation: web shells on the firewall reached via requests to a legitimate login.jsp file using the Behinder framework; creation of VPN user accounts with certificate pairs; DNS response modification for victim domains to enable man-in-the-middle capture of CMS admin credentials and session cookies; and deployment of PupyRAT, Pantegana and Sliver on web servers [S1][S2][S3].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing security gateways (firewall management portals) and the DNS and web/CMS tiers behind them are key cyber terrain. STEP 2: The actor exploited the gateway before a patch existed, so patch status alone is not protective; exposed management interfaces are the decisive variable [S1][S4]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is gateway zero-day, then web shell and rogue VPN accounts, then DNS tampering to harvest CMS credentials, then RAT deployment on web servers [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is repeated edge-device exploitation against South Asian and regional organizations. MDCOA is use of a gateway foothold to hijack DNS and credentials for onward access to partner or coalition web infrastructure. Candidate indicators: unexpected requests to login.jsp on the firewall, new VPN accounts and certificates, unexplained DNS answer changes, and Sliver or PupyRAT artifacts on web servers [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor advisories for edge devices and require management-interface exposure inventories. (2) Authorities: confirm who may direct emergency disabling of WAN-exposed administration portals on mission networks and partner-hosted services. (3) Mission assurance: plan fallback for DNS and web services if resolvers or gateways are suspect, and audit VPN account lists. (4) Coordination: share indicators with vendors and partner nations in South Asia; Sophos contacted affected organizations directly [S4].

identification.summary: Earth Alux is a China-linked cyberespionage group named by Trend Micro. Trend Micro describes it as exploiting vulnerable services on internet-exposed servers, implanting the GODZILLA web shell, and then delivering the VARGEIT and COBEACON backdoors for long-term data collection and exfiltration [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro first saw the group in the second quarter of 2023, mostly in Asia-Pacific; it was also seen in Latin America around mid-2024 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Earth Alux is a Trend Micro cluster name. No Microsoft name or MITRE group ID was found in the sources gathered. The 'China-linked' label is Trend Micro's assessment as relayed by secondary coverage; the primary report page could not be fetched in this session [S1][S2].

attribution.confidence: Trend Micro describes the group as China-linked; no confidence level or state-sponsor identification was found in the sources gathered [S1][S2].
attribution.basis: Trend Micro's own assessment; the cited coverage does not state the specific technical basis for the China link. Not corroborated by any government attribution found [S1][S2].

actors.objectives: Long-term data collection and exfiltration from compromised networks (espionage) [S1][S2].

targeting.notes: Sector list and primary-target countries are as reported in secondary coverage of Trend Micro's report; the list may not be complete [S1][S2].

capabilities.summary: Initial access is by exploiting vulnerable services on exposed servers, followed by GODZILLA web shell implantation [S1][S2]. The main backdoor VARGEIT is multi-channel and configurable: it can collect drive information, monitor processes, manipulate files, run command lines and inject further tools, with C2 over HTTP, TCP, UDP, ICMP, DNS and Microsoft Outlook (Graph API and drafts folder), the Outlook channel being the one most often seen [S2]. COBEACON (a Cobalt Strike Beacon) serves mainly as a first-stage backdoor; VARGEIT deploys RAILLOAD (DLL side-loading loader) and RAILSETTER (persistence and timestomping) [S2]. Later MASQLOADER variants can strip security products' NTDLL hooks [S2]. The group was observed testing its tools with Chinese-community open-source utilities ZeroEye and VirTest before deployment [S1][S2]. COBEACON is launched via MASQLOADER or the RSBINJECT shellcode loader; VARGEIT loads tools into a newly started Microsoft Paint process [S1][S2].

diamond.technology: Internet-exposed servers with vulnerable services; mail platform (Microsoft Outlook/Graph) abused as C2; endpoints with NTDLL-hook-based security tooling [S2].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing web servers and mail infrastructure (Exchange/Outlook cloud mailboxes) in government, telecom and IT-services networks are key terrain [S1][S2]. STEP 2: The actor operates mainly in APAC with expansion to Latin America, relevant to INDOPACOM-adjacent partner networks and contractors [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Template is exposed-service exploitation, GODZILLA web shell, COBEACON/VARGEIT, DLL side-loading and persistence, then collection and exfiltration; C2 hides in legitimate Outlook Graph traffic [S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued long-term espionage against APAC government and telecom targets. MDCOA is use of foothold in IT-service or telecom providers to reach downstream customers (not evidenced in sources; hypothesis). Candidate indicators: new web shells on exposed servers, Graph API access to draft messages from servers, DLL side-loading from unusual paths, timestomped files, NTDLL unhooking behavior [S2].

(1) Situational awareness: track inventory and patch status of internet-exposed servers and monitor mail-API (Graph) anomalies. (2) Authorities: hunting on partner or contractor networks requires coordination under existing agreements; no actor-specific authority guidance is supported by sources. (3) Mission assurance: assess dependence on telecom and IT-service providers in APAC theaters. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3/DIB partners and allied CERTs in affected countries [S1][S2].

provenance.importedSummary: Earth Alux is a China-linked APT group known for conducting cyberespionage attacks across various sectors, including government, technology, and telecommunications. They primarily exploit vulnerable services in exposed servers to gain initial access, implanting web shells like GODZILLA and deploying backdoors such as VARGEIT and COBEACON. The group employs tools like RSBINJECT and MASQLOADER for lateral movement and network discovery, while also utilizing RAILSETTER for persistence through mspaint injection. Their operations have predominantly targeted the APAC region and have extended to Latin America, with a focus on exfiltrating sensitive information to attacker-controlled cloud storage.

identification.summary: Earth Baxia is Trend Micro's name for a suspected China-based threat actor that, per Trend Micro's September 2024 report, targeted a Taiwanese government organization and likely other Asia-Pacific countries using spear-phishing and exploitation of GeoServer CVE-2024-36401 [S1][S2]. Operators deployed customized Cobalt Strike components and a new backdoor Trend Micro named EAGLEDOOR [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro tied the activity to suspicious behavior detected in July 2024 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Name is Trend Micro's Earth-series designation; no Microsoft name or MITRE group ID was found in the sources gathered. Trend Micro's own Earth Lusca (a separate cluster) was returned in searches but no source gathered states an Earth Baxia/Earth Lusca relationship; do not merge them.

attribution.confidence: Trend Micro assessed the group likely operates from China; coverage describes this as a suspicion, not a confirmed attribution [S1][S2].
attribution.basis: Secondary coverage of Trend Micro reports that a Cobalt Strike watermark checked on Shodan linked mostly to machines in China, and that some servers were hosted on Alibaba cloud or located in Hong Kong [S2][S3]. No government attribution or state-sponsor assignment was found.

targeting.notes: Trend Micro named a Taiwanese government organization as the initial victim and said other APAC countries were likely affected [S1]. Security Affairs and The Hacker News report the group primarily targeted government agencies, telecommunications and energy firms in the Philippines, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan and Thailand [S2][S3].

capabilities.summary: Initial access via spear-phishing emails and exploitation of GeoServer CVE-2024-36401, a remote code execution flaw (CVSS 9.8) that let the actor download or copy malicious components [S1][S2]. Uses GrimResource and AppDomainManager injection to deploy additional payloads [S1]. Deploys customized Cobalt Strike with modified internal signatures and a changed configuration structure for evasion [S1][S2]. EAGLEDOOR is a new backdoor supporting multiple communication protocols for information gathering and payload delivery [S1][S2].

diamond.infrastructure: Some servers on Alibaba cloud or in Hong Kong per press coverage of Trend Micro's findings [S2][S3]; full IOC list exists in a Trend Micro file not reviewed.
diamond.victim: Taiwanese government organization, and government, telecommunications and energy organizations across the Philippines, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan and Thailand [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing, unpatched GeoServer instances and email users susceptible to spear-phishing [S1][S2].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing geospatial servers (GeoServer) and government email are key terrain in Taiwan and neighboring APAC states [S1][S2]. STEP 2: A critical unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2024-36401) gives the actor a fast path before patching [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Template is spear-phish or GeoServer exploit, then Cobalt Strike, then EAGLEDOOR [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued access operations against APAC government, telecom and energy targets; MDCOA is reuse of other public-facing exploits for the same chain. Candidate indicators: unexpected GeoServer child processes, AppDomainManager config abuse, .msc (GrimResource) files in mail, and Trend Micro-published IOCs [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track Trend Micro IOCs and GeoServer exposure in partner-nation and supported networks [S1][S2]. Authorities: sharing on allied APAC victims requires coordination through appropriate partner and CTI channels. Mission assurance: patch or isolate GeoServer, harden email against .msc/.NET loader lures, and hunt for modified Cobalt Strike [S1]. Coordination: notify partner-nation CERTs in affected states [S2][S3].
