identification.summary: Earth Berberoka (also GamblingPuppet) is a Chinese-speaking-linked threat cluster named by Trend Micro researchers Daniel Lunghi and Jaromir Horejsi in 2022. It mainly targets online gambling sites using multiplatform malware (Windows, Linux, macOS) [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro published the first public report in April 2022 [S1].
identification.notes: Check Point's 2026 'Gambling Goblin' cluster is linked to Earth Berberoka with medium-to-high confidence by Check Point; treat it as a linked cluster, not a merged one [S4][S5]. Microsoft has no known mapping for this actor in the record. MITRE group ID is not in the record.

attribution.sponsor: Not attributed to a state. Trend Micro describes the malware as historically attributed to Chinese-speaking actors [S1]. Check Point describes Gambling Goblin as Chinese-speaking [S4].
attribution.confidence: Check Point assesses the Gambling Goblin link to Earth Berberoka with medium-to-high confidence [S4][S6].
attribution.basis: Malware lineage and reuse: PlugX, Gh0st RAT and PuppetLoader [S1]; oRAT codebase and operator routes shared with 2022 Earth Berberoka activity [S4].

actors.objectives: Not stated in the sources gathered as a state objective. Trend Micro reports that primary targets are gambling websites in China [S1]. Check Point reports that the linked 2025-2026 cluster hijacks sites to promote gambling and fuel SEO fraud [S4][S5].

sectors: Brazilian government and education sites (Gambling Goblin, linked cluster)
regions: Brazil (Gambling Goblin, linked cluster, since mid-2025) [S4][S6]
targeting.notes: Trend Micro also observed non-gambling victims: one education-related government institution, two IT services companies and one electronics manufacturer [S1]. Regional scope of the 2025-2026 Brazil activity rests on Check Point's linkage, not on Trend Micro [S4].

capabilities.summary: Upgraded older malware (PlugX, Gh0st RAT) plus PuppetLoader, a five-stage loader that hijacks loaded modules and hides payloads in modified BMP image files, one stage using a flawed RC4 implementation [S1][S2]. Tools target Windows, Linux and macOS [S1]. Distribution observed included a fake Adobe Flash Player installer (15 downloads in China, Dec 2020-Apr 2022) and a backdoored chat app called MiMi [S2]. The linked Gambling Goblin cluster installs malicious Apache modules that proxy visitors to phishing pages, and uses Linux tools DownPro, AlphaAgent, oRAT, a 3snake-based credential stealer and an SSH brute-forcer [S4][S6].

diamond.infrastructure: Compromised legitimate web servers, including Brazilian government sites, and phishing networks in Vietnamese, Spanish and English, with daily-generated domains [S4][S6]. Indicator files for 2022 activity are listed in Trend Micro's record but were not opened.
diamond.victim: Gambling sites and customers, plus a few non-gambling organizations; later Brazilian government and education sites [S1][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Not determined. Activity appears financially or SEO-fraud oriented in recent reporting, but this is not settled [S4].
diamond.technology: Windows, Linux and macOS endpoints; Apache web servers [S1][S4].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing web servers (Apache) and gambling or casino platforms are the relevant terrain; no military targets appear in the sources. STEP 2: The group reuses mature RATs and builds multiplatform loaders, giving it reach across Windows, Linux and macOS [S1][S4]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is lure or compromised site, then loader, then RAT or Apache module [S2][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued financially or SEO-motivated compromise of web servers and gambling-related organizations. MDCOA is repurposing hijacked government web infrastructure for broader phishing or malware hosting. Candidate indicators: unexpected Apache modules, BMP files carrying payloads, SSH brute-force against Linux hosts [S4].

(2) Authorities: any action against compromised foreign government sites belongs to host-nation or law-enforcement channels. (3) Mission assurance: audit Linux web servers for unauthorized Apache modules and credential theft. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partner CERTs; Brazilian government sites were affected [S4].

provenance.importedSummary: According to TrendMicro, Earth Berberoka is a threat group originating from China that mainly focuses on targeting gambling websites. This group's campaign uses multiple malware families that target the Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms that have been attributed to Chinese-speaking actors. Aside from using tried-and-tested malware families that have been upgraded, such as PlugX and Gh0st RAT, Earth Berberoka has also developed a brand-new complex, multistage malware family, which has been dubbed PuppetLoader.

identification.summary: Trend Micro describes Earth Freybug as a cyberthreat group active since at least 2012 that conducts espionage and financially motivated activity, and as a subset of APT41 [S2]. Trend Micro's 2 April 2024 report described a campaign in which the group used DLL hijacking and API unhooking through a previously undocumented malware it named UNAPIMON [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro: active since at least 2012 [S2]. The UNAPIMON campaign was reported 2024-04-02 [S3].
identification.notes: Earth Freybug is a Trend Micro cluster name. Trend Micro says its TTPs are similar to the activity Cybereason reported as Operation CuckooBees [S2]. Secondary coverage lists APT41 aliases such as Winnti, Wicked Panda, Brass Typhoon (formerly Barium), Axiom, Bronze Atlas and HOODOO [S2][S4]. These are aliases of the broader APT41 set, not of Earth Freybug, so none were added here.

attribution.confidence: Trend Micro characterizes Earth Freybug as a subset of APT41, a China-linked group [S2][S4]. RH-ISAC's write-up states the report matched TTPs of Operation CuckooBees, which it describes as widely attributed to Winnti/APT41 [S3]. No government attribution of Earth Freybug specifically was found.
attribution.basis: Trend Micro TTP comparison with Operation CuckooBees [S3]; vendor characterization as an APT41 subset [S2].

actors.objectives: Trend Micro describes the group as focused on espionage and financially motivated activity [S2]. Specific collection requirements in the UNAPIMON campaign are not stated in the sources reviewed.

targeting.notes: Trend Micro says the group attacks organizations across various sectors and countries; the sources reviewed did not name specific sectors, countries or victims for the UNAPIMON campaign [S3].

capabilities.summary: Trend Micro reports use of living-off-the-land binaries together with custom malware, plus DLL hijacking and API unhooking [S2][S3]. In the observed chain a process in the legitimate VMware Tools binary vmtoolsd.exe used schtasks.exe to create a remote scheduled task that ran a pre-deployed batch file (cc.bat) for reconnaissance and to launch further tasks [S2]. A later batch step reportedly side-loaded a DLL (TSMSISrv.dll) via the SessionEnv service to load UNAPIMON into a cmd.exe process [S5]. UNAPIMON is a C++ DLL, neither packed nor obfuscated, that uses Microsoft Detours to hook CreateProcessW and unhook API hooks in child processes, preventing security tools from monitoring them [S3][S5]. How the VMware Tools process was initially compromised is unknown; exploitation of external-facing servers is suspected [S2].

campaigns.summary: Trend Micro states the group has been active since at least 2012; no specific campaigns from that period are cited in the sources reviewed.

campaigns.name: UNAPIMON campaign
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro published analysis of an Earth Freybug intrusion using a vmtoolsd.exe process to create remote scheduled tasks running cc.bat, then DLL side-loading to deploy the UNAPIMON API-unhooking malware, with TTPs similar to Operation CuckooBees.

diamond.adversary: Cluster described by Trend Micro as an APT41 subset, China-linked, active since at least 2012 [S2][S4].
diamond.capability: LOLBins, custom malware (UNAPIMON), DLL hijacking/side-loading, Microsoft Detours-based API unhooking, scheduled tasks and batch scripts [S2][S5].
diamond.victim: Organizations across various sectors and countries; none named in sources reviewed [S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Espionage and financially motivated activity per Trend Micro [S2].
diamond.technology: Windows hosts running VMware Tools (vmtoolsd.exe), Task Scheduler and the SessionEnv service; endpoint security that relies on API hooking [S5].

gaps: Trend Micro's primary report could not be fetched or confirmed in search results, so it is not cited; details rest on secondary coverage (The Hacker News, RH-ISAC, Dark Reading, BleepingComputer).
Victim sectors, countries and number of victims are not identified in the sources reviewed.
Initial access vector is unknown; exploitation of external-facing servers is only suspected [S2].
C2 infrastructure and indicators were not captured.
Only one dated campaign (April 2024) was found; no earlier Earth Freybug campaigns were located, and activity after April 2024 was not found.
Relationship to the rest of APT41 (and to Microsoft's Brass Typhoon naming) is a vendor characterization (subset); the cluster boundary is not independently verified.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID or Microsoft name mapping was found for Earth Freybug.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Virtualized Windows servers running VMware Tools and Task Scheduler are the relevant terrain [S5]. STEP 2: The group's defense-evasion approach (unhooking API monitoring in child processes) degrades hook-based EDR visibility on affected hosts [S3][S5]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is a trusted process (vmtoolsd.exe) creating remote scheduled tasks that run batch files, then DLL side-loading to load UNAPIMON [S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage-focused intrusion using LOLBins and custom tooling against organizations in multiple sectors [S2]. MDCOA, which is speculative as the sources do not show it, is the same unhooking capability applied to defense-sector networks to run follow-on tools unseen. Candidate indicators: vmtoolsd.exe spawning schtasks.exe or cmd.exe, creation of remote tasks running cc.bat, TSMSISrv.dll loaded via SessionEnv, and hooks on CreateProcessW added by Detours [S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: because EDR hook visibility can be blinded, supplement with kernel/ETW and process-lineage telemetry and track the Trend Micro and APT41 reporting [S3]. (2) Authorities: hunting on contractor or partner hosts requires the appropriate owner or DIB CS coordination; confirm authority before acting. (3) Mission assurance: apply least privilege and restrict admin accounts, as Trend Micro recommends, on virtualization and management hosts [S3]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3 and partners, noting that victim and infrastructure data are unavailable and attribution is vendor-level only [S2].

provenance.importedSummary: Earth Freybug, identified as a subset of APT41, is a cyberthreat group active since at least 2012, engaging in espionage and financially motivated activities across various sectors worldwide. The tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) used in this campaign are similar to the ones from a campaign (Operation CuckooBees) described in an article published by Cybereason. They employ a diverse toolkit, including LOLBins and custom malware, to execute sophisticated cyberespionage attacks. The group's recent tactics involve DLL hijacking and API unhooking through a newly discovered malware named UNAPIMON, which prevents child processes from being monitored. This technique was observed in a vmtoolsd.exe process creating remote tasks to deploy malicious batch files for reconnaissance and backdoor access. UNAPIMON's simplicity and use of Microsoft Detours for defense evasion highlight the group's evolving methods and the need for vigilant security measures, such as restricting admin privileges and adhering to the principle of least privilege. Earth Freybug's persistence and creativity in refining their techniques underscore the ongoing threat they pose and the importance of proactive cybersecurity practices.

identification.summary: Earth Krahang is the Trend Micro name for a China-linked intrusion set that Trend Micro reported in March 2024 as having been active since early 2022 and focused mainly on government organizations worldwide [S1][S2]. Trend Micro counted at least 70 compromised organizations in 23 countries, 48 of them government bodies, and 116 targeted organizations in 35 countries; other coverage cites 45 countries, so counts vary by source [S3][S4]. The group exploits public-facing servers, sends spear-phishing emails, builds VPN servers on compromised hosts, brute-forces email credentials, and uses access to one government to attack other governments [S1][S5].
identification.firstObserved: Early 2022 per Trend Micro reporting published 2024-03-18 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Trend Micro links Earth Krahang to Earth Lusca but treats it as a separate intrusion set because it has independent infrastructure and unique backdoors [S1][S2]. CYFIRMA, by contrast, lists Earth Krahang as an alias of Earth Lusca, so cluster boundaries differ by vendor [S2]. Trend Micro also raised a possible link to i-Soon, framed as a possibility and not a confirmed attribution [S3][S4]. No Microsoft actor name or MITRE group ID is cited here.

attribution.sponsor: Trend Micro describes the group as China-linked; no government attribution is cited in the gathered sources [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: Trend Micro states the Earth Lusca and i-Soon connections as assessments with caveats: Earth Krahang could be another penetration team under the same company as i-Soon, but this is a possibility and not a confirmed attribution [S3][S4]. Vendors disagree on whether Earth Krahang is distinct from Earth Lusca [S1][S2].
attribution.basis: Trend Micro recovered samples, configuration files and attack-tool logs from the group's servers after operational mistakes, and observed shared infrastructure and tactics with Earth Lusca [S1][S2][S5].

actors.objectives: Cyberespionage against government institutions, with stolen email credentials used to exfiltrate mail [S1][S5].

targeting.notes: Trend Micro counted 70 confirmed compromises in 23 countries (48 government) and 116 targets in 35 countries; Security Affairs cites 45 countries [S3][S4]. Lures referenced geopolitical topics such as a Malaysian Ministry of Defense circular, ICJ hearings on Guyana versus Venezuela, and a Malaysian defense minister visit to Hungary [S2].

capabilities.summary: Initial access via spear-phishing (RAR archives containing LNK files that install backdoors) and exploitation of public-facing servers, including Oracle Web Applications Desktop Integrator CVE-2022-21587 and Openfire CVE-2023-32315; backdoors are sometimes delivered through web shells [S2][S3]. Tooling named in coverage: Cobalt Strike, RESHELL (a simpler .NET backdoor), and XDealer (tracked as DinodasRAT by ESET, with Windows and Linux versions), plus PlugX and ShadowPad listed in HivePro's summary [S2][S3][S7]. Post-exploitation includes SoftEther VPN for persistence and access to internal networks, remote desktop enablement, credential dumping, network scanning, brute-forcing of email accounts, and a Python script to exfiltrate Zimbra mail [S1][S2]. Compromised government webservers and mail accounts host payloads, proxy traffic and send phishing to other governments [S1][S5].

campaigns.name: Earliest observed activity
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro says it has tracked the activity since early 2022.

campaigns.name: Trend Micro public disclosure
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro published on 2024-03-18 its report describing about 70 compromised organizations in 23 countries, 48 of them government, with a Southeast Asia focus, and its possible links to Earth Lusca and i-Soon.

diamond.adversary: China-linked intrusion set that Trend Micro treats as separate from but related to Earth Lusca, with a possible i-Soon connection [S1][S3].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing with RAR/LNK droppers, public-facing server exploits, RESHELL, XDealer/DinodasRAT, Cobalt Strike, SoftEther VPN, and email brute-forcing [S2][S3][S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised government webservers and mail accounts used to host payloads, proxy traffic and send phishing; VPN servers created on compromised hosts; actor-run servers whose logs Trend Micro recovered [S1][S5].
diamond.victim: Government organizations (48 confirmed compromised of about 70), mostly in Southeast Asia [S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection against governments, using geopolitical lures tied to regional defense and international legal events [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing servers (Oracle, Openfire, Zimbra), Windows and Linux hosts, and email systems with weak credentials [S2][S7].

gaps: Trend Micro's primary report (trendmicro.com) could not be fetched in this session; details rest on search-result summaries and secondary coverage and should be verified against it.
Counts conflict across sources (23 versus 35 versus 45 countries); the basis for each figure was not verified.
Cluster boundary with Earth Lusca (and other vendor names for it) is unresolved; vendors disagree on whether it is a distinct group.
The i-Soon link is explicitly a possibility; no confirmed attribution or government statement was found.
No Earth Krahang activity after March 2024 was found in searches; current status is unknown.
PlugX and ShadowPad use appears only in secondary summaries and was not confirmed in the primary report.
No MITRE group ID or Microsoft name was identified.
Sectors beyond government (telecoms, post offices, media) and the IMDA advisory were not verified and were removed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Government mail servers, public-facing web and collaboration servers, and inter-government trust relationships are key terrain, since the actor abuses one government's infrastructure to reach others [S1][S5]. STEP 2: The actor favors Southeast Asia but has reached the Americas, Europe and Africa, so coalition and partner governments are in the threat area [S3]. STEP 3: The template is spear-phishing or exploitation of an edge server, then web shell or RESHELL/XDealer, then SoftEther VPN, credential dumping and mail collection [S2][S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued government mail and document collection, including phishing of partner governments from compromised accounts. MDCOA is use of a compromised partner or coalition government account to deliver a backdoor to US or allied defense personnel under a geopolitical lure. Candidate indicators: RAR archives with LNK files from known government senders, new SoftEther VPN services on servers, unexpected web shells on Openfire or Oracle systems, repeated failed email logins, and Linux hosts running unfamiliar systemd/SysV persistence [S2][S1][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track exploitation of edge-server CVEs (CVE-2022-21587, CVE-2023-32315) and partner-government compromises that could cascade to US-bound email [S2]. (2) Authorities: coordinate any defensive action on partner or contractor systems through the proper owners and legal channels; this analysis assigns none. (3) Mission assurance: treat inbound mail from partner governments as potentially compromised and enforce attachment filtering and multi-factor authentication to blunt email brute-forcing [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partner CERTs, especially in Southeast Asia, and with DC3 and DIB contacts for contractor-hosted servers.

provenance.importedSummary: Earth Krahang is an APT group targeting government organizations worldwide. They use spear-phishing emails, weak internet-facing servers, and custom backdoors like Cobalt Strike, RESHELL, and XDealer to conduct cyber espionage. The group creates VPN servers on infected systems, employs brute force attacks on email accounts, and exploits compromised government infrastructure to attack other governments. Earth Krahang has been linked to another China-linked actor, Earth Lusca, and is believed to be part of a specialized task force for cyber espionage against government institutions.

identification.summary: Earth Lamia is Trend Micro's name for a China-nexus intrusion set that Trend Research says has been active since at least 2023 and that mainly exploits web application vulnerabilities [S1][S3]. Google Threat Intelligence Group tracks Earth Lamia as UNC5454 [S4]. Microsoft has no mapping in this record; no Microsoft name was found.
identification.firstObserved: At least 2023 (Trend Micro) [S1][S3]. The PULSEPACK backdoor was first seen in attacks in August 2024 [S3].
identification.notes: Trend Micro names Earth Lamia; GTIG uses UNC5454 [S4]. Trend Micro reportedly links the cluster to REF0657 (Elastic), STAC6451 (Sophos) and CL-STA-0048 (Unit 42), per a search summary of the Trend report; the original report page could not be opened to confirm [S1]. Keep these as vendor-cluster overlaps, not merged facts. AWS names Earth Lamia and, separately, Jackpot Panda; GTIG says no public indicators exist to assess a relationship between them [S4][S5].

attribution.confidence: Trend Micro assesses the activity as a China-nexus intrusion set [S1]. GTIG and AWS describe related React2Shell exploitation as China-nexus; GTIG states the Earth Lamia/Jackpot Panda link comes from AWS reporting, not its own assessment [S4][S5]. AWS notes shared anonymization infrastructure among Chinese groups makes definitive attribution challenging [S5]. No government attribution found.
attribution.basis: Trend Micro research evidence (details not verified here) [S1]; AWS honeypot observations of exploitation attempts from infrastructure historically linked to named groups [S5].

targeting.notes: Trend Micro says targeting has shifted over time from financial services, to logistics and online retail, and most recently to IT firms, universities and government organizations [S1][S3]. An aggregator (strobes.co) also lists Latin America and the Middle East; that is not confirmed in Trend Micro coverage seen here.

capabilities.summary: Initial access is mainly through exploitation of web application flaws, frequently scanning for SQL injection (Trend Micro suspects sqlmap) and exploiting known vulnerabilities in public-facing servers [S1][S3]. Trend Micro lists CVE-2024-27198 (JetBrains TeamCity), CVE-2024-51378 (CyberPanel) and CVE-2025-31324 (SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer) among exploited flaws [S1]. Custom tooling includes the modular .NET backdoor PULSEPACK (TCP C2 in 2024) and the privilege-escalation tool BypassBoss [S1][S3]. The group uses DLL sideloading to run Cobalt Strike and Brute Ratel shellcode [S1][S3]. AWS reported Earth Lamia exploiting React2Shell (CVE-2025-55182) within hours of its 3 December 2025 disclosure [S5][S4].

campaigns.summary: AWS reported China-nexus groups including Earth Lamia and Jackpot Panda began exploiting the flaw within hours of the 3 December 2025 disclosure; GTIG relayed the AWS finding and gave no UNC5454-specific tooling [S4][S5].

diamond.capability: Web application exploitation, SQL injection, PULSEPACK, BypassBoss, DLL sideloading, Cobalt Strike and Brute Ratel [S1][S3].
diamond.victim: Financial, logistics, retail, IT, education and government organizations in Brazil, India and Southeast Asia [S1][S3].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing web applications and servers with unpatched or SQL-injectable flaws (TeamCity, CyberPanel, SAP NetWeaver, React Server Components) [S1][S5].

gaps: Trend Micro's primary report, AWS's primary blog and the Google Cloud and trade-press pages could not be fully opened (fetch failures); several details rest on search-result summaries and should be verified against the originals.
Sponsor, tasking and objectives are not stated in sources gathered.
Attribution rests on vendor assessments; AWS notes definitive attribution is challenging due to shared infrastructure [S5].

Overlaps with REF0657 (Elastic), STAC6451 (Sophos, which deployed Mimic ransomware) and CL-STA-0048 (Unit 42) not independently confirmed; Earth Lamia itself has not been observed using ransomware per Trend Micro summary [S1].
Relationship between Earth Lamia and Jackpot Panda is unknown; GTIG says no public indicators [S4].
No Microsoft actor name found; MITRE group ID not assigned in this record.
Infrastructure details and indicators not gathered.
Forescout's Chaya_004 (SAP NetWeaver CVE-2025-31324 exploitation) was not linked to Earth Lamia in any source found; do not merge.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing web applications, developer/CI servers (TeamCity), hosting control panels, ERP middleware (SAP NetWeaver) and React/Next.js servers are key terrain, especially for IT, university and government organizations in Brazil, India and Southeast Asia [S1][S5]. STEP 2: Exploitation within hours of disclosure (React2Shell) narrows the patch window to near zero [S5]. STEP 3: Template is web-app exploit or SQL injection, then PULSEPACK or Cobalt Strike/Brute Ratel via DLL sideloading, then privilege escalation with BypassBoss [S1][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued opportunistic exploitation of newly disclosed web flaws against regional IT, education and government targets. MDCOA is use of compromised IT service providers or partner government networks as a path to coalition or DoD-adjacent partners in the region. Candidate indicators: SQL injection scanning against web apps, DLL sideloading by legitimate signed binaries, and unexpected Cobalt Strike/Brute Ratel beacons [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track exploited-vulnerability advisories for web frameworks and enterprise middleware and push mitigation status to partner networks in Southeast Asia and Latin America. (2) Authorities: partner-network hunting depends on host-nation consent and DCO authorities; coordinate before action outside DODIN. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize patching and WAF coverage of internet-facing apps supporting mission systems and contractors. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3 and allied CERTs; note attribution is vendor-level and clusters overlap, so prioritize containment over naming [S4].

identification.summary: Earth Naga is Trend Micro's name for a China-aligned cyber espionage intrusion set that Trend describes as sharing compromised access with Earth Estries in what it calls a 'Premier Pass-as-a-Service' model [S1]. A Malpedia profile summarising the Trend report describes it as targeting government agencies, telecommunications and military-related manufacturers in the APAC region [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Search-result summaries of the Trend Micro report assess the Earth Estries and Earth Naga cooperation to date to at least late 2023 [S1]. First activity of Earth Naga itself is not established in sources opened.
identification.notes: Name is Trend Micro's (Earth- prefix). Search summaries of the Trend report equate Earth Naga with Flax Typhoon; other secondary profiles also list RedJuliett, Ethereal Panda and Storm-0919. These were not verified against the primary report or against Microsoft, Recorded Future or CrowdStrike, so no alias is added and the clusters are not merged [S1].

attribution.basis: Trend Micro characterises the activity as China-aligned [S1]. No sponsoring organisation or government attribution was found in sources reviewed.

targeting.notes: Trend Micro's report summary cites government, telecommunications and retail targets across APAC [S1]. Malpedia's claims of NATO-country and Latin America targeting could not be confirmed in re-check and were removed.

capabilities.summary: Malpedia's summary links Earth Naga to Draculoader and ShadowPad C&C infrastructure and to establishing SSH connections through compromised mail servers [S2]. Trend's central finding is that Earth Estries handed compromised assets to Earth Naga for continued exploitation, which complicates detection and attribution [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: Earth Naga is an APT group that has persistently targeted high-value organizations, including government agencies, telecommunications, and military-related manufacturers, primarily in Taiwan and the broader APAC region. They have been linked to the use of Draculoader and ShadowPad C&C infrastructure, demonstrating sophisticated TTPs such as establishing SSH connections through compromised mail servers. identification.summary: Earth Wendigo is a Trend Micro-named threat actor that has targeted Taiwanese government organizations, research institutions and universities since May 2019, using JavaScript injected into a widely used Taiwanese webmail system to exfiltrate email [S1][S2]. Trend Micro found no clear connection to previously known attack groups and named the actor itself [S2]. Trend Micro also observed separate spear-phishing emails with malicious links sent to politicians and activists who support Tibet, the Uyghur region or Hong Kong, which it treated as a distinct series of attacks [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: 2019-05 (start of the Taiwan webmail campaign per Trend Micro) [S1][S2].
identification.notes: The Google Drive spear-phishing results that surfaced in searches belong to a different Trend Micro cluster (Earth Preta) and must not be merged with Earth Wendigo. The webmail product is not named in the retrieved summaries.

attribution.confidence: Trend Micro named the actor itself because it saw no clear connection to earlier groups [S2]. No state attribution was confirmed in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Trend Micro January 2021 research [S1]. No sponsoring organization or country is named in the sources gathered.

actors.objectives: Email theft from Taiwanese government, research and university targets [S1][S2]. The Tibet, Uyghur and Hong Kong lures suggest interest in individuals associated with those causes [S1]; the sources gathered do not state a sponsor or tasking.

sectors: Politicians and activists (Tibet, Uyghur region, Hong Kong causes)
targeting.notes: The politician and activist targeting was reported by Trend Micro as separate from the Taiwan webmail operation [S1][S2].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing emails posing as a shopping-coupon ad carry hidden obfuscated JavaScript, triggered through the webmail search-suggestion feature to evade static checks [S2][S5]. The primary route is XSS injection into the webmail system; if that fails, the actor registers a malicious script as a Service Worker, which can intercept and manipulate HTTPS requests, hijack login credentials and add malicious scripts to the webmail page [S1][S5]. The final-stage backdoor opens a WebSocket channel; its single command, get('URL'), makes the victim's browser request a URL from the webmail server and return the response, which lets the server read email and attachments [S5][S2]. Related scripts stole cookies and webmail session keys and spread via victims' email signatures [S2]. Trend Micro reported the XSS flaw was fixed in January 2020, so only unpatched servers remained exposed [S2]. Python malware compiled as Windows executables was found to be shellcode loaders for code likely Cobalt Strike [S5].

diamond.adversary: Unnamed actor tracked by Trend Micro as Earth Wendigo; no sponsor stated in sources [S2].
diamond.capability: XSS injection into webmail, Service Worker persistence, WebSocket-driven browser-side email theft, obfuscated JavaScript lures, Python Cobalt Strike-style loaders [S2][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Attacker servers delivering follow-on scripts and a WebSocket server directing the victim browser [S2][S5]; specific domains and IPs not captured here.
diamond.victim: Taiwanese government, research institutions and universities; separately politicians and activists tied to Tibet, Uyghur region and Hong Kong causes [S1][S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Email collection against Taiwanese institutions and Tibet/Uyghur/Hong Kong supporters; no sponsor stated in sources.
diamond.technology: Unpatched webmail with an XSS flaw, and browser Service Worker capability, which let the actor persist and read mail from inside the victim's authenticated session [S2][S5].

gaps: Trend Micro's report was not opened directly (fetch failed); details come from search-result summaries of it and from SecurityWeek/Cyble coverage that was not individually fetched [S1][S5].
The webmail product is not named in the retrieved material.
No aliases or MITRE ATT&CK group ID found; no Microsoft name mapping checked.
No activity after January 2021 found in the searches run.
Indicators (domains, IPs, hashes) not captured.
Overlap with other China-nexus clusters was not assessed by Trend Micro per the retrieved text [S2].
No state or country attribution was confirmed; earlier aggregator (Malpedia/MISP) China labels could not be verified and were removed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Browser-accessed webmail and the user sessions inside it are key terrain; Taiwanese government and academic mail holds the target data [S1][S2]. STEP 2: The actor exploited a known webmail XSS that was patched in January 2020, so unpatched web applications are the exposed seam [S2]. STEP 3: Template is lure email, then XSS or Service Worker, then WebSocket browser proxy, then bulk mail retrieval from inside the authenticated session, which leaves little endpoint malware [S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued email collection against Taiwanese public-sector and academic organizations. MDCOA, speculative and not stated in sources, would be the same technique against allied or coalition webmail used during a Taiwan contingency. Candidate indicators: unexpected Service Worker registrations on webmail origins, WebSocket connections from webmail pages to unfamiliar hosts, obfuscated script in search-suggestion or signature fields [S2][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track web-application patch status for any webmail used by partner or coalition staff; the reported flaw was an old, fixed vulnerability [S2]. (2) Authorities: browser-side email theft occurs on partner or host-nation systems, so coordination runs through the owning organization, not US-controlled networks. (3) Mission assurance: treat webmail as untrusted for sensitive planning traffic where webmail patching cannot be verified. (4) Coordination: share indicators such as Service Worker and WebSocket anomalies with partner CERTs; attribution is unsettled, so prioritize detection over naming.

provenance.importedSummary: Earth Wendigo is a threat actor from China that has been targeting several organizations — including government organizations, research institutions, and universities in Taiwan — since May 2019, aiming to exfiltrate emails from targeted organizations via the injection of JavaScript backdoors to a webmail system that is widely used in Taiwan. The threat actor also sent spear-phishing emails embedded with malicious links to multiple individuals, including politicians and activists, who support movements in Tibet, the Uyghur region, or Hong Kong.

identification.summary: Edalat-e Ali (Ali's Justice; also spelled Edalate Ali, Adalat Ali) is an anti-government hacktivist persona that has leaked security-camera footage and internal documents from Iranian prisons and the judiciary and has interrupted Iranian state broadcasts [S1][S3][S4][S5][S6]. RFE/RL reports the group describes itself as made up of Iranians living and working inside Iran, intent on exposing alleged human rights abuses and seeking the release of political prisoners; this is a self-description, not independently verified [S6].
identification.firstObserved: August 2021 (leak of Evin prison CCTV footage, the earliest incident in the sources gathered) [S1].
identification.notes: Name means 'Ali's Justice'. Not a Microsoft-named actor and no MITRE ATT&CK group. Do not merge with the separate January 2022 'EvilPlayout' intrusion into IRIB documented by Check Point, which that report does not attribute to this group [S7].

attribution.confidence: No government or vendor attribution of Edalat-e Ali to a state sponsor was found in the sources gathered. The group claims to be domestic Iranians opposed to the regime [S6]; this is unverified.
attribution.basis: Group's own claims and statements relayed by media (Iran International, RFE/RL) [S2][S3][S6]. Iranian officials confirmed the authenticity of the Evin footage [S1], and Tasnim acknowledged the October 2022 broadcast was 'hacked for a few moments by anti-revolutionary agents' [S4].

actors.objectives: Expose alleged human rights abuses and judicial repression inside Iran, embarrass Iranian officials and state media, and encourage antigovernment protest [S1][S2][S4][S5][S6].

sectors: State broadcasting (IRIB streaming platform and news channel, state TV and radio)
targeting.notes: Evin prison CCTV footage released August 2021 [S1]; Ghezel Hesar prison videos and documents sent to Iran International in February 2022 [S3]; Telewebion live stream during an Iran-UAE football match on 2022-02-01 [S2]; state TV evening news on 2022-10-08 [S4]; Revolution Day speech by President Raisi on 2023-02-11 [S5]; judicial case-management documents released February 2024 [S6].

capabilities.summary: The sources show access to internal CCTV systems and prison computers (Evin, Ghezel Hesar), a judiciary case-management system holding more than 3 million documents (per the group's claim), and the ability to insert video and audio into live streams or broadcasts for seconds to about a minute [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5][S6]. Initial access methods, tooling and infrastructure are not described in the sources gathered. For October 2022, a state broadcaster spokesman said the incident was not a hack but internal 'vandalism and infiltration', so the technical means in that case are disputed [S4].

campaigns.name: Evin prison CCTV leak
campaigns.summary: Leaked videos from Tehran's Evin prison cameras showing guard abuse of prisoners were published by outside media starting 22 August 2021; Iran's prison chief acknowledged 'unacceptable behaviours' on 24 August and the judiciary later said cases were opened against guards. Hackers said the breach occurred months earlier.

campaigns.name: Telewebion live-stream hijack
campaigns.summary: Group interrupted the live stream of the state broadcaster's web platform during an Iran-UAE football match with a message urging protest.

campaigns.name: Ghezel Hesar prison leak
campaigns.summary: Group sent videos, files and prison documents to Iran International to demonstrate it had accessed Ghezel Hesar prison computers; documents reportedly listed prisoners arrested in the November 2019 protests.

campaigns.name: State TV news interruption
campaigns.summary: Evening news was briefly replaced with an image of Khamenei with crosshairs and flames and the text 'The blood of our youths is on your hands'; Tasnim acknowledged a brief hack while a broadcaster spokesman called it internal vandalism.

campaigns.name: Revolution Day speech disruption
campaigns.summary: Group disrupted the online broadcast of President Raisi's Revolution Day speech for about a minute, called for withdrawing money from government banks and joining protests on 16 February.

campaigns.name: Judiciary case-management leak
campaigns.summary: Group published a large set of documents from the judiciary's case management system, including Revolutionary Court Branch 26 material that RFE/RL says appears to show actions against Persian-language journalists abroad.

diamond.adversary: Self-described domestic anti-government hacktivists; membership, leadership and any outside support unknown [S6].
diamond.capability: Access to CCTV and internal prison and judiciary systems and to live broadcast or streaming feeds; exact techniques not reported [S1][S3][S5][S6].
diamond.victim: Iranian prisons, the judiciary, and state broadcasters (IRIB-related platforms and channels) [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Opposition to the Iranian government, timed to protest movements and national events such as Revolution Day and the 2022 protest wave [S4][S5][S6].
diamond.technology: Surveillance camera systems, prison and court IT systems, and live streaming or playout paths for state media [S1][S2][S5][S6].

gaps: Initial access, tools and infrastructure are not documented in the sources gathered; no technical report on this group was found.
Group identity, size and any state or foreign backing are unverified; only the group's self-description is available [S6].

Relationship to other Iranian opposition personas is unclear. One search summary stated that another hacktivist group, Tapandegan, promoted the Evin footage and credited Edalat-e Ali; the primary article was not opened.
An earlier debut action against Mashhad airport in May 2018 was mentioned in a search summary from a threat-intel profile; it was not confirmed in a source opened here.
Dates for the Evin hack itself are inconsistent across reports; only the leak date (August 2021) is supported [S1].
Whether the October 2022 incident was an external hack or insider action is disputed [S4].
Whether the group is linked to the January 2022 IRIB 'EvilPlayout' intrusion: Check Point's report treats that separately and no link is supported [S7].

Most pages could not be opened directly (fetch failures); several claims rest on search-result summaries of Iran International, RFE/RL, Al Jazeera and Check Point pages. Imported leads (Security Affairs, Hackread) were not read in full.
No Microsoft name or MITRE ATT&CK mapping exists for this group.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Iranian state broadcast chains, prison CCTV networks and judiciary case-management systems are the terrain the group has reached [S1][S3][S4][S6]. STEP 2: The actor is anti-regime and domestic by its own claim, so it is a regime-internal security problem, not a threat to US or coalition networks, based on the sources gathered [S6]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is access to an internal system, a later timed release or broadcast interruption tied to protests or national events, and delivery of material to diaspora media [S3][S5][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is further leaks and short broadcast disruptions timed to protest anniversaries and state events. MDCOA is a longer-duration takeover of broadcast or streaming systems during a crisis. Candidate indicators are unannounced protest-timing calls on social media, group logos on streams, and document dumps sent to Persian-language outlets [S2][S5][S6]. For US planners the main value is as an indicator of Iranian regime internal stability and information control, and as a source of open-source reporting; it is not a validated threat to DoD systems.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track the group's claims through open media and treat them as unverified until confirmed by officials or corroborating reporting, as with the Evin footage [S1][S6]. (2) Authorities: any US action touching this actor or Iranian networks would need separate legal review; the sources give no basis for operational action. (3) Mission assurance: no direct impact on US systems is shown in the sources. (4) Coordination: share notable disruptions with regional and IW or influence-analysis cells because activity is timed to political events [S4][S5].

provenance.importedSummary: Edalat-e Ali is a hacktivist group known for disrupting Iranian state-run TV and radio transmissions during significant events, such as the Revolution Day ceremonies. They have also targeted government facilities, releasing security camera footage to expose abuses and draw attention to human rights violations. The group has used their hacks to call for protests against the Iranian regime and have displayed anti-government messages during their disruptions. Edalat-e Ali has been active in releasing sensitive information and footage to embarrass Iranian officials and highlight injustices within the country.

identification.summary: Educated Manticore is Check Point Research's name for an Iranian-aligned activity cluster first publicly reported in April 2023, which Check Point said overlaps strongly with Phosphorus (Microsoft: Mint Sandstorm) [S2]. It used the PowerLess backdoor delivered through ISO images with Iraq-themed decoys in Arabic, English and Hebrew [S2]. In June 2025 Check Point reported the cluster running spear-phishing against Israeli journalists, cybersecurity experts and computer science professors [S4][S5].
identification.firstObserved: Publicly reported by Check Point Research in 2023-04 [S2]. Earlier activity date not stated in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: Check Point tracks this as a cluster, not a named state unit. In 2023 it said it lacked sufficient knowledge to place PowerLess activity within the wider Iranian landscape and so gave it its own name [S2]. In 2025 Check Point said the cluster aligns with activity the wider community tracks as APT42, Charming Kitten or Mint Sandstorm [S5]. Other vendor names for the broader Phosphorus family cited in coverage: APT35, TA453, Cobalt Illusion, ITG18, Yellow Garuda [S2]. Do not merge facts from those clusters into this record without cluster-specific sourcing.

attribution.sponsor: Iran. Check Point says the cluster is believed to work for the IRGC Intelligence Organization (IRGC-IO) [S5].
attribution.confidence: Check Point (2023) described strong overlap with Phosphorus/Mint Sandstorm but declined to fully attribute the activity [S2]. Check Point (2025) stated the IRGC-IO assessment as a belief [S5]. No government attribution found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Check Point tooling and infrastructure analysis (PowerLess backdoor, ISO lures, phishing kits) as relayed in secondary coverage; I could not open the Check Point reports directly [S2][S4][S5].

actors.objectives: Espionage and credential theft against Israel-linked individuals and the research community, including academics and cybersecurity experts [S2][S4][S5]. Specific collection requirements are not stated in the sources gathered.

sectors: Technology sector (executives and researchers impersonated as lures)
targeting.notes: 2023: decoy content from the Arab Science and Technology Foundation led Check Point to conclude the research community may have been targeted [S2]. 2025: victims included Israeli journalists, high-profile cybersecurity experts and computer science professors from leading Israeli universities; Check Point cautioned that the true scope is likely wider geographically and by industry [S5][S6].

capabilities.summary: 2023: updated PowerLess backdoor delivered via ISO images (and possibly other archives) carrying an Iraq-themed lure and a custom in-memory downloader; loaders used .NET executables built as Mixed Mode Assemblies, a technique Check Point called rarely seen in the wild [S2]. Check Point noted at the time that attacks resulting from these infections had not yet been observed [S2]. 2025: spear-phishing by email and WhatsApp using fictitious assistants to technology executives or researchers; initial messages contained no links; victims were steered to fake Gmail login pages or Google Meet invitations, some hosted on Google Sites pages mimicking Meet [S5][S6]. The phishing kits were React single page applications with minified, obfuscated code and supported Google password, SMS, email-code and app-based 2FA flows, enabling real-time relay of MFA tokens [S6]. Check Point reported messages appeared AI-assisted and that the group used more than 130 unique domains, one or two per targeted individual (per press quoting a Check Point researcher) [S5][S6].

campaigns.name: PowerLess ISO campaign against Israel-linked targets
campaigns.summary: Check Point reported an improved arsenal: ISO-delivered lures in Arabic, English and Hebrew with Iraq-related academic decoys, an in-memory downloader, and the PowerLess implant loaded through Mixed Mode Assembly .NET binaries [S2].

campaigns.name: Spear-phishing of Israeli technology academics, journalists and cybersecurity experts
campaigns.summary: Email and WhatsApp approaches by impersonated assistants led to fake Gmail or Google Meet pages and a React SPA kit that harvested credentials and 2FA codes, supported by 130+ domains [S4][S5][S6].

diamond.adversary: Iran-aligned cluster; Check Point believes it works for IRGC-IO and overlaps APT42/Charming Kitten/Mint Sandstorm [S2][S5].
diamond.capability: PowerLess backdoor, ISO lures, Mixed Mode Assembly loaders (2023); AI-assisted social engineering, WhatsApp/email approach, React SPA phishing kit with 2FA relay (2025) [S2][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: More than 130 domains and numerous subdomains, one or two per targeted individual, per press quoting Check Point; fake Gmail and Google Meet pages, Google Sites lures [S5][S6].
diamond.victim: Israeli academics, journalists, cybersecurity experts and researchers [S2][S5][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection against Israel-linked individuals; Check Point's 2025 report is covered by press alongside Iran-Israel tension, but that framing is the outlets', not a stated Check Point objective [S5].
diamond.technology: Consumer cloud identity (Google accounts, Gmail, Meet), WhatsApp messaging, and MFA that can be relayed in real time [S6].

gaps: I could not open the Check Point primary reports (2023 and 2025) or the Check Point blog from this environment; findings rely on search-result summaries of Check Point and secondary coverage. Verify details against research.checkpoint.com before use [S4].
Whether 2023 infections led to follow-on intrusions is not stated; Check Point said none had been observed at the time [S2].
Exact relationship to APT42, APT35/Charming Kitten and Mint Sandstorm is only characterized as overlap or alignment; Microsoft's own mapping of this cluster was not located.
Earliest activity date, malware C2 details, victim counts and any non-Israeli targeting are not available in the sources gathered.
The 130+ domain figure comes from press quoting a Check Point researcher; the figure and indicator list were not verified against the report.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is personal and institutional identity (Google accounts, WhatsApp) of researchers, academics and cyber experts who sit near government and defense work. STEP 2: The actor uses one or two disposable domains per victim and AI-polished, link-free first contact, which defeats blocklists and early filtering [S5][S6]. STEP 3: Template is rapport-building through an impersonated assistant, then a fake Gmail or Meet page that relays passwords and MFA codes [S6]; earlier template was ISO, in-memory downloader, PowerLess [S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued credential harvesting against Israel-linked experts and academics. MDCOA is extension of the same approach to allied-government or DoD-adjacent researchers and contractors, using personal accounts as a path to institutional data. Candidate indicators: unsolicited WhatsApp or email contact from unknown technology-sector assistants, newly registered per-target domains, Google Meet or Gmail lookalike pages, and ISO files arriving as lures [S2][S5][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: personal-account and messaging-app phishing against personnel and affiliated researchers sits outside most enterprise telemetry; add reporting channels for it. (2) Authorities: monitoring personal accounts is constrained; rely on awareness training, voluntary reporting and partner sharing rather than collection. (3) Mission assurance: prefer phishing-resistant MFA, since the kit relays SMS, email-code and app-based 2FA in real time [S6]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with Israeli and allied CERTs and industry partners, noting that vendor cluster boundaries (APT42, Charming Kitten, Mint Sandstorm) are not identical.

provenance.importedSummary: Educated Manticore is an Iranian APT group aligned with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, primarily engaged in espionage targeting government, military, and academic sectors. The group employs spear-phishing tactics, utilizing custom backdoors like POWERLESS and phishing kits designed as SPAs to harvest credentials. Their operations have included impersonating credible figures to lure victims and using ISO images to initiate infection chains. Educated Manticore's activities are characterized by rapid domain setup and aggressive spear-phishing campaigns, particularly against Israeli individuals.

identification.summary: Elderwood is the name Symantec gave in September 2012 to a systematic espionage group that reused components of an infrastructure it called the 'Elderwood platform' and that Symantec tracked back to the 2009 Operation Aurora attacks on Google and other companies [S1][S2]. Symantec reported the group had exploited at least eight zero-day vulnerabilities since late 2010, all in Internet Explorer or Adobe Flash Player, and that it was moving from spear-phishing toward watering-hole attacks against defense supply chain targets [S2][S6]. Symantec tied a December 2012 Internet Explorer zero-day (CVE-2012-4792) served from the Council on Foreign Relations website to the same group [S6][S7]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as G0066, a suspected Chinese cyber espionage group reportedly responsible for Operation Aurora [S8].
identification.firstObserved: 2009: Symantec tracks the group back to the 2009 Operation Aurora attacks [S2].
identification.notes: Symantec says the name comes from a source-code variable used by the attackers [S2]. Malpedia lists Elderwood, Elderwood Gang, G0066, SIG22 and SNEAKY PANDA; MITRE lists Elderwood Gang, Beijing Group and Sneaky Panda [S8]. No Microsoft Typhoon/Storm name was found for this cluster in the sources gathered. Symantec separately named 'Hidden Lynx' in 2013 and linked it to Aurora through shared malware; CrowdStrike tracked that group as 'Aurora Panda'. These are distinct vendor clusters from Elderwood/Sneaky Panda and should not be merged without primary evidence [S9].

attribution.sponsor: Suspected People's Republic of China. Google stated the Aurora attacks originated in China [S2]; MITRE describes Elderwood as a suspected Chinese cyber espionage group [S8].
attribution.confidence: Symantec's 2012 report did not name China or a geographic origin and said only that the group's sophistication probably indicated support from organized crime or a nation state [S2]. MITRE's characterization is 'suspected' [S8]. No US government attribution of the Elderwood cluster by name was found in the sources gathered; 2013 press reporting citing unnamed US officials described the Google breach as by Chinese hackers [S5].
attribution.basis: Symantec analysis of shared infrastructure, packer license and code artifacts (for example a misspelled 'HeapSpary' function) linking successive zero-day campaigns [S2][S6]; MITRE ATT&CK group entry [S8].

actors.objectives: Strategic espionage. Google initially pointed to Gmail accounts of Chinese human rights activists and intellectual property [S5]; US officials later told the Washington Post the Google intrusion reached a database of law-enforcement and FISA surveillance orders, apparently to identify Chinese intelligence operatives under US surveillance [S5]. Symantec reported that the group's primary targets were usually members of the defense supply chain [S2].

sectors: Defense industrial base and defense supply chain manufacturers [S2]
Think tanks / foreign policy organizations (Council on Foreign Relations website) [S6][S7]
regions: United States (Council on Foreign Relations watering hole) [S7]

capabilities.summary: Repeated use of zero-day exploits in Internet Explorer and Adobe Flash Player, at least eight from 2010 to fall 2012 and a ninth (CVE-2012-4792) in December 2012 [S2][S6]. Aurora used an Internet Explorer zero-day (CVE-2010-0249) delivered via spear-phishing links in email and instant messages to drop the Hydraq remote access trojan [S1][S2]. From 2012 the group increasingly used watering-hole (strategic web compromise) attacks, [S2][S7]. Symantec described shared tooling ('Elderwood platform'), a common commercial packer license, and reuse of exploit components across campaigns [S2][S6]. MITRE lists associated software including PoisonIvy, Hydraq, Briba, Naid, Wiarp, Vasport, Pasam, Nerex and Linfo [S8].

campaigns.name: Operation Aurora
campaigns.summary: Intrusions against Google and other companies using the IE zero-day CVE-2010-0249 to install a remote access trojan, described by McAfee in January 2010; Symantec later tied the Elderwood group to these attacks.

campaigns.name: Aurora surveillance-database disclosure
campaigns.summary: Washington Post reporting, citing unnamed US officials, said the Google intruders accessed a database of surveillance orders including FISA orders.

campaigns.name: Elderwood zero-day series
campaigns.summary: Symantec counted at least eight zero-days in IE and Flash Player exploited since late 2010, four in about 16 weeks in spring and summer 2012, mainly against defense supply chain targets.

campaigns.name: CVE-2012-1889 watering hole
campaigns.summary: Symantec linked a June 2012 site serving CVE-2012-1889 with a movie.swf file to the Elderwood Project.

campaigns.name: Symantec 'The Elderwood Project' report
campaigns.summary: Symantec published its report describing the Elderwood platform, the shift to watering-hole attacks, and the defense supply chain focus.

campaigns.name: Council on Foreign Relations watering hole (CVE-2012-4792)
campaigns.summary: The CFR website was compromised to serve an IE 6-8 zero-day; Symantec assessed it as a continuation of the Elderwood Project; Microsoft later issued out-of-band fix MS13-008.

diamond.adversary: Suspected PRC espionage group (Symantec: likely nation-state or organized-crime backed; MITRE: suspected Chinese) [S2][S8].
diamond.capability: Serial IE and Flash zero-days, Hydraq and related backdoors, commercial packer, shared 'Elderwood platform' exploit components [S1][S2][S6][S8].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised legitimate websites used as watering holes (e.g., CFR), spear-phishing links via email and instant message [S1][S7].
diamond.victim: Defense supply chain manufacturers, technology and internet firms (Google), human rights activists and NGOs, think tanks [S2][S5][S7][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on PRC dissidents, US technology and defense IP, and US counterintelligence activity (surveillance orders) [S5].
diamond.technology: Unpatched Internet Explorer 6-8 and Adobe Flash Player on Windows endpoints; trust in frequently visited policy and industry websites [S1][S6][S7].

gaps: Original Symantec 'The Elderwood Project' PDF and Symantec Connect blog could not be opened; details come from search summaries and press coverage of them [S2][S6].
The Washington Post article was not opened directly; reliance is on secondary coverage [S5].
MITRE ATT&CK G0066 page and CFR Cyber Operations Tracker 'Sneaky Panda' entry could not be fetched; alias and description data are from search-result summaries.
No Microsoft threat actor name identified for Elderwood; Microsoft mapping not checked.
Relationship between Elderwood/Sneaky Panda and Symantec's Hidden Lynx / CrowdStrike's Aurora Panda is unresolved; shared Aurora malware does not establish identity [S9].
No public activity explicitly attributed to Elderwood after early 2013 was found; current status is unknown.
No US government attribution naming Elderwood or a specific PRC organization was found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes user endpoints running browsers and plug-ins, and the third-party websites (policy, industry, supplier) that DoD and DIB personnel routinely visit [S7]. STEP 2: Historic reliance on browser and Flash zero-days means patch status alone does not bound the threat; defense supply chain firms are an indirect path to defense programs [S2][S6]. STEP 3: Doctrinal template is strategic web compromise or spear-phishing link, browser exploit, RAT such as Hydraq, then collection of IP and sensitive databases [S1][S2][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent IP theft from DIB suppliers via watering holes. MDCOA is access to counterintelligence or sensitive legal-process data, as reported for the Google surveillance-order database [S5]. Candidate indicators: unexpected script injection on frequently visited partner sites, heap-spray exploit pages targeting legacy browsers, and Hydraq-family beacons [S1][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness should track compromise of external websites frequented by the force, not only DoDIN assets [S7]. (2) Zero-day use means mitigation (browser isolation, plug-in removal) must be pre-authorized rather than waiting on vendor patches [S6]. (3) Mission assurance depends on DIB supplier hygiene; coordinate with DC3 and the DIB CS program when supplier compromise is suspected [S2]. (4) Coordinate with law enforcement and counterintelligence, since the reported Aurora objective included surveillance-order data [S5].

identification.summary: ELECTRIC PANDA is a CrowdStrike adversary name. CrowdStrike presented it in a 2013 CrowdCasts webinar alongside GIBBERISH PANDA and TEST PANDA [S4]. CrowdStrike uses the PANDA suffix for China-based actors [S5]. In April 2020 the name appeared in a US Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) bulletin reported by Politico [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: CrowdStrike CrowdCasts webinar naming the actor: 2013 [S4]. Activity start date is not stated in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: The name is not widely used by other vendors. A report quoted in the Politico coverage says it is not a widely accepted designation for a state-sponsored group [S1]. No source gathered maps ELECTRIC PANDA to a Microsoft name, a MITRE ATT&CK group, or to another vendor's cluster such as APT27 or Emissary Panda. Do not merge it with those clusters.

attribution.sponsor: Chinese government, as attributed by CrowdStrike according to the Politico coverage of the DCSA bulletin [S1]. The name's PANDA suffix is CrowdStrike's convention for China-based actors [S5].
attribution.confidence: The DCSA bulletin, as reported, said activity was from 'highly likely' Electric Panda actors [S1]. This describes confidence that the activity matched the actor, not confidence in state sponsorship. No formal government attribution to a named PRC agency was found.
attribution.basis: CrowdStrike naming [S4][S5]; DCSA bulletin to cleared contractors as relayed by Politico and syndicated coverage [S1][S2]. The underlying bulletin and CrowdStrike technical reporting were not opened.

targeting.notes: Per the DCSA bulletin as relayed by CyberWire summarizing Politico, 38 cleared contractor facilities were targeted since 1 February 2020 and roughly 600 connections were tied to Electric Panda actors; targeted sectors reportedly included health care technology, aerospace, naval and telecommunications [S2]. identification.summary: ELUSIVE COMET is a name used by the Security Alliance (SEAL) for a threat actor that lures cryptocurrency professionals into fake interviews or meetings on Zoom and then gets them to grant remote control of their computer, enabling malware installation and wallet theft [S1][S2][S4].
identification.notes: The earliest dated reporting found is April 2025 (Trail of Bits post of 2025-04-17) [S1]; SEAL's own report date was not retrieved and earlier activity may exist. Vendor-style name; no Microsoft name or MITRE group ID was found in the sources consulted.

attribution.basis: Trail of Bits, as relayed by secondary reporting, linked the methods to the Bybit heist of February 2025, which public reporting attributes to Lazarus (North Korea) [S1][S6]. Other reporting says the campaign resembles activity previously associated with Lazarus but that attribution is unconfirmed [S7]. No government attribution of ELUSIVE COMET itself was found.

actors.objectives: Financial gain: theft of cryptocurrency from individuals and executives, for example more than $100,000 drained from the wallets of Emblem Vault's CEO [S4][S8]. Reporting attributes millions of dollars in losses to the group [S8].

sectors: Venture capital and crypto media (as lure personas)
Cybersecurity vendors (Trail of Bits CEO targeted)
targeting.notes: Known targets named in sources are the Trail of Bits CEO (fake 'Bloomberg Crypto' interview request) and the Emblem Vault CEO [S1][S4]. Geographic scope was not stated in the sources consulted.

capabilities.summary: Social engineering rather than technical exploitation: operators approach targets on X, use Calendly links and Gmail addresses, join Zoom calls under the display name 'Zoom' so the remote-control request looks like a native system prompt, and exploit users habituated to clicking Approve [S1][S2][S9]. In the Emblem Vault case the victim was tricked into allowing a malware install; the payload was reported as GOOPDATE, which gave full device control and exposed credentials and wallets [S4][S10]. The attacker also took over the victim's X account to message contacts with the same scam [S10]. Zoom permits guests to request remote control by default, so success depends on the victim approving [S11].

provenance.importedSummary: ELUSIVE COMET is a threat actor responsible for significant cryptocurrency theft through sophisticated social engineering attacks, particularly leveraging Zoom's remote control feature. Their attack methodology involves manipulating legitimate workflows and exploiting human-centric vulnerabilities rather than technical flaws. The actor employs tactics such as social proof, time pressure, and interface manipulation to deceive targets. Organizations can mitigate risks by implementing technical controls to disable the remote control feature and deploying email boundary protections like DMARC, SPF, and DKIM.

identification.summary: Emerald Sleet (formerly THALLIUM) is a North Korean threat actor that Microsoft says stayed highly active through 2023. It spear-phishes prominent individuals with North Korea expertise and often impersonates academic institutions and NGOs [S1]. Microsoft says it targets diplomats and Korean Peninsula experts in government, think tanks and NGOs, media and education, and assesses the motive as intelligence collection [S2]. Since January 2025 Microsoft has seen the actor trick targets into running PowerShell as administrator and pasting code the actor supplies [S3]. Microsoft and OpenAI also observed it using large language models (LLMs) for reconnaissance, vulnerability research and phishing content [S1][S11].
identification.firstObserved: Kaspersky's 2013 'Kimsuky' report dates the earliest signs of activity to 2013-04-03 and the first Kimsuky Trojan samples to 2013-05-05 [S8]. Microsoft was tracking the group as THALLIUM by 2019 [S4].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Emerald Sleet (formerly THALLIUM). Microsoft says Emerald Sleet overlaps with the actors other researchers call Kimsuky and Velvet Chollima [S1]. Microsoft's naming map lists THALLIUM, VELVET CHOLLIMA, RGB-D5, Black Banshee, Kimsuky and Greendinosa as other names. It lists APT43 and Konni separately, under Opal Sleet [S5]. Material that vendors publish under Kimsuky, Springtail [S10] or TA427 [S9] is mapped to this record by alias, and boundaries may not match Microsoft's exactly. Mandiant's APT43 reporting is not merged here because Microsoft maps APT43 to Opal Sleet [S5]. MITRE tracks the group as Kimsuky (G0094) [S14].

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea. US Treasury describes Kimsuky as subordinate to the Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB), the DPRK's primary foreign intelligence service [S7]. A May 2024 FBI, State Department and NSA advisory says Kimsuky is administratively subordinate to the 63rd Research Center, an element of the RGB [S6].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft calls Emerald Sleet a 'North Korean state actor' [S3]. In 2019 Microsoft said THALLIUM is 'believed to operate from North Korea' [S4]. US Treasury sanctioned Kimsuky as an RGB-subordinate entity on 2023-11-30 [S7]. These government statements name Kimsuky, which Microsoft maps to Emerald Sleet [S5]. Kaspersky's 2013 report only surmised North Korean origin from target profiles, Korean-language compile paths and registrant names [S8].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and actor tracking, joint Microsoft and OpenAI LLM-abuse research, and a 2019 civil court action [S1][S2][S3][S4]. US Treasury designation [S7]. Joint FBI, State Department and NSA advisory [S6]. Vendor technical reporting from Kaspersky, Proofpoint and Symantec [S8][S9][S10].

actors.objectives: Microsoft assesses the motive as intelligence collection on North Korea-related policy, gathered from diplomats and Korean Peninsula experts [S2]. Through LLM-informed reconnaissance, the actor sought out think tanks, government organizations and experts focused on North Korean defense issues or its nuclear weapons program [S1]. Its 2022 impersonation campaign asked North Korea experts for their views on security issues and offered payment to review a document on the North Korean nuclear program [S12]. The 2024 joint US advisory describes Kimsuky posing as journalists, academics and East Asia experts to collect information for the regime [S6].

sectors: Government agencies and services, including diplomats [S2][S3]
Individuals working in international affairs, especially Northeast Asia [S3]
Nuclear non-proliferation, world-peace and human-rights organizations and experts [S4]
regions: North America, South America, Europe and East Asia (2025 PowerShell campaign) [S3]
United States, Japan and South Korea (2019 THALLIUM targets) [S4]
South Korea (2013 Kimsuky campaign; 2024 Gomir and GoBear activity) [S8][S10]
targeting.notes: Microsoft's victim set centers on people with North Korea or Northeast Asia expertise rather than on infrastructure [S1][S2][S3]. Treasury describes the group's targets as government, research and media figures, mainly in South Korea, Japan and the US [S7].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering is the core capability. The actor builds rapport over time while posing as officials, journalists, academics or think-tank staff, then sends spear-phishing emails [S1][S3][S6][S9][S12]. In 2019, THALLIUM's spoofed Microsoft-themed credential phishing led to mailbox access and forwarding rules that sent new mail to actor-controlled accounts [S4]. From December 2023 the group abused lax DMARC policies to spoof personas, and from February 2024 it added web beacons to profile targets [S6][S9]. In 2025 it ran ClickFix-style lures: victims were told to paste PowerShell as administrator, which installed a browser-based remote desktop tool and registered the device for actor access [S3]. Proofpoint saw similar lures deliver QuasarRAT [S13]. Its malware includes Linux (Gomir) and Windows (GoBear) backdoors spread through trojanized South Korean software installers [S10]. The 2013 Kimsuky malware included a module for stealing HWP documents [S8]. LLM use covers vulnerability research (CVE-2022-30190), basic scripting, phishing content and reconnaissance [S1][S11].

diamond.adversary: DPRK state actor tracked by Microsoft as Emerald Sleet (THALLIUM), which US Treasury and a joint US advisory place under the RGB [S3][S6][S7].
diamond.capability: Rapport-building spear-phishing and impersonation, credential phishing with mail-forwarding rules, PowerShell paste-and-run lures, remote desktop tooling, QuasarRAT, GoBear and Gomir backdoors, and LLM-assisted reconnaissance [S1][S3][S4][S10][S13].
diamond.infrastructure: Typosquatted and Microsoft-lookalike domains (50 seized in 2019), spoofed sender domains with weak DMARC policies, free webmail personas, web beacons, and remote servers that host certificates and register devices [S3][S4][S9].
diamond.victim: Diplomats, Korean Peninsula and Northeast Asia experts, think tanks, NGOs, government, media and academia in the US, South Korea, Japan, Europe and the Americas [S2][S3][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection on foreign policy toward the DPRK, nuclear issues and Korean Peninsula security in support of the regime [S1][S2][S6].
diamond.technology: Email trust (DMARC misconfiguration, sender spoofing), cloud mailbox rules, Windows PowerShell with administrator rights, and South Korean security and PKI software installers [S3][S4][S6][S10].

gaps: Cluster boundary: Microsoft maps APT43 and Konni to Opal Sleet, not Emerald Sleet, while many vendors treat APT43 and Kimsuky as one actor. Mandiant APT43 reporting, including cybercrime self-funding, is excluded until reconciled [S5].
Proofpoint TA427 and Symantec Springtail findings are mapped here by alias; neither source confirms the boundary matches Microsoft's Emerald Sleet [S9][S10].

The primary documents could not be opened: the IC3/FBI May 2024 advisory and the Treasury press release (blocked), plus the Microsoft On the Issues 2019 post, the Proofpoint blog and Kaspersky Securelist (DNS failures). Content is taken from search snippets and press coverage.
The full Microsoft write-up of the 2025 PowerShell tactic was seen only as an X thread summary. Victim counts and outcomes are not public.
No public reporting gathered here shows Emerald Sleet targeting US military networks or conducting disruptive operations.
An unverified search summary claims QR-code credential phishing by Emerald Sleet in May 2025; no primary source was found, so it is excluded.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): The key terrain is people, not networks: personal and work email of policy, diplomatic, academic and think-tank staff working on Korean Peninsula issues, plus organizational email domains with weak DMARC policies [S2][S3][S6]. STEP 2 (effects): Spoofed trusted personas undermine email-based trust. Compromised mailboxes with forwarding rules give persistent collection without implants [S4][S9]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Benign rapport-building email from a spoofed expert or official, then a lure (PDF, 'secure document', or 'device registration'), then credential capture or PowerShell paste-and-run, then remote desktop or RAT, then mail and document collection [S3][S4][S13]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection against DPRK-policy, nuclear and alliance-planning experts through impersonation and paste-and-run lures [S1][S3]. MDCOA is the compromise of a planner or liaison mailbox that gives sustained access to exercise, alliance or nuclear-policy correspondence [S4][S6]. Candidate indicators include unsolicited expert or official outreach that escalates to document review requests, instructions to run PowerShell as administrator, new inbox forwarding rules, spoofed domains failing DMARC alignment, and web-beacon tracking pixels in first-contact emails [S3][S4][S6][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Track Emerald Sleet lure themes and personas, such as South Korean officials, Japanese diplomats and think-tank staff. Monitor for PowerShell-as-admin and remote-desktop registration events and mailbox-rule changes [S3][S4][S9][S13]. Authorities: Most victims are civilian think tanks, academics and personal accounts outside the DODIN. Response relies on FBI and partner notification and on private-sector actions such as Microsoft's 2019 civil domain seizure and its account disablement with OpenAI [S1][S4][S6]. Mission assurance: Enforce DMARC quarantine or reject on mission-partner domains, restrict PowerShell for standard users, and train staff who handle Korean Peninsula topics to verify unsolicited expert contact out of band [S3][S6]. Coordination: Share indicators with USFK and INDOPACOM stakeholders and with ROK and Japanese partners, which mirrored the 2023 sanctions, and with industry reporters such as Microsoft and Proofpoint [S7][S9].

provenance.importedSummary: • APT43 is a prolific cyber operator that supports the interests of the North Korean regime. The group combines moderately-sophisticated technical capabilities with aggressive social engineering tactics, especially against South Korean and U.S.-based government organizations, academics, and think tanks focused on Korean peninsula geopolitical issues. • In addition to its espionage campaigns, we believe APT43 funds itself through cybercrime operations to support its primary mission of collecting strategic intelligence. • The group creates numerous spoofed and fraudulent personas for use in social engineering, as well as cover identities for purchasing operational tooling and infrastructure. • APT43 has collaborated with other North Korean espionage operators on multiple operations, underscoring the major role APT43 plays in the regime’s cyber apparatus.
