identification.summary: Check Point describes EvilWeb as a pro-Russian hacktivist group created in March 2024 that targeted American and European entities in support of the Russian narrative, using a hack-and-leak method in parallel with traditional DDoS attacks [S1]. It claimed to have obtained data from various high-profile American organizations [S1]. Its Telegram channel had 1,146 members as of 2024-09-03 [S1].
identification.notes: Do not confuse with Evil Corp (Indrik Spider), a separate financially motivated Russian cybercrime group; the name similarity is coincidental in the sources reviewed. A Russian-language wiki entry (cyclowiki) names a leader 'Levis'; this was not corroborated and is not used. Malpedia lists the group under a Russia country tag [S5].

attribution.basis: Check Point characterizes the group only as 'pro-Russian' [S1]; Malpedia tags it Russia [S5]. No reviewed source ties it to a Russian government organization, and none is asserted here.

actors.objectives: Check Point states the group acted in support of the Russian narrative [S1]. During #FreeDurov it joined a campaign demanding release of Telegram founder Pavel Durov after his arrest in France [S1][S2].

targeting.notes: Check Point says EvilWeb targeted various American and European entities and claimed data from high-profile American organizations [S1]. The #FreeDurov campaign as a whole targeted more than 50 French targets, primarily with DDoS [S1]; specific sectors hit by EvilWeb itself could not be confirmed from accessible text.

capabilities.summary: The group operates a hack-and-leak model alongside conventional DDoS attacks [S1]. It publicizes claims via a Telegram channel [S1]. Strobes notes no exploited CVEs attributed to it (secondary, undated; not cited as fact). Claimed data thefts were not independently verified in the sources reviewed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Environment: EvilWeb is a low-sophistication, publicity-driven hacktivist actor aligned with Russian narratives that targets US and European entities [S1]. MLCOA: opportunistic DDoS and claimed hack-and-leak against Western public-facing sites when geopolitical triggers arise, as with #FreeDurov, which saw 50+ French targets hit mainly by DDoS [S1], with limited disruption [S2][S3]. MDCOA: leak of genuine data from a US organization amplified by pro-Russian channels [S1]. Candidate indicators: Telegram announcements joining named operations (#Free... hashtags), target lists, and claimed leak posts [S1]. Evidence is thin; reassess if new reporting emerges.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: monitor open-source Telegram claims by hacktivist groups, noting claims can be exaggerated and impact is often minimal [S2][S3]. Authorities: monitoring public channels is open-source collection; any defensive response to DDoS on civilian sites follows owner/operator and national cyber authorities. Mission assurance: ensure public-facing DoD web services have DDoS mitigation and verify leak claims before attributing to compromise. Coordination: share indicators with sector and law-enforcement partners; no sourced basis for further specifics.

identification.summary: Femwar02 is a name given in media and threat-intelligence aggregator reporting to an apparently pro-Russian ransomware actor linked to the February 2026 ransomware attack on Sapienza University of Rome. [S2][S4][S5] Italian press (Corriere della Sera, as relayed by trade media) said the attack used the Bablock (Rorschach) ransomware and may be connected to Femwar02; the university has not confirmed this. [S2][S4] Strobes and Malpedia list no campaigns before the Sapienza incident. [S5][S6]
identification.notes: The Femwar02 link rests on press reporting and aggregator entries, not on an official attribution or a vendor technical report that I could open. [S2][S4] The official university notice does not name the ransomware strain or group. [S7] Bablock/Rorschach is a separate malware family first documented by Check Point and Group-IB in 2023 and used against victims before 2026, so the malware does not by itself identify this actor. [S8][S9]

attribution.confidence: Low. Attribution to Femwar02 and Bablock is media-reported and unconfirmed by the university or Italian authorities in the sources reviewed. [S2][S4]
attribution.basis: Corriere della Sera reportedly tied the attack to Bablock and possibly to Femwar02. [S2][S4] Aggregator and Malpedia-style entries describe the actor as pro-Russian, citing that the malware leaves Russian-language files unencrypted; I could not verify that behavior in a primary technical report. [S5][S6] No state sponsor is named in any source reviewed.

actors.objectives: Not established. The ransom link with a 72-hour countdown reported after the Sapienza attack suggests financial extortion as at least a stated aim, though that detail is reported as alleged. [S2][S3]

targeting.notes: The only incident attributed to Femwar02 in the sources is Sapienza University of Rome, beginning 2026-02-02 per press reporting (the university's later notice dates the attack 2026-02-01). [S1][S2][S5][S7] The university later said about 400 physical and virtual servers were affected, disrupting institutional portals and the InfoStud platform, with data on affected systems encrypted. [S7] Separately, Group-IB reported that Bablock/Rorschach as a malware family hit organizations in several countries including Italy; that is family-level, not Femwar02-specific. [S9]

capabilities.summary: Reporting on the Sapienza case describes Bablock/Rorschach ransomware with hybrid encryption, partial file encryption and Group Policy propagation. [S4][S5][S6] Check Point's 2023 analysis of Rorschach found code similarities to leaked Babuk source and LockBit 2.0 (I/O completion port thread scheduling), ransom notes inspired by Yanluowang and DarkSide, and loading via DLL side-loading of a Palo Alto Cortex XDR Dump Service Tool. [S8] Check Point reported very fast encryption in controlled tests. [S8][S9] Initial access vector for Sapienza is not reported in the sources reviewed.

provenance.importedSummary: Femwar02 is a previously unknown pro-Russian ransomware threat actor that emerged in early 2026, linked to a major cyberattack on Italy's Sapienza University of Rome in February 2026, which caused a full network shutdown and operational disruptions. The group deploys Bablock (also known as Rorschach), a next-generation ransomware strain first identified in 2023 that features fast hybrid encryption (curve25519 and hc-128), partial file encryption for speed, direct system calls to evade detection, and domain-wide propagation via Group Policy on Windows Domain Controllers. Bablock shares code similarities with LockBit 2.0 but incorporates elements from other families like Babuk and DarkSide, often delivered via encrypted payloads, DLL sideloading with tools like DarkLoader, and exploits such as those in Zimbra or phishing. Notably, the malware skips encrypting files written in Russian, reinforcing its pro-Russian alignment, with no prior attributions or campaigns documented before the Sapienza incident.

identification.summary: Ferocious Kitten is the name Kaspersky gave to an Iran-based espionage actor. Kaspersky says it has run surveillance against Persian-speaking individuals inside Iran since at least 2015 [S1][S2]. The group uses Persian-language Office decoy documents with malicious macros to install a custom Windows implant, MarkiRAT [S1][S2][S3]. MarkiRAT records keystrokes and clipboard content, uploads and downloads files, and runs arbitrary commands. Some variants hijack the Telegram and Chrome applications to stay persistent [S2][S4]. In July 2026 Recorded Future linked a new cluster, TAG-182, to MarkiRAT distribution through fake VPN and media-player apps. It cited tradecraft overlaps with Ferocious Kitten but did not assess an organizational link [S6].
identification.firstObserved: Kaspersky traced MarkiRAT activity back to at least 2015 [S1][S2]. The actor became publicly known in June 2021 after a lure document uploaded to VirusTotal in March 2021 was highlighted on Twitter [S2][S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft has no name for this actor: 'Ferocious Kitten' does not appear in Microsoft's public naming map as retrieved on 2026-10-15 [S8]. MITRE tracks the group as G0137 and lists BITSAdmin and MarkiRAT as its software [S7]. Kaspersky says some TTPs resemble those of Domestic Kitten (C2 domains reused for years) and Rampant Kitten (Telegram execution hijacking and KeePass data theft). These are TTP similarities, not shared attribution [S1][S4]. Recorded Future's TAG-182 is a separate cluster with overlapping tooling. Keep it distinct from Ferocious Kitten [S6].

attribution.sponsor: Iran (vendor assessment). Kaspersky describes the actor as appearing to be based in Iran and conducting domestic surveillance [S1][S4]. Recorded Future assesses that the related TAG-182 cluster is almost certainly an element of Iran's state surveillance apparatus [S6].
attribution.confidence: Kaspersky's assessment rests on victimology and on similarity to other Iran-focused surveillance actors, and its reporting names no sponsoring Iranian organization [S1][S2]. Recorded Future says its TAG-182/Ferocious Kitten overlaps support an operational connection, but more evidence is needed to judge whether the two clusters are organizationally linked [S6]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Persian-language lures that depict anti-regime protests or resistance camps [S2]; payloads built for software popular in Iran (Telegram, Psiphon) [S2][S3]; long-term C2 reuse and Telegram hijacking similar to Domestic Kitten and Rampant Kitten [S1][S4]; overlapping BITS job strings, file-naming patterns and C2 configurations between TAG-182 and historical MarkiRAT activity [S6].

actors.objectives: Domestic surveillance of Persian speakers, especially people tied to opposition or anti-regime activity, including theft of credentials, keystrokes, clipboard content and files [S1][S2][S3]. Recorded Future assesses that TAG-182 also targets Iranians abroad [S6].

sectors: Users of censorship-circumvention tools (Psiphon, VPN apps) and Telegram
regions: Iranian diaspora / anti-government movements abroad (TAG-182, per Recorded Future) [S6]
targeting.notes: Kaspersky's victim set is Persian-speaking individuals who appear to be in Iran [S1]. Lures pose as images or videos of protests or resistance camps against the Iranian government [S2]. TAG-182 promotes its malicious downloads through Instagram posts and staged websites [S6]. No government, military or DIB victims are reported in the cited sources.

capabilities.summary: Initial access through spearphishing Office documents with malicious macros, disguised as images or videos [S2][S7]. MarkiRAT records keystrokes and clipboard content, transfers files and runs commands [S2]. Picus also lists screenshots, file-system searches for target file types and credential stores, and staged exfiltration over HTTP(S) [S9]. Some MarkiRAT variants hijack the Telegram and Chrome launchers to stay persistent [S2][S4]. One variant is a backdoored build of the Psiphon circumvention VPN [S3][S4]. The group uses Windows BITS (BITSAdmin) for downloads [S7][S6] and file masquerading such as right-to-left override [S7]. Kaspersky saw signs of Android implants (APK/DEX files hosted on C2) but obtained no samples [S4]. In 2026 TAG-182 spread MarkiRAT through fake Android apps posing as VPNs and media players, such as 'Pis2ray VPN', 'YEPlayer' and 'YEMPlayer', promoted mainly on Instagram [S6]. Secondary vendor write-ups say the group exploited MSHTML CVE-2021-40444 to deliver a PowerShell stealer [S9]. That claim is not confirmed in SafeBreach's primary reporting (see gaps) [S5].

diamond.capability: MarkiRAT Windows implant (keylogging, clipboard capture, file transfer, command execution); Telegram and Chrome launcher hijacking; trojanized Psiphon; BITSAdmin; macro-laden decoy documents; suspected Android implants [S1][S2][S4][S6][S7].

gaps: The primary Kaspersky Securelist report [S1] and the Recorded Future report/PDF [S6] could not be fetched (DNS blocked). Their details come from search-result summaries and secondary coverage.
The Chinese intelligence firm that first analyzed the implant (mentioned in the imported summary) is not named in the sources gathered.

The SafeBreach publication date (2021-11-24) comes from secondary coverage. The primary blog was not opened.

No Android Ferocious Kitten sample has been publicly confirmed. Kaspersky reported only indirect evidence [S4]. For TAG-182, secondary coverage differs on whether the Android apps carry MarkiRAT itself or whether the MarkiRAT seen is the Windows variant (e.g. 'svehost.exe'). Check against the primary report [S6].
No sponsoring Iranian organization (MOIS, IRGC or other) is named in the cited sources, and no government attribution or indictment was found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (environment): The operational environment is personal Windows and Android devices of Persian-speaking users and the tools they rely on: Telegram, Chrome, Psiphon and sideloaded VPN or media apps [S2][S4][S6]. For DoD this matters mainly for personnel, partners, linguists or sources with Iranian ties, and for information-environment monitoring of Iranian domestic and diaspora populations. STEP 2 (effects): Iranian internet restrictions push targets toward circumvention tools, which the actor then trojanizes. Expect campaigns to follow censorship and connectivity events [S3][S6]. STEP 3 (threat model): The template is a Persian-language lure (protest imagery or a fake VPN or media app), then macro or sideload execution, then MarkiRAT with BITS downloads, then persistence through Telegram or Chrome launcher hijacking, then collection of keystrokes, clipboard and files [S2][S6][S7]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued surveillance of dissidents and diaspora through fake circumvention apps during unrest or after connectivity is restored [S6]. MDCOA is the same tooling turned against US-affiliated persons of Iranian heritage or partner-force personnel to collect contacts and credentials for counterintelligence targeting. That extension is an analytic inference not reported in the sources. Candidate indicators: BITS jobs pulling executables to user-writable paths; Telegram or Chrome shortcuts pointing to non-standard executables; Psiphon or 'Pis2ray'/'YEPlayer'/'YEMPlayer' binaries from unofficial sources; RTLO characters in attachment names; and macro-enabled Persian-language documents [S2][S6][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: This actor targets individuals, not networks, so DODIN telemetry is unlikely to see it. Awareness depends on vendor reporting (Kaspersky, Recorded Future) and on Force Protection and counterintelligence channels [S1][S6]. (2) Authorities: Activity against foreign nationals and diaspora falls mostly outside DoD cyber authorities. Coordinate with counterintelligence (AFOSI, DCSA) and with interagency partners for any US-person victims. (3) Mission assurance: Restrict sideloaded VPN and media apps on mobile devices used by linguists, partner liaisons and influence-operations personnel. Hunt for BITS abuse and Telegram/Chrome launcher tampering on any managed Windows endpoints [S6][S7]. (4) Coordination: Share indicators of fake circumvention apps with partners supporting Iranian information-environment operations, and track the unresolved TAG-182/Ferocious Kitten relationship rather than merging the clusters [S6].

provenance.importedSummary: Ferocious Kitten is an APT group that has been active against Persian-speaking individuals since 2015 and appears to be based in Iran. Although it has been active over a large timespan, the group has mostly operated under the radar until a lure document was uploaded to VirusTotal and was brought to public knowledge by researchers on Twitter. Subsequently, one of its implants was analyzed by a Chinese intelligence firm. Kaspersky then expanded some of the findings on the group and provided insights on additional variants. The malware dropped from the aforementioned document is dubbed MarkiRAT and is used to record keystrokes and clipboard content, provide file download and upload capabilities as well as the ability to execute arbitrary commands on the victims machine. Kaspersky were able to trace the implant back to at least 2015, along with variants intended to hijack the execution of the Telegram and Chrome applications as a persistence method. Interestingly, some of the TTPs used by this threat actor are reminiscent of other groups operating in the domain of dissident surveillance. For example, it used the same C2 domains across its implants for years, which was witnessed in the activity of Domestic Kitten. In the same vein, the Telegram execution hijacking technique observed in this campaign by Ferocious Kitten was also observed being used by Rampant Kitten, as covered by Check Point.

identification.summary: FIN1 is a FireEye designation for a financially motivated threat group first identified during an investigation at a financial-industry organization, where the group's activity dated back several years [S1]. The group deployed numerous malicious files and utilities that its developers referred to as the 'Nemesis' malware ecosystem, and used them to access victim environments and steal cardholder data [S1]. Coverage of the research describes it as the longest-running cybercrime group FireEye tracked [S5].
identification.firstObserved: Coverage of FireEye's December 2015 report states FireEye observed FIN1 activity dating to at least 2010 [S4][S5].
identification.notes: Name is FireEye's (now Mandiant); no Microsoft weather-name mapping was found in the sources gathered, and no cited source maps FIN1 to another vendor's cluster. Do not merge with FIN7/Carbanak or other FIN-numbered groups; none of the gathered sources link them. The original FireEye blog could not be opened (host unreachable from the research environment), so statements rely on the existing record text and secondary coverage of that report [S1].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor identified. FireEye characterized FIN1 as financially motivated (criminal) [S1].
attribution.confidence: FireEye assessed that FIN1 may be located in Russia or a Russian-speaking country; this is a suspicion, not a confirmed attribution [S1][S5].
attribution.basis: Language settings in many of the group's custom tools [S1][S5].

actors.objectives: Theft of data that is easily monetized from financial-sector victims, including payment card numbers, track data, ATM PIN numbers, and cardholder names and addresses [S1].

targeting.notes: Sector list from FireEye's description of the group [S1]. The known investigation was at a single unnamed financial-industry organization [S1][S5]. Victim geography is not stated in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: Operated a custom malware ecosystem called Nemesis, whose backdoors support multiple network protocols and C2 channels and offer file transfer, screen capture, keystroke logging, process injection and task scheduling [S4][S3]. In early 2015 the group added a utility, named BOOTRASH by FireEye, that modifies the Volume Boot Record so Nemesis loads before Windows; it builds a virtual file system in unallocated space between partitions, so components sit outside the Windows file system, evade OS integrity checks and antivirus scanning, and survive OS reinstallation [S2][S4]. FireEye advised a complete physical wipe of systems compromised with the bootkit [S2][S4]. FireEye noted that bootkits are rarely seen among targeted threat actors [S5].

campaigns.summary: FireEye reports a multi-year intrusion at a financial-industry organization in which FIN1 used Nemesis to steal cardholder data; trade press coverage follows the same month [S1][S2][S3][S4].

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated group, suspected Russia or Russian-speaking country based on tool language settings [S1][S5].
diamond.capability: Nemesis backdoor ecosystem and BOOTRASH Volume Boot Record bootkit [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.victim: Banks, credit unions, ATM operators, transaction processors and financial business services; one unnamed financial organization in the known case [S1][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Cybercrime for profit: monetizable card and ATM data [S1].
diamond.technology: Windows hosts with bootable disk structures (VBR, unallocated inter-partition space) and card-data environments at financial institutions [S2][S4][S1].

gaps: FireEye's original blog post could not be opened; all details beyond the existing record text come from secondary press coverage of it [S1].
Initial access vector, C2 infrastructure, and victim count/geography are not stated in the sources gathered.
No activity after 2015 was found; whether FIN1 is still active, was renamed, or merged into another cluster is unknown.
No alias or MITRE ATT&CK group mapping was found in the sources gathered; the existing record has no MITRE group id.
Dates for several press articles are given only to month (December 2015) based on reporting of FireEye's release; verify exact publication dates.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is financial-sector card-processing and ATM-management networks, and the boot sectors of hosts within them [S1][S2]. STEP 2: Pre-OS persistence defeats OS integrity checks and AV and survives reimaging, so standard remediation may leave the adversary in place [S2][S4]. STEP 3: Template is long-dwell access, Nemesis backdoors for collection (keylogging, screenshots, file transfer), then cardholder data theft [S1][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued theft of card and ATM data from financial institutions. MDCOA, an extrapolation not stated in sources, is reuse of boot-level persistence against a defense-contractor or military financial-services provider. Candidate indicators: unexpected modification of the Volume Boot Record, data in unallocated space between partitions, and reinfection after OS reimage [S2][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: criminal, not state-directed, per FireEye, so treat as a DIB/financial-services risk to personnel pay, ATM and card systems rather than a mission-system threat [S1]. (2) Authorities: remediation requiring full physical wipe has operational and legal implications for owned versus commercial systems [S2]. (3) Mission assurance: plan for rebuild from known-good media instead of reimaging in place [S2][S4]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with financial-sector partners and law enforcement channels; no source here documents specific DoD involvement.

provenance.importedSummary: FireEye first identified this activity during a recent investigation at an organization in the financial industry. They identified the presence of a financially motivated threat group that they track as FIN1, whose activity at the organization dated back several years. The threat group deployed numerous malicious files and utilities, all of which were part of a malware ecosystem referred to as ‘Nemesis’ by the malware developer(s), and used this malware to access the victim environment and steal cardholder data. FIN1, which may be located in Russia or a Russian-speaking country based on language settings in many of their custom tools, is known for stealing data that is easily monetized from financial services organizations such as banks, credit unions, ATM operations, and financial transaction processing and financial business services companies.

identification.summary: FIN13 is a financially motivated threat actor that Mandiant has tracked since 2017. Mandiant describes it conducting long-term intrusions against organizations in Mexico to gather information and carry out fraudulent money transfers, rather than smash-and-grab ransomware [S1]. Mandiant reports that the group relies heavily on custom passive backdoors, web shells and tunnelers rather than frameworks such as Cobalt Strike, with a median dwell time of about 2.5 years [S1]. Sygnia separately tracks an overlapping cluster as Elephant Beetle (TG2003), which it says steals millions of dollars from finance and commerce organizations, mainly in Latin America [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Mandiant: tracked since 2017, with activity going back as early as 2016 [S1]. Sygnia: had tracked Elephant Beetle for about two years when it published in January 2022 [S2][S3].
identification.notes: Mandiant name: FIN13 [S1]. Sygnia name: Elephant Beetle, also tracked as TG2003 [S2][S3]. Secondary reporting on Sygnia's research states that Sygnia noted similarities or overlaps with Mandiant's FIN13 [S3]; MITRE ATT&CK tracks the group as FIN13 (G1016) and the imported record lists Elephant Beetle and TG2003 as associated names [S7]. No Microsoft name for this actor was found in the sources gathered.

attribution.sponsor: None. Mandiant and Sygnia describe a financially motivated criminal actor; neither source makes a nation-state attribution [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: Mandiant makes no nation-state or geographic attribution; it notes Spanish-language strings in the SHELLSWEEP web shell, the GASCAN fraud tool and targeted database artifacts [S1]. The FIN13 to Elephant Beetle linkage is stated by Sygnia as an overlap, not as an identity [S3].
attribution.basis: Mandiant incident-response data covering more than five years of intrusions [S1]; Sygnia incident-response engagements [S2][S3].

actors.objectives: Financial theft: long, quiet reconnaissance of victim finance systems followed by fraudulent transactions, including point-of-sale and ATM-related fraud [S1]. Sygnia reports the group hides many small fraudulent transactions among legitimate activity to avoid detection [S2][S3].

regions: Mexico (Mandiant observed FIN13 operating exclusively against Mexico-based organizations over five years of data) [S1]
United States (secondary reporting says US-based firms were also affected) [S3]
targeting.notes: Mandiant says victims were large organizations, several with annual revenue in the millions to billions of USD, and that targeting a single country is rare: only 2.6% of financially motivated actors it tracks do so [S1]. Mandiant data is Mexico-only, while Sygnia's Elephant Beetle reporting extends to wider Latin America and some US firms; these cluster boundaries are not identical [S1][S3].

capabilities.summary: Initial access is primarily through exploitation of internet-facing servers. Mandiant saw indications of WebLogic and Apache Tomcat exploitation, though it could not confirm the specific vulnerabilities [S1]. Secondary reporting on Sygnia's research lists four exploited flaws: CVE-2017-1000486 (PrimeFaces), CVE-2015-7450 (WebSphere), CVE-2010-5326 and EDB-ID-24963 (both SAP NetWeaver). It also describes a focus on legacy Java applications on Linux, especially WebSphere and WebLogic, and obfuscated WAR archives [S4]. Mandiant documents a large custom toolset: BLUEAGAVE (a PowerShell/Perl passive backdoor), SIXPACK (ASPX tunneler), SWEARJAR (Java backdoor using DNS TXT), MAILSLOT (email-based C2), HOTLANE, BUSTEDPIPE, PORTHOLE, CLOSEWATCH, SPINOFF, DRAWSTRING, NIGHTJAR, LATCHKEY and a trojanized KeePass. Its fraud tool GASCAN sends ISO 8583 payment messages [S1]. The group also uses public tools such as Mimikatz, ProcDump, Invoke-WMIExec/SMBExec, NMAP and GOBOT2, and operates on both Windows and Linux [S1]. Sygnia reports more than 80 unique tools and scripts [S2][S3]. At publication, Mandiant had not seen FIN13 deploy ransomware [S1].

diamond.technology: Legacy, unpatched Java application servers (WebLogic, WebSphere, Tomcat) on Linux and Windows; payment-switch and POS systems using ISO 8583 [S1][S4].

gaps: Sygnia primary report and blog (blog.sygnia.co and the January 2022 PDF) could not be opened; Elephant Beetle details rely on press release listing and secondary coverage [S2][S3][S4].
Imported record lists country 'RU'; no cited source supports a Russian origin. Mandiant makes no geographic attribution and notes Spanish-language artifacts [S1]. Treat the origin as unknown.
Exact nature and strength of the FIN13 to Elephant Beetle overlap (shared tools, infrastructure or victims) is not documented in the sources gathered.
Some secondary coverage describes FIN13 as linked to ransomware, which conflicts with Mandiant's statement that it had not observed ransomware deployment [S1]; unverified.

The 2024 AllaKore RAT campaign link to FIN13 is tentative and contested in coverage; BlackBerry's original report was not opened [S5][S6][S8]. Later vendor reporting reportedly assigned this activity to a different named group; not verified here.
No public reporting found on FIN13 activity after 2022 attributed with confidence by Mandiant or Google Threat Intelligence.
NetWitness FIN13/Elephant Beetle paper and the MITRE ATT&CK G1016 page could not be fetched directly; MITRE data comes from the imported dataset [S7].
No Microsoft threat-actor name located for FIN13.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (environment): Key terrain is internet-facing legacy Java application servers (WebLogic, WebSphere, Tomcat, SAP NetWeaver) and the internal finance systems behind them: payment switches, POS, ATM and treasury applications [S1][S4]. STEP 2 (effects): Unpatched, years-old CVEs remain viable entry points, and multi-year dwell (median about 2.5 years) means compromise may predate current baselines [S1][S4]. STEP 3 (threat model): Exploit a public-facing server, drop a web shell or passive backdoor, tunnel inward, steal credentials, run reconnaissance on finance applications, then inject fraudulent transactions hidden among legitimate ones [S1][S2]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued quiet financial fraud against large Latin American organizations, including their US-linked subsidiaries [S1][S3]. MDCOA is long-term access to a financial institution or payment processor that serves DoD personnel or partner-nation forces in the region, enabling large-scale fraud or data theft. Candidate indicators: new JSP, ASPX or PHP files on Java or IIS servers; processes listening on high ephemeral ports (for example 65510-65512); unencrypted HTTP POST beacons to paths like /cpl/api.php; DNS TXT C2; anomalous ISO 8583 traffic or bursts of small transactions [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: FIN13 targets commercial and financial entities rather than DoD networks, so relevance is mainly to mission partners, contractors and financial services supporting operations in the USSOUTHCOM and USNORTHCOM areas; track legacy Java-server exposure on DODIN-adjacent systems [S1][S4]. (2) Authorities: this is criminal activity, so response falls primarily to law enforcement and partner-nation authorities, not military cyber forces; DoD's role is defensive hardening and information sharing. (3) Mission assurance: multi-year dwell argues for compromise-assessment hunts on legacy application servers, not just patching [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3, the DIB CS program and partner-nation CERTs in Mexico and Latin America.

provenance.importedSummary: Since 2017, Mandiant has been tracking FIN13, an industrious and versatile financially motivated threat actor conducting long-term intrusions in Mexico with an activity timeframe stretching back as early as 2016. Although their operations continue through the present day, in many ways FIN13's intrusions are like a time capsule of traditional financial cybercrime from days past. Instead of today's prevalent smash-and-grab ransomware groups, FIN13 takes their time to gather information to perform fraudulent money transfers. Rather than relying heavily on attack frameworks such as Cobalt Strike, the majority of FIN13 intrusions involve heavy use of custom passive backdoors and tools to lurk in environments for the long haul.

identification.summary: China-based, PRC-linked actor that gains and holds long-term access to networks with minimal malware, relying on built-in OS tools and legitimate software such as a SoftEther VPN bridge. Microsoft first exposed it for targeting Taiwanese organizations [S1]. US agencies later tied it to Integrity Technology Group, a Beijing company that ran a botnet of over 260,000 compromised SOHO, IoT and network devices [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Active since mid-2021 per Microsoft [S1]. The associated Raptor Train botnet dates to May 2020 per Lumen [S4]. The FBI-attributed botnet has operated since mid-2021 [S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Flax Typhoon. Microsoft maps Storm-0919 and ETHEREAL PANDA to it [S6]. Lumen also lists RedJuliett (Recorded Future) as overlapping [S4]; this encyclopedia holds a separate RedJuliett record from your import. Flax Typhoon has no MITRE ATT&CK group page as of the 2026-09-23 data [S7].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China. Integrity Technology Group (Yongxin Zhicheng), a publicly traded Beijing company, controlled the botnet infrastructure [S2]. OFAC sanctioned it for supporting Flax Typhoon computer network exploitation, citing use of Integrity Tech-linked infrastructure against multiple victims from summer 2022 to fall 2023 [S3].
attribution.confidence: Formal US government attribution through the FBI/CNMF/NSA joint advisory (Sep 2024) [S2] and OFAC designation (Jan 2025) [S3]. Microsoft attributes the 2023 Taiwan campaign to Flax Typhoon and describes the actor as China-based [S1].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry [S1]; FBI court-authorized operation and analysis of botnet management infrastructure [S2]; Lumen Black Lotus Labs infrastructure analysis, including Tier 3 management activity during Chinese working hours [S4]; Treasury findings [S3].

actors.objectives: Espionage through long-term, low-noise access. Microsoft assesses that observed behavior suggests intent to perform espionage and maintain access across sectors, though it had not observed the actor act on final objectives in the 2023 campaign [S1]. The botnet gave the actor a proxy layer to hide its operations and a DDoS capability [S2].

sectors: Military, defense industrial base and telecommunications (botnet-enabled targeting per FBI)
regions: Southeast Asia, North America and Africa (smaller numbers of victims, per Microsoft)
United States (botnet-enabled targeting; thousands of US devices in the botnet)
targeting.notes: Sector and region data from Microsoft [S1]; US and military/DIB targeting from FBI statements and the joint advisory as reported [S2][S5]. Botnet devices were spread across North America, South America, Europe, Africa, Southeast Asia and Australia [S2].

capabilities.summary: Exploitation of known vulnerabilities in public-facing servers, then web shells such as China Chopper [S1]. Privilege escalation with Juicy Potato; credential theft with Mimikatz [S1]. Persistence by enabling RDP and replacing the Sticky Keys accessibility binary to launch Task Manager with SYSTEM privileges, plus a SoftEther VPN bridge renamed to mimic Windows components and installed as a service [S1]. Infrastructure: Raptor Train, a tiered botnet built on the Mirai-variant 'Nosedive' implant across SOHO routers, IP cameras, NAS and IoT devices [S2][S4].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: In a Taiwan contingency, the cyberspace OE includes Taiwanese government and industrial networks and the global pool of compromised consumer and SOHO devices used as proxy terrain. STEP 2: A botnet of this scale lets adversary traffic appear to come from domestic residential and small-business addresses, which degrades geolocation-based attribution and blocklisting. STEP 3: The template is web shell, then privilege escalation, then RDP plus Sticky Keys, then a SoftEther VPN tunnel, then quiet access with no observed final action. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent espionage access in Taiwanese and allied networks. MDCOA is using the botnet for DDoS against Taiwanese or US targets during a crisis while maintaining espionage footholds. Candidate indicators: new outbound SoftEther or VPN services masquerading as Windows binaries, changes to accessibility executables, and spikes in SOHO-sourced authentication attempts against DIB portals [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Shared situational awareness should include botnet infrastructure intelligence, such as FBI and partner-shared C2 and node lists, so that defensive cyber forces can recognize proxy-sourced traffic. (2) Coordinate with allied partners, Taiwan especially, through established channels. Flax Typhoon victims are predominantly non-US, so DoD visibility depends on partner sharing. (3) Disruption precedents: the 2024 court-authorized FBI operation shows that domestic botnet takedown is a law-enforcement lead. DoD options against foreign-hosted tiers fall under separate authorities and require deconfliction. (4) DDoS readiness: JCC2 planning should include upstream mitigation coordination for public-facing DoD and DIB services.

provenance.importedSummary: Flax Typhoon is a Chinese state-sponsored threat actor that primarily targets organizations in Taiwan. They conduct espionage campaigns and focus on gaining and maintaining long-term access to networks using minimal malware. Flax Typhoon relies on tools built into the operating system and legitimate software to remain undetected. They exploit vulnerabilities in public-facing servers, use living-off-the-land techniques, and deploy a VPN connection to maintain persistence and move laterally within compromised networks.

relatedRecords.note: Lumen Black Lotus Labs lists RedJuliett (Recorded Future) as overlapping Flax Typhoon in its Sept 2024 Raptor Train reporting. Microsoft's mapping does not list RedJuliett under Flax Typhoon. Kept as separate records.

identification.summary: Cloudflare's Cloudforce One tracks FlyingYeti as a Russia-aligned threat actor that primarily targets Ukrainian defense entities and whose TTPs closely resemble those of UAC-0149, a cluster CERT-UA tracked earlier [S1][S3]. Cloudflare says that since 2024-04-26 it has taken measures to stop the actor launching a phishing espionage campaign; secondary coverage dates its detection to 2024-04-18, which the primary report does not confirm [S1][S5]. The campaign used debt-themed lures, a WinRAR exploit (CVE-2023-38831) and the COOKBOX PowerShell malware [S1][S2]. Microsoft says its Storm-1837 designation overlaps with activity other providers track as Flying Yeti and lists UAC-0149 [S4].
identification.firstObserved: SOC Prime, summarizing CERT-UA, reports UAC-0149 activity against Ukraine since at least autumn 2023 [S3]. Microsoft says Storm-1837 targeting of Ukrainian military devices was observed since December 2023 [S4]. Cloudflare's own FlyingYeti reporting centers on April-May 2024 [S1].
identification.notes: Name mapping rests on vendor statements of overlap, not on identical datasets. Cloudflare says FlyingYeti TTPs closely resemble UAC-0149 [S1]. Microsoft says Storm-1837 overlaps with Flying Yeti and lists UAC-0149 [S4]. Microsoft's name is a temporary 'Storm' designation, not a finalized weather-themed name [S4]. Do not merge facts across the three vendor clusters without the primary reports.

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor or specific organization is named in the sources gathered. Cloudflare describes the actor as Russia-aligned [S1]; Microsoft describes Storm-1837 as Russia-based [S4].
attribution.confidence: Cloudflare states the group's activity suggests alignment with Russian interests [S1]. Microsoft calls Storm-1837 a Russia-based actor without naming a government entity [S4]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Cloudflare cites Russian-language code comments and operational hours matching the UTC+3 time zone, per secondary coverage of its report [S5]. TTP resemblance to CERT-UA's UAC-0149 [S1][S3]. Targeting of Ukrainian military entities [S1][S4].

actors.objectives: Espionage against Ukrainian military and defense-related personnel, including access to devices used by drone operators [S1][S4]. Cloudflare describes the 2024 campaign as phishing espionage that also reached civilian targets [S1][S2].

regions: Ukraine; Cloudflare says about 94% of targeted devices were in Ukraine [S2]
targeting.notes: Cloudflare says the group mostly targets Ukrainian military entities and that this campaign pushed into civilian targets [S1][S2]. Full victim count is unknown because the campaign was disrupted early [S2]. Microsoft says Storm-1837 focuses on devices used by Ukrainian drone operators [S4].

capabilities.summary: Phishing delivered by email and Signal messages, using RAR archives that exploit WinRAR CVE-2023-38831 to run a script that opens a decoy and launches PowerShell tied to COOKBOX [S2][S3]. COOKBOX is a PowerShell backdoor that runs further commands; it sends an identifier in the X-Cookie HTTP header, persists through a registry Run key, and uses dynamic DNS (reported as NoIP) and Cloudflare Workers for C2 [S3]. Cloudflare reports the actor used Cloudflare Workers to fetch a WinRAR file hosted on GitHub, and decoy pages hosted on GitHub mimicking Kyiv's Komunalka housing site [S2][S5]. Microsoft says Storm-1837 uses a range of PowerShell backdoors (one called Cookbox by CERT-UA) and an Android backdoor, Griselda, which CERT-UA says is based on the Hydra banking malware and collects cookies, contacts and keystrokes [S4]. Cloudflare says its disruption stretched the actor's timeline from days to weeks and cost one instance nearly eight hours of debugging [S2][S5].

campaigns.name: FlyingYeti debt-themed WinRAR/COOKBOX campaign
campaigns.summary: Cloudflare says that since 2024-04-26 it has acted to prevent FlyingYeti launching a phishing campaign (secondary coverage says detection was 2024-04-18) using spoofed payment notices that exploited fear of losing housing and utilities after Ukraine's eviction and utility-cutoff moratorium ended in January 2024. A malicious RAR exploited CVE-2023-38831 to run a CMD file delivering COOKBOX. SOC Prime reports CERT-UA issued an alert on 2024-04-18 on a new UAC-0149 COOKBOX wave.

campaigns.name: Cloudflare disruption and public report
campaigns.summary: Cloudflare says it acted against the campaign from late April, disrupted it in mid-May as the actor was about to deploy the final COOKBOX payload, and published its findings on 2024-05-30 using detections, code takedowns and third-party cooperation.

diamond.adversary: Russia-aligned (Cloudflare) or Russia-based (Microsoft) actor, tracked as FlyingYeti, UAC-0149 and Storm-1837; no sponsor named [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: Phishing via email and Signal, CVE-2023-38831 WinRAR exploit, COOKBOX PowerShell backdoor, Griselda Android backdoor [S2][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Cloudflare Workers, GitHub-hosted decoy pages and archives, dynamic DNS, and in one Microsoft-observed case Telegram API and Mega [S2][S3][S4][S5].
diamond.victim: Ukrainian military personnel and drone operators, plus civilians targeted by debt-themed lures; about 94% of targeted devices in Ukraine [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Exploits Ukrainian financial stress after the moratorium on evictions and utility cutoffs ended, in the context of Russian-aligned espionage against Ukraine's military [S1][S5].
diamond.technology: Unpatched WinRAR, PowerShell and script hosts on Windows endpoints, Signal as a delivery channel to military users, and Android devices used by operators [S3][S4].

gaps: Cloudflare's primary report could not be opened directly in this session; Cloudflare details come from search-result excerpts and secondary coverage (The Register, Dark Reading, The Hacker News, SOC Prime) [S2][S5].
CERT-UA's original alerts (the early-2024 and 2024-04-18 alerts) were not opened; SOC Prime is a secondary source and cites CERT-UA#9522 for the April alert [S3].
No government attribution, sponsor organization or personnel were found; Russia-alignment rests on vendor inference [S1][S4].
Whether FlyingYeti, UAC-0149 and Storm-1837 are identical clusters is not established beyond vendor statements of overlap [S1][S4].
How Secret Blizzard gained control of the Storm-1837 backdoor is unresolved per Microsoft [S4].
Activity after mid-2024 was not found in the sources gathered.
Griselda was not corroborated in a CERT-UA primary document in this session [S4].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the personal and unit-level devices of Ukrainian (and potentially partner) operators, especially messaging apps such as Signal, plus Windows endpoints with outdated archive software [S3][S4]. STEP 2: The actor exploits local socio-economic stress (debt, utilities) and impersonates municipal services, and uses commodity cloud services (Cloudflare Workers, GitHub, dynamic DNS) that blend into normal traffic [S2][S5]. STEP 3: Template is lure via Signal or email, then malicious RAR using CVE-2023-38831, then script and PowerShell COOKBOX, then registry persistence and C2 with X-Cookie identifier [S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage phishing against Ukrainian military and drone-operator personnel with topical lures. MDCOA is use of the same delivery against partner-nation personnel supporting Ukraine, or hand-off of access to a more capable actor, as Microsoft observed when Secret Blizzard reused a Storm-1837 backdoor [S4]. Candidate indicators: WinRAR spawning cmd or PowerShell, new Run-key entries launching PowerShell, HTTP requests with an X-Cookie header to workers.dev or dynamic-DNS hosts, and GitHub-hosted decoy pages impersonating local services [S2][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track CERT-UA and vendor reporting on UAC-0149 and Storm-1837 and map to one tracking entry with noted overlaps [S1][S4]. (2) Authorities: any defensive action against third-party cloud services (GitHub, Cloudflare) should proceed through provider abuse channels and established legal authorities, as Cloudflare's own takedowns did [S2]. (3) Mission assurance: patch archive tools, restrict powershell.exe, wscript.exe, cscript.exe and mshta.exe per CERT-UA guidance, and brief personnel on messaging-app lures [S3]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partners, since Microsoft shows a lower-tier actor's access can be reused by a stronger actor [S4].

identification.summary: Russian military intelligence (GRU Unit 26165) cyber actor focused on strategic intelligence targets [S1]. Since 2022 it has focused on Ukraine's war effort and on Western logistics and technology companies that coordinate and deliver aid to Ukraine, including compromising IP cameras at border crossings to track shipments [S2]. It uses custom tools such as GooseEgg alongside public exploits [S1].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least 2004 [S3]. GooseEgg in use since at least June 2020, possibly April 2019 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Forest Blizzard (formerly STRONTIUM). Microsoft maps FANCY BEAR, APT28, Sofacy, Sednit and others to it [S5]; MITRE tracks it as APT28 (G0007) [S3]. Nineteen APT29 names that the source merge had placed on this record (e.g. Cozy Bear, NOBELIUM, Dark Halo) were moved to Midnight Blizzard.

attribution.confidence: US and UK governments attribute the actor to GRU Unit 26165 [S1]. A multinational joint advisory (21 May 2025) attributes the logistics-targeting campaign to Unit 26165 [S2].

actors.objectives: Strategic intelligence for the Russian military and state. Since 2022, collection on Ukraine and on the Western logistics and technology firms that move aid to Ukraine, including tracking shipments through compromised cameras, which agencies assess could enable sabotage or kinetic targeting [S2].

regions: NATO member states, Western Europe and North America
targeting.notes: Sector targeting from Microsoft [S1] and the 2025 joint advisory as summarized by the German BfV and coverage [S2][S4].

In the 2025 campaign: password spraying, spear-phishing and modification of Exchange mailbox permissions to maintain access [S2][S4]. Compromise of internet-connected IP cameras for surveillance [S2]. MITRE lists 93 techniques and 29 software entries, including X-Agent (CHOPSTICK), Zebrocy, LoJax, Drovorub and LAMEHUG [S3].

Earlier landmark events (2016 DNC intrusion and the 2018 DOJ indictment of GRU officers, Drovorub advisory, Ubiquiti EdgeRouter disruption in 2024) are not yet sourced in this profile.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The cyberspace OE includes commercial logistics providers, rail and port operators, and the IoT cameras along supply routes into Ukraine and NATO's eastern flank. These are intelligence collection points for the adversary. STEP 2: Compromised cameras turn the physical terrain itself into adversary ISR, which affects OPSEC for movements. STEP 3: The template is password spraying or phishing against mail accounts, then mailbox permission changes for persistence, then collection on shipments and schedules. In parallel, mass compromise of exposed cameras. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection on aid logistics to inform Russian targeting and diplomacy. MDCOA is using collected movement data to cue sabotage or strikes on aid shipments or nodes. Candidate indicators: new mailbox delegation or folder permissions, spray activity against logistics firms, and anomalous access to camera management interfaces near routes [S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Treat commercial partners' camera and mail exposure as part of force-protection planning for movements. (2) JCC2 situational awareness should take in partner and industry reporting on logistics-sector intrusions, since the victims are mostly private. (3) Authorities: hardening of commercial and allied camera networks is a partner-nation and owner responsibility. DoD influence is through contracts, requirements and liaison. (4) OPSEC: plan movement security assuming adversary visibility through compromised cameras on routes.

provenance.importedSummary: A 2015 report by F-Secure describe APT29 as: 'The Dukes are a well-resourced, highly dedicated and organized cyberespionage group that we believe has been working for the Russian Federation since at least 2008 to collect intelligence in support of foreign and security policy decision-making. The Dukes show unusual confidence in their ability to continue successfully compromising their targets, as well as in their ability to operate with impunity. The Dukes primarily target Western governments and related organizations, such as government ministries and agencies, political think tanks, and governmental subcontractors. Their targets have also included the governments of members of the Commonwealth of Independent States;Asian, African, and Middle Eastern governments;organizations associated with Chechen extremism;and Russian speakers engaged in the illicit trade of controlled substances and drugs. The Dukes are known to employ a vast arsenal of malware toolsets, which we identify as MiniDuke, CosmicDuke, OnionDuke, CozyDuke, CloudDuke, SeaDuke, HammerDuke, PinchDuke, and GeminiDuke. In recent years, the Dukes have engaged in apparently biannual large - scale spear - phishing campaigns against hundreds or even thousands of recipients associated with governmental institutions and affiliated organizations. These campaigns utilize a smash - and - grab approach involving a fast but noisy breakin followed by the rapid collection and exfiltration of as much data as possible.If the compromised target is discovered to be of value, the Dukes will quickly switch the toolset used and move to using stealthier tactics focused on persistent compromise and long - term intelligence gathering. This threat actor targets government ministries and agencies in the West, Central Asia, East Africa, and the Middle East; Chechen extremist groups; Russian organized crime; and think tanks. It is suspected to be behind the 2015 compromise of unclassified networks at the White House, Department of State, Pentagon, and the Joint Chiefs of Staff. The threat actor includes all of the Dukes tool sets, including MiniDuke, CosmicDuke, OnionDuke, CozyDuke, SeaDuke, CloudDuke (aka MiniDionis), and HammerDuke (aka Hammertoss). '

identification.summary: Adversary group targeting telecommunication and technology organizations.

Frontier Blizzard is Microsoft's name for a Russia-origin actor. Microsoft maps it to Google/Mandiant's UNC5792 [S1]. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) describes UNC5792 as a suspected Russian espionage cluster. It hijacks Signal accounts by altering legitimate Signal group-invite pages so that a victim who scans the code links their account to a device the actor controls [S2][S3]. In 2026, US government reporting linked UNC5792 to a broader campaign against Signal and WhatsApp accounts of officials. Press accounts say the campaign has compromised thousands of messaging accounts [S5][S6][S7].
identification.firstObserved: Publicly reported by GTIG on 2025-02-19, which describes activity in the preceding 'recent months' without giving specific start dates [S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Frontier Blizzard (origin Russia); the only other name Microsoft lists is UNC5792 [S1]. GTIG says UNC5792 partially overlaps with CERT-UA's UAC-0195 [S2][S4]. A partial overlap is not the same as identity, so do not merge UAC-0195 reporting wholesale. UNC4221 (CERT-UA UAC-0185) is a separate Russia-linked cluster. GTIG reported it together with UNC5792, and the 2026 US announcements also named it alongside UNC5792 [S2][S5][S6]; this profile does not merge its facts into Frontier Blizzard. No Microsoft narrative profile or blog post naming Frontier Blizzard was found.

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation. Press coverage of the June 2026 US announcements says UNC5792 is associated with officers of the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) Border Guards [S5][S6][S7].
attribution.confidence: GTIG (February 2025) called UNC5792 a 'suspected' Russian espionage cluster and gave no further confidence level [S2]. In June 2026 the FBI (in a public service announcement) and the State Department Rewards for Justice program tied UNC5792 to FSB Border Guards officers. This summary comes from press coverage; the primary US documents were not opened [S5][S6][S7]. Microsoft lists Frontier Blizzard's origin as Russia without public sponsor detail [S1].
attribution.basis: GTIG technical reporting on altered Signal invite pages and actor infrastructure [S2]. FBI PSA I-062626-PSA (2026-06-26), as reported by the press [S7]. State Department Rewards for Justice offer of up to $10 million, as reported by the press [S5][S6]. Microsoft naming mapping [S1].

actors.objectives: Espionage collection from secure messaging. Device linking gives the actor real-time copies of a victim's Signal messages [S2]. GTIG frames the wider Russian Signal campaign around wartime demand for Ukrainian military and government communications [S2][S3]. 2026 reporting describes collection against US and NATO government, diplomatic, defense and media targets [S5][S6].

targeting.notes: The 2025 reporting focuses on Ukrainian military users of Signal [S2][S3]. GTIG did not list UNC5792 victims individually. It described the general target pool for these Russian Signal operations as military personnel, politicians, journalists, activists and other at-risk groups, and assessed that the tactics would likely spread beyond Ukraine [S2][S3]. The 2026 target list (US officials, diplomats, NATO member-state officials, defense staff and journalists) comes from US government announcements as reported by the press [S5][S6].

capabilities.summary: UNC5792 does not exploit flaws in Signal's encryption. It abuses Signal's legitimate linked-devices feature: phishing delivers altered Signal group-invite pages, and the page's JavaScript redirect is replaced with an sgnl://linkdevice URI. A victim who scans the code links an actor-controlled device, which then receives the victim's messages in real time [S2][S3]. GTIG notes that device linking is a low-signature form of access: few detections exist for newly linked devices, so access can persist unnoticed [S2]. The actor's lookalike domains imitate Signal group and security pages (for example signal-group[.]site and signal-security[.]online) [S2]. In 2026 the FBI reported a tactic shift, as reported by the press. Operators now persuade targets to reveal their Signal Backup Recovery Key, which lets them restore a backup and read the full message history, in addition to verification codes and 2FA credentials [S7].

campaigns.name: Signal device-linking via altered group invites
campaigns.summary: GTIG reports that UNC5792 altered Signal group-invite pages to link victims' accounts to actor devices, chiefly targeting Ukrainian military users. Signal added device-linking warnings in response.

campaigns.name: FBI/CISA warning on messaging-app account takeover
campaigns.summary: A joint FBI/CISA announcement warns that Russian intelligence is phishing Signal and other messaging users for verification codes. It reports that thousands of accounts were accessed. The announcement did not name UNC5792 at this stage.

campaigns.name: Signal Backup Recovery Key phishing; Rewards for Justice offer
campaigns.summary: An FBI/CISA PSA (I-062626-PSA) updates the March 2026 warning: operators now solicit Signal Backup Recovery Keys, and the PSA names UNC5792 and UNC4221. The State Department offers up to $10 million for information on UNC5792, which it links to FSB Border Guards officers.

diamond.adversary: Russian operators that the US government ties to the FSB Border Guards, per press reporting [S5][S6][S7]. Google GTIG calls the cluster a suspected Russian espionage actor [S2].
diamond.capability: Social engineering that abuses Signal device linking through altered group invites and QR codes. Since 2026 it also includes phishing for Signal Backup Recovery Keys and verification codes [S2][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: Lookalike Signal domains, for example add-signal-group[.]com, signal-groups[.]tech and signal-security[.]site, hosting modified invite pages [S2].
diamond.victim: Ukrainian military Signal users (2025). US, NATO, diplomatic, defense and media personnel on Signal and WhatsApp (2026) [S2][S5][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection of private communications in support of Russia's war in Ukraine and against Ukraine's Western backers [S2][S5].
diamond.technology: Consumer end-to-end encrypted messaging apps (Signal, WhatsApp), specifically their device-linking and backup-recovery account features [S2][S7].

gaps: No Microsoft blog post or profile naming Frontier Blizzard was found. The name-to-UNC5792 mapping rests only on Microsoft's naming feed [S1], so Microsoft's own observations, scope and confidence are unknown.

The primary documents (FBI PSA I-062626-PSA, the March 2026 FBI/CISA PSA, and the State Department Rewards for Justice notice) could not be opened. Their attribution wording and details here come from press coverage [S5][S6][S7].

The press says the 2026 US announcements tie UNC5792 to FSB Border Guards and UNC4221 to actors working for Russian military services. Which specific techniques (backup-key phishing, WhatsApp targeting) belong to UNC5792 rather than UNC4221 is not clear from the coverage.
The UAC-0195 overlap is described only as 'partial' by GTIG [S2]. The CERT-UA primary reporting on UAC-0195 was not reviewed.
The press reports 'thousands' of compromised accounts [S6], but the share attributable to UNC5792 is unknown.
There is no MITRE ATT&CK group entry for UNC5792/Frontier Blizzard.
Activity before 2025 and the actor's start date are not established.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain is personal and official use of consumer encrypted messaging (Signal, WhatsApp) by commanders, staffs, liaison officers and NATO partners. Account-level features such as linked devices and backup recovery are the attack surface, not the crypto [S2][S7]. STEP 2 (effects): A single successful lure gives persistent, low-signature, real-time message access, and backup-key theft can expose full message history. The compromise sits outside DoD network sensors [S2][S7]. STEP 3 (threat model): The actor delivers a lure (a group invite, a security alert or a support message), the victim scans a QR code or hands over a code or key, and the actor links a device or restores a backup to collect messages [S2][S7]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued social-engineering collection against US and NATO officials, diplomats and defense personnel on Signal and WhatsApp, adapting as platforms add protections [S5][S6][S7]. MDCOA is undetected long-term access to accounts used to coordinate operations or partner support, enabling compromise of plans, personnel identities and locations, or follow-on impersonation of trusted contacts [S2][S5]. Candidate indicators: unexpected linked devices in Signal settings; messages that ask for verification codes or Backup Recovery Keys; Signal group invites hosted on lookalike domains such as signal-group[.]site or signal-security[.]online [S2][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Because the activity targets personal and commercial messaging accounts [S2][S5], it is largely invisible to DODIN sensors. Awareness depends on user reporting, OPSEC reviews of linked devices, and FBI/CISA and vendor reporting [S2][S7]. Authorities: The victims' accounts are commercial services. Response relies on user remediation (removing linked devices, regenerating backup keys), FBI/IC3 reporting, and coordination with the platforms rather than DoD cyber authorities [S7]. Mission assurance: Commanders should treat any operationally relevant content on consumer messaging apps as potentially exposed, and direct periodic linked-device audits and backup-key rotation [S2][S7]. Coordination: Share indicators and lure examples with FBI, CISA, NATO partners and Ukraine-facing liaison elements, since the reported targets span US, NATO and Ukrainian personnel [S2][S5][S6].

identification.summary: GCMAN is a financially motivated criminal group publicly named by Kaspersky Lab in February 2016, alongside Metel and Carbanak 2.0, for APT-style intrusions into banks [S1][S2]. MITRE describes it as a group that targets banks to transfer money to e-currency services [S5]. Kaspersky says the name comes from the group's use of the GCC compiler, which is rare among malware writers [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Publicly disclosed by Kaspersky on 2016-02-08 [S2]. ETDA lists first seen as 2016 [S6]. Kaspersky's earliest intrusion date is not established in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: Kaspersky says there is no direct connection between the Carbanak, Metel and GCMAN attacks; Golovanov called Metel and GCMAN copycats of Carbanak in some respects [S2]. Keep the three clusters separate. No Microsoft naming applies; Microsoft does not appear to track this actor under a weather-based name in the sources gathered. No aliases are stated by a cited source.

attribution.confidence: No state sponsor is stated in the sources gathered. ETDA classifies the motivation as financial crime [S6]. Kaspersky found victims only in Russia and suspected the activity is more widespread [S3][S2]; this is a victimology statement, not an attribution of origin.
attribution.basis: Kaspersky Lab incident-response and analysis reporting [S1][S2]; MITRE ATT&CK summary of Kaspersky reporting [S5]. The country code RU in this encyclopedia's imported record is not supported by a cited statement of actor origin and should not be treated as attribution.

actors.objectives: Direct financial theft: moving money out of bank systems to multiple e-currency services [S5][S3].

regions: Russia (the only victims Kaspersky identified; three financial institutions per press coverage) [S3]
targeting.notes: Kaspersky said it suspects infection is much more widespread than the Russian victims it identified [S3][S2].

capabilities.summary: Initial access by spear-phishing a financial institution with a malicious RAR archive that launches an executable instead of the Word document it imitates [S2][S6]. Lateral movement with legitimate and penetration-testing tools including PuTTY, VNC and Meterpreter [S3][S6]. The group located servers handling financial transactions and set up cron jobs to automate transfers to multiple e-currency services, mostly on weekends; Secondary reporting of Kaspersky's findings cites a cron script generating transactions at about $200 per minute [S3]. Press coverage of Kaspersky's findings reports the group waited about a year and a half after initial compromise before taking money in one incident [S3]. Malware was built with the GCC compiler [S2]. MITRE lists PuTTY and VNC use for lateral movement [S5].

campaigns.name: Kaspersky public disclosure of GCMAN with Metel and Carbanak 2.0
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky reports GCMAN bank intrusions with automated cron-driven transfers to e-currency services, with victims identified only in Russia, and publishes indicators of compromise.

campaigns.name: Long-dwell bank intrusion with delayed cash-out
campaigns.summary: In one incident reported in press coverage of Kaspersky research, about 18 months passed between initial compromise and the start of money theft; the incident date and victim are not given in the sources gathered.

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated criminal group named GCMAN by Kaspersky; individual identities, affiliation and origin not established [S1][S6].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing with malicious RAR archive, PuTTY, VNC, Meterpreter, GCC-compiled malware, cron-scheduled automated transfers [S3][S6][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Not described in the cited material available to me; Kaspersky published IOCs that I could not open [S2].
diamond.victim: Banks and financial institutions; Russian victims identified [S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Profit motive. Kaspersky frames the group as part of a trend of criminals adopting APT-style methods against banks [S2].
diamond.technology: Bank servers that handle financial transactions and the ability to push transfers to e-currency services without relying on malware on endpoints; use of scheduled jobs on servers [S3].

gaps: Could not open the primary Securelist report, the MITRE page, PCWorld or ETDA directly (fetch failed); details come from search-result summaries of those pages and Kaspersky's press release coverage. Validate against the Securelist report [S1].
Exact dates, victims and loss totals of GCMAN intrusions are not established; the 18-month dwell time appears only in press coverage [S3].
Actor origin, membership, and any link to Carbanak or Metel are unknown; Kaspersky states no direct connection [S2].
Infrastructure, malware hashes and IOCs were published by Kaspersky but not reviewed here [S2].
Whether the group remains active after 2016 is unverified; a third-party summary suggests Securelist lists it as inactive since 2017, which I could not confirm.
Some secondary Q&A sites add details (log deletion, specific payment services, ATT&CK mappings beyond PuTTY/VNC) that I did not rely on.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the bank server tier that originates or relays payment transactions, plus staff mailboxes. The group is a criminal actor, so relevance to DoD is mainly via financial-sector disruption and partner-nation banking, not direct DoD networks. STEP 2: Environment features include weak monitoring of scheduled jobs on transaction servers and reliance on legitimate admin tools that blend in. STEP 3: Template is spear-phish with RAR, long dwell with PuTTY/VNC/Meterpreter, then cron-scheduled transfers to e-currency services, favoring weekends [S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-volume automated theft from banks. MDCOA is use of the same access methods against financial entities supporting military pay or logistics. Candidate indicators: new cron entries on transaction servers, RAR attachments launching executables, unexpected PuTTY/VNC on servers, and weekend transaction bursts [S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: financial-sector criminal reporting is a low-priority feed unless military-affiliated financial systems are affected. (2) Authorities: this is a criminal matter, so response runs through law enforcement and financial regulators rather than offensive or defensive cyber operations authorities. (3) Mission assurance: protect payment and pay-system servers with monitoring of scheduled tasks and remote-admin tools. (4) Coordination: share indicators through established sector and DC3 channels where DoD-linked financial services are involved.
