identification.summary: Ghost Blizzard is the Microsoft name for a Russia-origin actor that Microsoft maps to BROMINE, Berserk Bear, TG-4192, Koala Team, Blue Kraken, Crouching Yeti and Dragonfly [S1]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as Dragonfly (G0035): a cyber espionage group attributed to Russia's FSB Center 16 that has targeted defense and aviation companies, government entities, ICS-related companies and critical-infrastructure sectors worldwide through supply-chain, spearphishing and drive-by compromise [S2]. The group is best known for long-running access operations against Western energy companies, including trojanized ICS vendor software (2013-2014) [S3][S4] and the 'Dragonfly 2.0' campaign against energy firms in Europe and North America [S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least 2010 [S2]. Symantec (as reported in 2017 coverage): active since at least 2011 [S5]. The US indictment covers activity from about 2012 to 2017-2018 [S9].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Ghost Blizzard (former Microsoft name BROMINE) [S1]. US and UK government statements describe the team as a unit within FSB Center 16, also known as Military Unit 71330 [S9][S10][S13]. Cisco Talos tracks 'Static Tundra', which it assesses with high confidence is a subset of Berserk Bear active since at least 2015; that is a sub-cluster, not a full alias [S11]. The imported summary in this record came from Dragos's ALLANITE profile; Dragos tracks ALLANITE (and DYMALLOY) as its own ICS-focused clusters, so ALLANITE details should not be merged into Ghost Blizzard without Dragos's own mapping (see gaps).

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation, Federal Security Service (FSB) Center 16 (Military Unit 71330), per US indictment and UK government attribution [S9][S10][S13].
attribution.confidence: The UK NCSC assessed it 'almost certain' that FSB Centre 16 carried out a malign cyber programme against critical IT systems and national infrastructure in Europe, the Americas and Asia [S10]. A US grand jury in the District of Kansas indicted three FSB Center 16 officers (Pavel Akulov, Mikhail Gavrilov, Marat Tyukov) on 2021-08-26; the indictment was unsealed on 2022-03-24 [S9][S13]. In August 2025 the FBI attributed exploitation of Cisco devices to FSB Center 16 actors, and Cisco Talos assessed with high confidence that the related Static Tundra cluster is a subset of Berserk Bear [S11]. Microsoft's public mapping lists the actor as Russia-origin; no Microsoft confidence statement was found [S1].
attribution.basis: US criminal indictment and State Department Rewards for Justice offer [S9][S12][S13]; UK FCDO/NCSC attribution [S10]; joint DHS/FBI and CISA/FBI advisories [S6][S8]; German BSI/BfV/BND memo [S7]; vendor reporting from Symantec, F-Secure/Netresec and Cisco Talos [S3][S4][S5][S11].

actors.objectives: Long-term espionage and pre-positioned access to critical infrastructure, especially energy. Symantec assessed that Dragonfly 2.0 aimed both to learn how energy facilities operate and to gain access to operational systems, and that this access could enable disruption [S5]. The 2014 trojanized-software campaign was assessed by Symantec as giving the group a beachhead that could enable sabotage, though it focused on espionage at the time [S3]. German agencies warned in 2020 that the group sought to anchor itself permanently in IT networks and possibly reach OT networks [S7]. Public reporting has found no disruptive attack by this actor [S7][S8].

sectors: Energy: electricity grid operators, generation firms, petroleum pipeline operators [S3]
Nuclear (including Wolf Creek Nuclear Operating Corporation) [S6][S10][S12]
ICS / industrial equipment vendors and supply-chain suppliers [S3][S4][S6]
US state, local, territorial and tribal (SLTT) government; US federal agencies [S8][S9]
Telecommunications, higher education and manufacturing (Static Tundra sub-cluster) [S11]
regions: Europe, including Spain, France, Italy, Germany, Poland, Turkey and Switzerland [S3][S5][S7]
Roughly 135 countries per the US indictment [S9]
North America, Asia, Africa and Europe (Static Tundra) [S11]
targeting.notes: The US indictment alleges the Dragonfly 2.0 phase targeted more than 3,300 users at over 500 US and international companies and entities, including US government agencies [S9]. DHS/FBI described staging through smaller, less secure supply-chain organizations before reaching intended energy targets [S6].

capabilities.summary: Supply-chain compromise of ICS vendor websites to trojanize legitimate software installers with the Havex/Oldrea RAT (for example a European PLC maker's driver package available for at least six weeks in June-July 2013) [S3][S4]; custom malware Backdoor.Oldrea and Trojan.Karagany [S3]; spearphishing (including template-based credential harvesting with the Phishery toolkit) and watering-hole websites [S5][S6]; use of common administration tools rather than zero-days after initial access [S5]; network reconnaissance and collection of ICS information inside energy networks [S6]; exploitation of public-facing vulnerabilities including Citrix CVE-2019-19781, Fortinet CVE-2018-13379, Exchange CVE-2020-0688, Exim CVE-2019-10149 and Netlogon CVE-2020-1472 [S8]; and exploitation of Cisco Smart Install CVE-2018-0171 to collect configuration files from thousands of network devices and modify configurations for access [S11].

campaigns.name: Trojanized ICS vendor software (Dragonfly / Havex)
campaigns.summary: Dragonfly compromised ICS equipment vendors and placed the Havex/Oldrea RAT in legitimate software downloads, including a PLC driver package (June-July 2013) and a wind-turbine/biogas management vendor's software (April 2014).

campaigns.name: Public exposure of Dragonfly / Energetic Bear
campaigns.summary: Symantec and F-Secure publicly report the campaign against energy firms in the US and Europe; F-Secure counts 88 Havex variants and 146 C2 servers.

campaigns.name: Dragonfly 2.0 begins
campaigns.summary: Symantec reports renewed activity from late 2015 against energy companies in Europe and North America, using phishing, watering holes and trojanized software.

campaigns.name: Wolf Creek nuclear plant targeting
campaigns.summary: Center 16 targets networks associated with the Wolf Creek nuclear plant in Kansas; the UK says there was no negative impact.

campaigns.name: DHS/FBI alert TA18-074A
campaigns.summary: US government attributes a multi-stage campaign, active since at least March 2016, against energy, nuclear, water, aviation and critical manufacturing to Russian government actors.

campaigns.name: German energy and water supply-chain compromises
campaigns.summary: BSI, BfV and BND warn operators that Berserk Bear had long-standing compromises in German energy, water and power companies via supply chains.

campaigns.name: SLTT and aviation network intrusions (AA20-296A)
campaigns.summary: CISA/FBI report targeting of dozens of US SLTT and aviation networks since at least September 2020, with data exfiltrated from at least two servers by 1 October 2020.

campaigns.name: US indictment unsealed; UK attribution
campaigns.summary: DOJ unseals the Kansas indictment of three FSB Center 16 officers for the Dragonfly campaigns; the UK attributes the programme to FSB Centre 16.

campaigns.name: Cisco Smart Install exploitation (Static Tundra)
campaigns.summary: FBI warns that FSB Center 16 actors exploited CVE-2018-0171 to harvest configurations from thousands of US critical-infrastructure network devices; Cisco Talos tracks the activity as Static Tundra, a Berserk Bear subset.

campaigns.name: Rewards for Justice offer
campaigns.summary: US State Department offers up to $10 million for information on the three indicted FSB officers.

diamond.adversary: FSB Center 16 (Military Unit 71330); three officers indicted in the US (Akulov, Gavrilov, Tyukov) [S9][S10][S13].
diamond.capability: Havex/Oldrea and Karagany malware; trojanized ICS software; spearphishing and watering holes; public-facing VPN, Citrix, Exchange and Cisco Smart Install exploits [S3][S5][S8][S11].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised ICS vendor download sites [S3][S4]; compromised small supply-chain organizations used as staging targets [S6]; watering-hole websites [S5][S6]; Havex C2 servers (146 counted by F-Secure) [S3].
diamond.victim: Energy, nuclear, water and aviation organizations, ICS vendors, US SLTT and federal government, and network devices at telecom, education and manufacturing organizations [S3][S6][S8][S11].
diamond.socioPolitical: Russian state interest in mapping and holding access to Western critical infrastructure, especially energy [S5][S7][S10].
diamond.technology: Windows enterprise networks bridging to ICS environments; trusted vendor update channels; internet-facing VPN/remote-access appliances and legacy Cisco IOS devices with Smart Install enabled [S3][S6][S8][S11].

gaps: Microsoft has published little actor-specific reporting under the Ghost Blizzard name; only Microsoft's public name mapping was found [S1]. learn.microsoft.com could not be fetched.

Primary government documents could not be opened (cisa.gov, justice.gov and ic3.gov blocked): TA18-074A, AA20-296A, the Akulov indictment and the FBI August 2025 PSA are cited through press or search-result coverage [S6][S8][S11][S13].
Symantec's 2014 and 2017 Dragonfly reports, Secureworks IRON LIBERTY, Dragos ALLANITE/DYMALLOY and the MITRE G0035 page could not be fetched; facts rely on search excerpts and press coverage.

Cluster boundaries: Dragos tracks ALLANITE and DYMALLOY separately; the imported ALLANITE summary may not describe Ghost Blizzard as Microsoft scopes it. Cisco Talos's Static Tundra is described as a subset of Berserk Bear, not the whole group [S11]. MITRE also keeps a separate Dragonfly 2.0 entry (G0074) [S2].

The UK FSB factsheet (updated December 2023) reportedly lists Turla/Snake/Venomous Bear names alongside Energetic Bear under the FSB structure; whether this reflects one unit or a grouping by parent organisation was not verified [S10].
Sources disagree on campaign end dates (indictment summaries give 2012-2017 or 2012-2018) [S9].
Activity after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, aside from the 2025 Cisco device exploitation, is not documented in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is the IT/OT boundary at energy, nuclear, water and aviation facilities, the vendor software-update channels that feed them, and internet-facing VPN, Citrix, Exchange and legacy Cisco network devices [S3][S6][S8][S11]. Installations relying on commercial utilities inherit this exposure. STEP 2 (effects): The actor has used trusted vendor downloads and smaller suppliers to reach hardened targets, so a defended perimeter does not bound the threat [S3][S6]. Unpatched years-old CVEs remain viable entry points [S11]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Supply-chain or phishing/watering-hole access, then credential harvest, admin-tool lateral movement, ICS reconnaissance and screenshots, with persistence and no observed disruption [S5][S6][S8]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued quiet access and collection of ICS and network-device configuration data from critical infrastructure [S7][S11]. MDCOA is use of that pre-positioned access to disrupt energy or other utility operations during a crisis, which Symantec and German agencies flagged as possible but which has not been observed [S5][S7]. Candidate indicators: unexpected Smart Install (TCP 4786) traffic or configuration exfiltration from Cisco devices [S11]; SMB/credential-harvesting template injections in phishing documents [S5]; new local accounts and remote access on engineering hosts; anomalous downloads from ICS vendor sites [S3][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Track the actor's targeting of commercial energy, water and aviation providers and of SLTT networks that support installations, alongside DODIN assets, since the reported victims sit largely outside DoD networks [S6][S8]. Authorities: Most likely victims are private-sector or civil-government owners, so response relies on coordination with CISA, FBI and DOE rather than DoD action on those networks [S6][S8][S9]. Mission assurance: Prioritise mission-relevant dependencies on commercial power and on legacy network devices; patch or disable Cisco Smart Install and harden internet-facing remote-access appliances named in advisories [S8][S11]. Coordination: Share indicators across energy-sector ISACs and allied partners, since the UK, Germany and the US have each reported the same actor [S7][S9][S10].

provenance.importedSummary: Adversaries abusing ICS (based on Dragos Inc adversary list). ALLANITE accesses business and industrial control (ICS) networks, conducts reconnaissance, and gathers intelligence in United States and United Kingdom electric utility sectors. Dragos assesses with moderate confidence that ALLANITE operators continue to maintain ICS network access to: (1) understand the operational environment necessary to develop disruptive capabilities, (2) have ready access from which to disrupt electric utilities. ALLANITE uses email phishing campaigns and compromised websites called watering holes to steal credentials and gain access to target networks, including collecting and distributing screenshots of industrial control systems. ALLANITE operations limit themselves to information gathering and have not demonstrated any disruptive or damaging capabilities. ALLANITE conducts malware-less operations primarily leveraging legitimate and available tools in the Windows operating system.

identification.summary: Group-IB designates GHOST STADIUM as a Chinese-speaking, financially motivated threat actor running a large phishing and ticket-fraud operation against FIFA World Cup 2026 fans, using a custom React-based kit that clones fifa.com and its single sign-on login flow [S1][S3][S7]. More than 300 of the 4,300+ FIFA-impersonating domains Group-IB tracked are actively running fraudulent infrastructure, with roughly 3,800 more parked or dormant [S3][S4]. Group-IB describes GHOST STADIUM as one of four independent threat actors it identified targeting the tournament, with six fraud schemes in parallel [S1][S4]. This is a fraud/cybercrime cluster, not a state-sponsored APT, per the cited reporting [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: Not confirmed; the wider FIFA-impersonating domain registrations date from August 2025 [S1][S3]
identification.notes: Group-IB tracks four independent actors in the World Cup fraud ecosystem; only GHOST STADIUM is named in the cited material, and facts about the other three or about generic 'World Cup scam' reporting by other vendors must not be merged into this cluster [S1][S4]. Silent Push reports a separate hunt for 227 matching phishing domains; its relationship to Group-IB's cluster is not established in the material reviewed [S6]. The 2,513 credential-pair figure appears in secondary reporting; Dataproof attributes the credentials mostly to infostealers (Vidar and Lumma named per that outlet), not to this kit's phishing [S3].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor identified; assessed by Group-IB as a financially motivated, Chinese-speaking criminal actor [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: Group-IB characterizes the actor as Chinese-speaking and financially motivated; the confidence level is not stated in the secondary sources reviewed [S1][S2].
attribution.basis: Group-IB-based reporting points to Chinese-language notes in the source code and an interface switching across 11 languages as indirect evidence of a Chinese-speaking developer [S2]. Shared Meta Pixel IDs across 300+ domains link the cluster [S7]. The original Group-IB text could not be opened, so the full basis is unverified.

actors.objectives: Financial gain through fake premium ticket sales, resale of tickets tied to hijacked FIFA accounts, and credential theft; Group-IB estimates premium ticket fraud alone at $71 million to $474 million, with total losses potentially reaching billions [S1][S2][S4]. GovInfoSecurity/BankInfoSecurity report a different range of $470 million to $1 billion [S5].

sectors: Consumers / sports fans (World Cup ticket buyers)
regions: Global (FIFA World Cup 2026 audience; kit supports 11 languages)
targeting.notes: Victims are individual fans buying tickets; FIFA is impersonated rather than breached [S1][S4]. The kit supports 11 languages [S4]. Lures offered tickets as cheap as $60 for seats officially priced in the thousands [S3][S4].

capabilities.summary: Custom React single-page phishing kit closely cloning fifa.com and its single sign-on flow, with an interface supporting 11 languages [S1][S4][S7]. Pages include a parameter (p1:reset:userPassword) that authorizes password reset, letting the attacker lock out the legitimate user after capturing credentials and resell tickets tied to the account [S3]. Traffic is acquired mainly through paid Facebook ads, with Meta Pixel IDs shared across the cluster; Telegram and WhatsApp links are secondary channels [S3][S4][S7]. Infrastructure is large-scale domain registration with hyphenated FIFA-name variants, many parked for later activation [S1][S3]. Related parallel schemes in the wider ecosystem include credential phishing, fake ticket sales and counterfeit merchandise [S1][S4].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: the operational environment is the commercial internet and social-media ad ecosystem around FIFA World Cup 2026; relevant to DoD mainly through personnel, families and installations in the host or travel context, not military networks. Step 3: the actor is a criminal cluster with scalable kit and domain infrastructure and no stated state ties [S1][S2][S4]. Step 4: MLCOA is continued ad-driven ticket fraud and credential theft with new domains activated through the tournament [S3][S6]; MDCOA is account-takeover reuse of stolen credentials against users who share passwords with official or work accounts (inference). Candidate indicators: hyphenated FIFA-name domains, shared Meta Pixel IDs, SSO-flow clones of fifa.com [S1][S3][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: treat as a force-protection and personnel-awareness issue rather than a threat to mission systems, since the evidence shows consumer-targeted fraud [S1][S4]. Authorities: DoD has no authority to act on commercial fraud infrastructure; takedowns and ad removal go through registrars, Meta and law enforcement. Mission assurance: reduce credential reuse between personal and official accounts and block known lookalike domains on government-managed devices. Coordination: share indicators with Group-IB, Silent Push and relevant law-enforcement/CTI channels through established unclassified sharing paths.

provenance.importedSummary: GHOST STADIUM is a Chinese-speaking, financially motivated threat actor operating a sophisticated phishing campaign across over 300 domains, utilizing a custom React-based phishing kit that closely mimics FIFA's official website and exploits the PingIdentity SSO login flow. The campaign has the potential to generate financial losses estimated between $71 million and $474 million from premium ticket fraud alone, with total losses potentially reaching billions. GHOST STADIUM employs Facebook Ads as a primary traffic acquisition channel and has been linked to 2,513 compromised FIFA credentials available on dark-web markets. The actor is part of a broader fraud ecosystem that includes multiple parallel schemes, such as credential phishing and counterfeit merchandise sales.

identification.summary: GhostRedirector is a previously unknown threat actor that ESET described in September 2025 and assessed as China-aligned with medium confidence in its blog post (its press release says 'very likely') [S1][S2][S3]. ESET reports it compromised at least 65 Windows servers since August 2024, identified in a June 2025 scan, mainly in Brazil, Thailand, Vietnam and the United States [S2]. It uses a passive C++ backdoor (Rungan) and a malicious native IIS module (Gamshen) that alters responses only for Googlebot to provide SEO fraud as a service, boosting rankings for gambling sites [S1][S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: At least August 2024, per ESET as relayed by secondary reporting [S3][S5].
identification.notes: ESET created the name GhostRedirector; no other vendor name or Microsoft mapping was found in the sources gathered [S1]. ESET could not tie the activity to any known group [S5]. Gamshen is conceptually similar to IIS-module SEO fraud previously described for DragonRank (BadIIS), but sources describe an overlap in technique only, and ESET reportedly found no evidence linking the two [S3][S4][S5]. Findings here come largely from secondary coverage of ESET's research because the primary blog could not be fetched.

attribution.confidence: ESET assesses the actor is China-aligned with medium confidence [S3][S5]. No government attribution or state sponsor was found in the sources gathered. This record does not claim state sponsorship.
attribution.basis: ESET cites hard-coded Chinese strings in the tooling, a code-signing certificate issued to a Chinese company (reported as Shenzhen Diyuan Technology via TrustAsia), and a password containing the Mandarin word 'huang' used for an account the group created [S4][S5][S7].

actors.objectives: ESET reports the observed objective is SEO fraud as a service: Gamshen injects backlinks to gambling sites into responses served to Googlebot to raise their search rankings, particularly sites aimed at Portuguese speakers [S2][S3][S5][S7]. Persistent access to the servers via backdoors and rogue administrator accounts supports this [S1][S7]. No espionage objective is stated in the sources gathered.

regions: Peru (named by some outlets, not in ESET's release)
targeting.notes: Sectors are as listed by The Hacker News from ESET's research [S3][S4]. ESET reportedly believes the group focused on Latin America and Southeast Asia, since many US-located victim servers appear leased to companies based in Brazil, Thailand and Vietnam [S2]. Outlets differ on country lists (Peru appears in The Record and The Register) [S4][S6].

capabilities.summary: Initial access is most likely SQL injection against public-facing applications, followed by PowerShell and CertUtil to download payloads [S2][S7]. Privilege escalation uses tools based on public EfsPotato and BadPotato exploits, which create or modify a user account and add it to the administrators group [S7]. Custom tooling includes Rungan (passive C++ backdoor that runs commands), Gamshen (native IIS module, Googlebot-only response manipulation), Comdai (library with backdoor features: networking, admin account creation, file execution, directory listing, service and registry manipulation) and Zunput (collects IIS-hosted site information and drops ASP, PHP and JavaScript web shells) [S1][S3][S7]. The legitimate remote tool GoToHTTP was also abused [S7]. Some samples were validly code-signed [S7].

diamond.adversary: China-aligned, medium confidence, financially or commercially oriented SEO fraud operator per ESET; no known-group tie [S3][S5].
diamond.capability: SQL injection access, PowerShell/CertUtil staging, Potato-family privilege escalation, Rungan, Gamshen, Comdai, Zunput, GoToHTTP, signed binaries [S1][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised Windows IIS servers used to host the malicious module and web shells [S1][S3]. C2 infrastructure details were not obtained.
diamond.victim: Internet-facing Windows/IIS servers across education, healthcare, insurance, transportation, technology and retail, mainly in Brazil, Thailand, Vietnam and the US [S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing IIS servers with SQL-injectable web applications; trust placed in search-engine crawler traffic and in code-signing certificates [S2][S7].

IOCs (hashes, C2 domains, IPs) were not retrieved.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing IIS servers and the web applications behind them are the relevant terrain, including servers leased to organizations in Latin America and Southeast Asia [S2][S3]. STEP 2: Exposed SQL-injectable applications and weak server monitoring favor the actor [S2]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is SQL injection, PowerShell/CertUtil download, Potato-style privilege escalation, rogue admin account, Rungan/Gamshen persistence [S2][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued opportunistic server compromise for SEO fraud. MDCOA, which the sources do not show but the access supports, is that the same footholds on government- or DoD-adjacent hosting in the covered regions could be repurposed by this or another actor. Candidate indicators: unexpected native IIS modules, new local administrator accounts, GoToHTTP installs, web shells in dynamic directories, CertUtil or PowerShell downloads from web server processes, and responses differing for Googlebot user agents [S1][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track IIS module inventories and web-server process child activity on mission-relevant and partner-hosted servers. (2) Authorities: activity on commercial or partner-nation servers sits outside DoDIN authorities; route through owners or CERT channels. (3) Mission assurance: reputational and SEO abuse is low direct impact, but the same access could enable other actors, so prioritize patching SQL injection and removing unneeded admin accounts. (4) Coordination: share ESET-derived indicators with DC3 and partner CERTs in Brazil, Thailand and Vietnam where relevant [S2][S3].

provenance.importedSummary: GhostRedirector is a China-aligned threat actor that has compromised at least 65 Windows servers across various sectors, primarily in Brazil, Thailand, and Vietnam. It employs a passive C++ backdoor named Rungan and a malicious IIS module called Gamshen to maintain persistent access and manipulate search engine results for SEO fraud. The actor utilizes public exploits like EfsPotato and BadPotato for privilege escalation and abuses code-signing certificates to evade detection. GhostRedirector's operations involve installing remote access tools, creating rogue administrator accounts, and leveraging SQL injection vulnerabilities to execute PowerShell for downloading malicious payloads.

identification.summary: Gingham Typhoon is a China-based espionage group that Microsoft calls the most active actor in the South Pacific. In summer 2023 Microsoft observed it targeting nearly every South Pacific Island country with complex phishing campaigns against international organizations, government entities and the IT sector [S1]. The July 2024 Five Eyes-led advisory lists GINGHAM TYPHOON as an industry name that overlaps with APT40, along with Kryptonite Panda, Leviathan and Bronze Mohawk [S3]. Under its earlier Microsoft name GADOLINIUM, the group historically focused on the maritime and health industries. It later expanded to Asia Pacific organizations, higher education and regional government [S2]. Mandiant ties APT40 to China's naval modernization effort [S4]. Governments in the United Kingdom (2021), New Zealand (2024) and Samoa (2025) have publicly attributed activity to APT40 [S10][S11][S12].
identification.firstObserved: Mandiant: operating since at least 2013 [S4]. Microsoft (2020): compromising targets for nearly a decade [S2]. The 2021 US indictment covers hacking from 2011 to 2018 [S5]. The FBI/CISA advisory AA21-200A, as summarized in search results, says the group has been active since at least 2009 [S6].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Gingham Typhoon. Microsoft reporting used the name GADOLINIUM in 2020 [S2]. Microsoft's threat-actor naming table, as summarized in search results, lists Gingham Typhoon as the new name for GADOLINIUM and maps APT40, Leviathan, TEMP.Periscope and Kryptonite Panda to it [S13]. Other names include APT40, TEMP.Periscope and TEMP.Jumper (Mandiant) [S4]; Leviathan, Kryptonite Panda and Bronze Mohawk [S3]; and TA423 / Red Ladon (Proofpoint / PwC) [S7]. MITRE tracks the group as Leviathan (G0065) [S8].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China, Ministry of State Security (MSS). Earlier reporting places the group in Haikou, Hainan, with tasking from the MSS Hainan State Security Department [S3][S5][S6].
attribution.confidence: The authoring agencies of the July 2024 advisory (led by ASD's ACSC with CISA, NSA, FBI, UK NCSC, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, NCSC-NZ, Germany's BND and BfV, South Korea's NIS, and Japan's NISC and NPA) assess that APT40 conducts malicious cyber operations for the PRC MSS [S3]. In July 2021 the US Department of Justice charged three alleged Hainan State Security Department officers and one contractor [S5]. Mandiant assesses with moderate confidence that APT40 is a state-sponsored Chinese cyber espionage operation [S4]. Microsoft describes Gingham Typhoon as China-based but does not name a sponsoring agency in the sources gathered [S1]. On 19 July 2021 the UK NCSC judged it highly likely that APT40 is linked to the MSS and highly likely sponsored by the MSS Hainan State Security Department, as part of a coordinated allied statement [S12]. In March 2024 New Zealand's GCSB/NCSC said its technical assessment let it confidently link the 2021 parliamentary compromise to APT40, a PRC state-sponsored group [S10]. In February 2025 Samoa's SamCERT called APT40 state-sponsored without naming China directly, linking to the 2024 multinational advisory [S11].
attribution.basis: Mandiant's technical indicators: activity centered on China Standard Time (UTC+8), C2 domains registered through China-based resellers, a C2 administration IP in Hainan, and logins from systems with Chinese language settings [S4]. A 2021 indictment names Ding Xiaoyang, Cheng Qingmin and Zhu Yunmin (alleged Hainan State Security Department officers) and Wu Shurong, operating through the front company Hainan Xiandun Technology Development Co. [S5]. A multinational government advisory in 2024 [S3]. UK NCSC assessment [S12]; New Zealand NCSC technical assessment reinforced by partners' analysis of similar events [S10].

actors.objectives: Strategic espionage supporting PRC geopolitical and economic priorities. Specific goals include support to China's naval modernization [S4], intelligence on Belt and Road Initiative partner states [S1][S4], and collection against South Pacific governments and against vocal critics of the Chinese government amid regional diplomatic competition [S1]. The 2021 indictment also charged conspiracy to commit economic espionage, covering theft of trade secrets and research [S5].

sectors: Government, including executive offices and trade-related departments [S1][S3]
IT sector and internet service providers [S1]
Energy and heavy-industry manufacturing, including offshore wind maintenance in the South China Sea [S7]
Critical infrastructure networks in the Blue Pacific (per SamCERT) [S11]
regions: South Pacific Island countries, including Papua New Guinea [S1] and Samoa [S11]
Southeast Asia and South China Sea claimant states, including Cambodia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia [S4][S5]
Europe, including the United Kingdom, Germany, Belgium, Norway, Switzerland and Austria [S4][S5]
Canada, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and Hong Kong [S4][S5]
targeting.notes: Microsoft says much of the South Pacific targeting reflects a yearslong focus on the region. It observed Gingham Typhoon events from June 2023 to January 2024 [S1]. Mandiant ties the choice of countries to Belt and Road Initiative interests [S4]. Country lists differ between sources: Mandiant's text and its figure list different countries [S4].

capabilities.summary: Initial access comes through spearphishing with malicious attachments and links, strategic web compromises, and exploitation of public-facing web servers followed by web shells [S4]. The group weaponizes newly disclosed exploits within days [S4]. The 2024 advisory says APT40 can rapidly adapt public proof-of-concept exploits for new vulnerabilities, still succeeds with vulnerabilities as old as 2017, and is relying less on procured or leased C2 infrastructure [S3]. It also abuses stolen VPN and remote-desktop credentials [S4]. Tools include AIRBREAK, FRESHAIR, BEACON, PHOTO, BADFLICK, China Chopper, HOMEFRY, MURKYTOP and DISHCLOTH [S4]. Microsoft documented C2 through cloud services: commands hidden in TechNet profiles (2016) and GitHub repositories (2018); Outlook Tasks C2 (2019); and a modified PowerShell Empire using OneDrive via the Microsoft Graph API with Azure AD applications (2020) [S2]. Proofpoint and PwC reported the ScanBox reconnaissance framework delivered through a fake Australian news site in 2022 [S7]. Fake online personas, spoofed domains and stolen credentials appear in the 2021 indictment [S5]. MITRE lists 17 software entries for G0065 [S8]. The 2024 advisory, as reported, says APT40 uses compromised devices, including end-of-life or unpatched SOHO routers, as operational infrastructure and last-hop redirectors; regularly uses web shells early in intrusions; prefers exploiting public-facing infrastructure over user-interaction techniques such as phishing; and has exploited Log4J (CVE-2021-44228), Atlassian Confluence (CVE-2021-26084) and Microsoft Exchange flaws [S14]. SamCERT reported fileless malware, modified commodity malware and long periods of undetected pre-positioning before exfiltration [S11].

campaigns.summary: Microsoft observed Gingham Typhoon targeting nearly every South Pacific Island country, including large-scale targeting of multinational organizations in Papua New Guinea. Victims included government, trade departments, ISPs, a transportation entity and critics of the Chinese government.

diamond.adversary: PRC MSS-linked operators, previously reported as tasked by the Hainan State Security Department and using the front company Hainan Xiandun [S3][S5]. Microsoft tracks them as Gingham Typhoon [S1].
diamond.capability: Spearphishing, strategic web compromise, rapid public-exploit adaptation and web shells [S3][S4]. Malware includes BADFLICK, PHOTO, China Chopper and HOMEFRY [S4]. Also used: cloud-service C2 such as OneDrive/Graph API with modified PowerShell Empire [S2], and the ScanBox reconnaissance framework [S7].
diamond.infrastructure: C2 domains registered through China-based resellers, plus a Hainan-based administration IP [S4]. Legitimate cloud services (TechNet, GitHub, Outlook, OneDrive, Azure AD apps) used as C2 [S2]. Fake news websites and spoofed domains [S5][S7]. Declining use of procured or leased C2 [S3]. Compromised SOHO devices used as last-hop redirectors [S14].
diamond.victim: South Pacific governments, international organizations, ISPs and IT firms [S1]. Also maritime, defense, engineering, health and university targets in the US, Europe and Southeast Asia [S2][S4][S5], and Australian government and media [S3][S7]. New Zealand parliamentary networks (2021) [S10] and Samoan government and critical infrastructure networks [S11].
diamond.socioPolitical: Geopolitical and diplomatic competition in the South Pacific; Belt and Road partner states; South China Sea disputes; and China's naval modernization [S1][S4].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing web servers and unpatched public applications [S3][S4]. VPN and remote-desktop access [S4]. Microsoft 365 / Azure AD cloud services abused for C2 [S2].

gaps: Microsoft's threat-actor naming page (learn.microsoft.com) could not be fetched (DNS failure); the Gingham Typhoon = GADOLINIUM = APT40 mapping rests on a search-result summary of that page [S13] and the 2024 joint advisory alias list [S3].

The full text of joint advisory AA24-190A was not opened. CVE and SOHO details come from press coverage [S14] and search summaries; secondary coverage pairs CVE numbers inconsistently (e.g., CVE-2021-31207 listed under Confluence), so verify CVE mappings against the primary advisory.
The DOJ indictment and press release (justice.gov) and CISA AA21-200A were not opened. Facts come from press and search-result coverage [S5][S6].

The start date is inconsistent across sources (2009, 2011, 2013, 'nearly a decade' before 2020).

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Relevant terrain includes Indo-Pacific partner networks, especially South Pacific Island governments, ISPs and international organizations [S1], plus Australian government networks [S3][S7]. It also includes maritime, naval-research and defense-industrial networks in the US and allied states [S4][S5]. Partner and ISP networks in the region are shared terrain for coalition operations. STEP 2 (effects): Rapid weaponization of public exploits [S3][S4] shrinks patch windows for internet-facing services. C2 over legitimate cloud services [S2] reduces the value of domain and IP blocking. STEP 3 (adversary template): Spearphishing or web-server exploitation, then web shell or first-stage backdoor, then credential theft (HOMEFRY, VPN/RDP credentials), then lateral movement with native tools, then RAR staging and exfiltration [S4]. Cloud-API C2 is an alternate branch [S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is sustained espionage against Pacific and Southeast Asian partner governments and maritime/defense research, timed to diplomatic and Belt and Road events [S1][S4]. MDCOA is compromise of partner ISPs or government executive offices that support coalition operations, giving persistent access to shared communications [S1]. Candidate indicators: exploitation attempts against newly disclosed CVEs on edge web servers within days of disclosure [S3]; web-shell creation; anomalous Azure AD application consent or Graph API OneDrive traffic [S2]; lookalike news or vendor domains in phishing [S5][S7]; and logon activity on UTC+8 working hours [S4]. Additional indicator: inbound access from residential or SOHO router address space acting as last-hop redirectors [S14]. Pacific legislative and small-state government networks with limited defensive capacity are demonstrated targets [S10][S11].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Fuse partner reporting (ASD's ACSC, NCSC-NZ, Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, UK NCSC) with US advisories, since the 2024 advisory was multinational and Australia-led [S3]. Track Microsoft reporting on South Pacific activity [S1]. Authorities: Much of the activity is in partner-nation and commercial networks (ISPs, IT firms, universities) [S1][S5], so action depends on partner consent, hunt-forward agreements, and coordination with FBI/CISA for domestic victims [S5][S6]. Mission assurance: Prioritize patching and web-shell hunting on DoD and DIB internet-facing servers, and monitor cloud tenants for malicious Azure AD applications [S2][S3][S4]. Coordination: Coordinate with Microsoft and cloud providers, which have previously suspended actor Azure AD applications [S2]. Coordinate with allied CERTs for Pacific Island and Southeast Asian partners targeted around Belt and Road and South China Sea issues [S1][S4]. Partner attribution precedent now includes New Zealand (2024) and Samoa (2025) [S10][S11]; Pacific partner CERTs are relevant coordination nodes for shared indicators.

identification.summary: GOBLIN PANDA is CrowdStrike's name for a China-linked espionage actor also tracked as Cycldek and Conimes, focused mainly on Southeast Asia, above all Vietnam [S1][S3][S4]. CrowdStrike says its targets have mostly been in the defense, energy and government sectors [S1][S2]. Kaspersky describes Cycldek as a Chinese-speaking APT that targets high-profile entities in Southeast Asia and judges it more capable than its reputation suggests [S3][S6].
identification.firstObserved: CrowdStrike first observed GOBLIN PANDA activity in September 2013 [S1][S2]. Kaspersky reports Cycldek activity since at least 2013 and code lineage back to 2014 [S3][S6].
identification.notes: Microsoft has no storm-name mapping recorded in this record (msName is empty). Kaspersky and some secondary sources list APT 27 as an alias of Cycldek; Microsoft maps APT27 to Linen/Circle Typhoon, so that alias is not adopted here (see gaps). Kaspersky splits NewCore malware into BlueCore and RedCore variants linked to two sub-clusters that share code and infrastructure and may be offshoots of one larger entity [S3][S4][S6].

attribution.confidence: Vendors label the actor Chinese-speaking or China-linked (CrowdStrike, Kaspersky) [S1][S3][S6]. No government attribution or sponsoring organization was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Vendor telemetry and malware analysis by CrowdStrike (2018) and Kaspersky (2020), including code and infrastructure overlap between malware clusters [S1][S3][S6].

actors.objectives: Espionage against government, defense and energy entities in Southeast Asia, with theft of data including from air-gapped systems via USB media [S1][S2][S4][S5].

targeting.notes: CrowdStrike reports defense, energy and government targeting, with Vietnamese-language decoys in 2018; C2 indicators pointed to Laos though Laotian targets were not confirmed [S1][S2]. Kaspersky reported government targets in Vietnam, Thailand and Laos [S4][S5]. Central Asia targeting could not be verified and was removed.

capabilities.summary: 2018 spear-phishing used Vietnamese-language Word decoys exploiting CVE-2012-0158 to drop the side-loading implant CrowdStrike calls QCRat [S1][S2]. Kaspersky's 2020 research described the NewCore RAT (BlueCore and RedCore variants; RedCore adds a keylogger and RDP logger) and USBCulprit, a tool that exfiltrates data via USB media and is relevant to air-gapped networks [S3][S4][S5][S6]. CrowdStrike lists PlugX and HttpTunnel as the actor's primary malware [S1]; other reporting lists and CVE-2017-11882 and CVE-2018-0802 as additional Office exploits; these were seen only in search-result summaries [S2][S5].

diamond.capability: Office exploit spear-phishing, QCRat, NewCore (BlueCore/RedCore) and USBCulprit [S1][S4][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: C2 indicators pointing to Laos were observed in 2018; Kaspersky notes shared code and infrastructure across clusters. Detailed infrastructure was not reviewed [S1][S6].
diamond.victim: Government, military, defense and energy organizations, mainly in Vietnam, plus Thailand and Laos [S1][S4][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: CrowdStrike reports heavy activity in late spring and early summer 2014 during South China Sea tensions, which suggests regional strategic-intelligence tasking (analyst inference) [S1].
diamond.technology: Legacy Microsoft Office vulnerabilities, removable USB media and air-gapped networks [S1][S4].

gaps: WebFetch could not reach securelist.com, crowdstrike.com or fortinet.com (DNS failure); findings rest on search-result summaries and secondary coverage, not the primary reports. Primary documents not opened: Kaspersky 'Cycldek: Bridging the air-gap', CrowdStrike August 2018 post, Fortinet playbook, CrowdStrike 2020 Global Threat Report, Thales 2022 handbook.
No reporting dated after 2020 was found in searches; current activity level is unknown.
State sponsor, tasking organization and any government attribution are not established in gathered sources.
Naming conflict: Kaspersky and secondary sources list APT 27 as a Cycldek alias, but Microsoft maps APT27 to Linen/Circle Typhoon. Do not merge these clusters without primary evidence.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID or Microsoft storm name is recorded for this actor.
Initial access beyond Office-exploit lures, and exact victim counts, are not documented in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is regional government, defense and energy networks in Vietnam, Thailand and Laos, including air-gapped enclaves reachable by removable media [S4][S5]. STEP 2: The actor reuses old Office exploits, so unpatched legacy Office installations are the exposed surface [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is localized-language spear-phishing, then side-loaded implant (QCRat/NewCore), then USB-based collection (USBCulprit) [S1][S4][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued regional government and defense espionage. MDCOA is USB-borne collection against partner or coalition air-gapped systems during regional crisis. Candidate indicators: Vietnamese-language decoy documents, DLL side-loading by signed binaries, and unexpected USB-resident executables [S1][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track regional partner-nation government and defense incidents attributable to Cycldek/GOBLIN PANDA. (2) Authorities: partner-network support depends on host-nation agreements; pursue through established channels. (3) Mission assurance: enforce removable-media controls and legacy Office patching on enclaves supporting regional operations [S1][S4]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partners and reconcile vendor names (GOBLIN PANDA, Cycldek, Conimes) in reporting [S1][S3].

identification.summary: GoldFactory is the name Group-IB uses for a financially motivated, Chinese-speaking cybercrime group that develops and operates mobile banking malware (GoldDigger, GoldDiggerPlus, GoldKefu, GoldPickaxe for Android and iOS) against victims chiefly in Vietnam and Thailand [S1][S3]. Group-IB describes it as well organized and closely connected to the Gigabud malware family, and says it has been active since at least mid-2023 [S3][S5]. In December 2025 Group-IB reported a wave of modified legitimate banking apps hitting Indonesia, Thailand and Vietnam since October 2024, plus a pre-release test build it calls Gigaflower, a new Gigabud variant [S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: 2023-06 (Group-IB: active since at least mid-2023; GoldDigger reported 2023-10) [S3][S5]
identification.notes: Single-vendor cluster (Group-IB); no Microsoft name or MITRE group ID identified in sources reviewed. Whether Gigabud and GoldFactory are directly the same operators is described in coverage as unresolved ('close connections') [S3]. Group-IB publications were seen only as search-result excerpts and secondary coverage; the primary pages could not be fetched.

attribution.confidence: Group-IB assesses GoldFactory as a Chinese-speaking cybercrime group [S3][S5]. No state sponsorship is asserted in the sources reviewed.
attribution.basis: Group-IB links the cluster by shared code and naming conventions across the 'Gold' malware families, and by close connections to Gigabud [S3]. The language assessment is Group-IB's, as relayed by secondary coverage [S3][S5].

actors.objectives: Financial gain: theft of banking credentials, personal data, ID documents and facial recognition data, then account takeover and unauthorized transfers, including using AI face-swap deepfakes to defeat facial verification [S2][S3].

sectors: Banking and financial services customers (retail mobile banking users)
targeting.notes: GoldPickaxe lures impersonated Thai government services, including a Digital Pension app [S2]. Group-IB's December 2025 report counts 300+ modified banking-app samples and almost 2,200 infections in Indonesia; first cases of that wave were in Thailand, with Vietnam following and Indonesia surging from mid-2025 [S5][S6]. Lures impersonate government entities and trusted local brands, in one case Vietnam's EVN utility via Zalo [S5][S6]. Victims, not government or military networks, are the target set.

capabilities.summary: Social-engineering-led mobile malware operations. Android: GoldDigger abuses Accessibility Service to capture on-screen text including passwords; GoldDiggerPlus embeds GoldKefu, uses web fakes impersonating 10 Vietnamese banks and can place real-time calls to victims [S3]. GoldPickaxe (iOS and Android, derived from GoldDigger) collects facial data, ID documents and SMS [S1][S3]. iOS delivery first abused TestFlight, then tricked victims into installing an MDM profile giving broad device control [S2][S3]. Operators use AI face-swap services to produce deepfakes from stolen biometrics [S2][S3]. In the 2025 wave, legitimate banking apps are repackaged and modified to capture data and enable remote control [S5][S6]. Gigaflower is described as a pre-release test version of a new Gigabud variant with experimental features such as text recognition and QR scanning of ID card images [S5]. Lure delivery includes phone calls, messengers and fake Google Play pages leading to RATs such as Gigabud, MMRat or Remo [S5][S6].

campaigns.summary: Group-IB reported GoldPickaxe.iOS and an Android version stealing facial data, ID documents and SMS, with deepfake-enabled bypass of facial verification. iOS delivery moved from TestFlight to MDM profile, with Thai government (Digital Pension) lures. Thai police reportedly confirmed criminals used captured face scans to bypass facial recognition. HKCERT issued a public alert on 2024-02-20 [S1][S2][S3][S4].

campaigns.summary: First cases of the later wave of repackaged banking apps appeared in Thailand in October 2024, followed by Vietnam in late 2024 to early 2025 [S5][S6].

campaigns.name: Indonesia surge
campaigns.summary: Infections rose sharply in Indonesia from mid-2025; Group-IB counted 300+ modified-app samples and almost 2,200 Indonesian infections [S5][S6].

campaigns.name: Group-IB 'Turning apps into gold' report and Gigaflower
campaigns.summary: Group-IB published findings on modified banking apps used against Indonesia, Thailand and Vietnam, and a pre-release Gigaflower build as a new Gigabud variant [S5][S6].

diamond.adversary: GoldFactory, Chinese-speaking cybercrime group per Group-IB, with close ties to the Gigabud ecosystem [S3][S5].
diamond.capability: Custom Android/iOS trojans, MDM abuse, AI face-swap deepfakes, repackaged banking apps [S2][S3][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Fake Google Play pages, messenger links (LINE/Zalo-type channels), phone-call social engineering, fake government and brand apps [S2][S5][S6]. Specific C2 and domains not captured.
diamond.victim: Retail banking customers in Vietnam, Thailand and Indonesia [S3][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Profit-driven fraud; no political aim stated in sources reviewed [S3].
diamond.technology: Android and iOS mobile platforms, TestFlight and MDM enrollment, accessibility services, facial-recognition banking checks, repackaged banking apps [S2][S3][S6].

gaps: Primary Group-IB reports (goldfactory-ios-trojan, turning-apps-into-gold) were visible only in search results and could not be opened; details rely on secondary coverage.
No Microsoft name, MITRE group ID, or government attribution found.
Relationship between GoldFactory and Gigabud operators is described only as 'close connections'; direct identity unconfirmed [S3].
No arrests or takedowns of operators found; Thai police statement is reported only secondhand [S3].
Infrastructure indicators, financial loss totals and operator identities not captured.
Exact publication day of the December 2025 report not verified.
Group-IB figures on 27 apps, 63% Indonesia share, 48 Gigaflower commands, hooking-tool names and the 50+ Vietnamese institutions count could not be confirmed and were removed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. The actor is a criminal threat to personnel and families rather than to military networks. Step 1-2: operating environment includes Southeast Asian mobile banking users and personal devices; relevant terrain is app stores, MDM enrollment, messenger platforms and facial-verification banking [S2][S6]. Step 3-4 MLCOA: continued fraud against SE Asian retail banking users via impersonated government and brand lures, expanding country by country (Thailand, Vietnam, Indonesia) [S5][S6]. MDCOA: expansion to other regions (Group-IB notes signs of geographic expansion) or to enterprise bring-your-own-device users, using stolen biometrics against corporate or financial verification [S3]. Candidate indicators: sideloaded banking apps, unexpected MDM profiles or TestFlight invitations, accessibility permission requests, unsolicited calls and messenger links from supposed utilities or agencies [S2][S5][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: brief deployed and stationed personnel in Southeast Asia on mobile-banking fraud lures and biometric theft [S2][S5]. Authorities: this is criminal activity; response is through law enforcement and host-nation channels, with force protection and personnel-security advisories rather than offensive action. Mission assurance: restrict sideloading and unmanaged MDM enrollment on personal devices used for official duties and avoid sharing ID documents or face scans via apps [S2][S3]. Coordination: share indicators with security forces, counterintelligence and host-nation CERTs (Thai banking CERT and HKCERT already issued alerts) [S2][S4].

provenance.importedSummary: GoldFactory is a threat actor group attributed to developing sophisticated mobile banking malware targeting victims primarily in the Asia-Pacific region, specifically Vietnam and Thailand. They utilize social engineering to deliver malware to victims' devices and have close connections to the Gigabud malware family. GoldFactory's Trojans, such as GoldPickaxe and GoldDigger, employ tactics like smishing, phishing, and fake login screens to compromise victims' phones and steal sensitive information. Their evolving malware suite demonstrates a high level of operational maturity and ingenuity, requiring a proactive and multi-faceted cybersecurity approach to detect and mitigate their threats.

identification.summary: ESET describes GopherWhisper as a previously undocumented China-aligned APT group that targets governmental institutions in Mongolia [S1][S2]. ESET found it in January 2025 after discovering a new backdoor, LaxGopher, on the system of a Mongolian government institution [S2][S5]. Most of its tools are written in Go, with a C++ fallback backdoor, SSLORDoor [S1]. It uses Discord, Slack, Microsoft 365 Outlook and file.io for command and control (C2) and exfiltration [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: ESET assesses the group has been active since at least November 2023 (as reported by secondary coverage); ESET first discovered it in January 2025 [S3][S5].
identification.notes: No Microsoft actor name or MITRE ATT&CK group ID was found for GopherWhisper in the sources gathered. The name is ESET's. ESET reportedly found no links between the toolset and known groups, which led to a new cluster designation [S5]. Do not merge with other China-aligned clusters without vendor evidence.

attribution.confidence: ESET characterizes the group as China-aligned and says the activity looks like cyber espionage, but reportedly did not tie it to a specific entity [S1][S3]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Per coverage of ESET's report: Slack and Discord message timestamps cluster in 08:00-17:00 UTC+8 (China Standard Time), and a Slack locale setting and VMware machine timestamps point the same way [S3]. The toolset reportedly showed no links to known groups [S5].

actors.objectives: ESET characterizes the activity as cyber espionage against a Mongolian government institution [S1][S3]. Specific collection requirements are not stated in the sources gathered. CompactGopher compresses files and uploads them to file.io, which indicates document collection [S3].

regions: Possible additional victims in unidentified locations and sectors [S2]
targeting.notes: The confirmed victim is a Mongolian governmental institution, with about 12 infected systems reported there [S4][S7]. ESET's analysis of C2 traffic via attacker-controlled Discord and Slack suggests dozens of other entities were compromised; their locations and sectors are unknown [S2][S3]. The imported record says Central Asia; that regional claim was not found in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: ESET documents a toolset of custom Go backdoors LaxGopher (Slack C2), RatGopher (Discord C2) and BoxOfFriends (Microsoft 365 Outlook draft messages via the Microsoft Graph mail REST API), the injector JabGopher, the exfiltration tool CompactGopher (compresses files and uploads to file.io), the loader FriendDelivery, and the C++ backdoor SSLORDoor [S2][S3][S4]. The group abuses legitimate cloud services for C2 and exfiltration, tested malware on these platforms, then reused the same accounts for live operations without clearing logs [S3][S4]. The initial access vector was not found in the sources gathered.

campaigns.name: Discovery on Mongolian government system
campaigns.summary: ESET found the previously undocumented LaxGopher backdoor on a system at a Mongolian government institution.

campaigns.name: ESET public disclosure
campaigns.summary: ESET published 'GopherWhisper: A burrow full of malware' and a press release on 2026-04-23, reporting about 12 infected systems at the Mongolian institution and likely dozens of other victims.

diamond.adversary: China-aligned espionage group tracked by ESET as GopherWhisper; working hours consistent with UTC+8 [S1][S3].
diamond.capability: Go-based backdoors, injector, loader and exfiltration tool, plus a C++ fallback backdoor, using legitimate cloud services for C2 [S2][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Attacker-controlled Slack and Discord workspaces and channels, Microsoft 365 Outlook accounts (draft messages), file.io for exfiltration [S2][S3]. Per ESET, Slack and Discord API tokens were obtained, allowing retrieval of C2 messages [S2].
diamond.victim: A Mongolian governmental institution (about 12 systems), with dozens of other unidentified victims suspected [S2][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Espionage against a Mongolian government body by a China-aligned actor [S1][S3]. Policy drivers were not stated in the sources gathered.
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints and enterprise use of Slack, Discord and Microsoft 365 Outlook, whose traffic is generally allowed and blends with legitimate use [S2][S3].

gaps: I could not open the primary ESET report (welivesecurity.com) or white paper; WebFetch failed with a DNS error on every host tried. Content is drawn from search-result summaries of ESET and secondary coverage, so details need checking against the primary report.
Initial access vector not found in the sources gathered.
Sponsor and tasking are unknown; no government attribution or Microsoft/MITRE mapping was found.
Identity, location and sectors of the 'dozens' of other suspected victims are unknown [S2].
The imported record's Central Asia victim claim and its reference to CompactGopher/JabGopher specifics were not independently confirmed beyond the sources cited.
The November 2023 start date is from secondary coverage, not the primary report.
Full IOCs (hashes, workspace IDs) are in ESET's report and were not retrieved.

The hendryadrian.com mirror was not seen in search results and was removed along with claims resting only on it (July 2024 Outlook account/tooling timeline, JabGopher svchost.exe detail; SSLORDoor raw SSL socket C2 and in-memory svchost.exe detail also removed).

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is government endpoints and the enterprise SaaS channels (Slack, Discord, Microsoft 365 Outlook) that the actor uses for C2; these are typically allowed through boundary controls [S2][S3]. STEP 2: The actor's use of allowed cloud services reduces the value of domain and IP blocklists [S3]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is backdoor deployment (Go tools), C2 via chat or mail-draft channels, then file compression and upload to file.io [S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against Mongolian and possibly other regional government entities. MDCOA is reuse of the same tradecraft against partner-nation government networks relevant to coalition operations; this is an inference, not a sourced finding. Candidate indicators: unapproved Slack or Discord clients or API token use on government hosts, Graph API mail-draft creation by non-mail processes, and uploads to file.io [S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track ESET's IOCs and fold SaaS-abuse detections (chat API tokens, draft-message Graph calls, file.io egress) into hunt plans [S2][S3]. (2) Authorities: monitoring or blocking of commercial chat services on government networks needs owner and policy approval; coordinate before action. (3) Mission assurance: assume cloud-service C2 may bypass perimeter allowlists; verify which SaaS tenants and clients are authorized. (4) Coordination: the confirmed victim is a foreign government, so sharing runs through partner and vendor channels; the platform providers (Slack, Discord, Microsoft) can disable abused accounts.

provenance.importedSummary: GopherWhisper is a China-aligned APT that routes C2 traffic through legitimate enterprise platforms like Slack, Discord, and Microsoft 365 Outlook to evade detection. Its toolkit includes the LaxGopher backdoor for Slack, RatGopher for Discord, and CompactGopher for data exfiltration via file.io. The group employs DLL side-loading via JabGopher and uses raw OpenSSL socket C2 on port 443 with the SSLORDoor backdoor. GopherWhisper has targeted Mongolian government entities and is assessed to have additional unidentified victims in Central Asia.

identification.summary: Granite Typhoon (formerly GALLIUM) is a China-linked cyberespionage actor. It first became known for compromising telecommunications providers by exploiting unpatched internet-facing services such as WildFly/JBoss, then deploying web shells and off-the-shelf credential and lateral-movement tools [S1]. In June 2022 Unit 42 reported that the group had expanded beyond telecommunications to financial institutions and government entities and was using a new RAT, PingPull [S2]. In 2023 Unit 42 tied the same cluster (Alloy Taurus) to a Linux PingPull variant and a new backdoor, Sword2033 [S3]. It also attributed, with moderate confidence, one of three China-nexus clusters active against a Southeast Asian government to Alloy Taurus [S4].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE and Unit 42 describe the group as active since at least 2012 [S5]. Microsoft's 2019 report covered activity observed mainly from 2018 to mid-2019 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Granite Typhoon (formerly GALLIUM). The Hacker News coverage of Unit 42's September 2023 report gives Granite Typhoon as an alias for Alloy Taurus, while Unit 42's own report lists GALLIUM [S4]. In Microsoft's taxonomy, 'Typhoon' indicates origin or attribution to China [S9]. Unit 42 tracks the group as Alloy Taurus and describes Alloy Taurus as also known as GALLIUM and Softcell [S2]. MITRE tracks it as GALLIUM (G0093) [S5]. Cluster boundary caution: SentinelLabs assessed the 2023 Middle East telecom intrusions as highly likely the work of a Chinese cyberespionage group in the nexus of Gallium and APT41, with the exact grouping unclear [S8].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (vendor assessments only; no government attribution found in the sources gathered). MITRE describes GALLIUM as likely Chinese state-sponsored [S5]. Unit 42 calls the group a likely Chinese state-sponsored group, citing its geographic and sector focus, technical skill and use of known Chinese threat-actor malware and TTPs [S2].
attribution.confidence: Vendor assessments only, at the 'likely' level [S2][S5]. Microsoft's 2019 GALLIUM report does not attribute the group to a specific state [S1]; Microsoft's later 'Typhoon' name signals China origin or attribution under its taxonomy [S9]. Unit 42 attributed its 2023 Southeast Asian government cluster (CL-STA-0045) to Alloy Taurus with moderate confidence [S4].
attribution.basis: Tooling overlap with known Chinese actors, including China Chopper, Poison Ivy and Gh0st-derived malware [S1][S2]; consistent targeting of telecommunications and government entities [S2]; infrastructure hosted in mainland China, Hong Kong SAR and Taiwan [S1].

actors.objectives: Intelligence collection from telecommunications providers [S1][S2]. Targeting later widened to government and financial entities, consistent with broader espionage [S2][S4].

sectors: Financial institutions and public financial administrators [S2][S4]
Critical infrastructure and public healthcare (Southeast Asian government cluster, shared across three actors) [S4]
regions: Southeast Asia, Europe and Africa (historic telecom targeting) [S2]
Afghanistan, Australia, Belgium, Cambodia, Malaysia, Mozambique, the Philippines, Russia and Vietnam (entities linked to 2022 infrastructure) [S2]
An unnamed Southeast Asian government (Alloy Taurus cluster activity from early 2022 into 2023) [S4]
South Africa and Nepal (2023 Linux PingPull/Sword2033 activity) [S3]
Middle East telecommunications providers (Q1 2023; SentinelLabs places the actor in the Gallium/APT41 nexus) [S8]
targeting.notes: Telecommunications has been the most consistent focus [S1][S2]. Unit 42's 2022 country list comes from targeted entities tied to GALLIUM infrastructure, not confirmed compromises [S2].

capabilities.summary: Initial access is mainly through exploiting unpatched internet-facing services, notably WildFly/JBoss, with public exploits; this needs no phishing or user interaction [S1]. In later activity Unit 42 and SentinelLabs reported exploitation of Exchange servers [S4][S8]. After access, the group installs web shells (China Chopper and BlackMould, a native IIS web shell based on China Chopper) and moves laterally mainly with compromised domain credentials and PsExec [S1]. Common tools are HTRAN, Mimikatz, NBTScan, Netcat, PsExec, Windows Credential Editor and WinRAR [S1]. Malware includes a modified Poison Ivy that Microsoft said appeared unique to GALLIUM and QuarkBandit, a modified Gh0st RAT. The group changed their communications to evade existing signatures, installed SoftEther VPN on internal systems for persistence, and signed at least one credential dumper with a stolen certificate [S1]. PingPull (2022) is a RAT with variants using ICMP, HTTP(S) or raw TCP for C2; its ICMP use exploits the fact that few organizations inspect ICMP [S2]. In 2023 the group added a Linux PingPull variant, which only 3 of 62 vendors flagged when it was reported, and the Sword2033 backdoor for file upload, download and command execution [S3].

campaigns.name: GALLIUM telecom intrusions (Microsoft)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reported GALLIUM exploiting WildFly/JBoss and using web shells, Mimikatz, PsExec, SoftEther VPN and modified Poison Ivy and Gh0st-variant malware against telecommunications providers, mainly from 2018 to mid-2019.

campaigns.name: PingPull expansion
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 reported the new PingPull RAT and expansion to government and finance targets, with infrastructure linked to entities in nine countries.

campaigns.name: Southeast Asian government intrusions (CL-STA-0045)
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 attributed CL-STA-0045, one of three China-nexus clusters active against the same Southeast Asian government, to Alloy Taurus with moderate confidence; the activity began in early 2022, continued through 2023, and exploited Exchange servers to deploy web shells for long-term espionage.

campaigns.name: Operation Tainted Love (Middle East telecoms)
campaigns.summary: SentinelLabs reported Q1 2023 intrusions against Middle East telecom providers through internet-facing Exchange servers, with custom Mimikatz-based credential theft (mim221). It assessed the activity as an evolution of Operation Soft Cell tooling and judged it highly likely to be a Chinese cyberespionage group in the nexus of Gallium and APT41, with the exact grouping unclear.

campaigns.name: Linux PingPull and Sword2033
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 reported a Linux PingPull variant and the new Sword2033 backdoor used against targets in South Africa and Nepal.

diamond.adversary: China-linked espionage operators that vendors assess as likely state-sponsored [S2][S5]. No named individuals or units appear in the sources gathered.
diamond.capability: Public exploits for internet-facing servers; China Chopper and BlackMould web shells; Mimikatz, WCE, PsExec and HTRAN; modified Poison Ivy and QuarkBandit; PingPull for Windows and Linux; Sword2033 [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: C2 mainly on dynamic DNS subdomains (ddns.net, myftp.biz); domains hosted in mainland China, Hong Kong SAR and Taiwan; Taiwan-based servers, apparently exclusive to GALLIUM, used for web shell connections [S1]; SoftEther VPN inside victim networks [S1].
diamond.victim: Telecommunications providers, government entities and financial institutions in Southeast Asia, Europe, Africa and elsewhere [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Government targeting supports broader intelligence requirements [S4].
diamond.technology: Unpatched internet-facing application and mail servers (WildFly/JBoss, IIS, Exchange) and networks that do not inspect ICMP [S1][S2][S8].

gaps: No Unit 42 primary reports could be fetched (2022 PingPull, 2023 Linux PingPull, 2023 SE Asia clusters); facts come from search-result summaries and press coverage [S2][S3][S4].

Microsoft's threat-actor naming table could not be opened, and Microsoft's 2023 taxonomy post does not list Granite Typhoon. The Granite Typhoon = Alloy Taurus mapping relies on press coverage of Unit 42 reporting [S4][S9].

Neither the MITRE ATT&CK page nor the SentinelLabs page could be fetched; content relies on search-result coverage [S5][S8]. Cybereason's Operation Soft Cell reporting (2019) was not included because no verified source URL was retained.

Cluster boundary: Unit 42 treats Softcell as a GALLIUM alias, while SentinelLabs placed 2023 Middle East activity in the Gallium/APT41 nexus. Shared or leaked tooling (Poison Ivy, China Chopper, Mimikatz) limits confidence in these links [S2][S8].
The CrowdStrike alias PHANTOM PANDA and the imported 'Red Dev 4' alias were not confirmed in any source opened.
No government attribution, indictment, sanctions or joint advisory naming this group was found. The sponsoring organization (MSS, PLA or contractor) is unknown.
No well-sourced activity after 2023 was found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (define the OE): Key terrain is telecom provider networks that hold call detail records, plus internet-facing application and mail servers (WildFly/JBoss, IIS, Exchange) at telecom, government and finance entities [S1][S2][S8]. STEP 2 (describe effects): Unpatched public-facing services give a foothold with no user interaction, and ICMP-based C2 can evade networks that do not inspect ICMP [S1][S2]. STEP 3 (adversary template): the actor exploits a public-facing server, installs a China Chopper or BlackMould web shell, harvests credentials with Mimikatz or WCE, moves laterally with PsExec, persists with RATs (PingPull, Poison Ivy, QuarkBandit) or SoftEther VPN, and stages data with WinRAR [S1][S2]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is sustained, low-cost collection of subscriber metadata and government data from partner-nation telecom and government networks [S1][S4]. Candidate indicators: new web shells on IIS or JBoss servers; anomalous ICMP payloads; SoftEther VPN on servers; C2 on dynamic DNS (ddns.net, myftp.biz); tools signed with stolen certificates; Linux hosts beaconing over HTTPS to unfamiliar domains [S1][S2][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track exploitation of internet-facing servers and ICMP C2 patterns across DoD-adjacent and partner telecom networks in regions the group has targeted (Southeast Asia, Africa, Europe, Middle East) [S1][S2][S8]. Authorities: most of the targeted terrain is commercial or partner-nation telecom outside the DODIN, so response depends on partner nations and private providers rather than direct DoD action [S2]. Coordination: share indicators (web shells, PingPull, Sword2033, dynamic DNS C2) with partner CERTs and providers, and reconcile vendor names (Granite Typhoon, GALLIUM, Alloy Taurus, Softcell) in shared reporting without merging the APT41 cluster [S1][S2][S3][S8].
