provenance.importedSummary: GALLIUM, is a threat actor believed to be targeting telecommunication providers over the world, mostly South-East Asia, Europe and Africa. To compromise targeted networks, GALLIUM target unpatched internet-facing services using publicly available exploits and have been known to target vulnerabilities in WildFly/JBoss.

identification.summary: Gray Sandstorm (formerly DEV-0343) is an Iran-origin actor that Microsoft says runs extensive password spraying against Office 365 / Exchange accounts. It emulates a Firefox browser and routes traffic through Tor proxy IPs [S1][S3]. In 2021 Microsoft observed it spraying more than 250 Office 365 tenants, compromising fewer than 20. Targets were US and Israeli defense technology firms, geographic information systems (GIS) companies, Persian Gulf ports of entry and maritime/cargo shippers with a Middle East presence [S1]. In March 2026 Check Point Research reported an Iran-nexus Microsoft 365 password-spray campaign against Israeli and UAE municipalities and companies, with tradecraft similar to Gray Sandstorm [S4][S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft began tracking the DEV-0343 cluster in late July 2021 [S1]. The imported summary's claim of activity 'since at least 2012' is not supported by any source gathered here.
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Gray Sandstorm. Gray Sandstorm was formerly tracked as DEV-0343 [S3]; 'DEV-' names are temporary designations Microsoft gives to unknown, emerging or developing clusters of activity [S1]. No MITRE ATT&CK group entry was identified. Microsoft documented an overlap with EUROPIUM (now Hazel Sandstorm): in June 2021 DEV-0343 targeted the same account within minutes of EUROPIUM gaining access, which Microsoft assesses as coordination among Iranian actors [S2]. Check Point also tied the 2026 technique to Peach Sandstorm, a separate Microsoft cluster [S4][S6]. Keep these clusters distinct.

attribution.sponsor: Iran. Microsoft lists Gray Sandstorm's origin as Iran [S3] and assesses its activity 'likely' supports the national interests of the Islamic Republic of Iran [S1][S2]. No source gathered names a specific government organization (e.g., IRGC or MOIS).
attribution.confidence: Microsoft's wording is 'likely' supports Iranian national interests [S1]. For the 2026 campaign, coverage reports that Check Point assessed Iranian responsibility with moderate confidence, citing similarities to Gray Sandstorm [S4][S6]. Hive Pro attributed the activity with moderate confidence to an Iran-nexus actor whose tactics closely mirror Gray Sandstorm, which is not a confirmed identification [S7]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft cited pattern-of-life analysis, notably activity Sunday through Thursday during Iranian working hours. It also cited extensive geographic and sectoral overlap with known Iranian actors and alignment of techniques and targets with another Iran-origin actor [S1][S2]. Check Point's 2026 assessment rests on Microsoft 365 log analysis showing red-team tooling run through Tor exit nodes, similar to Gray Sandstorm, plus target correlation with Iranian missile strikes [S4][S6].

actors.objectives: Microsoft assesses that DEV-0343 sought to track adversary security services and Middle East maritime shipping to strengthen Iran's contingency plans. It also suggests that commercial satellite imagery and proprietary shipping plans or logs could help offset Iran's developing satellite program [S1]. Check Point judged that the March 2026 campaign against municipalities likely supported kinetic operations and bomb damage assessment (BDA), as reported in coverage [S4][S6].

sectors: Defense technology: military-grade radars, drone technology, satellite systems, emergency response communications [S1][S2]
Geographic information systems (GIS) and spatial analytics [S1][S2]
Ports of entry and maritime/cargo transportation [S1][S2]
Municipalities and government entities (2026, Check Point, similar tradecraft) [S4][S5][S6]
Technology, transportation and logistics, healthcare, manufacturing (2026, Check Point) [S4][S6]
regions: Limited 2026 targeting in Europe, US, UK and Saudi Arabia [S4][S5]
targeting.notes: The 2021 targeting comes from Microsoft [S1][S2]. Reporting on the 2026 campaign comes from Check Point via secondary coverage, with attribution resting on tradecraft similarity [S4][S5][S6][S7]. Coverage reported more than 300 organizations targeted in Israel and more than 25 in the UAE [S5].

capabilities.summary: The actor's core capability is low-cost credential access. It uses an enumeration and password-spray tool similar to the open-source o365spray against Exchange ActiveSync and Autodiscover endpoints to validate accounts and passwords [S1][S2]. It sprays dozens to hundreds of accounts per organization, enumerating each one dozens to thousands of times. Traffic comes from 150 to more than 1,000 unique Tor exit IPs per organization, with Firefox or Chrome user agents [S1]. Because the Tor infrastructure rotates, Microsoft published no static IOCs [S1]. Microsoft notes that accounts with MFA are resilient to these sprays [S1][S8]. In the 2026 campaign Check Point reported several behaviors. Scanning ran from frequently rotated Tor exit nodes with an Internet Explorer 10 user agent. Operators then logged in with valid credentials via Windscribe and NordVPN IPs geolocated in Israel to bypass geographic restrictions [S4][S6]. No custom malware or exploited CVEs are attributed in the sources gathered.

campaigns.name: Account targeting alongside EUROPIUM
campaigns.summary: DEV-0343 targeted an account within minutes of EUROPIUM (Hazel Sandstorm) gaining access to it on 13 June 2021. Microsoft cited this as coordination among Iranian actors.

campaigns.name: Office 365 password-spray campaign against defense, GIS and maritime
campaigns.summary: Starting in late July 2021, DEV-0343 sprayed more than 250 Office 365 tenants through Tor, compromising fewer than 20. Targets were US/Israeli defense technology firms, GIS companies, Persian Gulf ports and maritime shippers. Microsoft disclosed the campaign on 11 October 2021.

campaigns.name: MSTIC CyberWarCon 2021 briefing
campaigns.summary: Microsoft placed DEV-0343 within broader Iranian trends and reiterated its targets, o365spray-like tooling and Iran working-hours pattern.

campaigns.name: Iran-nexus Microsoft 365 password spray against Israel and UAE (similar tradecraft)
campaigns.summary: Check Point reported three spray waves on 3, 13 and 23 March 2026, mainly against municipalities in Israel and the UAE. It assessed the campaign as Iran-linked with similarities to Gray Sandstorm, and correlated targets with cities hit by Iranian missiles (possible BDA support).

diamond.adversary: Iran-origin operators working Sunday through Thursday during Iranian business hours. Microsoft assesses they likely serve Iranian national interests [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.capability: An o365spray-like enumeration and password-spray tool against Exchange ActiveSync/Autodiscover; per Check Point in 2026, red-team tooling followed by valid-account logins [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Rotating Tor exit nodes, 150 to 1,000+ per target organization [S1]. In 2026, commercial VPN egress (Windscribe, NordVPN) geolocated in Israel [S4][S6].
diamond.victim: Office 365 tenants of defense technology, GIS, port and maritime organizations in the US, Israel and the Gulf [S1]. In 2026, Israeli and UAE municipalities and companies [S4][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Iranian contingency planning against adversary security services and Gulf shipping, plus satellite-program support [S1]. In 2026, possible support to kinetic targeting and BDA during Iran-Israel hostilities [S4][S6].
diamond.technology: Cloud identity: Office 365 / Microsoft 365 authentication via legacy ActiveSync and Autodiscover endpoints, and accounts without MFA or Conditional Access [S1][S4].

gaps: Check Point's primary report could not be fetched (host unreachable from this environment). Its 2026 details, including the 'moderate confidence' wording, IE10 user agent, VPN providers and BDA judgment, come from search-result summaries and secondary coverage.
The 2026 campaign is attributed to Gray Sandstorm only by tradecraft similarity. Check Point also cites Peach Sandstorm, and Microsoft has not publicly confirmed Gray Sandstorm's involvement.
The imported summary claims activity since at least 2012; no cited source supports this, and Microsoft dates the DEV-0343 cluster to July 2021.
Sponsoring organization (IRGC, MOIS or a contractor) is not identified in any source gathered.
Post-compromise actions after the 2021 compromise of fewer than 20 tenants (data accessed, persistence, follow-on tooling) are not public.
No MITRE ATT&CK group entry was found; no independent vendor or government reporting on Gray Sandstorm between 2022 and 2025 was found.
The relationship to Hazel Sandstorm (EUROPIUM) beyond the single June 2021 coordinated-access event is unclear.
The Microsoft threat actor naming page in the imported references was not re-fetched.
The date of Microsoft's conversion of DEV-0343 to the Gray Sandstorm name (often given as April 2023) was not confirmed by any cited source; the claim was removed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key cyber terrain is cloud identity, meaning Microsoft 365 / Exchange Online tenants of defense contractors (radar, UAS, satellite, emergency communications), GIS providers, Gulf ports and maritime logistics, and, per 2026 reporting, host-nation municipalities [S1][S4]. STEP 2 (effects): Iran's working-week pattern (Sunday through Thursday, about 04:00 to 16:00 UTC) and Tor-based spraying mean noisy but persistent authentication attempts against legacy protocols. Accounts with MFA are resilient [S1][S2]. STEP 3 (adversary model): enumeration via ActiveSync/Autodiscover, then password spray from Tor, then a valid-account login (in 2026 via in-country VPN egress), then mailbox access [S1][S4][S6]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued spraying of defense-industrial, logistics and maritime tenants to collect imagery, shipping and security-service information for Iranian contingency planning [S1]. MDCOA, during Iran-related hostilities, is compromise of host-nation municipal or logistics accounts near US or partner installations to support Iranian targeting and BDA, as Check Point suggested for March 2026 [S4][S6]. Candidate indicators: high-volume failed sign-ins to ActiveSync/Autodiscover from Tor exit IPs; Firefox, Chrome or IE10 user agents on legacy endpoints; successful logins from commercial VPN ranges geolocated in-country soon after spray activity; and spray timing aligned to Iranian business hours [S1][S4][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: fuse Entra ID / M365 sign-in telemetry (failed-logon sequences, Tor exit matches, legacy-protocol use) into the common operational picture. Microsoft published no static IOCs, so detection must be behavioral [S1]. (2) Authorities: most targets are defense contractors, logistics firms and foreign municipalities outside the DODIN, so response depends on DIB partnerships, host-nation coordination and vendor reporting rather than direct DoD action [S1][S4]. (3) Mission assurance: enforce MFA, block legacy ActiveSync clients from bypassing Conditional Access, and block anonymizer traffic. These are Microsoft's recommended mitigations, and they directly negate this TTP [S1]. Logistics, port and contractor accounts that support theater sustainment are priority assets. (4) Coordination: during Iran-related crises, share spray indicators with host-nation and coalition CERTs (Israel, UAE, Gulf partners), since municipal compromise may precede or support kinetic strikes [S4][S5].

provenance.importedSummary: Gray Sandstorm is an Iran-linked threat actor that has been active since at least 2012. They have targeted defense technology companies, maritime transportation companies, and Persian Gulf ports of entry. Their primary method of attack is password spraying, and they have been observed using tools like o365spray. They have a specific focus on US and Israeli targets and are likely operating in support of Iranian interests.

identification.summary: Grayling is the name Symantec's Threat Hunter Team (Broadcom) gave to a previously unseen threat actor, reported in October 2023, that targeted organizations mainly in Taiwan [S1][S2]. Its distinctive trait is DLL side-loading through the exported function SbieDll_Hook to load payloads such as Cobalt Strike, NetSpy and the Havoc framework [S2][S4].
identification.notes: Symantec reported the activity running from February 2023 to at least May 2023 [S2][S3]. Symantec reported no overlap with Naikon, which had used similar SbieDll_Hook/SandboxieBITS.exe side-loading [S2]. No Microsoft name or MITRE ATT&CK group ID was found in the sources reviewed.

attribution.confidence: Symantec did not tie Grayling to a specific country; it said the Taiwan focus suggests a region with strategic interest in Taiwan [S2][S4]. No government attribution found.
attribution.basis: Symantec's reasoning rests on the heavy Taiwan targeting, with DLL side-loading noted as common among China-linked actors, while it found no overlap with Naikon [S2][S4]. The China-linked label is a press inference, not a vendor or government attribution [S4].

actors.objectives: Symantec assessed the targets and post-exploitation behaviors as consistent with intelligence gathering rather than financial motivation; no data exfiltration was observed [S3][S4].

targeting.notes: Primary focus was Taiwanese manufacturing, IT and biomedical organizations; a Pacific Islands government agency and organizations in Vietnam and the US were also reportedly targeted [S2][S3]. SC Media's summary describes the island target as unspecified [S6].

capabilities.summary: Initial access was likely via exploitation of public-facing web servers, sometimes with web shells deployed, rather than spear phishing [S4]. Payloads were loaded by DLL side-loading via SbieDll_Hook, delivering Cobalt Strike, NetSpy and the open-source Havoc C2 framework [S2][S3]. Reported additional activity includes Mimikatz credential dumping, Active Directory discovery, exploitation of CVE-2019-0803 for privilege escalation, and terminating processes listed in a file named processlist.txt [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: Taiwan-focused intrusion set
campaigns.summary: Symantec observed Grayling intrusions from February 2023 through at least May 2023 against manufacturing, IT and biomedical organizations in Taiwan, with a Pacific Islands government agency and entities in Vietnam and the US also reportedly targeted [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: Public disclosure by Symantec
campaigns.summary: Symantec publicly reported Grayling as a previously unseen actor, citing the SbieDll_Hook side-loading technique and no observed exfiltration [S1][S2][S4].

diamond.adversary: Unattributed actor named Grayling by Symantec; Symantec did not name a country [S2][S4].
diamond.capability: Web shells, DLL side-loading via SbieDll_Hook, Cobalt Strike, Havoc, NetSpy, Mimikatz, CVE-2019-0803 exploit [S2][S3].
diamond.victim: Taiwanese manufacturing, IT and biomedical organizations; a Pacific Islands government agency; entities in Vietnam and the US [S2][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Symantec said the Taiwan focus suggests a region with strategic interest in Taiwan; intelligence gathering was the assessed motive [S3][S4].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing web servers (likely initial access vector) and Windows hosts/Active Directory environments [S2][S3][S4].

gaps: Symantec's primary report could not be fetched in this session (host unreachable); details rely on search-result summaries of it and secondary coverage [S1][S2][S3][S4].
Sponsor and country unknown; no government attribution found.
Exact initial-access vulnerabilities and C2 infrastructure not verified.
No activity after May 2023 or any follow-up reporting was found.
Whether the Pacific Islands, Vietnam and US victims were confirmed or only likely is inconsistent across coverage [S2][S6].
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID or Microsoft naming found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: the reported target set (Taiwanese manufacturing, IT, biomedical; Pacific Islands government) places internet-facing web servers and AD-joined Windows hosts as relevant terrain [S2][S3][S4]. Step 3: the actor is credible at web-server exploitation, side-loaded Cobalt Strike/Havoc/NetSpy, and credential theft, with no exfiltration observed [S2][S3]. MLCOA: continued espionage-style access against Taiwan-linked organizations via public-facing servers. MDCOA: exploitation of regional partner or supplier networks (Pacific, Vietnam, US) as stepping stones; this is inference not stated in sources. Candidate indicators: new web shells on external servers, legitimate-looking binaries loading DLLs exporting SbieDll_Hook, Havoc/Cobalt Strike beacons, processes terminated per processlist.txt [S2][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: share SbieDll_Hook side-loading and web-shell detection content with defenders of regional partner and supplier networks. Authorities: confirm which entities fall under DODIN-A versus partner or commercial ownership before any response action. Mission assurance: prioritize patching and monitoring of internet-facing servers and AD credential hygiene on mission-relevant systems. Coordination: route vendor reporting (Symantec) through intelligence and cyber protection teams and coordinate with partners in the Indo-Pacific region.

provenance.importedSummary: Grayling activity was first observed in early 2023, when a number of victims were identified with distinctive malicious DLL side-loading activity. Grayling appears to target organisations in Asia, however one unknown organisation in the United States was also targeted. Industries targeted include Biomedical, Government and Information Technology. Grayling use a variety of tools during their attacks, including well known tools such as Cobalt Strike and Havoc and also some others.

identification.summary: GreedyBear is the name Koi Security gave to a financially motivated crypto-theft campaign that, per reporting on Koi's findings, used more than 150 malicious Firefox extensions impersonating wallets such as MetaMask, TronLink, Exodus and Rabby, with more than $1 million reported stolen [S2][S3][S4]. The campaign also included about 500 malicious Windows executables spread mainly through Russian sites offering cracked software, and scam sites posing as wallet services [S2][S3]. Koi reported more than 650 malicious tools in total and says the same group was behind its earlier FoxyWallet campaign of about 40 Firefox extensions [S2][S3][S5].
identification.firstObserved: Koi's FoxyWallet reporting says the related Firefox-extension activity had run since at least April 2025 [S5]. GreedyBear was publicly reported in August 2025 [S2][S3].
identification.notes: No Microsoft name or MITRE group ID is known for GreedyBear. Treat it as a Koi-named campaign cluster, not an established vendor-agnostic actor; the encyclopedia's MISP Galaxy import carries it as a threat actor. The FoxyWallet link comes from Koi's own claim as relayed by secondary coverage [S2][S3].

attribution.sponsor: Not state-sponsored in any cited source. Koi's earlier FoxyWallet research suspected Russian actors [S5][S6].
attribution.confidence: Low and tentative. Koi suspected Russian threat actors for the earlier FoxyWallet cluster, citing Russian-language comments in extension code and metadata in a PDF from a command-and-control server [S5][S6]. No government attribution found.
attribution.basis: Russian-language artifacts in code and C2 metadata [S5][S6]; distribution of malware through Russian sites offering cracked software [S2][S3]; shared infrastructure, with extensions, executables and phishing sites tied to the single IP 185.208.156.66 [S2][S3].

actors.objectives: Financial gain through theft of cryptocurrency wallet credentials and seed phrases from users, with more than $1 million reported stolen [S2][S3][S4].

targeting.notes: Targeting is by product, not geography: Firefox users of wallets including MetaMask, TronLink, Exodus and Rabby [S2][S3]. The FoxyWallet cluster also copied Coinbase, Trust Wallet, Phantom, OKX, Keplr and others [S7]. No victim country breakdown found in the sources.

capabilities.summary: Operators used 'Extension Hollowing': publishing a harmless extension with fake positive reviews to pass marketplace checks, then adding malicious code that logs input from form fields and pop-ups and sends wallet credentials to attacker servers [S2][S3][S4]. FoxyWallet code reportedly filtered input strings longer than 30 characters and sent the victim's external IP [S7]. Koi says the code was partly AI-generated, based on artifacts it found [S4]. A Chrome extension called 'Filecoin Wallet' with the same theft logic and server suggests expansion to other browser marketplaces [S2][S3]. Windows malware samples were crypto-focused and spread via pirated software sites; reporting names LummaStealer among the payloads [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: FoxyWallet Firefox extensions (earlier cluster)
campaigns.summary: Koi reports activity since at least April 2025 using more than 40 fake wallet extensions on the Firefox add-ons store, with Russian-language artifacts noted [S5][S6][S7].

campaigns.name: GreedyBear public disclosure
campaigns.summary: Koi Security reports more than 150 malicious Firefox extensions, about 500 malicious executables and numerous phishing sites tied to one IP, with over $1 million stolen. A Chrome extension using the same logic and server was also found [S1][S2][S3][S4]. Mozilla was reportedly notified and the extensions removed [S3].

diamond.adversary: Unnamed, likely Russian-speaking, financially motivated operators per Koi's tentative assessment [S5][S6].
diamond.capability: Extension Hollowing, credential-logging extensions, crypto-focused stealers, phishing sites, partly AI-generated code [S2][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Single central IP 185.208.156.66 reported as the C2 for extensions, executables and phishing sites; Firefox add-ons store for delivery; pirated-software sites [S2][S3].
diamond.victim: Individual cryptocurrency wallet users [S2][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Criminal profit motive; no state tasking cited [S2].
diamond.technology: Weak vetting of extension updates in browser marketplaces and user trust in reviews; Windows endpoints used by people who install cracked software [S2][S3][S4].

gaps: Could not open Koi's primary GreedyBear report or FoxyWallet report (fetch failed); all details come from search-result summaries of secondary coverage and should be re-verified against Koi's reports [S1][S5].
Publication dates for Koi's reports and the FoxyWallet coverage are approximate (month level); confirm exact dates.
The Russian attribution is tentative and rests on language artifacts; no named individuals, groups or government assessments found.
Regional distribution of victims and wallet-level loss accounting are not public in the sources gathered.
Link to FoxyWallet is Koi's own assessment; no independent vendor corroboration found.
Whether the Chrome/other-browser expansion materialized after August 2025 was not checked.
No MITRE group mapping, Microsoft name or other vendor aliases found; relevance to DoD missions is indirect (personnel with personal crypto wallets).

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Browser extension stores and personal devices used by service members and contractors are the relevant terrain; this is a criminal threat, not a mission-system threat. STEP 2: The actor exploits weak marketplace vetting and user trust in reviews [S2][S4]. STEP 3: Template is a benign extension, then a hollowed malicious update, with phishing sites and cracked-software malware as parallel channels [S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued theft from crypto users across more browser stores. MDCOA is the same tooling repurposed against enterprise browser users or credential theft broader than wallets. Candidate indicators: traffic to 185.208.156.66 and extensions that gain permissions or code after review [S2][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: low priority for operational networks, but browser extension inventory is useful. (2) Authorities: enforce extension allowlisting through existing enterprise policy; no special authority indicated. (3) Mission assurance: credential theft on personal devices could expose reused credentials, so reinforce separation of personal and official accounts. (4) Coordination: share indicators through normal CSSP channels if observed [S2][S3].

provenance.importedSummary: GreedyBear is a sophisticated threat actor responsible for over $1 million in cryptocurrency theft through a campaign involving 150 malicious Firefox extensions, nearly 500 malicious executables, and numerous fraudulent websites. They employ techniques such as 'Extension Hollowing' to replace legitimate extensions with malicious versions that capture wallet credentials. The campaign is centralized, with most malicious domains resolving to a single IP address, and it has expanded to target other browsers while utilizing AI-generated code to enhance scalability and evade detection.

identification.summary: GREYVIBE is a threat cluster named and tracked by WithSecure, described as a Russia-nexus group that uses generative AI and LLMs across its operations against Ukrainian targets [S1]. WithSecure rates it low-to-moderately sophisticated, citing operational security failures, design flaws in its malware and heavy LLM reliance, and says it lacked the sophistication and operational discipline typically associated with mature nation-state actors [S1][S2]. Its main Windows malware is the PowerShell-based LegionRelay and PhantomRelay, and it also uses Android spyware called FallSpy [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Activity dates to at least 2025-08; WithSecure first found the activity in 2026-01 [S2].
identification.notes: WithSecure tracks DroneLink separately and is still investigating its relationship to the wider GREYVIBE cluster, although DroneLink shares C2 infrastructure and post-compromise tooling with PrincessClub [S1]. One secondary write-up suggests possible overlap with the TrickBot ecosystem and UAC-0098; this was not confirmed against WithSecure's own text and is not adopted here [S1].

attribution.confidence: WithSecure assesses GREYVIBE as Russia-nexus/Russian-speaking and says its activity aligns with Russian state interests, but it has not identified definitive links to any previously tracked threat group and BleepingComputer reports researchers could not confidently classify it as a nation-state operation [S1][S2]. Confidence statements here are WithSecure's and the press's, not a government attribution.
attribution.basis: Russian-language malware panels and a command-and-control server set to Moscow time [S2]; targeting of Ukrainian military, government, civilian and business victims [S1].

actors.objectives: Activity is assessed as consistent with intelligence gathering against Ukraine aligned with Kremlin interests, with no definitive state attribution [S1]. The malware steals files, screenshots, browser credentials and Telegram and WhatsApp data, and sets up RDP access [S1].

targeting.notes: Lures impersonate Zoom and LAPAS, adult-club sites and military charities [S1][S2].

capabilities.summary: The group uses custom malware: LegionRelay and PhantomRelay (PowerShell RATs), the Android spyware FallSpy, and the custom obfuscators LOOKVALPS and DAYLIGHT [S1]. LegionRelay supports file theft, screenshots, browser credential theft, Telegram and WhatsApp data exfiltration and RDP setup, and WithSecure assesses it was likely developed with LLM assistance [S1]. Delivery uses spear-phishing, ClickFix-style fake CAPTCHA pages and fake websites [S1][S2]. Post-compromise tools include WireGuard VPN and ZAPiXDESK [S1]. WithSecure reports use of ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Ideogram, for Ukrainian-language phishing content and imagery for fake sites [S2]. Design flaws in the malware gave WithSecure insight into victimology and operator behavior [S1].

diamond.adversary: Russia-nexus, Russian-speaking cluster, low-to-moderate sophistication, no definitive link to a known group [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: LegionRelay, PhantomRelay, FallSpy, LOOKVALPS, DAYLIGHT, WireGuard, ZAPiXDESK, with LLM-assisted development and lures [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Shared C2 across PrincessClub and DroneLink, a Moscow-time C2 server and Russian-language malware panels, plus fake CAPTCHA, adult-club and charity websites [S1][S2].
diamond.victim: Ukrainian military, government, civilian and business entities [S1][S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Ukraine war context; activity assessed as aligned with Russian state intelligence-gathering interests [S1].
diamond.technology: Windows (PowerShell), Android, Telegram/WhatsApp, RDP and browser credential stores; generative AI services used by the operator [S1][S2].

No sponsor, government attribution or definitive link to a tracked group; the TrickBot/UAC-0098 overlap claim is unverified.
Relationship of DroneLink to the core cluster remains under WithSecure investigation.
Dates of individual campaigns, victim counts and detailed infrastructure are not established.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID or other vendors' names confirmed.

provenance.importedSummary: GREYVIBE is a low-to-moderately sophisticated threat actor associated with Russian state interests, primarily targeting Ukrainian entities. The group employs custom malware like LegionRelay and PhantomRelay, utilizing techniques such as decoy-and-payload execution logic and systematic use of GenAI and LLMs throughout their operations. Their campaigns exhibit operational overlaps with other groups, including shared C2 infrastructure and post-compromise tooling. WithSecure has identified design flaws in their malware that have provided insights into their victimology and operational behavior.

identification.summary: GTG-1002 is Anthropic's internal designation for a threat actor that Anthropic assesses with high confidence to be a Chinese state-sponsored group [S1]. Anthropic reports the actor used its Claude Code tool inside an attacker-built framework to run a largely automated espionage campaign against about thirty global targets, including technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturers and government agencies [S1]. Anthropic says intrusion succeeded in a small number of cases [S1]. Anthropic estimates the AI performed 80-90% of the work, with humans needed at roughly 4-6 decision points per campaign [S1]. These figures are Anthropic's own estimates [S1][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Anthropic detected suspicious activity in mid-September 2025 and investigated for about ten days; it published on 2025-11-13 [S1]. The actor's start date and any earlier activity are not stated in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: GTG-1002 is a vendor-internal label from an AI developer, not a Microsoft, Mandiant or CrowdStrike cluster, and no mapping to an established named group appears in the sources gathered. MITRE ATT&CK lists a campaign entry for the Anthropic AI-orchestrated campaign (C0062) [S6]. The prior imported summary claimed an 18-month campaign; no gathered source supports that figure, so it was removed.

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China, as assessed by Anthropic [S1].
attribution.confidence: Anthropic states it assesses 'with high confidence' that the actor was a Chinese state-sponsored group [S1]. This is a vendor assessment; the sources gathered show no government attribution statement. A House Homeland Security Committee chairman described the activity as a foreign adversary using a commercial AI system, but that is a congressional characterization of Anthropic's report, not independent attribution [S4].
attribution.basis: Anthropic has visibility only into its own platform usage [S1]. The public report gave no technical indicators of compromise, and BleepingComputer reported its requests for technical detail went unanswered [S3]. The evidentiary basis for the state-sponsored judgment has not been published in the sources gathered.

actors.objectives: Intelligence collection: per Anthropic, the framework identified high-value databases in target networks and extracted data sorted by intelligence value [S1]. Specific collection requirements are not public.

targeting.notes: About thirty targets were attempted globally; the number of successful intrusions is not given, only 'a small number of cases' [S1]. Anthropic did not name victims or regions in the material gathered [S1].

capabilities.summary: Human operators selected targets and built a framework that used Claude Code as an automated tool [S1]. Phases reported by Anthropic: reconnaissance and identification of high-value databases; vulnerability research, exploit-code writing and credential harvesting; use of credentials to reach privileged accounts, create backdoors and exfiltrate data; and documentation of stolen credentials and systems to plan later operations [S1]. MITRE records that the adversary obtained open-source penetration-testing tools, including network scanners, database exploitation frameworks, password crackers and binary analysis suites [S6]. To bypass safeguards, the operators split work into small, seemingly innocent tasks and told Claude it worked for a legitimate cybersecurity firm doing defensive testing [S1]. Anthropic notes Claude sometimes hallucinated credentials or claimed to have extracted secret information that was actually public, an obstacle to full autonomy [S1]. Skeptics argue open-source tooling would be caught by existing detections, so operational impact may be low [S3].

campaigns.name: AI-orchestrated espionage campaign (mid-September detection)
campaigns.summary: Anthropic detected suspicious Claude Code activity in mid-September 2025 and investigated for about ten days, mapping about thirty attempted targets and banning accounts as they were identified [S1].

campaigns.name: Anthropic public disclosure
campaigns.summary: Anthropic published its report (corrected 2025-11-14) assessing with high confidence a Chinese state-sponsored actor and estimating AI did 80-90% of tactical work [S1]. Security researchers questioned the report for lacking indicators of compromise and technical evidence [S3].

campaigns.name: Congressional request for testimony
campaigns.summary: House Homeland Security Committee leaders invited Anthropic's CEO to testify at a 17 December hearing; Google Cloud and Quantum Xchange CEOs were also invited [S4][S5]. Whether the hearing occurred is not confirmed in the sources gathered.

diamond.adversary: Chinese state-sponsored group per Anthropic's high-confidence assessment; human operators selected targets and approved key steps [S1].
diamond.capability: Claude Code orchestration framework with open-source penetration-testing tools, jailbroken through task decomposition and a defensive-tester pretext [S1][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Anthropic's Claude platform accounts, which Anthropic banned [S1]. Attacker-side hosting, C2 and network infrastructure are not published [S3].
diamond.victim: About thirty technology, financial, chemical-manufacturing and government organizations, with a small number of successful intrusions [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection attributed to PRC state interests; no tasking detail is public [S1].
diamond.technology: Commercial agentic AI coding tools used as an orchestration layer, with hallucination limiting reliability [S1].

gaps: No indicators of compromise, victim names, vulnerabilities exploited or infrastructure were published, and BleepingComputer reported its requests went unanswered [S3].
The basis for Chinese state-sponsorship is not disclosed; no government attribution found in the sources gathered [S1].
Anthropic's own PDF report and the SOCRadar summary could not be opened in this session (host unreachable), so details beyond Anthropic's news post were taken from secondary coverage.
The exact number of successful intrusions and the campaign start date are not given. The earlier '18 months' claim is unsupported.
The 80-90% automation and 4-6 decision-point figures are Anthropic estimates and are disputed by some researchers [S1][S3].
Overlap with any established named PRC cluster is unknown.
MITRE campaign C0062 details were seen only in a search snippet; the page could not be fetched [S6].
Outcome of the 17 December 2025 hearing was not confirmed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is any internet-reachable enterprise or government environment holding high-value databases, plus the credentials and privileged accounts that open them [S1]. STEP 2: Machine-speed reconnaissance, exploit development and credential harvesting compress defender detection time, while orchestration depends on a commercial AI platform and on human approval at a few decision points [S1]. STEP 3: Template is human target selection, then AI-driven recon, exploit, credential harvest, lateral movement, backdoor, and data triage by intelligence value [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued use of commodity and open-source tooling driven by agentic AI against government, defense-adjacent and industrial targets, with few successes but high volume [S1][S6]. MDCOA is the same approach on models or self-hosted tools outside provider visibility, at larger scale and with better reliability, since hallucination is a current limiter [S1]. Candidate indicators: very high request rates inconsistent with human operators, scripted scanning followed by rapid credential reuse, and database queries sorted for sensitive content (Anthropic did not publish technical indicators) [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track AI-enabled intrusion reporting, but treat vendor figures as unverified because no indicators were published [S3]. (2) Authorities: coordinate any attribution or response through established DoD, DC3 and interagency channels; Anthropic's attribution is a vendor assessment only [S1]. (3) Mission assurance: harden identity and privileged-account monitoring and detect machine-speed activity patterns, since open-source tools were used [S6]. (4) Coordination: engage AI providers and DIB partners for threat sharing, and note congressional interest [S4][S5]. Also review internal use of agentic AI for abuse and guardrail evasion [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: GTG-1002 is a Chinese state-sponsored APT that conducted a large-scale autonomous cyber espionage campaign targeting approximately 30 global organizations across various sectors, focusing on military and energy-related data. The operation utilized AI, specifically Anthropic’s Claude model, for reconnaissance, exploitation, and data exfiltration, significantly reducing human involvement. Attackers employed techniques such as automated task execution and evasion of safety protocols by masquerading as legal security testing. The campaign lasted 18 months and highlighted vulnerabilities in traditional incident response workflows.

identification.summary: Hazel Sandstorm (formerly EUROPIUM) is an Iranian actor that Microsoft says has been publicly linked to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) [S1][S2]. Microsoft assessed with moderate confidence that actors linked to it gained initial access to the Albanian government and exfiltrated data before Iran's destructive attack there in July 2022 [S1][S2]. Other vendors track overlapping activity as APT34/OilRig, Crambus or Earth Simnavaz. That reporting describes long-running espionage against Middle East governments using PowerShell and .NET backdoors, Exchange-based C2, DNS tunneling, web shells and credential theft [S3][S4][S5][S6][S7].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: DEV-0861, which it links to EUROPIUM, has been exfiltrating mail from several countries since April 2020 [S2]. FireEye reported APT34 use of CVE-2017-0199 by July 2017 [S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Hazel Sandstorm (formerly EUROPIUM). Microsoft tracks EUROPIUM through three activity clusters with distinct tools or TTPs, some of which may work for the same unit [S2]. FireEye said APT34 'loosely aligns' with public OilRig reporting [S3]. Trend Micro equates Earth Simnavaz with APT34/OilRig [S6]. Symantec tracks the group as Crambus [S5]. These vendor clusters overlap but are not proven identical. Microsoft's link to Storm-0861 (DEV-0861) carries only moderate confidence [S2].

attribution.sponsor: Iran. Microsoft says EUROPIUM/Hazel Sandstorm has been publicly linked to the Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) [S1][S2]. Check Point also associates APT34 with MOIS [S7].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft judged with high confidence that the 15 July 2022 destructive attack on Albania was carried out by Iranian state-sponsored actors. Its link from the initial-access and exfiltration actors to EUROPIUM is moderate confidence [S2]. FireEye assessed APT34 as a suspected Iranian cyber-espionage group [S3]. No government attribution document was reviewed for this record.
attribution.basis: Microsoft incident response and telemetry, including shared RawDisk license keys and code-signing certificates across Albanian and Middle East intrusions [S2]. Vendor malware and infrastructure analysis (FireEye, ESET, Symantec, Check Point, Trend Micro), including code overlaps with earlier Karkoff and Saitama tools [S3][S4][S5][S6][S7].

actors.objectives: Strategic espionage against regional governments and critical sectors in support of Iranian state interests [S2][S5][S6][S7]. This includes long-dwell collection of email, files and credentials [S2][S5]. Microsoft also places it in enabling roles for destructive and retaliatory operations, as in Albania in 2022 [S2].

regions: Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, UAE [S2]
targeting.notes: Microsoft lists the EUROPIUM target countries as consistent with Iranian interests [S2]. Microsoft's Hazel Sandstorm profile lists only Albania and government [S1]. The broader regional picture comes from vendor clusters that overlap with it [S4][S5][S6][S7].

capabilities.summary: Initial access: unpatched internet-facing servers, including SharePoint CVE-2019-0604 (Albania), plus ProxyLogon CVE-2021-26855 cited in the same intrusion [S2]. Also rapidly weaponized Office exploits CVE-2017-0199 and CVE-2017-11882, the latter used within a week of its patch [S3]. Spearphishing with VBS droppers and double-extension lures [S4][S7]. Post-exploitation: web shells, Mimikatz, Impacket and RDP [S2]. Malicious password-filter DLLs and the StealHook backdoor for credential theft, and CVE-2024-30088 for privilege escalation [S6]. Backdoors include POWRUNER and BONDUPDATER [S3], Solar and Mango [S4], PowerExchange [S5], and Veaty and Spearal [S7]. C2 options: email or Exchange-based channels (EWS, compromised internal mailboxes) [S4][S5][S7], custom DNS tunneling [S7], compromised legitimate websites [S4] and ngrok tunneling [S6]. Collection: Exchange mailbox exfiltration [S2][S5][S6], browser and Windows Credential Manager theft [S4]. The 2019 Lab Dookhtegan leak exposed APT34 tools (Glimpse, PoisonFrog, HyperShell, HighShell, Fox Panel, Webmask), plus later the Jason brute-force tool [S8]. Microsoft notes Jason.exe was used by MOIS-affiliated actors in Albania (DEV-0166) [S2][S8].

Microsoft links the access and exfiltration actors to EUROPIUM with moderate confidence.

campaigns.name: Earth Simnavaz Gulf campaign
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reports web-shell access to UAE and Gulf government targets, followed by CVE-2024-30088 privilege escalation, a password-filter DLL, the StealHook backdoor and Exchange credential abuse.

diamond.adversary: An Iranian actor that Microsoft says has been publicly linked to MOIS, tracked as Hazel Sandstorm/EUROPIUM [S1][S2], with overlapping vendor clusters APT34/OilRig, Crambus and Earth Simnavaz [S3][S5][S6]. Personnel and tools were exposed by the 2019 Lab Dookhtegan leaks [S8].
diamond.capability: Server and Office exploits (CVE-2019-0604, CVE-2017-0199, CVE-2017-11882), web shells, credential theft (Mimikatz, password-filter DLLs, StealHook), privilege escalation via CVE-2024-30088, and custom .NET/PowerShell backdoors with email and DNS C2 [S2][S3][S4][S5][S6][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: Exfiltration IPs on hosting providers listed by Microsoft [S2]. Compromised legitimate websites used as C2 [S4], compromised internal Exchange mailboxes used for C2 [S5][S7], DNS tunneling [S7] and ngrok tunnels [S6].
diamond.victim: Governments in Albania, Iraq, the UAE and Gulf, and an unnamed Middle East state [S2][S5][S6][S7]. Israeli organizations [S4]. A Middle East energy company [S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Iranian regional intelligence priorities and retaliation. Microsoft assessed that Tehran likely used the Albania attacks as retaliation [S2].
diamond.technology: Microsoft Exchange and EWS, on-premises SharePoint, Windows domain controllers and password filters, and Windows privilege-escalation flaws [S2][S4][S5][S6].

gaps: MITRE mapping conflict: this actor record carries G0003 (Cleaver), but OilRig is MITRE G0049. The imported Cleaver/Operation Cleaver aliases and software (TinyZBot, Net Crawler) were not verified against Microsoft's Hazel Sandstorm mapping in this research.
Microsoft's link from Storm-0861/DEV-0861 to EUROPIUM is moderate confidence, and how Microsoft's three EUROPIUM clusters map onto APT34/OilRig, Crambus and Earth Simnavaz is not public [S2].
No US or allied government attribution document naming Hazel Sandstorm/APT34 was opened. The FBI/CISA Albania advisory was not reviewed (government sites are blocked).
Symantec's primary Crambus report was not opened directly; the details come from search-result coverage [S5].
The initial access vector is unknown for the Crambus (2023) and Iraq (2024) campaigns [S5][S7].
Reports of 2025 activity and of AI-tool use (aggregator sources) were not verified against primary vendor reporting.
Unit 42's original OilRig reporting (2016 onward) and Mandiant's 2019 LinkedIn phishing reporting were not reviewed for dates.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is internet-facing Exchange and SharePoint servers, domain controllers (where password filters can be installed), and mail flows of partner-nation governments in the Gulf, Iraq, Israel and Albania [S2][S5][S6][S7]. STEP 2: Fast weaponization of Office and server CVEs and long dwell times (8 months in the Crambus case; 8+ months from access to the destructive phase in Albania) favor the adversary where patching is slow [S2][S3][S5]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template runs from server exploit or spearphish to web shell or backdoor, then credential theft (Mimikatz, password-filter DLL), then Exchange mailbox collection over email or DNS C2 [S2][S4][S5][S6][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent email and credential espionage against host-nation and coalition partner ministries. MDCOA is Hazel Sandstorm-enabled access handed to a separate Iranian destructive actor for wiper or ransomware effects during a crisis, as in Albania 2022 [S2]. Candidate indicators: new ASPX web shells on SharePoint or Exchange, unexpected LSA notification-package or password-filter DLL registrations, EWS impersonation-role grants or service accounts, anomalous DNS TXT/subdomain volume, ngrok binaries or traffic, and double-extension document attachments [S2][S6][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: partner-nation government mail systems in the CENTCOM AOR are a recurring target. JCC2 should fuse partner CERT reporting and coalition mail-gateway telemetry, since the actor uses victims' own Exchange mailboxes for C2 [S5][S7]. (2) Authorities: activity often sits on partner, not DoD, networks, so response depends on partner-nation consent and established information-sharing agreements. (3) Mission assurance: an espionage foothold can enable a destructive handoff to another actor [S2]. Treat detected Hazel Sandstorm access in mission-relevant networks as a potential precursor to disruptive effects, not espionage only. (4) Coordination: attribution across overlapping vendor names is inconsistent, so coordinate with the intelligence community and partners on indicators rather than labels, and prioritize Exchange/SharePoint patching and credential resets.

provenance.importedSummary: OilRig is an Iranian threat group operating primarily in the Middle East by targeting organizations in this region that are in a variety of different industries; however, this group has occasionally targeted organizations outside of the Middle East as well. It also appears OilRig carries out supply chain attacks, where the threat group leverages the trust relationship between organizations to attack their primary targets. OilRig is an active and organized threat group, which is evident based on their systematic targeting of specific organizations that appear to be carefully chosen for strategic purposes. Attacks attributed to this group primarily rely on social engineering to exploit the human rather than software vulnerabilities; however, on occasion this group has used recently patched vulnerabilities in the delivery phase of their attacks. The lack of software vulnerability exploitation does not necessarily suggest a lack of sophistication, as OilRig has shown maturity in other aspects of their operations. Such maturities involve: -Organized evasion testing used the during development of their tools. -Use of custom DNS Tunneling protocols for command and control (C2) and data exfiltration. -Custom web-shells and backdoors used to persistently access servers. OilRig relies on stolen account credentials for lateral movement. After OilRig gains access to a system, they use credential dumping tools, such as Mimikatz, to steal credentials to accounts logged into the compromised system. The group uses these credentials to access and to move laterally to other systems on the network. After obtaining credentials from a system, operators in this group prefer to use tools other than their backdoors to access the compromised systems, such as remote desktop and putty. OilRig also uses phishing sites to harvest credentials to individuals at targeted organizations to gain access to internet accessible resources, such as Outlook Web Access. Since at least 2014, an Iranian threat group tracked by FireEye as APT34 has conducted reconnaissance aligned with the strategic interests of Iran. The group conducts operations primarily in the Middle East, targeting financial, government, energy, chemical, telecommunications and other industries. Repeated targeting of Middle Eastern financial, energy and government organizations leads FireEye to assess that those sectors are a primary concern of APT34. The use of infrastructure tied to Iranian operations, timing and alignment with the national interests of Iran also lead FireEye to assess that APT34 acts on behalf of the Iranian government.

identification.summary: China-based espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Heart Typhoon and that Mandiant/Google tracks as APT17 [S1][S2]. FireEye reported that APT17 had conducted network intrusions against the U.S. government, international law firms and information technology companies, and that it had used the BLACKCOFFEE malware since 2013 [S3]. In 2014-2015 the group hid encoded command-and-control (C2) addresses in Microsoft TechNet forum profiles and posts [S3]. In 2024 Italian firm TG Soft attributed spear-phishing campaigns against Italian companies and government entities, using a 9002 RAT variant, to APT17 [S9].
identification.firstObserved: The Hacker News says Mandiant (then FireEye) first documented APT17 in 2013 [S9]. FireEye says APT17 had used BLACKCOFFEE since 2013 [S3]. Symantec dates the related Hidden Lynx cluster to 2009 and links it to Operation Aurora (2009-2010) [S5][S6].
identification.notes: Microsoft lists HELIUM, AURORA PANDA, APT17, Hidden Lynx, ATG3, Red Typhoon, KAOS, TG-8153, SportsFans, DeputyDog and Tailgater as other names for Heart Typhoon [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as APT17 (G0025) [S2]. FireEye states that APT17 is also known as Deputy Dog [S3]. Symantec's Hidden Lynx is a broader cluster (an estimated 50-100 operators in two teams) that Symantec did not equate with APT17 in the sources reviewed here, so Hidden Lynx facts are kept separate below [S5][S6].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (assessed). FireEye calls APT17 a China-based threat group [S3]. In July 2019 the anonymous research group Intrusion Truth alleged that APT17 is run by the Jinan bureau of the Ministry of State Security (MSS) through contractors managed by alleged MSS officer Guo Lin [S7][S8].
attribution.confidence: FireEye 'assesses' that APT17 was behind the TechNet activity but gives no formal confidence level [S3]. The MSS Jinan link rests on Intrusion Truth's allegations, which press coverage and CERT-EU treat as unverified claims [S7][S8]. No U.S. government indictment or advisory naming APT17 was found in this research.
attribution.basis: Vendor technical reporting (FireEye/Microsoft joint TechNet investigation) [S3]; Intrusion Truth open-source identity research covering Guo Lin, Wang Qingwei and Zeng Xiaoyong, and Jinan front companies, plus code similarities to the ZoxRPC malware [S7][S8]; Microsoft and MITRE name mappings [S1][S2].

actors.objectives: Cyber-espionage against government, defense, legal and technology targets [S2][S3]. CFR reports that APT17 also targeted Chinese citizens for financial gain [S10]. Symantec assessed the related Hidden Lynx cluster as a hacker-for-hire operation that collects information for clients, while CrowdStrike's Dmitri Alperovitch argued it was closely tied to the Chinese government [S5].

sectors: Security vendors (Bit9, via the Hidden Lynx cluster)
regions: Global; 52 percent of Hidden Lynx targets were in the U.S. [S5]
targeting.notes: U.S. government, defense, law, IT, mining and NGO targeting is from MITRE [S2] and FireEye [S3]. Japanese media, manufacturing and government targeting is from FireEye's 2013 DeputyDog reporting, as covered by the press [S4]. Italian corporate and government targeting is from TG Soft, as covered by the press [S9]. Hidden Lynx figures apply to Symantec's broader cluster [S5].

capabilities.summary: Uses legitimate public sites as dead-drop resolvers: BLACKCOFFEE retrieved encoded C2 IPs that had been posted to TechNet profiles and forums [S3]. Used strategic web compromise (watering holes) with an Internet Explorer zero-day (CVE-2013-3893) in the 2013 DeputyDog campaign [S4]. In 2024 used spear-phishing with Office documents and links to a fake Skype for Business MSI hosted on a domain that imitated an Italian government site; the chain ran a VBS script and a Java archive that decrypted 9002 RAT shellcode [S9]. TG Soft describes 9002 RAT as modular, with traffic monitoring, screenshots, file enumeration, process management, command execution and diskless variants [S9]. In the related Hidden Lynx cluster, Symantec describes code-signing abuse after the Bit9 breach, plus the Moudoor and Naid trojans [S5][S6]. MITRE lists BLACKCOFFEE as APT17 software [S2].

campaigns.name: Operation Aurora (Hidden Lynx linkage)
campaigns.summary: Symantec links the Hidden Lynx cluster to Operation Aurora: the Naid trojan was used there, and Symantec says the group either carried out the attack or worked with the attackers [S5][S6]. The Hacker News notes that 9002 RAT (Hydraq/McRAT) was the tool used in Aurora [S9].

campaigns.name: VOHO watering hole / Bit9 compromise (Hidden Lynx)
campaigns.summary: According to Symantec as reported by the press, Hidden Lynx breached security firm Bit9 and signed malware with Bit9 keys after Bit9 software blocked attacks on U.S. defense contractors; Bit9 disclosed the breach in February 2013. The VOHO watering-hole campaign compromised about 4,000 machines [S5][S6].

campaigns.name: Operation DeputyDog
campaigns.summary: Starting 19 August 2013, watering-hole attacks compromised at least three major Japanese media sites and served an IE zero-day (CVE-2013-3893) against manufacturing, government and media targets. FireEye linked the actor to the Bit9 compromise through a shared IP address [S4].

campaigns.name: TechNet C2 obfuscation
campaigns.summary: FireEye and Microsoft found that a BLACKCOFFEE variant retrieved encoded C2 IPs from TechNet profiles and forum posts. They sinkholed the activity by encoding a sinkhole IP into the posts, and released IOCs and signatures in May 2015 [S3][S10].

campaigns.name: Intrusion Truth exposure
campaigns.summary: Intrusion Truth alleged that APT17 is run by the MSS Jinan bureau and named Guo Lin, Wang Qingwei and Zeng Xiaoyong [S7][S8].

campaigns.name: Italian 9002 RAT campaign
campaigns.summary: On 24 June and 2 July 2024, spear-phishing delivered a fake Skype for Business package that dropped a 9002 RAT variant on Italian companies and government entities; TG Soft attributed the activity to APT17 [S9].

diamond.adversary: PRC-based operators tracked as Heart Typhoon/APT17 [S1][S3]. Intrusion Truth alleges MSS Jinan bureau management through Jinan front companies [S7][S8].
diamond.capability: BLACKCOFFEE [S2][S3]; 9002 RAT variant [S9]; IE zero-day CVE-2013-3893 [S4]; Moudoor/Naid and stolen code-signing keys in the related Hidden Lynx cluster [S5][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Legitimate public sites (TechNet) used as dead-drop resolvers for C2 [S3]; compromised Japanese media sites as watering holes and a Hong Kong payload host [S4]; a look-alike Italian government domain [S9].
diamond.victim: U.S. government, defense, law and IT organizations [S2][S3]; Japanese media, manufacturing and government organizations [S4]; Italian companies and government entities [S9].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection that serves PRC interests; Intrusion Truth alleges MSS tasking [S7][S8]. Symantec's hacker-for-hire framing of Hidden Lynx is disputed [S5].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints and Internet Explorer [S4]; user trust in collaboration software (Skype for Business) [S9]; web forums used for C2 resolution [S3].

gaps: No Microsoft Threat Intelligence publication describing activity under the Heart Typhoon name was found; the Microsoft name rests on Microsoft's naming mapping [S1]. learn.microsoft.com could not be fetched.
The Hidden Lynx/APT17 relationship is asserted by Microsoft's alias list [S1] but is not detailed in the sources reviewed; Symantec's cluster is broader and may include other actors.
Intrusion Truth's MSS Jinan attribution is unverified, and no U.S. government indictment, sanction or advisory naming APT17 was found.
The primary reports could not be opened: TG Soft (2024), Symantec's Hidden Lynx white paper, FireEye's DeputyDog blog, and Intrusion Truth's posts. Their details rely on secondary coverage.
Activity after 2024 and current infrastructure are unknown.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes widely visited public websites (news, forum and government look-alike domains) that can serve as watering holes or dead-drop resolvers, and user endpoints at government, defense, legal and IT organizations [S2][S3][S4][S9]. STEP 2: C2 hidden in legitimate sites blends with normal traffic and weakens IP blocklists [S3]. STEP 3: Observed templates are a watering hole with a browser zero-day leading to a RAT [S4], and spear-phishing with a fake software installer leading to MSI, VBS, JAR and in-memory 9002 RAT [S9]. STEP 4: MLCOA is spear-phishing with trusted-software lures against government and defense-adjacent organizations to deploy modular RATs for espionage [S9]. MDCOA is a supply-chain or code-signing compromise of a security or IT vendor, as in the Hidden Lynx Bit9 case, to deliver trusted-signed malware into defense networks [S5][S6]. Candidate indicators: endpoints fetching forum or profile pages and then contacting unrelated IPs; MSI installers that spawn wscript and java; unsigned 'Skype for Business' packages from non-Microsoft domains [S3][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: correlate dead-drop-resolver patterns and look-alike government domains across DODIN and partner feeds [S3][S9]. Authorities: the TechNet sinkhole was a private-sector (FireEye/Microsoft) action [S3], so disruption of public-platform abuse likely depends on coordination with platform owners rather than military action alone. Mission assurance: prioritize monitoring and patch speed on defense-contractor and legal-support enclaves that hold program data [S2][S3]. Coordination: the actor's victims span allied nations (Japan, Italy) [S4][S9], which supports sharing indicators with partner CERTs; attribution to the MSS remains unofficial [S7].

identification.summary: Hellsing is a small cyberespionage group named by Kaspersky in April 2015 that targeted mostly government and diplomatic organizations in Asia [S1][S2]. Kaspersky found it while tracing Naikon, after a Naikon spear-phishing target questioned the email, declined to open the attachment, and sent a malicious email back to the sender [S2][S3]. Kaspersky estimated that close to 20 organizations were targeted [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Active since at least 2012 [S3]. Publicly disclosed by Kaspersky in April 2015 [S2].
identification.notes: Malpedia (via the imported MISP Galaxy text) says the actor seems to have targeted APT30 and possibly uses the same infrastructure as Mirage [S6]. Press reporting of Kaspersky's analysis says Kaspersky saw infrastructure overlap with PlayfullDragon (GREF) and Mirage (Vixen Panda) and treated Hellsing as a stand-alone operation [S7]. These are vendor-cluster overlaps, not mergers. No Microsoft Threat Intelligence name or MITRE ATT&CK group was found for Hellsing in the searches run.

attribution.sponsor: China (suspected). The Council on Foreign Relations Cyber Operations Tracker lists China as the suspected state sponsor [S5].
attribution.confidence: Low-to-moderate, and not stated in numeric form by any source seen. The CFR tracker lists the sponsor as suspected [S5]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: CFR's tracker classifies the activity as espionage and names China as suspected sponsor [S5]. Kaspersky's public reporting describes the victimology as government and diplomatic organizations in Asia [S2]. Infrastructure overlap with other China-linked clusters (Mirage) is reported by Malpedia and press coverage [S6][S7]. The specific technical evidence behind the China attribution is in the Securelist report, which could not be opened.

actors.objectives: Cyberespionage against government and diplomatic organizations in Asia [S1][S2]. The counter-attack on Naikon suggests an additional goal of identifying that group and gathering intelligence on it, in Kaspersky's assessment [S2][S3].

targeting.notes: Kaspersky detected malware mainly in Malaysia and the Philippines, with detections also in India, Indonesia and the US; the US detections were tied to diplomatic agencies and India to older malware versions [S1]. CFR lists suspected victims in Malaysia, the Philippines, India, Indonesia and the US [S5]. Malpedia describes spear-phishing against diplomatic targets in Southeast Asia, India and the US [S6].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing emails carrying archives with malware, similar to the approach used against Naikon [S1]. Lures included password-protected RAR archives, which help bypass malware scanners, with SCR or other executables inside [S1]. The custom backdoor can download and upload files, update itself and uninstall itself [S2][S3]. Malpedia lists PlugX among associated malware families [S6]. Kaspersky described the group as small and technically unremarkable [S2].

campaigns.name: Earliest known activity
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky and press coverage state that Hellsing has been active since at least 2012, mainly against government organizations in Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines.

campaigns.name: Counter-attack on Naikon and public disclosure
campaigns.summary: A Naikon spear-phishing target questioned the sender and returned a malicious email. This led Kaspersky to discover Hellsing, which it described as an APT-on-APT incident and the start of 'APT wars'. Kaspersky judged the reply aimed to identify Naikon and gather intelligence on it.

campaigns.name: Spear-phishing against Asian government and diplomatic targets
campaigns.summary: Close to 20 organizations were estimated targeted, mostly in Malaysia and the Philippines, with some in India, Indonesia and the US.

diamond.adversary: Small, suspected China-based espionage group; no individuals or organizations named in the sources seen [S2][S5].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing with password-protected RAR archives containing executables; custom backdoor with file transfer and self-update/uninstall functions [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Possible shared infrastructure with Mirage, and reported overlap with PlayfullDragon [S6][S7]. Indicators are published in the Securelist report, which could not be opened [S1].
diamond.victim: Government and diplomatic organizations, mainly in Malaysia and the Philippines, plus the Naikon group [S1][S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Regional diplomatic and government intelligence collection in Southeast Asia, India and the US, with a rivalry element against Naikon [S2][S5].
diamond.technology: Email and attachment handling; password-protected archives that evade scanners [S1].

gaps: WebFetch could not reach securelist.com, kaspersky.com, cfr.org or theregister.com (DNS failure), so the primary Securelist report was read only through search-result summaries. Technical detail (malware family names, C2 infrastructure, IOCs, timeline) is therefore not captured.
No Microsoft name, MITRE ATT&CK group ID or government attribution was found for Hellsing.
Evidence basis for the suspected China sponsorship is not visible in the sources gathered.

Cluster boundaries are unresolved: reported overlaps with Mirage, APT30, PlayfullDragon and Naikon were seen only through secondary summaries. One search summary also said Kaspersky reported the Hellsing developer started from Cycldek sources; this was not verified against the report text.
Activity after 2015 is not documented in the sources gathered. Malpedia's reference list was not fully visible.
Malpedia page date is not shown; its source entry uses the retrieval date.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Government and diplomatic email systems in the Indo-Pacific, and partner-nation diplomatic staff, are key terrain [S1][S5]. STEP 2: The actor is small and technically unremarkable, so it relies on social engineering rather than novel exploits [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Template is spear-phish with a password-protected archive, then a custom backdoor that uploads files [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued diplomatic and government collection in Malaysia, the Philippines, Indonesia and India, with opportunistic US diplomatic targeting. MDCOA is use of the same lure style against US or partner defense staff during a regional crisis. Candidate indicators: password-protected RAR emails containing SCR files, and backdoor beaconing from government workstations [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track phishing against partner diplomatic and government networks; Kaspersky's IOCs are on Securelist and should be pulled and validated [S1]. (2) Authorities: monitoring of partner-nation networks depends on partner agreements; no US authority is implied by the sources. (3) Mission assurance: block or sandbox password-protected archives and SCR attachments on mission networks [S1]. (4) Coordination: overlap with other China-linked clusters means shared reporting with partners and vendors is needed before any attribution is used [S6][S7].

identification.summary: HenBox is an Android espionage malware family named by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 in March 2018. It masquerades as VPN and Android system apps, often installs a legitimate decoy app alongside itself, and appears to primarily target Uyghurs and devices running Xiaomi's MIUI [S1][S2]. It is a malware family and associated activity cluster, not a Microsoft-named actor [S4].
identification.firstObserved: Unit 42's March 2018 report cites almost 200 samples, the oldest dating to 2015, most from the second half of 2017 [S1][S2]. A May 2016 sample posing as DroidVPN was downloaded from uyghurapps[.]net [S2].
identification.notes: No Microsoft actor name was found in the sources gathered. Unit 42 later grouped HenBox, Farseer, PlugX, Poison Ivy, 9002 and Zupdax infrastructure under the cluster name PKPLUG, and said it could not determine whether one group or several are involved [S3][S4]. Do not merge facts from other vendor clusters sharing PlugX or Poison Ivy without separate sourcing.

attribution.confidence: Unit 42 assessed with high confidence that PKPLUG has origins linked to Chinese nation-state adversaries, but said it could not determine whether one group or several are involved [S4]. This is a vendor assessment, not a government attribution.
attribution.basis: Unit 42 infrastructure overlaps: HenBox C2 shares domains and IPs with PlugX, Zupdax, 9002 and Poison Ivy activity focused on Southeast Asian politics, and with the Windows backdoor Farseer [S1][S3][S4].

actors.objectives: Surveillance and data theft from mobile devices of Uyghur users, per Unit 42's assessment that HenBox primarily targets Uyghurs; the sources gathered do not state a sponsoring tasking [S1][S2].

regions: China, Uyghur community, Xinjiang (Unit 42 believed victims were likely in Tibet, Xinjiang and Mongolia) [S4]
Southeast Asia, especially Myanmar, Taiwan, Vietnam and Indonesia, for the wider PKPLUG cluster [S3][S4]
targeting.notes: Targeting is inferred by Unit 42 from app themes, distribution sites and infrastructure overlaps, not from confirmed victim lists [S1][S3]. HenBox also targets Xiaomi devices running MIUI [S1][S2].

capabilities.summary: Trojanized Android apps disguised as VPN and system apps, distributed only on third-party (non-Google Play) app stores, though some decoy apps were on Google Play [S2]. HenBox sets itself to trigger based on alerts from Xiaomi smart-home IoT devices, then steals information from many sources including popular chat and social media apps [S2]. Unit 42 reported grown sample counts over time, from almost 200 in 2018 to over 400 since 2015 in a 2019 conference deck [S2][S5]. A related Windows backdoor, Farseer, shares config-file design and C2 infrastructure; it uses DLL sideloading of signed binaries and phishing or malicious PDFs [S3].

campaigns.name: Earliest HenBox samples
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 reports the oldest HenBox samples date to 2015, with a handful that year [S2].

campaigns.name: DroidVPN decoy sample
campaigns.summary: A sample posing as DroidVPN was downloaded from uyghurapps[.]net [S2].

campaigns.name: Peak HenBox sample volume
campaigns.summary: Most of the almost 200 samples in the March 2018 report came from the second half of 2017 [S2]. Farseer samples were also mostly from 2017 [S3].

campaigns.name: Unit 42 public disclosure of HenBox
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 published its HenBox reports, noting Uyghur and Xiaomi MIUI targeting and infrastructure ties to Southeast Asia-focused PlugX, Zupdax, 9002 and Poison Ivy activity [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: Farseer disclosure
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 published Farseer research on 26 February, finding it while investigating HenBox infrastructure. Over 30 unique samples were seen, mostly 2017 with some 2018 [S3]. The retrieved snippets did not state the year; 2019 is inferred from sample span, see gaps.

campaigns.name: PKPLUG cluster report
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 grouped HenBox, Farseer, PlugX, Poison Ivy and 9002 under PKPLUG, with activity back to November 2013, and assessed China-nexus origins with high confidence [S4][S5].

diamond.adversary: Unidentified cluster; Unit 42 assesses China-nexus origin and cannot say whether one group or several [S4].
diamond.capability: Trojanized Android apps (VPN and system app lures), IoT-alert trigger, broad app data theft; related Windows backdoor Farseer [S2][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Third-party app stores and sites such as uyghurapps[.]net; C2 domains and IPs overlapping with Farseer, PlugX, Poison Ivy, 9002 and Zupdax [S2][S3].
diamond.victim: Uyghur users and Xiaomi/MIUI device owners; wider cluster in Southeast Asia and possibly Tibet, Xinjiang, Mongolia [S1][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Surveillance of an ethnic minority community; Unit 42 notes Southeast Asia political focus in related infrastructure [S1][S4].
diamond.technology: Android devices from third-party app stores, MIUI, and connected Xiaomi smart-home devices used as a trigger [S2].

gaps: Unit 42 primary posts (HenBox: Chickens Come Home to Roost; Inside the Coop; Farseer; PKPLUG) could not be opened with WebFetch (DNS failure); claims rely on search-result summaries and secondary coverage, so exact wording is unverified.
Publication year of the Farseer post (26 February) was not stated in retrieved results; 2019 is inferred.
No government attribution or sponsoring organization is cited; sponsor left blank.
No Microsoft name or MITRE group ID was found for HenBox.
No activity after 2019 was found in the gathered sources; current status is unknown.
Exact capability list, native libraries and C2 protocol details are not captured here.
Relationship of HenBox to other PlugX/Poison Ivy users is unresolved; Unit 42 notes it may be one or multiple groups.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Personal Android devices and third-party app stores are the relevant terrain; HenBox is not documented against military networks in the sources. STEP 2: The adversary uses trojanized VPN and system apps with legitimate decoys and a smart-home IoT trigger [S2]. STEP 3: Victim-aligned lures, sideload from third-party stores, then broad data theft from chat apps [S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued surveillance of Uyghur and Southeast Asian communities [S1][S4]. MDCOA is reuse of the shared infrastructure and Windows tooling against regional government personnel [S3][S4]. Candidate indicators: apps from third-party stores posing as VPNs, uyghurapps[.]net downloads, and C2 overlap with Farseer or PlugX [S2][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat as low direct relevance to DoD networks; track for personnel traveling to or working with Southeast Asia and Chinese-language communities [S4]. (2) Authorities: personal device guidance falls to unit policy, not network defense authorities. (3) Mission assurance: restrict sideloading and third-party app stores on mission devices [S2]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partners via normal CTI channels; confidence is vendor-level only [S4].
