identification.summary: China-based cyber-espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Hexagon Typhoon and maps to APT12, NUMBERED PANDA, Calc Team, DNS-Calc, HYDROGEN, Red Anubis and HORDE [S1]. MITRE ATT&CK describes APT12 as a group attributed to China that has targeted media outlets, high-tech companies and multiple governments [S4]. Mandiant reported that APT12 compromised the New York Times in October 2012 and in August 2014 ran spear-phishing campaigns against Taiwanese government organizations, with possibly related activity against technology firms in Taiwan and Japan [S2]. Mandiant also documented a repeated pattern: after public exposure, the group paused briefly and then retooled [S2]. FireEye observed renewed, retooled activity in May 2013 [S10], and Zscaler reported a suspected IXESHE-linked watering-hole campaign against Taiwanese government networks in late 2016, while stopping short of confirming APT12 [S11].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro reported the IXESHE campaign active since at least July 2009 against East Asian targets [S6]; MITRE associates Ixeshe malware with APT12 [S4]. Arbor Networks (as reported by Mandiant) dated RIPTIDE/Etumbot campaigns to March 2011 [S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Hexagon Typhoon. Microsoft lists HYDROGEN, NUMBERED PANDA, Calc Team, Red Anubis, APT12, DNS-Calc and HORDE as other names [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as APT12 (G0005) with associated names IXESHE, DynCalc, Numbered Panda and DNSCALC [S4]. Mandiant uses APT12 and lists 'Calc Team' as an alias [S3]. MISP Galaxy lists BRONZE GLOBE (Secureworks), BeeBus, Group 22 and Crimson Iron as synonyms [S8]. Do not confuse this actor with APT5 / Mulberry Typhoon (MANGANESE). The imported summary text in this record described APT5 and has been replaced.

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China. Mandiant says APT12 is 'believed to be a cyber espionage group thought to have links to the Chinese People's Liberation Army' [S2][S3]. MITRE records the group as attributed to China [S4], and Microsoft lists its origin as China [S1].
attribution.confidence: Mandiant's PLA link is hedged ('believed to be', 'thought to have links') and does not name a specific unit [S2][S3]. FireEye's Ned Moran said the company was 'almost certain' the 2013 retooled activity came from the same group that attacked the New York Times [S10]. Zscaler explicitly did not confirm APT12 for the 2016 CNACOM campaign, citing only 'strong reasons for suspicion' [S11]. MISP Galaxy, citing CFR data, records China as the suspected state sponsor with an attribution-confidence value of 50 [S8]. No government indictment or formal government attribution naming APT12 or Hexagon Typhoon was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Vendor technical reporting from Mandiant/FireEye on malware families, delivery documents and Taiwan-focused targeting [S2][S3][S10]; Trend Micro IXESHE research [S6]; CrowdStrike and FireEye reporting cited by MITRE [S4][S5][S7]; Zscaler malware-similarity analysis for 2016 activity [S11]; Microsoft's naming map [S1].

actors.objectives: Cyber espionage consistent with broader PRC goals, especially PRC self-interest regarding Taiwan, according to Mandiant [S2][S3]. The New York Times intrusion coincided with the paper's reporting on the wealth of Premier Wen Jiabao's relatives, pointing to intelligence collection on media coverage of the PRC leadership [S9][S2]. 2013 targeting of an organization that shapes international finance and economic policy suggests economic-policy collection as well [S10].

sectors: Government (including Taiwanese government ministries and networks) [S2][S6][S11]
regions: East Asia (IXESHE targeting since at least July 2009) [S6]
targeting.notes: The August 2014 HIGHTIDE campaign targeted multiple Taiwanese government organizations between 22 and 28 August 2014, with lures sent from apparently valid but compromised Taiwanese government accounts [S2]. Related THREEBYTE and WATERSPOUT activity hit a Taiwanese technology company and a Japanese high-technology company, but Mandiant did not firmly attribute those two campaigns to APT12 [S2]. The 2016 CNACOM watering hole used a compromised Taiwanese public-service website to deliver an IXESHE variant to Taiwanese government targets; Zscaler's attribution to APT12 is suspected only [S11].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing with weaponized Word and PDF attachments exploiting Office, Adobe Reader and Flash vulnerabilities (Trend Micro lists CVE-2009-4324, CVE-2009-0927, CVE-2011-0609 and CVE-2011-0611; Mandiant lists CVE-2012-0158 for 2014) [S2][S4][S6]. The group sends lures from compromised but legitimate accounts [S2][S3]. Trend Micro reported IXESHE C2 using dynamic DNS and previously compromised servers [S6]. Custom HTTP backdoors include RIPTIDE (Etumbot to Arbor), a proxy-aware backdoor with RC4-encrypted C2; its modified successor HIGHTIDE; and THREEBYTE and WATERSPOUT, which Mandiant says are possibly related [S2][S3]. It also used Ixeshe, Aumlib and the HTRAN connection-proxy tool [S4][S6][S10]. Per CrowdStrike reporting cited by MITRE, it derived C2 ports from IP octets ('DNS calculation') and used blogs and WordPress for C2 [S4][S5]. The group retools rapidly after disclosure: network-protocol changes to Aumlib and Ixeshe in 2013 to evade IDS signatures [S10], and RIPTIDE protocol and string changes after the June 2014 Arbor report [S2]. Suspected 2016 activity added strategic web compromise with a CVE-2016-0189 Internet Explorer exploit [S11].

campaigns.name: IXESHE campaign begins
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reports IXESHE targeted attacks active since at least July 2009 against East Asian governments, Taiwanese electronics manufacturers and a telecommunications company, using PDF exploits and C2 on compromised servers.

campaigns.name: Trend Micro 'IXESHE: An APT Campaign' published
campaigns.summary: Public exposure of the IXESHE operation; MITRE cites it for spear-phishing attachments, client exploits and HTRAN use.

campaigns.name: New York Times compromise
campaigns.summary: Attackers persisted in the Times network for about four months, coinciding with its Wen Jiabao investigation published 25 Oct 2012; disclosed by the paper in January 2013. Mandiant later attributed the intrusion to APT12.

campaigns.name: CrowdStrike 'Whois Numbered Panda' profile
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike profiles the group as Numbered Panda; MITRE cites it for DNS-calculated C2 ports and blog/WordPress C2.

campaigns.name: Retooled Aumlib and Ixeshe operations
campaigns.summary: FireEye observes the NYT attackers resume in early May 2013 with updated Aumlib (against an international finance/economic-policy organization) and Ixeshe (against entities in Taiwan), with protocol changes to evade IDS; published August 2013.

campaigns.name: Retooling after Arbor Etumbot disclosure
campaigns.summary: Arbor publishes on the RIPTIDE (Etumbot) backdoor used March 2011 to May 2014; Mandiant then sees APT12 modify RIPTIDE into HIGHTIDE.

campaigns.name: HIGHTIDE spear-phishing against Taiwan government
campaigns.summary: 22-28 August 2014 CVE-2012-0158 Word lures from compromised Taiwanese government accounts deliver HIGHTIDE; possibly related THREEBYTE and WATERSPOUT lures hit a Taiwanese technology company and a Japanese high-tech company.

campaigns.name: CNACOM strategic web compromise (suspected)
campaigns.summary: From 7 Nov 2016 an iframe injected into a major Taiwanese public-service website's registration page served a CVE-2016-0189 exploit delivering an IXESHE variant to Taiwanese government targets; Zscaler suspects but does not confirm APT12.

diamond.adversary: PRC-based espionage operators that Mandiant believes have links to the PLA; Microsoft calls the group Hexagon Typhoon and MITRE tracks it as APT12 [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.capability: Exploit documents (CVE-2012-0158 and Adobe/Flash CVEs); IE exploit CVE-2016-0189 in suspected 2016 activity; RIPTIDE, HIGHTIDE, THREEBYTE, WATERSPOUT, Ixeshe and Aumlib backdoors; HTRAN proxying; rapid retooling after disclosure [S2][S4][S6][S10][S11].
diamond.infrastructure: Hard-coded HTTP C2 servers, including direct-IP C2 and dynamic-DNS domains [S2][S6]; previously compromised servers used as C2 [S6]; compromised legitimate email accounts used to send lures [S2]; blogs and WordPress used for C2, with ports derived by DNS calculation [S4][S5]; a compromised Taiwanese public-service website used as a watering hole in suspected 2016 activity [S11].
diamond.victim: Taiwanese government ministries and networks, journalists and media (New York Times), defense contractors, finance/economic-policy organizations, telecommunications, and high-tech and electronics firms in Taiwan and Japan [S2][S3][S6][S9][S10][S11].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection that supports PRC strategic goals, especially regarding Taiwan, and intelligence on foreign media coverage of PRC leadership [S2][S3][S9].
diamond.technology: Unpatched Microsoft Office and Adobe client software on Windows endpoints, plus trust in email from known colleagues [S2][S4].

gaps: No vendor or government reporting naming APT12/Hexagon Typhoon after the suspected December 2016 Zscaler CNACOM report was found in the searches run; current activity level, tooling and any re-designation are unknown [S11].
Microsoft has published no actor profile or blog content for Hexagon Typhoon that was found; only the naming map supports the Microsoft name [S1].

Primary documents not opened (hosts unreachable from this environment): CrowdStrike 'Whois Numbered Panda' [S5], Trend Micro IXESHE white paper [S6], FireEye 'Survival of the Fittest' [S7], Zscaler CNACOM blog [S11], TechCrunch and PCWorld articles [S9][S10], CFR APT12 entry, Secureworks BRONZE GLOBE profile and Arbor 'Illuminating the Etumbot APT Backdoor'. Claims from these rely on search-result excerpts or MITRE/Mandiant citations.

2013 press coverage of the New York Times breach attributed it to 'Chinese hackers' generally; the APT12 label comes from Mandiant's later 2014 reporting [S2][S9]. The original NYT article and Mandiant engagement details were not reviewed.
PLA link is a hedged vendor assessment (Mandiant). No specific PLA unit or MSS/contractor tie is public in the sources gathered, and no government attribution was found.
2016 CNACOM attribution to APT12 is suspicion based on targeting and malware similarity only [S11]; secondary coverage gives the sandbox-escape CVE inconsistently (CVE-2015-0116 vs CVE-2015-0016).

Alias boundary issue: MISP Galaxy's APT12 entry lists TG-2754 with the same identifier as BRONZE GLOBE [S8], but this encyclopedia maps TG-2754 to Mulberry Typhoon (APT5). Needs reconciling against Secureworks' own profiles.
THREEBYTE and WATERSPOUT campaigns were not positively attributed to APT12 by Mandiant [S2].
Aliases BeeBus, Group 22, Crimson Iron, Poisoned Flight and IXESHE-as-actor come from aggregator data (MISP) [S8], not from vendor reports reviewed here.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is user endpoints running Office and PDF readers, and the email trust relationships between government personnel, especially in Taiwan and Japan and partner organizations that work with them [S2]. STEP 2 (effects): Because email arrives from compromised colleague accounts, sender-reputation filtering is weakened. The group's quick retooling after disclosure shortens the shelf life of published signatures [S2]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Spear-phish (or, in suspected 2016 activity, a watering hole on a government-used website filtering for target IP ranges [S11]) with an exploit document from a compromised trusted account, then an HTTP backdoor (RIPTIDE/HIGHTIDE-class) with RC4-encrypted C2 or DNS-calculated ports, then document collection; HTRAN can be used to hide C2 origin [S2][S4][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued spear-phishing espionage against Taiwan-focused government, defense-industrial and media targets [S2][S3]. MDCOA is a renewed or rebranded campaign against US and partner organizations that support Taiwan, using new tooling released immediately after any public exposure [S2]. Candidate indicators: injected iframes on government-used websites serving IE exploits [S11]; Word documents exploiting CVE-2012-0158 or newer Office flaws; executables dropped as word.exe or winword.exe in user Temp directories; HTTP beacons with anomalous User-Agent/URI patterns to direct IPs or dynamic-DNS domains; C2 ports that look computed from IP octets [S2][S4][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: public reporting on this actor stops in 2016 (suspected only) in the sources gathered [S11], so treat any detection as a prompt to check current vendor reporting rather than to rely on 2014 IOCs [S2]. (2) Authorities: activity traced to commercial media or partner-nation government networks lies outside DoD defensive authorities and needs interagency and partner coordination [S2]. (3) Mission assurance: phishing from compromised partner accounts threatens DODIN users who correspond with Taiwan and Japan counterparts; prioritize patching Office and PDF readers and inspecting attachments [S2][S4]. (4) Coordination: share retooling observations quickly with partners, because Mandiant and FireEye report the actor changes tools and protocols within weeks to months of disclosure [S2][S10].

provenance.importedSummary: We have observed one APT group, which we call APT5, particularly focused on telecommunications and technology companies. More than half of the organizations we have observed being targeted or breached by APT5 operate in these sectors. Several times, APT5 has targeted organizations and personnel based in Southeast Asia. APT5 has been active since at least 2007. It appears to be a large threat group that consists of several subgroups, often with distinct tactics and infrastructure. APT5 has targeted or breached organizations across multiple industries, but its focus appears to be on telecommunications and technology companies, especially information about satellite communications. APT5 targeted the network of an electronics firm that sells products for both industrial and military applications. The group subsequently stole communications related to the firm’s business relationship with a national military, including inventories and memoranda about specific products they provided. In one case in late 2014, APT5 breached the network of an international telecommunications company. The group used malware with keylogging capabilities to monitor the computer of an executive who manages the company’s relationships with other telecommunications companies

identification.summary: HiddenArt is the name Enea's AdaptiveMobile Security unit assigned to a mobile-network signalling threat actor (a 'platform') that it believes with a high degree of confidence originates from Russian network sources [S1][S4]. Enea says it sustains a capacity to remotely access the personal devices of targeted individuals worldwide, and periodic reconnaissance was seen in at least 7 target mobile networks [S2]. Enea's presentation describes it as a core-network signalling actor whose main behaviour is location tracking and voice/SMS interception, in bursts with long gaps [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Publicly disclosed February 2022 in the 'Spectrum of Violence' research [S2]. Enea says the 'Hidden' part of the name reflects a feature the platform has used for 5+ years [S2]; the first-detection date is not stated in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: Single-vendor designation (Enea / AdaptiveMobile Security). No MITRE ATT&CK group ID and no Microsoft name were found. Malpedia lists no malware families for it and cites only the 2022 Enea write-up [S4]. A search summary of the Enea blog says the name's 'Art' element refers to the Old Irish word for bear; the blog page could not be opened to confirm [S1].

attribution.sponsor: Enea assesses with a high degree of confidence that HiddenArt originates from Russian network sources [S1]. Enea's sources gathered do not confirm a specific state organization or government control; this is a vendor assessment, not a government attribution.
attribution.confidence: Enea states it believes 'with a high degree of confidence' that the platform originates from Russian network sources [S1][S4]. Enea also notes that the actor's disguise makes attribution much harder [S1].
attribution.basis: Enea correlated signalling data across networks, tracking recurring Global Titles, message sequences and routing paths; individual messages can look like legitimate signalling when seen alone [S1]. The detailed basis for the Russia assessment is not available in the sources I could open [S1].

actors.objectives: Enea describes the activity as location tracking and voice and SMS interception of targeted individuals [S3]. Search summaries of Enea's blog say targets were mainly VIP individuals, many with Russian links [S1]. The actor's ultimate tasking is not stated in the sources gathered.

sectors: Mobile network operators (infrastructure attacked via core signalling) [S2]
Individual subscribers, described by Enea as mainly VIPs [S1]
regions: Global; periodic reconnaissance in at least 7 target mobile networks worldwide [S2]
targeting.notes: Specific operators, countries and victim names are not given in the sources gathered. The AdaptiveMobile white paper frames mobile-network attacks in the context of hybrid warfare [S2].

capabilities.summary: Core-network (SS7) signalling attacks for location tracking and voice/SMS interception, delivered in bursts [S1][S3]. Enea reports the actor tries to make its source SCCP Global Titles as similar as possible to real, non-malicious GTs of legitimate network nodes, which could evade operators with weaker firewalls; the messages appeared to come from GTs linked to a group of African networks [S1]. Enea's presentation also gives a working theory, based on captured traffic, that the actor injects attack requests using spoofed global titles and copies responses to itself [S3]. No malware families are listed [S4].

campaigns.name: Enea/AdaptiveMobile 'Spectrum of Violence' disclosure
campaigns.summary: Enea's AdaptiveMobile Security disclosed HiddenArt, found using its SIGIL signalling intelligence platform, with periodic reconnaissance against at least 7 mobile networks worldwide [S2].

campaigns.name: Enea presentation 'The Hidden Global Battlefield'
campaigns.summary: Presentation hosted by ENISA describes HiddenArt as a core-network signalling actor focused on location tracking and voice/SMS interception, active in bursts. The date comes from the file name only [S3].

diamond.adversary: Unnamed operator of a signalling platform that Enea assesses originates from Russian network sources [S1].
diamond.capability: SS7 location tracking and voice/SMS interception; GT spoofing to resemble legitimate GTs [S1][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: SS7 signalling access appearing from GTs linked to a group of African networks (per Enea blog summary); actual operator access points are not identified [S1].
diamond.victim: Targeted individuals, mainly VIPs per Enea, and at least 7 mobile networks reconnoitred worldwide [S1][S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Enea places the activity within hybrid-warfare use of mobile networks [S2].
diamond.technology: Legacy SS7 signalling interconnects and operators with weak signalling firewalls [S1].

gaps: Could not open the Enea blog, the Enea press release, the ENISA-hosted slides or the white paper (host unreachable); findings rely on search-result summaries of them. Verify against the primaries before use.
Blog publication date not confirmed; 'Spectrum of Violence' dated February 2022 from the Enea press release listing, and the slide deck date (2022-06) is inferred from its file name [S2][S3].
No government or third-party corroboration of Russian attribution; the basis is a single vendor's assessment [S1].
Victim networks, countries, individual targets and exact first-detection date are not public in the sources gathered.
No malware, tooling or ATT&CK mapping; no overlap analysis with other Russian actors.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Mobile operator core signalling (SS7 interconnect, Global Title translation) is key terrain, and the targets are subscribers' phones reached through it [S1][S2]. STEP 2: The actor operates through the network, not the handset, so device security controls do not see it [S2]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is bursty reconnaissance, then location tracking and voice/SMS interception, using GTs spoofed to resemble legitimate ones [S1][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued covert tracking and interception of VIP individuals across multiple operators. MDCOA is use of the same access to track or intercept deployed personnel or leaders in a crisis or hybrid conflict (the white paper's framing) [S2]. Candidate indicators: recurring GTs and message sequences, location-query bursts on subscribers from unfamiliar GTs, and signalling from GTs resembling legitimate peers [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: personnel and VIP use of commercial mobile networks, especially roaming, is exposed to signalling-layer tracking and interception that the user cannot detect [S1][S2]. (2) Authorities: operator signalling defenses are owned by carriers and regulators, not DoD; DoD action is mostly guidance and coordination [S2]. (3) Mission assurance: avoid reliance on SMS and voice over commercial networks for sensitive coordination and use end-to-end encrypted channels. (4) Coordination: use host-nation and carrier channels and signalling-intelligence sharing for reports of anomalous GTs [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: It was observed that a mobile network threat actor designated as ‘HiddenArt’ actively sustains a capacity to remotely access the personal devices of targeted individuals around the world on an ongoing basis. Since detecting this threat actor, periodic reconnaissance activities were observed in at least 7 target mobile networks around the world and given the wide geographic distribution of these targeted mobile operators, it is probable that the threat actor is active on a global scale.

identification.summary: Houken is the name France's ANSSI (CERT-FR) gave to an intrusion set that exploited three Ivanti Cloud Services Appliance (CSA) zero-days (CVE-2024-8190, CVE-2024-8963, CVE-2024-9380) against French organizations from September 2024 [S1][S2][S3]. ANSSI assesses that the operators likely seek valuable initial accesses to sell to a state-linked actor wanting intelligence, and that the actor might correspond to a private entity selling access and data to several state-linked bodies [S2][S3]. The operators use many open-source tools, mostly written by Chinese-speaking developers, plus custom webshells and, in some cases, a rootkit [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: Campaign detected in September 2024; ANSSI says activity could date back to 2023 [S2][S3]. CERT-FR published its report CERTFR-2025-CTI-009 on 2025-07-01 [S3].
identification.notes: ANSSI names the set Houken. Per Infosecurity Magazine, CERT-FR assessed Houken as run by the same actor Google's GTIG/Mandiant tracks as UNC5174 [S3]; The Hacker News frames the overlap as tradecraft similarity that raises the possibility of a common operator [S2]. Do not merge the two vendor clusters' facts; UNC5174 facts below are labeled as Mandiant's [S4][S5]. No Microsoft Typhoon/Storm name for Houken was found in the sources gathered.

attribution.sponsor: No government attribution located. ANSSI describes a Chinese-linked, likely access-broker operator supplying state-linked customers; it does not name a specific PRC agency in the coverage reviewed [S2][S3]. Mandiant (for UNC5174, the cluster ANSSI links to Houken) said that actor showed indications of acting as a contractor for China's Ministry of State Security [S4][S5].
attribution.confidence: ANSSI's Houken-to-UNC5174 link is reported as an assessment of same operator [S3]; other coverage describes it as similarity in tradecraft [S2]. Mandiant's moderate-confidence statement applies to its assessment that the custom tooling and SUPERSHELL framework are unique to a PRC actor, not to the MSS-contractor link, which it worded as 'indications' [S4][S5]. Confidence level of ANSSI's wording could not be verified against the primary PDF.
attribution.basis: ANSSI incident-response findings in French organizations [S1][S2]; overlap in tooling such as VShell and GOREVERSE between Houken and Mandiant's UNC5174 reporting [S2][S4]; use of open-source tools by Chinese-speaking developers [S1][S2].

actors.objectives: Obtain and monetize initial access to sensitive networks, likely for sale to state-linked actors seeking intelligence, with some direct data theft and occasional profit-driven activity such as cryptomining on one victim system [S2][S3].

sectors: Defense, media and telecom (Western targets, broad ANSSI targeting view)
regions: France (Ivanti CSA campaign, victims in government, telecom, media, finance, transport) [S2][S3]
Southeast Asia, including Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia [S3]
China including Hong Kong and Macau (NGOs) [S2]
targeting.notes: Targeting statements come from secondary coverage of the ANSSI report [S2][S3]. A secondary outlet reported a South American foreign ministry among victims; not verified in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: Exploited three Ivanti CSA zero-days (CVE-2024-8190, CVE-2024-8963, CVE-2024-9380) before the Ivanti advisory was published, starting early September 2024 [S1][S2][S3]. After access, operators deployed custom PHP webshells, modified legitimate scripts, and in some cases installed a custom rootkit for persistence [S1][S2]. Named open-source tools include Neo-reGeorg, Behinder (Ice Scorpion), Suo5, ffuf and VShell [S3]; secondary summaries of the ANSSI report also name GOREVERSE and a sysinitd kernel-module rootkit [S1]. A cryptominer was found on one victim, which ANSSI called uncommon for this actor [S2]. For UNC5174 (Mandiant's cluster), custom SNOWLIGHT, GOHEAVY and GOREVERSE tools and the SUPERSHELL framework were reported in 2024 [S4][S5].

Included for context only; ANSSI's link to Houken is an assessment, not established fact in these sources.

campaigns.name: Houken Ivanti CSA zero-day campaign against France
campaigns.summary: From early September 2024 the actor exploited CVE-2024-8190, CVE-2024-8963 and CVE-2024-9380 on Ivanti CSA devices, hitting French government, telecom, media, finance and transport organizations, and deployed webshells, open-source tools and in some cases a rootkit. Activity reportedly ran into late 2024 and may have started in 2023.

campaigns.name: ANSSI/CERT-FR publishes Houken report
campaigns.summary: CERT-FR report CERTFR-2025-CTI-009 names the Houken intrusion set, assesses it as the same actor as UNC5174, and states both were still active in mid-2025.

diamond.adversary: Chinese-linked operator assessed by ANSSI as an access broker, possibly a private entity selling access and data to state-linked bodies; ANSSI links it to UNC5174 [S2][S3].
diamond.capability: Ivanti CSA zero-days, custom PHP webshells, rootkit, and open-source tooling (Neo-reGeorg, Behinder, Suo5, ffuf, VShell) [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised Ivanti CSA appliances as footholds [S2][S3]. Actor C2 infrastructure details are in the ANSSI PDF, which could not be opened.
diamond.victim: French government, telecom, media, finance and transport organizations; also Southeast Asian government and education, and NGOs in China/Hong Kong/Macau [S2][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Access brokerage serving state-linked intelligence customers, with some financial self-enrichment [S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing network appliances (Ivanti CSA) with unpatched or unknown flaws; Linux hosts where a rootkit was used [S1][S2].

gaps: The primary CERT-FR report (CERTFR-2025-CTI-009) could not be fetched in this session (fetch tool DNS failure); all details come from search-result summaries and secondary coverage. Exact IOCs, infrastructure, timeline and confidence wording are unverified.
Strength of the Houken-UNC5174 link is reported inconsistently (same actor vs. tradecraft similarity) [S2][S3]. Treat as one assessment, not merged clusters.
No government (US/FR) attribution to a named PRC agency found; whether Houken customers are MSS, PLA or others is unknown.
No Microsoft or MITRE ATT&CK group entry was located for Houken.
Reports of a South American foreign ministry victim and OVH-hosted infrastructure were not verified.
Sysdig's UNC5174 reporting (SNOWLIGHT to VShell) appeared in results but was not opened or dated.
Activity after mid-2025 is not covered in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing edge appliances (Ivanti CSA and similar VPN/remote-access devices) in government, telecom and transport networks are key cyber terrain because they are the foothold [S2][S3]. STEP 2: The actor exploits zero-days before advisories, so patch status alone does not provide assurance, and compromised devices may be resold to other actors [S2][S3]. STEP 3: The template is edge-appliance zero-day, webshell, open-source tunneling/RAT tools, and sometimes a Linux rootkit [S1][S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued opportunistic exploitation of edge devices to build a portfolio of access for state-linked customers. MDCOA is that access being handed to an espionage or pre-positioning customer against allied government or telecom networks in a crisis. Candidate indicators: unexpected PHP files or modified scripts on appliances, Neo-reGeorg/Behinder/Suo5 traffic patterns, unauthorized kernel modules on Linux hosts, and unexplained cryptominer processes [S1][S2][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track edge-appliance zero-day disclosures and vendor advisories, and assume exposure before a patch exists [S2][S3]. (2) Authorities: appliance forensics and takedown on partner or contractor networks need coordination through DC3/DIB CS or host-nation channels; confirm authorities before acting. (3) Mission assurance: inventory mission-critical systems reachable via exposed appliances and prepare to isolate them. (4) Coordination: share indicators with allies (ANSSI/CERT-FR published the source report) and note that one access may be reused by multiple actors, so containment should precede attribution [S2][S3].

provenance.importedSummary: Houken is a Chinese state-sponsored threat actor that exploits zero-day vulnerabilities in Ivanti Cloud Services Appliance devices to gain initial access to critical infrastructure networks, particularly in France. The group employs a sophisticated rootkit alongside open-source tools, primarily developed by Chinese-speaking authors, to maintain persistence and control over compromised systems. Houken is suspected to operate as an initial access broker, selling footholds in targeted networks to other threat actors for further exploitation.

identification.summary: Houndstooth Typhoon is Microsoft's name for a China-origin threat actor. Microsoft's public naming map links it to HASSIUM (its former Microsoft name), CrowdStrike's DRAGNET PANDA, and the labels 'isoon' and 'deepclif' [S1][S2]. The 'isoon' label points to the Chengdu-registered PRC security contractor i-Soon (Anxun Information Technology / Sichuan Anxun). Reporting describes i-Soon as an APT-for-hire contractor serving the Ministry of Public Security (MPS) [S3][S5]. A February 2024 leak exposed i-Soon's internal documents, tools and target lists [S3][S4][S5]. In March 2025 US prosecutors charged i-Soon executives and employees, together with two MPS officers [S6][S7][S10].
identification.firstObserved: CrowdStrike reports that DRAGNET PANDA has been active since at least 2015 [S9]. The 2025 US indictment covers i-Soon intrusion activity from about 2016 through 2023 [S6][S10].
identification.notes: Microsoft publishes the naming but, in the sources found, no narrative profile of Houndstooth Typhoon. Its activity therefore has to be read through what other vendors report on DRAGNET PANDA and on i-Soon. Do not assume those clusters are identical [S1][S2][S9]. Keep the cluster boundary in mind: ESET assesses that its FishMonger cluster (Earth Lusca / Aquatic Panda) is operated by I-SOON [S8], but Microsoft maps AQUATIC PANDA to Charcoal Typhoon, not to Houndstooth Typhoon [S1]. SentinelOne notes that the leak suggests i-Soon was behind activity previously attributed to several different named threat actors [S3].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China. According to coverage of the March 2025 indictment, i-Soon carried out intrusions at the direction of, or for sale to, the MPS and the Ministry of State Security (MSS) [S6][S10]. In some cases it hacked first and then tried to sell the stolen data [S10].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft assigns China as the origin of Houndstooth Typhoon but publishes no confidence statement in the naming map [S1]. US prosecutors made charging allegations (not convictions) against i-Soon personnel and two MPS officers [S6][S7]. ESET assesses with high confidence that FishMonger conducted Operation FishMedley and states that it independently determined FishMonger is operated by I-SOON. That is a vendor assessment about the FishMonger cluster [S8].
attribution.basis: Microsoft's naming map [S1]; the February 2024 i-Soon document leak, whose authenticity and source were not independently confirmed although it matched prior reporting [S3][S4][S5]; press coverage of the March 2025 DOJ indictment [S6][S7][S10]; ESET research [S8]; CrowdStrike's DRAGNET PANDA profile [S9].

actors.objectives: Intelligence collection for PRC security services. Targets include dissidents, critics, religious minorities and media, alongside foreign-government espionage [S6][S9][S10]. SentinelOne describes i-Soon as a company that competes for low-value hacking contracts from many government agencies [S3]. Press coverage of the indictment says i-Soon charged MSS and MPS customers roughly $10,000 to $75,000 per compromised email inbox and worked with at least 43 MSS or MPS bureaus [S10].

sectors: Foreign government ministries, including foreign affairs ministries [S6][S10]
US federal and state government agencies [S10]
Defense / intelligence (the Defense Intelligence Agency is cited as a target) [S6]
Dissidents and critics of the PRC; Tibetan groups [S6][S9]
regions: Asia: multiple governments [S10]; India, Thailand, Vietnam and South Korea per the leaked data [S5]
targeting.notes: Victim lists come from three different evidence bases: the leak [S3][S5], the indictment [S6][S10] and the CrowdStrike DRAGNET PANDA profile [S9]. None of them is attributed by Microsoft to Houndstooth Typhoon specifically. The FishMedley victims ESET reported in 2022 (governments, NGOs, Catholic charities and think tanks in Taiwan, Thailand, Hungary, Turkey, France and the US) belong to ESET's FishMonger cluster and are kept separate here [S8].

capabilities.summary: According to the leaked i-Soon documents, the company offered: remote access trojans for Windows x64/x86 with keylogging, remote shell, registry and service management, and system reconnaissance; a Twitter/X account tool that can obtain the account email and phone number, read private messages and post as the victim; and malware with command-and-control infrastructure [S4][S5]. Some leaked records show custom hardware devices built for stealing data from victim networks [S4]. Indictment coverage stresses email-inbox compromise sold to MSS and MPS customers [S10]. ESET reports that the FishMonger cluster, which it ties to I-SOON, used ShadowPad, SodaMaster and Spyder implants [S8].

diamond.adversary: i-Soon (Anxun), a Chengdu-registered PRC contractor serving the MPS and MSS; named executives Wu Haibo (CEO) and Chen Cheng (COO); MPS officers Wang Liyu and Sheng Jing named as tasking officials [S3][S6][S10]. Microsoft tracks it as Houndstooth Typhoon [S1].
diamond.capability: Windows RATs, a social-media account takeover tool, custom hardware for data theft, and email-inbox compromise for hire [S4][S5][S10]. ShadowPad, SodaMaster and Spyder in the ESET FishMonger cluster [S8].
diamond.infrastructure: Malware command-and-control infrastructure described in the leaked documents [S4]. Specific infrastructure indicators were not obtained for this record.
diamond.victim: Dissidents, religious organizations, media, Asian foreign ministries, US federal and state agencies, and NATO and several Asian governments named in the leaked data [S3][S5][S6][S10].
diamond.socioPolitical: PRC domestic-security priorities (dissidents, Tibetan groups, religious minorities, critical media) combined with foreign-government intelligence. Delivered through a commercial contracting market that sells stolen access and data to many security-service bureaus [S3][S9][S10].
diamond.technology: Email accounts, Windows endpoints and social-media accounts are the main technical surfaces described [S4][S5][S10].

gaps: Microsoft has not published a narrative Houndstooth Typhoon profile in the sources found. The only Microsoft evidence is the naming map entry (HASSIUM, DRAGNET PANDA, isoon, deepclif) [S1].

Cluster boundary is unresolved. Microsoft maps 'isoon' to Houndstooth Typhoon but AQUATIC PANDA to Charcoal Typhoon, while ESET and the FBI tie FishMonger / Aquatic Panda to I-SOON [S1][S8]. Which i-Soon operations Microsoft counts as Houndstooth Typhoon is unknown.
No public source was found that explicitly links CrowdStrike's DRAGNET PANDA to i-Soon. The linkage rests on Microsoft's mapping [S1][S9].
The meaning and origin of the 'deepclif' label is unknown.

Primary documents were not opened: the DOJ indictment and press release, the FBI wanted notices, and the full SentinelOne, ESET and CrowdStrike pages (fetch blocked). Indictment details rely on press coverage.
The authenticity of the 2024 leak and the identity of the leaker are not confirmed [S3].
No Houndstooth Typhoon infrastructure indicators, CVEs or recent (2025-2026) activity were found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is email accounts, Windows endpoints and social-media accounts of government, defense-intelligence, media and diaspora-adjacent personnel, including foreign ministries of Asian partners and NATO [S3][S5][S6][S10]. STEP 2: A contractor model with many customer bureaus produces broad, opportunistic, volume-driven targeting. Sellable inbox access is the payoff [S3][S10]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is account or endpoint compromise, then a RAT with keylogging and remote shell, then mailbox and message collection, then sale or delivery of the data to MPS or MSS customers [S5][S10]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued mailbox compromise of partner-nation foreign ministries and US agencies for resale to security services. MDCOA is harvesting of partner or NATO communications that exposes coalition planning or personnel. Candidate indicators: anomalous mailbox access or forwarding rules on official accounts, unauthorized sign-ins to social-media accounts, and RAT behaviour (keylogging, new services or registry changes) on Windows hosts [S5][S10].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track partner-nation and NATO reporting, because the leak shows coalition partners were targeted [S3][S5]. (2) Authorities: the actor is a commercial contractor indicted by DOJ [S6], so coordinate with law-enforcement and intelligence partners before any response actions. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize identity and email hardening for personnel in intelligence-linked roles, given the reported DIA targeting [S6]. (4) Coordination: overlapping vendor names (Houndstooth Typhoon, Charcoal Typhoon, FishMonger, Aquatic Panda) can split reporting. Correlate across names in JCC2 rather than merging them [S1][S8].

identification.summary: HummingBad is an Android malware family that Check Point research says it has tracked since February 2016. It installs a persistent rootkit, generates fraudulent ad revenue and installs additional fraudulent apps [S1][S3]. Check Point tied it to Yingmob, a Beijing-based ad company that also runs a legitimate ad analytics business [S1][S3]. This is a criminal ad-fraud operation, not a state-sponsored APT group; the record's 'group' framing refers to the Yingmob-linked development team [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Check Point tracking from February 2016 per coverage [S3]; public attribution report published mid-2016 [S1][S2]. Lookout dates the related Shedun family to November 2015 [S4][S5].
identification.notes: Naming conflict: Lookout argued HummingBad is Shedun (also called GhostPush, AndroidOS_libskin, right_core) [S4][S5], while ElevenPaths concluded it is a distinct threat [S6]. Cheetah Mobile's 'Hummer' is reported by secondary coverage to be the same malware as HummingBad, based on shared infrastructure and the rooting file right_core.apk [S6]. These vendor cluster boundaries are not merged here. The record's existing '85 million devices' figure describes devices that installed at least one of roughly 200 Yingmob apps, not devices infected with HummingBad; about 10 million devices downloaded a malicious one [S2].

attribution.sponsor: Commercial: Check Point attributes the operation to Yingmob, a Chinese (Beijing) advertising company [S1][S3]. No government sponsorship is asserted in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Check Point presents the Yingmob link as a finding from its research; the sources do not give a formal confidence level [S1][S3].
attribution.basis: Check Point says malware samples led to Yingmob repositories, and that HummingBad shares command-and-control server addresses and enterprise-certificate use with the iOS malware YiSpecter, which it also links to Yingmob [S1][S3]. Check Point describes a 25-person 'Development Team for Overseas Platform' working on several projects [S2].

actors.objectives: Financial: fraudulent ad revenue from fake ad clicks and fraudulent app installs. Check Point estimated more than $300,000 per month, about $3,000 per day from clicks and about $7,500 per day from fraudulent installs [S1][S2]. Check Point also warned that control of the infected devices could be sold or turned to data theft [S1][S3].

regions: China (about 1.6 million devices per Check Point)
India (about 1.35 million devices per Check Point)
targeting.notes: Check Point reports most affected devices in China and India [S2][S3]. Targeting is opportunistic and consumer-focused; no sector-specific or government targeting is stated in the sources gathered. The Check Point report raises, but does not document, a risk of data theft or sale of device access [S1][S3].

capabilities.summary: Check Point describes a staged infection: a first component attempts to gain root access with a rooting exploit, and if that fails a second component shows a fake system update notification to trick the user into granting system-level permissions [S1][S3]. Once established it keeps a persistent rootkit, clicks ads fraudulently and installs additional fraudulent apps [S1][S3]. Lookout notes that the exploits used by related rooting-adware families are not new and have been used by popular rooting tools [S5].

campaigns.summary: Lookout reported the Shedun rooting-adware family in November 2015. Lookout later said HummingBad is another name for Shedun, a claim ElevenPaths disputed [S4][S5][S6].

campaigns.name: Check Point begins tracking HummingBad
campaigns.summary: Coverage of Check Point research says it tracked the HummingBad rootkit and ad-fraud malware from February 2016 [S3].

campaigns.name: Check Point attribution to Yingmob

campaigns.name: Lookout: spike in Shedun, also known as HummingBad
campaigns.summary: Lookout published a blog post describing a rise in Shedun detections and treating HummingBad as the same family [S4]. Secondary coverage reports Cheetah Mobile counting about 1.4 million infections per day in the first half of 2016 for its 'Hummer' trojan [S6].

diamond.adversary: Yingmob, a Beijing ad company with a 25-person overseas-platform development team, per Check Point [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Android rooting exploits, fake system-update prompt, persistent rootkit, fraudulent clicks and installs [S1][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: A control panel referencing about 200 apps, and C2 addresses shared with the iOS malware YiSpecter [S1][S2].
diamond.victim: Android consumers, concentrated in China and India [S2][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Commercial ad-fraud motive inside a legitimate ad-tech business; no state tasking is stated [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Unpatched or rootable Android devices and users who accept fake system update prompts; app distribution through channels that host Yingmob apps [S1][S3].

gaps: I could not open the Check Point blog, the Check Point report PDF, or the news articles with WebFetch (DNS failure in this environment). Details here come from search-result summaries of those pages and need confirmation against the primary documents [S1][S2][S3].
Exact publication dates are month-level for several sources; day-level dates were not confirmed except for the Lookout post (2016-07-07) [S4].

Unresolved vendor disagreement over whether HummingBad is a distinct family (Check Point, ElevenPaths) or Shedun renamed (Lookout); relationship to Cheetah Mobile's Hummer rests on secondary coverage [S4][S6].
No public evidence gathered of state sponsorship, victim data theft, or sale of device access; Check Point's warnings are risk statements [S1][S3].
Activity after 2016, and any Yingmob response or enforcement action, were not found in the sources gathered.
The record has no MITRE ATT&CK group ID; no group mapping was verified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Personal and BYOD Android phones, and unmanaged third-party app stores, are the relevant terrain; the sources show consumer targeting, not defense targeting [S2][S3]. STEP 2: The actor is a commercial ad-fraud operator with a development team, rooting exploits and an app-distribution pipeline; its stated aim is revenue [S1][S2]. STEP 3: The template is a trojanized app, rooting exploit, fake system-update prompt, persistent rootkit, then fraudulent ad and install traffic [S1][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued ad fraud on consumer devices in China and India, with incidental exposure of personnel devices. MDCOA, which the sources raise only as a risk, is Yingmob or a buyer repurposing rooted devices for data theft or as a botnet [S1][S3]. Candidate indicators: rooted or persistently modified Android devices, unexpected fake system update prompts, and unexplained app installs and ad traffic [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat this as a commodity mobile-malware risk to personnel devices, not a tracked state actor; monitor mobile threat defense telemetry for rooting and fake update prompts [S1][S3]. (2) Authorities: mobile device management and BYOD policy, not offensive or defensive cyberspace operations, govern the response. (3) Mission assurance: keep rooted or unmanaged Android devices off sensitive networks and away from official data [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators through normal CTI and mobile-security channels; the family-naming disputes mean indicators should be matched by sample hash, not family name alone [S4][S6].

provenance.importedSummary: We have investigated their intrusions since 2013 and have been battling them nonstop over the last year at several large telecommunications and technology companies. The determination of this China-based adversary is truly impressive: they are like a dog with a bone. HURRICANE PANDA's preferred initial vector of compromise and persistence is a China Chopper webshell – a tiny and easily obfuscated 70 byte text file that consists of an ‘eval()’ command, which is then used to provide full command execution and file upload/download capabilities to the attackers. This script is typically uploaded to a web server via a SQL injection or WebDAV vulnerability, which is often trivial to uncover in a company with a large external web presence. Once inside, the adversary immediately moves on to execution of a credential theft tool such as Mimikatz (repacked to avoid AV detection). If they are lucky to have caught an administrator who might be logged into that web server at the time, they will have gained domain administrator credentials and can now roam your network at will via ‘net use’ and ‘wmic’ commands executed through the webshell terminal.

identification.summary: IcePeony is a China-nexus APT cluster named by the nao_sec research team, described as active since at least 2023 and previously unknown, targeting government agencies, academic institutions and political organizations in India, Mauritius and Vietnam [S1][S3][S4]. It gains access mainly through SQL injection against public-facing web servers, then uses web shells or its custom IIS module backdoor IceCache [S1][S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: At least 2023, per nao_sec as relayed by secondary coverage [S3][S4].
identification.notes: Name coined by nao_sec; no Microsoft name is known from the sources gathered. Malpedia lists related families IceCache and IceEvent [S5]. IceCache is distinct from CrowdStrike's IceApple IIS framework; do not merge the two (search results only noted the similarity of IIS focus) [S2].

attribution.confidence: nao_sec and the secondary coverage describe the group as 'China-nexus'; no government attribution was found in the sources gathered [S3][S4].
attribution.basis: Researcher inference from working-hour patterns (roughly 14 hours of activity per day, no Sunday activity, suggested to match China's '996' IT work schedule) and from victim selection resembling China's maritime strategy interests; secondary coverage presents both as possibilities, not confirmed facts [S2][S3][S4].

actors.objectives: Credential theft from government and related targets appears to be the main goal; researchers suggest the targeting fits Chinese national interests, possibly maritime strategy toward Indian Ocean countries. This is analyst inference, not confirmed [S3][S4].

regions: South and Southeast Asia (government agencies, per Virus Bulletin slide summary)
targeting.notes: nao_sec reportedly saw over 200 attempts against various Indian government websites in the logs it analyzed [S3].

capabilities.summary: Initial access via SQL injection on public-facing web servers, followed by web shells or the custom IIS module IceCache [S1][S3]. The server left as an open directory in early July 2024 exposed Cobalt Strike 4.8, frp, sqlmap, Impacket, reGeorg, suo5, Stowaway and craXcel, plus IceCache client malware and about two weeks of shell command history [S2]. Malpedia associates the families IceCache and IceEvent with the group [S5].

diamond.socioPolitical: Targeting of Indian Ocean and neighboring governments is suggested by researchers to fit Chinese maritime strategy; unconfirmed [S3][S4].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing web servers vulnerable to SQL injection and IIS hosts that can run malicious modules [S2][S3].

gaps: The primary nao_sec post and the Virus Bulletin slides could not be fetched (host unreachable in this environment); facts rely on search-result summaries of them and secondary coverage [S1][S2].
Exact IceCache capabilities (credential theft functionality) were not verified from the primary report.
No sponsor, government attribution or vendor naming (e.g., Microsoft) found; relationship to other China-nexus clusters is unknown.
No reporting found for 2025 or 2026 activity.
Specific victim organizations, CVEs and IOCs not gathered. The 996 and maritime-strategy links are inference only.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing web servers, especially IIS hosts of government and academic sites, are key terrain. STEP 2: The group relies on common tools and SQL injection rather than zero-days, and its operators appear to work a regular schedule, with no Sunday activity reported [S2][S3]. STEP 3: Template is SQL injection, then web shell or IceCache, then credential theft and tunneling (frp, suo5) [S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued credential harvesting against South and Southeast Asian governments. MDCOA is the same web-server access pattern turned against partner-nation or DoD-adjacent sites supporting Indo-Pacific operations. Candidate indicators: unexpected IIS modules, SQL injection attempts against web applications and new web shells [S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track partner-nation government web compromises in the Indo-Pacific as indicators of Chinese collection interest. (2) Authorities: coordination of incident support to partner nations runs through established channels, not unilateral action. (3) Mission assurance: inventory and monitor IIS web servers and registered modules on DoD-connected sites. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partners and the DIB through existing reporting channels.

provenance.importedSummary: IcePeony is a China-nexus APT group that has been active since at least 2023, targeting government agencies, academic institutions, and political organizations in countries such as India, Mauritius, and Vietnam. They primarily employ SQL injection techniques to exploit vulnerabilities in publicly accessible web servers, subsequently installing web shells or executing malware like IceCache to facilitate credential theft. IcePeony operates under harsh work conditions, potentially adhering to the 996 working hour system, and shows a particular interest in the governments of Indian Ocean countries. Their activities suggest alignment with China's national interests, possibly related to maritime strategy.

identification.summary: Long-running cyber-espionage actor tracked as Inception / Inception Framework (Blue Coat, Symantec, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42) and Cloud Atlas (Kaspersky, Check Point, F.A.C.C.T., Positive Technologies) [S1][S2][S4][S5]. It relies on spear-phishing with weaponized Office documents, layered script-based implants and command and control over legitimate cloud services [S1][S3][S5]. In December 2014 Kaspersky assessed that Cloud Atlas represents a rebirth of the RedOctober operation that it exposed in 2013 [S4]. Check Point reported that after February 2022 its targeting narrowed to Russia, Belarus and conflict-affected parts of Ukraine and Moldova [S2], and Kaspersky reported that more than 80% of 2024 VBCloud targets were in Russia [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Active since at least 2014 per Unit 42 [S1] and Symantec, as reported by Security Affairs (since at least May 2014) [S6]. Kaspersky saw the first Cloud Atlas attacks in August 2014 and links the actor to RedOctober, which it exposed in 2013 [S4].
identification.notes: No Microsoft name was identified for this actor in the sources gathered. Brandefense lists the aliases Inception Framework, Blue Odin, Cloud Atlas, Clean Ursa, ATK116, G0100 and OXYGEN [S9]. MITRE tracks it as Inception (G0100) [S10]. Kaspersky's RedOctober link rests on a shared compression method, compiler setup and overlapping targets in Russia, Kazakhstan and Belarus. It is a vendor assessment, not proof of the same operator [S4]. Palo Alto Networks noted in 2014 that both the Inception and Cloud Atlas campaigns used CloudMe for command and control [S5]. Sources disagree on whether Blue Coat or Symantec coined the name 'Inception Framework' [S9].

attribution.confidence: No sponsor was identified in the open sources gathered. The Record's coverage of F.A.C.C.T.'s December 2023 reporting describes the group as state-backed but names no sponsoring country [S7]. Security Affairs, reporting on Symantec and Akamai research, describes Inception as nation-state-backed without naming the state [S6]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Vendor reporting covers tradecraft and targeting but names no sponsoring state [S1][S2][S7]. Since 2022 the targeting has centred on Russia and Belarus [S2][S3]. Kaspersky's RedOctober lineage assessment rests on code and target overlap [S4].

actors.objectives: Strategic intelligence collection against government, diplomatic and strategic-industry targets [S4][S5][S9]. The tooling is built for reconnaissance, system profiling and document theft [S1][S3]. Brandefense characterizes the goal as collection of diplomatic communications, government documents and related research [S9].

sectors: Executives in oil, finance and engineering; military officers; government officials [S5][S9]
Agro-industrial enterprises and state-owned research organizations [S7]
Defense sector (Russia, 2025, per Positive Technologies coverage) [S8]
Energy, defense, aerospace, research and media organizations [S9]
regions: Russia-controlled or contested areas of Ukraine and Moldova (2022) [S2]
Smaller 2024 VBCloud victim sets in Belarus, Canada, Moldova, Israel, Kyrgyzstan, Turkey and Vietnam [S3]
Africa, Europe and the Middle East (Brandefense profile) [S9]
targeting.notes: The 2014 lures referenced diplomatic car sales [S4]. Unit 42 saw the group in 2017 against government targets in Europe, Russia and Central Asia [S1]. Check Point says the post-2022 shift narrowed its scope but did not change its tactics [S2]. The 2023 lures appealed for support to Russian soldiers in the 'special military operation' [S7]. The cross-regional sector list comes from secondary profiles and is not tied to dated campaigns [S9].

capabilities.summary: Initial access is spear-phishing with Word documents. Kaspersky saw a CVE-2012-0158 variant in 2014 [S4]. Later campaigns used remote-template retrieval with Equation Editor exploits CVE-2017-11882 and CVE-2018-0802 [S1][S3][S7]. In 2014 the documents dropped a Visual Basic script that installed the loader and payload rather than writing a PE backdoor to disk [S4]. Command and control ran over CloudMe WebDAV storage [S5]. In 2018 Symantec reported that the group hid its origin behind chains of hijacked UPnP home routers, which needed no custom malware on the routers [S6]. In 2018 Unit 42 named POWERSHOWER, a PowerShell reconnaissance backdoor that cleans up after itself [S1]. Check Point reported a DLL in 2022 that proxies connections through victim machines [S2]. Kaspersky's 2024 reporting describes an HTA-to-VBShower chain that deploys PowerShower (network probing and payload download) and VBCloud (system information and file theft) [S3]. In 2025 Positive Technologies observed several new TLS certificates issued in a single day for fresh infrastructure [S8].

diamond.adversary: Unattributed espionage actor tracked as Inception / Cloud Atlas since 2014. Kaspersky assesses lineage from RedOctober [S1][S4][S7].
diamond.capability: Weaponized Office documents using remote templates and Equation Editor exploits; VBS/HTA loaders; the VBShower, PowerShower/POWERSHOWER and VBCloud implants; a victim-side proxy DLL [S1][S2][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Cloud storage used for C2 (CloudMe WebDAV) [S5]; chains of hijacked UPnP home routers used as proxies [S6]; regularly refreshed domains and TLS certificates [S8].
diamond.victim: Diplomatic, government, defense, research and agro-industrial organizations, now mainly in Russia and Belarus [S2][S3][S4][S7][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Targeting narrowed to Russia, Belarus and contested areas of Ukraine and Moldova after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, which suggests intelligence requirements tied to that conflict [S2]. No sponsoring state is named [S7].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints running Microsoft Office with unpatched Equation Editor; consumer routers exposing UPnP; legitimate cloud storage services [S1][S3][S5][S6].

gaps: No sponsoring state is named in open sources. Neither a government attribution nor a Microsoft name was found.

The primary Kaspersky Securelist reports could not be opened: securelist.com was blocked by the session proxy. Details of the VBCloud report and of the 2025 to early-2026 reports (including the PowerCloud tool) rest on search summaries and secondary coverage.
The original Blue Coat (2014), Symantec (2018) and F.A.C.C.T. (2023) reports were not opened. They are cited through secondary coverage.
Positive Technologies research (2024-2025) on Google Sheets C2 and Yandex.Disk-hosted modules was seen only in Russian-language summaries and has no confirmed date. It is not included as a campaign.
The Akamai 65,000-router UPnProxy botnet is only 'related' to Inception per coverage. Do not attribute the whole botnet to this actor.
Kaspersky's Cloud Atlas-RedOctober linkage and the merging of the Inception and Cloud Atlas vendor clusters are vendor assessments.
Brandefense's sector and region list (Africa, Middle East, aerospace, media) is not tied to dated primary campaign reporting.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The operational environment includes diplomatic, government and defense networks and the cloud-storage and consumer-router infrastructure that the actor abuses for C2 and anonymization [S1][S5][S6]. STEP 2: Legacy Office Equation Editor flaws (CVE-2017-11882, CVE-2018-0802) remain usable years after patching. This shows that unpatched Office clients are the decisive terrain [S1][S3]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template runs from a themed spear-phish to a remote template or Equation Editor exploit, then an HTA/VBS loader (VBShower), then PowerShell reconnaissance (PowerShower), then file theft (VBCloud) over cloud or proxied C2 [S1][S3][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against Russian and Belarusian government, defense and research targets; US and allied equities face spillover risk through the smaller victim sets in other countries [S2][S3][S8]. MDCOA is retasking against diplomatic or coalition entities with geopolitical lures, using residential-router proxy chains to frustrate attribution and blocking [S4][S6]. Candidate indicators: Word documents that fetch remote templates over HTTP; EQNEDT32 spawning mshta or wscript; VBS files with randomized names in user profile directories; outbound WebDAV to cloud storage; PowerShell reconnaissance followed by self-cleanup [S1][S3][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: the current focus is on Russia and Belarus [S2][S3], so this actor is lower priority for DoDIN defense. Track it for retargeting signs, such as lures themed on coalition or diplomatic issues [S4]. (2) Authorities: no sponsoring state is named [S7], so any response beyond network defense needs careful attribution coordination; do not treat vendor lineage claims as government attribution [S4]. (3) Mission assurance: verify that Equation Editor is removed or disabled and that remote-template loading is restricted on mission systems, since the actor reuses years-old exploits [S1][S3]. (4) Coordination: its anonymization relies on consumer UPnP routers and legitimate cloud storage [S5][S6], so takedown or blocking requires coordination with cloud providers and partners rather than simple IP blocking.

identification.summary: IndigoZebra is a suspected Chinese-speaking cyber-espionage group that has targeted Central Asian governments since at least 2014 [S1][S8]. Kaspersky first named it in its Q2 2017 APT Trends report, describing activity against former Soviet republics using Meterpreter, Poison Ivy, xDown and a previously unknown backdoor it called xCaon [S6][S5]. In July 2021 Check Point Research reported a spear-phishing campaign against the Afghan National Security Council that delivered BoxCaon, a new xCaon variant that uses Dropbox for command and control [S1][S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Activity since at least 2014: Check Point found about 30 xCaon samples, the earliest from 2014 [S1][S4]. First public naming was Kaspersky's Q2 2017 APT Trends report (dated 2017-08-08 per Malpedia) [S6][S7].
identification.notes: No Microsoft name for IndigoZebra was found in the searches run for this record (Microsoft's naming mapping could not be opened); the encyclopedia keeps the vendor name IndigoZebra. MITRE tracks the group as G0136 [S8]. Check Point described the 2021 Afghan activity as only 'believed' to be IndigoZebra, based on malware links to the earlier xCaon cluster [S2][S4].

attribution.sponsor: Suspected China-linked. Kaspersky listed IndigoZebra among Chinese-speaking actors [S5][S6], and Check Point called it a Chinese-speaking group [S2]. Check Point named no government sponsor [S2][S4].
attribution.confidence: Vendor assessment only. Kaspersky made no definitive attribution in 2017 [S5]. Check Point's language is 'Chinese-speaking' and 'believed to be' IndigoZebra [S2][S4]. Malpedia's 'Chinese state-sponsored' label is stronger than the primary vendors' wording [S7]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Malware lineage (xCaon to BoxCaon) and code overlap linking the 2021 Afghan intrusions to earlier Central Asian activity [S1][S4]. Kaspersky noted ties to other Chinese-speaking actors in 2017 [S5].

actors.objectives: Political and government espionage against Central Asian states, including Afghanistan's National Security Council and political entities in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan [S1][S3][S4].

targeting.notes: Check Point telemetry showed the HTTP-based xCaon variants mainly targeted political entities in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan [S3]. Check Point said the campaign may extend beyond the three named countries; these were the ones it could confidently tie to the victim list [S2].

capabilities.summary: Kaspersky's 2017 report described a toolset of Meterpreter, Poison Ivy, xDown and the custom xCaon backdoor [S5][S6]. The xCaon family (about 30 samples since 2014) used HTTP for C2 [S1]. BoxCaon, the 2021 variant, uses an attacker-controlled Dropbox account as C2. It creates a unique folder per victim, reads commands from a sub-folder named 'd', and writes results back to Dropbox, so its traffic blends with legitimate HTTPS cloud-storage use [S1][S5]. BoxCaon's features are narrow: file download and upload, command execution, and returning results. That is enough to stage further reconnaissance and lateral-movement tools [S1]. Initial access in 2021 was by spear-phishing that impersonated the Administrative Office of the President of Afghanistan, with a password-protected RAR archive leading to a backdoor dropped as 'spools.exe' [S3][S4]. MITRE lists Poison Ivy, xCaon and BoxCaon as associated software [S8].

campaigns.name: Check Point BoxCaon report

diamond.adversary: Suspected Chinese-speaking espionage operators; government sponsorship not confirmed by the reporting vendors [S2][S4][S5].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing with government-impersonation lures and password-protected RAR archives; custom xCaon/BoxCaon backdoors; commodity Poison Ivy, Meterpreter and xDown [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: HTTP C2 for older xCaon variants; attacker-controlled Dropbox account with a per-victim folder structure for BoxCaon [S1][S5].
diamond.victim: Afghan National Security Council; government and political entities in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan; former Soviet republics more broadly [S1][S2][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection on Central Asian governments [S1][S4].
diamond.technology: Abuse of trusted cloud storage (Dropbox) as C2, and trust in inter-agency email from senior government offices [S1][S3].

gaps: The Check Point Research report, Check Point blog, Kaspersky Securelist report and MITRE page could not be fetched in this session (network errors). Facts are drawn from search-result excerpts and secondary coverage of those documents and should be verified against the originals.
No Microsoft name was confirmed; Microsoft's MicrosoftMapping.json could not be accessed.
No public reporting after 2021 was found; current activity status is unknown.
No government attribution or indictment was found. Malpedia's 'state-sponsored' label goes beyond what Kaspersky and Check Point state.
Whether the 2021 intrusions succeeded in exfiltrating data, and the full victim set beyond Afghanistan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, are not public in the sources gathered.
Specific IOCs (Dropbox tokens, domains, hashes) were not retrieved; secondary claims about a hardcoded bearer token were not verified against Check Point.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Relevant terrain is the email and cloud-storage traffic of Central Asian partner governments' national security and presidential offices, plus coalition personnel who exchange mail with them [S1][S4]. STEP 2: Allowed cloud-storage services (Dropbox) give the actor C2 that blends into normal HTTPS. Long-running custom tooling since 2014 shows patience and persistence [S1]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is a spear-phish impersonating a senior government office, then a password-protected RAR, then the xCaon/BoxCaon backdoor, then Dropbox-based tasking, then follow-on reconnaissance tools [S1][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection on Central Asian government policy and security deliberations through impersonation phishing. MDCOA is use of a compromised partner-government mailbox to phish US or coalition personnel working regional security issues, giving access to shared planning data; this is an extrapolation, not observed. Candidate indicators: password-protected RAR attachments claiming senior-office origin, endpoints making Dropbox API calls with no sanctioned Dropbox use, and a new 'spools.exe' or similar look-alike system binary [S1][S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: flag Dropbox and other cloud-storage API traffic from mission and partner-liaison enclaves, because BoxCaon C2 resembles legitimate use [S1]. (2) Authorities: activity is vendor-attributed only, so treat it as a suspected PRC-linked espionage threat and avoid overstating government attribution in products [S2][S4]. (3) Mission assurance: harden email trust paths with Central Asian partner governments, since lures impersonated a presidential office [S3]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partner-nation CERTs in Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and the region, and with commercial vendors, because public reporting has been sparse since 2021.

identification.summary: The Infrastructure Destruction Squad is a Telegram-based threat actor brand that KELA describes as presenting itself as politically motivated but appearing largely profit-driven, active since at least June 2025, centered on selling access and developing Malware-as-a-Service offerings [S1]. Malpedia lists Dark Engine as an alias and describes ICS/SCADA-targeted incidents with a surge in June 2025 [S2]. The group has stated that Dark Engine is a separate organization linked to its channel only through 'friends' [S1].
identification.notes: The group posts in English, Russian and Chinese and says its members are mostly in China with others in Russia, Belarus and the United States (self-described, per KELA) [S1]. The existing encyclopedia record lists country RU; no reviewed source supports that and it conflicts with the group's self-description [S1]. Not to be confused with the 2023 Cyber Anarchy Squad (separate Ukrainian-aligned group) [S1].

attribution.basis: No reviewed source attributes the group to a state sponsor. KELA assesses it as appearing largely profit-driven despite political framing [S1]. Member nationality claims are self-reported [S1].

actors.objectives: KELA assesses the brand is largely profit-driven, selling access and developing MaaS products, despite a politically motivated presentation [S1]. Claimed intrusions also serve publicity: its Venice post said it was 'simply here to deliver a message' [S4].

sectors: Industrial control systems / SCADA (metallurgy, food processing) [S2]
targeting.notes: All infrastructure intrusions are self-reported claims on Telegram; independent confirmation was not found [S4][S5].

capabilities.summary: KELA reports the group's best-known product is the BLACKNET-00 ransomware builder, first offered for sale in April 2026 at a $300 price point [S1]. The channel advertises a 'TRK25 Advanced SCADA' scanning tool for sale and a claimed 'VoltRuptor ICS' tool for sabotaging control devices [S5]. A claimed French hydro intrusion reportedly used an exposed VNC service [S5]. Malpedia also ties the alias to a fake-CAPTCHA/SEO-poisoning WordPress credential-harvesting campaign [S2]; this link is unverified here.

identification.summary: Infy, also called Prince of Persia, is a long-running Iranian-linked espionage group named by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 in 2016 after a malware family called Infy [S5]. Unit 42 traced the operation back about a decade, and SafeBreach later dated activity to 2007 [S5][S1]. The group went quiet publicly after the 2016 takedown, returned in 2017 with a new malware family called Foudre [S7], and was reported as still active in late 2025 and early 2026 [S1][S3][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Unit 42 (2016) described a campaign running for about a decade [S5]. A secondary summary of SafeBreach research says activity was traced to 2007 [S1]; accounts of the start date differ across vendors.
identification.notes: Aliases seen in sources: Prince of Persia, Foudre (malware family, also used as a group label), Operation Mermaid, APT-C-07 [S2]. Foudre is the downloader and victim profiler; Tonnerre is the second-stage implant [S2]. Microsoft has no mapped name for this group in this record; msName is empty. Not to be confused with other Iranian clusters tracked by Microsoft.

attribution.sponsor: Iran. SafeBreach assesses the group is a state-sponsored actor operated by the Iranian regime [S4]. Unit 42 attributed it to Iran on infrastructure grounds [S5].
attribution.confidence: SafeBreach calls the evidence solid proof of state sponsorship, based on C2 maintenance stopping during Iran's January 2026 national internet shutdown [S4]. This is vendor assessment only; no government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Unit 42 observed numerous Iranian domains on IP addresses neighboring known C2 servers, suggesting a possible Iranian hosting reseller [S5]. About one third of victims in the 2016 sinkhole data were in Iran [S6]. C2 maintenance stopped on 2026-01-08 when Iran imposed a nationwide internet shutdown, and resumed shortly before restrictions eased [S4].

actors.objectives: Long-term surveillance and intelligence collection on individuals, including dissidents and academics, per SafeBreach [S2]. Unit 42 described targeting of governments and businesses of multiple nations as well as Iranian citizens [S5].

capabilities.summary: Custom malware lineage: Infy and Infy M (2016) [S5], Foudre (reported 2017, with anti-takeover features to prevent C2 sinkholing) [S7], and Tonnerre second stage [S2]. SafeBreach reported Foudre v34 and Tonnerre v12-18 and v50 builds, with Tonnerre v50 detected in September 2025 [S4]. C2 uses a domain generation algorithm; Tonnerre v50 redirects to a Telegram group and bot, the first Telegram use since 2016, likely replacing FTP exfiltration [S4]. A variant called Tornado v51 supports HTTP and Telegram C2 and generates domains via a new DGA and via fixed names decoded from blockchain data; it is dropped using a one-day WinRAR flaw (likely CVE-2025-8088 or CVE-2025-6218) that places it in the startup folder [S3]. Foudre is believed distributed via phishing email [S2].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the individual endpoint and personal communications, especially Windows systems used by dissidents, academics and diaspora, plus Telegram as a C2 channel [S2][S4]. STEP 2: The actor is selective and long-lived, rebuilds after exposure, and is tied to Iranian national network conditions [S4][S7]. STEP 3: Template is phishing or a booby-trapped archive exploiting a recent WinRAR flaw, Foudre profiling, then Tonnerre or Tornado collection and exfiltration over FTP or Telegram, with DGA C2 [S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-volume surveillance of individuals, with rapid C2 rotation after any public exposure [S3][S4]. MDCOA is expansion to US or coalition-linked personnel or contractors using the same delivery chain. Candidate indicators: Telegram bot traffic from non-messaging hosts, DGA-pattern domain lookups, files extracted by WinRAR into startup folders, and Foudre/Tonnerre artifacts [S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor reporting for new Foudre/Tonnerre/Tornado versions; activity correlates with Iranian national internet status, which may serve as an indicator of state tasking [S4]. (2) Authorities: this actor mainly targets individuals, so defensive action on personal devices is outside DoD authority; coordinate with law enforcement and the intelligence community for any DoD-affiliated victims. (3) Mission assurance: patch WinRAR and similar archive tools and control Telegram egress on government networks [S3][S4]. (4) Coordination: share DGA and C2 indicators with DC3 and partners; note that the actor rebuilt infrastructure after exposure, so indicators age quickly [S4][S7].
