provenance.importedSummary: Infy is a group of suspected Iranian origin. Since early 2013, we have observed activity from a unique threat actor group, which we began to investigate based on increased activities against human right activists in the beginning of 2015. In line5with other research on the campaign, released prior to publication of this document, we have adopted the name “Infy”, which is based on labels used in the infrastructure and its two families of malware agents. Thanks to information we have been able to collect during the course of our research, such as characteristics of the group’s malware and development cycle, our research strongly supports the claim that the Infy group is of Iranian origin and potentially connected to the Iranian state. Amongst a backdrop of other incidents, Infy became one of the most frequently observed agents for attempted malware attacks against Iranian civil society beginning in late 2014, growing in use up to the February 2016 parliamentary election in Iran. After the conclusion of the parliamentary election, the rate of attempted intrusions and new compromises through the Infy agent slowed, but did not end. The trends witnessed in reports from recipients are reinforced through telemetry provided by design failures in more recent versions of the Infy malware.

identification.summary: IronHusky is a Kaspersky-named, Chinese-speaking espionage actor that Kaspersky says has operated since at least 2017 [S1][S5]. Kaspersky linked it to the MysterySnail remote access trojan (RAT) in 2021, when MysterySnail was found alongside the Windows zero-day CVE-2021-40449 [S2][S3]. In 2025 Kaspersky reported a new MysterySnail version against government organizations in Mongolia and Russia [S1][S5].
identification.firstObserved: At least 2017 per Kaspersky [S1][S5]. CSO reports that older China-based infrastructure reused by MysterySnail goes back to 2012 [S3].
identification.notes: No Microsoft name is mapped in this record. No alias is stated in the sources gathered. Secondary coverage gives different start dates (2012 versus 2017), which come from separate claims: 2017 is the group's activity and 2012 is reused C2 infrastructure [S3][S7].

attribution.confidence: Kaspersky describes IronHusky as a Chinese-speaking threat actor [S1][S5]. Kaspersky tied MysterySnail to IronHusky because early variants showed code and functionality overlap with IronHusky-attributed malware and reused C2 addresses of the Chinese-speaking actor dating back to 2012 [S3][S7]. This is a vendor assessment; no government attribution or state sponsor was found.
attribution.basis: Malware code overlap and reused C2 infrastructure reported by Kaspersky [S3][S7].

actors.objectives: Kaspersky-derived coverage describes the activity as espionage against IT companies, defense contractors, diplomatic entities and government organizations [S3][S5][S7].

sectors: Aviation and research institutes (per the imported record, not independently confirmed)
targeting.notes: The 2021 MysterySnail activity hit IT companies, defense contractors and diplomatic entities [S3][S7]. In 2025 the targets were government organizations in Mongolia and Russia [S1][S5]. Only Windows Server systems were observed attacked with the 2021 exploit [S7].

capabilities.summary: The 2021 intrusions used an elevation-of-privilege exploit for CVE-2021-40449, a use-after-free in the Win32k driver, fixed by Microsoft on 12 October 2021; it was deployed against Windows servers in late August and early September 2021 [S7]. The payload was the MysterySnail RAT, which collects system information and contacts a C2 server for further commands [S7]. The 2025 version is delivered through a malicious MMC script disguised as a document from Mongolia's National Land Agency (ALAMGAC); the script downloads a ZIP second stage and a decoy DOCX, and sets persistence through registry changes [S5]. The updated RAT supports almost 40 commands, and a lighter variant, MysteryMonoSnail, supports 13 commands and uses WebSocket for C2 [S5][S6]. C2 uses public file storage and the piping-server project [S5]. Earlier reporting says the group used common Chinese-speaking tools such as PlugX and PoisonIvy [S3].

diamond.infrastructure: C2 addresses reused from older Chinese-speaking activity dating to 2012; public file storage and piping-server project in 2025; WebSocket C2 for MysteryMonoSnail [S3][S5][S7].
diamond.victim: Government, military/defense contractor, IT and diplomatic entities in Mongolia and Russia [S3][S5].

The original Kaspersky/Securelist articles (2021 and 2025) could not be opened (fetch failed); details come from search-result summaries and secondary coverage and should be verified against the primary text.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Windows Server hosts at IT firms, defense contractors and diplomatic entities, and government endpoints that open official-looking documents, are the exposed terrain [S5][S7]. STEP 2: The actor has persisted across at least 2017 to 2025 with rebuilt tooling after reporting, so expect re-tooling rather than disappearance [S1][S5]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is zero-day or script-based delivery, then MysterySnail RAT with public-service C2 [S5][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against Mongolian and Russian government targets. MDCOA is use of a new privilege-escalation zero-day against Windows servers of defense or IT suppliers. Candidate indicators: unexpected MMC (.msc) script execution from downloads, new registry persistence keys, outbound connections to public file-storage services or piping-server hosts, and WebSocket C2 from servers [S5][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Kaspersky and Microsoft reporting on Win32k and similar server privilege-escalation flaws; patch timelines matter because the 2021 exploit preceded the patch [S7]. (2) Authorities: this record shows no US-specific victims, so relevance is as a partner-region and supplier-risk indicator; confirm reporting and sharing authorities before any action. (3) Mission assurance: harden Windows Server and restrict MMC script execution for document-style lures [S5]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with contractor and partner networks through established DIB channels.

Since their initial attacks ceased in 2018, they have been working on a new remote access trojan dubbed MysterySnail.

identification.summary: North Korean state-sponsored actor focused on stealing cryptocurrency, usually by socially engineering developers and staff at blockchain firms and their vendors [S1][S3]. US government advisories track the same activity as TraderTraitor [S1][S3][S5]. In July 2023 GitHub, which Microsoft owns, named Jade Sleet as the actor behind a social-engineering campaign that used repository invitations and malicious npm dependencies [S1][S2]. The FBI has tied TraderTraitor to the theft of about $308 million from DMM Bitcoin in 2024 and about $1.5 billion from Bybit in February 2025 [S5][S6]. Reporting in 2026 links the actor to the KelpDAO/LayerZero bridge exploit and to an intrusion at an India-based IT services firm that used macOS backdoors [S9][S10][S12].
identification.firstObserved: US advisory AA22-108A (April 2022) describes TraderTraitor activity since at least 2020 [S3]. The Microsoft/GitHub public naming of Jade Sleet dates to July 2023 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Jade Sleet (in-development name Storm-0954). Microsoft's naming map lists LABYRINTH CHOLLIMA (CrowdStrike) as an alias [S13]. GitHub equated Jade Sleet with CISA's TraderTraitor [S1]. FBI statements on the DMM Bitcoin and Bybit thefts list Jade Sleet, UNC4899 and Slow Pisces as other names for TraderTraitor [S5][S6]. Mandiant says UNC4899 likely corresponds to TraderTraitor [S4]. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 tracks the activity as Slow Pisces [S8]. AA22-108A groups TraderTraitor under the broader Lazarus Group / APT38 / BlueNoroff umbrella [S3]. Keep that umbrella separate from this specific cluster. MITRE ATT&CK has no Group ID assigned in this record.

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea. Mandiant assesses UNC4899 as a cryptocurrency-focused element within the DPRK Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB) [S4].
attribution.confidence: The FBI publicly attributed the Bybit theft (2025-02-26 PSA) and the DMM Bitcoin theft (December 2024, with DC3 and Japan's National Police Agency) to TraderTraitor, i.e. to North Korea [S5][S6]. Mandiant assesses with high confidence that UNC4899 is an RGB element, and assesses that UNC4899 'likely' corresponds to TraderTraitor [S4]. In coverage of the LayerZero incident report, Mandiant and CrowdStrike attribute the KelpDAO operation to TraderTraitor/UNC4899 [S10]. GitHub attributed the July 2023 campaign to Jade Sleet [S1].
attribution.basis: Joint FBI/CISA/Treasury advisory AA22-108A [S3]. FBI attributions of specific thefts [S5][S6]. Mandiant incident response, including an OPSEC slip in which UNC4899 connected directly from a Pyongyang netblock during the JumpCloud intrusion [S4]. GitHub/Microsoft telemetry [S1]. Vendor reporting from Unit 42, Safe{Wallet}/Mandiant and LayerZero [S7][S8][S10].

actors.objectives: Revenue generation for the DPRK state through theft of cryptocurrency from exchanges, DeFi protocols, wallet and custody providers, and individuals [S3][S5][S6]. The actor also gains access to software and service providers so it can compromise their downstream cryptocurrency customers [S4][S7].

sectors: Cryptocurrency wallet and custody software providers [S5][S7]
Play-to-earn gaming and crypto-focused venture capital [S3]
Identity/SaaS service providers used as supply-chain pivots [S4]
IT services, DevOps and fintech personnel [S12]
targeting.notes: The actor targets people more than perimeter devices. Developers, DevOps engineers and executives at crypto firms or their suppliers are approached through fake recruiter or developer personas on LinkedIn, GitHub, Slack and Telegram [S1][S2][S5][S8][S12]. GitHub said most targets were connected to blockchain, cryptocurrency or online gambling, with a few in cybersecurity [S1].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering through fake recruiters and developers, using job-interview 'coding challenges' and repository invitations. These lead victims to clone and run trojanized projects or malicious npm dependencies [S1][S2][S5][S8]. AA22-108A describes trojanized cryptocurrency applications for Windows and macOS [S3]. The actor runs supply-chain operations: it compromised JumpCloud's commands framework to reach downstream customers [S4], and it compromised a Safe{Wallet} developer laptop, hijacking AWS session tokens to bypass MFA and tamper with front-end JavaScript that Bybit signers used [S7]. Unit 42 documents gated, in-memory payload delivery (RN Loader, RN Stealer) that steals SSH keys and AWS, Kubernetes and Google Cloud configuration files from macOS hosts [S8]. Mandiant observed macOS keychain theft and persistence through backdoors and plist files within 24 hours of access [S4]. In 2026 the actor used a booby-trapped Terraform project with typosquatted provider registries, plus Rust macOS backdoors: FLATROOF (Telegram exfiltration) and ROOFDECK (Nostr-relay C2) [S12]. It also manipulated RPC responses and ran DDoS against healthy nodes to defeat a bridge verifier [S10]. After thefts, the actor quickly launders funds across thousands of addresses and multiple blockchains [S6].

diamond.adversary: DPRK RGB-linked crypto-theft cluster (Jade Sleet / TraderTraitor / UNC4899 / Slow Pisces) [S1][S4][S5][S8].
diamond.capability: Recruiter and coding-challenge lures; trojanized repositories and npm packages; supply-chain compromise of SaaS and wallet providers; macOS stealers and backdoors (RN Loader, RN Stealer, FLATROOF, ROOFDECK); cloud session-token theft [S1][S4][S7][S8][S12].
diamond.infrastructure: Fake personas on LinkedIn, GitHub, Slack and Telegram; GitHub-hosted repositories; ORB proxy infrastructure (one direct connection from Pyongyang observed); typosquatted HashiCorp registries; Telegram and Nostr relays for C2 and exfiltration [S1][S4][S8][S12].
diamond.victim: Developers, DevOps staff and executives at crypto exchanges, DeFi/bridge protocols, wallet providers, and their IT and SaaS suppliers in the US, Japan, India and elsewhere [S1][S4][S5][S6][S12].
diamond.socioPolitical: Sanctions-evading revenue generation for the DPRK regime [S3][S6].
diamond.technology: Developer workstations (often macOS), package managers, CI/IaC tooling, cloud consoles and multisig signing front ends [S4][S7][S8][S12].

gaps: No Microsoft Threat Intelligence profile of Jade Sleet was found in the searches. The Microsoft-side description comes from GitHub's July 2023 post, and that post was not fetched directly (github.blog was unreachable); content comes from search summaries and SecurityWeek coverage [S1][S2].

Primary US government documents (AA22-108A, the FBI PSA on Bybit, the FBI/NPA statement on DMM Bitcoin) could not be opened. Their content here comes from search summaries and press coverage [S3][S5][S6].

The Microsoft naming map links LABYRINTH CHOLLIMA (CrowdStrike) to Jade Sleet [S13], but no CrowdStrike source was found confirming this mapping or naming the CrowdStrike designation used for Bybit or KelpDAO. Treat the CrowdStrike alias as unverified.

Mandiant hedges the UNC4899 = TraderTraitor equivalence as 'likely' [S4]. FBI statements treat Jade Sleet, UNC4899 and Slow Pisces as the same cluster [S5][S6]. Cluster boundaries may still differ between vendors.
Relationship to the broader Lazarus/APT38/BlueNoroff umbrella and to other Microsoft Sleet actors (e.g., Sapphire Sleet, Citrine Sleet, Moonstone Sleet) is not resolved in the sources gathered.

SentinelOne's original 2026 report on FLATROOF/ROOFDECK and LayerZero's primary incident report were not opened. Details come from the CSA research note and The Defiant [S10][S12]; the FLATROOF/ROOFDECK details were not corroborated in fact-check searches.
No MITRE ATT&CK Group ID is recorded for this cluster.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): The relevant cyberspace terrain is the people layer (developers, DevOps engineers, executives) and the developer toolchain: GitHub, npm, Terraform/IaC registries, cloud session tokens and SaaS administration frameworks. Perimeter devices matter less [S1][S4][S7][S12]. STEP 2 (effects): Any DoD or DIB element with cryptocurrency, fintech, or third-party SaaS and identity dependencies inherits risk from supplier compromise. JumpCloud and Safe{Wallet} show one supplier compromise reaching many downstream victims [S4][S7]. STEP 3 (threat evaluation): The template is recruiter or developer persona, then trojanized repository or coding challenge, then macOS stealer or backdoor, then theft of cloud and SSH credentials, then supply-chain pivot or direct asset theft, then rapid multi-chain laundering [S4][S6][S8][S12]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued job-lure targeting of crypto, fintech and DevOps staff to fund the DPRK [S8]. MDCOA is applying the same developer-workstation and SaaS supply-chain tradecraft to an identity or IT provider serving defense customers; JumpCloud is the precedent [S4]. Candidate indicators: unsolicited 'coding test' repositories run on corporate hosts; unexpected npm or Terraform provider sources and typosquatted registries; Telegram or Nostr-relay traffic from developer Macs; anomalous use of cloud session tokens; SaaS command or agent frameworks executing unfamiliar scripts [S1][S4][S8][S12].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Track supplier and SaaS compromise reporting, plus FBI attributions of crypto thefts, as early warning of the actor's current tradecraft. Its supply-chain intrusions reach downstream customers within days [S4][S6]. (2) Authorities: The activity sits largely in private-sector and FBI law-enforcement lanes [S5][S6]. DoD roles are mostly defending its own networks and supporting partners, so coordinate through the appropriate interagency channels. (3) Mission assurance: Developer and DevOps workstations, IaC pipelines and identity platforms should be treated as mission-relevant terrain. Brief cleared personnel on fake recruiter and coding-test lures [S8][S12]. (4) Coordination: Share indicators with DC3 and DIB partners; DC3 joined the DMM Bitcoin attribution [S5]. Expect vendor names (Jade Sleet, TraderTraitor, UNC4899, Slow Pisces) to differ across reports [S5][S6].

identification.summary: Jasper Sleet is Microsoft's name for North Korea's remote IT worker activity. Microsoft says the workers are mainly focused on making money for the North Korean government [S1]. Operatives use stolen, rented or fabricated identities to get hired into remote IT, software and web development roles. Once hired, they collect salaries that are laundered back to the DPRK and at times steal data or extort their employers [S1]. Microsoft says the workers have used AI since 2024 to scale the operation, and it describes AI use at every stage: getting hired, staying hired and misusing access [S1][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft says it has tracked this global operation since at least early 2020 [S1]. The January 2025 DOJ indictment that Microsoft cites describes fraudulent work from 2018 to 2024 [S1][S6].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Jasper Sleet, formerly tracked as Storm-0287 [S1][S2]. Microsoft tracks other North Korean clusters that use similar fraudulent-employment techniques separately, including Storm-1877 and Moonstone Sleet [S1]. Microsoft has since renamed Storm-1877 to Coral Sleet [S2][S4]. Microsoft's naming mapping lists no other-vendor aliases for Jasper Sleet [S2]. US DOJ actions against the DPRK IT worker scheme do not use Microsoft's cluster names [S5][S6][S7].

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea). Microsoft says the remote IT workers generate revenue for the North Korean government and likely fall under a particular leadership structure in North Korea [S1].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributes the activity to North Korea and attributed at least one 2025 incident response case to Jasper Sleet [S1][S3]. The US government attributes the broader remote IT worker scheme to the DPRK through indictments and guilty pleas, but it does not use the name Jasper Sleet [S5][S6][S7].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and machine-learning detection of suspect accounts. Microsoft also found a public repository in October 2024 that held suspected workers' photos, resumes, accounts and payment-tracking records [S1]. Microsoft's Incident Response team (DART) investigated a case involving PiKVM devices [S3]. Microsoft also cites DOJ indictments [S1][S6].

actors.objectives: The primary objective is to generate revenue for the DPRK, which Microsoft says violates international sanctions [S1]. Secondary objectives are stealing intellectual property, source code and trade secrets, and extorting employers by threatening to release stolen data [S1]. Microsoft's incident response reporting also cites deploying malicious tools and sending profits to state programs [S3]. In a related DOJ case, workers in the scheme reached ITAR-controlled data at a California defense contractor [S8].

sectors: Information technology and software development (remote roles)
Fortune 500 companies (via staffing and contracting firms)
Defense industrial base (ITAR data exposure in a DOJ case)
regions: Global; Microsoft says targeting has broadened to various industries worldwide [S1]
targeting.notes: The historic focus on US technology, critical manufacturing and transportation companies, and the shift to global targeting, come from Microsoft [S1]. The targeted roles are IT, software development, web development and administrator jobs [S1]. Microsoft says the workers are most often located in North Korea, China and Russia [S1]. The defense-contractor ITAR exposure comes from DOJ case reporting that does not name Jasper Sleet [S8].

capabilities.summary: Identity fraud: personas are stolen, rented from willing people or bought from fraud services, then matched to the target's location. The workers back them with email, GitHub, LinkedIn and freelance-site profiles [S1]. AI: Faceswap is used to place operatives' faces onto stolen ID documents and headshots, and voice-changing software is used in interviews [S1][S4]. Generative AI is used to analyze job postings, build culturally fitting names, polish resumes and keep up job performance [S4]. Facilitators validate identities, open accounts, receive company laptops and run laptop farms [S1]. Remote access: IP-based KVM devices (PiKVM, TinyPilot) and RMM tools (JumpConnect, RustDesk, TeamViewer, AnyViewer, AnyDesk) [S1]. Microsoft DART observed PiKVM used as an out-of-band channel that bypassed EDR and exfiltrated data [S3]. Evasion: VPNs (notably Astrill VPN), VPSs and proxies; workers also avoid turning on cameras [S1].

campaigns.name: Microsoft begins tracking the remote IT worker operation
campaigns.summary: Microsoft says it has tracked the global operation since at least early 2020. US government reporting it cites found more than 300 US companies unknowingly employed these workers between 2020 and 2022.

campaigns.name: Public repository exposure
campaigns.summary: Microsoft found a public repository with photos of suspected workers, resumes, email accounts, wallet information and payment-tracking sheets.

campaigns.name: DOJ indictment of Jin Sung-Il, Pak Jin-Song and three facilitators
campaigns.summary: Two North Korean nationals and three facilitators were charged over work obtained from at least 64 US companies between 2018 and 2024. Payments from ten of those companies totaled at least $866,255. Microsoft cites this case in its Jasper Sleet reporting.

campaigns.name: Microsoft disruption and DOJ coordinated nationwide actions
campaigns.summary: Microsoft published its Jasper Sleet profile and suspended 3,000 known Outlook/Hotmail accounts created by North Korean IT workers. The same day, DOJ announced an arrest, two indictments, searches of 29 suspected laptop farms in 16 states, and seizures of 29 financial accounts and 21 websites. DOJ says the schemes involved more than 100 US companies. The DOJ materials do not use the Jasper Sleet name.

campaigns.name: Five facilitators plead guilty
campaigns.summary: DOJ announced guilty pleas from five facilitators in schemes that affected more than 136 US companies and generated over $2.2 million for the DPRK. The cluster is not named.

campaigns.name: DART PiKVM incident response
campaigns.summary: Microsoft DART traced four compromised accounts that connected PiKVM devices to employer workstations, which led to data exfiltration, to Jasper Sleet.

campaigns.name: AI-as-tradecraft reporting
campaigns.summary: Microsoft describes Jasper Sleet using AI across the lifecycle to get hired, stay hired and misuse access. Microsoft says it has disrupted thousands of accounts linked to fraudulent IT worker activity.

diamond.adversary: DPRK remote IT workers, most often located in North Korea, China and Russia, supported by willing facilitators in the US and elsewhere [S1][S5].
diamond.capability: Identity fraud enhanced by AI (Faceswap, voice changers, generative AI for resumes and job analysis); facilitator-run laptop farms; KVM devices and RMM tools; data theft and extortion [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Facilitator-hosted company laptops; PiKVM and TinyPilot devices; Astrill VPN, VPSs and proxies; consumer Outlook/Hotmail accounts; GitHub, LinkedIn and freelance profiles; and facilitator bank accounts used for laundering [S1][S3].
diamond.victim: Organizations hiring remote IT and software staff. The historic focus was US technology, critical manufacturing and transportation, and targeting has since gone global [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Sanctions evasion and revenue generation for the DPRK government [S1].
diamond.technology: Remote-hiring and onboarding processes, staffing and contracting intermediaries, and the legitimate credentials issued to new hires [S1][S3][S4].

gaps: No MITRE ATT&CK group ID is recorded for Jasper Sleet, and Microsoft's naming mapping lists no other-vendor aliases [S2]. Mappings to other vendors' DPRK IT worker clusters were not confirmed by any cited source, so none are added.

Cluster boundaries are unclear. Microsoft says Storm-1877 (now Coral Sleet) and Moonstone Sleet use similar fraudulent-employment techniques, but it does not publicly explain how it separates them from Jasper Sleet [S1][S4].
The DOJ indictments and pleas cover the DPRK IT worker scheme but do not use Microsoft's names. Which defendants map to Jasper Sleet rather than other clusters is not established [S5][S6][S7].

Date discrepancy: Microsoft dates the indictment of two North Korean nationals and three facilitators to January 3, 2025, while press coverage reported the announcement on January 23-24, 2025 [S1][S6].
The DOJ primary documents on justice.gov could not be opened. Details come from search summaries and press coverage [S5][S6][S7][S8].
The total number of operatives, total revenue attributable to Jasper Sleet, and victim identities in the PiKVM incident are not public [S1][S3].

The publication date of Microsoft's 'Imposter for hire' post (S3), given here as December 11, 2025, could not be confirmed from search results; the post's content (four accounts tied to PiKVM devices, traced to Jasper Sleet) was confirmed [S3].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the hiring and onboarding pipeline (staffing firms, contractors, freelance platforms), identity systems (Entra ID) and remote-access paths into developer and administrator workstations [S1][S3]. STEP 2: Remote work and contractor-heavy staffing at DIB and IT support providers widen the attack surface. Insider-type access bypasses perimeter defenses, and KVM hardware bypasses EDR [S1][S3][S8]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is fabricated persona, AI-assisted interview, hire, facilitator laptop farm with KVM or RMM, and long-term access. Payroll is laundered to the DPRK, with optional data theft or extortion [S1][S4]. STEP 4: The MLCOA is revenue generation from remote IT jobs at US and allied firms [S1]. The MDCOA is a placed worker at a defense contractor or DoD IT provider stealing ITAR or source-code data, or handing access to other DPRK operators [S1][S3][S8]. Candidate indicators: impossible or atypical travel sign-ins involving China or Russia; Astrill VPN egress; unsanctioned RMM tools (AnyDesk, RustDesk, TeamViewer); PiKVM or TinyPilot devices on endpoints; new hires who avoid cameras; and personas reused across employers [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: combine HR and contractor-vetting data with identity telemetry, such as Microsoft's 'Sign-in activity by a suspected North Korean entity Jasper Sleet' alert, so insider-risk cases appear in the cyber picture [S1][S4]. (2) Authorities: most activity is fraud and sanctions evasion handled by DOJ and FBI. Any cyber response on contractor networks requires law enforcement and counterintelligence coordination, and Microsoft advises not tipping off suspects [S1][S5]. (3) Mission assurance: enforce least privilege and RMM and KVM controls for remote developers and administrators on DoD-adjacent contracts, because an ITAR exposure has already occurred [S1][S3][S8]. (4) Coordination: work with DC3, the DIB CS program and staffing vendors on identity verification and on sharing persona indicators.

identification.summary: JINX-0164 is a name used by Wiz Research for a financially motivated cluster, disclosed in late May 2026, that targets cryptocurrency organizations and software developers, almost entirely on macOS [S5][S7]. Intrusions start with fake recruiter approaches on LinkedIn that steer victims to a fake video-conferencing page, which delivers the AUDIOFIX Python infostealer/RAT; the actor then moves from developer laptops into code repositories and CI/CD pipelines [S5][S6][S7]. In April 2026 it trojanized version 9.4.1 of the npm package @velora-dex/sdk to deliver the MINIRAT Go backdoor [S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: Activity dates to at least mid-2025 per Wiz [S5][S7]. Public disclosure: Wiz, late May 2026 [S5][S7].
identification.notes: JINX-0164 is a Wiz-assigned cluster name, not a Microsoft name; no Microsoft actor name or MITRE group was found in the sources gathered. The trojanized npm version is 9.4.1 (published 2026-04-07; clean baseline 9.4.0; reverted in 9.4.2 about three hours later per SafeDep/OpenSourceMalware); one secondary outlet's '4.9.1' is a typo [S6]. Wiz is reported as noting consistency with DPRK financially motivated groups without confirmed overlap or formal attribution (see attribution).

attribution.confidence: Wiz tracks the cluster as financially motivated and, as reported by secondary outlets, has not formally attributed it to a state actor, though it notes consistency with DPRK financially motivated groups [S5][S7]. This record's imported country field (KP) is not supported by a primary source gathered here.
attribution.basis: Per secondary coverage, Wiz assesses the activity as consistent with North Korean financially motivated groups (BlueNoroff, Contagious Interview, UNC1069/Sapphire Sleet) but with distinct infrastructure and no confirmed overlap; it has not formally attributed the cluster to DPRK [S5][S7]. A Cloud Security Alliance research note is reported as saying the actor does not appear to operate at the scale of large North Korea-linked crypto thefts while using similar foundational techniques [S3]. These are technique-level similarities, not attribution.

actors.objectives: Financial gain: theft of cryptocurrency and wallet credentials from developers, plus access to code and CI/CD systems at crypto firms for follow-on compromise [S5][S7].

targeting.notes: Targeting is by role and sector (macOS-using developers at crypto organizations) rather than by geography; regions not stated in the sources gathered [S5][S7].

capabilities.summary: Credible LinkedIn recruiter personas and fake meeting pages spoofing Teams-style conferencing; a shell script that profiles the system and fetches payloads from a fake driver-store domain; AUDIOFIX (Python macOS infostealer/RAT) and MINIRAT (lightweight Go backdoor sharing C2 with AUDIOFIX) [S5][S6][S7]. After initial access the actor injected AUDIOFIX into internal repositories with commits disguised under other developers' names, so colleagues building from them were infected [S5]. It also compromised an npm publisher account (not the GitHub source) to push a trojanized package [S6]. Secondary coverage says AUDIOFIX targets 51 cryptocurrency wallet browser extensions [S7].

diamond.adversary: Unattributed financially motivated cluster; technique overlap with North Korea-linked UNC1069 reported but no state link established [S5][S7].
diamond.capability: AUDIOFIX, MINIRAT, shell-script loader, fake conferencing pages, repository and npm tampering [S5][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Lookalike/fake conferencing and driver-store domains; VPN exit nodes reported in the imported record are not confirmed in sources gathered.
diamond.victim: macOS-using developers and engineering teams at crypto firms; downstream npm consumers [S5][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Financial crime; no state tasking established [S5][S7].
diamond.technology: macOS developer endpoints, LinkedIn as a contact channel, npm publishing credentials, CI/CD systems that auto-resolve packages [S5][S6].

gaps: Primary Wiz report, Hacker News and CSA pages could not be fetched (host unreachable); details rest on search-result summaries and secondary write-ups.
Wiz primary text not fetched; npm version 9.4.1 taken from SafeDep and OpenSourceMalware.

Victim count, losses, and geography not found.
VPN exit node use and full domain/IOC list not verified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Developer workstations (macOS), source repositories, package registry accounts and CI/CD runners are key terrain; for DoD this maps to software factories and contractor developers, though sources show only crypto-sector targeting. STEP 2: The actor exploits trust in recruiters, meeting links and upstream packages rather than software vulnerabilities [S5][S6]. STEP 3: Template: LinkedIn lure, fake meeting page, shell script, AUDIOFIX, repository/commit tampering, CI/CD access, package publishing [S5][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued crypto-developer targeting for theft. MDCOA is the same tradecraft aimed at defense software developers or widely used packages to seed supply-chain access; this is analyst projection, not sourced. Candidate indicators: unexpected npm releases without matching git tags, commits under a developer's name from unusual hosts, outbound traffic to datahub[.]ink, cloud-sync[.]online, byte-io[.]us [S5][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track package-integrity and registry-account alerts for mission software. (2) Authorities: developer endpoints and CI/CD often sit with contractors or program offices; clarify who may isolate or investigate. (3) Mission assurance: protect signing keys, publish tokens and pipeline secrets; require artifact-to-source verification. (4) Coordination: share IOCs through DC3/DIB channels; treat attribution to state actors as unconfirmed [S3][S5].

provenance.importedSummary: JINX-0164 is a financially motivated threat actor active since mid-2025, primarily targeting software developers through recruitment-themed social engineering to steal cryptocurrencies and conduct supply chain attacks. Their operations have focused on macOS devices, utilizing malware such as AUDIOFIX and MINIRAT, with a notable supply chain compromise involving the trojanization of an npm package. The actor employs a shell script for initial system profiling and payload delivery, often spoofing legitimate services like Microsoft Teams and cryptocurrency companies. JINX-0164's infrastructure includes numerous lookalike domains and utilizes VPN exit nodes for accessing victim systems.

identification.summary: Larva-24005 is AhnLab ASEC's name for a sub-group of Kimsuky, which ASEC describes as receiving North Korean support [S1]. ASEC reported it using compromised servers as phishing infrastructure against people involved with North Korea and university professors researching the regime, with phishing aimed at South Korea and Japan [S1]. In a later ASEC profile, the cluster was tied to intrusions into South Korean software, energy and financial organizations, using BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) in some cases, MySpy, RDPWrap and KimaLogger or RandomQuery keyloggers [S2][S3][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Activity since at least October 2023 per ASEC-based reporting [S3][S4]; one advisory says September 2023 [S6].
identification.notes: ASEC treats Larva-24005 as a sub-group of Kimsuky [S1]. Kimsuky is tracked by other vendors under different names; this record does not merge those facts with ASEC's cluster. Strobes states no exploited CVEs are attributed to the actor, which conflicts with ASEC's BlueKeep reporting [S2]; ASEC is treated as authoritative.

attribution.sponsor: North Korea (DPRK), as assessed by AhnLab ASEC, which calls Larva-24005 a Kimsuky sub-group that receives North Korean support [S1].
attribution.confidence: Not stated in the sources reviewed. This is a vendor (AhnLab ASEC) assessment; no government attribution to Larva-24005 specifically was found.
attribution.basis: ASEC's linkage of the cluster to Kimsuky [S1][S3][S4]. The underlying technical evidence for the linkage was not available because the ASEC pages could not be opened (see gaps).

actors.objectives: Collection of credentials and information from individuals involved with North Korea and academics researching the regime, via phishing [S1]. Persistent remote access and keystroke capture on compromised hosts in South Korean software, energy and financial organizations [S3][S4].

regions: A threat advisory lists additional countries, including the US, Canada, Germany, UK, China, Singapore and others [S5][S6]
targeting.notes: Reporting differs on Japan: headlines say attacks on South Korea and Japan, but ASEC's profile describes breached South Korean firms with phishing sent to South Korea and Japan, so Japan appears to be a phishing target rather than a confirmed set of breached victims [S4]. The wider country list comes from a secondary advisory and may reflect victim or phishing recipients [S5].

capabilities.summary: Breaches servers in Korea, sets up a web server and PHP environment there, and uses them for phishing; pages were stored under the IIS_USER account and XAMPP home folder, with traces later deleted [S1]. Phishing emails posed as Zoom meeting links or web portal login pages [S1]. Initial access included BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) in some systems, although an RDP scanner found on one system showed no evidence of use, and phishing exploiting Equation Editor CVE-2017-11882 was another route [S3][S4]. Post-compromise, a dropper installed MySpy (system information collection) and RDPWrap to keep RDP access, followed by KimaLogger or RandomQuery keyloggers [S3][S4].

campaigns.name: Start of observed intrusion activity
campaigns.summary: ASEC-based reporting says the campaign against South Korean software, energy and financial firms has been active since at least October 2023; a Hivepro advisory says September 2023 [S3][S4][S6].

campaigns.name: Phishing emails targeting Japan (ASEC report)
campaigns.summary: ASEC reported Larva-24005 used compromised Korean servers as phishing infrastructure and attack base against North Korea-related individuals and professors, and also against Japan, with Zoom-link and portal-login lures and BlueKeep, RDPWrap and a custom keylogger used on infrastructure [S1].

campaigns.name: ASEC APT group profile
campaigns.summary: ASEC published a longer Larva-24005 profile covering intrusions at South Korean software, energy and financial companies and tooling (MySpy, RDPWrap, KimaLogger, RandomQuery) [S2][S4].

campaigns.name: Secondary press coverage
campaigns.summary: The Hacker News and Security Affairs reported ASEC's findings, attributing the cluster to Kimsuky; ThaiCERT followed on 2025-04-23 [S3][S4][S5].

diamond.adversary: Larva-24005, an AhnLab-named Kimsuky sub-group, assessed by ASEC as North Korea-supported [S1].
diamond.capability: BlueKeep exploitation, CVE-2017-11882 phishing, MySpy, RDPWrap, KimaLogger and RandomQuery keyloggers, and PHP/web phishing kits [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised servers in Korea running IIS/XAMPP with PHP used to host phishing pages and as a C2 base [S1].
diamond.victim: North Korea-focused individuals and academics, South Korean software, energy and financial organizations, and Japanese phishing recipients [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on North Korea policy and research communities, consistent with ASEC's Kimsuky linkage [S1].
diamond.technology: Internet-exposed unpatched Windows RDP (BlueKeep), Microsoft Office Equation Editor, IIS/XAMPP web servers, email [S1][S3][S4].

gaps: ASEC primary reports (asec.ahnlab.com/en/86535 and /87554) could not be opened (host unreachable); details rely on search-result summaries and secondary coverage.
Exact first-observed date conflicts (September vs October 2023) [S6][S3].
Attribution confidence and technical basis for the Kimsuky linkage are not stated in accessible sources.
Whether Japanese and other-country entities were breached or only phishing recipients is unclear [S4][S5].
No MITRE group ID, Microsoft name or government attribution identified.
Indicators (hashes, domains, IPs) were not retrieved.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: the environment of interest is Korean and Japanese academic, policy and enterprise networks plus exposed Windows RDP and IIS/XAMPP servers [S1][S3]. Step 3 (adversary): a Kimsuky sub-group using compromised third-party servers for phishing [S1]. MLCOA: continued Zoom or portal-login phishing against North Korea experts, hosted on newly compromised servers, with keyloggers and RDPWrap for persistence [S1][S3]. MDCOA: broader victim set across the countries listed in secondary advisories [S5]. Candidate indicators: new RDPWrap installs, IIS_USER or XAMPP web roots holding phishing pages, KimaLogger or RandomQuery artifacts, BlueKeep probing [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: share phishing and tooling indicators from ASEC with allied and academic partners once primary indicators are retrieved [S1]. Authorities: activity concerns civilian and allied networks, so response would run through host-nation or owner channels rather than DoD authorities. Mission assurance: ensure legacy Windows RDP hosts are patched against CVE-2019-0708 and Office against CVE-2017-11882 [S3][S4]. Coordination: AhnLab and Korean/Japanese CERTs hold the primary data [S1][S5].

provenance.importedSummary: Larva-24005 is a threat actor that breaches servers in Korea to establish a web server and PHP environment for phishing attacks, primarily targeting individuals involved with North Korea and university professors researching the regime. They exploit the BlueKeep vulnerability for initial access and utilize RDPWrap and a custom keylogger post-compromise. Phishing emails are crafted to appear as legitimate communications, often containing malicious URLs or compressed files. The actor has been observed storing phishing pages in the IIS_USER account and XAMPP home folder, although traces of these pages were later deleted.

identification.summary: Lemon Sandstorm is Microsoft's name for an Iran-origin threat actor formerly tracked by Microsoft as RUBIDIUM and also known as Pioneer Kitten [S1]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as Fox Kitten (G0117), describes a suspected nexus to the Iranian government, and reports activity since at least 2017 against entities in the Middle East, North Africa, Europe, Australia and North America [S2][S4]. Its signature is mass exploitation of known vulnerabilities in internet-facing VPN and edge appliances, followed by hands-on intrusion with largely open-source and dual-use tools [S2][S5][S6][S11]. Microsoft implicated RUBIDIUM in the Pay2Key and N3tw0rm ransomware campaigns against Israel in late 2020 and early 2021 [S3]. An August 2024 FBI/CISA/DC3 advisory, as reported in the press, describes the same cluster selling or brokering network access to ransomware affiliates (ALPHV/BlackCat, NoEscape, RansomHouse) alongside separate espionage against Israel and Azerbaijan [S11][S12][S13]. Microsoft cites that warning in its October 2024 healthcare ransomware report [S14].
identification.firstObserved: Active since at least 2017, per MITRE ATT&CK and CrowdStrike as summarized by MITRE [S2][S4], and per press coverage of the 2024 joint advisory [S12].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Lemon Sandstorm (formerly RUBIDIUM). Microsoft's naming feed lists RUBIDIUM and PIONEER KITTEN as other names [S1]. MITRE G0117 lists Fox Kitten, UNC757, Parisite, Pioneer Kitten, RUBIDIUM and Lemon Sandstorm [S2]. Press coverage of the 2024 advisory gives the same alias set and says the operators used the online handles 'Br0k3r' and, in 2024, 'xplfinder' [S11][S12]. Parisite is Dragos's name, and Dragos's reporting focuses on ICS-related targeting [S2][S10]. Vendor clusters overlap but are not guaranteed to be identical; see gaps.

attribution.sponsor: Iran. Microsoft lists the actor's origin as Iran [S1]. Press coverage of the August 2024 FBI/CISA/DC3 advisory reports the FBI's assessment that the actors are associated with the Government of Iran and use the Iranian company name 'Danesh Novin Sahand' as a cover [S12][S13]. The sources gathered do not name a specific Iranian organization (for example IRGC or MOIS) as sponsor.
attribution.confidence: US government: the FBI assesses, per press reporting on the 2024 advisory, that the actors are associated with the Government of Iran [S12][S13]. CISA's 2020 alert, as cited by MITRE, described an 'Iran-based' actor [S6][S2]. Microsoft attributes Pay2Key and N3tw0rm to RUBIDIUM but publishes no confidence level [S3]. MITRE and CrowdStrike use 'suspected nexus' wording [S2][S4][S10]. Fortinet's incident responders, as reported by The Hacker News, tie a 2023-2025 Middle East intrusion to Lemon Sandstorm based on tradecraft overlaps [S15]. Morphisec, as reported by The Hacker News, assesses that Pay2Key.I2P is linked to Fox Kitten [S16]. None of the advisory texts were opened for this record.
attribution.basis: FBI/CISA/DC3 joint advisory (2024) as reported by Help Net Security, BleepingComputer and Infosecurity Magazine [S11][S12][S13]; Microsoft threat intelligence and naming [S1][S3][S14]; MITRE ATT&CK procedure mapping drawn from ClearSky, CrowdStrike, CISA, Check Point and Fortinet [S2][S4][S5][S6][S7][S8][S9]; MISP galaxy [S10]; vendor reporting on 2025 activity [S15][S16].

actors.objectives: Dual-track. (1) Espionage: gaining and maintaining access to entities holding information of likely intelligence interest to the Iranian government, per CrowdStrike as carried in MISP [S10]; ClearSky called the 2020 campaign 'espionage-offensive' [S5]. Press reporting on the 2024 advisory says the group also intrudes into organizations in Israel and Azerbaijan to steal sensitive technical data [S12][S13]. (2) Monetization and disruption: brokering access to ransomware affiliates for a share of ransom payments [S11][S12]; reporting on the advisory says the FBI viewed the 2020 Pay2Key campaign as an information operation against Israel-based infrastructure rather than a bid for ransom [S12]. In 2025, Pay2Key.I2P reportedly offered affiliates a higher profit share for attacks on Iran's enemies, including Israel and the US [S16].

sectors: ICS-related entities (per Dragos, as cited in MISP) [S10]
Middle East critical infrastructure (2023-2025 Fortinet case) [S9][S15]
targeting.notes: Targeting is opportunistic, driven by exposure of vulnerable internet-facing VPN, firewall and remote-access appliances, not by sector alone [S2][S6][S11]. US victims in the 2024 advisory coverage are mostly ransomware access targets; Israel and Azerbaijan are espionage targets [S12]. Sector list for 2017-2021 comes from MITRE [S2].

capabilities.summary: Initial access comes through n-day exploitation of edge devices. 2020 reporting covered Fortinet, Pulse Secure and Palo Alto VPNs [S2][S5][S6]. 2024 advisory coverage adds Citrix NetScaler, F5 BIG-IP, Ivanti, Palo Alto PAN-OS GlobalProtect (CVE-2024-3400) and Check Point gateways (CVE-2024-24919) [S11][S12]. In the 2023-2025 Fortinet case, initial access was via compromised SSL VPN credentials [S15]. Persistence relies on web shells (including China Chopper), scheduled tasks, newly created accounts and the sticky-keys backdoor [S2][S6][S11]. Tunneling and C2 use ngrok, SSHMinion, FRPC, Go Proxy, Plink and AWS-hosted C2, and MITRE associates SystemBC with the group [S2][S4][S6][S9]. The Fortinet case also featured custom malware: the HanifNet .NET backdoor, HXLibrary and NeoExpressRAT, plus MeshCentral. Fortinet reported at least five novel malware families [S15]. Credentials are dumped from LSASS, NTDS and KeePass [S2][S6]. Ransomware involvement spans the actor's own Pay2Key in 2020 [S7][S8], hands-on help to ALPHV/NoEscape/RansomHouse affiliates in encrypting victims [S11][S12], and the 2025 Pay2Key.I2P RaaS, which Morphisec reports is tied to Mimic ransomware capabilities [S16].

diamond.adversary: Iran-origin actor that the FBI associates with the Government of Iran; cover company Danesh Novin Sahand; personas Br0k3r and xplfinder; Microsoft Lemon Sandstorm (formerly RUBIDIUM) [S1][S11][S12].
diamond.capability: N-day edge-device exploitation; web shells; tunneling tools (ngrok, FRPC, Plink, SSHMinion); SystemBC; custom backdoors HanifNet and NeoExpressRAT; credential dumping; Pay2Key and Pay2Key.I2P ransomware [S2][S4][S9][S12][S15][S16].
diamond.infrastructure: Reverse tunnels and proxies to actor C2, including ngrok and AWS-hosted servers [S2]; criminal-forum personas for access sales [S11][S12]; Keybase and Twitter for Pay2Key victim contact [S2][S7].
diamond.victim: US schools, municipalities, financial and healthcare organizations (access brokering); Israeli, Azerbaijani and UAE targets; Middle East critical infrastructure; historically oil and gas, defense and government in multiple regions [S2][S12][S15].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection for Iran [S10][S12] combined with revenue and pressure operations against Israel and the US, intensified after the June 2025 conflict [S3][S16].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing VPN, firewall and ADC appliances (Fortinet, Pulse/Ivanti, Palo Alto, Citrix, F5, Check Point); Windows AD; cloud and Teams collaboration data [S2][S6][S11][S12].

gaps: The 2024 FBI/CISA/DC3 advisory (IC3 PDF and CISA AA24-241A page) was not opened; its content is taken from press coverage [S11][S12][S13]. One search summary noted the IC3 PDF may carry a different product ID (AA24-233A); unverified.
Cover-company spelling varies in coverage ('Danesh Novin Sahand' vs 'Sahan'); confirm in the primary advisory [S13].

Older primary documents were not opened; their content comes from MITRE ATT&CK and MISP. These include CrowdStrike's PIONEER KITTEN profile, ClearSky's Fox Kitten and Pay2Kitten reports, CISA AA20-259A, Check Point's Pay2Key alert, the Fortinet 2025 report and Dragos PARISITE.

Fortinet's 2025 report itself was not opened. Its attribution wording and confidence, and the victim's identity, rest on The Hacker News coverage [S15]. A search summary of other coverage said the intrusion may trace to May 2021; unverified.
The Pay2Key.I2P attribution to Fox Kitten is Morphisec's assessment; no government confirmation was found [S16]. The links to Mimic ransomware and a reported Linux variant are unverified.
Some secondary sources (Truesec, Paubox) claim IRGC ties and a close link to Peach Sandstorm; these were not verified in primary reporting and are excluded.
Microsoft has no public dedicated Lemon Sandstorm profile; Microsoft coverage here is the naming feed, the 2021 MDDR blog and the 2024 healthcare report [S1][S3][S14].

Cluster boundaries: Parisite (Dragos), UNC757 (Mandiant) and Fox Kitten/Pioneer Kitten are mapped together by MITRE, MISP and the 2024 advisory coverage [S2][S10][S12]. Microsoft's own mapping lists only RUBIDIUM and PIONEER KITTEN [S1].
ICS targeting rests on MISP's summary of Dragos reporting; OT impact is unverified [S10].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Internet-facing VPN, firewall and ADC appliances (Fortinet, Ivanti/Pulse, Palo Alto, Citrix, F5, Check Point) are key cyber terrain [S2][S11][S12]. Victimology includes US municipal, education, finance and healthcare networks, Israeli, Azerbaijani and UAE targets, and Middle East critical infrastructure. These overlap with base support services, host nations and coalition partners [S12][S15]. STEP 2 (effects): Every new edge-device CVE widens the target set within days. Ransomware partnerships turn espionage access into availability effects [S11][S12]. STEP 3 (adversary template): n-day or stolen-credential VPN access; web shell or new account; tunnel (ngrok, FRPC, Plink, SystemBC) or custom backdoor (HanifNet, NeoExpressRAT); credential dumping; RDP/SMB movement; then data theft and/or a handoff to ransomware affiliates [S2][S6][S12][S15]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet, multi-year access for intelligence collection, with opportunistic access sales [S12][S15]. MDCOA is crisis-time activation of brokered or long-held access to encrypt or disrupt partner-nation critical infrastructure or DIB and installation-support networks, consistent with Pay2Key.I2P's pro-Iran affiliate incentives [S16]. Candidate indicators: exploitation of newly disclosed edge-device CVEs; new local or domain accounts after VPN logins from unfamiliar sources; scheduled tasks named like system services; outbound ngrok/FRP/MeshCentral traffic; VSS-based NTDS access; and forum offers of domain-admin access to sector peers [S2][S6][S12][S15].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Track patch and compromise-assessment status of edge appliances across the DODIN, DIB and mission partners. The actor reuses stolen VPN credentials and persists after patching [S6][S15]. (2) Authorities: Activity blends state espionage with criminal ransomware [S12]. Incidents may need joint FBI, CISA and DC3 handling, and early clarity on lead agency, particularly for DIB and municipal or healthcare providers that support installations [S12][S14]. (3) Mission assurance: The Fortinet case shows two years of undetected dwell and attempted re-entry after eviction [S15]. Plan for credential resets, threat hunting and offline backups for mission-critical and ICS-adjacent systems. (4) Coordination: Share edge-exploitation and tunneling indicators with Israeli, Gulf and Azerbaijani partners and US critical-infrastructure sectors [S12]. Map vendor aliases (Pioneer Kitten, Fox Kitten, UNC757, Parisite, Br0k3r) so partner reporting links to one cluster [S1][S2][S11].

provenance.importedSummary: PIONEER KITTEN is an Iran-based adversary that has been active since at least 2017 and has a suspected nexus to the Iranian government. This adversary appears to be primarily focused on gaining and maintaining access to entities possessing sensitive information of likely intelligence interest to the Iranian government. According to DRAGOS, they also targeted ICS-related entities using known VPN vulnerabilities. They are widely known to use open source penetration testing tools for reconnaissance and to establish encrypted communications.

identification.summary: Leopard Typhoon is Microsoft's name for a China-origin actor formerly tracked by Microsoft as LEAD [S1]. Microsoft maps WICKED PANDA, TG-2633, TG-3279, Mana, KAOS, Red Diablo and Winnti Group to it [S1]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the actor as Winnti Group (G0044). MITRE describes a group with Chinese origins, active since at least 2010, that heavily targeted the gaming industry and has since widened its targeting [S2]. In its January 2017 post on German industrial attacks, Microsoft described how Windows Defender ATP flags Winnti-related activity by the LEAD and BARIUM activity groups [S3]. Microsoft described LEAD as the industrial-espionage group that steals code-signing certificates to sign its malware [S3].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least 2010 [S2]. Kaspersky first publicly reported the group in 2013 [S8].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Leopard Typhoon (legacy element name LEAD) [S1]. MITRE match: Winnti Group (G0044) [S2]. Cluster boundary caution: Microsoft separates LEAD from BARIUM (now Brass Typhoon), describing BARIUM as focused on electronic gaming, multimedia and internet content and using social-media rapport and malicious macro, .chm or .lnk first stages [S3]. Microsoft also lists WICKED PANDA under both Leopard Typhoon and Brass Typhoon [S1]. Several vendors do not draw this line. Symantec groups Winnti, APT41, Barium, Blackfly and Wicked Panda together [S9]. LAC's RevivalStone reporting is covered as 'Winnti (APT41)' and overlaps Trend Micro's Earth Freybug, an APT41 subset [S10]. 'Winnti' is also a malware family name used by several groups [S2]. Reports titled 'Winnti' may therefore describe Brass Typhoon activity rather than Leopard Typhoon.

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (origin per Microsoft's naming mapping) [S1]. German public broadcaster ARD reported in 2019 that analysis of Winnti code pointed to a group likely working for the Chinese government [S7].
attribution.confidence: No Microsoft confidence statement on state sponsorship of Leopard Typhoon was found; Microsoft assigns China as the origin [S1]. MITRE describes Chinese origins [S2]. In 2019, a DCSO executive said 'we can assume that there is a very targeted tasking by the Chinese state,' while noting definite proof was impossible [S6]. That statement concerns Winnti intrusions in Germany and is not a government attribution. No US government indictment, advisory or sanction naming Leopard Typhoon or LEAD was found in this research.
attribution.basis: Microsoft naming mapping and 2017 Windows Defender ATP reporting [S1][S3]; MITRE ATT&CK group record [S2]; vendor reporting from ESET, Symantec and LAC [S4][S5][S9][S10]; German press investigations reported by AFP and Reuters [S6][S7].

actors.objectives: Industrial and commercial espionage. A threat-actor card summarizing Microsoft's 2017 reporting says LEAD sought research materials, process documents and project plans [S11]. Microsoft said LEAD steals code-signing certificates and uses them to sign its malware in later attacks [S3]. Supply-chain compromise of software and game developers supports both espionage and onward access [S4][S5]. ESET found a cryptominer as the final payload of the 2019 gaming supply-chain attack and said a financial motive could not be ruled out [S4].

sectors: Online and video game developers and publishers [S2][S4][S5]
Materials and energy (Winnti/APT41-labeled reporting; boundary unclear) [S9][S10]
regions: South Korea and Taiwan (2020 game developers) [S5]
Thailand and wider Asia (2019 gaming supply chain; small numbers in Brazil, Peru, Turkey and Russia) [S4]
Switzerland (Roche) and other multinationals named by ARD, including Marriott, Lion Air, Sumitomo and Shin-Etsu [S7]
targeting.notes: Microsoft's 2017 post addresses German industrial victims [S3]. Victim lists from 2019 German press reporting attribute infections to 'Winnti' malware, not to a Microsoft-named cluster [S6][S7]. Materials, energy and Japan targeting comes from vendors that merge Winnti with APT41, so it may belong to Brass Typhoon under Microsoft's taxonomy [S9][S10].

capabilities.summary: Microsoft said LEAD uses Winnti malware for long-term access and signs malware with stolen code-signing certificates [S3]. A threat-actor card summarizing the same reporting says initial access typically came from emailed Winnti installers, with brute-forced logins, SQL injection and unpatched web servers also used [S11]. MITRE attributes Winnti for Windows, PlugX and PipeMon to the group [S2]. ESET reported supply-chain compromise of game developers' build environments, so that malware shipped inside legitimate software. ESET also reported the PortReuse backdoor and continued use of ShadowPad variants [S4]. In 2020, ESET reported the modular PipeMon backdoor, which persisted as a Print Processor and was signed with a likely stolen certificate. In one case the actor reached a build orchestration server [S5]. Winnti/APT41-labeled reporting from 2023-2025 describes the Winnkit backdoor and heavier use of open-source tools [S9]. It also describes ERP SQL injection, China Chopper and Behinder web shells, abuse of a maintenance provider's shared account, and a 'Winnti v5.0' RAT with rootkit and loader [S10][S12].

campaigns.name: Kaspersky exposure of Winnti
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky first publicly reported the Winnti group in 2013. Security Affairs says the researchers assessed it as active since 2007.

campaigns.name: German conglomerate intrusion
campaigns.summary: Microsoft cited German press reports that intruders used Winnti as their main implant to keep access to a conglomerate's network from February 2016. Reuters, citing media reports at the time, describes a 2016 Winnti attack on ThyssenKrupp.

campaigns.name: Microsoft LEAD/BARIUM reporting
campaigns.summary: Microsoft described how Windows Defender ATP detects LEAD and BARIUM activity linked to Winnti in German industrial attacks, and separated LEAD (industrial espionage, certificate theft) from BARIUM (gaming and media).

campaigns.name: Bayer intrusion
campaigns.summary: Bayer confirmed in April 2019 that it detected Winnti infections in early 2018 and cleaned up the systems with DCSO and North Rhine-Westphalia police. Bayer said no data was stolen.

campaigns.name: Asian gaming supply-chain attacks
campaigns.summary: ESET reported compromised game builds distributing malware, with victims concentrated in Thailand and Asia and a custom XMRig miner as the final payload.

campaigns.name: German DAX and multinational victims (ARD)
campaigns.summary: ARD reported Winnti infections. Siemens, Henkel and Roche confirmed they were affected by Winnti; BASF and Covestro confirmed only that they had been attacked. All said no sensitive information was lost.

campaigns.name: PortReuse and ShadowPad arsenal (ESET)
campaigns.summary: ESET documented the PortReuse backdoor and active ShadowPad variants, and warned an Asian mobile hardware and software manufacturer that it was compromised.

campaigns.name: PipeMon against Korean and Taiwanese game developers
campaigns.summary: ESET found the PipeMon backdoor at MMO developers in South Korea and Taiwan, linked to Winnti by shared C2 domains. The actor reached a build orchestration server in at least one case.

campaigns.name: Operation CuckooBees (overlapping cluster)
campaigns.summary: Cybereason reporting, as covered by Dark Reading, describes Winnti theft of trade secrets from technology and manufacturing companies. Attribution is shared with APT41/BARIUM.

campaigns.name: Blackfly against materials sector (overlapping cluster)
campaigns.summary: Symantec reported Blackfly targeting two subsidiaries of an Asian conglomerate in materials and composites in late 2022 to early 2023, using Winnkit and open-source tools.

campaigns.name: RevivalStone (overlapping cluster)
campaigns.summary: LAC reported, as covered in February 2025, Winnti intrusions into Japanese manufacturing, materials and energy firms. Access came through ERP SQL injection and spread through a maintenance provider to three more organizations.

diamond.adversary: China-origin actor that Microsoft calls Leopard Typhoon (formerly LEAD) [S1][S3]. MITRE tracks it as Winnti Group (G0044) [S2]. Several vendors fold it into APT41 [S9][S10].
diamond.capability: Winnti RAT and rootkit, PlugX, PipeMon, PortReuse and ShadowPad; malware signed with stolen certificates; software supply-chain tampering [S2][S3][S4][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: C2 domains reused across campaigns, which ESET used to link PipeMon to Winnti [S5]; compromised developer build environments and build orchestration servers [S4][S5]; a trusted maintenance provider's shared account (RevivalStone) [S10].
diamond.victim: Game developers and players in Asia [S4][S5]; German industrial, chemical and pharmaceutical multinationals [S3][S6][S7]; Asian hardware manufacturers [S4]; Japanese manufacturing, materials and energy firms (overlapping cluster) [S10].
diamond.socioPolitical: German commentators linked the targeting to China's economic goals, and DCSO suggested Chinese state tasking [S6]. Intellectual property and certificate theft support commercial and technology advancement [S3][S11].
diamond.technology: Windows enterprise networks, code-signing trust, software build pipelines, internet-facing ERP and web applications, and outsourced IT maintenance relationships [S3][S4][S5][S10].

gaps: Microsoft has not published a profile under the name Leopard Typhoon that could be found. Microsoft's 2017 LEAD post was seen only as a search result and could not be fetched (DNS failure), so its details here come from search summaries and the ETDA card [S3][S11].

The boundary between Leopard Typhoon (LEAD) and Brass Typhoon (BARIUM/APT41) is unresolved. Microsoft separates them, but Symantec, LAC and others merge 'Winnti' with APT41. CuckooBees, Blackfly and RevivalStone are recorded as overlapping clusters, not confirmed Leopard Typhoon activity [S1][S3][S9][S10].
German 2019 victim reporting attributes infections to Winnti malware, which several groups share. Which Microsoft cluster was responsible is not stated [S2][S7].

Primary vendor reports were not opened because WebFetch could not resolve the hosts: ESET white papers, Symantec Blackfly, LAC RevivalStone, Cybereason CuckooBees, and Kaspersky 2013/2015. Content comes from search summaries and press coverage.
No US government indictment, advisory or sanction naming Leopard Typhoon or LEAD was found. The September 2020 DOJ APT41 indictments concern Wicked Panda/APT41 and were not reviewed for this record.
Microsoft maps the names TG-2633, TG-3279, Mana, KAOS and Red Diablo to Leopard Typhoon, but their originating reports were not identified [S1].
No reporting from 2025-2026 specific to Leopard Typhoon was found; the most recent Winnti-labeled activity found is the 2024 RevivalStone campaign [S10][S12].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1 (operational environment): the relevant terrain is commercial software and game build pipelines, code-signing infrastructure, internet-facing ERP and web servers, outsourced IT maintenance accounts, and industrial, chemical and pharmaceutical R&D networks [S3][S4][S5][S10]. Defense-industrial-base suppliers fall within this terrain. Step 2 (effects): signed malware and trojanized legitimate software weaken signature-based trust. Long dwell times, such as Bayer detecting infections in early 2018 that were disclosed in 2019, show durable access [S3][S4][S6]. Step 3 (adversary template): initial access by phishing a Winnti installer, web or SQL injection, or a supply-chain compromise. Persistence follows through Winnti RAT and rootkit, PipeMon or ShadowPad, then lateral movement through shared or provider accounts and theft of documents and certificates [S4][S5][S10][S11]. Step 4: the MLCOA is continued IP and certificate theft from manufacturing, materials and technology firms in Asia and Europe [S3][S7][S9][S10]. The MDCOA is the use of stolen signing certificates or a compromised build server to push trojanized updates into software DoD or its suppliers use. This is inferred from the 2019-2020 supply-chain activity; no documented campaign against DoD exists [S4][S5]. Candidate indicators: binaries signed with certificates from unrelated vendors; unexpected Print Processor registrations; new web shells (China Chopper, Behinder) on ERP or web servers; anomalous use of maintenance-provider shared accounts; DNS to C2 domains reused from prior Winnti campaigns [S5][S10].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track certificate revocations, vendor and game-studio supply-chain compromises, and Winnti, PipeMon and ShadowPad detections. Account for shared Winnti malware when attributing [S2][S4][S5]. Authorities: observed victims are almost entirely private-sector firms in Germany, Japan and Asia, so DoD action toward exposed suppliers would normally run through DC3 and DIB partnership and interagency channels, not direct DODIN operations [S6][S7][S10]. Mission assurance: the main DODIN risk is trust in signed third-party software and managed-service accounts. Prioritize allow-listing that does not rely on signature alone, and monitor provider access [S3][S10]. Coordination: deconflict with partners that track Brass Typhoon/APT41, since vendors merge the clusters, and with allied CERTs such as Germany's and Japan's, which have handled Winnti cases [S1][S6][S9][S10].

provenance.importedSummary: Winnti Group is a threat group with Chinese origins that has been active since at least 2010. The group has heavily targeted the gaming industry, but it has also expanded the scope of its targeting. Some reporting suggests a number of other groups, including Axiom, APT17, and Ke3chang, are closely linked to Winnti Group.

identification.summary: Lilac Typhoon is the Microsoft name for the threat actor it earlier tracked as DEV-0234, with China as its listed origin [S4]. In June 2022 Microsoft named DEV-0234 and DEV-0401 among the 'multiple adversaries and nation-state actors' exploiting the Atlassian Confluence remote code execution flaw CVE-2022-26134 [S1][S2][S3]. Public reporting on the actor beyond this one Microsoft mention is very limited.
identification.firstObserved: Earliest public reference found: Microsoft Threat Intelligence post of 2022-06-11 naming DEV-0234 as exploiting CVE-2022-26134 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft maps Lilac Typhoon to DEV-0234 only; it lists no other vendor names [S4]. Third-party profiles (Malpedia, Strobes) repeat the DEV-0234 alias and the China attribution and cite the June 2022 Microsoft post [S6]. In the same June 2022 statement Microsoft named DEV-0401, which SecurityWeek describes as a separate China-based ransomware operator (LockFile, AtomSilo, Rook) [S3]. Keep DEV-0401 activity separate from Lilac Typhoon. The payload list commonly attached to this actor (Cobalt Strike, web shells, botnets, coin miners, ransomware including Cerber2021) describes everything Microsoft saw across all CVE-2022-26134 exploitation. It is not attributed to DEV-0234 specifically [S2][S3].

attribution.sponsor: China (Microsoft 'Origin/Threat' designation) [S4]. No public source found names a specific PRC organization (MSS, PLA, MPS) or contractor.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft lists the origin as China [S4] and grouped DEV-0234 with the 'nation-state actors' exploiting CVE-2022-26134 [S1]. Microsoft did not publish a confidence level in the sources found. No government attribution of DEV-0234 or Lilac Typhoon was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry, reported in a 2022-06-11 social media post [S1] and covered by trade press [S2][S3], plus Microsoft's naming mapping [S4]. No technical report on this actor was found.

sectors: Organizations running internet-facing Atlassian Confluence Server or Data Center (cross-sector) [S1][S5]
targeting.notes: The only documented targeting is opportunistic exploitation of vulnerable Confluence Server/Data Center instances in June 2022 [S1][S2]. Confluence Cloud was not affected [S7]. No victims, sectors or regions attributable to DEV-0234 specifically were found in public sources.

capabilities.summary: Microsoft reported that DEV-0234 exploited CVE-2022-26134 [S1][S2][S3]. That flaw is an unauthenticated OGNL-injection remote code execution vulnerability in Confluence Server and Data Center, patched by Atlassian on 2022-06-03 [S5][S7]. Microsoft said exploitation of the flaw across all actors delivered Cobalt Strike, web shells, botnets (Mirai, Kinsing), coin miners and ransomware (Cerber2021) [S2][S3]. Microsoft did not state which of these payloads DEV-0234 used. The actor quickly weaponized an n-day edge/collaboration-server vulnerability within about a week of disclosure [S1][S7]. That is the only capability the sources support.

campaigns.name: Exploitation of Atlassian Confluence CVE-2022-26134
campaigns.summary: Microsoft named DEV-0234 (now Lilac Typhoon) and DEV-0401 among the adversaries and nation-state actors exploiting the Confluence OGNL-injection RCE flaw shortly after Atlassian's 2022-06-03 patch. Across all actors, observed payloads included Cobalt Strike, web shells, botnets, coin miners and Cerber2021 ransomware.

diamond.adversary: China-origin actor tracked by Microsoft as Lilac Typhoon (formerly DEV-0234) [S4]; no named individuals or units in public sources.
diamond.capability: Exploitation of Confluence CVE-2022-26134 (unauthenticated OGNL-injection RCE) [S1][S5]; specific post-exploitation tooling not attributed [S2][S3].
diamond.victim: Internet-exposed Confluence Server/Data Center instances (opportunistic) [S1][S5]; no named victims.
diamond.technology: On-premises Atlassian Confluence Server and Data Center versions before the June 2022 fixes [S5][S7].

gaps: No Microsoft blog post or technical report specific to DEV-0234/Lilac Typhoon was found. Its public record rests on a single 2022-06-11 Microsoft post and press coverage of it [S1][S2][S3].

Microsoft did not say which CVE-2022-26134 payloads (Cobalt Strike, web shells, coin miners, botnets, Cerber2021) DEV-0234 used. The imported summary's statement that this actor deployed all of them is not supported at actor level.
Whether DEV-0234 is espionage-motivated, financially motivated or both is unknown. Microsoft's 'nation-state actors' phrasing covers the group of actors named, not DEV-0234 specifically.

The imported reference (Security Boulevard coverage of CISA/NSA/FBI advisory AA22-279A, Oct 2022) could not be opened. Whether that advisory lists CVE-2022-26134 among CVEs exploited by PRC state-sponsored actors was not verified, and the advisory does not name Lilac Typhoon or DEV-0234 in any source seen.
The imported Risky Business newsletter reference could not be opened; its relevance is unverified.

Volexity first detected in-the-wild CVE-2022-26134 exploitation, which involved BEHINDER and China Chopper web shells [S7]. Nothing in the sources links that intrusion to DEV-0234, so it is not merged here.
No overlaps with other vendors' clusters are published (no MITRE ATT&CK group ID). Third-party profiles (Malpedia) appear to restate the Microsoft post [S6].
Activity after 2022 under the Lilac Typhoon name was not found in public reporting.
Primary pages from therecord.media, securityweek.com and malpedia could not be fetched (network blocked); their content was taken from search-result excerpts.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): internet-facing on-premises Confluence and similar collaboration servers on DoD, DIB and mission-partner networks are relevant key terrain, because they store planning and engineering documentation [S1][S5]. STEP 2 (effects): an unauthenticated RCE gives the actor immediate server-level access, and mass exploitation started within days of disclosure, so the defender has very little time to patch [S1][S7]. STEP 3 (threat model): the evidenced template is opportunistic exploitation of a public n-day in a collaboration server [S1][S2]. Follow-on tooling for this actor is undocumented; across actors it included web shells, Cobalt Strike, coin miners and ransomware [S2][S3]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is opportunistic exploitation of newly disclosed edge or collaboration-server RCEs to gain footholds. MDCOA is persistent access to unpatched collaboration servers holding operational planning data, used for collection or handed off to other PRC actors. Candidate indicators: OGNL-injection patterns in Confluence request URIs, new JSP/web-shell files in Confluence directories, Confluence service processes spawning shells or downloaders, and unexpected outbound connections from Confluence hosts [S5][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track the exposure and patch state of collaboration servers (Confluence and similar) in JCC2 views. Treat CISA KEV additions such as CVE-2022-26134 as triggers for an immediate exposure check [S7]. (2) Authorities: Microsoft's DEV-0234 attribution is a vendor assessment without government corroboration, so response actions should rest on observed exploitation, not on the actor name [S1][S4]. (3) Mission assurance: account for internal wikis and knowledge bases that hold mission data when assessing compromise impact. (4) Coordination: many criminal and state actors exploited the same flaw [S2][S3]. Deconflict attribution with DC3/DIB CS partners and CISA, and prioritize containment over actor naming.

provenance.importedSummary: Lilac Typhoon is a threat actor attributed to China. They have been identified as exploiting the Atlassian Confluence RCE vulnerability CVE-2022-26134, which allows for remote code execution. This vulnerability has been used in cryptojacking campaigns and is included in commercial exploit frameworks. Lilac Typhoon has also been involved in deploying various payloads such as Cobalt Strike, web shells, botnets, coin miners, and ransomware.

identification.summary: China-based state-sponsored espionage actor that Microsoft says has focused on stealing intellectual property since 2012, targeting government, defense, strategic planning and human rights organizations [S1]. It is known for drive-by compromises (watering holes) and for relying on existing exploits. In July 2025 it exploited on-premises SharePoint vulnerabilities [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: active since 2012 [S1]. Operation Iron Tiger reporting dates to 2015 [S6].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Linen Typhoon (formerly IODINE). Microsoft maps TG-3390, Lucky Mouse, Emissary Panda, APT27, UNC215, Hippo, BOWSER, Wekby2 and Red Phoenix to it [S4]. Microsoft lists APT27 and EMISSARY PANDA under both Linen and Circle Typhoon; APT6 and DEV-0322 belong to Circle Typhoon only and were removed from this record's aliases. MITRE tracks the group as Threat Group-3390 (G0027) [S3].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China. The March 2025 US indictments describe APT27 members operating in the PRC hacker-for-hire ecosystem, at times at the direction of the Ministry of Public Security (MPS) and Ministry of State Security (MSS) [S2].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Collaboration servers (on-premises SharePoint) and government-hosted websites are key terrain. They hold planning documents and can be turned into watering holes. STEP 2: Rapid uptake of newly disclosed collaboration-server CVEs narrows the defender's window to days. STEP 3: The template is a watering hole or public exploit, then web shell or RAT, then document collection from collaboration platforms. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent IP and policy theft from government and defense targets. MDCOA is mass exploitation of a newly disclosed enterprise vulnerability across DoD-adjacent organizations during a crisis to harvest planning data. Candidate indicators: new web shells on SharePoint servers, unexpected ASPX files, and outbound traffic from collaboration servers to unfamiliar hosts [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Emergency patch and mitigation tracking for collaboration platforms should feed JCC2 situational awareness in near real time when a CVE like ToolShell drops. (2) Multiple PRC actors exploited the same SharePoint flaw, so attribution to a single actor may be slow; prioritize containment over naming. (3) Coordinate with DC3 and the DIB CS program for contractor-hosted collaboration servers. (4) Watering-hole risk extends to coalition and government websites personnel visit; include web-traffic telemetry in hunt planning.
