provenance.importedSummary: The FBI issued a rare bulletin admitting that a group named Advanced Persistent Threat 6 (APT6) hacked into US government computer systems as far back as 2011 and for years stole sensitive data. The FBI alert was issued in February and went largely unnoticed. Nearly a month later, security experts are now shining a bright light on the alert and the mysterious group behind the attack. “This is a rare alert and a little late, but one that is welcomed by all security vendors as it offers a chance to mitigate their customers and also collaborate further in what appears to be an ongoing FBI investigation,” said Deepen Desai, director of security research at the security firm Zscaler in an email to Threatpost. Details regarding the actual attack and what government systems were infected are scant. Government officials said they knew the initial attack occurred in 2011, but are unaware of who specifically is behind the attacks. “Given the nature of malware payload involved and the duration of this compromise being unnoticed – the scope of lateral movement inside the compromised network is very high possibly exposing all the critical systems,”Deepen said.

identification.summary: LongNosedGoblin is a China-aligned APT group named by ESET Research, which announced it on 18 December 2025 [S1][S2][S4]. It targets governmental entities in Southeast Asia and Japan for cyberespionage [S2][S4]. Its most distinctive trait is abuse of Windows Group Policy to deploy malware and move laterally [S1][S4]. It uses cloud services such as OneDrive and Google Drive for command and control [S7].
identification.firstObserved: ESET traces activity to at least September 2023 and first noticed the group's malware in 2024 in a Southeast Asian government network [S5].
identification.notes: ESET is the originator of the name; no Microsoft name or MITRE group ID was found in the sources gathered. ESET judges the NosyDoor backdoor is probably shared among several China-aligned actors, so tool presence alone does not identify this group [S1][S3]. ESET reports similarities to ToddyCat and tooling resembling Erudite Mogwai but treats LongNosedGoblin as distinct [S7]. Cisco Talos tracks a separate cluster, UAT-8302, that uses NetDraft, which Talos says ESET calls NosyDoor; Talos describes a close operating relationship between clusters rather than identity [S9]. Keep these cluster boundaries separate.

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor or government agency is named in the sources gathered. ESET characterizes the group as China-aligned [S2][S4].
attribution.confidence: ESET's confidence level is not stated in the secondary coverage reviewed; the primary ESET report could not be opened.
attribution.basis: ESET's assessment of targeting, tooling and tradecraft, as relayed by press coverage [S2][S4][S5]. Cisco Talos separately assesses with high confidence that UAT-8302 is a China-nexus APT, and links its NetDraft malware to ESET's NosyDoor; this is Talos's assessment of its own cluster, not of LongNosedGoblin [S9].

actors.objectives: Cyberespionage against governmental entities in Southeast Asia and Japan [S2][S4]. Browser-history collection is used to select higher-interest victims for further tooling [S7].

targeting.notes: ESET first found the malware in a Southeast Asian government network in 2024 [S5]. Many victims received NosyHistorian but only a small subset also received NosyDoor, indicating selective follow-on targeting [S7]. Specific countries were not identified in the sources gathered. A NosyDoor variant seen in an EU country used Yandex Disk, which ESET ties to other actors' use of the tool, not necessarily this group [S10].

capabilities.summary: Modular custom malware ecosystem. NosyHistorian collects browser history from Chrome, Edge and Firefox to choose victims for further tooling [S7]. NosyDoor is a backdoor that uses Microsoft OneDrive for C2 in the campaigns ESET observed [S1][S5]. Other tools reported include NosyStealer, NosyLogger and NosyDownloader [S3]. Malware is deployed through Group Policy, which implies domain controller access and domain administrator credentials [search summary of S4]. A September 2025 wave used Group Policy to deliver NosyHistorian and a possible Cobalt Strike loader [S3]. Initial access was not established in most cases, as attackers were already inside the networks ESET examined [S7].

diamond.adversary: China-aligned espionage group per ESET; no sponsor named [S2][S4].
diamond.capability: NosyHistorian, NosyDoor, NosyStealer, NosyLogger, NosyDownloader, a possible Cobalt Strike loader, and Group Policy deployment [S3][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: Cloud services (OneDrive, Google Drive) used as C2 [S1][S7]. Specific domains and IPs were not captured from the primary report.
diamond.victim: Governmental entities in Southeast Asia and Japan [S2][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Government-focused espionage by a China-aligned actor in the Indo-Pacific; no further motive stated in sources gathered [S2][S4].
diamond.technology: Windows Active Directory and Group Policy as a deployment channel; Chrome, Edge and Firefox browser data; trusted cloud storage services as C2 [S1][S7].

gaps: The primary ESET WeLiveSecurity report could not be opened (fetch failed); details come from the ESET press release listing and secondary coverage found via search. Verify tool descriptions, IoCs and confidence wording against it.
Initial access vector is not established in the sources gathered [S7].
Specific victim countries and the exact victim count are unclear; victim count is not stated in the sources gathered.
ESET's formal confidence level and any government attribution are not available.
Relationship to ToddyCat, Erudite Mogwai and Talos UAT-8302 is unresolved [S7][S9].
No Microsoft actor name or MITRE ATT&CK group ID was identified; ATT&CK mapping is pending.
Whether activity continued after the September 2025 wave is unknown.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Active Directory domain controllers and Group Policy objects are key cyber terrain in government networks; browser data on user workstations supports target selection [S1][S7]. STEP 2: The actor already holds domain administrator-level access in observed cases, so perimeter-focused defenses alone are insufficient [search summary of S4][S7]. STEP 3: Template is pre-existing privileged access, then NosyHistorian harvest of browser history, then selective NosyDoor deployment, with C2 over OneDrive or Google Drive blending into normal cloud traffic [S1][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against Southeast Asian and Japanese government entities using Group Policy deployment. MDCOA is use of the same shared tooling against allied or partner government networks in the Indo-Pacific. Candidate indicators: new or modified Group Policy objects pushing executables or scheduled tasks, unexpected DLLs such as oci.dll, browser-history access by unknown processes, and OneDrive or Google Drive API traffic from servers or workstations that do not normally use them [S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: monitor GPO change auditing and domain controller logs and track vendor reporting on shared NosyDoor/NetDraft tooling [S9]. (2) Authorities: coordinate any partner-network assistance through established agreements; vendor attribution here is not government attribution. (3) Mission assurance: protect domain admin credentials and segment tier-0 assets, since Group Policy access implies full domain control [search summary of S4]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with Indo-Pacific partners given the Southeast Asia and Japan focus [S2].

provenance.importedSummary: LongNosedGoblin is a China-aligned APT group targeting governmental entities in Southeast Asia and Japan for cyberespionage. The group employs Group Policy for malware deployment and utilizes cloud services like Microsoft OneDrive and Google Drive as C&C servers. Their operations feature a modular malware ecosystem, including backdoors, browser data stealers, and PowerShell-based downloaders that execute multi-stage payloads in memory. LongNosedGoblin's tactics emphasize reconnaissance-driven targeting and the abuse of trusted enterprise mechanisms, allowing for stealthy persistence within compromised networks.

identification.summary: Madi (also spelled Mahdi) is a cyber-espionage campaign disclosed in July 2012 by Kaspersky Lab and Seculert, who sinkholed its command-and-control servers and monitored it [S1]. Over roughly eight months they identified more than 800 victims, mostly in Iran and Israel, including people working on Iranian and Israeli critical-infrastructure projects, Israeli financial institutions, Middle Eastern engineering students and government bodies [S1]. The name comes from a file, mahdi.txt, dropped on infected machines [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Seculert tracked variants of the same malware back to December 2011 [S4]. Public disclosure was 2012-07-17 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Kaspersky uses 'Madi' and Seculert uses 'Mahdi' [S6]. This is a named campaign and malware family, not a vendor-tracked actor with a Microsoft name or MITRE group ID; no Microsoft name is assigned. Victim-distribution figures differ by dataset (see gaps).

attribution.confidence: No source gathered attributes Madi to a government. Seculert found Farsi strings and Persian-calendar dates in components, and its CTO said the author was fluent in Persian [S2][S4]. Symantec suggested an unknown Farsi-speaking individual with a broad agenda [S4]. Kaspersky and Seculert found no apparent connection to Flame and did not speculate on a sponsor [S4]. Seculert's CTO later said mounting evidence suggested the malware was built by Iranians, primarily to spy on people inside Iran [S3].
attribution.basis: Language artifacts (Farsi strings, Persian-calendar dates), victim set, and early C2 hosting in Tehran before servers moved to Canada, per Seculert as reported by press [S4][S3]. These are circumstantial vendor observations, not government attribution.

actors.objectives: Surveillance of selected individuals and organizations: the malware stole files, logged keystrokes, captured screenshots and recorded audio [S1][S5]. Spied-on applications included Gmail, Hotmail, Yahoo! Mail, ICQ, Skype, Google+ and Facebook, plus ERP/CRM and financial systems [S1]. The sponsor's strategic intent is not established in the sources gathered.

sectors: Critical infrastructure project personnel (Iran and Israel)
regions: Later victims reported in the United States and Germany [S3]
targeting.notes: Sinkhole counts reported by press: at least 387 computers in Iran, 54 in Israel, 14 in Afghanistan, 6 in the UAE and 4 in Saudi Arabia [S6]. Symantec's data put about 72 percent of targets in Israel, a figure that may reflect Symantec's customer base [S5]. Seculert reported more than 150 new victims since June, including some tied to the US and Germany [S3].

capabilities.summary: Spread by rogue emails using basic social engineering, with specially crafted PowerPoint files; lures included a missile-test video and a copy of a Daily Beast article on Israel-Iran electronic warfare [S2][S5]. The Trojan stole files, logged keystrokes, took screenshots at set intervals, recorded audio and could update itself [S1][S5]. Kaspersky called the malware crude, yet the operators sustained surveillance [S2][S5]. A variant compiled 25 July 2012 added monitoring of Jabber and VKontakte conversations and uploaded stolen data to the server without waiting for commands [S6].

campaigns.summary: Seculert traced variants of the malware to December 2011, when the C2 domain was hosted on a server in Tehran; main servers later moved to Canada.

campaigns.name: Continued victim growth
campaigns.summary: Seculert reported more than 150 new victims since June 2012, including some tied to the US and Germany. The first victim using a 'Flame' prefix began contacting C2 in early June; researchers found no apparent link to Flame.

campaigns.name: Public disclosure and sinkholing
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky Lab and Seculert announced Madi after sinkholing the C2 servers; more than 800 victims over about eight months, mostly in Iran and Israel. Symantec published its own analysis the next day.

campaigns.name: New variant after C2 takedown

campaigns.name: Follow-up reporting of continued infections

diamond.adversary: Unknown, Persian-speaking developer(s); Farsi strings and Persian-calendar dates in code. No government attribution in the sources gathered [S2][S4].
diamond.capability: Email-delivered PowerPoint lures with a Trojan providing file theft, keylogging, screenshots, audio capture and self-update [S1][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Four C2 servers sinkholed by Kaspersky and Seculert; early hosting in Tehran, later in Canada [S1][S4].
diamond.victim: Individuals and organizations in Iran and Israel tied to infrastructure projects, finance, engineering and government, plus smaller numbers elsewhere [S1][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Iran-Israel tension supplied the lure themes (missile test, electronic-warfare article) [S2][S5]. Sponsor motive is not established.
diamond.technology: Reliance on user opening of Office attachments and on commonly used webmail, messaging and business-application accounts that were monitored [S1][S5].

gaps: No sponsor is established. Language clues are circumstantial and do not identify a state actor [S2][S4].
Victim distribution conflicts: sinkhole data (Kaspersky/Seculert) pointed mostly to Iran, while Symantec reported about 72 percent in Israel; the cause is not resolved in the sources [S5].

The Securelist 'Madi Campaign' Parts I and II, the CFR Cyber Operations Tracker entry, the Symantec blog (archived) and Threatpost article listed in the record could not be opened in this session; technical detail here relies on press coverage.
Several press sources are cited at month-level dates because exact publication days were not visible.
No activity after late 2012 was found; whether the operators persisted or retooled is unknown.
Overlap with Flame was examined by researchers who found no apparent connection [S4]; no link to other named actors is established.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the user endpoint and its webmail, messaging and ERP/CRM accounts, not hardened infrastructure [S1]. STEP 2: The adversary used a low-sophistication Trojan with topical lures and sustained collection, so persistence rather than technical novelty is the threat [S2][S5]. STEP 3: The template is a themed email with a PowerPoint attachment, then Trojan install, then keylogging, screenshots, audio and file theft to C2 [S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-cost surveillance of individuals tied to regional infrastructure, finance and government. MDCOA is retooled variants that add messaging platforms and rapid exfiltration, as the July 2012 variant did [S6]. Candidate indicators: unexpected PowerPoint attachments with geopolitical lures, mahdi.txt on hosts, and periodic outbound uploads from user workstations [S3][S5]. Relevance to US forces is indirect and historical; the sources show limited US victimization [S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat this as a historical regional-espionage case study; no current activity was found. (2) Authorities: sinkholing was done by private vendors, so any takedown of similar infrastructure needs legal review and partner coordination. (3) Mission assurance: protect planners' personal and commercial webmail and messaging accounts, which this campaign targeted [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with vendors and partners, noting that takedown did not end the campaign, since a new variant appeared after C2 domains were shut down [S6].

identification.summary: MalKamak is a name Cybereason gave to an Iranian threat group it says has been operating since at least 2018 and was first publicly reported in October 2021 [S1][S2]. Cybereason's Nocturnus and Incident Response teams tracked its activity as Operation GhostShell, an espionage campaign against aerospace and telecommunications firms [S1][S3]. The group's main tool is ShellClient, a previously undocumented RAT that evaded antivirus and used Dropbox for command and control [S1][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Cybereason: ShellClient development dates to at least November 2018; the vendor first responded to the activity in July 2021 and published in October 2021 [S1][S3][S5].
identification.notes: MalKamak is a Cybereason cluster name. Microsoft has no mapped name in this encyclopedia record. ETDA's threat group card, as summarized in search results, lists no alias other than MalKamak and Operation GhostShell as the campaign name, both from Cybereason [S7]. Cybereason notes possible links to Chafer (APT39) and Agrius but assesses MalKamak as distinct; these clusters are kept separate here [S2][S3].

attribution.sponsor: Iran, as assessed by Cybereason; ETDA's card, as summarized in search results, lists the group as state-sponsored [S1][S7]. No government attribution found.
attribution.confidence: Cybereason said it is confident, based primarily on code analysis, that MalKamak is an Iranian group [S5]. Cybereason described links to Chafer (APT39) and Agrius as possible but not enough for a firm link [S2][S3].
attribution.basis: Cybereason code analysis [S5]. Overlap with Chafer was shared credential-dumping and persistence methods. Overlap with Agrius was similar coding style and conventions, plus a ShellClient-associated domain that resolved to the same IP addresses as a domain used by Agrius's IPsec Helper malware. A Cybereason analyst speculated that a former member of Chafer or Agrius could now be involved, or that the three groups share tooling; this is speculation, not a confirmed link [S3].

actors.objectives: Cybereason assessed the campaign aimed to steal sensitive information about critical assets, organizations' infrastructure and technology [S3]. Motivation is listed as information theft and espionage in ETDA's card, as summarized in search results [S7].

targeting.notes: Cybereason reported at least 10 affected organizations in the aerospace and telecom sectors, mostly in the Middle East with some in the U.S., Russia and Europe [S3][S6]. Individual victims were not named in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: ShellClient evolved from a basic reverse shell into a fuller espionage backdoor, with development dating to at least 2018 [S3][S5]. Version 4 is a modular PE using Costura to compress modules with zlib, and it stores most strings as bytes decoded at runtime to evade string-based detection [S5]. It profiles hosts (BIOS and MAC data, network details, installed antivirus, public IP via ipinfo[.]io) to derive a per-host agent ID [S5]. C2 uses the Dropbox API with an embedded key; data is AES-encrypted with a hardcoded key; victims poll a commands folder every two seconds and upload results to an agents folder [S5]. Persistence and SYSTEM privileges come from a service named nhdService, shown as Network Hosts Detection Service [S5]. Operators dumped credentials from lsass using an executable named lsa.exe that Cybereason suspects is a SafetyKatz variant but did not obtain [S4][S5]. Lateral movement used WMI, PAExec and net use [S4]. Initial access vector was not identified in the sources gathered.

diamond.adversary: Iranian group MalKamak per Cybereason, with possible but unconfirmed ties to Chafer and Agrius [S2][S5].
diamond.capability: ShellClient RAT (Costura/zlib modular build, byte-encoded strings), lsa.exe credential dumping, WMI/PAExec/net use lateral movement [S4][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Dropbox accounts and API used as C2 with AS and CS folders; a ShellClient-associated domain shared IP addresses with an Agrius IPsec Helper domain [S3][S5].
diamond.victim: At least 10 aerospace and telecom organizations, mostly Middle East, plus U.S., Russia and Europe [S3][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Espionage collection on critical assets, infrastructure and technology of aerospace and telecom firms [S3][S7].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints with antivirus that relied on signatures/strings, and permissive egress to cloud storage such as Dropbox [S5].

gaps: Initial access vector is not stated in the sources gathered.
The Cybereason primary report could not be fetched (host unreachable from this environment); details rely on trade-press and search-result summaries of it [S1][S3][S5].
No reporting of MalKamak or ShellClient activity after October 2021 was found.
Victims are unnamed, and no government attribution or sponsor entity (for example IRGC or MOIS) is given.
Relationship to Chafer (APT39) and Agrius is unresolved; do not merge clusters [S2][S3].
MITRE ATT&CK has no group ID for MalKamak in this record; technique mapping not verified.
Version-by-version ShellClient evolution (2018 to v4) was not mapped in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Aerospace and telecom networks, and endpoints with permitted cloud-storage egress, are key terrain; aerospace firms overlap the defense industrial base [S3]. STEP 2: The actor operated undetected from at least 2018 until 2021 and relied on antivirus evasion and traffic blending with Dropbox [S3][S5]. STEP 3: Template is a persistent ShellClient service with SYSTEM rights, credential dumping from lsass, then lateral movement via WMI, PAExec or net use, with Dropbox C2 [S4][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued quiet collection against aerospace and telecom targets in the Middle East, U.S. and Europe. MDCOA, an assessment not stated by sources, is use of access in telecom or aerospace firms to support regional contingency planning. Candidate indicators: new service named nhdService (Network Hosts Detection Service), processes polling Dropbox API about every two seconds, outbound requests to ipinfo[.]io/ip from servers, and lsass access by unknown executables such as lsa.exe [S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track ShellClient indicators and Dropbox-abuse detections across DIB and telecom partners; the primary report's IOCs should be pulled by an analyst with access [S3]. (2) Authorities: blocking or monitoring cloud-storage egress on contractor networks depends on owner authority; coordinate through DC3 and DIB cybersecurity channels. (3) Mission assurance: telecom and aerospace dependencies may be exposed; identify supplier systems that support mission-critical networks. (4) Coordination: attribution is vendor-only and linkage to Chafer or Agrius is unresolved, so prioritize detection and containment over naming [S2][S3].

identification.summary: Manatee Tempest (formerly DEV-0243) is a financially motivated, ransomware-associated group that Microsoft says overlaps with activity other vendors track as EvilCorp [S2][S3]. Microsoft cites the Dridex banking trojan as one of the earliest campaigns that made the group notorious [S2]. CrowdStrike, tracking the group as INDRIK SPIDER, says it has operated Dridex since June 2014 and expanded into targeted 'big game hunting' ransomware with BitPaymer in 2017 [S5]. Microsoft says the group buys access from DEV-0206 (Mustard Tempest), supplies custom Cobalt Strike loaders, deployed WastedLocker, then in-house PhoenixLocker and Macaw, and from about November 2021 the LockBit 2.0 RaaS payload [S1][S3]. In October 2024 the UK NCA, with the US and Australia, sanctioned Evil Corp members and described links to Russian intelligence services [S10][S11].
identification.firstObserved: CrowdStrike: Dridex operations since June 2014 [S5]. Microsoft gives no first-seen date for Manatee Tempest [S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Manatee Tempest; 'DEV-0243 is now tracked as Manatee Tempest' per Microsoft's April 2023 naming update [S2]. Microsoft's Security Insider profile lists EvilCorp as an alias [S3]. Mandiant tracks a highly overlapping cluster as UNC2165 and the FakeUpdates access chain separately as UNC1543 [S7]. CrowdStrike uses INDRIK SPIDER [S5][S13]. The access broker DEV-0206 / Mustard Tempest (SocGholish/FakeUpdates) is a separate Microsoft cluster that hands off access; do not merge their facts [S1]. Per the imported actor record, Microsoft's naming map also lists INDRIK SPIDER under Mustard Tempest; this record keeps Manatee Tempest as the Russia-origin ransomware cluster.

attribution.sponsor: Russia-based financially motivated criminal group with documented ties to Russian intelligence services, not a state unit. US Treasury (2019) said leader Maksim Yakubets worked for the FSB as of 2017 [S6]. The UK NCA (2024) said the group cultivated ties with the FSB, SVR and GRU, aided by Yakubets' father-in-law Eduard Benderskiy, a former senior official of the FSB's Vympel unit [S10].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft describes overlap between Manatee Tempest and EvilCorp, without a stated confidence level [S2]. Mandiant assesses with high confidence that UNC2165 shifted to LockBit to hinder attribution and evade sanctions, and calls UNC2165 highly likely the latest incarnation of Evil Corp [S7][S8]. State-link claims are made by US Treasury (2019) and the UK NCA (2024), not by Microsoft [S6][S10].
attribution.basis: US Treasury OFAC designations and DOJ indictments of Yakubets and Igor Turashev in December 2019, as reported [S6]; UK/US/Australian sanctions and a US indictment of Aleksandr Ryzhenkov in October 2024, as reported [S10][S11][S13]; Microsoft telemetry on DEV-0206 to DEV-0243 handoffs [S1][S2]; CrowdStrike and Mandiant malware and intrusion analysis [S5][S7].

actors.objectives: Primarily financial: Dridex credential theft and wire fraud against banks, then ransomware extortion of organizations [S5][S6]. Treasury said Dridex losses exceeded $100 million [S6]. Secondary state-aligned tasking is alleged: Treasury said Yakubets was tasked with projects for the Russian state, including acquiring confidential documents through cyber means [S6], and the NCA, as reported, said Russian intelligence services tasked the group with cyber attacks and espionage operations against NATO allies [S10][S13]. Since 2021 the group has used RaaS brands such as LockBit to hide its identity and evade sanctions [S1][S7].

sectors: Organizations running domain-joined VMware ESXi hypervisors [S4]
regions: Global: Dridex victims in over 40 countries [S6]
targeting.notes: Targeting is opportunistic, shaped by the access DEV-0206/FakeUpdates infections provide, then narrowed to high-value organizations [S1][S5][S7]. NCC Group reportedly said the group did not steal or threaten to publish victim data in WastedLocker operations [S12]. Details of the alleged NATO espionage targets were not disclosed [S10].

capabilities.summary: Custom malware development across a decade: the Dridex banking trojan with repeated module and anti-analysis updates [S5]; BitPaymer ransomware, with Dridex typically installed before BitPaymer deployment [S5]; WastedLocker, Hades, PhoenixLocker and Macaw ransomware [S1][S3][S7]; and custom Cobalt Strike loaders resembling Blister inner payloads [S1]. Initial access commonly comes from the SocGholish/FakeUpdates chain run by DEV-0206/UNC1543, including FakeUpdates delivered through existing Raspberry Robin infections in 2022 [S1][S2][S7]. Hands-on-keyboard lateral movement resembles nation-state and penetration-testing tradecraft [S5]. Since about November 2021 the group has used the LockBit RaaS payload to avoid attribution [S1][S7]. In 2024 Microsoft named Manatee Tempest among ransomware operators using the 'ESX Admins' technique (CVE-2024-37085) to gain full control of domain-joined ESXi hypervisors [S4]. Aleksandr Ryzhenkov is reported to be a LockBit affiliate [S11][S13].

gaps: Primary government documents (Treasury OFAC 2019 and 2024 releases, DOJ indictments, NCA 'Evil Corp: Behind the Screens' report) were not opened; details rely on press coverage of them.
Coverage of the NCA report differs on whether SVR and GRU ties were established or only sought. The nature, dates and targets of the alleged NATO espionage operations are undisclosed.
Microsoft gives no confidence level for the Manatee Tempest/EvilCorp overlap. Vendor cluster boundaries among Manatee Tempest, UNC2165 and INDRIK SPIDER may not coincide exactly.
Microsoft's naming map reportedly lists INDRIK SPIDER under both Manatee Tempest and Mustard Tempest (per imported record); the mapping file was not re-verified this session.
No public reporting from 2025-2026 on Manatee Tempest activity was found; current operational status, and whether the group still deploys LockBit after Operation Cronos, is unknown.
Garmin attribution to Evil Corp came from NCC Group as reported; Arete IR called the evidence inconclusive, and payment was never confirmed by Garmin [S12].
Which ransomware Manatee Tempest deployed in the 2024 ESXi attacks is not specified by Microsoft [S4].
CrowdStrike's October 2024 blog and The Register/Infosecurity coverage could not be fetched; claims from them rely on search-result summaries.

Fact-check 2026-10-14: a TechRadar source (since removed) not found in search and removed with its sole-sourced claims (earnings since 2011, at least $300M, CNI/government targeting). Microsoft S1-S4, CrowdStrike S5 and Computing S12 URLs were not re-verified by search this pass.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (environment): Key terrain is enterprise Windows endpoints exposed to browser-update lures and removable media, Active Directory, and domain-joined ESXi hypervisors hosting mission systems [S1][S2][S4]. STEP 2 (effects): A single SocGholish or Raspberry Robin foothold can be sold onward, so commodity infections on DoD or DIB networks are pre-ransomware warning, not noise [S1][S2]. ESXi encryption can take down many virtualized services at once [S4]. STEP 3 (threat model): access broker handoff, Cobalt Strike loader, credential theft and lateral movement, then mass encryption under a RaaS brand that hides the operator [S1][S5][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is financially motivated ransomware against large organizations including healthcare, deployed under another brand's payload [S1][S5]. MDCOA is state-tasked intrusion against NATO-member targets under criminal cover, using ransomware access for espionage or disruption [S6][S10][S13]. Candidate indicators: fake browser update ZIP/JS downloads executed by wscript, Raspberry Robin USB LNK infections, unexpected Cobalt Strike beacons after those infections, and creation of an 'ESX Admins' AD group [S1][S2][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track SocGholish/FakeUpdates and Raspberry Robin detections across DODIN segments as leading indicators, and include ESXi/AD hygiene status in mission-assurance dashboards [S1][S2][S4]. (2) Authorities: Evil Corp and named members are under US, UK and Australian sanctions, so any ransom-payment discussion by mission partners or contractors raises OFAC issues; coordinate with legal before engaging [S6][S11]. Criminal-cover operations with alleged intelligence tasking blur the line between law enforcement and military response [S10][S13]. (3) Mission assurance: plan for simultaneous loss of virtualized services and test restoration of hypervisor clusters [S4]. (4) Coordination: brand-based attribution is unreliable because the group uses LockBit and other RaaS payloads, so share indicators with FBI, CISA, DC3 and coalition partners (NCA) and avoid naming an actor from the ransom note alone [S1][S7][S11].

provenance.importedSummary: INDRIK SPIDER is a sophisticated eCrime group that has been operating Dridex since June 2014. In 2015 and 2016, Dridex was one of the most prolific eCrime banking trojans on the market and, since 2014, those efforts are thought to have netted INDRIK SPIDER millions of dollars in criminal profits. Throughout its years of operation, Dridex has received multiple updates with new modules developed and new anti-analysis features added to the malware. In August 2017, a new ransomware variant identified as BitPaymer was reported to have ransomed the U.K.’s National Health Service (NHS), with a high ransom demand of 53 BTC (approximately $200,000 USD). The targeting of an organization rather than individuals, and the high ransom demands, made BitPaymer stand out from other contemporary ransomware at the time. Though the encryption and ransom functionality of BitPaymer was not technically sophisticated, the malware contained multiple anti-analysis features that overlapped with Dridex. Later technical analysis of BitPaymer indicated that it had been developed by INDRIK SPIDER, suggesting the group had expanded its criminal operation to include ransomware as a monetization strategy.

identification.summary: Mango Sandstorm (formerly MERCURY; also tracked as MuddyWater) is an Iranian nation-state actor that Microsoft assesses with high confidence is affiliated with Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) [S1][S2]. Microsoft reports it mainly targets organizations in the Middle East and those doing business with Middle Eastern victims [S1]. In 2022 it exploited Log4j 2 vulnerabilities in internet-facing applications, including SysAid Server instances at Israeli organizations [S1]. In 2023 it enabled a destructive hybrid on-premises and cloud attack carried out by its likely partner Storm-1084 (DEV-1084) under the DarkBit persona [S2][S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft renamed MERCURY to Mango Sandstorm in its April 2023 taxonomy change; Sandstorm is Microsoft's family name for Iranian actors [S1][S2][S4]. Microsoft equates MERCURY with the MuddyWater name used by US Cyber Command [S1] and calls Mango Sandstorm 'a.k.a. MuddyWater' [S3]. Storm-1084 (formerly DEV-1084, DarkBit persona) is a separate Microsoft cluster that Microsoft assesses likely partnered with Mango Sandstorm; its destructive actions should not be merged into Mango Sandstorm's profile [S2]. Other vendor aliases in the base record (Seedworm, Static Kitten, TA450, Boggy Serpens, etc.) were not re-verified in this pass; see gaps.

attribution.sponsor: Iran, Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) [S1][S2][S3].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft assesses with high confidence that MERCURY/Mango Sandstorm is affiliated with MOIS [S1]. Microsoft reports that US Cyber Command publicly described MuddyWater as 'a subordinate element within the Iranian Ministry of Intelligence and Security' [S1][S2]. Microsoft's 2024 Iran report calls Mango Sandstorm 'MOIS-linked' [S3].
attribution.basis: Microsoft Threat Intelligence telemetry and incident analysis [S1][S2]; Microsoft's citation of the public US Cyber Command attribution of MuddyWater to MOIS [S1][S2]. The Cyber Command primary statement was not opened directly in this research pass.

actors.objectives: Microsoft's reporting shows access operations against Middle Eastern, especially Israeli, organizations [S1]. It also shows Mango Sandstorm providing access that let a partner cluster (Storm-1084) carry out destruction and disruption disguised as criminal ransomware [S2][S3]. That pattern supports both espionage-style access and Iranian state-directed destructive effects against Israel [S2][S3].

sectors: Organizations running vulnerable internet-facing applications (SysAid Server, VMware products affected by Log4j 2) [S1]
Hybrid on-premises and Microsoft cloud (Azure/Microsoft 365) enterprise environments [S2]
regions: Middle East, and organizations doing business with Middle Eastern victims [S1]
targeting.notes: The sources gathered in this pass do not break targeting down by sector; sector data from other vendors and from US government advisories still needs verification (see gaps).

capabilities.summary: Opportunistic exploitation of unpatched internet-facing applications, including Log4j 2 (Log4Shell) in SysAid Server and VMware applications in 2022 [S1]. Follow-on access uses web shells, new local administrator accounts, and startup-folder and registry autostart persistence [S1]. Credential theft uses Mimikatz and SQL-server credential dumping [S1][S2]. Lateral movement uses WMI, RemCom, remote scheduled tasks and encoded PowerShell [S1][S2]. Tunneling and remote access use Ligolo-based tools, Venom proxy, OpenSSH, RPort, and the eHorus remote monitoring product [S1][S2]. The actor also sends spear-phishing from compromised mailboxes with commercial remote-access tools such as ScreenConnect [S1]. In the 2023 hybrid attack, the actors compromised an Azure AD Connect server and used AADInternals to extract connector-account credentials. Microsoft attributes the AADInternals use with high confidence. The actors then abused Global Administrator access, OAuth application permissions and mailbox delegation. Storm-1084 used this access to delete Azure resources and deploy ransomware through Group Policy [S2]. Microsoft notes the actors often waited weeks or months between stages [S2].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Internet-facing enterprise applications (help-desk/ITSM servers such as SysAid, VMware services) and identity synchronization servers (Azure AD Connect) are key cyber terrain. Compromising them gives access to both on-premises and cloud environments [S1][S2]. STEP 2 (effects): Microsoft's reporting shows the actor waiting weeks to months between stages. Access gained for espionage can later be handed to a destructive partner, so dwell time is effectively preparation of the environment [S2]. STEP 3 (adversary template): exploit an N-day in an exposed application, then web shell and local admin account. Next comes credential theft (Mimikatz, SQL dumping), WMI/RemCom lateral movement, and Ligolo/eHorus/RPort tunneling. The actor then pivots to Azure AD Connect and uses AADInternals to escalate to Global Administrator [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent access and collection against Israeli and Middle Eastern organizations and their partners via unpatched public-facing applications and phishing from compromised mailboxes [S1]. MDCOA is a staged handoff to a destructive partner using a fake ransomware persona. That partner deletes cloud resources and deploys encryption via Group Policy against a partner-nation or US-affiliated hybrid enterprise during a regional crisis [S2][S3]. Candidate indicators: new local administrator accounts on internet-facing servers; RemCom, Ligolo (e.g., vpnui.exe), Venom, eHorus, RPort or unexpected ScreenConnect installs; AADInternals execution on Azure AD Connect hosts; OAuth apps newly granted full_access_as_app; new 'Send on behalf' mailbox delegations; NETLOGON-share payloads distributed via new GPOs [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: correlate on-premises indicators (web shells, tunneling tools) with cloud identity events (Global Admin activity, OAuth consent, Azure resource deletions). Microsoft's 2023 case moved from on-premises to cloud destruction within hours once Global Admin was obtained [S2]. (2) Authorities: the DarkBit-style criminal persona can mislead early characterization. Microsoft assessed the persona as masking Iranian state involvement, so treat ransomware events at Israeli or Middle Eastern partner organizations as potential state-directed activity until assessed otherwise [S2][S3]. (3) Mission assurance: enforce MFA on all privileged and synchronization accounts and prioritize patching of internet-facing Log4j-affected applications. Treat Azure AD Connect servers as tier-0 assets [S1][S2]. (4) Coordination: Mango Sandstorm provides access and a separate cluster carries out effects, so share indicators across both Microsoft clusters and with coalition partners in the region. Detecting the access phase is the main opportunity to prevent the destructive phase [S2].

identification.summary: Marigold Sandstorm is Microsoft's name for an Iran-origin actor that Microsoft previously tracked as DEV-500 (DEV-0500) [S4][S5]. MITRE ATT&CK maps Marigold Sandstorm and DEV-0500 to Moses Staff (G1009), a suspected Iranian group that has mainly targeted Israeli companies since at least September 2021 and says it aims to cause damage by leaking stolen data and encrypting networks without demanding a ransom [S1][S2]. Microsoft's February 2024 Iran report calls Moses Staff an 'IRGC-run cyber persona' [S8]. Secureworks tracks the operator behind the Moses Staff and Abraham's Ax personas as COBALT SAPLING [S10].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least September 2021 [S1]. Kaspersky says Moses Staff was first seen on underground forums in September 2021 [S11].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Marigold Sandstorm (formerly DEV-500). Microsoft's mapping file lists DEV-500 and VENGEFUL KITTEN as other names but not 'Moses Staff' [S4]. The Sandstorm family name denotes Iran attribution [S5]. The Moses Staff equivalence comes from MITRE ATT&CK, which cites Microsoft's July 2023 naming page [S1][S6], and from MISP Galaxy [S7]. Microsoft's February 2024 report refers to 'Moses Staff' as a persona and does not use the name Marigold Sandstorm [S8]. Abraham's Ax (from November 2022) is a second persona that Secureworks assesses is likely run by the same operator (COBALT SAPLING) [S10].

attribution.sponsor: Iran. Microsoft describes Moses Staff as an IRGC-run cyber persona [S8], and its naming taxonomy places Marigold Sandstorm in the Iran (Sandstorm) family [S4][S5]. Secureworks believes COBALT SAPLING is Iranian in origin [S10]. MITRE uses 'suspected Iranian' [S1].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft states the IRGC link as fact in a February 2024 report but does not give a confidence level in the passage reviewed [S8]. Secureworks assesses the Moses Staff/Abraham's Ax link as likely [S10]. MITRE ATT&CK hedges ('suspected Iranian') [S1]. Kaspersky refers to Moses Staff as 'alleged to be an Iranian hacker group' [S11]. The sources gathered contain no US or Israeli government attribution.
attribution.basis: Microsoft Threat Intelligence assessment [S8] and naming mapping [S4]. Secureworks CTU analysis of shared iconography, videography, leak sites and malware artifacts [S10]. Technical reporting by Check Point (November 2021) and Cybereason (February 2022), as summarized by MITRE [S1][S2][S3].

actors.objectives: Politically motivated disruption and hack-and-leak operations. Moses Staff openly states it aims to damage Israeli companies by leaking stolen data and encrypting networks without asking for a ransom [S1][S2]. Microsoft places the persona inside Iran's IRGC-run cyber-enabled influence activity [S8]. Secureworks reports that the Abraham's Ax persona targets Saudi government ministries. It assesses this is likely a response to Saudi Arabia's leadership role in improving relations between Israel and Arab states. Secureworks adds that such personas give the Government of Iran plausible deniability [S10].

regions: Italy, India, Germany, Chile, Turkey, the UAE and the United States [S1][S3]
targeting.notes: Israeli companies are the primary focus [S1][S2]. Targeting outside Israel and the sector list come from Cybereason's February 2022 reporting, as summarized by MITRE [S1][S3]. Saudi targeting is attributed to the Abraham's Ax persona, which Secureworks links to the same operator [S10]. Several victim claims (an Israeli power plant, a defense ministry, security cameras) are the persona's own claims and are only partly confirmed [S8][S12][S13].

capabilities.summary: Initial access through known vulnerabilities in internet-facing infrastructure such as Microsoft Exchange, followed by obfuscated ASPX web shells [S1][S2]. PyDCrypt is a PyInstaller-compiled loader tailored to each victim. It opens firewall rules for SMB, NetBIOS and RPC to spread through the network, then drops DCSrv [S1][S2]. DCSrv is a time-triggered encryptor built on the open-source DiskCryptor and its signed drivers. It encrypts whole drives and offers no ransom path, so it works as a wiper [S1][S2]. PsExec is used for lateral movement [S1]. Since at least November 2021 the group has used StrifeWater, a reconnaissance RAT with screenshot, file-collection and module-download functions [S1][S3]. Stolen data goes to leak sites and Telegram/social channels. Leaked material has been reused by other Iran-linked personas, for example Cyber Avengers in October 2023 [S8][S11][S12].

diamond.capability: Exchange/public-facing exploitation, obfuscated web shells, PyDCrypt, DCSrv (DiskCryptor-based full-disk encryption), StrifeWater RAT, PsExec, and hack-and-leak publicity [S1][S2][S3][S12].
diamond.infrastructure: Web shells on compromised IIS/Exchange servers and StrifeWater C2 [S1][S2][S3]. Leak sites shared across personas, plus Telegram and X accounts used for claims [S8][S12].
diamond.victim: Mainly Israeli companies and government-linked entities. Also organizations in Italy, India, Germany, Chile, Turkey, the UAE and the US, and Saudi ministries via Abraham's Ax [S1][S3][S10].
diamond.socioPolitical: Anti-Israel hack-and-leak meant to cause damage and psychological effect rather than profit [S1][S2]. Abraham's Ax aims to disrupt Israel-Saudi normalization [S10]. The personas give Iran deniability within IRGC influence activity [S8][S10].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is internet-facing Exchange/IIS servers and flat Windows networks where SMB and RPC can be opened between hosts [S1][S2]. Israeli and partner-nation government, energy, utility and manufacturing organizations make up the relevant part of the environment, along with Saudi ministries via the Abraham's Ax persona [S1][S3][S10]. STEP 2 (effects): Whole-disk encryption with no recovery path works as a wiper. Leaks and Telegram claims add an influence layer that IRGC-linked media amplify, so perceived effects can exceed real ones [S1][S2][S8]. STEP 3 (adversary template): exploit an Exchange server, drop an obfuscated web shell, run StrifeWater reconnaissance, steal data, then spread PyDCrypt via opened firewall rules and PsExec. This ends in time-triggered DCSrv encryption and a public leak through persona channels [S1][S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is hack-and-leak with destructive encryption against Israeli entities, timed to political events, with claims recycled by sister personas [S8][S11][S12]. MDCOA is the same template against partner-nation energy or utility providers supporting coalition operations, combined with false or exaggerated outage claims to shape perceptions during a crisis [S8]. Candidate indicators: new ASPX files under IIS aspnet_client paths, bulk netsh firewall changes that allow SMB/RPC/NetBIOS, DiskCryptor drivers on servers, StrifeWater beacons, and Moses Staff or Abraham's Ax Telegram/X posts naming a partner organization [S1][S2][S3][S12].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track patch status of internet-facing Exchange/IIS assets across DODIN and mission-partner enclaves, and monitor persona leak channels as early warning [S1][S2][S12]. (2) Authorities: no-ransom encryption is destructive state-linked activity rather than criminal extortion [S1][S8]. Responses may need DCO and interagency coordination, and public attribution claims should credit the assessing source (Microsoft, Secureworks). (3) Mission assurance: keep offline backups and recovery plans for full-disk encryption, and segment networks to resist bulk SMB/RPC firewall changes [S1][S2]. (4) Coordination: Israeli and Gulf partners are primary targets [S1][S10]. Share indicators with coalition CERTs, and coordinate public messaging to counter exaggerated persona claims amplified by IRGC-linked media [S8].

identification.summary: Russian foreign intelligence (SVR) cyber-espionage actor that conducts long-term, patient intrusions against governments, diplomatic entities, NGOs and IT service providers, mainly in the US and Europe [S1]. Responsible for the SolarWinds supply-chain compromise (attributed 2021) [S3] and the 2023–2024 breach of Microsoft's corporate email [S1]. Known for identity- and cloud-focused tradecraft: password spraying, OAuth application abuse and residential proxy networks [S1].

capabilities.summary: Identity and cloud tradecraft: password spraying from residential proxies against accounts without MFA, abuse of legacy OAuth applications to grant itself mailbox access (full_access_as_app) through Exchange Web Services [S1]. Large-scale spear-phishing with signed RDP configuration files that map local resources to actor-controlled servers (Oct 2024, thousands of targets in over 100 organizations) [S2]. Supply-chain compromise (SolarWinds Orion) [S3]. MITRE lists 66 techniques and 49 software entries, including the 'Duke' malware families, WellMess and Cobalt Strike [S4].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The cyberspace OE includes cloud identity tenants (Entra ID/M365), SaaS providers and IT service providers. For this actor, key terrain is identity infrastructure, not network perimeters. STEP 2: Residential-proxy sourcing defeats IP reputation and geolocation, so detection terrain is authentication telemetry. STEP 3: The template is low-and-slow password spray, then a foothold in an overlooked or legacy account without MFA, then OAuth app abuse or privilege grants, then mailbox and document collection. A parallel option is a supply-chain or provider compromise. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent collection on NATO and US government decision-making and on IT providers. MDCOA is a supply-chain compromise of a DoD or DIB software or cloud provider giving broad access during a crisis. Candidate indicators: new OAuth app consents or role grants (full_access_as_app), spray patterns against legacy accounts, and RDP files arriving by email [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Identity is the primary sensor: JCC2 situational awareness must include cloud sign-in and app-consent logs from DoD and partner tenants. (2) Third-party risk: a breach at a provider (cloud, IT service, software vendor) is a DoD event, so reporting agreements with providers are part of C2. (3) MFA and legacy-account hygiene across test and non-production tenants is a mission assurance requirement. (4) Counterintelligence fusion: SVR collection is foreign intelligence, so coordinate cyber findings with CI channels.

provenance.importedSummary:
APT29 is threat group that has been attributed to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). They have operated since at least 2008, often targeting government networks in Europe and NATO member countries, research institutes, and think tanks. APT29 reportedly compromised the Democratic National Committee starting in the summer of 2015.

In April 2021, the US and UK governments attributed the SolarWinds Compromise to the SVR; public statements included citations to APT29, Cozy Bear, and The Dukes. Industry reporting also referred to the actors involved in this campaign as UNC2452, NOBELIUM, StellarParticle, Dark Halo, and SolarStorm.

identification.summary: Iranian state-sponsored actor associated with an intelligence arm of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). It runs long-term espionage through targeted phishing and social engineering against dissidents, journalists, academics, think tanks, policymakers and government officials. One subgroup rapidly weaponizes newly public vulnerabilities against critical-infrastructure targets [S1]. It targeted a 2024 US presidential campaign [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: FireEye identified APT35 operations dating back to 2014 (imported record). Microsoft reports a subgroup moving from reconnaissance to direct targeting of US critical infrastructure from late 2021 to mid-2022 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Mint Sandstorm (formerly PHOSPHORUS). Microsoft maps CHARMING KITTEN, APT35, Newscaster and Parastoo to it [S5]. MITRE tracks it as Magic Hound (G0059) [S4]. Google/Mandiant's APT42 overlaps with part of this activity, and coverage of the 2024 election case uses 'Mint Sandstorm or APT42' interchangeably. This encyclopedia holds a separate APT42 record; vendor cluster boundaries differ.

attribution.confidence: Microsoft assesses the IRGC association, corroborated by Mandiant, Proofpoint and Secureworks; the US Treasury sanctioned elements of the group in 2022 citing IRGC sponsorship [S1]. Formal US attribution through the 2024 indictment of three named IRGC employees for the campaign hack [S3].

actors.objectives: Intelligence collection in support of IRGC priorities: monitoring dissidents and activists, collecting on foreign policy, defense and nuclear-related experts, and gaining access to critical infrastructure that could support retaliation [S1]. In 2024 it ran a hack-and-leak operation against a US presidential campaign, attempting to pass stolen material to people it believed were tied to the opposing campaign [S3].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering is the core tradecraft: tailored spear-phishing, impersonation and credential harvesting, including multi-week rapport building before delivery [S1][S3]. A subgroup weaponizes public proofs of concept within days: Zoho ManageEngine CVE-2022-47966 (exploited the day the PoC appeared), IBM Aspera Faspex CVE-2022-47986 (within five days) and Log4Shell [S1]. Custom tooling includes Drokbk and Soldier (.NET implants) and CharmPower (modular PowerShell backdoor delivered through template injection) [S1].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The OE includes the personal accounts and devices of staff, policy advisers and family members, because this actor works through people more than networks. STEP 2: In a US–Iran crisis, expect collection against planners, think tanks and media plus opportunistic access to US port, energy and transit infrastructure. STEP 3: The template is persona-driven rapport building, then credential phishing or a malicious template, then a PowerShell or .NET implant. In parallel, a separate team exploits newly published CVEs within days. STEP 4: MLCOA is intensified phishing of government, military and policy personnel to inform IRGC decision-making. MDCOA is hack-and-leak or opportunistic infrastructure disruption timed to political events or military action. Candidate indicators: new lookalike domains for US government or think-tank brands, phishing that references real conferences or interviews, and exploitation within days of a public PoC [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Personnel-centric defense: phishing-resistant MFA and reporting channels for personal accounts of key staff are C2 protection measures. (2) Patch tempo as an operational metric: the subgroup's days-to-exploit window means JCC2 situational awareness should track exposure time on internet-facing systems, not just patch compliance. (3) Information environment: hack-and-leak threats require coordination with public affairs and counterintelligence before material surfaces. (4) Authorities: election and campaign infrastructure defense is led by the FBI and CISA, so DoD's role is limited to its own personnel and networks.

identification.summary: MirrorFace is a China-linked cyber-espionage actor that mainly targets Japan. ESET first documented it in 2022, when it went after Japanese political entities ahead of an election [S2]. In January 2025, Japan's National Police Agency (NPA) and its national cybersecurity center publicly attributed a campaign to it that had run since 2019 and sought information on Japan's national security and advanced technology [S1][S9]. In 2024 it reached beyond Japan: ESET reported its first known European target (a Central European diplomatic institute) [S3], and Trend Micro reported targets in Taiwan and India [S4]. Its signature tools are LODEINFO and NOOPDOOR (which ESET calls HiddenFace), plus the revived ANEL backdoor [S3][S4][S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: Japanese police: active since at least 2019 [S1]. Trend Micro: LODEINFO used exclusively by Earth Kasha since 2019 [S4]. Trend Micro's 2025 reporting says Earth Kasha has run espionage since at least 2017 [S7].
identification.notes: Trend Micro tracks the overlapping cluster as Earth Kasha [S4][S5][S7], and Security Affairs reports Japan's advisory as treating MirrorFace and Earth Kasha as the same group [S1]. Cybereason reports a related LODEINFO/NOOPDOOR intrusion set as 'Cuckoo Spear' and links it to APT10 [S8]. The encyclopedia maps APT10 to Microsoft's Purple Typhoon record. No source gathered gives a separate Microsoft name for MirrorFace, so it is kept as a related sub-cluster rather than merged. MITRE tracks the group as G1054 [S11].

attribution.sponsor: China-linked. Japan's NPA describes the campaigns as systematic cyberattacks linked to China [S1][S9]. No source gathered names a specific PRC ministry or unit for MirrorFace itself.
attribution.confidence: Government attribution: Japan's NPA and its national cybersecurity center publicly attributed the 2019-2024 campaigns to MirrorFace in January 2025 [S1][S9]. Vendor positions changed over time. In 2022 ESET tracked MirrorFace as a separate entity and said it could not link it to a known APT group despite speculation about APT10 [S2]. In March 2025, after observing the APT10-associated ANEL backdoor, ESET assessed MirrorFace as a subgroup under the APT10 umbrella and noted this aligned with Kaspersky and Cybereason [S3]. Trend Micro says Earth Kasha is believed to be part of the wider APT10 umbrella [S7].
attribution.basis: Japanese government advisory (reported through press coverage) [S1][S9]; shared exclusive tooling (LODEINFO, NOOPDOOR/HiddenFace) and reuse of ANEL, which was previously tied to APT10 [S3][S5][S6]; vendor telemetry from ESET, Trend Micro, JPCERT/CC and Cybereason [S2][S3][S4][S6][S8].

actors.objectives: Espionage and theft of information. Japan's police say the goal was information on Japan's national security and advanced technology [S1][S9]. ESET describes the aim as espionage and exfiltrating files of interest [S2], and Trend Micro judged the primary motivation to be theft of victims' information and data [S4]. The 2022 targeting of a political party before the July 2022 House of Councillors election shows interest in Japanese domestic politics [S2].

sectors: Advanced technology, including aerospace, semiconductor and manufacturing [S4][S6][S9]
targeting.notes: JPCERT/CC says early targets were media, political organizations, think tanks and universities, and that the focus shifted to manufacturers and research institutions from 2023 [S6]. Trend Micro says the 2024 move back to spear-phishing reflects a shift from enterprise targets to individuals [S5].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing with malicious attachments and links, including OneDrive-hosted ZIP archives that contain macro-enabled droppers [S1][S5][S7]. In 2023 the group exploited internet-facing VPN and edge devices: Array AG (CVE-2023-28461), Proself (CVE-2023-45727), FortiOS/FortiProxy (CVE-2023-27997) and Citrix [S4][S6]. Its custom backdoors are LODEINFO, NOOPDOOR/HiddenFace (shellcode injected into legitimate processes, loaded through XML or DLL side-loading, with encrypted code stored in the registry) and ANEL (loaded by ANELLDR through DLL side-loading) [S3][S5][S6]. It also uses Cobalt Strike [S4]. Newer tradecraft includes a customized AsyncRAT run inside Windows Sandbox to evade security controls, abuse of Visual Studio Code remote tunnels [S3], an updated ANEL that can run Beacon Object Files in memory, and NOOPDOOR that uses DNS-over-HTTPS to hide C2 lookups [S7]. MITRE lists the group's software, including MirrorStealer, DOWNIISSA and NOOPLDR [S11].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The operational environment includes allied Japanese government, political, think-tank and defense-industrial networks, Taiwanese government institutions, and diplomatic bodies that engage on Japan [S1][S3][S7]. Internet-facing VPN appliances and personal or cloud email are key terrain [S4][S5]. STEP 2: Patches to edge devices (Array, Fortinet, Citrix) and controls on Windows Sandbox, VS Code tunnels and DoH egress shape the actor's access [S3][S4][S7]. STEP 3: The model runs from a tailored spear-phish (OneDrive ZIP, macro document, event-themed lure) or an edge-device exploit, to DLL side-loaded ANEL, LODEINFO or NOOPDOOR, to credential theft and file exfiltration [S3][S5][S6][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued spear-phishing of individuals in Japan- and Taiwan-related policy, research and diplomatic communities to collect security and technology information [S1][S5][S7]. MDCOA is exploitation of edge devices at defense-industrial or coalition partners, establishing durable NOOPDOOR access that harvests alliance planning or advanced-technology data during a regional crisis [S4][S6]. Candidate indicators: unexpected VS Code tunnel processes or code.exe network sessions; Windows Sandbox (.wsb) launched on non-developer hosts; signed binaries side-loading unknown DLLs; encrypted blobs in the registry; DoH traffic from endpoints; OneDrive-delivered ZIPs with macro-enabled Excel files [S3][S6][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Japanese government (NPA) and JPCERT/CC advisories alongside vendor reporting, because allied disclosures preceded or complemented vendor reporting [S1][S6]. (2) Authorities: the actor targets allied and partner networks (Japan, Taiwan, European diplomatic bodies), so most response actions sit with host nations; DoD action centers on its own networks and information sharing [S1][S3][S7]. (3) Mission assurance: harden and monitor internet-facing VPN appliances on DODIN and Defense Industrial Base enclaves that support Indo-Pacific operations, and restrict VS Code tunnels and Windows Sandbox where not required [S3][S4]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with Japanese counterparts, USINDOPACOM components and DC3/DIB partners, and deconflict naming (MirrorFace, Earth Kasha, APT10/Purple Typhoon) in shared reporting [S1][S3][S7].

identification.summary: Moafee is a China-based cyber espionage group named by FireEye in September 2014 research that described it as operating from Guangdong Province and targeting military and government organizations involved in the South China Sea dispute [S1][S2][S3]. FireEye reported targets that included organizations within the US defense industrial base [S3]. FireEye described Moafee alongside a second group, DragonOK, which shares custom backdoors, RATs and the HTRAN proxy tool but was assessed as a distinct group with a different mission and location [S1][S3]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks Moafee as G0002 [S4].
identification.firstObserved: Publicly named by FireEye in September 2014 [S1][S2][S3]. The start date of its activity is not stated in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: Microsoft name: none found in the sources gathered. Cluster boundary: FireEye treats Moafee (Guangdong) and DragonOK (Jiangsu) as separate groups that may be subgroups with their own mission focus [S1][S3]. This encyclopedia's imported record merges DragonOK, BRONZE OVERBROOK and Shallow Taurus into Moafee; the sources gathered here describe DragonOK as a related but separate cluster, and no gathered source mapped BRONZE OVERBROOK or Shallow Taurus to either name. Post-2014 campaigns below are DragonOK reporting and are labeled as such. Press coverage spells the name variously as Moafee, Moafree and Moafe [S3].

attribution.confidence: FireEye assessed Moafee as a China-based group operating from Guangdong Province [S1][S2][S3]. No government attribution or named state sponsor appears in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: FireEye research released in September 2014 ahead of its full 'Operation Quantum Entanglement' report, as covered by trade press [S1][S2][S3]; MITRE ATT&CK group entry G0002 [S4].

actors.objectives: Political and military espionage against government and military organizations with interests in the South China Sea dispute, per FireEye reporting [S2][S3]. FireEye contrasted this with DragonOK's economic espionage against high-tech and manufacturing companies [S1][S3].

targeting.notes: FireEye reported Moafee targets as military and government organizations involved in the South China Sea dispute, including organizations within the US defense industry [S2][S3]. Related cluster DragonOK targeted high-tech and manufacturing companies in Japan and Taiwan [S1][S2], and later Japan with possible targeting of Taiwan, Tibet and Russia [S6]. Specific Moafee victim countries are not named in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: FireEye reported that Moafee and DragonOK used similar TTPs, including custom-built backdoors and remote-administration tools, shared malware implants and social-engineering approaches, and the HTRAN proxy tool [S1][S2][S3]. MITRE ATT&CK notes binary padding for defense evasion and lists PoisonIvy among associated software [S4]. FireEye said the shared tooling may reflect collaboration, common training, a common toolkit supply chain, or a combination, and noted a possible third group using the same TTPs [S1][S3].

campaigns.name: Operation Quantum Entanglement (FireEye)
campaigns.summary: FireEye reported two China-based groups operating in parallel: Moafee, from Guangdong, targeting government and military organizations tied to the South China Sea dispute, including US defense industry targets, and DragonOK, from Jiangsu, targeting high-tech and manufacturing firms in Japan and Taiwan. Both used shared custom backdoors, RATs and HTRAN.

diamond.capability: Custom backdoors and RATs shared with DragonOK, the HTRAN proxy tool, PoisonIvy, and binary padding for evasion [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Proxied C2 using HTRAN [S2][S3]. No specific domains or IPs appear in the sources gathered.
diamond.victim: Government and military organizations involved in the South China Sea dispute, and US defense industrial base organizations [S2][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence on the South China Sea territorial dispute in support of Chinese interests, per FireEye's targeting description [S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Users' susceptibility to social engineering, and Windows hosts that run custom implants [S1][S4].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The relevant environment includes government, military and defense-industrial networks of South China Sea stakeholders, including US DIB contractors [S2][S3]. STEP 2: Spearphishing and custom RATs mean user mailboxes and endpoints are the primary avenues of approach [S1][S5]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is socially engineered delivery, then a custom backdoor or PoisonIvy, with C2 relayed through HTRAN proxies [S1][S3][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent collection of policy and military planning information related to South China Sea issues from government and DIB targets. MDCOA is coordinated collection across allied and partner networks during a maritime crisis, using shared toolkits that blur attribution between related clusters [S1][S3]. Candidate indicators: HTRAN proxy activity, PoisonIvy or NewCT-family implants, binary-padded executables, and themed phishing to personnel working on the South China Sea [S3][S4][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: shared tooling across Moafee, DragonOK and a possible third group means detections of these malware families should be correlated across clusters rather than assigned to one actor [S1][S3]. (2) Authorities: DIB targeting implies coordination with contractors under DIB cybersecurity information-sharing mechanisms [S3]. (3) Mission assurance: protect planning data on South China Sea and Indo-Pacific operations held on mission-partner networks [S2][S3]. (4) Coordination: regional partners named as DragonOK targets (Japan, Taiwan) may hold telemetry relevant to the shared toolkit [S1][S6].

identification.summary: Mofang is a cyber-espionage group that Dutch security firm Fox-IT named and publicly exposed in June 2016. Fox-IT assesses it as almost certainly operating out of China and probably government-affiliated [S1][S2]. MITRE ATT&CK describes it as a likely China-based group that has run focused attacks on government and critical infrastructure in Myanmar and other countries, and says the name comes from its frequent practice of imitating a victim's infrastructure [S4]. The group relies on social engineering rather than exploits, delivering its custom ShimRat and ShimRatReporter tools [S1][S2][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Fox-IT reporting (via SecurityWeek): active since at least February 2012 [S2]. MITRE ATT&CK: observed since at least May 2012 [S4]. Fox-IT published its report on 2016-06-15 [S1].
identification.notes: MITRE ATT&CK group ID G0103 [S4]. The imported record lists BRONZE WALKER (Secureworks CTU) and Superman as aliases, but no cited source in this file confirms either name, so neither is added to aliasesAdd. Start dates differ: February 2012 in Fox-IT-derived press coverage [S2] versus May 2012 in MITRE [S4].

attribution.sponsor: Suspected People's Republic of China government affiliation (vendor assessment only) [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: Fox-IT says the actor almost certainly operates out of China and is probably government-affiliated [S1][S2]. MITRE describes it as a likely China-based group [S4]. These are vendor and knowledge-base assessments, not government attribution; no US or allied government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Fox-IT's analysis of tooling, infrastructure and target selection, which it links to investments or technological advances that could threaten the Chinese sphere of influence [S1][S2]. Press coverage reports that targeting of the Myanmar Kyaukphyu special economic zone lined up in time with a tender later won by China's CITIC group [S2].

actors.objectives: Politically and economically motivated information theft. Fox-IT links Mofang's target selection to investments or technological advances that could be perceived as a threat to China's sphere of influence [S1]. Press reporting says experts believe information taken from Myanmar government organizations and the Singapore firm CPG Corporation could have helped a Chinese company win the Kyaukphyu infrastructure tender. This is an expert inference, not a confirmed outcome [S2].

sectors: Engineering and consulting firms involved in Myanmar infrastructure (CPG Corporation) [S2]
targeting.notes: Fox-IT suspects there are more victims than the countries it lists [S1]. In 2015-2016 the reported targeting centers on Myanmar and on organizations with interests in Myanmar's Kyaukphyu special economic zone [S2].

capabilities.summary: Mofang does not use exploits for initial infection. It relies on social engineering, usually email inviting targets to open attached files or follow links [S1][S2]. The only exploits reported in its toolset are previously known privilege-escalation exploits built into the malware [S2]. Its custom tools ShimRat (a remote access trojan) and ShimRatReporter (used for automated initial discovery) date back to at least 2012 [S2][S4]. MITRE lists two software entries for the group, ShimRat (S0444) and ShimRatReporter (S0445). It also lists spearphishing attachments and links, user execution, and encrypted or compressed payloads among the group's techniques [S4]. The group's name comes from its practice of imitating victim infrastructure, such as lookalike domains [S4].

campaigns.name: Early ShimRat operations
campaigns.summary: Mofang has been active since at least February 2012 (MITRE: May 2012), targeting government, military, critical infrastructure, automotive and weapons organizations in several countries including India, Germany, Canada, the United States, Singapore and South Korea [S2][S4].

campaigns.name: Kyaukphyu special economic zone targeting
campaigns.summary: In mid-2015 Mofang attacked Myanmar government organizations and the Singapore-based firm CPG Corporation, which had won a 2014 consulting tender for the Kyaukphyu SEZ. CITIC was later declared winner of an infrastructure tender in early 2016. Experts believe stolen information could have helped the Chinese bidder, though this is not confirmed [S2].

campaigns.name: Fox-IT public exposure
campaigns.summary: Fox-IT published its Mofang threat report, describing the group as almost certainly China-based and probably government-affiliated [S1][S3].

diamond.adversary: A likely China-based espionage group that Fox-IT assesses as probably government-affiliated [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: Social-engineering lures carrying the custom ShimRat RAT and ShimRatReporter discovery tool. The malware has built-in, previously known privilege-escalation exploits, and payloads are encrypted or compressed [S2][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Infrastructure that imitates the victim's own, which is the source of the 'Mofang' name [S4]. Specific domains and IP addresses are in the Fox-IT report, which was not opened for this file.

diamond.socioPolitical: Targeting tracks Chinese strategic and economic interests, such as Myanmar's Kyaukphyu SEZ, where China's CNPC had invested and CITIC won an infrastructure tender [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints reached through email and user execution of attachments or links [S2][S4].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1 (operational environment): concern centers on organizations tied to Chinese strategic investments and infrastructure projects, especially in Myanmar and South/Southeast Asia, and on defense and weapons-industry partners in allied nations [S1][S2]. Step 2 (effects): exposure is mainly loss of confidentiality of negotiating positions, tender data and defense-industrial information. No destructive activity is reported [S1][S2]. Step 3 (threat evaluation): low-sophistication initial access through social engineering, with no exploit-based entry; custom ShimRat tooling; and infrastructure that imitates victims [S2][S4]. Step 4: MLCOA is spearphishing with attachments or links aimed at government and partner organizations involved in China-linked economic projects, followed by ShimRat discovery and data theft [S2][S4]. MDCOA is long-term access to defense-industrial or military networks in partner nations, exposing weapons or program data [S2]. Candidate indicators include lookalike domains that mimic the victim organization [S4], email attachments that drop compressed or encrypted payloads [S4], and unexpected shim database installation (inferred from the ShimRat name; validate).
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Mofang's reported activity is from 2012-2016, with no recent public reporting, so treat it as a historical case study of economically motivated PRC-linked espionage rather than a current tracked threat [S1][S2][S4]. Authorities: attribution is vendor-only (Fox-IT, MITRE), so any defensive action should rest on observed indicators rather than government attribution [S1][S4]. Mission assurance: the threat to deployed or partner-nation networks comes mainly from user-targeted phishing, so user awareness and email and attachment controls are the main mitigations [S1][S2]. Coordination: the targeting of partner governments (for example Myanmar) and defense industry in allied countries [S2] suggests information sharing with partners and the defense industrial base.
