identification.summary: North Korean threat actor that Microsoft named in May 2024 (formerly Storm-1789). Microsoft says it runs both financially motivated and espionage operations against software and IT, education and defense industrial base targets [S1]. Its signature tradecraft is social engineering through fake companies, fake job offers and personas on LinkedIn, Telegram and freelancing platforms. Through those channels it delivers trojanized PuTTY, malicious npm packages and a fully functional malicious tank game [S1]. It deployed its own FakePenny ransomware in April 2024 [S1]. In February 2025 it began deploying Qilin ransomware-as-a-service payloads, its first use of ransomware not built in-house [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: earliest dated activity is trojanized PuTTY delivery in early August 2023 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Moonstone Sleet (formerly Storm-1789) [S1]. Microsoft reports that early activity strongly overlapped with Diamond Sleet, including reuse of Comebacker code. The group later moved to its own infrastructure and attacks, and the two groups have since run concurrent operations [S1]. Microsoft's mapping file lists CrowdStrike's LABYRINTH CHOLLIMA as a related name [S9], but CrowdStrike's LABYRINTH CHOLLIMA is a broader, older cluster (see gaps) [S8]. Checkmarx initially attributed the group's npm packages to Jade Sleet before separating them out by code style [S3][S4]. Datadog tracks an npm cluster called Stressed Pungsan that overlaps with Moonstone Sleet [S5]. MITRE tracks the group as G1036 [S10].

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea). Microsoft describes Moonstone Sleet as a North Korean threat actor [S1] and later as 'a North Korean state actor' [S2].
attribution.confidence: Attribution to North Korea is Microsoft's assessment [S1][S2]. No government attribution of Moonstone Sleet by name was found in the sources gathered. Bitdefender describes Moonstone Sleet's role in the 2025 'Korean Leaks' campaign as only 'potential' involvement [S6][S7].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry, code overlap with Diamond Sleet (Comebacker) and infrastructure analysis [S1]. Checkmarx found indicators linking npm packages to Moonstone Sleet [S3][S4].

actors.objectives: Microsoft assesses dual goals: intelligence collection, such as credential and intellectual-property theft from defense and aerospace firms, and revenue generation through ransomware, possibly also remote IT-worker employment [S1]. Microsoft says the move to Qilin RaaS continues the financially motivated line of effort [S2].

sectors: Defense industrial base and aerospace, including defense technology, drone technology and aircraft parts makers [S1]
Individual software developers and job seekers [S1][S3]
Financial services, potentially, via an MSP compromise in South Korea [S6][S7]
regions: Global; Microsoft does not name specific countries [S1]
South Korea (potential link through the 2025 Korean Leaks campaign) [S6][S7]
targeting.notes: Microsoft lists aerospace and defense intrusions in December 2023, April 2024 and May 2024 [S1]. The public npm registry gives the group access to an open-ended pool of developers [S3][S4]. Microsoft has not identified a Moonstone Sleet supply-chain attack, but warns that its access to software companies would pose a high risk [S1].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering with fake companies (StarGlow Ventures, C.C. Waterfall, DeTankZone) and fake recruiters or job applicants on LinkedIn, Telegram, freelancing sites and email [S1][S2]. Trojanized PuTTY delivered with the SplitLoader multi-stage dropper [S1]. npm packages disguised as skills tests, which Checkmarx says use a 'single-package approach' that runs at install time [S1][S3][S4]. A fully playable blockchain tank game (DeTankWar/DeTankZone) that delivers the custom YouieLoad loader [S1]. LSASS credential theft with Procdump and Mimikatz [S1]. Custom FakePenny ransomware, with one $6.6M Bitcoin ransom demand [S1]. Qilin RaaS ransomware deployed at a limited number of organizations since late February 2025 [S2].

The Hacker News reports more than 1 million files and 2 TB stolen from 28 victims.

diamond.adversary: North Korean state actor per Microsoft (formerly Storm-1789), with early overlap with Diamond Sleet [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: SplitLoader, YouieLoad, FakePenny, malicious npm packages, Mimikatz and Procdump against LSASS, and Qilin RaaS [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Fake company websites and domains such as starglowventures[.]com, ccwaterfall[.]com and detankwar[.]com; C2 domains such as mingeloem[.]com and matrixane[.]com; and the public npm registry [S1][S3].
diamond.victim: Software, IT, education, defense and aerospace organizations and individual developers; potentially South Korean financial firms reached through an MSP [S1][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: DPRK requirements for both foreign intelligence and hard-currency revenue, pursued by the same operators [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Developer trust in open-source packages, freelance and recruiting platforms, and shared tools such as PuTTY; MSP remote-management trust relationships [S1][S3][S6].

gaps: Microsoft's mapping links Moonstone Sleet to LABYRINTH CHOLLIMA [S9]. CrowdStrike's LABYRINTH CHOLLIMA is an older cluster (also UNC4034/Temp.Hermit) that CrowdStrike split into three adversaries in January 2026 [S8]. Which CrowdStrike sub-cluster, if any, corresponds to Moonstone Sleet is not stated in the sources gathered. Do not import LABYRINTH CHOLLIMA or Bureau 121 facts wholesale.
No government attribution or indictment naming Moonstone Sleet was found. The DPRK organizational sponsor (for example, which RGB element) is unverified.

Moonstone Sleet's role in Korean Leaks is described only as 'potential' [S6][S7]. The Bitdefender primary report and the CrowdStrike blog could not be fetched (host unreachable); details come from search summaries and secondary coverage.
BleepingComputer's coverage of Microsoft's March 2025 Qilin statement could not be fetched. The exact publication day and the victims are unknown.
No sources from 2026 describe new Moonstone Sleet operations, so current activity is unverified.
Overlap boundaries with Datadog's Stressed Pungsan and with Diamond Sleet and Jade Sleet npm activity are not fully resolved [S1][S3][S5].
The scale and placements of Moonstone Sleet's IT-worker job seeking are undocumented [S1].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the developer and contractor workforce: personal devices used for job hunting, npm and other package registries, and MSP management channels into DIB and aerospace suppliers [S1][S3][S6]. STEP 2: Recruiting platforms (LinkedIn, Telegram, freelance sites) and open package registries put the first contact outside DoD-controlled networks, which limits visibility before compromise [S1][S2]. STEP 3: The template is a persona and fake-company lure, then a trojanized tool, skills-test package or game, then a loader (SplitLoader or YouieLoad), then LSASS credential theft and IP theft, with ransomware optional (FakePenny or Qilin) [S1][S2]. STEP 4: The MLCOA is continued job-lure and npm-package intrusions against defense and aerospace contractors and developers to steal credentials and IP. The MDCOA is turning access at a software vendor or MSP into a supply-chain compromise or ransomware against DIB suppliers that support Air Force programs, a risk Microsoft flags [S1][S6]. Candidate indicators: Procdump run against LSASS; connections to known Moonstone Sleet domains; unsolicited job or skills tests that require running PuTTY or npm code; Defender detections such as SplitLoader, YouieLoad or PennyCrypt [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: fuse Microsoft and vendor npm and package-registry reporting into the JCC2 common operational picture for DIB and aerospace partners, because the first intrusion step happens off-network [S1][S3]. (2) Authorities: the activity mixes espionage with criminal ransomware (FakePenny, Qilin), so incidents may fall under law-enforcement as well as DoD and DC3 lanes. Classify carefully and coordinate early [S1][S2]. (3) Mission assurance: treat contractor developer workstations, build pipelines and MSP connections as mission-relevant terrain; ransomware against a key supplier could degrade sustainment [S1][S6]. (4) Coordination: work with the DIB CS program and industry partners on fake-recruiter and fake-company indicators; brief personnel about job and game lures [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: Moonstone Sleet is a North Korean-linked threat actor executing both financially motivated attacks and espionage operations. The group previously overlapped significantly with another North Korean-linked entity, Lazarus Group, but has differentiated its tradecraft since 2023. Moonstone Sleet is notable for creating fake companies and personas to interact with victim entities, as well as developing unique malware such as a variant delivered via a fully functioning game.

identification.summary: Mora_001 is the name Forescout's Vedere Labs uses for a ransomware operator that exploited two Fortinet authentication-bypass flaws, CVE-2024-55591 and CVE-2025-24472, in FortiOS and FortiProxy to obtain super-admin access, then deployed a ransomware strain Forescout calls SuperBlack [S1][S2][S3]. Forescout says the actor shows a distinct operational signature and post-exploitation playbook that sets it apart from other ransomware operators, including LockBit affiliates [S1][S3]. The SuperBlack encryptor was reportedly built from a leaked LockBit 3.0 builder with LockBit branding removed [S3]. Intrusions were seen from late January to early March 2025 [S2][S5].
identification.firstObserved: Forescout reported intrusions between late January and early March 2025 [S2][S5].
identification.notes: Name used is the Forescout designation Mora_001; no Microsoft name is known for this record. The ransom note reuses a TOX chat ID previously associated with LockBit, so it overlaps with LockBit-related infrastructure; this does not make Mora_001 a LockBit affiliate by itself, and Forescout treats it as an independent actor [S3].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor is stated in the sources gathered. The record's country field (RU) is not supported by an attribution statement in the cited sources beyond Forescout's observation of Russian-language artifacts [S2].
attribution.confidence: Forescout (as reported by secondary coverage) links Mora_001 to the LockBit ecosystem but treats it as an independent actor; researchers see links rather than a clear affiliation [S2][S3]. No government attribution found.
attribution.basis: Shared TOX ID in the ransom note with LockBit, a leaked LockBit 3.0 builder used for SuperBlack, and Russian-language artifacts, as reported from Forescout [S2][S3].

actors.objectives: Financially motivated double extortion: data is exfiltrated first and then encrypted [S2][S3].

targeting.notes: Victim sectors and countries were not named in the coverage reviewed. Forescout confirmed at least three cases and said others could exist [S2]. Within victim networks the actor prioritized domain controllers, authentication servers, database servers and file servers [S2][S3]. Initial access depends on internet-exposed Fortinet management interfaces; ShadowServer data cited by The Register put India (4,631) and the US (3,863) as the top countries for exposed unpatched firewalls for CVE-2024-55591, which is exposure data and not confirmed victims [S3].

capabilities.summary: Initial access via authentication bypass in FortiOS and FortiProxy (CVE-2024-55591, CVE-2025-24472) on devices with exposed management interfaces, giving super_admin privileges [S2][S3]. CVE-2024-55591 was exploited as a zero-day before Fortinet's 14 January 2025 disclosure, and a public proof of concept appeared on 27 January with exploitation reportedly within 96 hours [S2][S3]. Persistence through new privileged accounts and local users imitating legitimate VPN users, scheduled scripts, and syncing with backup firewalls [S2]. SuperBlack is based on the leaked LockBit 3.0 builder with LockBit branding removed and a custom exfiltration module [S2][S3].

diamond.adversary: Ransomware operator tracked by Forescout as Mora_001, with Russian-language artifacts and links to the LockBit ecosystem, but not a confirmed LockBit affiliate [S2][S3].
diamond.capability: Fortinet authentication bypass exploits, rogue admin accounts, exfiltration, and the SuperBlack encryptor from the LockBit 3.0 builder [S2][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Exposed Fortinet management interfaces are the entry point. The ransom note contains a TOX ID tied to LockBit [S3]. Specific indicator values were not retrieved.
diamond.victim: Organizations with internet-exposed, unpatched FortiOS/FortiProxy; sectors not named in sources reviewed [S2][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Financially motivated extortion; no stated political objective [S2].
diamond.technology: Perimeter firewalls with management interfaces exposed to the internet, and domain controllers, authentication, database and file servers behind them [S2][S3].

gaps: Forescout's original blog (S1) could not be fetched in this environment; details come from search summaries and secondary coverage, so wording and exact figures should be checked against it.
Victim sectors, countries and the full victim count are not public in sources gathered; only at least three confirmed cases are reported [S2].
TOX ID value, IP addresses and file hashes were not retrieved.
No activity after March 2025 was found; whether the actor is still active is unknown.
Basis for the record's RU country tag is only Russian-language artifacts; no government or vendor attribution to a Russian state or location was found.
No Microsoft or MITRE name was found for this actor.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing FortiOS/FortiProxy management interfaces and the domain controllers, authentication, database and file servers behind them are key cyber terrain [S2][S3]. STEP 2: Weaponization of a public proof of concept within about 96 hours narrows the patch window; exposed interfaces were the enabling condition [S3]. STEP 3: The observed template is authentication bypass, rogue super-admin and VPN-lookalike accounts, exfiltration, then encryption [S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued opportunistic double-extortion of organizations with exposed, unpatched Fortinet devices. MDCOA is the same access method applied to a defense-industrial or installation network to cause encryption and data loss during a crisis. Candidate indicators: unexpected admin accounts on firewalls, new local users imitating VPN users, management-interface logins from unfamiliar IPs, and large outbound transfers before encryption [S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Maintain situational awareness of Fortinet advisories and track patch status of perimeter devices [S3]. (2) Confirm authorities to disable or restrict management-interface exposure and to hunt on contractor and mission-partner networks. (3) Mission assurance: protect domain controllers and authentication servers and keep offline backups, since the actor targets these [S2]. (4) Coordinate with DC3 and the DIB CS program and CISA for ransomware reporting; attribution to LockBit versus a distinct actor is unsettled, so prioritize containment over naming [S2][S3].

provenance.importedSummary: Mora_001 is a threat actor exhibiting a distinct operational signature that combines opportunistic attacks with ties to the LockBit ecosystem. The actor has been observed exploiting CVE-2024-55591 and CVE-2025-24472 vulnerabilities affecting Fortinet devices. The ransom note associated with Mora_001 includes the same TOX ID used by LockBit, indicating a potential affiliation or shared communication channels. Their post-exploitation patterns suggest a structured playbook that differentiates them from other ransomware operators, including LockBit affiliates.

identification.summary: Moshen Dragon is a China-aligned cyberespionage cluster named by SentinelLabs in May 2022 that targeted telecommunication providers in Central Asia [S1][S2][S4]. It sideloaded ShadowPad and PlugX through DLL search order hijacking of legitimate security-vendor software [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: May 2022 (date of SentinelLabs public reporting, as relayed by secondary coverage); earlier activity start date not confirmed in sources gathered [S1][S2].
identification.notes: No Microsoft name is recorded for this cluster. Secondary reporting says researchers saw tactical overlap with Nomad Panda (RedFoxtrot) but SentinelLabs tracks the groups separately [S1].

attribution.confidence: SentinelLabs describes the cluster as China-aligned [S1][S4]. No government attribution found in sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Malware choice (ShadowPad, PlugX) and TTP overlap with other China-linked groups, as reported by SentinelLabs via secondary coverage [S1].

actors.objectives: Espionage against the telecommunications sector in Central Asia, as characterized by SentinelLabs [S1][S4]. Specific collection requirements are not stated in the sources gathered.

targeting.notes: Specific victim organizations and countries are not named in the secondary sources gathered [S1][S2].

capabilities.summary: Five malware 'triads' (loader, DLL, payload sets) that use DLL search order hijacking against signed security software from Symantec, Trend Micro, BitDefender, McAfee and Kaspersky to sideload ShadowPad and PlugX [S1][S2]. Additional tools reported are an LSA notification package for credential harvesting, the passive backdoor GUNTERS, and Impacket for lateral movement and exfiltration [S1][S4]. SentinelLabs said it could not determine the initial infection vector [S2]. The abuse relies on a Windows design weakness, not vulnerabilities in the security products [S2].

campaigns.name: SentinelLabs disclosure of telecom targeting in Central Asia
campaigns.summary: SentinelLabs published 'Moshen Dragon's Triad-and-Error Approach', reporting ShadowPad and PlugX sideloading against Central Asian telecom operators [S1][S2].

diamond.adversary: China-aligned espionage cluster tracked as Moshen Dragon by SentinelLabs [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: ShadowPad and PlugX delivered via DLL search order hijacking of security-vendor binaries; LSA notification package; GUNTERS passive backdoor; Impacket [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.victim: Telecommunication providers in Central Asia [S1][S4].
diamond.technology: Windows hosts running security software whose signed binaries load DLLs from writable search paths [S2].

gaps: Could not open the primary SentinelLabs report or other pages (DNS failure in this environment); all facts rely on search-result summaries of secondary coverage and must be verified against the original.
Initial access vector was not determined by SentinelLabs [S2].
Victim names, countries, timeline and dwell time are not identified in the sources gathered.
No sponsor or government attribution found. Overlap with RedFoxtrot/Nomad Panda (reported by Recorded Future as likely tied to PLA Unit 69010) is TTP-level only; do not merge clusters [S1].
No Microsoft name, MITRE group ID or post-2022 activity was found.
Infrastructure indicators (domains, IPs, hashes) not collected.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Telecommunications providers and the endpoints and servers running security software are relevant terrain for coalition and partner-nation communications in Central Asia [S1][S4]. STEP 2: Security-vendor binaries are trusted by defenders, so sideloading hides in plain sight [S2]. STEP 3: The pattern is unknown access, then DLL-sideloaded ShadowPad/PlugX, credential theft via an LSA notification package, lateral movement with Impacket [S1][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued telecom-sector espionage in Central Asia. MDCOA (low-evidence extrapolation) is use of telecom access to support collection against partner governments. Candidate indicators: legitimate AV executables running from unusual directories, unsigned DLLs beside signed binaries, new LSA notification packages, Impacket-style lateral movement [S1][S2][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track partner-nation telecom compromise reporting for Central Asia [S1]. (2) Authorities: hunting on partner or commercial telecom networks requires host-nation or provider consent. (3) Mission assurance: do not assume signed security-vendor binaries are benign; add DLL load-path monitoring [S2]. (4) Coordination: share indicators through established vendor and partner channels; initial access is unknown, so avoid over-specific guidance [S2].

provenance.importedSummary: Moshen Dragon is a Chinese-aligned cyberespionage threat actor operating in Central Asia. They have been observed deploying multiple malware triads and utilizing DLL search order hijacking to sideload ShadowPad and PlugX variants. The threat actor also employs various tools, including an LSA notification package and a passive backdoor known as GUNTERS. Their activities involve targeting the telecommunication sector and leveraging Impacket for lateral movement and data exfiltration.

identification.summary: China-based espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Mulberry Typhoon (formerly MANGANESE) and that Mandiant and MITRE track as APT5 [S1][S8][S9]. MITRE says it primarily targets the telecommunications, aerospace and defense industries in the U.S., Europe and Asia and has a strong interest in compromising networking devices and their software, including with zero-day exploits [S8]. Microsoft reported in 2023 that Mulberry Typhoon targeted the US defense industrial base, most notably with a zero-day exploit against devices (CVE-2022-27518) [S1]. In December 2022 NSA published threat-hunting guidance on APT5's exploitation of Citrix ADC [S4][S5].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: active since at least 2007 [S8]. 2019 press coverage of FireEye reporting also says the group has been active since 2007 [S7].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Mulberry Typhoon (formerly MANGANESE) [S1][S9]. MITRE associates Mulberry Typhoon, MANGANESE, BRONZE FLEETWOOD, Keyhole Panda and UNC2630 with APT5 [S8]. NSA-related coverage calls APT5 also UNC2630 and MANGANESE [S4][S6]. Mandiant itself only assessed UNC2630 as possibly tied to APT5, based on a trusted third party's evidence that it could not independently confirm [S2]. 2019 coverage of FireEye reporting describes APT5 as several subgroups with distinct tactics and infrastructure [S7].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (suspected). Mandiant suspected UNC2630 operates on behalf of the Chinese government [S2]. Its May 2021 update says UNC2630 and UNC2717 are believed to be affiliated with the Chinese government [S3]. Coverage of the NSA guidance calls APT5 a Chinese state-sponsored group [S5][S6].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft describes Mulberry Typhoon as China-based [S1]. NSA publicly attributed the CVE-2022-27518 exploitation to APT5 in December 2022, according to press coverage of the advisory [S4][S5]. Mandiant held the UNC2630 to APT5 link at low-to-moderate confidence ('may have ties'; 'not able to definitively connect') [S2]. 2019 coverage notes that FireEye had not formally attributed APT5 to a nation-state [S7].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and reporting [S1]; Mandiant incident response at Pulse Secure victims, plus third-party linkage to historic APT5 campaigns [S2][S3]; NSA threat-hunting guidance, which this record relies on through press reporting [S4][S5][S6]; MITRE ATT&CK group entry [S8].

actors.objectives: Espionage aimed at defense, aerospace and telecommunications targets [S1][S8]. Mandiant judged that Pulse Secure-era activity sought to steal credentials, keep long-term persistent access to victim networks and access or exfiltrate sensitive data, in support of key Chinese government priorities [S3]. Earlier VPN-exploitation coverage reported spying on pricing and bidding information [S7].

sectors: Government, high tech, education, transportation and financial (broader Pulse Secure campaign, not UNC2630 alone) [S3]
targeting.notes: Microsoft groups Mulberry Typhoon with Circle Typhoon and Volt Typhoon as China-based groups targeting the US DIB. It says their targets occasionally overlap but they are distinct actors with different infrastructure and capabilities [S1]. Mandiant's May 2021 sector list covers the whole Pulse Secure campaign (UNC2630 and UNC2717) [S3].

capabilities.summary: Exploits edge and network appliances, including zero-days: Pulse Secure CVE-2021-22893 alongside older flaws [S2], Citrix ADC/Gateway CVE-2022-27518 [S1][S4], and, per 2019 coverage, Pulse Secure CVE-2019-11510 and Fortinet CVE-2018-13379 [S7]. CVE-2022-27518 allowed unauthenticated remote code execution on appliances configured as a SAML SP or IdP [S4]. UNC2630 deployed purpose-built Pulse Secure implants: SLOWPULSE, which modifies legitimate Pulse Secure files to bypass or log credentials in authentication flows, including some 2FA, plus RADIALPULSE, THINBLOOD, ATRIUM, PACEMAKER, SLIGHTPULSE and PULSECHECK [S2]. Later families include BLOODMINE, BLOODBANK, CLEANPULSE and RAPIDPULSE [S3]. Operators patched devices for persistence that survived upgrades, removed webshells to evade detection and cleared logs [S3]. MITRE also lists Mimikatz, Skeleton Key, PoisonIvy, gh0st RAT and PcShare [S8].

diamond.adversary: China-based espionage operators tracked as Mulberry Typhoon/APT5. UNC2630 is a possibly related Mandiant cluster [S1][S2][S8].
diamond.capability: Zero-day and n-day exploits for VPN and application-delivery appliances; trojanized appliance binaries (SLOWPULSE family); webshells; credential theft; log tampering [S2][S3][S4][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised edge appliances (Pulse Secure, Citrix ADC, Fortinet) serve as access and persistence points [S2][S4][S7]. Microsoft says Mulberry Typhoon's infrastructure is distinct from that of Circle and Volt Typhoon [S1].
diamond.victim: US defense industrial base, aerospace and telecommunications companies (including satellite communications) and technology firms in the U.S., Europe and Asia [S1][S2][S7][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection supporting key Chinese government priorities against Western defense and telecom sectors [S1][S3].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing SSL VPN and ADC appliances with SAML or authentication roles, which sit outside EDR coverage and have limited forensic visibility [S2][S3][S4].

gaps: The NSA advisory 'APT5: Citrix ADC Threat Hunting Guidance' (December 2022) could not be opened; its content is cited through press coverage [S4][S5][S6].
No Microsoft report dedicated to Mulberry Typhoon was found. Microsoft's public description is limited to the 2023 East Asia report [S1].
Original FireEye reporting on APT5's 2007 origins and subgroups was not retrieved; it is cited through 2019 press coverage [S7].
The UNC2630 to APT5 link rests on an unnamed third party per Mandiant [S2]. Some press coverage overstates it as confirmed; treat Pulse Secure-era facts as UNC2630, not as definitively APT5.
Microsoft says Mulberry, Circle and Volt Typhoon targets overlap, but finds insufficient evidence to tie the groups together [S1].
No 2024-2026 public reporting attributing new activity to Mulberry Typhoon or APT5 was found in this research pass.
The vendor sources gathered here do not substantiate the CrowdStrike (Keyhole Panda) and Secureworks (BRONZE FLEETWOOD) alias mappings beyond MITRE's listing [S8].
No sponsoring organization (MSS, PLA or contractor) is named in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the edge: SSL VPN concentrators, Citrix ADC/Gateway and SAML-integrated access appliances on DIB, aerospace and telecom networks that connect to DoD programs [S1][S2][S4]. STEP 2: These appliances often fall outside EDR coverage and retain few logs. The actor patches appliance binaries and clears logs, so absence of evidence is weak [S2][S3]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is appliance exploit (zero-day or fresh n-day), then trojanized authentication components or a webshell, then credential harvest, then internal access and data staging [S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet, long-term credential theft and data collection from DIB and telecom networks via edge devices [S3]. MDCOA is a rapid mass-exploitation wave against a newly discovered appliance zero-day across DoD-adjacent contractors, with implants that survive vendor patching and upgrades, giving persistent access to program data during a crisis [S1][S3]. Candidate indicators: modified Pulse Secure or Citrix system files and integrity-check failures, unexpected webshells on appliances, gaps or truncation in appliance logs, and authentication successes that bypass MFA [S2][S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: JCC2 should track edge-appliance inventory and patch state, plus vendor integrity-check results, for DoD and mission-partner networks, because this actor's entry point is the appliance [S2][S4]. (2) Authorities: most observed victims are DIB companies [S1][S2]. Response depends on DC3/DIB CS sharing, CISA and NSA advisories and contractor cooperation rather than DoD-owned terrain. (3) Mission assurance: an appliance patch alone does not remove a persistence patcher [S3]. Plan for rebuild or replacement and credential resets on systems behind compromised appliances. (4) Coordination: Mulberry, Circle and Volt Typhoon target the same DIB sector but are distinct actors [S1]. Deconflict hunts and reporting by actor, and avoid merging indicators across clusters.

identification.summary: Russian covert influence operation that Microsoft's Threat Analysis Center (MTAC) tracked as Storm-1516 and described as Kremlin-aligned [S1][S2]. Its signature is a fabricated video, often with a paid actor posing as a whistleblower or citizen journalist, laundered through newly created websites that imitate local or well-known media outlets and then amplified by influencers [S1][S2][S9]. France's VIGINUM analyzed 77 Storm-1516 operations documented from the operation's emergence through 5 March 2025 [S8]. NewsGuard assessed in December 2025 that Storm-1516 had overtaken Russian state media (RT and Sputnik) as the leading source of false Russia-Ukraine claims it tracks, based on roughly 400 debunked narratives [S6][S7].
identification.firstObserved: VIGINUM dates the operation's start to March 2023 [S8].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Neva Flood (formerly Storm-1516), per the encyclopedia's imported Microsoft naming mapping; not re-verified in this research pass. Recorded Future tracks a closely related network as CopyCop, which it links to John Mark Dougan, the Moscow-based Center for Geopolitical Expertise (CGE) and the GRU [S4][S5]. VIGINUM treats Storm-1516 and CopyCop as overlapping rather than identical, and links Storm-1516 to sub-clusters including former Prigozhin troll-farm staff and Dougan's fake-news sites [S8]. Keep CopyCop website counts and Storm-1516 operation counts separate.

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation. VIGINUM attributes central coordination to Yury Khoroshenky, whom it describes as a suspected officer of Russian military intelligence (GRU) [S8]. The US Treasury said the GRU directed and funded the CGE and US-based facilitators who built an AI server and at least 100 imitation news websites for 2024 US election interference [S10]. The EU sanctioned Dougan in December 2025 as responsible for the Storm-1516 campaign, and the German government publicly blamed Russia for using Storm-1516 against its federal election [S11].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft (MTAC) labels Storm-1516 Kremlin-aligned [S1][S2]. VIGINUM (French government) states its investigations confirm involvement of individuals and organizations close to the Russian state, including Dougan [S8]. Recorded Future assesses CopyCop is very likely operated by Dougan with CGE and GRU support [S4][S5]. Treasury's December 2024 designation of the CGE describes a GRU-funded website network but, in the coverage reviewed, does not name Storm-1516 or Dougan [S10]. Dougan denies working for the Russian government [S3].
attribution.basis: Microsoft MTAC election reporting [S1][S2]; VIGINUM technical report (via secondary coverage) [S8]; Recorded Future Insikt Group CopyCop reporting [S4][S5]; US Treasury OFAC sanctions on CGE and Valery Korovin (via press coverage) [S10]; EU sanctions and German government statement (via CORRECTIV) [S11]; investigative reporting by CORRECTIV [S3].

actors.objectives: Undermine Western support for Ukraine and shape elections in target countries in Russia's favor [S1][S9]. Bloomberg's 2026 analysis of Storm-1516 videos found more than 40% aimed at undermining support for Ukraine and about one-third targeted elections in countries other than the US [S9]. NewsGuard found false narratives aimed at France closely followed French expressions of support for Ukraine [S7].

sectors: News media (impersonation of outlets and real journalists) [S1][S4]
regions: Ukraine (narratives about Ukraine and its leadership) [S6][S9]
targeting.notes: Targets track Russian foreign-policy priorities: the US election in 2024, then Germany ahead of its February 2025 election, and France following its support for Ukraine [S1][S3][S7]. Canada and Moldova targeting is from Recorded Future's CopyCop reporting, an overlapping cluster [S4].

capabilities.summary: Production of staged or AI-manipulated videos featuring actors posing as whistleblowers or citizen journalists [S1][S9]. Rapid creation of fake news websites that imitate local outlets, sometimes registered only days before use, with large reserves of dormant sites prepared in advance (more than 100 German-named sites before the 2025 election) [S1][S2][S3]. Generative AI used to rewrite the same story for each site [S3]; Recorded Future reports self-hosted, uncensored Llama 3 models, likely GRU-financed, and over 300 inauthentic CopyCop websites in 2025 [S4]. Impersonation of media outlets, political parties, fact-checkers and real journalists [S4]. Amplification through pro-Russian influencers, Telegram channels and hashtags on X [S2][S3].

diamond.adversary: Russian state-linked operators. VIGINUM names suspected GRU officer Yury Khoroshenky as coordinator [S8]. US-born Russia resident John Mark Dougan, sanctioned by the EU, produces content [S3][S11]. The GRU-funded CGE is sanctioned by Treasury [S10].
diamond.capability: Staged or AI-manipulated videos with paid actors [S1][S9]. AI-rewritten articles [S3]. Self-hosted Llama 3 content generation [S4]. Impersonation of outlets and journalists [S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Hundreds of imitation news domains, many created days before use or held dormant [S1][S3][S4]. Purpose-built video channels and influencer, Telegram and X amplification networks [S2][S3].
diamond.victim: Voters and information environments in the US, Germany, France, Canada and Moldova [S1][S3][S4]. Political leaders who are smeared [S1][S3]. Media brands and journalists whose identities are spoofed [S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Erode Western support for Ukraine and influence elections toward Kremlin-preferred outcomes [S1][S7][S9].
diamond.technology: Low-cost domain registration, generative AI, and social platforms with weak provenance signals; AI chatbots that repeat the false narratives [S3][S4][S7].

gaps: Primary documents not opened (fetch failed): VIGINUM/SGDSN Storm-1516 report, Microsoft MTAC reports, Recorded Future CopyCop reports, Treasury press release. Details rely on search-result coverage.
Microsoft's renaming of Storm-1516 to Neva Flood comes from the imported Microsoft mapping and was not re-verified in this pass; no Microsoft publication using the name Neva Flood was located.
Exact publication dates of the Recorded Future reports (S4, S5) and the VIGINUM report (S8) were not confirmed against the original pages.
Boundary between Storm-1516 (Microsoft/VIGINUM) and CopyCop (Recorded Future) is unresolved; VIGINUM calls them overlapping.
Alliance4Europe and co-authors link Storm-1516 to Prigozhin's Foundation to Battle Injustice (R-FBI); that report's date and details were not verified.

The Insider and Gnida Project report 2025 Storm-1516 fabrications aimed at Moldova, Armenia and France that used real journalists' identities; not included as cited events because publication dates were not confirmed.
Secondary coverage of the VIGINUM report says Khoroshenky is possibly assigned to GRU Unit 29155; this was not confirmed in the primary report.
No MITRE ATT&CK group entry exists; the actor is an influence operation, not an intrusion set, so cyber-intrusion TTPs are not documented.
Measured effects on voter behavior or policy outcomes are not documented; reach figures (views) are vendor and media estimates.
Secondary coverage states Clemson University's Media Forensics Hub first identified the operation in December 2023, before MTAC named it; the Clemson report was not located.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): The relevant terrain is the information environment of the US and allies that support Ukraine. This includes local-news brand trust, social platforms (X, Telegram), and AI chatbots that repeat narratives [S3][S7]. STEP 2 (effects): Pre-positioned dormant domain reserves let the actor surge within days of a political trigger, such as a coalition collapse or an election [S3]. STEP 3 (threat model): The template is fabricated video with an actor, then laundering through a fake local outlet created days earlier, then amplification by influencers and Telegram [S1][S2][S3]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued fabrications against leaders of pro-Ukraine states timed to aid decisions and elections [S7][S9]. MDCOA is a fabricated whistleblower video alleging misconduct by US or allied military personnel or units during a crisis, aimed at splitting coalition support. Candidate indicators: bursts of newly registered domains with local-news names, sites that share templates or AI-rewritten copy, and actor-led 'whistleblower' videos first posted on new channels [S1][S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track public reporting from VIGINUM, Microsoft MTAC, Recorded Future and NewsGuard, and monitor new domain registrations that imitate news outlets near allied elections [S3][S4][S8]. (2) Authorities: this is foreign malign influence aimed at civilian audiences. Response, including attribution and sanctions, has come through Treasury, the EU and allied governments, not military cyber channels [S10][S11]. DoD roles are mainly support and force protection. (3) Mission assurance: prepare rapid public-affairs and command responses to fabricated claims about personnel or operations, because fabricated videos gain millions of views quickly [S1][S2]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with allied agencies (e.g., VIGINUM) and interagency partners. Recognize vendor cluster differences (Storm-1516 vs CopyCop) when fusing reporting [S5][S8].

provenance.importedSummary: CopyCop is a Russian covert influence network that has established over 300 fictional media websites targeting the US, France, Canada, and other countries, primarily to disseminate pro-Russian and anti-Ukrainian narratives. The network employs TTPs such as deepfakes, fake interviews, and self-hosted LLMs for content generation, while also impersonating local media outlets and fact-checking organizations. Its operations are supported by the Moscow-based Center for Geopolitical Expertise and the GRU, aiming to undermine support for Ukraine and exacerbate political fragmentation in Western nations. CopyCop's influence content is amplified by a network of pro-Russian social media influencers and other Russian influence networks.

identification.summary: NICKEL ALLEY is Sophos Counter Threat Unit's name for a threat group that Sophos describes as operating on behalf of the North Korean government and conducting 'Contagious Interview' activity against technology-sector professionals [S1]. The group often builds a fake LinkedIn company page for credibility and maintains a coordinating GitHub account for malware delivery [S1]. Sophos states that since at least mid-2025 the group has used ClickFix lures to deliver the PyLangGhost RAT [S1]. Sophos also notes that in late 2025 the group established code repositories containing Visual Studio Code 'tasks', and that it conducts opportunistic npm attacks (compromised packages and typosquats) [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Since at least mid-2025 for ClickFix delivery of PyLangGhost, per Sophos [S1]. Earlier start date of NICKEL ALLEY itself not established in sources reviewed.
identification.notes: Sophos's NICKEL ALLEY is tied by Sophos to the Contagious Interview campaign [S1]. Other vendors track Contagious Interview / ClickFake Interview activity under their own names (e.g. Famous Chollima / Wagemole per SOCRadar; Sekoia's ClickFake Interview attributed to Lazarus Group in reporting) [S2][S3]. Cluster boundaries and overlap with NICKEL ALLEY were not verified; do not merge facts across these names.

provenance.importedSummary: NICKEL ALLEY is a North Korean threat group that targets technology professionals through fake job opportunities, employing social engineering tactics such as creating fraudulent LinkedIn pages and GitHub repositories for malware delivery. They utilize the ClickFix tactic to deploy the PyLangGhost RAT, which supports file exfiltration and system profiling, particularly focusing on Chrome cryptocurrency wallet data. The group has also leveraged Visual Studio Code tasks to execute commands for malware retrieval based on the victim's operating system. Their operations indicate a dual focus on cryptocurrency theft and potential supply chain compromise or corporate espionage.

identification.summary: Night Dragon is the name McAfee gave to a series of coordinated, covert intrusions against global oil, energy and petrochemical companies, described in a McAfee Foundstone/McAfee Labs white paper dated 10 February 2011 [S1]. Attackers used spear-phishing, social engineering, Windows vulnerabilities, Active Directory compromise and remote administration tools (RATs), and stole proprietary operations and project-financing information such as oil and gas field bid data [S1][S2]. McAfee's Dmitri Alperovitch said no zero-day exploits were used [S2]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as campaign C0002, with an older group object G0014 [S5].
identification.firstObserved: McAfee: activity began in November 2009 [S1][S2]. The ICS-CERT advisory says activity began in 2009 or possibly as early as 2007 [S3].
identification.notes: Night Dragon is a McAfee campaign name, not a Microsoft-named actor; no Microsoft name or mapping was found in the sources gathered. Treat it as a campaign label for one intrusion set in 2009-2011, not a continuing group. Third-party mirrors of ATT&CK data mention an alias 'Musical Chairs' but I could not verify it on a primary page, so it is not added as an alias.

attribution.confidence: McAfee said the tools and network activity pointed primarily to China, and described the evidence as circumstantial [S1][S2]. Some other researchers said they had detected the attacks but were less certain of McAfee's conclusions [S2]. McAfee traced C2 infrastructure to a person or hosting provider in Heze City, Shandong Province, China (sources differ on which) [S4]. Control Engineering reported that no one could say whether the Chinese government sanctioned the attacks or whether a private company was responsible (as reported in search results, not opened).
attribution.basis: McAfee cited Chinese-based tooling and network activity, and C2 infrastructure linked to Heze City, Shandong Province [S1][S4]. No government attribution to a named PRC organization was found in the sources gathered.

actors.objectives: Theft of sensitive proprietary operations and project-financing information, including financial documents on oil and gas field exploration and bid negotiations and operational details on oil and gas field production supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems [S1][S2].

regions: Companies, individuals and executives in Kazakhstan, Taiwan, Greece and the United States [S2]
McAfee said it saw evidence of the activity in virtually every region of the globe [S1]
targeting.notes: McAfee confirmed five victim companies, none named publicly [S2]. NERC rated risk to bulk power system reliability as MEDIUM, noting financial data appeared to be the primary target although successful exploits may reach industrial control and SCADA systems [S6]. ICS-CERT said the tools and techniques can be highly successful against any industry [S3].

capabilities.summary: Unsophisticated but effective: spear-phishing, social engineering, exploitation of Windows vulnerabilities, Active Directory compromise and commodity remote administration tools, with no zero-days [S1][S2]. McAfee's paper documents the zwShell RAT and its command-and-control (C2) infrastructure in an appendix [S1]. ATT&CK lists hosted C2 infrastructure, HTTP-based C2 and password cracking with Cain & Abel, and a third-party mirror lists gsecdump, PsExec and ASPXSpy [S5].

diamond.socioPolitical: Collection of bid, exploration and project-financing data suggests commercial and economic intelligence value; McAfee did not establish state tasking [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Windows and Active Directory enterprise networks, with exposure of SCADA-related operational data to intruders in corporate networks [S1][S2][S6].

Details such as the exact attack chain (for example web-server compromise and credential theft steps), full tool list and C2 indicators were not confirmed from opened sources.
Victim companies were never named publicly; the total number of victims beyond five confirmed is unknown.
No government attribution or Microsoft naming was found; sponsor is unresolved.
Whether Night Dragon activity continued after 2011 under another name is unknown.
The alias 'Musical Chairs' appears in third-party mirrors only and is unverified.
The Heze City/Shandong C2 link comes from McAfee-based press reporting; NERC text mentioning Shandong was not confirmed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Corporate networks of energy firms, Active Directory and bid or project-financing data stores are key terrain; SCADA data held on corporate systems is a secondary concern [S1][S2][S6]. STEP 2: Commodity tooling and no zero-days mean defenders' known-patch and credential hygiene gaps determine exposure [S2]. STEP 3: Template is spear-phishing or Windows exploitation, then Active Directory compromise, then RAT-based collection and exfiltration to leased C2 [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued economic and commercial intelligence theft from energy and defense-energy suppliers. MDCOA is use of the same footholds to reach operational technology data in a crisis; NERC judged this lower risk in 2011 [S6]. Candidate indicators: unexpected RAT beacons from corporate hosts, anomalous Active Directory authentication, and bulk transfers of bid or financial documents [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track energy-sector compromise of installations that support DoD fuel and power supply chains [S1][S6]. (2) Authorities: coordinate responses through owners of commercial networks and sector channels such as ICS-CERT and NERC rather than assuming DoD authority [S3][S6]. (3) Mission assurance: separate corporate IT from SCADA and OT networks and verify what operational data sits on corporate systems [S2][S6]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DIB and energy sector partners; attribution was circumstantial, so prioritize containment over naming [S2].

identification.summary: Nitro is the name Symantec gave in October 2011 to a series of targeted attacks that began against chemical-sector companies and used the PoisonIvy remote access Trojan delivered by spear-phishing email [S3]. Symantec judged the purpose to be industrial espionage [S3]. Palo Alto Networks (Unit 42) reported in October 2014 that a group it called Nitro was still active, using different malware (mainly Spindest, plus PCClient and Farfli variants) [S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: Symantec reporting describes the same infrastructure being used against human-rights groups from about late April 2011 and the motor industry in late May 2011, before the chemical-sector wave of roughly July to mid-September 2011 [S3][S2].
identification.notes: Whether the 2014 Unit 42 'Nitro' activity involves the same operators as 2011 is a vendor linkage via infrastructure overlap, not independently verified here [S5]. Covert Grove is a pseudonym Symantec gave to an individual tied to one C2 server, not a group name [S3][S7]. Microsoft has no known Typhoon/Sleet name mapping for Nitro in the sources gathered.

attribution.confidence: Symantec stated it could not determine whether the individual it called Covert Grove was the sole attacker, had only an indirect role, or was acting on behalf of one or more other parties [S3].
attribution.basis: Symantec traced one command-and-control server to a US-hosted machine owned by a man in his 20s in Hebei province, China, whom it pseudonymized Covert Grove [S3][S7]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered. Sponsor left blank; the imported record's country code CN rests on this single-server finding.

actors.objectives: Symantec assessed the goal of the chemical-industry wave as collecting intellectual property such as design documents, formulas and manufacturing processes [S3]. Trend Micro read the broader mix of chemical, human-rights, motor and defense targets as community-of-interest targeting to gather information for later, more precise attacks [S2].

regions: Press coverage of Symantec: about 48 organizations in about 20 countries, with most infected machines in the United States, Bangladesh and the United Kingdom [S3][S4]
2014: US and European organizations, plus a South Korean clothing manufacturer's website used to host malware [S6]
targeting.notes: Press accounts of Symantec's report give 29 chemical companies and 19 other firms, mostly defense [S3][S4]. Counts differ slightly across outlets. 2014 victim types come from SC Magazine's coverage of the Unit 42 report [S6].

capabilities.summary: 2011: spear-phishing emails posing as meeting invitations or security updates from business partners carried PoisonIvy, a freely available RAT; Symantec said no zero-day vulnerabilities were used and the attacks were not particularly sophisticated [S3][S4]. Trend Micro noted a human operator sits behind each PoisonIvy connection and can explore the network, steal data and install further malware, and mapped three distinct sets of C2 infrastructure from Symantec's samples, one using dynamic DNS domains [S2]. 2014: Unit 42 and SC Magazine reported mainly Spindest malware with PCClient and Farfli variants, with spear phishing and PoisonIvy absent from those cases, and compromised legitimate websites used to serve malware [S5][S6].

diamond.adversary: Unidentified operator(s); Symantec tied one C2 server to an individual in Hebei, China (pseudonym Covert Grove) but could not say if he acted alone or for others [S3].
diamond.capability: PoisonIvy RAT via spear phishing (2011); Spindest, PCClient and Farfli malware and compromised websites (2014) [S2][S5][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Three distinct C2 sets mapped by Trend Micro including dynamic DNS domains; a US-hosted server in 2011; IP resolution overlap used by Unit 42 to link 2014 samples [S2][S3][S5].

diamond.socioPolitical: Commercial and technical intelligence; Trend Micro viewed the wider targeting as intelligence gathering for later focused attacks [S2].
diamond.technology: Email gateways and endpoints exposed to socially engineered attachments, and legitimate websites that can be compromised to host malware [S3][S6].

gaps: Symantec white paper full text could not be opened; Symantec details here come via press reports [S3].
WebFetch could not reach unit42.paloaltonetworks.com or the seebug PDF; Unit 42 details come from search-result summaries and SC Magazine coverage.
No government or vendor attribution to a sponsor; the Covert Grove link is to one server and one individual only.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Defense industrial base and chemical/manufacturing suppliers hold design data and are the relevant terrain; email gateways and employee mailboxes are the entry points [S3][S6]. STEP 2: Evidence is of a low-sophistication actor using freely available tools and no zero-days, so basic email defenses matter [S3][S2]. STEP 3: Template is spear phish with a plausible business lure, then RAT with live operator, then lateral exploration and data theft [S2][S3]; by 2014 tooling and web-based delivery changed [S5][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued IP collection from defense and industrial firms. MDCOA is use of compromised supplier websites and varied custom malware to reach defense-adjacent targets. Candidate indicators: PoisonIvy or Spindest-family detections, dynamic-DNS C2 domains, and IPs overlapping Unit 42 indicators [S2][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor indicator sets for Nitro across contractor reporting [S5]. (2) Authorities: defense contractor networks are owned by industry; coordination runs through the DIB reporting channels rather than direct action. (3) Mission assurance: protect design and supply-chain data at chemical and manufacturing suppliers [S3]. (4) Coordination: attribution is weak, so share indicators without asserting a sponsor [S3].

provenance.importedSummary: These attackers were the subject of an extensive report by Symantec in 2011, which termed the attackers Nitro and stated: 'The goal of the attackers appears to be to collect intellectual property such as design documents, formulas, and manufacturing processes. In addition, the same attackers appear to have a lengthy operation history including attacks on other industries and organizations. Attacks on the chemical industry are merely their latest attack wave. As part of our investigations, we were also able to identify and contact one of the attackers to try and gain insights into the motivations behind these attacks.' Palo Alto Networks reported on continued activity by the attackers in 2014.

identification.summary: Russian-speaking cyber-espionage group that MITRE ATT&CK says has mainly targeted Central Asia, including local governments, diplomatic missions and individuals, since at least 2014, using Android and Windows malware written largely in Delphi [S1]. ESET named it Nomadic Octopus and presented it at Virus Bulletin 2018 as a previously undocumented group focused on diplomatic missions in the region [S4][S5]. Kaspersky tracks the same actor as DustSquad and documented its Delphi 'Octopus' Windows Trojan disguised as a Russian-interface Telegram client [S2][S3]. In April 2023 PRODAFT reported 'Paperbug', a surveillance campaign against high-ranking Tajik officials, telecom services and public service infrastructure, ongoing since 2020 [S8][S9].
identification.firstObserved: Kaspersky: campaign dating back to 2014 [S2][S6]. ESET: active since at least 2015 [S4][S6]. MITRE ATT&CK: since at least 2014 [S1].
identification.notes: Vendor names: Nomadic Octopus (ESET) and DustSquad (Kaspersky) [S1][S6]. Kaspersky says the name 'Octopus' was coined by ESET in 2017 after the 0ct0pus3.php script found on the actor's old C2 servers [S2]. MITRE tracks the group as G0133 and its Windows backdoor as Octopus (S0340) [S1]. No Microsoft (weather-taxonomy) name was found in the sources gathered. Scope differs between vendors: in 2018 ESET reported only one malware family, while Kaspersky reported Windows and Android malware [S6].

attribution.confidence: No government attribution found. Vendors describe the operators as Russian-speaking [S1][S2]. ESET's Anton Cherepanov told SecurityWeek the Russian-language inference rests on spear-phishing emails and Russian malware filenames [S6]. Kaspersky linked the Octopus Trojan to DustSquad with its similarity-based Attribution Engine and found no strong similarities tying Octopus to Zebrocy/Sofacy, even though some victims were infected with both [S2]. For Paperbug, coverage reports PRODAFT said the observed TTPs align with patterns associated with Russia-linked actors such as Sofacy, while also stating the ultimate motive is unknown [S8][S9].
attribution.basis: Language artifacts in lures and filenames [S6]; code-similarity analysis by Kaspersky [S2]; PRODAFT victim data and access to a C2 backend panel during the Paperbug investigation [S8].

actors.objectives: Political and diplomatic intelligence collection in Central Asia: ESET describes cyber espionage against diplomatic missions as the main goal and noted a campaign against a local political blogger, suggesting surveillance beyond high-value targets [S4][S5]. In Paperbug, operators periodically stole emails, documents and chat histories and took real-time screenshots of victims writing emails and contracts [S8][S9]. PRODAFT reportedly left the ultimate sponsor open, citing domestic opposition forces or intelligence gathering by Russia or China as possibilities [S9].

sectors: Public service infrastructure, including OT such as gas station systems [S8]
targeting.notes: In Paperbug, initial access to victims came through the compromised network of a Tajikistan-based telecom company; further access came from stolen documents, client contracts and credentials, weak network configurations and unpatched software [S8].

capabilities.summary: Custom Delphi malware: the Octopus Windows Trojan, delivered as a fake Russian-interface Telegram client in a ZIP lure, gives remote access, command execution, file upload and download, screenshots and searches for RAR archives, using third-party Delphi libraries for JSON-based C2 traffic and compression [S2][S3]. ESET's slides describe a documents collector and about 280 exfiltrated archives, mostly documents [S5]. Kaspersky also found Android malware [S6]. In Paperbug the group used an updated Octopus variant plus mostly public offensive tools, disguised tools as 'Google Update' and 'Java Update', sometimes deployed tools carelessly during victims' active hours, and ran several C2 servers [S8][S9]. MITRE lists the group's techniques separately [S1].

campaigns.summary: Surveillance of high-ranking Tajik officials, telecom services and public service infrastructure via a compromised Tajik telecom; government networks, individual computers and OT devices such as gas station systems compromised. PRODAFT published in April 2023.

diamond.adversary: Russian-speaking espionage operators tracked as Nomadic Octopus (ESET) and DustSquad (Kaspersky); no government attribution [S1][S2][S6].
diamond.capability: Delphi Octopus Trojan (Windows) and Android malware; document collector; screenshot capture, command execution and file transfer; public offensive tools disguised as software updaters [S2][S5][S8].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-run C2 servers (earlier ones hosted the 0ct0pus3.php script); multiple C2 servers in Paperbug, one of whose backend panels PRODAFT accessed; a compromised Tajik telecom network used as a pivot [S2][S8].
diamond.victim: Central Asian diplomatic missions, local governments, opposition figures and bloggers; Tajik senior officials, telecom and public-service infrastructure including OT devices [S1][S5][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Political surveillance in Central Asia, using regional events such as a possible Telegram ban and Kazakh opposition politics as lures [S2][S3]; sponsor left open by PRODAFT [S9].
diamond.technology: Popular messaging apps as a lure; Windows endpoints and Android devices; telecom carrier networks; operational technology such as gas station systems [S2][S6][S8].

gaps: No primary document could be opened directly: Securelist, PRODAFT, Virus Bulletin, SecurityWeek, Security Affairs, The Hacker News and Malpedia all failed to fetch (DNS errors). Facts come from search-result excerpts of these pages and should be checked against the originals.
The Paperbug report PDF (prodaft.com/m/reports/PAPERBUG_TLPWHITE-1.pdf, in the actor record) was not reviewed. Its IOCs, victim counts and C2 details are unverified.
A secondary search summary claimed Nomadic Octopus compromised 499 systems since January 2022. The source of this figure could not be identified, so it is excluded.

Sponsor is unknown. 'Russian-speaking' is a linguistic assessment. PRODAFT's comparison to Sofacy-like TTPs conflicts with Kaspersky's finding of no strong Octopus-Zebrocy/Sofacy ties; neither is government attribution.
No Microsoft name for this actor was found.
Some aggregator pages show an alias 'Golden Falcon' alongside DustSquad; no cited vendor source confirms it, so it was not added.
No public reporting after the April 2023 Paperbug disclosure was found; current activity status is unknown.
Exact publication dates for several 2018 and 2023 articles are given to month precision only.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The operational environment is Central Asian government, diplomatic and telecom networks, including the networks of partner nations and of US and coalition diplomatic or liaison elements in the region [S1][S8]. Regional telecom carriers are key terrain because Paperbug used one as an access point to downstream victims [S8]. STEP 2: Local mobile carriers and weak network configurations can expose traffic and endpoints of personnel who rely on host-nation services [S8]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is a socially engineered lure (fake messaging app, political-themed ZIP) or carrier-network pivot, then a Delphi backdoor or public tooling disguised as updaters, then document and screenshot collection [S2][S8]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet, long-running political surveillance of officials and diplomats, with collection of email, documents and chats [S8][S9]. MDCOA is use of telecom access to monitor coalition or partner communications, or misuse of the OT access shown in Paperbug (gas station systems) [S8]. Candidate indicators: unsigned Telegram-lookalike installers; processes named Google Update or Java Update in non-standard paths; periodic screenshot capture; outbound JSON-over-HTTP beacons from Delphi binaries; staging of RAR archives [S2][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: tag Central Asian partner-nation telecom and government networks as possible compromised transit, and treat host-nation carrier paths as untrusted [S8]. (2) Authorities: the actor targets foreign government and partner networks rather than the DODIN directly, so response options rely on information sharing with partners and the State Department rather than DoD defensive action on those networks. (3) Mission assurance: personnel deployed or traveling in Central Asia should use enterprise-managed messaging and avoid sideloaded apps, given the fake-Telegram lure [S2][S3]. (4) Coordination: report suspected indicators through CTI channels, and ask vendors (ESET, Kaspersky, PRODAFT) for updated reporting, since public data ends in 2023.

provenance.importedSummary: Prodaft researchers have published a report on Paperbug, a cyber-espionage campaign carried out by suspected Russian-speaking group Nomadic Octopus and which targeted entities in Tajikistan. According to Prodaft, known compromised victims included high-ranking government officials, telcos, and public service infrastructures. Compromised devices also included OT devices, besides your typical computers, servers, and mobile devices. In typical Prodaft fashion, the company also gained access to one of the group's C&C server backend panels.

identification.summary: Nylon Typhoon (formerly NICKEL) is a China-based espionage actor that Microsoft says uses exploits against unpatched systems to compromise remote access services and appliances, targeting government agencies, diplomatic organizations and NGOs in Central and South America, the Caribbean, Europe and North America [S1][S11]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the same group as Ke3chang (G0004), attributed to actors operating out of China, which has targeted oil, government, diplomatic, military and NGO organizations since at least 2010 [S3]. Microsoft reports that the actor achieved long-term access to several victims and ran regularly scheduled data exfiltration [S1]. Symantec reported the group, which it tracks as Flea, still attacking foreign ministries in the Americas in late 2022 and early 2023 with a new Microsoft Graph-based backdoor, Graphican [S12][S13].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: targeting since at least 2010 [S3]. Microsoft has tracked NICKEL since 2016 and tracked the operations it disclosed in 2021 since September 2019 [S1]. Latest dated public campaign found: late 2022 to early 2023 (Symantec, Flea) [S12][S13].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Nylon Typhoon (formerly NICKEL). Microsoft maps NICKEL, VIXEN PANDA, Playful Dragon, RedRiver, ke3chang, APT15 and Mirage to it [S4]. In 2021 Microsoft wrote that it 'observed some common activity' with actors known as APT15, APT25 and KeChang, which is an overlap statement rather than a one-to-one equivalence [S1]. Microsoft's Security Insider profile (dated 2024-01-25) lists APT15 and Vixen Panda as other names [S11]. Symantec's Flea is linked to APT15/Nickel in coverage of its 2023 report [S13]. MITRE lists Ke3chang, APT15, Mirage, Vixen Panda, GREF, Playful Dragon, RoyalAPT, NICKEL and Nylon Typhoon as associated names [S3]. The imported summary on this record described ESET's 'GREF' cluster (active since March 2017, Android BadBazaar campaigns against Uyghurs). That summary was not carried forward because no source gathered here ties that ESET cluster to Microsoft's Nylon Typhoon (see gaps).

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (state nexus). Microsoft describes NICKEL as a China-based threat actor [S1][S4], and MITRE attributes Ke3chang to actors operating out of China [S3]. None of the sources gathered names a specific PRC agency or unit.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributes the activity to NICKEL / Nylon Typhoon by name and assesses that China-based actors will keep targeting government, diplomatic and NGO sectors, likely for economic espionage or traditional intelligence collection [S1]. Microsoft did not publish a numeric or worded confidence level for state sponsorship. The December 2021 domain seizure was a civil action by Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit under a US District Court order, not a US government attribution [S1][S2]. Symantec assesses Flea as China-linked [S13]; that is a vendor assessment, not government attribution.
attribution.basis: Microsoft MSTIC telemetry and customer notifications, plus the DCU seizure of NICKEL-operated websites [S1][S2]; sign-in activity concentrated Monday to Friday, 08:00 to 17:00 China Standard Time [S1]; long-running vendor reporting summarized by MITRE ATT&CK (Mandiant, NCC Group, Intezer, ESET) [S3][S6][S7][S8][S9]; Symantec reporting on Flea/Graphican, as covered by the press [S12][S13]; Mandiant reporting on shared China-nexus ORB infrastructure [S5].

actors.objectives: Intelligence collection against foreign ministries, diplomatic entities, other government bodies and NGOs. Microsoft assesses this is likely in pursuit of economic espionage or traditional intelligence collection as China expands bilateral relations and Belt and Road partnerships [S1]. Mandiant's 2014 Operation Ke3chang report focused on attacks against Ministries of Foreign Affairs [S3][S9]. Symantec's 2022-2023 Flea victims were mainly foreign affairs ministries in the Americas, plus a government finance department, consistent with continued diplomatic intelligence collection [S12][S13].

sectors: Government, including ministries of foreign affairs and a finance department [S1][S9][S12][S13]
Private corporation in Central and South America (2022-2023) [S13]
regions: Central and South America, with a large share of activity against Central and South American governments [S1]
North America, including the United States [S1][S3]
Africa: Mali appears among the 29 countries Microsoft listed [S1]
Middle East: Mandiant lists it among regions historically targeted by APT15 and APT5 [S5]
targeting.notes: Microsoft's December 2021 list of 29 targeted countries: Argentina, Barbados, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Brazil, Bulgaria, Chile, Colombia, Croatia, Czech Republic, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, France, Guatemala, Honduras, Hungary, Italy, Jamaica, Mali, Mexico, Montenegro, Panama, Peru, Portugal, Switzerland, Trinidad and Tobago, United Kingdom, United States and Venezuela [S1]. In its 2021 Digital Defense Report summary, Microsoft names NICKEL among the four nation-state groups most active against the government sector from July 2020 to June 2021, mostly against government entities involved in international affairs [S10]. Symantec's 2022-2023 activity hit foreign ministries in the Americas, a corporation in Central and South America and one European victim [S12][S13].

capabilities.summary: Initial access through exploits against unpatched internet-facing Microsoft Exchange and SharePoint servers and remote-access appliances such as VPNs, including a Pulse Secure VPN vulnerability [S1]. MITRE also records VPN access using compromised accounts and stolen VPN certificates [S3][S6]. Credential theft uses keyloggers, Mimikatz, WDigest abuse and NTDSDump [S1]. Custom backdoors include Neoichor, Leeson, NumbIdea, NullItch and Rokum; several use the Internet Explorer COM interface for C2 hidden in legitimate-looking web pages, and implants are dropped into existing application paths to blend in [S1]. Stolen credentials are used for routine Microsoft 365 email collection through browser sign-ins and legacy Exchange Web Services, routed through commercial VPNs and actor infrastructure [S1]. Scheduled, incremental file collection is staged and archived with renamed RAR or 7-Zip [S1]. Earlier tooling includes RoyalCLI and RoyalDNS (DNS C2) and the SharePoint dumping tool spwebmember [S3][S6], the MirageFox RAT, an upgraded Mirage [S3][S7], and the Okrum backdoor, in use since December 2016 [S3][S8]. Mandiant reports that APT15 has used the provisioned ORB network SPACEHOP for reconnaissance scanning and vulnerability exploitation [S5]. In 2022-2023 the group (as Symantec's Flea) used Graphican, an evolution of the Ketrican backdoor (itself based on BS2005), which uses the Microsoft Graph API and OneDrive to retrieve encrypted C2 addresses and supports an interactive shell, file transfer, hidden process creation and hidden PowerShell execution [S12][S13]. The same campaign used the EWSTEW Exchange email-extraction backdoor, the Zerologon flaw CVE-2020-1472, Mimikatz, Pypykatz, Safetykatz and the public K8Tools toolkit [S12][S13].
