diamond.adversary: China-based espionage operators that Microsoft tracks as Nylon Typhoon (NICKEL) [S1][S4]. Sign-in activity clusters on weekdays from 08:00 to 17:00 China Standard Time, with possible shift-based scheduling [S1].
diamond.capability: Exploits for Exchange, SharePoint and VPN appliances. Credential theft with Mimikatz, WDigest, NTDSDump and keyloggers. Custom backdoors Neoichor, Leeson, NumbIdea, NullItch and Rokum [S1]. Legacy tools RoyalCLI, RoyalDNS, MirageFox and Okrum [S3][S6][S7][S8]. Graphican (Graph API/OneDrive C2), EWSTEW, Zerologon exploitation and K8Tools in 2022-2023 [S12][S13].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-operated websites used for C2, seized by Microsoft DCU in 2021 [S1][S2]. Hardcoded C2 servers return legitimate-looking HTML that hides Base64 shellcode [S1]. Commercial VPN providers carry account sign-ins [S1]. The SPACEHOP ORB network, provisioned by a single entity in China, uses relay servers hosted in Hong Kong or China [S5]. RoyalDNS used DNS for C2 [S3]. Graphican retrieves its C2 address from OneDrive through the Microsoft Graph API, hiding C2 lookup in legitimate cloud traffic [S12][S13].
diamond.victim: Foreign ministries and other government bodies, diplomatic entities and NGOs in Latin America, the Caribbean, Europe, North America and Mali [S1]. MITRE adds oil and military targets [S3]. Foreign ministries and a finance department in the Americas, plus one European victim, in 2022-2023 [S12][S13].
diamond.socioPolitical: Microsoft links the targeting to China's growing global influence, its bilateral relations and Belt and Road partnerships, with likely economic-espionage or traditional intelligence-collection aims [S1].
diamond.technology: Unpatched on-premises Exchange and SharePoint, remote-access VPN appliances, Microsoft 365 accounts reachable through legacy authentication (EWS), and Windows hosts where credentials are cached in memory [S1]. Microsoft 365 Graph API and OneDrive as C2 channels, and domain controllers unpatched for Zerologon [S12][S13].

gaps: No Microsoft reporting dated after 2021 with new Nylon Typhoon technical detail was found; the 2024 Security Insider profile is a summary [S11]. The latest dated campaign found is Symantec's 2022-2023 Flea/Graphican activity [S12][S13]. No 2024-2026 campaign reporting was found.
Microsoft's DCU announcement and the court filings could not be opened. Seizure details come from the MSTIC blog [S1] and press coverage reporting 42 domains [S2].

Symantec's Graphican report (S12) and most of its press coverage could not be opened (hosts blocked). Its details come from search-result summaries of Symantec and CSO Online coverage [S13]. Symantec's Flea name is not in Microsoft's mapping [S4], so the Flea-to-Nylon Typhoon link rests on Symantec's APT15/Nickel linkage.

Primary reports were not opened because their hosts were blocked: Mandiant Operation Ke3chang (2014), NCC Group RoyalCLI/RoyalDNS (2018), Intezer MirageFox (2018), ESET Okrum and Ketrican (2019), and Palo Alto Unit 42 TidePool. Their content is used only as summarized by MITRE ATT&CK.

Cluster boundary: ESET's 'GREF' (active since March 2017; Android BadBazaar trojanized Signal and Telegram apps targeting Uyghurs) appears in the imported summary, and MISP lists it as a separate entry from APT15. MITRE's GREF alias rests on older NCC Group reporting [S3]. No source gathered here establishes that ESET's GREF mobile activity belongs to Microsoft's Nylon Typhoon, so it is excluded.

Microsoft stated only 'common activity' with APT15, APT25 and KeChang in 2021 [S1]. APT25 is not in Microsoft's current Nylon Typhoon mapping [S4]. The exact boundary with Mandiant's APT15 and APT25 is unresolved.

Secureworks BRONZE PALACE, BRONZE DAVENPORT and BRONZE IDLEWOOD, plus the aliases Lurid, Metushy, Red Vulture, Social Network Team and Royal APT, are unverified. The Secureworks profile could not be opened.
No specific PRC sponsoring agency (MSS, PLA or contractor) and no US government indictment or advisory naming this actor was found.

Google Threat Intelligence's APT15 profile (sectors: trade, economic and financial, energy, military; ENFAL, BALDEAGLE, NOISEMAKER and MIRAGE malware) was read but carries no publication date, so it is not cited.
The Microsoft mapping file (S4) is a living document. Its date is the access date, not a publication date.

MITRE ATT&CK pages could not be opened directly this session. The G0004 description and aliases were confirmed through search results (version 3.1, modified 2025-04-04) [S3]; software and campaign C0052 details come from earlier reading of the ATT&CK bundle and were not re-verified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (define the OE): Key cyber terrain is internet-facing Exchange, SharePoint and VPN appliances, plus Microsoft 365 tenants that still allow legacy authentication (EWS). It matters most for foreign-affairs, diplomatic and partner-nation government networks in Latin America, the Caribbean, Europe and North America [S1]. STEP 2 (describe effects): Exposed and unpatched remote-access edges are the entry point. Shared ORB relay networks such as SPACEHOP spread source infrastructure across commercial VPS providers, which weakens IP-based blocking and attribution [S1][S5]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Exploit edge service or VPN, then dump credentials (Mimikatz, NTDSDump, WDigest, keylogger), then deploy an IE-COM backdoor in a legitimate software path, then collect mailboxes through M365/EWS sign-ins over commercial VPNs, then run recurring, date-filtered file collection archived with renamed RAR or 7-Zip [S1]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is quiet, long-term diplomatic and government intelligence collection with scheduled exfiltration from partner-nation ministries [S1]. MDCOA is persistent access to partner-nation foreign-affairs and military networks, or to shared coalition email, exposing coalition planning or negotiating positions (analyst extrapolation from the targeting [S1][S3]). Graphican shows the actor moving C2 into Microsoft Graph/OneDrive traffic, which blends with normal M365 use [S12][S13]. Candidate indicators: unexpected Graph API or OneDrive access by non-browser processes on servers; Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472) exploitation attempts against domain controllers [S12][S13]; EWS or legacy-auth sign-ins from commercial VPN ranges during 00:00-09:00 UTC on weekdays; WDigest UseLogonCredential being enabled; executables such as AcroRd64.exe or FoxitRdr64.exe in unexpected application folders; IE registry changes (IEHarden=0, ClearBrowsingHistoryOnExit=1); renamed rar.exe or 7z.exe with keyboard-walk passwords [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Fuse identity telemetry (legacy-auth and EWS sign-ins, VPN-sourced logons) with edge-device patch status. The actor relies on valid credentials after initial exploitation, so host-only sensing will miss mailbox collection [S1]. Track ORB/SPACEHOP-linked infrastructure as shared China-nexus terrain rather than as a single-actor indicator [S5]. Authorities: The 2021 disruption came through a private civil seizure (Microsoft DCU under a US District Court order), not government action [S1][S2]. Planners should not count such actions as DoD effects, and they should coordinate deconfliction with private-sector disruption efforts. Situational awareness should also cover cloud API telemetry, because Graph/OneDrive C2 bypasses traditional C2 domain blocking [S12][S13]. Mission assurance: Block legacy authentication, enforce MFA, apply the ASR rule against LSASS credential theft, and prioritize patching of Exchange, SharePoint and VPN appliances on DODIN and mission-partner enclaves [S1]. Coordination: Many victims are partner-nation and Western Hemisphere foreign ministries [S1]. Information sharing with partner nations and combatant commands, especially SOUTHCOM-area partners, is an analyst-inferred coordination need for protecting shared diplomatic and military communications.

provenance.importedSummary: GREF is a China-aligned APT group that has been active since at least March 2017. They are known for using custom backdoors, loaders, and ancillary tools in their targeted attacks. Recently, they have been attributed to two active Android campaigns that distribute the BadBazaar malware through malicious apps on official and alternative app stores. GREF has targeted Android users, particularly Uyghurs and other Turkic ethnic minorities outside of China, using trojanized versions of popular messaging apps like Signal and Telegram.

identification.summary:
Scattered Spider is a native English-speaking cybercriminal group active since at least 2022.   The group initially targeted customer relationship management (CRM) providers, business process outsourcing (BPO) firms, and telecommunications and technology companies before expanding in 2023 to gaming, hospitality, retail, managed service provider (MSP), manufacturing, and financial sectors. 
Scattered Spider relies heavily on social engineering, including impersonating IT and help-desk staff, to gain initial access, bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA), and compromise enterprise networks. The group has adapted its tooling to evade endpoint detection and response (EDR) defenses and used ransomware for financial gain.   
Scattered Spider had expanded into hybrid cloud and identity environments, using help-desk impersonation and MFA bypass to obtain administrator access in Okta, AWS, and Office 365.

identification.summary: Oka Flood is Microsoft's name for a Russia-based influence-operations actor that Microsoft previously tracked as Storm-1679 [S4]. Microsoft calls Storm-1679 a prolific Russian influence actor whose main tactic is spoofed content that imitates reputable media outlets [S1]. Microsoft says the Paris 2024 Olympics were a primary objective since at least summer 2023, when the actor released the fake documentary 'Olympics Has Fallen' with AI-generated audio imitating Tom Cruise's voice [S1][S2]. In September 2024 Microsoft reported that Storm-1679 shifted from the French election and the Olympics to content targeting Kamala Harris [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: Olympics-focused activity since at least summer 2023, with the fake documentary released on Telegram in June 2023 [S1][S2]. CheckFirst's related 'Operation Overload' reporting begins in 2023 [S5].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Oka Flood (formerly Storm-1679), listed as a Russian influence-operations actor [S4]. Researchers outside Microsoft (ISD, as relayed by the AI Incident Database) treat Operation Overload, Matryoshka and Storm-1679 as one campaign [S8]. CheckFirst names the newsroom-flooding campaign Operation Overload [S5][S6]. These are separate analytic clusters whose equivalence Microsoft has not confirmed in the sources gathered. Microsoft reports Storm-1679 alongside Storm-1099 (Doppelganger) and Storm-1516, but tracks them as separate actors [S1][S3].

attribution.sponsor: Russia (Microsoft: Russia-affiliated influence actor) [S1][S4]. No sourced attribution to a specific Russian government organization.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft describes Storm-1679 as a Russian influence actor but does not name a state sponsor in the sources reviewed [S1][S3]. CheckFirst found that some email accounts used in Operation Overload were accessed from Russian residential IP addresses [S6][S9]. CheckFirst's CEO, Guillaume Kuster, called this 'a red flag' but 'not proof of anything', and said it was unclear who was behind the campaign or whether it was state-backed [S9]. No US government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft Threat Analysis Center (MTAC) observation of content and amplification [S1][S2][S3]; Microsoft naming taxonomy [S4]; CheckFirst/Reset.Tech technical analysis of email infrastructure (Operation Overload cluster) [S5][S6].

actors.objectives: Microsoft says the actor's goals were to damage the International Olympic Committee's reputation, create expectations of violence at the Paris 2024 Games, and discourage spectators from attending [S1][S2]. Earlier Russia-aligned celebrity-video content pushed the false narrative that President Zelensky abuses drugs [S1][S7]. In 2024 the actor turned to US election narratives that disparaged Kamala Harris [S3]. CheckFirst says the related Operation Overload campaign aims to drain fact-checker and newsroom resources and to push Kremlin narratives through trusted information channels [S5].

sectors: National governments and political leaders (France/Macron; US presidential campaign) [S1][S3]
Media, newsrooms and fact-checkers (impersonated or flooded) [S1][S5]
regions: Ukraine and Ukrainian refugee communities (earlier campaigns) [S1]
Germany (2025 federal election, per AI Incident Database reporting on Matryoshka/Operation Overload) [S8]
targeting.notes: Before spring 2024, content was mostly in English with some French, German and other European languages. French-language content increased in spring 2024 [S1]. Germany targeting comes from the Matryoshka/Operation Overload cluster, not from Microsoft reporting [S8].

capabilities.summary: Influence-operations tradecraft rather than network intrusion. Documented techniques include: AI-generated voice imitation of celebrities (Tom Cruise) in a feature-length fake documentary with spoofed Netflix branding and fake reviews attributed to the New York Times, Washington Post and BBC [S1][S2]; doctored Cameo videos bought from US celebrities and re-edited with anti-Ukraine messaging [S1][S7]; fake news clips and video 'press releases' impersonating Euronews, France 24, the CIA and France's DGSI [S1]; likely digitally generated graffiti images and false-flag impersonation of militant groups [S1]; and bot-amplified accounts and Telegram channels [S1]. In the September 2024 Harris content, Microsoft found the actor used actors and conventional editing rather than generative AI [S3]. The related Operation Overload cluster sends mass email to newsrooms (at least 71,000 emails reported by September 2024, with the volume having trebled since June) and uses 'content amalgamation' across X, Telegram and Russia-aligned sites [S5][S6][S9].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): The information environment counts as key terrain. That includes Telegram, X, short-form video platforms, the brands of trusted Western media and agencies (CIA, DGSI, BBC, France 24), and fact-checking organizations [S1][S5]. STEP 2 (effects): The actor imitates trusted brands and celebrity voices cheaply, so audiences and newsrooms face content that looks authoritative. Verification capacity is the friendly vulnerability the actor exploits [S1][S5]. STEP 3 (adversary model): Pick a high-visibility event (Olympics, election). Produce spoofed media or a fake press release that hints at violence or scandal. Seed it on Telegram and amplify it with bots. Then email newsrooms asking them to 'verify' it [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 4 (COAs): The most likely COA (MLCOA) is fabricated news clips or fake official statements around major Western events and elections that discredit leaders and support for Ukraine [S1][S3]. The most dangerous COA (MDCOA) is a fabricated 'official' threat warning (for example, a spoofed CIA or allied intelligence press release) released during a real crisis or a major event with a US military presence, which would trigger panic, force-protection confusion or misdirected public affairs responses [S1]. Candidate indicators: content carrying spoofed logos of agencies or outlets that is absent from their official channels; new Telegram channels pushing event-specific fear narratives; bursts of verification-request emails to press and public affairs offices [S1][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Track impersonation of US government and DoD brands alongside media spoofing, since the actor has faked CIA press releases [S1]. Give public affairs and IO cells a shared picture of active fabricated narratives. (2) Authorities: This is an influence actor with no sourced network-intrusion activity. Responses fall mainly under IO, public affairs and interagency (State GEC successor functions, FBI FITF) lanes rather than DCO. Confirm authorities before any cyberspace response. (3) Mission assurance: Expect fabricated threat content around large events and exercises with a US presence. Prepare rapid authoritative messaging to prevent operational disruption [S1]. (4) Coordination: Share indicators with platform operators and allied counterparts (France, Germany) that are dealing with the same campaigns. Do not merge vendor clusters (Storm-1679, Operation Overload, Matryoshka) in reporting without noting the source of each [S5][S8].

provenance.importedSummary: Storm-1679 is a Russian disinformation group believed to be a spinoff of the Internet Research Agency, actively engaged in influence operations targeting the International Olympic Committee and the 2024 Olympic Games. The group has employed AI-generated content, including deepfake videos and fabricated narratives about violence, to discredit the IOC and instill fear among potential attendees. Their campaigns have been identified across multiple languages and platforms, utilizing techniques such as impersonation of media outlets and the creation of disinformation websites. Microsoft attributes significant disinformation activities related to the Olympics to Storm-1679, highlighting their focus on spreading falsehoods and promoting anti-Olympics messaging.

identification.summary: Russian-speaking, financially motivated ransomware group that Group-IB (as reported by the press) describes as unusual because it mainly attacks Russian organizations, which most Russian-speaking ransomware operators avoid [S1][S2]. Group-IB's first public reporting was in September 2020 and dated campaigns to spring 2020 [S1]. Kaspersky reported renewed activity in early 2025 [S6].
identification.firstObserved: Spring 2020 (campaigns since about March 2020 per Group-IB's 2022 reporting [S4]; first reported by Group-IB in September 2020 [S1]).
identification.notes: Group-IB also tracks the group as TinyScouts [S2][S4]. Coverage of the 2022 Linux report and of Brandefense's 2025 write-up differs on geographic scope: Group-IB-derived reporting describes mainly Russian targets [S2][S4], while Brandefense says Europe and the Americas are also targeted [S7]; the Brandefense claim is not corroborated by other gathered sources. The 2025 Kaspersky ransom-note use of the 'OldGremlin' name is reported as the first time the operators used the name themselves [S6].

attribution.confidence: Vendors describe the group as financially motivated and Russian-speaking [S1][S2][S6]. No government or state sponsorship attribution was found in gathered sources. Kaspersky links its 2025 incidents to earlier OldGremlin campaigns via consistent tactics and a reused cryptographic public key (Kaspersky's own assessment, as reported) [S6].
attribution.basis: Group-IB analysis of 2020-2022 campaigns (via press coverage) [S1][S2]; Kaspersky Threat Research on 2025 activity (via press-release coverage) [S6].

actors.objectives: Financial gain through large-scale ransomware extortion; Group-IB-derived reporting gives a maximum demand of $4.2 million in 2021 and $16.9 million in 2022 [S2][S4]. Kaspersky's 2025 report mentions the group earlier demanded nearly $17 million from one victim [S6].

targeting.notes: 2020 reporting: medical labs, banks, manufacturers and software developers [S1]. 2022: logistics, industry, insurance, retail, real estate, software development, banking [S2][S4]. 2025: manufacturing, healthcare, retail and technology [S6]. Brandefense claims Europe and the Americas as well [S7] (uncorroborated).

capabilities.summary: Targeted phishing email as initial access, with lures such as an invoice purporting to come from RBC and COVID-themed mails impersonating a Russian microfinance organization [S1]. A link downloads a ZIP containing the custom TinyNode backdoor or the TinyPosh trojan [S1]. Cobalt Strike is used for lateral movement, followed by domain admin credential theft, creation of a privileged account for persistence, deletion of server backups and encryption with TinyCryptor (aka decr1pt) several weeks after the attack began [S1]. A Go-built Linux variant of the TinyCrypt ransomware (AES-256-CBC, .crypt extension) was found in 2022 [S4]. Kaspersky's 2025 toolkit comprises a backdoor, a 'patcher' abusing a flaw in a legitimate Windows driver to disable protections, an encryptor, and a 'closethedoor' tool to isolate the host and remove traces, with Node.js used to run commands; typical dwell time before encryption is about 49 days [S6].

campaigns.name: Initial phishing campaigns (TinyNode/TinyCryptor)
campaigns.summary: Group-IB reports custom-tool operations (nine campaigns between May and August 2020 per the Sept 2020 report [S1]; Group-IB's later reporting counts activity since March 2020 [S4]) against Russian medical labs, banks, manufacturers and software developers; a successful attack in August 2020 hit a clinical diagnostics lab. Ransom demand cited at $50,000 in cryptocurrency.

campaigns.name: Retail-association impersonation campaign
campaigns.summary: Coverage of Group-IB reporting describes a single 2021 campaign in which the actor impersonated an association of online retailers; maximum demand that year was $4.2 million.

campaigns.name: Linux TinyCrypt variant and record demand
campaigns.summary: Group-IB reported a Go-built Linux version of TinyCrypt and a maximum ransom demand of $16.9 million in 2022; targets spanned logistics, industry, insurance, retail, real estate, software and banking.

campaigns.name: Return in 2025
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky reported new attacks from early 2025 against manufacturing, healthcare, retail and technology firms, with a new toolkit, about 49 days of dwell time, and first use of the 'OldGremlin' name in ransom notes and file paths.

diamond.adversary: Russian-speaking financially motivated ransomware group, also tracked by Group-IB as TinyScouts [S2][S4].
diamond.capability: Phishing, custom backdoors (TinyNode, TinyPosh), Cobalt Strike, TinyCryptor/TinyCrypt ransomware for Windows and Linux, BYOVD-style driver abuse in 2025 [S1][S4][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Phishing links hosting ZIP payloads [S1]; specific infrastructure details were not obtained.
diamond.victim: Mainly Russian banks, industrial, medical, software, logistics, insurance and retail organizations [S1][S2][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Financial extortion against Russian entities, atypical for Russian-speaking ransomware actors [S1].
diamond.technology: Windows and Linux enterprise networks reachable through email; Active Directory domain credentials; backups targeted for deletion [S1][S4].

gaps: Direct fetches of Group-IB, Kaspersky, The Hacker News and BleepingComputer pages failed in this environment; content relies on search-result summaries of those reports, and primary documents were not opened.
Year of the $16.9 million demand and details of the 2021 campaign come from secondary coverage [S4].
No sponsor, individuals, or law-enforcement action identified in gathered sources.
Brandefense claim of non-Russian targeting is uncorroborated [S7].
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID or Microsoft name was identified.
Initial access broker relationships, infrastructure and IOCs not gathered.
Hackread and Security Affairs URLs could not be confirmed in search results; those sources and the TinyFluff (2022) claims resting on them were removed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Email gateways, domain controllers and backup systems are key terrain in organizations the group targets [S1]. STEP 2: The group primarily victimizes Russian entities, so direct relevance to US/allied networks is limited and mainly as a model of criminal intrusion tradecraft [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Template is phishing, custom backdoor, Cobalt Strike, domain-admin theft, backup deletion, then long-dwell encryption (about 49 days in 2025) on Windows and Linux [S1][S4][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-volume, high-demand ransomware against Russian industry. MDCOA is expansion to non-Russian organizations, as one unverified vendor claim suggests [S7]. Candidate indicators: phishing mail with ZIP links impersonating trade bodies, Cobalt Strike beacons, new privileged accounts, loading of vulnerable Windows drivers, mass backup deletion [S1][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Long dwell time (about 49 days) gives a detection window; feed backup-deletion and new-admin-account alerts into situational awareness [S1][S6]. (2) Mission assurance: protect offline backups and Linux servers, since a Linux encryptor exists [S4]. (3) Authorities and coordination: treat as criminal activity; coordinate through normal law-enforcement and DC3/industry-sharing channels if any DoD-adjacent victim emerges. Relevance is low unless targeting shifts [S7].

provenance.importedSummary: OldGremlin is a Russian-speaking ransomware group that has been active for several years. They primarily target organizations in Russia, including banks, logistics, industrial, insurance, retail, and IT companies. OldGremlin is known for using phishing emails as an initial infection vector and has developed custom malware for both Windows and Linux systems. identification.summary: OnionDog is a name given by Qihoo 360's Helios Team (SkyEye Labs) in 2016 to an activity cluster that reportedly stole data from energy and transportation organizations in Korean-speaking countries, with activity traced back to October 2013 [S2]. In August 2017 Trend Micro assessed that OnionDog is not a targeted attack but a cyber drill, because several of the eight C&C IP addresses in the 360 report were linked to South Korea's National Cybersecurity Center (NCSC) [S1][S3].
identification.firstObserved: 360 Helios: activity traced back to October 2013 [S2].
identification.notes: The existing record's country value (KP) is not supported by any source gathered here; neither the 360 report coverage nor Trend Micro attributes OnionDog to North Korea [S1][S2]. The two vendor readings conflict (real APT per 360, drill per Trend Micro) and this record does not resolve them [S1][S2].

attribution.basis: No source gathered names a sponsor. 360 Helios described a group but the coverage reviewed names no state [S2]. Trend Micro, reviewing the same indicators, assessed the samples were linked to official South Korean cyber practices (the NCSC) and concluded this was a cyber drill, not a targeted attack [S1][S3].

sectors: Transportation (harbors, vessel traffic services, subways, public transportation)
targeting.notes: 360 Helios reported 2014 targeting of electric power and water resources corporations and other energy enterprises, and 2015 targeting of harbors, VTS, subways and public transportation [S2]. The existing record also lists government as a target; no source gathered here confirms this. All targeting claims derive from the 360 report and are disputed by Trend Micro [S1].

capabilities.summary: 360 Helios reported spear-phishing email lures, an early Trojan disguised as a Hangul (HWP) document using icons and file numbers, later use of a vulnerability in an upgraded Hangul version to embed malicious code in a genuine HWP file, and a USB worm to reach network-isolated targets [S2]. Helios reported 96 groups of malicious code and 14 C&C domains/IPs [S2]. Trend Micro reviewed the eight hardcoded C&C IPs and said the malware does no actual harm to systems and that about 200 unique samples are known [S1][S3].

diamond.adversary: Unknown. 360 described a group; Trend Micro assessed official South Korean (NCSC) cyber-practice activity [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing, malicious/fake HWP documents, Hangul vulnerability, USB worm for isolated networks [S2].

No sponsor or state attribution is stated in any source gathered; the KP country value in the original record is unsupported. A secondary vendor blog reportedly links OnionDog to Lazarus, but this was not verified and Qianxin's own report reportedly says no link was found; not used here.
The original 360/Qianxin report and Trend Micro appendix (hashes) could not be opened (WebFetch failed); details rely on search summaries and secondary coverage.
No aliases or MITRE group are established. Help Net Security, ETDA, Malpedia and CFR pages were not opened.
Actor objectives and any post-2017 activity are not documented in sources gathered.

identification.summary: North Korean actor within the Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB) that conducts cyber espionage against military, defense and technology targets to advance the regime's military and nuclear programs, and that has expanded into financial gain, including ransomware [S1][S2]. A US indictment unsealed in July 2024 charged an alleged member for Maui ransomware attacks on US hospitals [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft first observed the actor in 2014 [S1]; MITRE: active since at least 2009 [S4]. TigerRAT in use since 2020 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Onyx Sleet (formerly PLUTONIUM). Microsoft maps SILENT CHOLLIMA, StoneFly, DarkSeoul, Andariel and APT45 to it [S5]; MITRE tracks it as Andariel (G0138) [S4]. These names were previously merged into the Diamond Sleet (Lazarus) record and have been separated.

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea: Reconnaissance General Bureau [S2].
attribution.confidence: Formal US government attribution through the indictment of Rim Jong Hyok, announced 25 Jul 2024, which describes him as an RGB member associated with Andariel / Onyx Sleet / APT45 [S2]. Microsoft attributes the activity to Onyx Sleet [S1].
attribution.basis: DOJ indictment and FBI investigation [S2]; Microsoft telemetry [S1]; CISA-linked advisory reporting cited by Microsoft [S1].

actors.objectives: Intelligence collection supporting DPRK military and nuclear programs, primarily from military, defense and technology targets [S1]. Revenue generation through ransomware and possibly online gambling [S1][S2], with ransom proceeds laundered through Hong Kong-based facilitators [S2].

sectors: Military and defense (including US defense contractors and US Air Force bases)
targeting.notes: Regions and sectors from Microsoft [S1]. FBI-reported victims: five healthcare providers, four US defense contractors, two US Air Force bases and NASA OIG [S2].

capabilities.summary: Custom malware including TigerRAT (since 2020), SmallTiger (against South Korean defense and manufacturing), LightHand, ValidAlpha/BlackRAT and Dtrack [S1]. Custom ransomware, notably Maui, used against US hospitals [S1][S2]. MITRE lists 12 techniques for Andariel (G0138), including gh0st RAT and Rifdoor usage [S4]. The MITRE mapping is thin relative to the public reporting, so treat the ATT&CK list as incomplete.

campaigns.name: Maui ransomware against US healthcare
campaigns.summary: RGB-developed Maui ransomware encrypted medical testing and records systems at US hospitals; ransoms laundered via Hong Kong facilitators. Charged in the 2024 indictment.

campaigns.name: Indictment of Rim Jong Hyok
campaigns.summary: Kansas grand jury charges for conspiracy to commit computer hacking and money laundering; $10M reward; added to FBI Most Wanted. Victims include defense contractors, US Air Force bases and NASA OIG.

campaigns.name: TigerRAT / SmallTiger espionage
campaigns.summary: Custom RATs against defense, manufacturing and technology targets, primarily in South Korea, the US and India.

diamond.adversary: RGB operators; Rim Jong Hyok charged in 2024 [S2].
diamond.capability: TigerRAT, SmallTiger, LightHand, ValidAlpha, Dtrack; Maui ransomware [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-controlled C2; cryptocurrency ransom payment and laundering through Hong Kong facilitators [S2].
diamond.victim: Defense contractors, military installations, NASA OIG, US hospitals, South Korean defense and manufacturing, Indian targets [S1][S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Support to DPRK military and nuclear programs, plus sanctions-evading revenue [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Vulnerable internet-facing systems and weak healthcare IT resilience exploited for ransomware leverage [S2].

gaps: Primary indictment PDF and the joint technical advisory issued alongside it were not fetched (government sites blocked); the advisory identifier should be confirmed.
MITRE's Andariel technique list (12) is far smaller than the reported tradecraft; analyst mapping from Microsoft and advisory reporting is needed.
How ransomware revenue and espionage tasking are balanced within the group is not public.
Overlap with the Diamond Sleet record's historical 'Lazarus' events (e.g. DarkSeoul) should be reconciled.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The OE includes DIB contractors, military installations' IT and healthcare systems supporting military communities. This actor targets all three. STEP 2: Ransomware against hospitals near installations can degrade medical support to forces and families. STEP 3: The template is exploitation of internet-facing systems, then custom RATs for espionage, and in some cases ransomware deployment for revenue. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent espionage against defense and aerospace technology to support weapons programs. MDCOA is ransomware against healthcare or installation-support providers during a Korean Peninsula crisis, combining revenue with disruption. Candidate indicators: TigerRAT or SmallTiger detections, ransomware staging in healthcare networks, and intrusions at aerospace and defense suppliers [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Coordinate with USFK and INDOPACOM, and with South Korean partners, since South Korea is the primary target. (2) Include Defense Health Agency and community hospital partners in situational awareness for ransomware threats. (3) Financial disruption (seizures, sanctions) is a DOJ and Treasury lead but affects the actor's resources; track it as part of campaign assessment. (4) DIB CS program reporting is a primary sensor for this actor's espionage.

provenance.importedSummary:
Andariel is a North Korean state-sponsored threat group that has been active since at least 2009. Andariel has primarily focused its operations--which have included destructive attacks--against South Korean government agencies, military organizations, and a variety of domestic companies; they have also conducted cyber financial operations against ATMs, banks, and cryptocurrency exchanges. Andariel's notable activity includes Operation Black Mine, Operation GoldenAxe, and Campaign Rifle.

Andariel is considered a sub-set of Lazarus Group, and has been attributed to North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau.

North Korean group definitions are known to have significant overlap, and some security researchers report all North Korean state-sponsored cyber activity under the name Lazarus Group instead of tracking clusters or subgroups.

identification.summary: North Korea-linked espionage actor that Microsoft calls Opal Sleet (formerly OSMIUM) and that other vendors track as Konni and TA406 [S1][S4]. Microsoft reported that in March 2023 an attacker account attributed to Opal Sleet sent phishing emails to Russian diplomatic government entities [S2]. Proofpoint reported that from February 2025 the group, which it calls TA406, phished Ukrainian government entities with both credential-harvesting and malware lures [S4]. Later Konni reporting describes abuse of Google Find Hub to wipe South Korean victims' Android phones (activity from September 2025, reported November 2025) and an AI-assisted PowerShell backdoor aimed at blockchain developers (January 2026) [S11][S9].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Opal Sleet. Microsoft's mapping lists OSMIUM, VELVET CHOLLIMA, Planedown, Konni and APT43 as other names [S1]. Proofpoint says TA406 activity overlaps with what third parties track as Opal Sleet and Konni [S4]. Press coverage also gives Vedalia as an alias [S10]. Coverage of Genians' reporting describes KONNI as sharing targets and infrastructure with Kimsuky and APT37 [S11]. These are vendor cluster overlaps, not proof that the groups are identical.

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea), per vendor assessments [S2][S4].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributes the March 2023 phishing of Russian diplomatic entities to Opal Sleet by name [S2]. Proofpoint calls TA406 a North Korean state-sponsored actor, but says it could not confirm with full certainty that every observed operation was TA406's. Its attribution rests on technical overlaps and the choice of targets [S4]. No government attribution of Opal Sleet or Konni was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and threat-intelligence reporting [S2]; Proofpoint technical overlaps and targeting [S4]; Genians and Check Point reporting on Konni malware and infrastructure, via secondary coverage [S9][S10][S11].

actors.objectives: Strategic and political intelligence collection. Microsoft assessed that North Korean groups targeting Russia in 2023 were likely gathering intelligence [S2]. Proofpoint assessed that the 2025 Ukraine campaigns aimed to gather intelligence on how the Russian invasion was progressing, possibly to help North Korean leadership judge the risk to its own forces in the theater [S4]. The January 2026 targeting of blockchain and cryptocurrency developers suggests interest in that sector as well [S9].

sectors: Think tanks and policy experts, impersonated as lure personas [S4]
Individuals reached via KakaoTalk, including North Korea human-rights contexts [S11][S10]
Blockchain/cryptocurrency software developers and engineering teams [S9]
regions: Asia-Pacific: Japan, Australia, India (2026 developer campaign) [S9]
targeting.notes: Coverage of Check Point's reporting says Konni historically focused on South Korean government and academic targets [S9]. Proofpoint describes the move to Ukraine as a change from the group's earlier focus on Russia [S4].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing is the core access method. Lures include fictitious think-tank personas sending links to password-protected archives on external file hosts. Those archives hold HTML and CHM files with embedded PowerShell that profiles the host. The group also sends spoofed Microsoft security alerts to harvest credentials [S4]. Konni operators used KakaoTalk lures and stolen Google credentials to locate victims' Android devices and factory-reset them through Google Find Hub. They then used the victim's still-active KakaoTalk PC session to send malware to the victim's contacts [S11]. In January 2026 Check Point reported a heavily obfuscated, in-memory PowerShell backdoor that it assessed as AI-assisted. It persisted through a scheduled task disguised as OneDrive and dropped the legitimate SimpleHelp remote-management tool [S9][S10]. Genians' 'Operation Poseidon' reporting describes Google and Naver ad-redirect URLs that delivered LNK files, an AutoIt loader and EndRAT, with payloads and C2 hosted on compromised WordPress sites [S10].

campaigns.name: Phishing of Russian diplomatic entities
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reported that an attacker account attributed to Opal Sleet sent phishing emails to Russian diplomatic government entities. Microsoft did not name the victims.

campaigns.name: TA406 targeting of Ukrainian government
campaigns.summary: Proofpoint reported credential-harvesting and malware phishing against Ukrainian government entities, using think-tank personas and HTML/CHM payloads. It assessed the aim as intelligence on the progress of Russia's invasion.

campaigns.name: Google Find Hub remote-wipe campaign
campaigns.summary: Genians (reported November 2025) described KONNI using stolen Google credentials to locate and factory-reset South Korean victims' Android devices, then spreading malware through their KakaoTalk PC sessions.

campaigns.name: AI-assisted PowerShell backdoor against blockchain developers
campaigns.summary: Check Point reported phishing with fake project documentation that delivered an obfuscated PowerShell backdoor and SimpleHelp. Samples were linked to Japan, Australia and India.

campaigns.name: Operation Poseidon (ad-redirect spear-phishing)
campaigns.summary: Genians-attributed Konni spear-phishing impersonated North Korean human-rights groups and South Korean financial institutions. It used Google and Naver ad-redirect URLs to deliver EndRAT.

diamond.adversary: North Korea-linked operators that Microsoft tracks as Opal Sleet and Proofpoint as TA406, also called Konni [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing with HTML/CHM/LNK payloads and embedded PowerShell; credential-harvesting pages; RATs including EndRAT; an AI-assisted PowerShell backdoor; abuse of the SimpleHelp RMM tool [S4][S11][S9][S10].
diamond.infrastructure: Freemail and Proton Mail sender accounts; external file-hosting services; compromised WordPress sites for payloads and C2; ad-redirect URLs; hijacked Google and KakaoTalk accounts [S4][S11][S10].
diamond.victim: Russian diplomatic entities; Ukrainian government entities; South Korean individuals and organizations; APAC blockchain developers [S2][S4][S11][S9].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on the Russia-Ukraine war and on Korean Peninsula issues in support of North Korean leadership [S2][S4].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints running PowerShell and CHM; Google accounts linked to Android devices; KakaoTalk desktop sessions; developer workstations [S4][S11][S9].

gaps: Microsoft has published no stand-alone Opal Sleet profile in the sources gathered. The only Microsoft-sourced campaign found is the March 2023 Russia phishing, known from press coverage of Microsoft's 2023 East Asia report; the report itself was not retrieved [S2].
Proofpoint's original blog could not be fetched. Its details come from search excerpts and secondary coverage, and the exact publication day (around 2025-05-13/14) is unconfirmed [S4].
The BleepingComputer article's exact date (late August or early September 2023) is unconfirmed.

Cluster boundaries: Microsoft's mapping lists VELVET CHOLLIMA and APT43 under Opal Sleet [S1], while other vendors commonly associate those names with Kimsuky. Coverage of Genians' reporting says KONNI overlaps with Kimsuky and APT37 [S11]. It is unresolved whether the 2025-2026 Konni campaigns from Genians and Check Point fall inside Microsoft's Opal Sleet boundary.
First-observed date is unverified. Secondary sources give different start years for Konni (2014 vs. about 2016), and no primary source was found.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID is confirmed for Opal Sleet/Konni.
No US government attribution or advisory naming Opal Sleet, Konni or TA406 was found.
Which North Korean organization (for example, an RGB element) sponsors the group is not established in the cited sources.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): The relevant cyberspace includes diplomatic and government email, personal cloud identities (Google/Naver) tied to mobile devices, messaging apps such as KakaoTalk, and developer workstations [S4][S11][S9]. STEP 2 (effects): The actor relies on social engineering rather than exploits of perimeter devices, so the decisive terrain is user identity and email/messaging trust [S4][S11]. STEP 3 (threat model): Think-tank or official persona -> link to archive or file host -> HTML/CHM/LNK running PowerShell -> reconnaissance and RAT or backdoor -> credential theft, sometimes followed by device wipe and contact-chain spread [S4][S11][S9][S10]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued credential and intelligence collection against government, diplomatic and policy targets on the Russia-Ukraine war and Korean issues [S2][S4]. MDCOA is the use of stolen cloud credentials to wipe devices and blind victims during operations, as seen in the Find Hub campaign [S11]. Candidate indicators: unsolicited think-tank 'senior fellow' outreach; password-protected archives holding CHM/HTML files; scheduled tasks posing as OneDrive; unexpected SimpleHelp installs; Google/Naver ad-redirect links leading to LNK downloads; unexpected Find Hub remote-reset events [S4][S9][S10][S11].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Fuse vendor reporting under all aliases (Opal Sleet, Konni, TA406, OSMIUM) while keeping cluster caveats visible [S1][S4][S11]. Authorities: The reported activity is espionage against government and diplomatic targets, so defensive responses fall mainly under DODIN/DCO and partner information-sharing channels, and the cited sources contain no government attribution [S2][S4]. Mission assurance: Personnel who deal with the Korean Peninsula, Ukraine or Russia policy face phishing aimed at personal and official accounts. Protecting cloud identities and device-management features such as Find Hub reduces the risk of losing data and devices [S4][S11]. Coordination: Coordinate with allied and partner CERTs (for example Ukraine and South Korea) and with commercial vendors whose telemetry covers the actor's lures [S4][S11][S9].

identification.summary: Operation BugDrop is a cyber-reconnaissance (espionage) campaign publicly disclosed by industrial cybersecurity firm CyberX in February 2017, named for its use of Dropbox to hold stolen data [S1][S3]. CyberX confirmed at least 70 victims across critical infrastructure, media and scientific research, mostly in Ukraine, with smaller numbers in Russia, Saudi Arabia and Austria [S1][S3]. The malware takes over PC microphones to record audio and also captured credentials, documents and screenshots [S1][S3].
identification.firstObserved: CyberX reported activity from no later than June 2016 [S1]. Public disclosure was February 2017 [S1][S3].
identification.notes: BugDrop is a campaign name coined by CyberX, not a vendor-assigned actor name; no Microsoft name or MITRE group exists for it. CyberX noted TTP and targeting similarities to Operation Groundbait (ESET, May 2016) but said the campaigns may be unrelated or that the actors changed methods after exposure [S2]. Do not merge the two clusters. The 600GB figure in one headline is not confirmed in the body text of the sources reviewed [S6].

attribution.confidence: CyberX did not identify the actors; it floated possibilities including Ukrainians spying on pro-Russian Ukrainians, Russians spying on Ukrainians, or a hired third party [S1]. Infosecurity Magazine's headline calls it state-sponsored [S3].
attribution.basis: CyberX's assessment of operational scale and targeting [S1][S3]. Malware reported as likely created in Russia, unconfirmed [S1]. No government attribution found in the sources reviewed.

actors.objectives: Intelligence collection through audio eavesdropping and theft of credentials, documents and screenshots from Ukrainian critical infrastructure, media and research targets [S1][S3].

targeting.notes: At least 70 confirmed victims [S1][S3]. Reporting on the CyberX findings says victims included people in Donetsk and Luhansk, as did Groundbait [S2].

capabilities.summary: Initial infection reportedly via phishing emails with malicious macros [S1][S2]. The malware used reflective DLL injection, a technique also seen in BlackEnergy and Duqu, to avoid the normal Windows loading path [S3]. DLLs were encrypted to evade antivirus and sandboxing [S3]. The malware checks for anti-malware software and monitoring tools such as Wireshark before running [S1]. It records from the PC microphone and captures credentials, documents and screenshots [S1]. Dropbox was the exfiltration channel and is hard to block in corporate networks [S1][S2]; free web hosting sites were used for command and control [S3]. CyberX estimated 2.5 to 3 GB per infected computer per day [S1].

campaigns.name: Operation Groundbait (related, separate cluster)
campaigns.summary: ESET disclosed Groundbait, which CyberX later compared with BugDrop for similar TTPs and targeting; the relationship is unconfirmed [S2].

campaigns.name: Earliest reported BugDrop activity
campaigns.summary: CyberX reported the campaign dated to no later than June 2016. The malware was reportedly compiled one month after ESET's Groundbait report [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: CyberX public disclosure
campaigns.summary: CyberX named Operation BugDrop, reporting at least 70 victims, mostly in Ukraine, and microphone-based eavesdropping with Dropbox exfiltration [S1][S3].

diamond.adversary: Unidentified; CyberX offered several candidate actor types and did not attribute [S1].
diamond.capability: Phishing with macros, reflective DLL injection, encrypted DLLs, anti-analysis checks, microphone capture, credential, document and screenshot theft [S1][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Dropbox for staging stolen data; free web hosting for command and control [S1][S3]. Groundbait operators by contrast registered their own domains [S2].
diamond.victim: At least 70 organizations in critical infrastructure, media and scientific research, mostly in Ukraine, plus Russia, Saudi Arabia and Austria [S1][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection against Ukrainian targets during the ongoing Ukraine conflict, with victims reported in Donetsk and Luhansk [S2]. Motive beyond collection is not stated in the sources.
diamond.technology: Windows PCs with attached microphones, Office macro execution, and permitted cloud storage traffic such as Dropbox [S1][S2][S3].

gaps: No attribution to a named actor or government in the sources reviewed; the 'state-sponsored' headline is not backed by quoted evidence [S1][S3].
The original CyberX report was not opened; WebFetch failed on all hosts (DNS errors) so only search-result summaries were used, and all details are secondhand.
Relationship to Operation Groundbait is unresolved [S2].
Whether BugDrop continued after February 2017 is unknown [S1].
Indicators (hashes, Dropbox accounts, hosting domains) were not gathered.
The 600GB figure in the Security Affairs headline is unverified [S6].
Source publication dates are approximate to the month, taken from search results and URL date patterns.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is workstations with microphones and Office macro execution in energy and infrastructure organizations, plus permitted cloud-storage egress paths [S1][S3]. STEP 2: The adversary exploits cloud-service traffic that is rarely blocked and avoids owned domains [S1][S2][S3]. STEP 3: Template is phishing with macro document, reflective DLL loading, microphone and document collection, then Dropbox exfiltration [S1][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection against Ukrainian-linked infrastructure and media. MDCOA is use of the same audio-capture access against sensitive deployed or coalition facilities (this extension is not shown in the sources). Candidate indicators: unexpected processes accessing audio devices, Office macro child processes, unapproved Dropbox traffic from servers or control-room workstations, and tools checking for Wireshark [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: include endpoint audio-device access and cloud-storage egress in mission-system monitoring [S1]. (2) Authorities: monitoring of user audio endpoints and cloud traffic requires clear authority and legal review; confirm before tasking. (3) Mission assurance: disable or physically cover microphones on sensitive workstations and restrict personal cloud storage [S1][S3]. (4) Coordination: attribution is unresolved, so share indicators through partners without naming a sponsor [S1].

identification.summary: Trend Micro named the actor behind this activity "DRBControl" after Talent-Jump Technologies contacted it in 2019 about a backdoor found during an incident response engagement [S1]. Trend Micro describes an APT campaign aimed at gambling and betting companies in Southeast Asia [S1]. Security Affairs reports the incident response was for a company based in the Philippines [S3].
identification.firstObserved: 2019 (Trend Micro was alerted in 2019; Dropbox expired the C2 tokens in August 2019) [S1]. Trend Micro's report was published around February 2020 per press coverage [S3].
identification.notes: This is a Trend Micro-named cluster/campaign. Trend Micro reports links to Winnti (shared mutexes, domain names, issued commands) and to Emissary Panda/APT27 (use of HyperBro, which it says appears exclusive to that group), but says the evidence is insufficient for a definitive link [S1][S4]. Do not merge facts from the Winnti, APT27 or Microsoft-named clusters into this record without vendor mapping.

attribution.confidence: Trend Micro reported overlaps with Winnti and Emissary Panda but stated there was not enough evidence to establish a definitive link [S4]. No government attribution found in sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Trend Micro cites shared mutexes, domain names and commands with Winnti, and use of the HyperBro backdoor, which it says appears exclusive to Emissary Panda [S1][S4].

actors.objectives: Trend Micro judged the main goal to be cyberespionage, because exfiltrated data was mostly databases and source code [S1][S3].

regions: Philippines (company in the originating incident response) [S3]

provenance.importedSummary: Operation DRBControl is a cyberespionage campaign targeting gambling companies in Southeast Asia, first identified in 2019. The operation involves the use of HyperBro malware and SysUpdate variants, with evidence of customer database and source code exfiltration. The threat actor has employed domain spoofing for command and control and has shown a consistent interest in the gambling industry. Trend Micro's analysis linked multiple tools and malware families to this campaign, indicating a sophisticated and evolving threat landscape.

identification.summary: Operation Emmental, also known as the Retefe gang, is a threat actor group that has been active since at least 2012. They primarily target customers of banks in countries such as Austria, Sweden, Switzerland, and Japan. The group has developed sophisticated malware, including a Mac alternative called Dok, to bypass two-factor authentication and hijack network traffic. They have also been observed using phishing emails to spread their malware. The group is believed to be Russian-speaking and has continuously improved their malicious codes over the years.

Operation Red Signature is the name Trend Micro gave to a 2018 information-theft supply chain attack against organizations in South Korea, in which attackers compromised the update server of an unnamed remote support solutions provider and used it to deliver 9002 RAT to selected targets [S1][S2]. The malware was signed with the provider's stolen code-signing certificate, and the update server was configured to serve malicious files only to clients in the IP ranges of targeted organizations [S1][S3]. Trend Micro worked with South Korean firm IssueMakersLab on the analysis [S1][S3].
identification.firstObserved: 2018-04 (a ShiftDoor sample signed with the stolen certificate dated 2018-04-08, so the certificate may have been stolen as early as April 2018 per Trend Micro; campaign discovered around end of July 2018) [S1][S3]
identification.notes: Trend Micro reported a separate GandCrab ransomware phishing campaign against South Korean targets in the same period; it is not part of Operation Red Signature [S4]. In 2021 Avast reported a backdoor on a US federal commission network whose second-stage oci.dll shared markers with an Operation Red Signature sample (rcview40u.dll); Avast did not name the actor, so this is a code-overlap lead and not a merged cluster [S5][S6]. The source set does not state the vendor of the compromised update server.

attribution.basis: The cited reporting does not attribute Operation Red Signature to a named actor or state; the encyclopedia's CN country tag is an upstream import (MISP Galaxy) that the sources reviewed here do not substantiate. Avast stated it could not attribute the 2021 US commission intrusion and only noted code overlap with Operation Red Signature [S5][S6].

actors.objectives: Trend Micro characterized the campaign as information-theft driven [S1][S3]. The follow-on IIS 6 WebDAV exploit (CVE-2017-7269) and SQL database password dumper point to interest in web server and database data [S3].

targeting.notes: Targets were organizations in South Korea; the update server delivered malicious files only to clients within the IP ranges of the targeted organizations [S1][S3]. The specific victim organizations and sectors were not identified in the sources reviewed.

capabilities.summary: Supply chain compromise of a remote support provider's update server, with theft of the vendor's code-signing certificate to sign malware, and IP-range-conditioned delivery so only chosen victims received payloads [S1][S3]. Payload was 9002 RAT, reportedly compiled 2018-07-17 and configured to go inactive by 2018-07-31, which suggests a short operational window [S2][S3]. 9002 RAT also installed an IIS 6 WebDAV exploit (CVE-2017-7269) and an SQL password dumper [S3]. Security Affairs reported a C2 server at 66.42.37.101 [S2]. Avast's later finding of oci.dll samples abusing WinDivert for traffic monitoring, with a decryptor resembling Operation Red Signature code, suggests the tooling or its source may have been reused [S5][S6].

campaigns.summary: A ShiftDoor sample signed with the compromised vendor certificate dated 2018-04-08 led Trend Micro to assess the certificate may have been stolen as early as April 2018 [S1][S3].

campaigns.summary: Avast reported backdoor files masquerading as oci.dll on the network of a small US federal commission; the second-version oci.dll shared markers with Operation Red Signature's rcview40u.dll. Avast could not attribute the activity and the victim did not engage [S5][S6].

diamond.adversary: Unattributed in cited sources [S1][S3].
diamond.capability: 9002 RAT, CVE-2017-7269 IIS 6 WebDAV exploit, SQL password dumper, stolen code-signing certificate, conditional update-server delivery [S3].
diamond.infrastructure: A compromised remote support provider update server; reported C2 at 66.42.37.101 [S2][S3].
diamond.victim: Organizations in South Korea selected by IP range [S1][S3].
diamond.technology: Remote support software update mechanism, code-signing trust, IIS 6 WebDAV and SQL database servers [S3].

gaps: Actor identity, sponsor and any vendor aliases are not stated in the sources reviewed; MISP Galaxy country tag CN unverified.
Name of the compromised remote support vendor and the victim organizations/sectors are not identified in the sources reviewed.
Trend Micro primary report and Avast primary report could not be opened (fetch unavailable); details rely on search-result excerpts and press coverage, and exact publication dates should be verified.
Relationship between the 2018 campaign and the 2021 Avast US commission intrusion is code overlap only; shared operator not established.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: the relevant environment is trusted third-party software update channels (remote support tools) and the web/database servers of targeted organizations [S3]. Step 3 (adversary): unattributed, with demonstrated capability to compromise a vendor update server, steal and abuse a code-signing certificate, and gate payloads by victim IP range [S1][S3]. MLCOA: further selective supply chain delivery of RATs against a limited victim set to collect web server and database data [S3]. MDCOA: reuse of the tooling against non-Korean government networks, as the 2021 Avast code-overlap finding suggests [S5][S6]. Candidate indicators: signed binaries from the vendor certificate outside normal release cadence, updates delivered only to some IP ranges, CVE-2017-7269 exploitation of IIS 6, oci.dll sideload anomalies with WinDivert use [S3][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: inventory remote support and auto-update software on mission networks and verify update integrity beyond signature checks, since the signature itself was stolen [S1][S3]. Authorities: defensive response on DODIN-owned systems falls to the owning network operators; vendor and allied (e.g., ROK) coordination goes through established intelligence and legal channels. Mission assurance: prioritize legacy IIS 6 and SQL servers and segment remote support tooling [S3]. Coordination: share indicators with allied partners and the affected vendor, and note that victims may not engage, as with the US commission in 2021 [S5].

provenance.importedSummary: The threat actors compromised the update server of a remote support solutions provider to deliver a remote access tool called 9002 RAT to their targets of interest through the update process. They carried this out by first stealing the company’s certificate then using it to sign the malware. identification.summary: AhnLab classifies cyberattacks against Korean companies and organizations that use Shadow Force and Wgdrop malware as Operation Shadow Force, a name taken from the Shadow Force malware the group mainly used [S1]. AhnLab's first confirmed attack was in March 2013, with activity likely before 2012 based on malware creation dates, and in 2020 AhnLab had not confirmed any link to a known group [S1]. A 2023 AhnLab report says the group has targeted South Korean organizations since 2013, mainly Windows servers [S2][S4]. The 2025 AhnLab/NCSC joint report tracks the successor activity as TA-ShadowCricket, first tracked as Larva-24013 [S5].
identification.firstObserved: March 2013 (first confirmed attack); likely active before 2012 [S1]. Virus Bulletin abstract says active since 2014 mainly in South Korea [S3].
identification.notes: No Microsoft name or MITRE group ID is known for this cluster. Dates of first activity differ across AhnLab documents (2012/2013 in the 2020 report [S1]; 2014 in the VB2023 abstract [S3]); not reconciled. The VB2023 abstract describes the group as 'reportedly' Chinese-speaking [S3].

attribution.confidence: Low. AhnLab stated in 2020 that it had not confirmed whether the attacker is associated with a known group [S1]. The Virus Bulletin 2023 abstract describes the group only as reportedly Chinese-speaking [S3]. No government attribution found.
attribution.basis: AhnLab malware analysis, certificate analysis and code-lineage work [S1][S3][S5].

regions: Asia-Pacific, including Maggie-infected MS-SQL servers with APAC concentration (Maggie link to Shadow Force is a hypothesis, not confirmed) [S3][S6]
targeting.notes: Sources describe targets as Korean companies and organizations and Windows servers, not specific industry sectors [S1][S2]. Sector list left empty.

capabilities.summary: Core malware is Shadow Force and Wgdrop [S1]. AhnLab's operation timeline lists an MS-SQL server intrusion by an unknown method, Htran (aio.exe) to download further malware, and a PE modifier (iatinfect.exe) that patches EXE files [S2][S4]. Malware has been signed with forged or stolen digital certificates of Korean companies [S1][S3]. After 2020 older backdoors were used less, with Viticdoor appearing and cryptocurrency miners installed alongside since December 2021 [S2][S4]. The actor has reused the same file names and similar tools since 2014, which aids detection [S2]. The 2025 joint report describes the successor cluster using IRC bots and backdoors against exposed Windows remote access and poorly managed MS-SQL servers [S5].

diamond.adversary: Unattributed actor tracked by AhnLab as Operation Shadow Force, later TA-ShadowCricket; reportedly Chinese-speaking [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.capability: Shadow Force, Wgdrop, Viticdoor, Htran, iatinfect.exe PE patcher, cryptocurrency miners, IRC bots [S1][S2][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised MS-SQL and Windows servers; forged or stolen Korean-company code-signing certificates [S1][S3]. IRC command infrastructure for TA-ShadowCricket [S5].
diamond.victim: Korean companies and organizations, mainly Windows servers [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Internet-exposed, poorly managed MS-SQL and Windows remote access services; trust in code-signed binaries [S1][S5].

gaps: Sponsor, motive and objective are not established in any source gathered; AhnLab stated no link to a known group was confirmed [S1].
Initial access vector is described as unknown (MS-SQL intrusion by unknown method) [S2][S4].

I could not open the AhnLab primary reports, the VB2023 paper/slides or the ASEC TA-ShadowCricket post (fetch failed); statements rely on search-result summaries and should be validated against the originals.

Search summaries disagreed on whether TA-ShadowCricket is the same actor as Shadow Force; the AhnLab/NCSC-focused result states Larva-24013 was linked to Shadow Force and reclassified [S5]. Confirm in the primary report.
Secondary coverage (not cited) calls TA-ShadowCricket China-linked and reports over 2,000 compromised systems; not verified against AhnLab text.
Whether the Maggie backdoor belongs to this group is a hypothesis raised by AhnLab, not a confirmed link [S3][S6].
Wgdrop details were not found beyond its naming as a defining malware family [S1].
Sector-level targeting is not documented in sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-exposed MS-SQL and Windows remote-access servers are key terrain, particularly in South Korea and the wider Asia-Pacific [S1][S5]. STEP 2: Weakly managed database servers and code-signing trust are exploitable seams [S1][S5]. STEP 3: Template is server intrusion, Htran-assisted tool download, PE patching for persistence, then backdoor or IRC bot, with miners as monetization [S2][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued opportunistic compromise of Korean and APAC Windows servers, which the available sources do not tie to a specific sector. MDCOA is use of a compromised, trusted-signed server as a staging node against allied networks in the theater; this is judgment and not shown in sources. Candidate indicators: iatinfect.exe or aio.exe on database servers, unexpected extended-stored-procedure DLLs on MS-SQL, IRC traffic from servers, and binaries signed with certificates later reported as leaked [S2][S3][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track AhnLab and Korean NCSC reporting on this cluster for ROK-hosted infrastructure that coalition networks may touch [S5]. (2) Authorities: activity is on Korean and third-country servers, so hunt or response actions off DoD networks need host-nation and legal coordination. (3) Mission assurance: harden and inventory any internet-exposed MS-SQL and RDP-type services supporting mission systems; miner activity is an early sign of server compromise [S2][S5]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with ROK counterparts and DC3 as appropriate; avoid assuming state sponsorship given low-confidence attribution [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: Operation Shadow Force is a group of malware that is representative of Shadow Force and Wgdrop from 2013 to 2020, and is a group activity that attacks Korean companies and organizations. The group's first confirmed attack was in March 2013, but considering the date of malware creation, it is likely to have been active before 2012. Since the malware used mainly by them is Shadow Force, it was named Operation Shadow Force, and it has not been confirmed whether the attacker is associated with a known group.

identification.summary: PassCV is a name first coined by Snorre Fagerland of Blue Coat Systems for a malware cluster; Cylance's SPEAR team later widened it to cover the malware and the APT group behind the larger C2 infrastructure and stolen Authenticode certificates [S1]. Cylance described the group as using many stolen code-signing certificates and as moving from older infrastructure to off-the-shelf RATs and custom code [S1]. Cylance said it identified eighteen previously undisclosed stolen certificates issued to companies and individuals in China, Taiwan, Korea, Europe, the United States and Russia [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Cylance's 2016-10-18 report is the main source. Cylance saw clues that more than one group might share the stolen certificates, but judged a single group using several public RATs more likely [S1]. The Blue Coat post that coined the name was not opened.

attribution.sponsor: The Council on Foreign Relations Cyber Operations Tracker lists China as the suspected state sponsor [S3]. Cylance, in the text reviewed, names no government sponsor [S1].
attribution.confidence: Low. The only sponsor statement found is a CFR tracker entry listing suspected Chinese sponsorship [S3]. Cylance noted that several groups might share the certificates [S1].
attribution.basis: CFR tracker entry [S3]. No technical attribution to a state organization was found in the sources reviewed.

actors.objectives: Cylance reported malware aimed at game developers, with code to harvest stored passwords and log keystrokes [S2]. The custom Saber RAT could hijack and steal in-game account information and items [S2]. The CFR entry says the actor stole digital certificates from game companies for use against other targets [S3]. The overall objective is not stated by the sources; the activity as described mixes data theft, theft of signing certificates and in-game asset theft.

sectors: Online video game developers and platforms [S2][S3]
regions: Certificate owners were in China, Taiwan, Korea, Europe, the United States and Russia [S1]
CFR lists suspected victim countries China, Taiwan, South Korea, the United States and Russia [S3]
targeting.notes: Infosecurity Magazine reports the group went after developers using the Unity engine and Cocos2d framework; the Pokemon Go reference in the headline is only an example of a Unity game and does not say that game was attacked [S2]. Phony resumes and CVs were used to deliver backdoors [S2].

capabilities.summary: Heavy use of stolen Authenticode certificates to sign malware [S1]. Obfuscated and signed versions of older RATs such as ZxShell and Ghost RAT [S2], plus a custom RAT called Saber with DDoS and in-game account theft functions [S2]. Cylance said the group began expanding into other off-the-shelf RATs and custom code, and noted a move into signed adware [S1][S2]. Delivery used phony resumes and CVs [S2].

campaigns.name: Signed malware targeting gaming companies
campaigns.summary: Cylance SPEAR published findings on eighteen new stolen certificates, C2 infrastructure and new custom RATs, with a cluster of activity aimed at game developers. CFR logged the incident in October 2016.

diamond.adversary: Unattributed; CFR lists suspected Chinese sponsorship, and Cylance leaned to a single group while noting possible certificate sharing [S1][S3].
diamond.capability: Stolen-certificate code signing; signed ZxShell, Ghost RAT and other RATs; custom Saber RAT; credential harvesting and keylogging [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Cylance described a large C2 infrastructure tied together with the stolen certificates; specific indicators were not reviewed [S1].
diamond.victim: Online game developers and platforms; certificate owners across several countries [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints that trust Authenticode-signed binaries; game engines such as Unity and Cocos2d as developer targets [S1][S2].

gaps: Fetching failed for every page tried (connection errors), so all content comes from search-result summaries; Cylance/BlackBerry, Infosecurity Magazine and CFR pages were not read in full.
The original Blue Coat (Fagerland) post that coined PassCV was not located; first-observed date unknown.
No government attribution or named operators found; the CFR China-sponsor entry is the only sponsor statement and its basis was not reviewed.
No activity after 2016 found in sources reviewed.
ETDA and Malpedia profiles exist but were not opened and carry no date seen; aliases are not confirmed by a cited source.
Infosecurity Magazine publication date was not seen; 2016-10 is inferred from its coverage of the Cylance report.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Code-signing trust and software-development environments are key terrain; stolen certificates let malware appear legitimate [S1]. STEP 2: Signed binaries can defeat reputation-based allowlisting [S1]. STEP 3: The observed pattern is resume or CV lure, then signed RAT, then credential and keystroke theft [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued theft of certificates and credentials from software developers. MDCOA is use of a stolen certificate from a defense software vendor to sign tooling aimed at DoD-adjacent targets. Candidate indicators: unexpected signed binaries from certificate owners that do not match the software, and ZxShell or Ghost RAT network behavior [S1][S2]. The sources describe gaming targets only, so relevance to DoD is an inference.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track revoked or abused code-signing certificates and feed them to allowlisting policy. (2) Authorities: certificate revocation and blocking requests run through the owning vendor and CAs rather than DoD authorities. (3) Mission assurance: do not treat a valid signature as proof of trust for software in contractor or developer pipelines. (4) Coordination: share indicators through DC3 and the commercial vendor community. Evidence is dated 2016 and thin.

provenance.importedSummary: The PassCV group continues to be one of the most successful and active threat groups that leverage a wide array of stolen Authenticode-signing certificates. Snorre Fagerland of Blue Coat Systems first coined the term PassCV in a blog post. His post provides a good introduction to the group and covers some of the older infrastructure, stolen code-signing certificate reuse, and other connections associated with the PassCV malware. There are several clues alluding to the possibility that multiple groups may be utilizing the same stolen signing certificates, but at this time SPEAR believes the current attacks are more likely being perpetrated by a single group employing multiple publicly available Remote Administration Tools (RATs). The PassCV group has been operating with continued success and has already started to expand their malware repertoire into different off-the-shelf RATs and custom code. SPEAR identified eighteen previously undisclosed stolen Authenticode certificates. These certificates were originally issued to companies and individuals scattered across China, Taiwan, Korea, Europe, the United States and Russia. In this post we expand the usage of the term ‘PassCV’ to encompass the malware mentioned in the Blue Coat Systems report, as well as the APT group behind the larger C2 infrastructure and stolen Authenticode certificates. We’d like to share some of our findings as they pertain to the stolen certificates, command and control infrastructure, and some of the newer custom RATs they’ve begun development on.
