provenance.importedSummary: PurpleHaze is a China-nexus threat actor tracked by SentinelLABS, linked to APT15, known for targeting critical infrastructure sectors such as telecommunications and government organizations. The actor has been associated with reconnaissance attempts against SentinelOne and has utilized ShadowPad, a modular backdoor platform, for cyberespionage and potential ransomware deployment. Investigations are ongoing to determine overlaps between ShadowPad intrusions and PurpleHaze activity, highlighting the extensive sharing of malware and operational practices among Chinese threat groups. The targeting of third-party service providers has raised significant concerns regarding operational security and supply chain monitoring.

identification.summary: China-based cyber-espionage group that CrowdStrike publicly attributed in June 2014 to People's Liberation Army (PLA) Unit 61486, part of the 12th Bureau of the PLA Third General Staff Department (3PLA), based in Shanghai [S1][S2]. CrowdStrike reported the group has operated since at least 2007 and focused on US defense and European satellite and aerospace targets [S1]. Coverage of the 62-page report describes targeting of the US space, aerospace and communications sectors through targeted email carrying exploits for productivity software and custom malware [S2][S3]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the group as Putter Panda (G0024) with associated names APT2 and MSUpdater [S6].
identification.firstObserved: CrowdStrike: activity since at least 2007 [S1][S2]. Public disclosure: 2014-06-09 [S1][S3].
identification.notes: No Microsoft weather-taxonomy name was found: the group does not appear in Microsoft's published threat actor naming mapping as retrieved on 2026-10-15 [S7]. The CrowdStrike name 'Putter' reflects phishing aimed at golf-playing victims [S8]. MITRE lists APT2 and MSUpdater as associated names [S6]. Other aliases in this record (4HCrew, SearchFire, SULPHUR, TG-6952) came from imported galaxy data and were not confirmed in the sources gathered. Putter Panda (Unit 61486) is a separate cluster from Comment Panda/APT1 (Unit 61398), although CrowdStrike reported infrastructure overlap between the two [S4][S9].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China, PLA Unit 61486 (3PLA 12th Bureau, Shanghai), per CrowdStrike [S1][S2]. MITRE ATT&CK repeats this attribution [S6].
attribution.confidence: This is a vendor attribution by CrowdStrike, not a US government attribution, and no indictment of Unit 61486 personnel appears in the sources gathered [S1][S2]. Some security experts questioned the findings and whether they would help defenders [S5]. China has denied similar accusations and asked for evidence [S2].
attribution.basis: CrowdStrike tied the actor handle 'cpyy', reported as Chen Ping, to Unit 61486. The links were registration of command-and-control domains and background details in personal photos that placed him at a Shanghai facility associated with the 3PLA 12th Bureau, a method CrowdStrike called 'hat-tribution' [S1][S4]. CrowdStrike also reported infrastructure overlap with Comment Panda (PLA Unit 61398 / APT1) and interaction between actors tied to both groups [S4][S9]. CrowdStrike said its intelligence partners had had the information for months before release [S2].

actors.objectives: Theft of trade and military secrets for the PRC. Collection focused on space, satellite, aerospace and communications technology from Western government agencies and defense contractors [S1][S2][S8].

targeting.notes: CrowdStrike described US defense and European satellite and aerospace targets [S1]. Reuters coverage describes Western government agencies and defense contractors as targets since 2007 [S2]. Named victims were not disclosed in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing, including golf-themed lures, delivering exploits for Adobe Reader and Microsoft Office, followed by custom malware [S3][S8]. MITRE attributes four software families to the group: 4H RAT, 3PARA RAT, pngdowner and httpclient [S6]. MITRE also describes droppers that hide payloads with RC4 or a 16-byte XOR key, persist through a Run-key value named 'McUpdate', inject DLLs into network-facing processes such as Outlook and Firefox, and try to terminate Sophos antivirus components [S6]. Command-and-control domains were procured by an individual CrowdStrike tied to the unit [S4].

campaigns.name: Start of reported Putter Panda operations
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike says the group has been active since at least 2007 against defense, satellite and aerospace targets.

campaigns.name: US indictment of five Unit 61398 (APT1) officers
campaigns.summary: This is context rather than a Putter Panda operation: the Justice Department unsealed charges against five members of a different PLA unit less than three weeks before the Putter Panda report.

campaigns.name: CrowdStrike Putter Panda report and 'hat-tribution'
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike published a 62-page report attributing the campaign to PLA Unit 61486 and naming Chen Ping ('cpyy'). The report covered US space, aerospace and communications targeting and infrastructure overlap with Comment Panda/APT1.

campaigns.name: Public skepticism of the attribution
campaigns.summary: Some security experts questioned the findings and whether they helped defenders.

diamond.adversary: PLA Unit 61486 (3PLA 12th Bureau, Shanghai) per CrowdStrike. CrowdStrike tied Chen Ping ('cpyy') to domain procurement [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing with Adobe Reader and Microsoft Office exploits; 4H RAT, 3PARA RAT, pngdowner and httpclient; RC4/XOR-obfuscated droppers; Run-key persistence; DLL injection; antivirus termination [S6][S8].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-registered command-and-control domains, procured by an individual CrowdStrike tied to the unit. Infrastructure overlapped with Comment Panda/APT1 [S4][S9].
diamond.victim: Space, satellite, aerospace and communications organizations, defense contractors and government agencies in the United States and Europe [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection of military and trade secrets on space and satellite technology. The report was published weeks after the May 2014 US indictment of Unit 61398 officers, and CrowdStrike framed the release as keeping up pressure on China [S2][S4].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints running vulnerable Adobe Reader and Microsoft Office; email as the initial vector; network-facing applications such as Outlook and Firefox used as injection hosts [S6][S8].

gaps: The primary CrowdStrike PDF report (imported reference URL on vox-cdn) and the CrowdStrike blog could not be opened. Details here come from search-result coverage, so technical claims should be checked against the original report.
No public reporting after 2014 attributed to Putter Panda or Unit 61486 was found. Current status after the 2015 PLA reorganization (Strategic Support Force, later Cyberspace Force) is unknown.
Microsoft has no published name for this group in its naming mapping (retrieved 2026-10-15). The 'SULPHUR' alias in imported data is unconfirmed and should not be read as a Microsoft attribution.
Aliases 4HCrew, SearchFire, TG-6952 and the APT2 equivalence come from imported galaxy data or MITRE; the original Mandiant and Secureworks documents asserting them were not reviewed.
Some third-party profiles mention targeting of Japan and research organizations; these claims were not confirmed in a dated primary source.
MITRE ATT&CK pages, Wikipedia, Threatpost and Infosecurity Magazine could not be fetched directly. MITRE details rely on search snippets of the G0024 entry (version 1.2, modified 2024-11).
The yoga-themed lures sometimes associated with this group could not be confirmed in the sources found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Space, satellite, aerospace and communications program data held by government agencies and defense contractors is the relevant key terrain. This includes contractor email systems and the Windows endpoints of engineers and program staff [S1][S2][S3]. STEP 2: Initial access depended on users opening documents that exploit Adobe Reader and Microsoft Office. Patch currency for document readers and email filtering therefore shapes the threat's freedom of action [S8]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is a tailored phishing email, sometimes keyed to personal interests such as golf, then a document exploit, a dropper with obfuscated payload, Run-key persistence ('McUpdate'), DLL injection into Outlook or Firefox, and RAT command and control over HTTP to actor-registered domains [S6][S8]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet, long-duration theft of space and satellite technical data from the defense industrial base. MDCOA is persistent access to satellite and communications program networks being used to support counterspace or targeting decisions during a crisis. That MDCOA is an extrapolation, not reported activity. Candidate indicators: Run-key values named McUpdate, unexpected termination of antivirus processes, injected DLLs in Outlook or Firefox, and connectivity checks to legitimate sites followed by outbound HTTP to unfamiliar domains [S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: the cluster's last public reporting dates to 2014, so JCC2 tracking should treat it as a historical PLA space- and aerospace-espionage template rather than a current named threat until new reporting appears [S1][S6]. (2) Authorities: the attribution is a vendor (CrowdStrike) assessment, contested by some experts and not backed by a US indictment of this unit in the sources gathered. Products should label it as vendor attribution [S1][S5]. (3) Mission assurance: space and satellite programs depend on contractor networks, so defense-industrial-base email and endpoint hygiene is a mission-assurance concern [S2][S3]. (4) Coordination: overlap with APT1 infrastructure argues for joint analysis with teams tracking other 3PLA-linked clusters, without merging the clusters [S4][S9].

identification.summary: RADIO PANDA is a name that the MISP Galaxy threat-actor cluster lists as a China-attributed actor with the synonym Shrouded Crossbow, and the same cluster lists Radio Panda and Circuit Panda among the synonyms of BlackTech (Palmerworm, Temp.Overboard, Earth Hundun, Manga Taurus, Canary Typhoon and others) [S8]. A September 2023 joint advisory by NSA, FBI, CISA and Japanese agencies lists Radio Panda as an alias of BlackTech (confirmed in search summary of the advisory [S4]; also relayed by [S5][S6]). BlackTech is described by Trend Micro as a cyber espionage group operating against targets in East Asia, particularly Taiwan, and occasionally Japan and Hong Kong [S2]. Trend Micro named Shrouded Crossbow as one of three campaigns (with PLEAD and Waterbear) that it linked to BlackTech and said they may be run by the same group [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro said Shrouded Crossbow was first observed in 2010 [S1]. Trend Micro dated PLEAD to 2012 [S8]. MITRE describes BlackTech activity since at least 2013 [S10].
identification.notes: Name mapping rests on aggregator and secondary sources, not on a vendor page for RADIO PANDA itself: the MISP cluster maps RADIO PANDA to the Shrouded Crossbow synonym [S8] and lists RADIO PANDA among BlackTech synonyms [S8]; press coverage of the 2023 advisory relays the same alias [S6]. Vendor names for the BlackTech cluster: Palmerworm (Symantec) [S3], Earth Hundun (Trend Micro) [S7], Manga Taurus (Unit 42, per Malpedia listing) [S9], Circuit Panda, Temp.Overboard, Canary Typhoon [S8]. Trend Micro itself says only that Shrouded Crossbow, PLEAD and Waterbear 'may' be run by one group [S2], so the equivalence of Shrouded Crossbow with the wider BlackTech cluster is a vendor hypothesis and not settled.

attribution.sponsor: The September 2023 advisory is titled as covering People's Republic of China-linked cyber actors [S6]. MITRE describes BlackTech as a suspected Chinese cyber espionage group [S10]. No specific PRC government organization is named in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Symantec did not tie the 2019-2020 Palmerworm campaign to a specific country; it noted that Taiwanese officials have publicly linked BlackTech to the Chinese government [S3]. Trend Micro described Shrouded Crossbow's operator as well-funded, an inference from the apparent purchase of BIFROST source code [S1]. The MISP Galaxy record for the RADIO PANDA name carries an attribution-confidence value of 50 for the name mapping itself [S8].
attribution.basis: Vendor technical reporting (Trend Micro [S1][S2][S7], Symantec [S3]), the joint US-Japan advisory as relayed by secondary coverage [S5][S6], and aggregator alias mappings [S8][S9].

actors.objectives: Trend Micro assessed that BlackTech campaigns are likely designed to steal targets' technology, based on mutexes and C2 domain names [S2]. Shrouded Crossbow focused on espionage-style backdoor access against Asian government contractors, privatized government agencies and several commercial sectors [S1]. The 2023 advisory describes pivoting from overseas subsidiaries into US and Japanese headquarters networks [S5].

regions: East Asia, particularly Taiwan, occasionally Japan and Hong Kong [S2]
Japan, Taiwan, China and the United States (Palmerworm 2019-2020) [S3]
United States and Japan headquarters, via international subsidiaries [S5]
targeting.notes: Targeting is drawn from sub-cluster reporting under different vendor names; it should not be read as the profile of a single separately confirmed 'Radio Panda' operation [S2][S8].

capabilities.summary: Shrouded Crossbow used three backdoors derived from BIFROST (BIFROSE, KIVARS, XBOW); Trend Micro inferred the operators bought and improved the source code, and delivered the malware by spear-phishing with booby-trapped attachments and decoy documents [S1]. BIFROSE used Tor for C2 and had a UNIX version; KIVARS added a 64-bit variant [S1]. Trend Micro estimated a development team of at least 10 people and more than 100 C2 servers [S1]. Palmerworm in 2019-2020 used stolen code-signing certificates, new backdoors named Consock, Waship, Dalwit and Nomri, and dual-use tools such as PuTTY, PsExec, SNScan and WinRAR [S3]. Trend Micro reports the Waterbear backdoor (more than ten versions since 2009), with a newer Deuterbear variant from 2022, and anti-debug, anti-sandbox and anti-AV features [S7]. The 2023 advisory describes router firmware tampering: downgrading to older legitimate firmware, hot patching in memory, loading unsigned bootloader and firmware, a built-in SSH backdoor activated by crafted TCP or UDP packets, and hiding activity from logs; the advisory names no CVE and says the technique is not limited to Cisco [S4][S5].

diamond.adversary: Suspected PRC-linked espionage group tracked as BlackTech and under many vendor names; Radio Panda is one listed synonym [S6][S8][S10].
diamond.capability: BIFROST-derived backdoors, PLEAD and Waterbear families, stolen code-signing certificates, dual-use tools, and router firmware modification [S1][S3][S5][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: More than 100 C2 servers and Tor use for Shrouded Crossbow [S1]; compromised public-facing branch routers used as proxies in the 2023 advisory [S5]. Further infrastructure detail is not in the sources gathered.
diamond.victim: Asian government contractors and commercial firms, Taiwan-centered East Asian targets, and US and Japanese multinationals via subsidiaries [S1][S2][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Technology theft and regional intelligence collection focused on Taiwan and Japan are the objectives vendors infer [S2]; no government tasking is documented in the sources gathered.
diamond.technology: Edge routers at subsidiary sites with trusted links to headquarters, and endpoints reachable by spear-phishing [S1][S5].

gaps: No vendor page for RADIO PANDA itself was opened; the CrowdStrike naming is known here only from a MISP Galaxy entry [S8] and from secondary coverage of the 2023 advisory [S6]. A 2013 CrowdStrike slide deck listing Radio Panda was seen in a search result but not opened and is not cited.
The primary advisory (AA23-270A on cisa.gov, also hosted on ic3.gov) could not be opened because government sites are blocked; its exact alias list and wording are unverified [S4].
MISP Galaxy treats RADIO PANDA as both a Shrouded Crossbow synonym and a BlackTech synonym; Trend Micro only says the two 'may' be the same group [S2][S8]. Confirm before merging the records.
Microsoft's own naming page for Canary Typhoon was not opened; the mapping comes from MISP Galaxy [S8].
Trend Micro's original 2015 Shrouded Crossbow paper and the 2017 BlackTech page could not be fetched (host unreachable); content relies on SecurityWeek and search summaries [S1][S2].
No activity after 2024 was found; current status and any 2025-2026 operations are unknown.
Specific PRC sponsor (MSS, PLA or contractor) is not identified in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is edge routers at overseas subsidiaries and contractor sites with trusted links to headquarters, plus the trust relationships between them [S5]. STEP 2: The actor operates against Taiwan, Japan and the US, and against government contractors, so DoD-adjacent suppliers and Indo-Pacific partners in technology, electronics and finance are in scope [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is spear-phishing or other initial access, backdoor with stolen-certificate signing, dual-use tools, and then pivoting through router trust and firmware tampering [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued technology and policy collection against Taiwan, Japan and regional contractors. MDCOA is persistent footholds in network edge devices used to reach defense-industrial or allied headquarters networks unnoticed in a crisis. Candidate indicators: unexpected firmware downgrades or bootloader changes, hidden SSH sessions absent from logs, anomalous EEM policies, trusted subsidiary-to-headquarters traffic from unusual hosts, and binaries signed with stolen certificates [S3][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track router firmware integrity and configuration baselines at contractor and partner sites as a mission-relevant cyber terrain item [S5]. (2) Authorities: monitoring of supplier and allied networks depends on contract and partner-nation agreements, so coordinate through DC3, the DIB cybersecurity program and host-nation channels rather than assuming direct access. (3) Mission assurance: treat subsidiary and partner links as untrusted segments and prepare to isolate them without losing mission data flow [S5]. (4) Coordination: align alias handling with intelligence staff because the same actor appears under many names and sources disagree on cluster boundaries [S2][S8].

identification.summary: RaHDit (Russian Angry Hackers Did It) is a pro-Kremlin hacktivist group that, per OFAC as relayed by secondary reporting, is allegedly composed of active and former Russian intelligence officers [S1][S2]. provenance.importedSummary: RaHDit is a pro-Kremlin hacktivist group known for orchestrating hack-and-leak operations, including the publication of personal information about Ukrainian military intelligence personnel and their associates. The group has been linked to Russian intelligence and has claimed to provide actionable intelligence to the Russian army. RaHDit operates a website called NemeZida, where they disclose sensitive data, and has been involved in disinformation campaigns supporting Russian narratives. Their activities include collaboration with other hacktivist groups and targeting Ukrainian cyberdefense efforts.

identification.summary: Rancor is a cyber espionage group that Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 first described on 26 June 2018. Unit 42 found it through attacks in Southeast Asia during 2017 and 2018, work that grew out of its research into the KHRAT Trojan [S1][S2]. Unit 42 said the group used two main malware families, DDKONG and PLAINTEE, against targets in countries including Singapore and Cambodia. Because the decoy documents drew on political news, Unit 42 judged that the group was targeting political entities [S1]. Check Point later tracked a seven-month Rancor spear-phishing campaign against Southeast Asian government entities, and Unit 42 reported repeated attempts against a Cambodian government organization using new custom malware called Dudell [S3][S6][S7].
identification.firstObserved: 2017. Unit 42 observed DDKONG in use from February 2017, and the earliest known PLAINTEE sample dates to October 2017 [S1][S2]. Check Point describes the group as active since at least 2017 [S3][S4].
identification.notes: No Microsoft (Typhoon) name for Rancor appears in the sources gathered. Palo Alto Networks tracks the group as Rancor Taurus, and the ETDA threat encyclopedia also lists the names Rancor Group and Rancor Taurus [S10]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as Rancor (G0075) and describes it as operating in Southeast Asia with politically themed lures [S9]. Secondary coverage reports Kaspersky-identified links between Rancor and DragonOK, and a link to the KHRAT operators, whom Unit 42 has associated with DragonOK. These are overlaps between clusters, not evidence that Rancor and DragonOK are the same group [S2][S10].

attribution.sponsor: Suspected China-nexus. ETDA lists the country as China [S10], and CFR's Cyber Operations Tracker describes Rancor as a China-linked group [S8]. Check Point said its 2019 report contained insights that 'might indicate' a Chinese origin [S3][S4]. No government attribution appears in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Low to moderate, vendor-only. Check Point's wording is hedged ('might indicate') [S3]. Unit 42 notes that Derusbi, which Rancor used, is believed to be unique to a small subset of Chinese cyber espionage groups [S6]. A Unit 42 analyst quoted by CyberScoop said Rancor's tools are all custom, either unique to Rancor or shared with a small cluster of Chinese espionage groups [S7].
attribution.basis: Malware overlap with a small set of China-associated groups (Derusbi; links to KHRAT and DragonOK) [S6][S7][S2]; Check Point's origin indicators [S3]; and consistent targeting of Southeast Asian governments and political entities [S1][S3].

actors.objectives: Espionage against Southeast Asian governments and political entities [S1][S3][S10]. Unit 42 inferred the political focus from decoys built on public political news, including material linked to the opposition Cambodia National Rescue Party [S1]. ETDA lists the group's motivation as information theft and espionage [S10].

targeting.notes: Cambodia appears in every major reporting window: decoys hosted on a Cambodian government website in 2018 [S1], and persistent attempts against a Cambodian government organization from December 2018 to January 2019 and again in mid-2019 [S6][S7]. Check Point reported five unnamed government targets in the region, according to secondary coverage [S4]. Unit 42 said the attempts against the Cambodian organization appear to have failed [S7].

capabilities.summary: Spear phishing is the main way in. Unit 42 did not see the original 2018 emails and inferred them from the decoy documents found on infected systems [S1]. In 2018, delivery used HTA files and DLL loaders that downloaded further malware and displayed decoy images or PDFs hosted on legitimate sites, including a Cambodian government website and, at least once, Facebook [S1]. The payloads were DDKONG and PLAINTEE, and PLAINTEE communicates over a custom UDP protocol [S1][S2]. In the 2018-2019 campaigns, the group sent Excel and other Office documents with macros, exploited known vulnerabilities, and sent lures from real government email accounts [S3][S4][S5]. It also used DLL side-loading through trusted signed executables [S3]. Unit 42 reported a new custom macro-based malware, Dudell, and attempts to install Derusbi or KHRAT [S6]. MITRE also records msiexec use to fetch installers over HTTP, certutil for tool transfer, scheduled-task persistence, and HTTP C2 [S9].

campaigns.name: DDKONG / PLAINTEE operations (Clusters A and B)
campaigns.summary: DDKONG was in use from February 2017, and PLAINTEE samples appeared from October 2017. Unit 42 linked two activity clusters through PLAINTEE. They targeted political entities in Singapore and Cambodia with HTA and DLL-loader lures.

campaigns.name: Unit 42 public disclosure of RANCOR
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 named the previously unidentified group RANCOR and published details on DDKONG, PLAINTEE, and decoys hosted on a Cambodian government website.

campaigns.name: Southeast Asian government spear-phishing campaign
campaigns.summary: From December 2018 to June 2019, Check Point tracked lures sent to government departments and embassies. The lures were updated over time, sent from real government email accounts, and used macros and known exploits to install backdoors.

campaigns.name: Attempts against a Cambodian government organization (Dudell)
campaigns.summary: From December 2018 to January 2019, the group sent weaponized Excel documents (Dudell) and tried to install Derusbi or KHRAT. A further script-based attempt followed in July 2019. Unit 42 said none of the attempts appear to have succeeded.

diamond.adversary: Rancor (Unit 42: Rancor Taurus), a suspected China-nexus espionage group. Vendor-only attribution [S1][S3][S10].
diamond.capability: Custom malware: DDKONG, PLAINTEE (custom UDP C2) and Dudell. Shared families: Derusbi and KHRAT. Delivery and execution via HTA, DLL loaders, side-loading, Office macros, known exploits, msiexec and certutil [S1][S3][S6][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Decoys hosted on legitimate sites, including a Cambodian government website and Facebook [S1]. Compromised or abused real government email accounts used as senders [S5]. HTTP-based C2 [S9].
diamond.victim: Government departments, embassies and political entities in Cambodia, Singapore and the wider Southeast Asia region [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Lures built from regional political news, including Cambodian opposition (CNRP) themes, around a period of Cambodian political tension. This points to collection of political intelligence on Southeast Asian governments [S1].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints running Microsoft Office with macros enabled or unpatched against known vulnerabilities. Trust in signed executables, which enables side-loading [S3][S9].

gaps: Primary documents could not be opened: WebFetch failed to resolve unit42.paloaltonetworks.com, research.checkpoint.com, cfr.org, thehackernews.com, cyberscoop.com and securityaffairs.com. Report details come from search-result excerpts of those pages.
The publication date of the Unit 42 Dudell report (S6) is listed as 2019-12-17 in search-result metadata; the exact date of the CyberScoop article (S7) was not confirmed beyond December 2019.
No Microsoft threat actor name for Rancor was found. Mapping to the Microsoft taxonomy is unverified.
No activity reported after 2019 was found in reliable sources. A secondary blog's claim that Dudell was 'discovered in 2024' conflicts with Unit 42 and was not used.
The Rancor/DragonOK/KHRAT relationship is stated only in secondary coverage of Kaspersky and Unit 42 research. The Kaspersky source itself was not located.
No government (USG or allied) attribution or sponsoring-agency identification (e.g., MSS or PLA unit) was found.
Thailand and Vietnam come from secondary sources (Security Affairs, ETDA) and are not confirmed in a primary vendor report reviewed here.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): The relevant terrain is Southeast Asian partner-nation government networks, embassies and political-party systems, especially Cambodia and Singapore, plus the legitimate government websites and email accounts the actor abuses for staging and delivery [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 2 (effects): Partner ministries' trust in mail from real government accounts weakens email-based defenses. This affects US engagement and coalition planning that runs through these partners [S3][S5]. STEP 3 (threat model): The template is a politically themed spear-phishing document (HTA, macro Excel or exploit document), then a loader or DLL side-load, then a custom backdoor (DDKONG, PLAINTEE, Dudell, Derusbi or KHRAT) with HTTP or custom UDP C2 and scheduled-task persistence [S1][S3][S6][S9]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is sustained, iterative phishing of partner ministries and embassies to collect political intelligence, retargeting after failed attempts [S3][S7]. MDCOA is compromising partner-government mail accounts and websites to send lures to US or coalition personnel engaged in the region. That second scenario is extrapolated from observed account and website abuse, not from reported targeting [S1][S5]. Candidate indicators: Office documents spawning msiexec or certutil downloads over HTTP; new schtasks /create entries; signed binaries loading DLLs from user-writable paths; unusual outbound UDP from workstations; decoys pulled from government or Facebook URLs [S1][S3][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Track partner-nation reporting and vendor feeds on Southeast Asian government phishing. Rancor reporting is sparse after 2019, so lack of reporting does not mean the group is inactive [S3][S6]. (2) Authorities: The victims are mainly foreign partner governments [S1][S3]. Defensive support is a matter for partner-engagement and information-sharing arrangements rather than DODIN authorities, except where DoD personnel or systems receive lures. (3) Mission assurance: Mission-partner and embassy-adjacent DoD users should treat mail from partner-government accounts as possibly compromised, and macro and HTA execution controls should be enforced [S3][S5]. (4) Coordination: Coordinate with interagency and partner CERTs (for example, Cambodian and Singaporean) to share decoy hashes and abused legitimate URLs. Attribution remains vendor-only and hedged, so products should describe it that way [S3][S10].

identification.summary: China-based nation-state activity group that Microsoft tracks as the primary threat group targeting nations that ring the South China Sea [S1][S2]. Microsoft reports that it consistently targets government ministries, military entities, and corporate entities connected to critical infrastructure, particularly telecoms, and that it has been particularly persistent since January 2023 [S1]. In June 2023 it successfully targeted military and executive entities in Indonesia and a Malaysian maritime system [S2]. Microsoft maps APT30, LotusBlossom and LOTUS PANDA to Raspberry Typhoon [S3]; vendor reporting under those names describes Southeast Asia-focused espionage going back to at least 2005 (FireEye, APT30) [S5] and continuing into 2025-2026 (Cisco Talos, Symantec and Rapid7 reporting on Lotus Blossom / Lotus Panda) [S8][S9][S10].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft does not state a first-observed date [S1][S2]. FireEye said APT30 had been conducting cyber espionage since at least 2005 [S5]. Cisco Talos said Lotus Blossom has conducted espionage since at least 2012 [S8]; coverage of the Rapid7 reporting says Lotus Blossom has been active since 2009 [S10].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Raspberry Typhoon (formerly RADIUM) [S1][S3]. Microsoft's public naming map lists RADIUM, LOTUS PANDA, LotusBlossom and APT30 as other names for Raspberry Typhoon without naming the vendor for each [S3]. Microsoft does not map Naikon, Spring Dragon, Billbug/Thrip or PLA Unit 78020 to Raspberry Typhoon [S3]; Symantec, however, treats Billbug, Lotus Blossom and Thrip as one group [S7], and press coverage of Talos lists Lotus Panda, Billbug, Spring Dragon and Thrip as Lotus Blossom aliases [S8]. MITRE tracks APT30 (G0013), Naikon (G0019), Lotus Blossom (G0030) and Thrip (G0076) as separate groups [S4]. Facts below are labelled by the reporting vendor's cluster name; do not assume every event is inside Microsoft's Raspberry Typhoon boundary.

attribution.sponsor: China. Microsoft describes Raspberry Typhoon as a nation-state activity group based out of China [S2]. FireEye assessed APT30 activity as state sponsored, most likely by the Chinese government [S5]. Talos describes Lotus Blossom as China-backed [S8]. No specific sponsoring organization (MSS or PLA) is named for the Microsoft cluster in the sources reviewed.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributes activity to Raspberry Typhoon by name without a stated confidence level [S1][S2]. FireEye: 'most likely' Chinese government (2015) [S5]. Unit 42: likely nation-state sponsored, country not named (2015) [S6]. Talos: high confidence that the 2025-reported campaigns are Lotus Blossom, based on exclusive use of Sagerunex [S8]. Symantec (2025): Chinese actors, with attribution to a single actor not determined, though indicators linked to Billbug [S9]. Rapid7: medium confidence that Lotus Blossom compromised Notepad++ update infrastructure [S10]. No government attribution of the Microsoft-defined cluster was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry in its East Asia reports [S1][S2] and naming map [S3]; vendor malware and infrastructure analysis by FireEye [S5], Palo Alto Unit 42 [S6], Symantec [S7][S9], Cisco Talos [S8] and Rapid7 [S10], mostly reviewed through press coverage.

actors.objectives: Long-term intelligence collection on governments, militaries and critical-infrastructure entities in South China Sea littoral and wider Southeast Asian states, consistent with Chinese strategic goals in the South China Sea [S1][S2]. FireEye described APT30 as focused on targets holding key political, economic and military information about the region, with activity spikes around ASEAN meetings [S5]. Microsoft's 2024 report places June 2023 Indonesia and Malaysia activity in the weeks before a rare multilateral naval exercise involving Indonesia, China and the United States [S2]. Symantec raised the concern that a compromised certificate authority could let the group sign malware with valid certificates [S7].

Aviation: air traffic control and air freight [S9]
Manufacturing, media and news agencies, construction [S8][S9]
Journalists and commercial organizations with regional information [S5]
regions: Nations ringing the South China Sea [S1]
Unnamed Southeast Asian countries (2024-2025 Symantec reporting) [S9]
India and wider Southeast Asia (APT30 coverage) [S5]
Central America (per coverage of Rapid7 reporting) [S10]
targeting.notes: Microsoft's 2024 report lists Raspberry Typhoon with Flax Typhoon and Granite Typhoon as actors behind observed events in or around the South China Sea [S2]. Regions and sectors beyond S1-S2 come from vendor clusters that Microsoft maps (APT30, LotusBlossom, LOTUS PANDA) [S3] or that Symantec equates with Lotus Blossom (Billbug) [S7].

capabilities.summary: Microsoft says Raspberry Typhoon typically conducts intelligence collection and malware execution against government and infrastructure targets [S1]. APT30 used a sustained, planned malware development effort, including tools able to reach air-gapped networks, according to FireEye coverage [S5]; MITRE's G0013 software list includes BACKSPACE, NETEAGLE, SHIPSHAPE, SPACESHIP and FLASHFLOOD [S4]. Lotus Blossom used spearphishing with decoy documents (reportedly CVE-2012-0158) to deliver the Elise backdoor [S6]. Symantec tied the 2022 activity to the Hannotog and Sagerunex backdoors [S7]. Talos reports Sagerunex variants that use Dropbox, Twitter and Zimbra webmail as C2 tunnels instead of VPS servers [S8]. Symantec's 2025 reporting describes DLL sideloading through legitimate Trend Micro and Bitdefender binaries, ChromeKatz and CredentialKatz browser credential stealers, a reverse SSH tool, and a timestamp-altering utility (datechanger.exe) [S9]. Rapid7 reports a hijacked Notepad++ update path delivering a trojanized NSIS installer that sideloaded via a renamed Bitdefender binary to launch the Chrysalis backdoor [S10].

diamond.adversary: China-based nation-state activity group (Microsoft: Raspberry Typhoon, formerly RADIUM) [S1][S2][S3]; overlapping vendor clusters APT30, Lotus Blossom/Lotus Panda and Billbug [S3][S5][S7][S8].
diamond.capability: Spearphishing with decoy documents and Elise [S6]; APT30 malware families [S4][S5]; Sagerunex and Hannotog backdoors [S7][S8]; DLL sideloading, Chrome credential stealers and reverse SSH [S9]; software-update hijacking delivering Chrysalis [S10].

diamond.victim: Government ministries, military, executive and defense entities, telecoms, maritime systems, aviation, certificate authorities and media in South China Sea and Southeast Asian states [S1][S2][S6][S7][S8][S9]; Notepad++ users selected for redirection [S10].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection that mirrors Chinese strategic goals in the South China Sea, timed around ASEAN meetings and a multilateral naval exercise involving the United States [S1][S2][S5].
diamond.technology: Government and military Windows networks, telecom and aviation infrastructure, PKI/certificate services, cloud services abused for C2, and software update mechanisms [S2][S7][S8][S9][S10].

gaps: Primary documents could not be opened: FireEye APT30 report (2015), Unit 42 Operation Lotus Blossom, Symantec Billbug (2022) and Lotus Panda (2025) blogs, Cisco Talos Lotus Blossom blog, Rapid7 Chrysalis report, Kaspersky Naikon/Spring Dragon and MITRE pages; content is drawn from search-result summaries and press coverage.

Cluster boundaries are unresolved. Microsoft maps only RADIUM, LOTUS PANDA, LotusBlossom and APT30 [S3]; MITRE keeps APT30, Naikon, Lotus Blossom and Thrip separate [S4]. Symantec merges Billbug/Thrip with Lotus Blossom [S7]. Naikon (and its PLA Unit 78020 attribution) is not verified as part of Raspberry Typhoon.

Microsoft has not publicly tied the 2025 Sagerunex, 2024-2025 Symantec or Notepad++ activity to Raspberry Typhoon by name; those links rest on Microsoft's alias mapping plus vendor attributions of differing confidence (Symantec could not pin the 2025 activity to a single actor; Rapid7 medium confidence).
Exact publication dates for the Talos (2025-03) and Rapid7 (2026-02) reports were taken from coverage, not the primary pages.
No sponsoring organization (MSS vs PLA) is named for the Microsoft cluster; no government attribution found.
Victims of the Notepad++ redirection and specific Raspberry Typhoon victim organizations after 2023 are not public in reviewed sources.
The claim of Central America targeting appears only in secondary coverage [S10] and is unverified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (Operational environment): Key terrain includes partner-nation government ministries, military and executive networks, telecom carriers, maritime and aviation systems, PKI providers, and software update channels in South China Sea littoral states [S1][S2][S7][S9][S10]. STEP 2 (Effects): Coalition and exercise planning shared with these partners is exposed through partner networks, and activity has been timed before multilateral naval exercises and ASEAN meetings [S2][S5]. STEP 3 (Threat model): spearphishing or trusted-software update hijack, DLL sideloading of signed security-vendor binaries, Sagerunex/Chrysalis-class backdoors with C2 over Dropbox, Twitter or Zimbra, browser credential theft and timestamp tampering [S6][S8][S9][S10]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is persistent, quiet collection from partner defense and foreign ministries and telecoms ahead of regional exercises and diplomatic events [S1][S2][S5]. MDCOA is use of a compromised certificate authority or software update channel to sign or push implants into many networks, including those connected to US forces [S7][S10]. Candidate indicators: unexpected Trend Micro or Bitdefender binaries loading DLLs from unusual paths; workstation traffic to Dropbox/Twitter/Zimbra APIs from non-browser processes; GUP.exe or updater processes fetching installers from non-vendor IPs; ChromeKatz/CredentialKatz artifacts; file timestamp anomalies [S8][S9][S10].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: fuse partner-nation and vendor reporting on Lotus Blossom/Lotus Panda/APT30 under the Raspberry Typhoon name while keeping vendor cluster labels visible, since attributions vary in confidence [S3][S8][S9][S10]. Authorities: most victims are partner-nation government and telecom networks [S1][S2][S9], so response depends on partner agreements and defend-forward or hunt-forward authorities rather than DODIN-only actions. Mission assurance: exercise and coalition planning data shared with Southeast Asian partners, and software update and PKI trust used by mission systems, are at risk [S2][S7][S10]; validate update integrity for third-party tools on mission networks. Coordination: synchronize with partner CERTs, and with the security vendors whose binaries are abused for sideloading, before and during regional exercises [S2][S9].

provenance.importedSummary: Microsoft has tracked Raspberry Typhoon (RADIUM) as the primary threat group targeting nations that ring the South China Sea. Raspberry Typhoon consistently targets government ministries, military entities, and corporate entities connected to critical infrastructure, particularly telecoms. Since January 2023, Raspberry Typhoon has been particularly persistent. When targeting government ministries or infrastructure, Raspberry Typhoon typically conducts intelligence collection and malware execution. In many countries, targets vary from defense and intelligence-related ministries to economic and trade-related ministries

identification.summary: In 2021, PwC started tracking a series of intrusions under the moniker of Red Dev 17 that they assess were highly likely conducted by a China-based threat actor. Their analysis suggests Red Dev 17 has been active since at least 2017. Red Dev 17's observed targets are mainly in India, and include the Indian military, a multinational India-based technology company, and a state energy company. They assess that it is highly probable that the threat actor behind intrusions associated with Red Dev 17 is also responsible for the campaign known in open source as Operation NightScout. Red Dev 17 is a user of the 8.t document weaponisation framework (also known as RoyalRoad), and abuses benign utilities such as Logitech or Windows Defender binaries to sideload and execute Chinoxy or PoisonIvy variants on victim systems. They identified capability and infrastructure links between Red Dev 17 and the threat actor they call Red Hariasa (aka FunnyDream APT), as well as infrastructure overlaps with Red Wendigo (aka Icefog, RedFoxtrot), and with ShadowPad C2 servers. At this time, they do not have sufficient evidence to directly link Red Dev 17 to any of these threat actors. However, They assess with realistic probability that Red Dev 17 operates within a cluster of threat actors that share tools and infrastructure, as well as a strong targeting focus on Southeast Asia and Central Asia.

Red Menshen is a China-nexus threat actor tracked by PwC, which published on the group in 2022 and assesses it is almost certainly China-based [S2][S7]. It is best known for BPFDoor, a passive Linux backdoor that uses a Berkeley Packet Filter to inspect traffic at kernel level and wait for a trigger packet [S1][S3]. Its main targets are telecommunications providers [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Publicly reported in 2022 (PwC TROOPERS 2022 talk; CFR dates its entry May 2022). A 2021 first-seen date could not be confirmed [S2][S7].
identification.notes: Trend Micro tracks the same activity as Earth Bluecrow [S1]. Malpedia lists Red Dev 18 and DecisiveArchitect as synonyms; CrowdStrike's 2022 report on DecisiveArchitect and its JustForFun implant is listed there [S7]. Malpedia is an aggregator, so treat vendor cluster equivalence as unconfirmed until the vendor reports are compared [S7]. The imported record has no Microsoft actor name and no MITRE group ID; none was found in sources reviewed.

attribution.confidence: PwC assesses the group is almost certainly China-based [S2][S7]. Rapid7 describes it as a China-nexus actor [S3]. One analysis noted no direct evidence linking the group to a specific Chinese military or intelligence entity, and a CFR entry lists China as the suspected state sponsor [S7]. No government attribution was found in the sources reviewed.
attribution.basis: Vendor assessments only (PwC, Trend Micro, Rapid7) [S1][S2][S3]. PwC also noted weekday-only activity, mostly 01:00-10:00 UTC, consistent with an 8 to 9 hour working window [S2][S7].

actors.objectives: Long-term espionage access to telecommunications networks, with the aim of spying on corporate and government entities, as described by Rapid7 [S3].

regions: South Korea, Hong Kong, Myanmar, Malaysia, Egypt (2024 activity per Trend Micro) [S1]
South Korea and Taiwan network-edge appliances (Rapid7, 2026) [S5][S6]
targeting.notes: Telecoms are the core target, with government, education and logistics also named [S2][S7]. Trend Micro telemetry showed telecom, finance and retail victims in 2024, e.g. telecom in South Korea (July and December 2024), Hong Kong (January 2024) and Myanmar (December 2024), a Malaysian retail case in October 2024, and an Egyptian financial case in September 2024 [S1]. PwC's slides also list the USA; this was only seen in a search summary [S7].

capabilities.summary: Signature tool is BPFDoor, a passive kernel-level Linux implant that opens no listening port and waits for a crafted trigger packet [S1][S3]. PwC reported post-exploitation with custom Mangzamel (including Golang variants), custom Gh0st, Mimikatz and Metasploit against Windows systems [S7]. Trend Micro found a controller able to open a reverse shell for lateral movement [S1]. Rapid7 (March 2026) reported about 300 samples, seven new variants (F to L), and two primary variants, httpShell and icmpShell, that hide the trigger in HTTPS traffic or relay over ICMP [S3]. Reporting says initial access often comes via internet-facing edge devices (Ivanti, Fortinet, Palo Alto, routers, VMware ESXi were cited in one summary, with no specific CVEs confirmed), followed by CrossC2, Sliver and TinyShell [S3]. Rapid7 (October 2026) found a new BPFDoor variant and BPF-enabled Rekoobe posing as the Korean anti-spam product SpamSniper, and an SMTP-speaking implant, AVERAT, on Taiwanese appliances [S5][S6]. C2 reportedly ran through VPS servers administered via compromised Taiwan-based routers used as VPN tunnels [S2][S7].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Telecom core and edge Linux servers, mail gateways, VPN/firewall appliances and routers are key cyber terrain; they carry traffic and subscriber data for host-nation and coalition partners in Asia and the Middle East [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 2: The implant evades perimeter controls by hiding in existing ports and mail or HTTPS traffic, so defenders get little network visibility [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 3: Observed template is edge-device foothold, then CrossC2/Sliver/TinyShell, then BPFDoor persistence, with weekday 01:00-10:00 UTC operator hours [S2][S3][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued quiet telecom espionage and tooling refresh in Asia. MDCOA is use of the same persistent access to monitor or disrupt partner-nation communications during a regional crisis (inference, not sourced). Candidate indicators: unexpected raw-socket/BPF filters on Linux hosts, daemon names mimicking SpamSniper, outbound SMTP-like sessions from appliances on TCP 25, ICMP relay between hosts [S1][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track partner-nation telecom and edge-appliance compromises reported by vendors and feed them to the common operating picture [S1][S5]. (2) Authorities: hunting on partner or commercial telecom infrastructure needs host-nation or owner consent; clarify before any action. (3) Mission assurance: assume Linux edge appliances supporting mission communications may be implanted; verify with kernel/BPF-level inspection rather than port scans [S1][S3]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partner CERTs and sector contacts; vendor detections (YARA/Suricata) came from Rapid7 for customers [S3].

provenance.importedSummary: Since 2021, Red Menshen, a China based threat actor, which has been observed targeting telecommunications providers across the Middle East and Asia, as well as entities in the government, education, and logistics sectors using a custom backdoor referred as BPFDoor. This threat actor uses a variety of tools in its post-exploitation phase. This includes custom variants of the shared tool Mangzamel (including Golang variants), custom variants of Gh0st, and open source tools like Mimikatz and Metasploit to aid in its lateral movement across Windows systems. Also, They have been seen sending commands to BPFDoor victims via Virtual Privat Servers (VPSs) hosted at a well-known provider, and that these VPSs, in turn, are administered via compromised routers based in Taiwan, which the threat actor uses as VPN tunnels. Most Red Menshen activity that has been observed took place between Monday to Friday (with none observed on the weekends), with most communication taking place between 01:00 and 10:00 UTC.131 This pattern suggests a consistent 8 to 9-hour activity window for the threat actor, with realistic probability of it aligning to local working hours.

identification.summary: Red Nue is the Malpedia/MISP name for a China-linked (Chinese-speaking) espionage cluster that TeamT5 and Kaspersky track as LuoYu [S1][S2][S3]. It is associated with the multi-platform LootRAT/ReverseWindow backdoor (Windows and macOS variants reported as Demsty; Android variant SpyDealer) and the Windows backdoor WinDealer [S1][S5]. TeamT5 presented the group at JSAC in January 2021 [S5]. Kaspersky reported in June 2022 that WinDealer is delivered through man-on-the-side interception of application update requests [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Dates differ by source: TeamT5 (via JPCERT/CC conference coverage) says activity has been observed since 2014 [S5]; Kaspersky and BlackBerry say since at least 2008 [S2][S4]; Malpedia says active since at least 2017 and WinDealer in use since at least 2019 [S1].
identification.notes: Aliases: Red Nue (Malpedia/MISP) and LuoYu (TeamT5, Kaspersky) [S1][S2]. No Microsoft Typhoon/Storm name was found in the sources gathered. The Malpedia 2017 start date conflicts with the vendor 2008/2014 dates; do not merge them [S1][S2][S5].

attribution.confidence: Kaspersky characterizes LuoYu as a Chinese-speaking APT actor [S2]; BlackBerry describes it as a sophisticated APT group linked to China [S4]. No source gathered attributes the group to a specific PRC government agency or contractor.
attribution.basis: Shared C2 servers tied samples across ReverseWindow, WinDealer and SpyDealer, per TeamT5's JSAC 2021 presentation as summarized in secondary coverage [S5]. Kaspersky later confirmed the Demsty-WinDealer link [S3]. Language and target profile are Kaspersky's basis for 'Chinese-speaking' [S2].

actors.objectives: Espionage against organizations in and around China, including foreign diplomatic organizations in China, academia, and defense, logistics, telecommunications and financial companies [S2][S6]. WinDealer functions include file search and transfer, screenshots and command execution, consistent with information collection [S3].

regions: China (vast majority of victims per Kaspersky)
Germany, Austria, United States, Czech Republic, Russia, India (Kaspersky)
Hong Kong, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan (per TeamT5)
targeting.notes: Kaspersky says the vast majority of LuoYu victims are in China, with additional victims in several other countries [S2]. TeamT5's sector and region list comes from JPCERT/CC conference summaries [S5]. Malpedia notes the 2019 WinDealer watering hole on a Chinese news website serving the diaspora [S1]. Diplomatic and academic groups are described as targets, not named victims [S2].

capabilities.summary: Multi-platform toolset: ReverseWindow/LootRAT (Windows, macOS as Demsty), SpyDealer (Android) and WinDealer (Windows); TeamT5 also lists Linux and Mac targeting [S1][S5]. WinDealer is modular and can capture screenshots, run commands, transfer files, search documents and perform ping-scan discovery [S3]. Its 2020 sample has no hard-coded C2 and instead generates addresses from a pool of about 48,000 ChinaNet addresses in Xizang and Guizhou [S6]. Delivery includes watering holes (including local news sites), and from about 2020 man-on-the-side replacement of update downloads for popular Asian apps such as QQ and WeChat [S2][S3][S6]. BlackBerry also describes man-on-the-side combined with watering-hole attacks on Android messaging apps [S4]. Kaspersky speculates the actor may be intercepting traffic at network level so it needs no real C2 servers [S6].

diamond.infrastructure: WinDealer picks C2 from about 48,000 ChinaNet addresses (Xizang, Guizhou) via an address-generation algorithm, with no fixed C2 [S6]; shared C2 servers linked the malware families [S5].
diamond.victim: Foreign diplomatic organizations in China, academia, defense, logistics, telecommunications and finance; mostly in China, plus several other countries [S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection on foreign missions and sensitive sectors in and near China; diaspora-focused watering hole in 2019 [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Software auto-update channels of popular Asian applications and unencrypted or interceptable network paths; Android messaging apps [S4][S6].

gaps: Securelist, JPCERT/CC and BlackBerry pages could not be opened (fetch blocked); facts rely on search excerpts and secondary coverage (Kaspersky press release, The Hacker News, Security Affairs) and should be checked against the originals.
Sponsor is not identified by any gathered source.
Start date conflict: 2008 (Kaspersky, BlackBerry), 2014 (TeamT5), 2017 (Malpedia).
No Microsoft name mapping found; no MITRE group ID.
Activity after 2022 was not found in the sources gathered.
The PwC reports listed in the original record were not reviewed.
Named victims and the network position enabling man-on-the-side interception are not public in gathered sources.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the software update path of popular regional applications, news sites popular with diaspora communities, and Android messaging apps used by personnel [S3][S4][S1]. STEP 2: The actor needs only an internet-connected victim for man-on-the-side delivery, so users on untrusted or in-country networks are exposed [S6]. STEP 3: Template is update-request interception or watering hole, then WinDealer or Demsty, then document search, screenshots and file transfer to dynamically generated C2 addresses [S3][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection against diplomatic and academic targets in China and Asia. MDCOA is use of update hijacking against travelers or deployed personnel on regional networks. Candidate indicators: application update downloads from unexpected sources or failing signature checks, and outbound connections to many ChinaNet addresses in Xizang or Guizhou [S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: personnel on China-region networks and personal Android devices are exposed; track travel and device policy. (2) Authorities: network-level interception occurs outside friendly networks, so response is limited to endpoint and policy measures. (3) Mission assurance: restrict auto-update of unmanaged applications on mission systems and enforce signed-update verification. (4) Coordination: share indicators with partners and diplomatic security elements, noting the sources are largely secondary and need validation.

provenance.importedSummary: Red Nue, active since at least 2017, is known for its use of the multi-platform LootRAt backdoor, also known as ReverseWindow. LootRAT has variants for Windows and Macintosh (reported in open source as Demsty), as well as an Android variant known as SpyDealer. Red Nue has also used another Windows backdoor known as WinDealer since at least 2019, when it deployed it to targets as part of a watering hole campaign on a Chinese news website for the Chinese diaspora community. Parts of Asia feature heavily in Red Nue's victimology.

identification.summary: Iranian destructive cyber actor that Microsoft tracked as DEV-0842 (now Storm-0842), the cluster that deployed ransomware and a wiper against the Albanian government on 15 July 2022 [S1]. Check Point tracks the activity as Void Manticore, a MOIS-affiliated group that runs the 'Homeland Justice' persona against Albania and the 'Karma' persona against Israel and uses custom wipers [S4]. Later vendor reporting ties the 'Handala' hack-and-leak persona to the same cluster, including the March 2026 Intune-based mass wipe at Stryker [S7][S8].
identification.firstObserved: Destructive deployment by DEV-0842 against Albania on 2022-07-15. Microsoft says other Iranian clusters held access from May 2021 [S1]. Mandiant saw a ROADSWEEP ransomware sample from Albania on 2022-07-22 [S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name in this record: Red Sandstorm. The Microsoft sources gathered here use DEV-0842/Storm-0842 [S1], and secondary 2026 reporting says Microsoft tracks the Handala cluster as Storm-0842 [S7][S8]. Microsoft splits the 2022 Albania operation across several clusters: DEV-0861 (initial access, mail exfiltration), DEV-0166 (mail exfiltration), DEV-0133 (probing) and DEV-0842 (ransomware and wiper) [S1]. Only the DEV-0842 role belongs to this record. Check Point describes a handoff in which Scarred Manticore gains access and then passes targets to Void Manticore [S4]. CrowdStrike's name is Banished Kitten [S7].

attribution.sponsor: Iran, Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS), per Check Point's assessment of Void Manticore [S4]. FBI and CISA attribute the 2022 Albania attacks to 'Iranian state cyber actors' [S2].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft has high confidence that Iranian government-sponsored actors carried out the 15 July 2022 destructive attack [S1]. Microsoft has moderate confidence that the initial-access and exfiltration actors are linked to EUROPIUM, which is publicly tied to MOIS [S1]. Mandiant made a moderate-confidence assessment that one or more actors operating in support of Iranian goals were involved, but tied the activity to no named group [S3]. Check Point links Void Manticore to MOIS [S4]. The Handala-to-Void Manticore link is a vendor assessment that secondary sources credit to Check Point in May 2024 [S7][S8].
attribution.basis: Microsoft incident response and telemetry [S1]; FBI investigation summarized in Joint Cybersecurity Advisory AA22-264A [S2]; Mandiant malware and persona analysis [S3]; Check Point research on overlaps in wipers and personas [S4]; secondary vendor analyses of the 2026 Stryker incident [S7][S8].

actors.objectives: Disruptive and destructive attacks combined with hack-and-leak influence operations that punish and intimidate states and organizations opposed to Iranian policy. These include Albania for hosting the MEK [S1][S3] and Israeli organizations [S4]. Microsoft assessed the 2022 Albania attack as retaliation for cyberattacks on Iran that Tehran blamed on Israel and the MEK [S1]. Handala claimed the 2026 Stryker attack as retaliation for a reported US strike [S8].

regions: United States-headquartered multinationals with global device fleets (Stryker, 2026) [S7][S8]
targeting.notes: Reporting says the Karma persona claimed attacks on more than 40 Israeli organizations [S4].

capabilities.summary: In Albania (July 2022), DEV-0842 deployed GoXml.exe ransomware and the cl.exe wiper, which uses the RawDisk driver rwdsk.sys. It also used a Defender-disabling tool and the Mellona.exe SMB distributor. Web shells, Mimikatz and Impacket were seen in the wider intrusion [S1]. FBI/CISA report that the actors deployed a ZeroCleare variant after defenders responded to the ransomware [S2]. Check Point-based reporting names custom wipers: CI Wiper and No-Justice/LowEraser in Albania, and an updated BiBi wiper with partition-table deletion in Israel [S4]. In 2026 the cluster shifted to abusing living-off-the-cloud administration. Reporting describes AiTM phishing and infostealer-derived session tokens used to compromise an Intune administrator, the creation of a new Global Administrator, and Microsoft Graph API calls that issued mass factory resets without custom malware [S7]. Hack-and-leak through Telegram personas and websites is a constant feature [S3][S4].

campaigns.name: Albania government destructive attack (Homeland Justice)
campaigns.summary: On 15 July, DEV-0842 deployed ransomware and a wiper that disrupted Albanian government websites and public services. Initial access, gained by other clusters through SharePoint CVE-2019-0604, dated to May 2021. The Homeland Justice persona leaked data and pushed anti-MEK messaging.

campaigns.name: Second Albania wave and US advisory
campaigns.summary: FBI/CISA report further Iranian destructive activity against Albania in September 2022, likely as retaliation for public attribution and the severing of diplomatic ties. The advisory notes about 14 months of prior access and use of a ZeroCleare variant.

campaigns.name: Karma persona attacks on Israeli organizations
campaigns.summary: Check Point-based reporting says the Karma persona claimed attacks on more than 40 Israeli organizations using an updated BiBi wiper, posting stolen data or evidence of wiped drives on Telegram.

campaigns.name: Check Point public exposure of Void Manticore
campaigns.summary: Check Point publishes research linking Homeland Justice and Karma to MOIS-affiliated Void Manticore and describing target handoff from Scarred Manticore.

campaigns.name: Stryker Intune mass-wipe (Handala)
campaigns.summary: On 11 March 2026, attackers using the Handala persona reportedly compromised Stryker's Intune administration and factory-reset a large device fleet. Device counts reach about 200,000 in some reports, and Stryker said no malware was found.

diamond.adversary: Iranian MOIS-affiliated destructive unit (Microsoft DEV-0842/Storm-0842; Check Point Void Manticore; CrowdStrike Banished Kitten) operating the Homeland Justice, Karma and Handala personas [S1][S4][S7].
diamond.capability: Custom wipers and ransomware (cl.exe, GoXml, ZeroCleare variant, CI Wiper, No-Justice/LowEraser, BiBi) [S1][S2][S4]; credential tools and web shells [S1]; in 2026, Intune and Graph API remote wipe through a compromised administrator identity [S7].
diamond.infrastructure: Telegram channels and persona websites used for leaks and claims [S3][S4]; access handed off from partner MOIS clusters (Scarred Manticore; EUROPIUM-linked actors in Albania) [S1][S4]; victim cloud management planes used as the delivery mechanism [S7].
diamond.victim: Albanian government and public services [S1][S2]; Israeli organizations [S4]; the global medtech firm Stryker [S7][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Retaliation tied to Albania hosting the MEK and to Israel/US conflict with Iran, amplified through influence messaging [S1][S3][S8].
diamond.technology: Windows domain environments, on-premises SharePoint (initial access by partner clusters), and cloud endpoint management (Microsoft Intune/Entra ID) [S1][S7].

gaps: Could not confirm in any source that Microsoft uses the name 'Red Sandstorm'. learn.microsoft.com could not be fetched. The cited Microsoft and secondary sources use DEV-0842/Storm-0842. A Wikipedia article (Handala Hack Team) surfaced in search with the alias 'Red Sandstorm' and attributes it to Iran International reporting, but the article could not be opened or dated.

Primary documents not opened: CISA/FBI AA22-264A (cisa.gov blocked), the Check Point Void Manticore and 'Bad Karma, No Justice' reports (fetch failed), the Mandiant ROADSWEEP blog, Unit 42's Handala wiper report, and Microsoft's March 2026 Intune hardening guidance. Details come from search-result coverage.
Microsoft assigns initial access in Albania to other clusters (DEV-0861, EUROPIUM-linked). Do not credit access-phase TTPs to Storm-0842 without checking.
Mandiant did not confirm that ROADSWEEP was the ransomware used in the government attack, and tied the activity to no named group [S3].

Stryker impact figures (device counts, 61 vs 79 countries, a 50 TB exfiltration claim) conflict across secondary sources and are unverified. One vendor claims MuddyWater pre-positioned access before the wipe; this is single-source.

Reported link between the unit and sanctioned MOIS deputy minister Yahya Hosseini Panjaki (and his reported 2026 death) comes only from Wikipedia citing Iran International. Treasury's September 2024 designation, as summarized in search results, concerns transnational repression, not cyber.
Sources disagree on whether the Karma persona was retired and replaced by Handala, or whether both were active at once.
First-activity date of the cluster before July 2022 is not established in public sources.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain is identity and management planes, meaning domain controllers, Entra ID Global Administrator roles and Intune or other MDM consoles, which can be turned into fleet-wide wipe mechanisms [S7]. It also includes internet-facing collaboration servers that partner MOIS clusters exploit for initial access [S1]. STEP 2 (effects): Destruction is timed to political events (MEK conference, diplomatic disputes, kinetic conflict), and hack-and-leak amplifies the psychological effect [S1][S2][S3]. STEP 3 (threat model): A partner cluster gains long-dwell access (about 14 months in Albania) and exfiltrates mail; this unit then deploys ransomware-styled wipers or abuses MDM remote wipe, and a persona claims the attack on Telegram [S1][S2][S4][S7]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is a hack-and-leak plus wiper attack against government or regional partner-nation networks during periods of Iran-Israel/US tension [S4]. MDCOA is an identity-plane compromise of a defense contractor or mission partner leading to mass MDM wipe of endpoints that support operations, as at Stryker [S7]. Candidate indicators: creation of new Global Administrator accounts; bulk Intune wipe or retire actions through Graph API; RawDisk driver (rwdsk.sys) loading; Defender-disable tooling; Telegram persona claims naming the organization [S1][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Track Handala, Homeland Justice and Karma persona channels as early warning, since claims and leaks accompany or follow attacks [S3][S4]. Watch for joint advisories on Iranian destructive activity [S2]. Authorities: Activity hits partner nations (Albania is a NATO member) and US companies, so response may require DCO coordination with mission partners and DIB/CISA/FBI channels rather than DoDIN-only actions [S2][S7]. Mission assurance: Enforce multi-admin approval and phishing-resistant MFA for MDM and identity admins, keep offline recovery for endpoints, and harden SharePoint and VPN edges used by access-broker clusters [S1][S7]. Coordination: Because access and destruction are split across MOIS clusters, hunt across the handoff boundary, so that detecting a partner's long-dwell access becomes a pre-strike warning for Storm-0842 effects [S1][S4].

provenance.importedSummary: Void Manticore is an Iranian APT group affiliated with MOIS, known for conducting destructive wiping attacks and influence operations. They collaborate with Scarred Manticore, sharing targets and conducting disruptive operations using custom wipers. Void Manticore's TTPs involve manual file deletion, lateral movement via RDP, and the deployment of custom wipers like the BiBi wiper. The group utilizes online personas like 'Karma' and 'Homeland Justice' to leak information and amplify the impact of their attacks.

identification.summary: RedGolf is Recorded Future's Insikt Group name for a threat activity group it assesses as highly likely Chinese state-sponsored, identified through a large cluster of new infrastructure tied to the custom Windows and Linux backdoor KEYPLUG [S1]. Insikt says RedGolf closely overlaps with activity reported publicly as APT41 and BARIUM [S1]. Insikt describes it as likely carrying out state-sponsored espionage in parallel with financially motivated operations for personal gain from at least 2014 onward [S1]. KEYPLUG use against US state governments was first publicly reported by Mandiant in March 2022 and attributed to APT41 [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Recorded Future: activity from at least 2014 for the overlapping APT41/BARIUM cluster [S1]. KEYPLUG intrusions reported by Mandiant from May 2021 to February 2022 [S2].
identification.notes: RedGolf is a Recorded Future cluster name, not a Microsoft name; no Microsoft mapping was confirmed in the sources gathered. Recorded Future states 'closely overlaps' with APT41/BARIUM, not that the clusters are identical [S1]. Press quoting an Insikt analyst says the groups are thought to be either the same or very closely affiliated [S5]. Facts about APT41 from Mandiant [S2] and the DOJ [S3][S4] describe that vendor/government cluster and are not asserted to be RedGolf-specific.

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China, per Recorded Future's assessment that RedGolf is highly likely a Chinese state-sponsored group [S1].
attribution.confidence: Recorded Future: highly likely Chinese state-sponsored [S1]. Some press coverage paraphrases this as 'likely' state-sponsored [S5]. China's Foreign Ministry denied the accusations, calling the report false information [S5][S7].
attribution.basis: Recorded Future infrastructure analysis of KEYPLUG command-and-control servers and tool overlap with APT41/BARIUM [S1][S5]. For the overlapping APT41 cluster, the US DOJ charged five Chinese nationals and two Malaysian nationals in September 2020, and prosecutors described the Chengdu 404 company as a front [S3][S4]. These are not indictments of RedGolf by name.

actors.objectives: Espionage against government and other organizations, alongside financially motivated activity, per Recorded Future's description of the overlapping APT41/BARIUM cluster [S1]. Mandiant observed personally identifiable information exfiltration from US state government victims but said the campaign goals were unknown and it could not rule out financial motivation [S2].

sectors: Industrial sectors in Italy (KEYPLUG, Tinexta report)
regions: United States (state governments, per Mandiant on APT41/KEYPLUG) [S2]
United States government entities reportedly targeted by RedGolf [S5]
targeting.notes: Insikt listed the sectors above for RedGolf and did not name specific victims [S1][S5]. Insurance and telecommunications victims come from Mandiant's APT41 reporting [S2]. The Italian KEYPLUG case is attributed to APT41 by Tinexta Cyber, not to RedGolf [S6].

capabilities.summary: KEYPLUG is a custom modular backdoor written in C++ with Windows and Linux variants. It supports HTTP, TCP, KCP over UDP and WSS for command and control [S2]. Mandiant saw APT41 use it with Cloudflare-fronted WSS C2 and dead drop resolvers in forum posts, ViewState deserialization, a USAHerds zero-day (CVE-2021-44207), Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228), SQL injection, Cobalt Strike BEACON, BADPOTATO, Mimikatz and DNS-based exfiltration [S2]. Insikt additionally saw RedGolf infrastructure using Cobalt Strike, PlugX and dynamic DNS domains, which are common among Chinese state-sponsored groups [S5]. Tinexta reported a .NET loader that decrypts the KEYPLUG payload with AES in a 2024 Italian case [S6].

campaigns.name: DOJ charges against APT41-linked individuals
campaigns.summary: The DOJ announced charges against seven people (five Chinese nationals, two Malaysian nationals) over hacking of more than 100 companies, from three indictments dated August 2019 and August 2020. Prosecutors described Chengdu 404 as a front company. This concerns the overlapping APT41 cluster, reported here via Dark Reading and a search listing of the DOJ release.

campaigns.name: APT41 KEYPLUG campaign against US state governments
campaigns.summary: Mandiant reported at least six US state government networks compromised, with initial access via ViewState deserialization, the USAHerds zero-day and Log4Shell. KEYPLUG Windows was heavily used June to December 2021 and KEYPLUG.LINUX deployed after Log4Shell exploitation. Two earlier victims were re-compromised in February 2022.

campaigns.name: Insikt report on RedGolf KEYPLUG infrastructure
campaigns.summary: Insikt identified a large cluster of new KEYPLUG infrastructure and attributed it to RedGolf. The Hacker News reported the cluster as 42 C2 IP addresses tracked as GhostWolf, seen from at least 2021 to 2023, alongside Cobalt Strike, PlugX and dynamic DNS domains. China denied the findings.

campaigns.name: KEYPLUG implant against Italian industries
campaigns.summary: Tinexta Cyber's Zlab reported a previously undetected KEYPLUG implant used against several Italian industries over months and linked it to APT41. This is a vendor attribution to APT41, not RedGolf.

diamond.adversary: Highly likely Chinese state-sponsored cluster overlapping APT41/BARIUM, with espionage and financially motivated activity [S1].
diamond.capability: KEYPLUG Windows and Linux backdoor, Cobalt Strike, PlugX, and for the overlapping APT41 cluster web-application exploitation including a zero-day and Log4Shell [S2][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Cluster of new KEYPLUG C2 servers (reported as 42 IPs, GhostWolf) and dynamic DNS domains [S1][S5]. APT41 used Cloudflare-fronted WSS C2 and forum dead drop resolvers [S2].
diamond.victim: Aviation, automotive, education, government, media, IT and religious organizations; US government entities reportedly [S1][S5]. APT41 victims include six US state governments [S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: State-aligned espionage coexisting with profit-seeking, consistent with the PRC contractor ecosystem described in the DOJ charges against APT41-linked individuals [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing web applications with exposed or default ASP.NET machine keys, unpatched Java logging libraries (Log4j), and mixed Windows/Linux server estates [S2].

gaps: The Recorded Future report text could not be opened (host unreachable from this environment); RedGolf claims rely on search-result summaries and press coverage of the report [S1][S5][S7].
The DOJ press release was not opened; DOJ details come from a search listing and Dark Reading coverage [S3][S4].
Exact overlap between RedGolf and APT41/BARIUM is unresolved: Recorded Future says 'closely overlaps' [S1].
No Microsoft actor name mapping for RedGolf was found; a search suggested BARIUM and Brass Typhoon are Microsoft names for APT41 but no primary Microsoft mapping was opened.
No victims named by Insikt; the 42-IP GhostWolf figure comes from secondary coverage only [S5].
No MITRE ATT&CK group entry for RedGolf confirmed.
Whether the 2024 Italian KEYPLUG activity is RedGolf is unknown [S6].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing web applications (ASP.NET, Java) and Windows/Linux servers at government and contractor-adjacent organizations are key terrain [S2]. STEP 2: The adversary exploits new vulnerabilities within hours (Log4Shell) and reuses a static machine key across installations, so patch windows are short [S2]. STEP 3: Template is web-app exploitation, then KEYPLUG with Cloudflare-fronted WSS C2, Cobalt Strike and credential theft, then data exfiltration including over DNS [S2][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage and opportunistic access against government and industry using KEYPLUG [S1]. MDCOA is rapid mass exploitation of a newly disclosed web-app flaw against DoD-adjacent hosts, combined with financially motivated activity that could mask intent [S1][S2]. Candidate indicators: Linux files split as xaa-xad, modified existing SYSTEM scheduled tasks, DNS queries carrying hex-encoded subdomains, and WSS traffic to Cloudflare ranges with an unusual SNI/host [S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track KEYPLUG and dynamic DNS infrastructure feeds and fold vendor reporting into hunt priorities [S1][S5]. (2) Authorities: attribution is vendor-level (Recorded Future); do not treat it as government attribution when tasking or reporting [S1]. (3) Mission assurance: inventory internet-facing ASP.NET/Java applications and rotate default machine keys [S2]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3 and partner networks; state and commercial victims in prior campaigns were in sectors adjacent to defense supply chains [S1][S2].
