identification.summary: Microsoft describes Sapphire Sleet as a North Korean state actor focused on the finance sector, especially cryptocurrency, venture capital and blockchain organizations, whose main motive is stealing cryptocurrency wallets to generate revenue [S2][S3][S4]. Its signature tradecraft is social engineering. Operators pose as venture capitalists or recruiters, set up fake Zoom or Teams meetings or skills assessments, and then get the victim to run a script that installs malware [S1][S3]. In 2026 Microsoft also attributed two npm software supply-chain compromises to it: Axios (March 2026) and Mastra (June 2026) [S2][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: cryptocurrency theft and computer network exploitation since at least 2020 [S1]; 'active since at least March 2020' [S2][S3][S4]. Mandiant tracks the overlapping UNC1069 cluster as active since at least 2018 [S7][S8].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Sapphire Sleet (legacy element name COPERNICIUM per Microsoft's mapping) [S5]. Microsoft says the actor is also tracked as UNC1069, STARDUST CHOLLIMA, Alluring Pisces, BlueNoroff, CageyChameleon and CryptoCore [S4][S5]. This record is linked to MITRE G0082 (APT38), but the Microsoft sources gathered here do not list APT38, BeagleBoyz or NICKEL GLADSTONE as Sapphire Sleet names. Keep the APT38 bank-heist history (2016 Bangladesh Bank and similar) separate from Sapphire Sleet's documented 2020+ cryptocurrency activity [S4][S6].

attribution.sponsor: Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea). Microsoft calls Sapphire Sleet a North Korean state actor [S2][S4]. MITRE attributes the linked APT38 group to the Reconnaissance General Bureau [S6], but no source gathered here ties Sapphire Sleet itself to a specific DPRK organization.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft assessed with high confidence that the June 2026 Mastra npm compromise is attributable to Sapphire Sleet [S4]. Microsoft attributed the infrastructure and Axios compromise to Sapphire Sleet without stating a confidence level [S2]. Google Threat Intelligence Group separately attributed the Axios compromise to UNC1069 [S8]. All of these are vendor assessments; no government attribution of Sapphire Sleet by name was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and incident analysis, including C2 hosting at Hostwinds, a VPS provider Microsoft says Sapphire Sleet commonly uses [S2][S3][S4]. GTIG cited reuse of the WAVESHAPER.V2 backdoor and infrastructure overlaps with known UNC1069 activity, as reported by Security Affairs [S8]. Kaspersky's attribution of the GhostCall/GhostHire campaigns is to BlueNoroff [S9][S10].

actors.objectives: Revenue generation for the DPRK through cryptocurrency theft. Microsoft says the actor's primary motivation is stealing cryptocurrency wallets [S2][S3][S4] and estimated that more than US$10 million in cryptocurrency was stolen from multiple companies over a six-month period [S1]. Access to credentials, keychains and developer environments supports follow-on theft [S3][S4].

sectors: Web3 firms and centralized exchanges (overlapping UNC1069/BlueNoroff reporting) [S7][S9]
Software developers and open-source maintainers; npm consumers and CI/CD pipelines [S2][S4][S9]
Job seekers approached through fake recruiting [S1][S3]
regions: Global; Microsoft gives no regional restriction [S1][S2]
India, Turkey, Australia, and parts of Europe and Asia (Kaspersky, BlueNoroff GhostCall/GhostHire since April 2025) [S9]
targeting.notes: Targeting is individual-centric. Executives, investors and developers are approached through LinkedIn and Telegram [S1][S3][S7][S9]. The 2026 npm compromises extended exposure to any developer workstation or CI/CD pipeline that installed the poisoned versions, even if the package was never imported in code [S4]. Kaspersky's regional data comes from its BlueNoroff cluster and may not match Microsoft's Sapphire Sleet boundaries [S9].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering is the core capability. Lures include fake venture-capital investment meetings, where a staged connection error prompts the victim to run a .scpt (macOS) or .vbs (Windows) 'fix', and fake recruiter skills assessments hosted on actor-controlled sites [S1]. In an April 2026 macOS intrusion, a 'Zoom SDK Update.scpt' padded with thousands of blank lines launched a curl-to-osascript chain. The chain deployed backdoors (e.g., 'services', 'com.google.chromes.updaters'), a fake password prompt whose capture was exfiltrated via the Telegram Bot API, and theft of browser data, keychain, crypto wallets (Ledger Live, Exodus), Telegram sessions, SSH keys and Apple Notes. It also modified the TCC database and persisted via LaunchDaemons and LaunchAgents [S3]. A June 2026 Teams-themed variant used 'MSTeams SDK Update.scpt' [S3]. Supply-chain capability: in the Axios compromise (axios 1.14.1/0.30.4), a fake dependency, plain-crypto-js@4.2.1, used an install hook to deliver OS-specific payloads for macOS, Windows and Linux [S2]. GTIG identified that payload as the WAVESHAPER.V2 backdoor [S8]. In the Mastra compromise, a takeover of a maintainer account pushed 140+ packages that depended on the typosquat easy-day-js. Its postinstall hook disabled TLS verification and staged a Node.js implant, followed by reflective .NET injection, a PowerShell backdoor, a Defender exclusion and a SYSTEM service [S4]. Mandiant reporting on overlapping UNC1069 describes ClickFix lures, AI-generated video in fake meetings and new families SILENCELIFT, DEEPBREATH and CHROMEPUSH [S7].

campaigns.name: Mastra npm supply-chain compromise
campaigns.summary: Through a takeover of a maintainer account, 140+ mastra/@mastra packages were published with the typosquat easy-day-js, whose postinstall hook installed a cross-platform implant; attributed by Microsoft to Sapphire Sleet with high confidence on 2026-06-19.

diamond.adversary: North Korean state actor tracked by Microsoft as Sapphire Sleet, overlapping with UNC1069, STARDUST CHOLLIMA, BlueNoroff and others [S4][S5].
diamond.capability: Persona-based social engineering (fake VC, recruiter, meeting support) leading to AppleScript/VBScript execution; macOS backdoors and credential stealers; npm install-hook supply-chain payloads; WAVESHAPER.V2 (per GTIG) [S1][S2][S3][S4][S8].
diamond.infrastructure: Fake LinkedIn recruiter profiles and skills-assessment sites [S1]; meeting-themed domains such as uw04webzoom[.]us [S3]; Hostwinds VPS C2 (e.g., sfrclak[.]com, 142.11.206.73:8000) [S2]; C2 at 23.254.164.92 and teams.onweblive[.]org [S4]; Telegram Bot API for credential exfiltration [S3]; hijacked Telegram accounts [S7].
diamond.victim: Individuals at cryptocurrency, blockchain, venture-capital and fintech organizations; developers and open-source maintainers; downstream npm consumers [S1][S2][S4][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Cryptocurrency theft to generate revenue for the DPRK [S2][S4].
diamond.technology: macOS Script Editor/osascript and TCC permissions; Windows VBScript and PowerShell; npm lifecycle (postinstall) scripts and semver caret ranges; browser wallet extensions and keychains [S2][S3][S4].

gaps: Cluster boundaries: this record is linked to MITRE G0082 (APT38), but the Microsoft sources gathered list UNC1069, STARDUST CHOLLIMA, Alluring Pisces, BlueNoroff, CageyChameleon and CryptoCore, not APT38, BeagleBoyz or NICKEL GLADSTONE. APT38-era bank heists should not be attributed to Sapphire Sleet without a source that explicitly links them [S4][S5][S6].
First-observed dates conflict: Microsoft says March 2020 [S2]; Mandiant says UNC1069 has been active since 2018 [S7][S8].

Kaspersky (BlueNoroff) and Mandiant (UNC1069) campaign details are mapped to Sapphire Sleet only through alias overlap; Microsoft has not confirmed that each named campaign is Sapphire Sleet activity [S7][S9].
Primary document not opened: GTIG's Axios attribution, used via secondary coverage [S8]; full Securelist GhostCall/GhostHire report (host unreachable), used via Kaspersky press materials [S9][S10].
No US government advisory or indictment naming Sapphire Sleet specifically was found; the specific RGB unit responsible is not established in the sources gathered.
Total cryptocurrency losses attributable specifically to Sapphire Sleet beyond Microsoft's >$10M six-month estimate [S1] are unknown, as are downstream victims of the Axios and Mastra compromises.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (Operational environment): Key terrain includes personnel identities on LinkedIn and Telegram, developer workstations, CI/CD pipelines and the npm dependency graph, all exploited in sourced activity [S1][S2][S4]. STEP 2 (Effects): Any installation of a poisoned package executes code with no user action beyond npm install, so build systems that pull public packages are exposed [S4]. macOS endpoints are directly targeted [S3]. STEP 3 (Threat evaluation): The template is a persona lure (VC, recruiter, meeting support), then a user-run .scpt/.vbs or ClickFix command, then a backdoor, then credential, keychain and wallet theft [S1][S3][S7]. A parallel path is maintainer account takeover, then a malicious dependency with an install hook, then a cross-platform implant [S2][S4]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued financially motivated social engineering against crypto and fintech staff, with incidental compromise of developers who also support DoD-adjacent software [S1][S3]. MDCOA is a supply-chain compromise of a widely used package pulled into DoD or DIB build pipelines, giving broad implant access that could be repurposed beyond theft (analyst extrapolation from [S2][S4]). Candidate indicators: Script Editor or osascript spawning curl; files named '*SDK Update.scpt'; unexpected LaunchDaemons or LaunchAgents such as com.google.webkit.service.plist; Telegram Bot API traffic from endpoints [S3]; npm installs of plain-crypto-js or easy-day-js; outbound traffic to Hostwinds-hosted IPs on port 8000; new Defender exclusions or an 'scdev' service [S2][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: feed software-composition and package-registry alerts (e.g., poisoned Axios or Mastra versions) into JCC2 common operating picture in near real time, because Microsoft reports a window of minutes to hours between malicious publication and detection or removal [S4][S8]. (2) Authorities: DoD software consumed from public registries and contractor development environments sit across DODIN and DIB boundaries; response requires coordination with DC3 and DIB partners rather than unilateral action. (3) Mission assurance: enforce dependency pinning, install with --ignore-scripts, and rebuild from a trusted baseline after exposure, as Microsoft recommends [S2]; harden macOS fleets against user-run AppleScript [S3]. (4) Coordination: vendor attribution differs by name (Microsoft Sapphire Sleet, GTIG UNC1069, Kaspersky BlueNoroff) [S2][S8][S9], so deconflict naming in intelligence products and prioritize indicator sharing over naming disputes.

provenance.importedSummary:
APT38 is a North Korean state-sponsored threat group that specializes in financial cyber operations; it has been attributed to the Reconnaissance General Bureau. Active since at least 2014, APT38 has targeted banks, financial institutions, casinos, cryptocurrency exchanges, SWIFT system endpoints, and ATMs in at least 38 countries worldwide. Significant operations include the 2016 Bank of Bangladesh heist, Bancomext  and Banco de Chile , along with software supply chain compromises and destructive malware attacks.

North Korean group definitions are known to have significant overlap, and some security researchers report all North Korean state-sponsored cyber activity under the name Lazarus Group instead of tracking clusters or subgroups.

identification.summary: China-based cyber-espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Satin Typhoon and maps to APT18, Wekby, Dynamite Panda, TG-0416 and SCANDIUM [S1]. Mandiant attributed the 2014 Community Health Systems breach, which exposed data on about 4.5 million patients, to the group under the name APT 18 [S3][S4]. FireEye reported in July 2015 that APT18 quickly weaponized the Hacking Team-leaked Flash zero-day CVE-2015-5119 in spearphishing campaigns launched before Adobe's July 8, 2015 patch [S2]. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 reported in May 2016 that Wekby used a new malware family, pisloader, that uses DNS requests for command and control [S6].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Satin Typhoon (formerly SCANDIUM). Microsoft maps SCANDIUM, DYNAMITE PANDA, COMBINE, TG-0416, SILVERVIPER, Red Wraith, APT18, Elderwood Group and Wekby to it [S1]. Vendor names reported in 2014 coverage: APT 18 (Mandiant), Dynamite Panda (CrowdStrike), TG-0416 (SecureWorks), Wekby (Palo Alto Networks), Scandium (Microsoft) [S3]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the group as APT18 (G0026) [S8]. Microsoft tracks Salmon Typhoon (APT4/SODIUM/MAVERICK PANDA) separately; those names do not belong to this record.

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (assessed by vendors; no government attribution found in sources gathered). Microsoft lists the actor's origin as China [S1]; security experts quoted in 2014 coverage said the group may have links to the Chinese government [S4].
attribution.confidence: Vendor assessment only. Mandiant attributed the Community Health Systems intrusion to APT 18 [S3][S4]; FireEye attributed the July 2015 Flash campaign to APT18 using a previously known APT18 C2 address [S2]. No indictment, sanctions or government advisory naming this actor was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Incident-response attribution by Mandiant [S3]; infrastructure overlap with previously known APT18 C2 (FireEye) [S2]; Volexity observation of Wekby C2 reused across years [S5]; malware lineage linking pisloader to HTTPBrowser (Unit 42) [S6].

actors.objectives: Espionage and intellectual-property theft. Mandiant said the group has been known to steal medical technology and pharmaceutical manufacturing intellectual property, while the 2014 Community Health Systems intrusion took patient personal data rather than medical device information [S3]. The motive for collecting bulk patient identity data was not publicly established [S3][S4].

sectors: Health and biotechnology, including hospital operators [S2][S3]
regions: United States (Community Health Systems; US-based organization targeted with pisloader) [S3][S6]
targeting.notes: Sector list for July 2015 comes from FireEye [S2] (search excerpts confirmed these sectors only for the combined APT3/APT18 activity; the APT18-specific list and victim count were not confirmed); Mandiant's broader sector description comes from 2014 interview coverage [S3]. FireEye described APT18's 2015 lures as nonspecific and likely reused across multiple targets [S2].

capabilities.summary: Rapid adoption of newly public exploits: APT18 used the Hacking Team-leaked Flash zero-day CVE-2015-5119 in 'Important: Flash Update' spearphishing emails that linked to a malicious SWF file, which delivered a Gh0st RAT variant [S2][S5]. FireEye said APT18 relied on procured (not compromised) infrastructure [S2]; Volexity noted a Singapore C2 IP reused in many Wekby attacks over prior years [S5]. Unit 42 reported pisloader, a variant tied to the HTTPBrowser family, using DNS TXT requests for C2 plus return-oriented programming and other anti-analysis techniques [S6]. In the 2014 Community Health Systems case, TrustedSec reported (citing anonymous sources close to the investigation) that the attackers stole credentials from a Heartbleed-vulnerable Juniper device and used them for VPN access; Mandiant did not confirm the initial access vector [S3][S7]. MITRE lists gh0st RAT, HTTPBrowser, hcdLoader, Pisloader and cmd as software used by the group [S8].

campaigns.name: Community Health Systems intrusion
campaigns.summary: Intrusions in April and June 2014 into the US hospital operator exposed non-medical identifiers of about 4.5 million patients; Mandiant attributed them to APT 18. TrustedSec claimed Heartbleed-enabled VPN credential theft as initial access; this was not confirmed.

campaigns.name: Hacking Team Flash zero-day spearphishing (CVE-2015-5119)
campaigns.summary: 'Important: Flash Update' emails led to a malicious SWF that delivered a Gh0st RAT variant calling back to a previously known APT18 C2. FireEye reported targeting in aerospace and defense, construction and engineering, education, health and biotechnology, high tech, telecommunications and transportation. Volexity reported the same activity under the Wekby name.

campaigns.name: Wekby pisloader DNS C2 attack
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 observed Wekby targeting a US-based organization with pisloader, an HTTPBrowser-related malware that uses DNS requests for command and control.

diamond.adversary: China-based espionage operators tracked as Satin Typhoon / APT18 / Wekby / Dynamite Panda [S1][S3]; no individual operators publicly named in sources gathered.
diamond.capability: Rapidly weaponized public exploits (CVE-2015-5119), Gh0st RAT, HTTPBrowser-family pisloader with DNS C2, and reported VPN credential abuse [S2][S6][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: Procured infrastructure, including a long-reused C2 IP in Singapore and a lure server masquerading as an Adobe download page [S2][S5].
diamond.victim: US organizations in aerospace and defense, engineering, health care, high tech, telecommunications, transportation and education; Community Health Systems patient data [S2][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Theft of medical, pharmaceutical and defense-relevant intellectual property, plus bulk personal data from a US health care provider [S3].
diamond.technology: Unpatched internet-facing remote-access devices (reported Heartbleed on Juniper VPN), browser plug-ins (Adobe Flash), and DNS as a C2 channel [S2][S6][S7].

gaps: No recent reporting (after 2016) specifically naming Satin Typhoon, APT18 or Wekby was found; current activity level is unknown.

First observed date not established from a primary source. Secondary summaries say 'active since about 2009' and claim PLA Navy affiliation; neither was verified in a primary source, so both are left out.

The existing record's aliases BRONZE EDISON, SAMURAI PANDA, PLA Navy and Wisp Team do not appear in Microsoft's Satin Typhoon mapping [S1]; the Secureworks BRONZE EDISON profile could not be opened to confirm its overlap.
Imported references to Sykipot (AlienVault, Trend Micro, SANS, CFR) may reflect MISP Galaxy merging of Elderwood/Sykipot activity with APT18; that link was not verified in the sources gathered.
The Heartbleed initial-access claim for Community Health Systems comes from TrustedSec's account citing anonymous sources and was not confirmed by Mandiant [S3][S7].

A July 2015 Zscaler report of HttpBrowser delivered via Hacking Team exploits against a financial services firm was attributed in coverage to Emissary Panda, a different cluster (Microsoft Linen Typhoon); it is excluded here even though HTTPBrowser is shared tooling.

Primary documents not opened: Secureworks BRONZE EDISON profile, Unit 42 pisloader post, Volexity post, Mandiant APT groups page, MITRE G0026 page (content taken from search-result summaries and the record's ATT&CK import).

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is internet-facing remote-access appliances (VPN gateways), end-user browsers and plug-ins, and DNS resolution paths, all of which the actor has reportedly used [S2][S6][S7]. STEP 2: The actor weaponized a leaked zero-day within days of its disclosure, so the patch window against it may be days or less [S2][S5]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is a generic spearphish or exploited edge device, then Gh0st RAT or an HTTPBrowser-family implant, then C2 over HTTP or DNS to procured infrastructure, then IP or PII theft [S2][S6][S7]. STEP 4: The MLCOA is opportunistic exploitation of newly disclosed vulnerabilities against defense-industrial-base, aerospace and health organizations to steal IP [S2][S3]. The MDCOA is credential theft from unpatched VPN appliances giving persistent access to defense-supporting networks and bulk personnel data [S3][S7]. Candidate indicators: 'Flash/software update' themed emails from look-alike domains, unusual DNS TXT query volume to rare domains, VPN logins with credentials reused from edge-device memory exposure, and contact with previously reported C2 such as 223.25.233.248 [S2][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track exploit publication and patch status for edge VPN devices and client software in near real time, given the actor's speed of exploit adoption [S2][S5]. (2) Authorities: attribution rests on vendor assessments only, with no government attribution in the sources gathered, so response actions should not presume a formal attribution [S3][S4]. (3) Mission assurance: health and personnel data systems that support installations are proven targets for bulk PII theft [S3]. (4) Coordination: share DNS-C2 and C2 IP indicators with DC3/DIB partners, because the targeted sectors overlap with aerospace and defense contractors [S2][S6].

identification.summary: Scarab APT was first spotted in 2015, but is believed to have been active since at least 2012, conducting surgical attacks against a small number of individuals across the world, including Russia and the United States. The backdoor deployed by Scarab in their campaigns is most commonly known as Scieron.

Scarlet Mimic is a threat group named by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 in January 2016 after a seven-month study of a multi-year espionage campaign against Uyghur and Tibetan activists and those interested in their causes [S1][S2]. Unit 42 also saw attacks against government organizations in Russia and India responsible for tracking activist and terrorist activity [S1][S2]. MITRE tracks the group as G0029 [S5].
identification.firstObserved: Unit 42 (January 2016) said the attacks began over four years earlier, i.e. roughly 2011 or before [S1]. Trend Micro first described the FakeM backdoor in 2013 [S2].
identification.notes: Unit 42 later tracks the cluster as Golfing Taurus (per imported record). Unit 42 found some IP overlap with Putter Panda (APT 2) but did not conclude the groups are the same [S1]. No Microsoft Typhoon/Storm name is mapped in this record. Do not merge with Earth Minotaur (Trend Micro, separate Tibetan/Uyghur Android actor) [S6].

attribution.sponsor: Not attributed to a government by the primary vendor. Unit 42 said it had no evidence directly linking the attacks to a government source, but that the activity supports an assessment that a group or groups with motivations similar to the stated position of the Chinese government is involved [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: Low to moderate as a state-aligned assessment; Unit 42 explicitly declined direct government attribution [S1]. Press coverage of Citizen Lab's work described the group as believed to work on behalf of Chinese authorities, which is a secondary characterization [S4].
attribution.basis: Targeting pattern against minority-rights activists and Russian/Indian counter-terror-related agencies, consistent with PRC positions [S1]; partial IP overlap with Putter Panda, not concluded to be the same group [S1].

actors.objectives: Information gathering on minority-rights activists (Uyghur and Tibetan) and their supporters, which Unit 42 assessed as the group's primary mission [S1].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is activist and diaspora communication accounts, personal and mobile devices, and regional counter-terror agency networks in Russia and India [S1]. STEP 2: Defenders in these groups often lack enterprise security and use cloud mail, which the actor exploited through credential phishing [S3]. STEP 3: Template is spear-phish or watering hole, then FakeM-family backdoor on Windows, Mac or Android, with mimicked messenger C2 [S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued collection against minority-rights activists. MDCOA is use of the same toolset and infrastructure against government or military personnel tied to counter-terror or regional security topics. Candidate indicators: Messenger-mimicking C2 traffic, mobile apps themed for Uyghur or Tibetan topics, reused C2 hosting fake Google login pages [S2][S3]. Low direct relevance to US DoD networks in sources gathered.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: treat as low-priority regional espionage threat with limited public reporting after 2016 [S1]. Authorities and coordination: targeting is primarily civil society, so response would be partner-nation or civilian-agency led rather than DoD; share indicators through existing intelligence channels. Mission assurance: personnel using personal mobile devices and cloud mail on activist-related or regional topics are the exposed population [S2][S3].

provenance.importedSummary: Scarlet Mimic is a threat group that has targeted minority rights activists. This group has not been directly linked to a government source, but the group’s motivations appear to overlap with those of the Chinese government. While there is some overlap between IP addresses used by Scarlet Mimic and Putter Panda, APT 2, it has not been concluded that the groups are the same. The attacks began over four years ago and their targeting pattern suggests that this adversary’s primary mission is to gather information about minority rights activists. We do not have evidence directly linking these attacks to a government source, but the information derived from these activities supports an assessment that a group or groups with motivations similar to the stated position of the Chinese government in relation to these targets is involved. The attacks we attribute to Scarlet Mimic have primarily targeted Uyghur and Tibetan activists as well as those who are interested in their causes. Both the Tibetan community and the Uyghurs, a Turkic Muslim minority residing primarily in northwest China, have been targets of multiple sophisticated attacks in the past decade. Both also have history of strained relationships with the government of the People’s Republic of China (PRC), though we do not have evidence that links Scarlet Mimic attacks to the PRC. Scarlet Mimic attacks have also been identified against government organizations in Russia and India, who are responsible for tracking activist and terrorist activities. While we do not know the precise target of each of the Scarlet Mimic attacks, many of them align to the patterns described above.

identification.summary: Scarred Manticore has been pursuing high-value targets for years, utilizing a variety of IIS-based backdoors to attack Windows servers. These include a variety of custom web shells, custom DLL backdoors, and driver-based implants.

Russian military intelligence (GRU) cyber unit responsible for most of the destructive and disruptive cyberattacks against Ukraine over the past decade, including the 2015 and 2016 power-grid outages, NotPetya (2017), and wipers deployed around the February 2022 invasion [S2][S3]. It combines espionage, sabotage and information operations, and paces its attacks to support Russian conventional military operations [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Publicly documented destructive activity since at least the December 2015 Ukraine grid outage; the 2020 DOJ indictment covers attacks from 2015 to 2019 [S2][S3]. Earlier espionage activity under the Sandworm name is reported in the imported references but was not re-verified here. Microsoft's BadPilot subgroup has been active since at least 2021 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Seashell Blizzard (formerly IRIDIUM). Microsoft maps Sandworm, VOODOO BEAR, APT44, UAC-0113, BE2 and BlackEnergy Lite to it [S8]. Mandiant upgraded the cluster to APT44 in April 2024 to separate it from APT28 (GRU Unit 26165) [S3].

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation: GRU Unit 74455, the Main Centre for Special Technologies (GTsST) of the Main Directorate of the General Staff [S1][S2][S3].
attribution.confidence: Formal US government attribution through the October 2020 indictment of six named Unit 74455 officers [S2]. Microsoft states the actor works on behalf of GRU Unit 74455 [S1]. ESET attributes the December 2025 Poland wiper attempt with medium confidence [S6].
attribution.basis: DOJ indictment evidence [S2]; long-running vendor forensics (Mandiant, ESET, Microsoft, Dragos) [S1][S3][S4][S6]; malware lineage across BlackEnergy, Industroyer/Industroyer2, NotPetya and later wipers.

actors.objectives: Support Russian military and political objectives through destructive and disruptive attacks, intelligence collection and influence operations, focused on Ukraine and increasingly on states supporting it [S1][S3]. Targets Western elections and institutions, including in NATO countries [S3]. Microsoft assesses its access subgroup exists to establish and hold access in sectors of interest to Russia, which can later enable destructive operations [S1].

regions: NATO and EU states, including Poland (Dec 2025 energy-sector wiper attempt)
United States, Canada, Australia and the United Kingdom (BadPilot focus in 2024)
Central Asia and the Middle East (BadPilot, 2023)
targeting.notes: Sector and region data from Mandiant [S3], Microsoft's BadPilot reporting [S1] and ESET [S6]. Ukrainian water and heating targeting as reported in ESET-derived coverage [S6].

capabilities.summary: Full-spectrum: espionage, destructive wipers and OT effects. OT capability is proven: Industroyer (2016), Industroyer2 against a Ukrainian substation (thwarted April 2022) [S5], and an October 2022 outage caused by executing native MicroSCADA binaries (scilc.exe), a living-off-the-land approach to OT [S4]. Wipers include NotPetya, KillDisk, CaddyWiper and DynoWiper (Poland, Dec 2025) [S2][S4][S6]. Initial access through edge devices and n-day exploits (Exchange CVE-2021-34473, Zimbra CVE-2022-41352, ScreenConnect CVE-2024-1709, FortiClient EMS CVE-2023-48788), with persistence through RMM tools (Atera, Splashtop), the ShadowLink Tor hidden-service tool and the LocalOlive web shell [S1]. Uses hacktivist-branded Telegram personas for influence [S3].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: For any EUCOM or NATO contingency, the cyberspace OE includes allied energy, heating, water and telecom OT, not just DoD networks. Poland in Dec 2025 shows NATO-state energy is in range. STEP 2: Sandworm times effects with kinetic operations, so cyber effects should be modeled alongside the adversary's fires and maneuver timeline, not as a separate line. STEP 3: The template is edge or n-day initial access (often prepared long in advance by BadPilot), then domain compromise, then pivot to SCADA management hosts, then OT effect using native tools, then wiper to destroy evidence and slow recovery. STEP 4: MLCOA is sustained espionage and access maintenance in allied energy and logistics with periodic destructive attacks in Ukraine. MDCOA is synchronized wiper and OT attacks on allied energy and logistics nodes supporting reinforcement of NATO's eastern flank. Candidate indicators: RMM tools (Atera, Splashtop) appearing without change records, Tor hidden-service persistence, new local admin accounts on SCADA management hosts, and abnormal MicroSCADA or engineering tool execution [S1][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Integrate allied CERT reporting (CERT-UA, Polish CSIRTs) and vendor ICS telemetry into shared situational awareness, since the earliest warning is often in partner OT networks. (2) Plan for degraded host-nation infrastructure: C2 resilience and mission assurance assessments should assume possible power and heating loss at staging areas. (3) Authorities: defense of allied civilian infrastructure is a host-nation lead. US cyber forces support through partner agreements and hunt-forward-type missions, which must be coordinated through EUCOM and USCYBERCOM channels. (4) Wiper resilience: offline backups and restoration drills for deployed mission systems are a C2 continuity requirement, not just an IT task.

identification.summary: Russian state cyber-espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Secret Blizzard and other vendors track as Turla, Snake, Uroburos, Venomous Bear and Waterbug [S1][S2][S4]. Microsoft says it seeks long-term access to systems for intelligence collection, generally looking for information of political importance, and it targets foreign affairs ministries, embassies, government offices and defense organizations worldwide [S2]. It regularly takes over the tools and infrastructure of other threat actors; Microsoft counts at least six such actors over seven years [S2]. Its flagship Kazuar backdoor has grown into a modular peer-to-peer botnet [S4]. In 2025 Microsoft confirmed for the first time that it can operate adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attacks at the internet service provider (ISP) level inside Russia [S1].
identification.firstObserved: ESET describes Turla as operating since at least 2004 [S5]. The French C4 says it has observed Turla targeting France since 2010 [S7].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Secret Blizzard. Microsoft lists the overlapping names VENOMOUS BEAR, Uroburos, Snake, Blue Python, Turla, Wraith, ATG26 and Waterbug [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as Turla (G0010). 'Snake' names both the actor (in some vendor reporting) and its long-running implant, which the US disrupted in 2023 [S6]. Kaspersky's WhiteBear is described as a parallel project or second stage of its Skipper Turla cluster, with a separate target focus [S9]. Microsoft tracks Storm-0156, Storm-1919 (Amadey), Storm-1837 and Aqua Blizzard as separate actors whose access Secret Blizzard has piggybacked on; they are not aliases [S2][S3][S4].

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation, Federal Security Service (FSB) Center 16. Microsoft cites CISA's attribution of Secret Blizzard to FSB Center 16 [S1][S2][S4], and US court documents in Operation MEDUSA attribute the Snake malware to a unit within FSB Center 16 [S6]. France's Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre (C4) attributes Turla to the FSB's 16th Centre [S7].
attribution.confidence: US government: attribution to FSB Center 16, stated in the 2023 MEDUSA court-authorized operation and the joint advisory, as reported by press [S6]. France: formal national attribution by the C4 on 2026-07-13, issued the same day as a French Foreign Ministry attribution statement and an EU High Representative statement [S7][S8]. Microsoft relies on CISA's attribution rather than stating its own confidence level [S1][S4]. ESET assesses with high confidence that Gamaredon collaborates with Turla [S5].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and joint analysis with Lumen Black Lotus Labs [S2][S3]; FBI technical operation against the Snake peer-to-peer network [S6]; French C4 and Foreign Ministry attribution statements [S7][S8]; ESET telemetry from Ukrainian machines [S5]; Kaspersky reporting on WhiteBear [S9].

actors.objectives: Strategic political and military intelligence collection through long-term, covert access [S2]. Priorities include foreign ministries, embassies and diplomats, including foreign embassies in Moscow [S1][S2]; Ukrainian military devices, including front-line systems [S3]; and government, diplomatic and defense targets in Europe and Central Asia [S4]. US court documents describe the group stealing sensitive documents from hundreds of systems in at least 50 countries [S6].

sectors: Foreign affairs ministries and embassies / diplomatic entities [S1][S2][S9]
Defense and military organizations, including Ukrainian military devices [S2][S3]
Intelligence services (Afghan General Directorate of Intelligence) [S2]
regions: At least 50 countries, including the United States, per US court documents (as reported) [S6]
targeting.notes: Tasking is selective. ESET saw Turla on only seven machines in Ukraine over about 18 months, against much wider Gamaredon compromise [S5]. Microsoft saw a custom survey tool deployed selectively to devices connecting from Starlink IP addresses, which Microsoft describes as a common signature of Ukrainian front-line military devices [S3]. In India, Secret Blizzard mostly harvested data that Storm-0156 had already staged rather than deploying malware directly [S2].

capabilities.summary: Kazuar is a modular peer-to-peer botnet built from Kernel, Bridge and Worker modules. A single elected Kernel leader limits outbound traffic, internal traffic uses Window Messaging, Mailslot and named pipes, and external C2 uses HTTP, WebSockets or Exchange Web Services [S4]. Delivery uses droppers such as Pelmeni, whose payload is often encrypted against the target's hostname [S4]. The group hijacks other actors' access: Storm-0156 C2 servers since November 2022 (using TwoDash, Statuezy, MiniPocket and a TinyTurla fork) [S2], Amadey bots and a Storm-1837 backdoor in Ukraine in 2024 to install Tavdig and KazuarV2 [S3], and Gamaredon tools that launched or installed Kazuar in 2025 [S5]. ApolloShadow malware, delivered through ISP-level AiTM and a captive-portal redirect, installs a trusted root certificate disguised as a Kaspersky installer, enabling TLS stripping; it also creates a local admin account named UpdatusUser [S1]. Microsoft assesses that this AiTM position is likely enabled by lawful-intercept systems, possibly SORM [S1]. The Snake implant ran a covert peer-to-peer network across compromised computers until the FBI disabled it in 2023 [S6]. Earlier operations used hijacked satellite connections and compromised websites for C2 [S9].

diamond.capability: Kazuar P2P botnet, Tavdig, TwoDash, Statuezy, MiniPocket, TinyTurla variants, ApolloShadow and the Snake implant; hijacking other actors' footholds; ISP-level AiTM [S1][S2][S3][S4][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Commandeered C2 and footholds belonging to Storm-0156, Amadey (Storm-1919), Storm-1837 and Gamaredon [S2][S3][S5]; Kazuar P2P relays with HTTP, WebSocket and EWS C2 [S4]; Snake's covert P2P network [S6]; ISP-level interception position in Russia [S1]; compromised websites and hijacked satellite links in earlier activity [S9].

gaps: Primary US documents (the DOJ MEDUSA announcement and the joint Snake advisory) were not opened; their details come from press coverage [S6]. The advisory identifier AA23-129A and the Ryazan facility detail were not verified.

The French C4 statement and the CERT-FR report (CERTFR-2026-CTI-004/005) could not be fetched; details come from search summaries of the C4 and French Foreign Ministry statements [S7][S8]. Press mentions of a specific FSB unit number (Unit 61240), a twelve-country scope and Polish water and energy sabotage are unverified. The sabotage claims may belong to a different FSB Center 16 activity set or EU statement, so do not attach them to Turla without the primary text.
The ESET Gamaredon x Turla report was not opened; findings come from search summaries of the ESET blog and press release [S5].
How Secret Blizzard gained control of the Storm-1837 backdoor and Amadey bots was still under investigation at the time Microsoft published [S3].
Microsoft's assessment that SORM or lawful-intercept systems enable the ISP-level AiTM is a likelihood judgement, not a confirmed mechanism [S1].
A CrowdStrike report dated July 2026 appeared in aggregator results but was not reviewed.
The Kaspersky WhiteBear URL and content come from the imported actor record; the publication month (2017-08) was not re-verified [S9].
Most aliases in the imported record (e.g., ATK13, ITG12, SIG23, UAC-0003/0024/0144, UNC4210) were not confirmed by the sources gathered here.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (environment): key terrain includes diplomatic and government networks, defense research enclaves, Exchange/EWS services, TLS trust stores, and host-nation ISP links serving deployed or diplomatic personnel, especially inside Russia [S1][S4][S8]. STEP 2 (effects): host-nation telecommunications cannot be trusted; ISP-level AiTM plus a rogue root certificate exposes credentials and tokens in transit [S1]. Footholds left by lower-tier actors (criminal botnets, other APTs) can become entry points for this actor [S2][S3][S5]. STEP 3 (threat model): access is gained by piggybacking on an existing foothold or by AiTM/captive-portal lure, followed by a loader (Tavdig, Pelmeni) and then the Kazuar P2P botnet, with an elected leader keeping C2 traffic low, and selective collection [S1][S3][S4]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is quiet, long-term collection from a small number of high-value diplomatic, government and defense hosts, plus selective targeting of front-line military devices in Ukraine [S2][S3][S5]. MDCOA is covert interception of coalition planning traffic through compromised ISP or host-nation infrastructure and in-memory implants on mission-relevant networks, giving persistent awareness of intentions during a crisis [S1][S4]. Candidate indicators: unexpected root certificates (including fake Kaspersky-branded installers), a local account named UpdatusUser, captive-portal redirects to unfamiliar domains, internal Mailslot or named-pipe chatter between hosts paired with a single host making outbound HTTP/WebSocket/EWS connections, and Tavdig/Kazuar artifacts on hosts already infected with commodity malware [S1][S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat any detection of commodity malware (e.g., Amadey) or another APT's implant on mission or partner networks as a possible Secret Blizzard staging point, and escalate hunting accordingly [S2][S3][S5]. (2) Authorities: the 2023 MEDUSA operation shows US law-enforcement authorities can disrupt this actor's infrastructure [S6]. Coordinate DoD defensive actions with FBI/DOJ and with allied attributions such as France's 2026 statement [S7]. (3) Mission assurance: personnel and devices operating on host-nation networks in Russia or contested regions should tunnel all traffic to trusted networks, as Microsoft recommends, and certificate-store monitoring should be part of baseline hardening [S1]. Starlink-connected tactical devices are a demonstrated reconnaissance filter for this actor [S3]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with State Department and embassy IT, allied CERTs (e.g., CERT-FR), Ukrainian partners and DIB partners, because victims span diplomatic, defense-industrial and coalition military domains [S1][S3][S7][S8].

sources.title: Introducing WhiteBear

provenance.importedSummary: As a part of our Kaspersky APT Intelligence Reporting subscription, customers received an update in mid-February 2017 on some interesting APT activity that we called WhiteBear. Much of the contents of that report are reproduced here. WhiteBear is a parallel project or second stage of the Skipper Turla cluster of activity documented in another private intelligence report “Skipper Turla – the White Atlas framework” from mid-2016. Like previous Turla activity, WhiteBear leverages compromised websites and hijacked satellite connections for command and control (C2) infrastructure. As a matter of fact, WhiteBear infrastructure has overlap with other Turla campaigns, like those deploying Kopiluwak, as documented in “KopiLuwak – A New JavaScript Payload from Turla” in December 2016. WhiteBear infected systems maintained a dropper (which was typically signed) as well as a complex malicious platform which was always preceded by WhiteAtlas module deployment attempts. However, despite the similarities to previous Turla campaigns, we believe that WhiteBear is a distinct project with a separate focus. We note that this observation of delineated target focus, tooling, and project context is an interesting one that also can be repeated across broadly labeled Turla and Sofacy activity. From February to September 2016, WhiteBear activity was narrowly focused on embassies and consular operations around the world. All of these early WhiteBear targets were related to embassies and diplomatic/foreign affair organizations. Continued WhiteBear activity later shifted to include defense-related organizations into June 2017. When compared to WhiteAtlas infections, WhiteBear deployments are relatively rare and represent a departure from the broader Skipper Turla target set. Additionally, a comparison of the WhiteAtlas framework to WhiteBear components indicates that the malware is the product of separate development efforts. WhiteBear infections appear to be preceded by a condensed spearphishing dropper, lack Firefox extension installer payloads, and contain several new components signed with a new code signing digital certificate, unlike WhiteAtlas incidents and modules.

identification.summary: SHADOW-EARTH-053 is a China-aligned threat group exploiting unpatched Microsoft Exchange Server vulnerabilities, specifically CVE-2021-26855, to conduct cyberespionage against government and defense-linked targets across Asia and Europe. The group primarily deploys ShadowPad malware, utilizing techniques such as credential dumping, tunneling tools, and lateral movement via WMIC. They have also been observed installing web shells for persistence and leveraging a custom ExchangeExport tool to extract high-value mailbox contents. Additionally, low-confidence associations with Noodle RAT and CVE-2025-55182 have been noted in their operations.

Storm-0062 is a Microsoft-tracked nation-state cluster (also tracked as DarkShadow and Oro0lxy by others). In October 2023 Microsoft said Storm-0062 had been exploiting the Atlassian Confluence Data Center and Server vulnerability CVE-2023-22515 in the wild since 14 September 2023 [S2][S3]. Press coverage of Microsoft's notice described the actor as China-linked [S3][S4]. The name 'Shadow Typhoon' could not be verified against a retrieved source and is treated as unconfirmed (see gaps).
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft-observed exploitation of CVE-2023-22515 began 2023-09-14 [S2][S3]. Earlier activity under this name is not established in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: The Oro0lxy alias is described by The Record as previously linked to a 2020 DOJ indictment involving China's Ministry of State Security [S4]; that link was not verified against the indictment text (see gaps).

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (reported). SecurityWeek, citing its own sources, said the Storm-0062 team has been observed conducting cyberespionage for China's Ministry of State Security [S2]. Microsoft's October 2023 notice called the actor a nation-state actor but did not name China, according to SecurityWeek and The Record [S2][S4].
attribution.confidence: Moderate-to-low for the specific state agency. Microsoft's statement says nation-state [S2]; the MSS link rests on unnamed sources in press reporting [S2]. Dark Reading and Petri describe Microsoft as attributing to a Chinese APT, which is the outlets' characterization [S3][S4].

targeting.notes: Victims of the Storm-0062 Confluence exploitation were not named in the sources gathered. Atlassian said multiple customers reported attacks in which external attackers created unauthorized Confluence administrator accounts [S2]. The affected product was the on-premises Confluence Data Center and Server editions [S2][S5].

capabilities.summary: Zero-day exploitation of CVE-2023-22515, a CVSS 10 (per Atlassian/SecurityWeek; some outlets cite 9.8) broken-access-control flaw in Confluence Data Center and Server 8.0.0 through 8.5.1 that is reachable without authentication [S2][S5]. Microsoft said any device with network access to a vulnerable application could exploit it to create an administrator account [S3]. Exploitation as a zero-day ran about three weeks before Atlassian's 2023-10-04 disclosure [S2][S3]. Public proof-of-concept exploits appeared soon after [S3]. Microsoft published four IP addresses seen sending exploit traffic: 192.69.90[.]31, 104.128.89[.]92, 23.105.208[.]154 and 199.193.127[.]231 [S3]. Post-exploitation tooling used by the actor is not described in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-exposed on-premises Confluence servers are key terrain because an unauthenticated flaw let attackers create administrators [S5]. STEP 2: The actor held a roughly three-week zero-day window before disclosure, and public PoCs followed [S2][S3]. STEP 3: Template is unauthenticated exploitation leading to administrator account creation [S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is further quiet zero-day or n-day use against collaboration servers. MDCOA is mass exploitation after PoC release against unpatched DoD-adjacent contractors. Candidate indicators: unexpected administrator accounts, and traffic from the four Microsoft-listed IPs [S3][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Track patch status and exposure of on-premises Confluence for situational awareness; CVE is on the KEV catalog [S5]. (2) Patching does not remove an existing intruder, so tasking should include hunting [S5]. (3) Attribution is vendor-level only and state agency is unconfirmed, so avoid government-attribution language [S2]. (4) Coordinate exposure checks with DIB contractors and share Microsoft-listed IPs through established channels [S3].

provenance.importedSummary: The cyberattack campaign that Microsoft uncovered was launched by a China-linked hacking group called Storm-0062. According to the company, the group is launching cyberattacks by exploiting a vulnerability in the Data Center and Server editions of Confluence. Those are versions of the application that companies run on-premises.

identification.summary: ShaggyPanther is a threat actor that primarily targets government entities in Taiwan and Malaysia. They have been active since 2008 and utilize hidden encrypted payloads in registry keys. Their activities have been detected in various locations, including Indonesia and Syria.

Shahid Hemmat is an IRGC-CEC affiliated hacking group linked to cyberattacks targeting U.S. critical infrastructure, including the defense industry and international transportation sectors. The group has been implicated in the hack of a booster station at the Municipal Water Authority in Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, which disrupted drinking water supply. Key figures within Shahid Hemmat include Manouchehr Akbari, Amir Hossein Hoseini, Mohammad Hossein Moradi, and Mohammad Reza Rafatnejad. The U.S. government is offering a $10 million reward for information on these individuals.
Shamoon Group is an Iran-linked threat actor associated with destructive Shamoon wiper operations targeting organizations in the Middle East, especially in the energy sector.

This group's activity was first observed in November 2013. It leverages a banking Trojan more commonly known as Shylock which aims to compromise online banking credentials and credentials related to Bitcoin wallets.

SharpPanda, an APT group originating from China, has seen a rise in its cyber-attack operations starting from at least 2018. The APT group utilizes spear-phishing techniques to obtain initial access, employing a combination of outdated Microsoft Office document vulnerabilities, novel evasion techniques, and highly potent backdoor malware.

Silent Librarian is the name used by Proofpoint (TA407) and others, and COBALT DICKENS by Secureworks, for an Iran-linked group that runs credential-phishing campaigns against universities using fake library and student-portal login pages [S3][S5][S6]. Press reporting on Proofpoint's profile ties the names Silent Librarian, Cobalt Dickens, TA407 and Mabna Institute together [S9]. The US indictment of nine people said to work for the Mabna Institute was unsealed in March 2018 [S1][S2]. Secureworks counted at least 380 universities in over 30 countries targeted as of September 2019 [S3].
identification.firstObserved: The Mabna Institute indictment, as reported, covers intrusions against universities beginning in 2013 [S8]. Records on the 2018 indictment describe the campaign as already large by March 2018 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Names are not perfectly interchangeable. The record's alias list pairs the Mabna Institute (the indicted company) with the Silent Librarian phishing activity; vendors such as Secureworks assess these as the same actor but that is a vendor judgment [S3]. RiskIQ observed a separate 2020 set of university phishing campaigns with similar tradecraft (domain shadowing) and named it Shadow Academy without attributing it to Mabna [S6]. Victim counts differ by source (176 vs 178 foreign universities; 320+ vs 380) [S1][S2][S3][S8].

attribution.sponsor: Iran. The 2018 US Treasury action stated the Mabna Institute acted for the benefit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) [S2]; the indictment is reported to say the firm also served other Iranian government clients [S1].
attribution.confidence: Treasury and DOJ made the Mabna-IRGC statements in 2018 (as reported) [S1][S2]. Secureworks assessed COBALT DICKENS as an actor bound to the Iranian government [S3]. Whether every later university phishing wave is Mabna activity is a vendor linkage, not a government finding; RiskIQ declined to link its 2020 Shadow Academy cluster to Mabna [S6].
attribution.basis: US DOJ indictment and OFAC designation of Mabna Institute and individuals, March 2018 (via press and Iran Watch coverage) [S1][S2]; superseding indictment of 17 defendants unsealed August 2026 (via press coverage) [S7][S8]; vendor reporting from Secureworks, Malwarebytes and Proofpoint (via press) [S3][S5][S9].

actors.objectives: Per the indictment as reported, the group stole academic data and intellectual property (more than 31 TB) from universities, companies and agencies, and sold the stolen articles through Iranian sites Megapaper.ir and Gigapaper.ir [S1][S8]. Treasury stated the Mabna Institute acted for the IRGC's benefit [S2].

sectors: Private-sector companies (at least 42 US and 11 foreign per the 2026 indictment)
regions: Foreign universities: 176 in 21 countries per Treasury; 178 per 2026 indictment [S2][S8]
Australia, United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Hong Kong and Switzerland in the July-August 2019 wave [S4]
targeting.notes: The 2018 indictment reportedly cites about 100,000 professor accounts targeted and 7,998 compromised [S1]. Secureworks counted at least 380 universities in over 30 countries by September 2019, many targeted repeatedly [S3]. Alleged victims also included the Labor Department, the UN and FERC [S1]. Proofpoint reports campaigns cluster around the back-to-school period, usually June to October [S9].

capabilities.summary: Low-volume, well-crafted spearphishing built on spoofed university branding and library or student-portal login pages [S9]. In 2019 Secureworks saw over 20 new Freenom domains and valid Let's Encrypt certificates on spoofed login pages, with lures sent from compromised university accounts [S3][S4]. In fall 2020 Malwarebytes saw mimic domains mainly on .ME, .TK and .CF, with lures updated for virtual classes [S5]. The 2018 indictment says compromised accounts were used to harvest research and email [S1]. No custom malware is described in the cited sources [S1][S3].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: higher-education networks and research partners (including DoD-funded labs) are the observed target set [S2][S8]. Step 3: the adversary uses low-volume credential phishing with lookalike domains and compromised-account lures, timed to the academic calendar [S4][S9]. Step 4 MLCOA: renewed June-October wave against university library and student portals, harvesting credentials for research and email access [S1][S9]. MDCOA: stolen faculty or partner credentials used to pivot into defense-related research or partner mail [S1]. Candidate indicators: newly registered lookalike university domains on free TLDs, new Let's Encrypt certificates for them, and lures sent from other universities' accounts [S3][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: share university-themed phishing indicators with affiliated academic and DIB research partners via existing ISAC/DC3 channels [S2][S8]. Authorities: monitoring of non-DoD university networks rests with those owners and with law enforcement; confirm authorities before any action. Mission assurance: enforce MFA on any DoD-affiliated academic accounts and monitor for email-forwarding abuse [S1]. Coordination: align with FBI and partner universities, noting the 2026 indictment may prompt retaliation or shifts in tradecraft (unverified).

provenance.importedSummary: Last Friday, Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein announced the indictment of nine Iranians who worked for an organization named the Mabna Institute. According to prosecutors, the defendants stole more than 31 terabytes of data from universities, companies, and government agencies around the world. The cost to the universities alone reportedly amounted to approximately $3.4 billion. The information stolen from these universities was used by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) or sold for profit inside Iran. PhishLabs has been tracking this same threat group since late-2017, designating them Silent Librarian. Since discovery, we have been working with the FBI, ISAC partners, and other international law enforcement agencies to help understand and mitigate these attacks.

identification.summary: Silk Typhoon (formerly HAFNIUM) is a Chinese espionage group. Microsoft describes it as well-resourced and technically efficient, able to quickly operationalize exploits for zero-day vulnerabilities in edge devices, and holding one of the largest targeting footprints among Chinese threat actors [S1]. It is best known for exploiting four on-premises Exchange Server zero-days in early 2021 [S1][S2]. Since late 2024 Microsoft has observed it shift toward IT supply-chain compromise: it steals API keys and credentials from privileged access management (PAM), remote monitoring and management, cloud application and cloud data management providers, then uses them to reach those providers' downstream customers [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft says it has tracked the actor since 2020 and observed Exchange zero-day exploitation beginning in January 2021 [S1]. The US indictment of two alleged HAFNIUM operators covers intrusions from February 2020 to June 2021, as reported by the press [S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Silk Typhoon (formerly HAFNIUM) [S1]. CrowdStrike tracks MURKY PANDA, active since at least 2023, and says that cluster's activity aligns with what industry tracks as Silk Typhoon. This is an overlap statement, not an identity [S5][S6]. MITRE tracks the group as HAFNIUM (G0125) [S10]. Some press coverage of the March 2025 APT27 / i-Soon indictments labels Yin Kecheng and Zhou Shuai 'Silk Typhoon', while other coverage of the same indictments uses APT27 and lists aliases such as Emissary Panda and Lucky Mouse. Those aliases sit under Linen Typhoon in this encyclopedia; see gaps [S9].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China, Ministry of State Security (MSS). A US indictment unsealed in July 2025 alleges that Xu Zewei and Zhang Yu acted at the direction of the MSS Shanghai State Security Bureau. Xu allegedly worked through Shanghai Powerock Network Co. Ltd., which prosecutors called an 'enabling' company (as reported by the press) [S3][S4].
attribution.confidence: In 2021 Microsoft attributed the Exchange campaign to HAFNIUM with high confidence, as a group assessed to be state-sponsored and operating out of China [S2]. In 2025 Microsoft called Silk Typhoon a Chinese state actor but stated no confidence level [S1]. The US government has charged alleged HAFNIUM operators criminally, which is an indictment, not a conviction [S3][S4]. Linking the 2024 Treasury breach to Silk Typhoon rests on Bloomberg reporting citing people familiar with the incident [S7].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and incident analysis [S1][S2]; a DOJ indictment and the extradition of Xu Zewei from Italy, known here through press coverage [S3][S4]; and CrowdStrike reporting on the overlapping MURKY PANDA cluster [S5][S6].

actors.objectives: Espionage. Microsoft says the data it seeks overlaps with China-based interests, US government policy and administration, and legal process and documents tied to law enforcement investigations [S1]. In 2020 the group allegedly sought COVID-19 vaccine, treatment and testing research from US universities, including one in Texas (as reported from the indictment) [S3][S4]. In the 2024 Treasury intrusion the group reportedly accessed unclassified information on potential sanctions actions [S7].

sectors: IT services and infrastructure, including MSPs and RMM providers [S1]
PAM, identity management, cloud application and cloud data management providers [S1][S5]
Government, including US federal (Treasury) and state and local [S1][S7]
Healthcare and infectious-disease or COVID-19 researchers [S1][S2][S3]
regions: Worldwide; Microsoft says targets are in the US and worldwide [S1]
targeting.notes: Microsoft says downstream victims of the late-2024 supply-chain activity were mostly state and local government and the IT sector [S1]. The FBI said the 2021 Exchange campaign victimized more than 12,700 US organizations (as reported in press coverage of the DOJ case) [S4].

capabilities.summary: Edge-device and server exploitation: Exchange CVE-2021-26855, -26857, -26858 and -27065 (2021); Citrix NetScaler CVE-2023-3519 and zero-days (early 2024); Palo Alto GlobalProtect CVE-2024-3400 (March 2024); and an Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day, CVE-2025-0282 (January 2025) [S1][S2]. CrowdStrike says MURKY PANDA also used zero-days against SaaS providers, and coverage of its report includes a Commvault product zero-day [S5][S6]. Credential access includes password spraying and corporate passwords leaked on public repositories such as GitHub [S1]. Post-exploitation includes web shells, Active Directory dumping, theft of key-vault secrets, and LSASS dumping with Procdump [S1][S2]. In 2021 the group used Covenant C2, Nishang and PowerCat, staged data with 7-Zip and exfiltrated to MEGA [S2]. The group moves from on-premises to cloud through AADConnect/Entra Connect servers. It abuses service principals and OAuth apps (including by adding credentials to already-consented apps) to pull mail, OneDrive and SharePoint data through Microsoft Graph and EWS, and it creates Entra ID apps disguised as legitimate services [S1]. It has abused delegated administrative privileges held by a Microsoft cloud solution provider [S5][S6]. For anti-forensics it clears logs and modifies timestamps [S1][S5]. Its toolset includes the Neo-reGeorg web shell and a Golang Linux RAT that CrowdStrike calls CloudedHope [S5][S6].

campaigns.name: COVID-19 research intrusions
campaigns.summary: The alleged operators Xu Zewei and Zhang Yu targeted US universities and immunology and virology researchers, including a Texas university, to obtain COVID-19 research, reportedly under MSS Shanghai State Security Bureau direction (as reported from the indictment).

campaigns.name: Exchange Server zero-day campaign (ProxyLogon chain)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft attributes exploitation of four on-premises Exchange zero-days, followed by web shells, LSASS dumping and mailbox exfiltration, to HAFNIUM. The FBI later said more than 12,700 US entities were victimized.

campaigns.name: Citrix NetScaler and GlobalProtect exploitation
campaigns.summary: Microsoft observed exploitation of NetScaler zero-days and of CVE-2023-3519, and in March 2024 zero-day exploitation of Palo Alto GlobalProtect CVE-2024-3400.

campaigns.name: US Treasury breach via BeyondTrust API key
campaigns.summary: A stolen BeyondTrust Remote Support SaaS API key gave access to Treasury workstations, including OFAC. Bloomberg attributed the breach to Silk Typhoon, citing people familiar with the incident. In January 2025 Treasury sanctioned Yin Kecheng over the Departmental Offices compromise; Treasury did not name Silk Typhoon in the sources gathered.

campaigns.name: IT supply-chain compromise
campaigns.summary: Microsoft says the group used API keys and credentials stolen from PAM, cloud application and data-management providers to access downstream tenants, mostly state and local government and IT-sector victims.

campaigns.name: Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day (CVE-2025-0282)

diamond.adversary: MSS-directed operators, including contractors. Xu Zewei of Shanghai Powerock Network Co. and Zhang Yu were allegedly tasked by the Shanghai State Security Bureau [S3][S4]. Microsoft calls the group a Chinese state actor [S1].
diamond.capability: Rapid zero-day and n-day exploitation of edge devices and servers (Exchange, NetScaler, GlobalProtect, Ivanti), web shells, credential and secret theft, and Entra ID / OAuth / service-principal abuse for cloud data theft [S1][S2]. The overlapping MURKY PANDA cluster adds Neo-reGeorg and CloudedHope [S5][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: No dedicated infrastructure. The group relies on covert networks of compromised Cyberoam appliances, Zyxel routers and QNAP devices, plus proxies, VPNs and short-lease VPS [S1]. In 2021 it operated mainly from leased US VPS and exfiltrated to MEGA [S2].
diamond.victim: US government at federal, state and local levels; IT service providers and SaaS vendors as stepping stones; and defense, healthcare and research, legal, higher education, think tanks, NGOs and energy [S1][S2][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence on US government policy and administration, legal and law-enforcement matters, sanctions deliberations and pandemic research, reflecting PRC state interests [S1][S3][S7].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing appliances and on-premises servers, hybrid identity (Entra Connect), multi-tenant and OAuth apps, and trust relationships between providers and customers (API keys, delegated admin privileges) [S1][S5].

gaps: No primary DOJ, Treasury or FBI documents could be opened (blocked); indictment and sanctions details come from press coverage [S3][S4][S7][S8].
The CrowdStrike MURKY PANDA blog post could not be fetched; details come from secondary coverage. CrowdStrike frames MURKY PANDA as aligning with Silk Typhoon, not as identical to it [S5][S6].
The Silk Typhoon attribution of the Treasury breach rests on Bloomberg's anonymous sourcing; the government sources gathered name Yin Kecheng, not Silk Typhoon [S7][S8].

Naming conflict: some press labels the March 2025 APT27 indictees (Yin Kecheng, Zhou Shuai) 'Silk Typhoon', while those aliases (APT27, Emissary Panda, Lucky Mouse) map to Linen Typhoon in this encyclopedia. The primary indictment text was not reviewed [S9].

Some press links Silk Typhoon or HAFNIUM to Mandiant's UNC5221, the cluster Google associated with Ivanti exploitation. This was not confirmed in a vendor primary source, so UNC5221 is not added as an alias.
Imported aliases ATK233, Operation Exchange Marauder, Red Dev 13 and 'timmy' were not verified in sources gathered.
The full extent of downstream victims of the 2024-2025 supply-chain activity and of the Commvault-related intrusions is not public in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes internet-facing VPN and edge appliances (Ivanti, NetScaler, GlobalProtect), hybrid identity servers (Entra Connect), and third-party IT, PAM, RMM and SaaS providers that hold API keys or delegated admin rights into DoD and DIB tenants [S1][S5]. STEP 2: The group can turn new edge-device CVEs into exploits within days. Its use of covert networks of compromised SOHO devices and short-lease VPS undermines IP-reputation blocking [S1]. STEP 3: The template is edge-device or provider compromise, then web shell, credential and key-vault theft, then a pivot to Entra ID through service principals or OAuth apps, then mail and SharePoint/OneDrive exfiltration via Graph or EWS, with log clearing [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent collection of policy, legal and sanctions-related email and documents from government and contractor tenants through compromised providers [S1][S7]. MDCOA is mass zero-day exploitation of a widely deployed edge product across DoD-adjacent networks during a crisis, as in the Exchange 2021 campaign with more than 12,700 US victims, to harvest planning data at scale [S2][S4]. Candidate indicators: new or renamed Entra ID apps with Office 365-themed names; new credentials added to consented apps; Graph or EWS mail access by service principals; unexpected web shells on edge devices or servers; admin-account resets through provider APIs; and logons from SOHO-device IP space [S1][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: fuse edge-appliance patch status and third-party provider access (API keys, delegated admin privileges) into the common operating picture, because the actor enters through these trust paths [S1][S5]. (2) Authorities: the activity crosses DoD, DIB, commercial SaaS and federal civilian networks (Treasury), so response requires coordinating DC3, CISA and FBI lanes rather than unilateral DoD action [S1][S7]. (3) Mission assurance: inventory and minimize standing provider privileges and multi-tenant app consents, and plan for credential and key rotation at the provider level after a compromise [S1]. (4) Coordination: law-enforcement actions (the Xu Zewei arrest and extradition) have not been assessed as stopping operations, so keep defensive posture independent of indictment news [S3][S4].

HAFNIUM, G0125

provenance.importedSummary: HAFNIUM primarily targets entities in the United States across a number of industry sectors, including infectious disease researchers, law firms, higher education institutions, defense contractors, policy think tanks, and NGOs. Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center (MSTIC) attributes this campaign with high confidence to HAFNIUM, a group assessed to be state-sponsored and operating out of China, based on observed victimology, tactics and procedures. HAFNIUM has previously compromised victims by exploiting vulnerabilities in internet-facing servers, and has used legitimate open-source frameworks, like Covenant, for command and control. Once they’ve gained access to a victim network, HAFNIUM typically exfiltrates data to file sharing sites like MEGA.In campaigns unrelated to these vulnerabilities, Microsoft has observed HAFNIUM interacting with victim Office 365 tenants. While they are often unsuccessful in compromising customer accounts, this reconnaissance activity helps the adversary identify more details about their targets’ environments. HAFNIUM operates primarily from leased virtual private servers (VPS) in the United States.

identification.summary: SilkSpecter is a Chinese financially motivated threat actor that orchestrates phishing campaigns targeting e-commerce shoppers, particularly during peak shopping seasons. They exploit legitimate payment processors like Stripe to exfiltrate Cardholder Data and Personally Identifiable Information through convincing fake e-commerce sites created using the oemapps SaaS platform. Their phishing infrastructure relies on Chinese-hosted CDN servers and utilizes deceptive elements such as the "trusttollsvg" icon and a "/homeapi/collect" endpoint to track victim interactions. Analysts have linked SilkSpecter to over 89 IP addresses and more than 4,000 domain names associated with phishing activities, predominantly using .top, .shop, .store, and .vip TLDs.

Sima is a group of suspected Iranian origin targeting Iranians in diaspora. In February 2016, Iran-focused individuals received messages purporting to be from Human RightsWatch's (HRW) Emergencies Director, requesting that they read an article about Iran pressing Afghanr efugees to fight in Syria. While referencing a real report published by HRW, the links provided for the Director’s biography and article directed the recipient to malware hosted elsewhere. These spear-phishing attempts represent an evolution of Iranian actors based on their social engineering tactics and narrow targeting. Although the messages still had minor grammatical and stylistic errors that would be obvious to a native speaker, the actors demonstrated stronger English-language proficiency than past intrusion sets and a deeper investment in background research prior to the attempt. The actors appropriated a real identity that would be expected to professionally interact with the subject, then offered validation through links to their biography and social media, the former of which itself was malware as well. The bait documents contained a real article relevant to their interests and topic referenced, and the message attempted to address to how it aligned with their professional research or field of employment. The referenced documents sent were malware binaries posing as legitimate files using the common right-to-left filenames tactic in order to conceal the actual file extension. All of these techniques, while common pretexting mechanisms, are a refinement compared to a tendency amongst other groups to simply continually send different forms of generic malware or phishing, in the hopes that one would eventually be successful.

SLIME88 is a China-nexus APT that has exploited the critical vulnerability CVE-2026-34197 in Apache ActiveMQ to deploy SoxAgent RAT, compromising Linux devices and establishing an ORB network tracked as GOBLIN14. The group has targeted IT and manufacturing entities in the US, South Korea, India, and France. Additionally, SLIME88 has aimed at Taiwan’s energy sector using phishing emails and fake certificate installers to deploy backdoor programs like AdaptixC2 and CobaltStrike. They often utilize Cloudflare to obscure their C2 IP addresses, evading detection.

The Smishing Triad is a Chinese-speaking threat group known for targeting postal services and their customers globally through smishing campaigns. They leverage compromised Apple iMessage accounts to send fraudulent messages warning of undeliverable packages, aiming to collect personally identifying information and payment credentials. The group offers smishing kits for sale on platforms like Telegram, enabling other cybercriminals to launch independent attacks. "Smishing Triad" has expanded its operations to target UAE citizens, using geo-filtering to focus on victims in the Emirates.

Microsoft describes Smoke Sandstorm as an Iranian nation-state actor, formerly tracked as BOHRIUM and DEV-0056. In September 2021 it compromised email accounts at a Bahrain-based IT integration company whose Bahrain Government clients were likely the ultimate target [S1]. Microsoft maps Mandiant's UNC1549 and CrowdStrike's IMPERIAL KITTEN to Smoke Sandstorm [S8]. Google Threat Intelligence (Mandiant) describes UNC1549 as an Iran-nexus espionage group targeting aerospace, aviation and defense organizations and their third-party suppliers [S3][S4]. Check Point tracks the overlapping cluster as Nimbus Manticore and reported a new backdoor, MiniFast, in 2026 [S7].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: earliest dated activity September 2021 [S1]. Mandiant: UNC1549 active since at least June 2022 [S3]. CrowdStrike: IMPERIAL KITTEN active since at least 2017 (reported by The Hacker News) [S6].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Smoke Sandstorm (formerly BOHRIUM, DEV-0056) [S1]. Microsoft's mapping lists IMPERIAL KITTEN and UNC1549 under Smoke Sandstorm [S8]. MITRE tracks NIMBUS MANTICORE as G1059 and lists UNC1549 and TA455 as associated names [S9]. The Hacker News lists GalaxyGato, Nimbus Manticore and Subtle Snail as other names for UNC1549 [S5]. Mandiant's 2024 report noted overlaps with both Tortoiseshell and Smoke Sandstorm/BOHRIUM [S3]. Cluster scopes differ by vendor; see gaps.

attribution.sponsor: Iran. Microsoft lists Iran as the country of origin [S1]. CrowdStrike assesses that IMPERIAL KITTEN likely fulfills Iranian strategic intelligence requirements associated with IRGC operations (as reported by The Hacker News) [S6]. Check Point and press coverage describe Nimbus Manticore as IRGC-affiliated [S7].
attribution.confidence: Mandiant assessed the Iran nexus of UNC1549 with moderate confidence, citing overlaps with Tortoiseshell, which has been linked to the IRGC [S3]. The 2025 GTIG report calls UNC1549 a suspected Iran-nexus, Iranian-backed group and does not name the IRGC [S4]. The IRGC link rests on vendor assessments; no government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and its 2022 civil legal action against BOHRIUM infrastructure [S1][S2]; Mandiant/GTIG incident response [S3][S4]; CrowdStrike and Check Point reporting, relayed by press coverage [S6][S7].

actors.objectives: Espionage. GTIG says UNC1549 primarily seeks network and IT documentation, intellectual property and email, and uses compromised organizations as pivots into their industry partners [S4]. Microsoft assesses that its Middle East targeting serves sectors of interest to the Iranian regime, including government, defense and transportation [S1].

sectors: Defense contractors and their third-party suppliers [S4]
Government (Bahrain Government via an IT integrator) [S1]
regions: Middle East: Bahrain [S1]; Israel and UAE [S3]
Europe and the United States (2026 Check Point reporting) [S7]
targeting.notes: Microsoft's BOHRIUM reporting stresses supply-chain-style access through IT integrators [S1]. GTIG emphasizes abuse of trusted third parties to reach defense primes [S4]. CrowdStrike's IMPERIAL KITTEN reporting focuses on Israeli transportation, logistics and technology firms [S6].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering with fake recruiter personas and job lures, used by BOHRIUM in 2022 and by UNC1549 through 2025 [S2][S3][S4]. Initial access through trusted third-party relationships and VDI breakouts from Citrix, VMware and Azure Virtual Desktop environments provided to partners [S4]. Custom backdoors and tunnelers: MINIBIKE and MINIBUS [S3]; TWOSTROKE, DEEPROOT, POLLBLEND, GHOSTLINE and LIGHTRAIL [S4]; MiniFast (2026) [S7]. Credential theft through DCSync (DCSYNCER.SLICK), Kerberoasting, AD CS abuse, browser-credential theft (CRASHPAD) and a fake Outlook prompt (TRUSTTRAP) [S4]. Heavy use of Microsoft Azure infrastructure for C2, including more than 125 Azure subdomains in 2024, and lookalike aerospace career domains [S3][S4]. Defense evasion through DLL search-order hijacking of legitimate vendor binaries, unique per-payload hashes, legitimately signed backdoors, reverse SSH tunnels and dormant backdoors that reactivate after eradication [S4]. CrowdStrike reports watering holes, VPN credential theft, one-day exploitation and IMAPLoader malware under IMPERIAL KITTEN [S6]. Check Point assesses that MiniFast code appears AI-assisted [S7].
