diamond.adversary: Iranian state-linked operators that Microsoft tracks as Smoke Sandstorm [S1]. Vendors link the overlapping clusters to the IRGC at varying confidence [S3][S6][S7].
diamond.capability: Recruiter and job lures; MINIBIKE/MINIBUS, TWOSTROKE, DEEPROOT, LIGHTRAIL and MiniFast; DCSync, Kerberoasting, AD CS abuse and RDP hijacking [S3][S4][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: Azure-hosted C2 (azurewebsites.net, cloudapp.azure.com), lookalike career domains, reverse SSH tunnel endpoints, ZeroTier and ngrok [S3][S4]. In 2022 Microsoft seized 41 BOHRIUM domains [S2].
diamond.victim: Aerospace, aviation and defense firms and their suppliers; government clients reached through IT integrators; transportation and technology firms in the Middle East, Europe, the US and India [S1][S2][S3][S4][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on defense and aerospace programs and on regional governments, aligned with Iranian regime interests [S1][S4]. Lures exploited the Israel-Hamas conflict [S3].
diamond.technology: Trust relationships between primes and suppliers, partner-facing VDI (Citrix, VMware, AVD), Active Directory and Azure AD Connect, and cloud hosting that blends with legitimate Azure traffic [S3][S4].

gaps: Cluster boundaries: Microsoft maps IMPERIAL KITTEN to Smoke Sandstorm [S8], but CrowdStrike's IMPERIAL KITTEN reporting (IMAPLoader, watering holes, since 2017) overlaps with Tortoiseshell-associated activity, and Mandiant noted overlaps with both Tortoiseshell and Smoke Sandstorm [S3][S6]. Do not merge IMPERIAL KITTEN facts into Smoke Sandstorm without vendor confirmation.
MITRE G1059 (NIMBUS MANTICORE) also lists Proofpoint's TA455; Microsoft's mapping does not name TA455 under Smoke Sandstorm. The encyclopedia keeps TA455 as a separate record [S8][S9].

Check Point's 2025 report on Nimbus Manticore expanding into Europe (MiniJunk, MiniBrowse) was referenced in searches but could not be opened (host unreachable), and its date was not confirmed. It is not cited.

Secondary coverage says Check Point observed three Nimbus Manticore waves from February to April 2026, coinciding with the US 'Operation Epic Fury', and a first use of SEO poisoning that impersonated Oracle SQL Developer. Sources for this were undated aggregator pages and were not verified against the primary report.
Kaspersky reporting (NodeRabbit, PollCat, fake coding tests) and Nextron reporting (a fake Ebix recruiter) on Nimbus Manticore surfaced only in search snippets and were not verified.
Dark Reading reported 2025 targeting expansion to the US, UAE, Qatar, Spain and Saudi Arabia; the article date was not confirmed, so it is not cited.
Primary documents not opened: Microsoft's 2022 BOHRIUM blog and civil action filing, CrowdStrike's IMPERIAL KITTEN report, and Check Point's research posts.
No government (USG) attribution or advisory specific to Smoke Sandstorm was found in the sources gathered.
Unit 42 reportedly found no confirmed breaches of targeted oil, gas or aviation firms in the 2026 activity (secondary snippet only, unverified).

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain includes defense-industrial-base suppliers, IT integrators and partner-facing VDI (Citrix, VMware, AVD) that bridge into prime contractors and government clients, as well as Active Directory and Azure AD Connect [S1][S4]. STEP 2 (effects): Supplier and integrator compromises let the actor bypass hardened primes, and Azure-hosted C2 blends with legitimate cloud traffic [S3][S4]. STEP 3 (adversary model): Recruiter or job lure, or a supplier pivot, then a custom backdoor (MINIBUS, TWOSTROKE, DEEPROOT, MiniFast), then DCSync and Kerberoasting, then RDP lateral movement, then collection of IT documentation, IP and email [S3][S4][S7]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is persistent espionage against aerospace, aviation and defense suppliers supporting US and partner programs, timed with regional conflict [S4][S7]. MDCOA is the use of supplier access and domain-controller credential resets to cause outages or set up follow-on disruption during an Iran-related crisis; GTIG notes that DC account password resets have already caused outages [S4]. Candidate indicators: job-themed archives from lookalike career domains; DLL side-loading of signed Fortinet, VMware, Citrix or NVIDIA binaries from unusual paths; new reverse SSH tunnels, ZeroTier or ngrok after remediation; DCSync from non-DC hosts; unexpected azurewebsites.net or cloudapp.azure.com beacons [S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: fuse DIB supplier compromise reporting with DoD network telemetry, because the actor reaches targets through third parties and partner VDI [S4]. (2) Authorities: much of the relevant terrain sits in contractor and cloud-provider space, so response depends on DC3 and the DIB CS program, cloud-provider takedowns (Microsoft's 2022 domain seizure is a precedent) and law-enforcement partners rather than DoD actions alone [S2][S4]. (3) Mission assurance: dormant backdoors reactivate after eradication, so restoration plans must include full credential and trust resets (including AD CS and Azure AD Connect) and post-remediation hunts [S4]. (4) Coordination: activity has tracked Middle East conflict cycles, so share indicators with coalition partners in Israel, the Gulf and Europe during escalation periods [S3][S7].

provenance.importedSummary: NIMBUS MANTICORE is a State Sponsored cyber espionage group associated with the Iranian Regime specifically the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). NIMBUS MANTICORE has employed social engineering attacks to include HR related themes and has leveraged custom malware against its victims. NIMBUS MANTICORE has sought sensitive information in victims’ environments to include network/IT documentation, intellectual property and emails. NIMBUS MANTICORE has also leveraged compromised organizations as pivot points to access other organizations of interest. NIMBUS MANTICORE has been active since 2021 and has targeted critical infrastructure organizations to include aviation, aerospace, telecommunications and defense and information technology related organizations within the United States, Australia, Midde East and Europe.

relatedRecords.note: MITRE's NIMBUS MANTICORE (G1059) lists Proofpoint's TA455 alongside UNC1549, which Microsoft maps to Smoke Sandstorm. Kept as separate records pending vendor-level confirmation.

identification.summary: SneakyChef is a threat actor known for using the SugarGh0st RAT to target government agencies, research institutions, and organizations worldwide. They have been active since at least August 2023, with a focus on leveraging old and new command and control domains. The group has been observed using lures in the form of scanned documents related to Ministries of Foreign Affairs and embassies. Talos Intelligence assesses with medium confidence that the operators are likely Chinese-speaking based on language preferences and specific targets.

Solntsepek is a threat actor group with ties to the Russian military unit GRU. They have claimed responsibility for a cyberattack on Kyivstar, a Ukrainian mobile operator, and have been linked to previous attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. Solntsepek has been associated with the Sandworm hacking group, known for their destructive cyberattacks, including the NotPetya worm. They have also engaged in hostile activities, such as revealing personal details of Ukrainian soldiers.

SpaceBears is a ransomware group believed to be based in Moscow, Russia, that has taken credit for several high-profile cyberattacks while primarily operating as a Data Broker. They currently list eight organizations on their Data Leak Site, focusing on medium to small-sized targets. Their methods suggest a reliance on basic extortion strategies rather than sophisticated malware tactics, with no advanced techniques or indicators of ransomware detected.

Spandex Tempest is Microsoft's name for the financially motivated cybercrime actor that Proofpoint tracks as TA505 and CrowdStrike as MONTY SPIDER [S1]. Proofpoint describes TA505 as responsible for the largest malicious spam campaigns it had ever observed, distributing Dridex, Locky, Jaff, The Trick and other malware at high volume through the Necurs botnet [S2]. From late 2018 the group shifted from ransomware-first spam toward backdoors and RATs (ServHelper, FlawedGrace, Get2/SDBbot) aimed heavily at financial institutions [S3][S4]. Fox-IT reported in 2020 that the group had moved toward running most of its operation itself, from initial infection through monetization, including a Clop data-leak site [S5].
identification.firstObserved: Proofpoint's timeline begins with Dridex campaigns in 2014 [S2]; the Proofpoint profile was published in September 2017 [S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft maps Spandex Tempest to MONTY SPIDER and TA505 and labels it 'Financially motivated' [S1]. Microsoft separately tracks Lace Tempest (DEV-0950), which it named as the actor behind the 2023 MOVEit Transfer exploitation linked to the Clop extortion operation [S1][S8]. US government advisories use 'CL0P Ransomware Gang, also known as TA505' [S7], so the industry label TA505 spans activity that Microsoft splits between Spandex Tempest and Lace Tempest. Mandiant tracks related activity as FIN11 and several UNC clusters, which it has treated as overlapping with but not identical to TA505 [S9][S11]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the group as TA505 (G0092).

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor identified in the sources gathered; Microsoft classifies Spandex Tempest as financially motivated [S1]. 2019 reporting on CyberInt research describes TA505 as believed to be Russian-speaking [S10].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft's mapping assigns TA505 and MONTY SPIDER to Spandex Tempest [S1]. The 'Russian-speaking' characterization is a vendor belief reported in press coverage, not a government attribution [S10].
attribution.basis: Microsoft naming taxonomy [S1]; Proofpoint campaign tracking from 2014 onward [S2][S3][S4][S6][S12]; Fox-IT analysis of Get2/SDBbot samples [S5]; CyberInt research as reported by SecurityWeek [S10].

actors.objectives: Financial gain through banking-trojan fraud, ransomware, remote-access tooling on financial and retail networks, and data-theft extortion [S1][S2][S3][S5]. Proofpoint describes the actor as opportunistic and trend-setting, changing tactics to follow the most profitable targets [S6].

regions: Global, not focused on a single region [S3]
Financial institutions in Greece, Singapore, UAE, Georgia, Sweden and Lithuania (Sept 2019) [S4]
Financial institutions in Chile, India, Italy, Malawi, Pakistan and South Korea, and US retailers (Dec 2018 to Feb 2019) [S10]
targeting.notes: Proofpoint assessed in 2019 that TA505 focused on financial institutions while alternating with wider campaigns against other verticals [S4]. Victim counts in the CISA Clop advisory (3,000+ US and 8,000+ global organizations) are attributed to the 'CL0P Ransomware Gang, also known as TA505' and should not be assigned to Spandex Tempest alone given Microsoft's separate Lace Tempest cluster [S7][S1].

capabilities.summary: High-volume malspam via the Necurs botnet delivering Dridex, Locky, Jaff, GlobeImposter and Philadelphia [S2][S12]. FlawedAmmyy RAT delivered through Quant Loader in 2018 [S12]. Delphi-based ServHelper backdoor and the full-featured FlawedGrace RAT (first observed November 2017), delivered by Word, Publisher and PDF lures in late 2018 [S3]. Get2 downloader from September 2019 delivering FlawedAmmyy, FlawedGrace, Snatch and the C++ SDBbot RAT [S4]. Abuse of the commercial Remote Manipulator System remote-administration tool against banks and retailers [S10]. HTML redirects in the infection chain and a 'CL0P^_- LEAKS' data-leak site by 2020 [S5]. In 2021, intermediate loaders written in Rebol and KiXtart (tracked by Morphisec as MirrorBlast) replaced Get2 and delivered an updated FlawedGrace [S6].

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated cybercrime actor tracked as Spandex Tempest / TA505 / MONTY SPIDER, reported as believed Russian-speaking [S1][S10].
diamond.capability: Necurs-delivered malspam; Dridex, Locky, GlobeImposter; FlawedAmmyy, ServHelper, FlawedGrace, Get2, SDBbot; Rebol/KiXtart loaders; commercial RMS tool [S2][S3][S4][S6][S10][S12].
diamond.infrastructure: Necurs botnet for spam distribution [S2][S12]; actor-registered domains with recurring naming patterns [S6]; HTML redirect pages and a Clop data-leak site [S5].
diamond.victim: Banks and financial institutions worldwide, retail, restaurants and hospitality, and broad multi-industry recipients [S3][S4][S6][S10].
diamond.socioPolitical: Profit-driven operations that follow the most lucrative monetization model, from banking fraud to ransomware and data-leak extortion [S5][S6].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints opened via Office macro, PDF and MSI lures; payment-heavy retail and banking networks [S3][S6][S10].

gaps: Microsoft has not published, in sources found, a dedicated Spandex Tempest profile; the Microsoft name is supported only by the MSTIC naming mapping [S1].

Cluster boundary: Microsoft separates Spandex Tempest (TA505) from Lace Tempest (DEV-0950, Clop/MOVEit), while CISA treats the CL0P gang as 'also known as TA505' and Mandiant uses FIN11/UNC clusters. Accellion, GoAnywhere and MOVEit activity is not confirmed as Spandex Tempest by Microsoft [S1][S7][S8][S9][S11].
Russian-speaking assessment comes from vendor reporting via press; no government attribution of nationality or state nexus located [S10].

Primary documents could not be opened (fetch blocked or DNS failure): Proofpoint blogs, Fox-IT/NCC Group article, CISA AA23-158A, Canadian Centre for Cyber Security TA505/Cl0p profile; details rely on search-result summaries.
Activity attributable specifically to Spandex Tempest after 2021 is not established in the sources gathered.
Imported actor record lists country RU; this is not confirmed by Microsoft, which labels the group only as financially motivated [S1].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The operational environment is email gateways, user Windows endpoints and, for support functions, financial and payment systems such as finance offices, base retail and contractor payroll [S3][S10]. STEP 2: High-volume campaigns of tens to hundreds of thousands of emails can overwhelm filtering, and the actor swaps loaders and payloads often, which shortens the useful life of signatures [S4][S6]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is an Office, PDF or MSI lure, then a loader (Get2, Rebol/KiXtart), then a RAT (FlawedGrace, SDBbot, ServHelper, FlawedAmmyy, RMS), followed by monetization through fraud, ransomware or Clop-branded data-leak extortion [S3][S4][S5][S6][S10]. STEP 4: MLCOA is opportunistic phishing that reaches DoD-adjacent finance or contractor users for credential and remote-access theft. MDCOA is ransomware or data-leak extortion against a mission-support contractor that degrades logistics or payroll during an operation. Candidate indicators: macro-enabled Excel or Word lures themed on invoices or insurance claims; MSI execution spawning Rebol or KiXtart interpreters; unexpected RMS/TektonIT remote-admin binaries; HTML redirect chains in phishing links [S3][S6][S10].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: include commodity-crime loader and RAT families in DODIN threat reporting, because this actor's tooling changes yearly [S4][S6]. (2) Authorities: this is a criminal, financially motivated actor [S1], so response will be primarily DCO-IDM and law-enforcement coordination rather than an adversary-state military response. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize contractors and support functions that handle payment and personnel data, given the actor's banking and retail focus and its data-leak extortion model [S3][S5]. (4) Coordination: track vendor naming differences (Spandex Tempest, TA505, Lace Tempest, FIN11, CL0P) in joint reporting to avoid double-counting or merging separate clusters [S1][S7][S9].

provenance.importedSummary: TA505, the name given by Proofpoint, has been in the cybercrime business for at least four years. This is the group behind the infamous Dridex banking trojan and Locky ransomware, delivered through malicious email campaigns via Necurs botnet. Other malware associated with TA505 include Philadelphia and GlobeImposter ransomware families.

identification.summary: Russian nation-state actor focused on email credential theft through tailored, rapport-building spear-phishing of individuals in international affairs, defense, logistics support to Ukraine, think tanks, academia, NGOs and government, mainly in NATO countries [S1][S2][S5]. Microsoft says its activity has historically supported both espionage and cyber-influence objectives [S1]. The UK NCSC and allied agencies assess it is almost certainly subordinate to FSB Centre 18 [S5][S6]. Since at least 2022-2023 it has added selective custom malware (SPICA, LOSTKEYS, and the NOROBOT/MAYBEROBOT chain) to its phishing operations [S4][S9][S11].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft has tracked the actor since 2017 [S2]. NCSC reporting (via coverage) describes activity since at least 2015, including spear-phishing of UK parliamentarians [S6].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Star Blizzard (formerly SEABORGIUM; renamed April 2023) [S2]. Microsoft says its indicators and tactics overlap with Callisto Group (F-Secure), TA446 (Proofpoint) and COLDRIVER (Google) [S2]. Google lists COLDRIVER as also known as UNC4057, Star Blizzard and Callisto [S4]. The December 2023 joint advisory (per search summary) lists SEABORGIUM, Callisto Group, TA446, COLDRIVER, TAG-53 and BlueCharlie as aliases [S5]. Ukraine's SSU associated Callisto with Gamaredon (ACTINIUM), but Microsoft said it had not observed technical intrusion links supporting that association [S2]. Citizen Lab's COLDWASTREL is assessed as a distinct actor targeting similar communities and must not be merged with Star Blizzard [S10][S12].

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation, Federal Security Service (FSB). The UK NCSC and partners assess Star Blizzard is almost certainly subordinate to FSB Centre 18 [S5][S6]. DOJ described the group as an operational unit within FSB Center 18 (per coverage of the October 2024 seizure) [S8].
attribution.confidence: Government: NCSC uses 'almost certainly' for Centre 18 subordination (December 2023), jointly with US and other Five Eyes agencies [S5][S6]. Microsoft calls it a Russian nation-state actor without a formal confidence rating [S1]. Google calls COLDRIVER 'Russian government-backed' without naming an agency [S4].
attribution.basis: Joint advisory and NCSC attribution statement [S5][S6]. US charges (December 2023) against Ruslan Peretyatko, described as an FSB Center 18 officer, and Andrey Korinets, with US Treasury and UK sanctions and a State Department reward of up to $10 million (per press coverage) [S7]. Microsoft and Google telemetry and infrastructure analysis [S1][S2][S4]. Microsoft civil action and DOJ domain seizures in October 2024 [S8].

actors.objectives: Intelligence collection in support of Russia's strategic interests, per Google [S4]. Microsoft assesses it likely supports traditional espionage and information operations rather than financial goals [S2]. In a small number of cases stolen material has been leaked, including hack-and-leak operations against UK officials and an NGO, and NCSC links it to leaks intended to interfere in UK politics [S4][S6]. It also targets exiled Russian opposition figures and Western civil society [S10].

sectors: Government and diplomacy, current and former officials [S3][S4]
Defense and intelligence consultancies; defense-industrial firms (from 2022) [S2][S5]
US government agencies including the intelligence community, DoD and defense contractors, State Department and Department of Energy facilities (2016-2022, per indictment coverage) [S7]
Think tanks and Russia-focused international-relations researchers [S2][S3]
NGOs, IGOs and civil society, including funders [S2][S8][S10]
regions: United States and United Kingdom (most targeted) [S2][S5]
Other NATO countries, with occasional Baltic, Nordic and Eastern European targeting [S2][S5]
targeting.notes: The actor mainly targets personal or NGO email accounts rather than corporate ones [S4][S5]. About 30% of Microsoft's nation-state notifications for this actor went to consumer email accounts [S2]. Microsoft observed targeting of more than 30 organizations in 2022 and more than 30 civil-society organizations between January 2023 and August 2024 [S2][S8].

capabilities.summary: Core tradecraft: reconnaissance of targets, fake social-media profiles and new webmail accounts impersonating trusted contacts, then benign rapport-building emails, often referencing a non-existent attachment, before any malicious link [S2][S5]. It harvests credentials with Evilginx adversary-in-the-middle pages, which capture passwords and MFA tokens [S1][S2]. Lures include custom PDFs, password-protected PDFs or Proton Drive links, and altered OneDrive notifications (July-August 2024) [S1]. Evasion includes HubSpot and MailerLite redirect URLs, multiple registrars, link shorteners, open redirects, Microsoft Safe Links abuse, browser fingerprinting, hCaptcha, a DNS/reverse-proxy service and randomized domains [S1]. Microsoft says it adopts TTPs for brief periods and changes them once they are publicly known [S1]. After compromise it exfiltrates mail and sets forwarding rules to dead-drop accounts [S2]. In November 2024 it used QR codes to link targets' WhatsApp accounts to actor-controlled devices, its first use of WhatsApp [S3]. Selective malware: the Rust backdoor SPICA, delivered as a fake PDF decryption tool and believed in use since November 2022 [S9]; LOSTKEYS, a VBS file stealer delivered through a ClickFix fake CAPTCHA and PowerShell chain (January-April 2025) [S4]; and, after LOSTKEYS was exposed, the COLDCOPY lure, NOROBOT DLL, YESROBOT Python backdoor and MAYBEROBOT PowerShell backdoor (May-June 2025) [S11].

diamond.adversary: FSB Centre 18-linked operators (NCSC: almost certainly) [S5][S6]. US charges name Ruslan Peretyatko, described as an FSB officer, and Andrey Korinets [S7].
diamond.capability: Evilginx AiTM credential and MFA-token theft; PDF, Proton Drive and OneDrive-themed lures; WhatsApp device linking; SPICA, LOSTKEYS and NOROBOT/YESROBOT/MAYBEROBOT malware [S1][S3][S4][S9][S11].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-registered domains across multiple registrars, VPS servers running Evilginx, a DNS/reverse-proxy service, email marketing platforms (HubSpot, MailerLite) as redirectors, link shorteners, and newly created webmail sender accounts (often Proton) [S1][S2]. Over 100 domains were seized in October 2024 [S8].
diamond.victim: Government, defense, think-tank, academic, NGO, journalist and politician targets in the US, the UK and NATO, often through personal email; Russian exiles [S2][S4][S5][S10].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on Russia, Ukraine and NATO policy; selective leaks intended to interfere in UK politics; targeting of Russian dissidents abroad [S4][S6][S10].
diamond.technology: Consumer and cloud email, phishable MFA, WhatsApp linked-device features, and Windows scripting (PowerShell via the Run dialog, rundll32) [S1][S3][S4][S11].

gaps: Primary government documents were not opened: the joint advisory, NCSC news pages, DOJ press release, indictment and Treasury designation were blocked. Their content comes from search summaries and press coverage [S5][S6][S7][S8].

Original Google TAG SPICA blog, GTIG October 2025 ROBOT-chain report, Citizen Lab 'Rivers of Phish' report and Zscaler's BAITSWITCH/SIMPLEFIX report were not opened; details come from search results and secondary coverage [S9][S10][S11].

Vendor naming: TAG-53 and BlueCharlie (Recorded Future), IRON FRONTIER (Secureworks) and GOSSAMER BEAR (CrowdStrike) come from the imported record or advisory alias lists and were not checked against the vendors' own reporting.
COLDWASTREL (Citizen Lab) and PwC's related tracking are assessed as distinct from COLDRIVER; the relationship is unresolved [S10][S12].
The SSU-proposed link to Gamaredon (ACTINIUM) is unconfirmed by Microsoft [S2].
Google could not confirm whether December 2023 Maltego-themed LOSTKEYS samples belong to COLDRIVER [S4].
The year of the Institute for Statecraft compromise differs across reports (2018 vs 2019) [S6].
No public reporting on activity after October 2025 surfaced in searches; search results showed NCSC PDFs re-hosted under 2026 paths, but their content could not be opened.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the personal email, cloud accounts and messaging apps (WhatsApp) of senior leaders, policy advisers, defense-industrial staff, Ukraine-assistance logistics personnel and their outside contacts. Much of this sits outside DoD network boundaries [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 2: Reliance on credible impersonation and phishable MFA makes identity the operating environment. Rapid TTP and infrastructure turnover after public exposure shortens indicator lifespan [S1][S3][S8]. STEP 3: The template is reconnaissance and a fake persona, a benign rapport email, a PDF, link or QR lure, Evilginx credential and token capture or WhatsApp device linking, then mailbox exfiltration and forwarding rules. A selective malware branch runs from a ClickFix fake CAPTCHA through PowerShell to LOSTKEYS or the NOROBOT/MAYBEROBOT chain [S1][S2][S3][S4][S11]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued credential phishing of personal accounts of US, UK and NATO defense and policy figures for intelligence on Ukraine support and Russia policy. MDCOA is a timed leak of stolen planning or political correspondence during a crisis or election to undermine allied cohesion [S4][S6]. Candidate indicators: unsolicited mail from known contacts on new webmail addresses; mail citing a missing attachment; password-protected PDFs or Proton Drive links; Safe Links-wrapped shortened URLs; new inbox forwarding rules; unexpected WhatsApp linked devices; PowerShell or rundll32 launched from the Run dialog after a CAPTCHA page [S1][S2][S3][S4][S11].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: victims are mostly personal and NGO accounts, so DoD sensors will miss much of this activity. JCC2 pictures should include partner reporting from NCSC, Microsoft and Google [S2][S4][S5]. (2) Authorities: personal accounts and commercial messaging platforms fall outside DODIN defensive authorities. Response there relies on FBI, DOJ and industry actions such as the October 2024 domain seizures [S7][S8]. (3) Mission assurance: phishing-resistant MFA and personal-account hygiene for key leaders and Ukraine-support staff reduce exposure to AiTM credential theft. Script-execution restrictions reduce ClickFix risk [S1][S4]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with Five Eyes partners and the DIB, and expect rapid infrastructure rebuilding after exposure [S5][S8].

provenance.importedSummary: The Callisto Group is an advanced threat actor whose known targets include military personnel, government officials, think tanks, and journalists in Europe and the South Caucasus. Their primary interest appears to be gathering intelligence related to foreign and security policy in the Eastern Europe and South Caucasus regions.

identification.summary: Storm-0133 is Microsoft's name for the cluster that other vendors track as HEXANE, Lyceum, Siamesekitten and Spirlin. Microsoft lists its origin as Iran [S1]. Secureworks CTU disclosed the group as LYCEUM in August 2019. CTU said it had been active since about April 2018 against organizations of strategic national importance, including oil and gas and possibly telecommunications [S2][S3]. Dragos separately disclosed it as HEXANE at Black Hat 2019 [S4]. Later public reporting covers telecom and ISP intrusions in the Middle East and Africa in 2021 [S5][S6], Israeli IT-sector targeting via fake job lures in 2021 [S7], and a custom DNS backdoor used against Middle Eastern energy and telecom targets in 2022 [S8][S9].
identification.firstObserved: 2018 (Secureworks: active since about April 2018; earliest campaign mid-2018 against South African targets) [S2]; Dragos also says active since 2018 [S4].
identification.notes: Microsoft's mapping equates Storm-0133 with HEXANE, Lyceum, Siamesekitten and Spirlin [S1]. The imported summary says the group has been 'active since at least 2014' and is 'linked to APT34'. Neither claim is supported by the sources gathered here, so both are excluded (see gaps). Storm-#### is Microsoft's designation for an emerging or developing cluster [S1].

attribution.sponsor: Iran (Microsoft lists Iran as origin) [S1]. No specific Iranian government organization is named in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft lists the cluster's origin as Iran [S1]. At disclosure in 2019, Secureworks CTU saw tradecraft resembling the Iranian groups COBALT GYPSY and COBALT TRINITY. CTU found no direct malware or infrastructure links and said technical evidence was insufficient for an attribution assessment [S2]. ClearSky described Siamesekitten/Lyceum as Iranian [S6][S7]. Zscaler ThreatLabz reporting describes the group as Iran-linked [S8].
attribution.basis: Vendor tradecraft comparison (Secureworks) [S2]; ClearSky campaign analysis [S7]; Zscaler analysis of an Iranian-military-themed lure [S8]; Microsoft naming taxonomy [S1]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.

actors.objectives: Espionage and access against strategically important energy and telecommunications organizations [S2][S5][S6]. Dragos assessed that telecom access could serve as a stepping stone to network-focused man-in-the-middle attacks [S4]. ClearSky assessed that 2021 targeting of Israeli IT and communications firms was most likely meant to enable supply-chain attacks [S7].

sectors: IT and communications service providers (supply chain) [S7]
Government (an African ministry of foreign affairs) [S6]
targeting.notes: Targeting staff in the 2019 Secureworks reporting were executives, HR staff and IT personnel [S2]. Victim names in the 2021 ISP and telecom intrusions were not disclosed [S6].

capabilities.summary: Initial access through credential harvesting by password spraying or brute force, followed by spearphishing with malicious Excel attachments that install the .NET RAT DanBot [S2]. Earlier tooling included PowerShell scripts alongside DanBot [S5]. In 2021 Kaspersky reported a shift from PowerShell scripts and DanBot to new C++ malware it named James and Kevin [S5]. In 2021 ClearSky reported a chain of fake-recruiter social engineering and impersonation of real Israeli firms on LinkedIn, with Excel lures dropping the Milan backdoor (which fetched DanBot), later replaced by the .NET backdoor Shark [S7]. Zscaler reported a custom .NET DNS backdoor in 2022 (DnsSystem, modified from open-source DIG.net). It was delivered by a macro-laden Word document posing as Iranian military news, persisted via the Startup folder, and used DNS hijacking with TXT-record command retrieval and A-record exfiltration [S8][S9].

campaigns.name: Middle East oil and gas campaign
campaigns.summary: After heavy toolkit testing on a public multi-vendor scanning service in February 2019, the group used password spraying and DanBot-laden Excel spearphishing against Middle Eastern oil and gas organizations.

campaigns.name: Public disclosure (LYCEUM / HEXANE)
campaigns.summary: Secureworks CTU disclosed LYCEUM. Dragos disclosed HEXANE at Black Hat 2019 as targeting oil and gas plus telecoms in the Middle East, Central Asia and Africa.

campaigns.name: Siamesekitten Israeli IT supply-chain targeting
campaigns.summary: ClearSky reports May-June 2021 fake job offers impersonating Israeli firms to deliver Milan and DanBot, with Shark replacing Milan in July 2021.

campaigns.name: ISP and telecom intrusions (Accenture / Prevailion)
campaigns.summary: Intrusions between July and October 2021 against ISPs and telecom operators in Israel, Morocco, Tunisia and Saudi Arabia and an African MFA.

campaigns.name: Tunisia activity (Kaspersky, VB2021)
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky reports a new Lyceum cluster against two Tunisian entities, including telecom and aviation, using new C++ malware James and Kevin.

campaigns.name: DnsSystem DNS-hijacking backdoor
campaigns.summary: Zscaler reports a .NET DNS backdoor delivered by Iranian-military-themed Word lures against Middle Eastern energy and telecom organizations.

diamond.adversary: Iran-origin cluster per Microsoft (Storm-0133). Tracked as HEXANE, Lyceum, Siamesekitten and Spirlin [S1]. The sponsoring organization is not publicly identified in the gathered sources [S2].
diamond.capability: Password spraying and brute force; Excel and Word macro lures; DanBot, Milan, Shark, James/Kevin and DnsSystem backdoors with DNS-based C2 [S2][S5][S7][S8].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-controlled DNS servers used for DNS tunneling and hijacking C2 [S8]. Phishing sites mimicking Israeli IT companies and fake LinkedIn profiles [S7]. A HivePro advisory lists IOCs such as the cyberclub[.]one domain [S9].
diamond.victim: Energy (oil and gas), telecom operators and ISPs, IT service providers, aviation, and a foreign ministry. Victims are located in the Middle East, North Africa, South Africa and Israel [S2][S4][S5][S6][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection against regional energy and communications infrastructure. Possible use of telecom access for man-in-the-middle operations (Dragos assessment) [S4]. Supply-chain access to Israeli organizations (ClearSky assessment) [S7].
diamond.technology: Reliance on DNS protocol C2 that blends with normal traffic [S8]. Exposure of single-factor enterprise accounts to password spraying [S2]. Trust in recruiters and HR channels [S7].

gaps: Primary documents not opened: Secureworks/Sophos blog (fetch blocked), Kaspersky VB2021 paper, ClearSky Siamesekitten report, Accenture CIFR/Prevailion PACT report, Zscaler ThreatLabz blog, Dragos HEXANE profile, Google 'Tool of First Resort' PDF (fetch failed). Facts rely on search-result summaries of secondary coverage.
Several source dates are approximate. The Kaspersky/Dark Reading item (S5) and the Heimdal/ClearSky item (S7) are dated by event timing, not a verified publication date.

No sponsoring Iranian organization (e.g., MOIS or IRGC) is named in any gathered source. Secureworks said evidence was insufficient for attribution in 2019. Do not upgrade vendor assessments to government attribution.
Imported summary claims 'active since at least 2014' and a link to APT34. Neither is supported by the gathered sources and both were excluded pending verification.

Aliases Chrono Kitten (CrowdStrike), MYSTICDOME and UNC1530 (Mandiant) come from the imported record. They were not confirmed in sources read here. The Google 'Tool of First Resort' report on Israel-Hamas war cyber activity may cover UNC1530 but could not be opened.
No public reporting from 2023 onward was found in this research pass. Current activity status is unknown.
ATT&CK G1001 page could not be fetched (DNS failure); technique and software lists come from the imported MITRE data, not this research.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain is regional telecom operators, ISPs, energy companies and IT service providers in the Middle East and North Africa. Partner-nation and host-nation networks supporting deployed forces likely transit these providers [S4][S6]. STEP 2 (effects): Compromised ISPs and telecoms could expose communications that transit them to interception or man-in-the-middle activity (Dragos assessment) [S4]. Compromised IT suppliers could provide downstream access (ClearSky assessment) [S7]. STEP 3 (threat model): Password spraying or recruitment-themed social engineering, then macro-laden Office lures, then a .NET or C++ backdoor with DNS-based C2 [S2][S7][S8]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is persistent espionage access inside regional telecom and energy organizations for collection [S2][S6]. MDCOA is use of telecom or ISP access to intercept or manipulate traffic of partner or US-associated networks during a regional crisis [S4]. Candidate indicators: bursts of failed logons consistent with password spraying [S2]; Office documents with AutoClose macros writing to Startup folders [S8]; anomalous DNS TXT-record query volume to rare domains [S8]; recruiter outreach impersonating legitimate firms [S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Track the security posture of partner-nation telecom and ISP carriers in the AOR, because this actor focused on that layer [S4][S6]. (2) Mission assurance: Assume transit over regional carriers may be observed. Rely on end-to-end encryption and avoid dependence on carrier-provided DNS [S4][S8]. (3) Detection: Prioritize DNS analytics and password-spray detection on DoD-adjacent and partner enclaves [S2][S8]. (4) Coordination and authorities: Activity against partner-nation infrastructure falls under host-nation and private-sector authorities. Coordinate through combatant command, partner CERTs and vendor reporting channels rather than acting unilaterally.

provenance.importedSummary: Lyceum is an Iranian APT group that has been active since at least 2014. They primarily target Middle Eastern governments and organizations in the energy and telecommunications sectors. Lyceum is known for using cyber espionage techniques and has been linked to other Iranian threat groups such as APT34. They have developed and deployed malware families like Shark and Milan, and have been observed using DNS tunneling and HTTPfor command and control communication.

identification.summary: Storm-0216 is Microsoft's name for a financially motivated ransomware operator that Microsoft associates with Twisted Spider and UNC2198 [S4][S5]. Proofpoint tracked TA2101 in late 2019, impersonating German, Italian and US government agencies to deliver Maze ransomware [S1][S2]. Mandiant's UNC2198 cluster covers IcedID-initiated intrusions that ended in Maze (July 2020) and Egregor (October 2020) deployment [S3]. In late 2023 Microsoft reported Storm-0216 hands-on-keyboard activity after Danabot infections, ending in Cactus ransomware [S4][S5].
identification.firstObserved: Proofpoint reported TA2101 campaigns between 16 October and 12 November 2019 [S1]. Mandiant created UNC2198 in June 2020 [S3].
identification.notes: Cluster boundaries differ by vendor: Proofpoint TA2101, Mandiant UNC2198 (which absorbed UNC2374 and UNC2414) and Microsoft Storm-0216 are mapped to one another by Microsoft and by press coverage [S3][S4][S5]. Mandiant says UNC2420 (Shathak/TA551) distributes the payloads UNC2198 used for access but treats it as a separate distribution cluster [S3]. Microsoft tracks Danabot as Storm-1044, a separate actor that hands off access [S4][S5].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor identified in the sources gathered; Mandiant describes UNC2198 as financially motivated [S3]. The source record lists country as RU; Microsoft is reported to describe Storm-0216 as Russia-based [S4].
attribution.confidence: Vendor assessments only. Mandiant assesses the objective is to monetize intrusions via ransomware and merged clusters through shared infrastructure and tooling, which it calls an analytical practice, not a definitive identity claim [S3]. Microsoft links Storm-0216 to Twisted Spider and UNC2198 [S4][S5].
attribution.basis: Shared Cobalt Strike team-server certificate (self-signed 'Oracle Inc', TCP 25055), WINDARC paths, code-signing certificate and RCLONE paths [S3]; Microsoft telemetry of Danabot-to-Storm-0216 handoff, as relayed in press coverage of Microsoft's posts [S4][S5]. Microsoft's original post was not opened.

actors.objectives: Financial gain through ransomware and data-theft extortion; Mandiant states UNC2198 aims to monetize intrusions by compromising networks with ransomware [S3].

sectors: Business and IT services (2019 TA2101 recipients)
targeting.notes: Targeting is opportunistic across industries. Mandiant says UNC2198 victims were primarily in North America across a breadth of industries [S3]. 2019 campaigns are from Proofpoint and secondary coverage [S1][S2]. 2023 victim sectors were not stated in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: 2019: macro-laden Word lures impersonating government agencies running PowerShell to download Maze [S1]. 2020 (UNC2198): IcedID delivered via MOUSEISLAND and PHOTOLOADER, WINDARC TeamViewer-hijacking backdoor, SYSTEMBC proxy, Cobalt Strike BEACON in about 90% of intrusions, Metasploit, KOADIC, Empire, BloodHound, lateral movement by WinRM, RDP, PsExec and SMB BEACON, privilege escalation with a CVE-2020-0787 exploit, RCLONE exfiltration before encryption, and Maze or Egregor deployment (PsExec for Maze, forced GPO updates for Egregor) with time-to-ransom of 5.5 and 1.5 days respectively [S3]. 2023: access via Danabot (private build, malvertising) after QakBot disruption, RDP lateral movement, Cactus ransomware [S4][S5].

campaigns.name: TA2101 government-impersonation campaigns
campaigns.summary: Lures impersonating the German Federal Ministry of Finance (lookalike .icu sender domains, RSA SecurID-themed document) delivering Maze via macro-enabled Word documents and PowerShell [S1]; secondary coverage adds Italian Revenue Agency and USPS impersonation [S2]. Activity ran 16 October to 12 November 2019.

campaigns.summary: Microsoft reported Danabot (Storm-1044) infections, spread via malvertising since November 2023, handed off to Storm-0216 for hands-on-keyboard activity and Cactus deployment, after the August 2023 QakBot takedown.

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated ransomware operator tracked as TA2101, UNC2198, Twisted Spider and Storm-0216 [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.capability: Phishing macros, IcedID/Danabot access, Cobalt Strike, WINDARC, SYSTEMBC, RCLONE, Maze, Egregor, Cactus [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Cobalt Strike team servers with self-signed 'Oracle Inc' certificate on TCP 25055; lookalike .icu sender domains in Germany; malvertising delivery for Danabot [S1][S3][S5].
diamond.victim: Organizations in Germany, Italy and the US in 2019; North American organizations across industries in 2020 [S1][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Criminal extortion; ransomware operators monetize intrusions [S3].
diamond.technology: Windows domains reachable via phishing-delivered loaders, RDP, PsExec and GPO; BITS privilege escalation CVE-2020-0787 [S3].

gaps: Microsoft's original Storm-0216 post could not be opened; details rely on secondary coverage [S4][S5]. Proofpoint's post was seen in search results only, not opened in full [S1].
Whether TA2101, UNC2198 and Storm-0216 are one continuous group is a vendor mapping, not independently verified; Mandiant itself cautions its cluster merges are analytic judgments [S3].
Relationship between the Maze/Egregor operators and the 2023 Cactus activity is not established in sources gathered beyond the Microsoft mapping.
Victim counts, ransom figures and 2024-2026 activity were not found.
CrowdStrike Twisted Spider and Secureworks GOLD VILLAGE profiles listed in the record were not opened; aliases are unverified beyond the record.
Country attribution (RU) is from the source record; no primary evidence was reviewed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Windows domain infrastructure, remote-access paths (RDP, TeamViewer-like tools) and email gateways at contractor and supporting organizations are relevant terrain; the actor is criminal, so effects fall on availability and data confidentiality [S3]. STEP 2: Time from access to ransom was 1.5 to 5.5 days in 2020, narrowing response windows [S3]. STEP 3: The template is phishing or malvertising, loader (IcedID/Danabot), Cobalt Strike, domain discovery, RCLONE exfiltration, then PsExec or GPO ransomware deployment [S3][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is opportunistic ransomware and extortion against commercial and supporting organizations. MDCOA is a ransomware outbreak against a DoD-supporting or healthcare-adjacent entity during a crisis, degrading mission support. Candidate indicators: rclone.exe in C:\PerfLogs, scheduled task named shadowdev, BEACON as int32.dll, new GPO pushes of executables, Danabot malvertising hits [S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track commodity loader activity (IcedID, Danabot) as precursors, since handoffs to ransomware operators occur within days [S3][S4]. (2) Authorities: criminal activity against US companies is law-enforcement-led; coordinate defensive response through established DIB and law enforcement channels rather than assuming military authority. (3) Mission assurance: protect domain controllers and GPO integrity, keep offline backups, and restrict RDP and remote tools [S3]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3/DIB partners and track takedown events (QakBot, August 2023) that cause actors to change tooling [S4].

provenance.importedSummary: Proofpoint researchers detected campaigns from a relatively new actor, tracked internally as TA2101, targeting German companies and organizations to deliver and install backdoor malware. The actor initiated their campaigns impersonating the Bundeszentralamt fur Steuern, the German Federal Ministry of Finance, with lookalike domains, verbiage, and stolen branding in the emails. For their campaigns in Germany, the actor chose Cobalt Strike, a commercially licensed software tool that is generally used for penetration testing and emulates the type of backdoor framework used by Metasploit, a similar penetration testing tool. Proofpoint researchers have also observed this actor distributing Maze ransomware, employing similar social engineering techniques to those it uses for Cobalt Strike, while also targeting organizations in Italy and impersonating the Agenzia Delle Entrate, the Italian Revenue Agency. We have also recently observed the actor targeting organizations in the United States using the IcedID banking Trojan while impersonating the United States Postal Service (USPS).

identification.summary: Storm-0247 is Microsoft's name for a China-origin threat actor that Microsoft maps to ToddyCat and Websiic [S1]. Kaspersky named ToddyCat in June 2022 and described an APT that compromised Microsoft Exchange servers to hit mainly government and military organizations in Europe and Asia, using two previously unknown tools, the Samurai backdoor and the Ninja Trojan [S2][S3]. Later Kaspersky reporting (2023-2025) describes an expanding toolkit focused on large-scale data collection and exfiltration, email theft and defense evasion [S5][S6][S7][S8].
identification.firstObserved: Kaspersky: first detected in December 2020, attacking Exchange servers [S2][S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Storm-0247 (origin China; other names ToddyCat, Websiic) [S1]. ToddyCat is Kaspersky's name [S2]. Websiic is the name ESET gave in March 2021 to a newly detected actor exploiting the Exchange ProxyLogon vulnerabilities [S4]. Most detailed reporting uses the ToddyCat name, and technical details here come from Kaspersky reporting as covered by trade press. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the group as ToddyCat (G1022).

attribution.sponsor: Microsoft lists the actor's origin as China [S1]. Trade-press coverage describes ToddyCat as China-linked or Chinese [S3][S7]. No cited source names a specific PRC government sponsor.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft's China origin label is a vendor assessment in its naming table and does not name a sponsoring agency [S1]. Coverage of Kaspersky's 2022 report does not clearly attribute ToddyCat to a Chinese state actor. Kaspersky's comment about a 'Chinese-speaking' group in the same period referred to a different group [S3]. No government attribution or indictment was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft's public threat-actor naming map [S1]. Kaspersky technical reporting from 2022 to 2025, carried in vendor press releases and trade press [S2][S3][S5][S6][S7][S8]. ESET's 2021 ProxyLogon reporting for the Websiic cluster [S4].

actors.objectives: Cyber espionage. The actor collects and exfiltrates sensitive data, at what Kaspersky calls 'industrial scale', from government and defense-related organizations [S2][S6]. From 2024-2025 it also stole email data and Microsoft 365 access tokens to keep reaching victim mailboxes [S8].

regions: Asia, including Taiwan and Vietnam in early intrusions [S2]
Kaspersky also reports related activity against entities in Afghanistan, India, Indonesia, Iran, Kyrgyzstan, Malaysia, Pakistan, Russia, Slovakia, Thailand, the UK and Uzbekistan [S2]
targeting.notes: Kaspersky reports that the group first hit Exchange servers in 2020-2021 and from September 2021 shifted to desktop machines of government and diplomatic entities in Asia [S2]. The 2024 reporting emphasizes government organizations in the Asia-Pacific region, some of them defense-related [S6].

capabilities.summary: Initial access: exploitation of Exchange servers, first through an unknown exploit that deployed the China Chopper web shell and then through ProxyLogon from February-March 2021 [S2][S3]. Custom implants: Samurai, a modular C# passive backdoor working on ports 80/443 and built mainly to run arbitrary C# code, and Ninja, a post-exploitation toolkit that lets several operators work on one host at once [S2][S3]. Exfiltration (2023): LoFiSe finds target files and Pcexter uploads archives to OneDrive. Kaspersky also reported a Dropbox uploader and a passive UDP backdoor, plus staging with 7z [S5]. Persistence and collection (2024): several redundant tunnels (reverse SSH, SoftEther VPN, Ngrok, FRP), some binaries renamed to look legitimate, and WAExp and TomBerBil for WhatsApp Web data and browser credentials [S6]. Defense evasion (2024-2025): abuse of CVE-2024-11859, a DLL search-order hijack in ESET's command-line scanner that requires admin rights, to load TCESB. TCESB uses BYOVD with a vulnerable Dell driver (CVE-2021-36276) and runs AES-decrypted payloads in memory [S7]. Email access (2025): TCSectorCopy reads disk sectors to copy Outlook OST files that Outlook has locked; the actor also used a PowerShell TomBerBil variant run from domain controllers over SMB, and SharpTokenFinder or ProcDump on Outlook.exe to recover Microsoft 365 tokens [S8].

campaigns.name: 'Industrial scale' data theft in Asia-Pacific

campaigns.name: ESET scanner DLL hijack / TCESB

campaigns.summary: Kaspersky described TCSectorCopy for copying OST files, a PowerShell TomBerBil variant seen in May-June 2024 incidents, and Microsoft 365 token harvesting.

diamond.adversary: Storm-0247 / ToddyCat. Microsoft labels it China-origin, and no specific state sponsor is named publicly [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Exchange exploitation (unknown exploit, ProxyLogon), China Chopper, Samurai, Ninja, LoFiSe, Pcexter, TomBerBil, TCESB (BYOVD), TCSectorCopy and token-harvesting tools [S2][S5][S6][S7][S8].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised on-premises Exchange servers [S2]. Legitimate cloud storage (OneDrive, Dropbox) used for exfiltration [S5]. Redundant tunnels through reverse SSH, SoftEther VPN, Ngrok and FRP [S6].
diamond.victim: Government, military/defense and diplomatic organizations in Europe and Asia, and in 2024 especially Asia-Pacific governments [S2][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Bulk collection of government and defense information and ongoing mailbox access are consistent with long-term state intelligence collection in Asia and Europe [S2][S6][S8].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing on-premises Exchange; Windows domain environments (domain controllers, SMB); Outlook OST files; Microsoft 365 tokens; security software with exploitable DLL loading (ESET scanner) [S2][S7][S8].

gaps: Primary Kaspersky Securelist reports (2022, 2023, 2024, 2025) could not be opened; their content here comes from Kaspersky press releases as summarized in search results and from trade-press coverage.
No cited source names a sponsoring PRC organization (MSS, PLA or a contractor). Microsoft's 'China' origin label gives no confidence level or basis.

Cluster boundaries: Microsoft merges ToddyCat (Kaspersky) and Websiic (ESET) under Storm-0247. The public evidence for the Websiic-ToddyCat link was not reviewed, and ESET's victim details for Websiic were not found.
MITRE ATT&CK page G1022 and ESET's March 2021 WeLiveSecurity report could not be fetched directly.
No Microsoft blog reporting specifically on Storm-0247 activity was found.
Some search results labeled ToddyCat as 'Russian' (a translation artifact of a localized page). That label is not supported and was not used.
Details of US or DoD-specific targeting are not reported in the cited sources.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is on-premises Exchange servers, domain controllers, and endpoints that hold Outlook mail stores and browser credentials in government, defense and diplomatic networks, especially partner-nation networks in the Asia-Pacific and Europe [S2][S6][S8]. STEP 2: Several redundant tunnels and cloud-storage exfiltration mean that removing one access path may not evict the actor [S5][S6]. STEP 3: The template runs from exploitation of an edge mail server to a web shell, then Samurai/Ninja, discovery and lateral movement over SMB, file staging with 7z, and exfiltration to OneDrive/Dropbox, followed by token theft for ongoing mailbox access [S2][S5][S6][S8]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet, persistent bulk collection from partner government and defense networks that keeps email access through stolen Microsoft 365 tokens. MDCOA is exploitation of a newly disclosed mail or edge-server flaw during a crisis to harvest coalition planning traffic, with BYOVD tooling (TCESB) used to blind endpoint security [S7][S8]. Candidate indicators: unexpected ESET command-line scanner binaries loading DLLs from non-system paths; vulnerable Dell driver loads; raw disk-sector reads that touch OST files; ProcDump against Outlook.exe; SoftEther/Ngrok/FRP binaries renamed to look like system tools; bulk uploads to OneDrive or Dropbox from servers [S5][S6][S7][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track the exposure of on-premises Exchange and mail token stores in mission-partner networks, since the actor's main victims are government and defense entities in allied regions [S2][S6]. (2) Authorities: much of the likely key terrain belongs to partner nations, so response depends on partner agreements and information-sharing channels, not DoD authorities alone. (3) Mission assurance: treat stolen Microsoft 365 tokens as continued compromise even after host cleanup; plan token revocation and credential resets alongside tunnel eradication [S6][S8]. (4) Coordination: abuse of security-vendor software (the ESET flaw) and a signed vulnerable Dell driver calls for coordination with endpoint-security owners and driver blocklisting across enclaves [S7].

identification.summary: InvisiMole is a cyber-espionage group first reported by ESET in 2018 in connection with targeted operations in Ukraine and Russia; ESET telemetry indicates it has operated since at least 2013 [S1][S2]. Its modular spyware includes two backdoor modules, RC2FM and RC2CL, with capabilities such as webcam and microphone recording, geolocation tracking and collection of recently accessed documents [S2][S3]. The record's Storm-0593 designation could not be verified in this fact-check.
identification.firstObserved: ESET: group active since at least 2013; malware first reported in 2018 [S2][S3].
identification.notes: The Storm-0593 to InvisiMole mapping is unverified (searches found no source linking them). InvisiMole is a separate group from Gamaredon; ESET describes them as distinct actors that cooperate [S3][S4]. CERT-UA tracks the activity as UAC-0035 as reported by SOC Prime [S7].

attribution.confidence: No government attribution of InvisiMole to a specific Russian organization was found in the sources gathered. ESET links InvisiMole operationally to Gamaredon (Russia-linked) but treats them as independent [S3][S4].
attribution.basis: ESET observed InvisiMole tools deployed on systems already compromised by Gamaredon, indicating cooperation between the two groups while ESET treats them as independent [S3][S4].

actors.objectives: Intelligence collection from military and diplomatic organizations and government bodies in Ukraine and Eastern Europe, using spyware that records audio and video, tracks location and collects documents [S3][S4][S7].

targeting.notes: ESET's 2018 report found the malware on a few dozen computers in Ukraine and Russia [S2]. The 2020 activity targeted a few high-profile military and diplomatic organizations in Eastern Europe from late 2019 to at least June 2020 [S3][S4].

capabilities.summary: Modular spyware with a wrapper DLL and two backdoor modules, RC2FM and RC2CL, offering nearly 100 espionage functions, including webcam and microphone access, screenshots and document theft [S2][S3]. The 2020 toolset added a DNS-tunnelling downloader for C2 communication [S3]. Operators gained initial access to targets via Gamaredon's prior compromise: InvisiMole tools were deployed only on systems already infected by Gamaredon [S3][S4]. In March 2022 CERT-UA reported spear-phishing with a ZIP containing an LNK that ran an HTA and VBScript to fetch the LoadEdge backdoor, which then pulled TunnelMode, RC2FM and RC2CL [S7].

campaigns.name: Long-running undetected spyware activity
campaigns.summary: ESET reports the malware went unnoticed until its products found it on compromised machines in Ukraine and Russia; only a few dozen computers were affected and a 2013 compile date remained in the samples.

campaigns.name: Military and diplomatic targeting with Gamaredon access
campaigns.summary: ESET reports a refreshed toolset deployed against a few high-profile military and diplomatic organizations in Eastern Europe, only on systems previously compromised by Gamaredon.

campaigns.name: CERT-UA warning on UAC-0035 spear-phishing
campaigns.summary: CERT-UA warned of spear-phishing against Ukrainian state bodies delivering LoadEdge, followed by TunnelMode, RC2FM and RC2CL (reported via SOC Prime secondary coverage).

diamond.adversary: InvisiMole (Storm-0593 designation unverified); cooperates with but is distinct from Gamaredon [S3][S4].
diamond.capability: RC2FM and RC2CL backdoors, DNS-tunnelling downloader, later LoadEdge and TunnelMode [S3][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: Initial access via systems already compromised by Gamaredon [S3][S4]; spear-phishing archives with LNK/HTA/VBScript chain in 2022 [S7]. C2 domains and hosting not captured in the sources gathered.
diamond.victim: Military, diplomatic and government organizations in Ukraine and Eastern Europe [S3][S4][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection against Ukrainian and regional military and diplomatic entities; the March 2022 campaign followed the start of the full-scale invasion, and a secondary report notes the LoadEdge compile date coincided with 24 February 2022 [S7].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints; shortcut and script-based delivery; exposure of already-compromised hosts to second-stage tooling [S3][S7].

gaps: The Microsoft Storm-0593 to InvisiMole mapping could not be confirmed by search; claims resting only on it were removed.
The CERT-UA advisory (cert.gov.ua/article/37829) was not opened; 2022 details come from secondary coverage [S7].
No InvisiMole campaign after March 2022 was found in searches; current status unknown.
MITRE ATT&CK group ID for InvisiMole was not confirmed from a source and the record's mitreGroupId remains blank.
Overlap with Gamaredon (a separate group) is cooperation, not merger; the nature of any tasking relationship is unknown.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is Ukrainian and Eastern European military and diplomatic endpoints, particularly hosts already compromised by Gamaredon, plus staff with webcams and microphones [S3][S4]. STEP 2: The adversary relies on a partner's prior access and on spear-phishing, so detecting the first-stage Gamaredon compromise is the main early warning [S3][S7]. STEP 3: Template is initial access (Gamaredon foothold or LNK/HTA/VBScript phishing), then downloader or LoadEdge, then RC2FM/RC2CL spyware with audio, video, location and document collection [S3][S7]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against Ukrainian and regional military and diplomatic targets. MDCOA is use of the same spyware against allied or coalition personnel and delegations in the region, exploiting their devices' sensors. Candidate indicators: DNS tunnelling traffic from endpoints, LNK files in unsolicited archives launching HTA/VBScript, and Gamaredon-associated infections preceding other implants [S3][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat Gamaredon detections as possible precursors to InvisiMole tooling and report them jointly. (2) Authorities: any response on partner networks in Ukraine or the region depends on host-nation and coalition agreements. (3) Mission assurance: devices of deployed personnel and delegations with webcams and microphones are exposed to audio and video collection. (4) Coordination: share indicators with CERT-UA and ESET-style vendor channels through established intelligence-sharing arrangements [S3][S7].

identification.summary: Storm-0940 is Microsoft's name for a Chinese threat actor that Microsoft says has been active since at least 2021 and obtains initial access through password spray and brute-force attacks, or by exploiting or misusing network edge applications and services [S1]. Microsoft observed it using credentials harvested by CovertNetwork-1658, a covert network of compromised small-office/home-office routers, sometimes on the same day the credentials were obtained [S1]. After access it uses scanning and credential-dumping tools for lateral movement, tries to reach network devices, installs proxy tools and remote access trojans for persistence, and attempts data exfiltration [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: active since at least 2021 [S1]. Microsoft began observing intrusions enabled by CovertNetwork-1658 password spraying in August 2023 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft tracks Storm-0940 (the actor) separately from CovertNetwork-1658 (the router network), which is also called xlogin and Quad7 (7777) [S1]. Microsoft assesses that multiple Chinese threat actors use credentials from CovertNetwork-1658, so the network is not exclusive to Storm-0940 [S1]. Public research on the botnet itself (Gi7w0rm, Sekoia, Team Cymru) predates Microsoft's actor naming; those vendors did not name Storm-0940 in the coverage reviewed [S3][S4].

attribution.confidence: Microsoft calls the actor Chinese and assesses that the CovertNetwork-1658 operator is located in China [S1]. Microsoft describes the hand-off of credentials between the network and Storm-0940 as evidence of a likely close working relationship [S1].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry on sign-in activity and on the same-day reuse of sprayed credentials [S1]. No government attribution or named sponsoring agency was found in the sources reviewed.

targeting.notes: Microsoft lists these sectors as 'among others' [S1]. Sekoia described the botnet as mainly used for brute-force attempts against Microsoft 365 accounts [S3]. Gi7w0rm earlier described low-volume brute-forcing of Microsoft Azure instances (October 2023) [S4]. Microsoft saw an increase in targeted Azure tenants between 8 and 30 October 2024 [S1].

capabilities.summary: Initial access through low-volume password spraying relayed via compromised SOHO routers (mostly TP-Link), plus brute force and exploitation or misuse of network edge applications [S1]. Microsoft says the spray submits very few attempts across many accounts, and in about 80 percent of cases only one sign-in attempt per account per day, so per-IP or per-account failure thresholds will not catch it [S1]. The router network was historically about 8,000 devices, about 20 percent spraying at once, average node uptime about 90 days [S1]. Routers are compromised through a remote-code-execution vulnerability that Microsoft says it is still investigating; the implant chain downloads a Telnet binary and the xlogin backdoor from a remote FTP server, opens a command shell on TCP 7777, then deploys a SOCKS5 server on TCP 11288 [S1]. Sekoia later reported operators developing new backdoors and reverse shells, and additional clusters on other devices (alogin on ASUS, rlogin on Ruckus, axlogin on Axentra NAS, zylogin on Zyxel VPNs) [S3]. After access, Storm-0940 uses scanning and credential-dumping tools, proxy tools and RATs; specific tool names are not given in the Microsoft post [S1].

campaigns.name: Quad7 (7777) botnet first publicly documented
campaigns.summary: Independent researcher Gi7w0rm first referenced the 7777 botnet, estimated at about 10,000 nodes and used for low-volume brute-forcing of Microsoft Azure instances. This is research on the botnet, not yet linked to Storm-0940 by name [S4].

campaigns.name: Password-spray-enabled intrusions begin
campaigns.summary: Microsoft begins observing intrusions enabled by CovertNetwork-1658 password spraying against its customers [S1].

campaigns.name: Team Cymru report on botnet 7777
campaigns.summary: Team Cymru counted 12,783 active bots over the 30 days to 5 August 2024 across the 7777 and a second 63256 (mostly ASUS) cluster, with seven management IPs [S4].

campaigns.name: Sekoia documents xlogin and sibling clusters
campaigns.summary: Sekoia describes xlogin (TP-Link, ports 7777 and 11288) and four sibling clusters, mainly used against Microsoft 365 accounts, and notes a decline in the xlogin botnet [S3].

campaigns.name: Microsoft names Storm-0940 and CovertNetwork-1658
campaigns.summary: On 31 October 2024 Microsoft publishes its assessment linking Storm-0940 to CovertNetwork-1658 credentials, notes network usage declined after the July and August 2024 vendor reports, and a rise in targeted Azure tenants from 8 to 30 October, which it says may be early evidence of new infrastructure with modified fingerprints [S1].

diamond.adversary: Chinese actor tracked by Microsoft as Storm-0940, in a likely close working relationship with the China-based CovertNetwork-1658 operator [S1].
diamond.capability: Low-volume password spray, brute force, edge-application exploitation, credential dumping, proxy tools and RATs [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: CovertNetwork-1658 / Quad7: compromised SOHO routers (mostly TP-Link) with xlogin shell on TCP 7777 and SOCKS5 on TCP 11288, about 8,000 devices, FTP-hosted implant downloads [S1]. Microsoft lists two spoofed user-agent strings and an Azure app ID in hunting guidance; it published no IPs, hashes or domains [S1].
diamond.victim: Think tanks, government, NGOs, law firms, defense industrial base in North America and Europe [S1].
diamond.technology: Cloud identity (Microsoft Entra/Azure AD, Microsoft 365) accounts lacking MFA or relying on legacy authentication, and unmanaged consumer routers used as proxies [S1][S3].

gaps: Sponsoring organization and strategic objectives are not stated in the sources reviewed; the encyclopedia country field (CN) comes from Microsoft's description.
The router vulnerability used to build CovertNetwork-1658 is unidentified; Microsoft said it was still investigating [S1].
Names of the post-compromise tools (credential dumpers, proxies, RATs) are not given in the Microsoft post [S1].
Which other Chinese actors use the same credentials is not public [S1].
No Storm-0940 reporting after November 2024 was found; current activity and whether new infrastructure materialized are unknown.
Sekoia's and Gi7w0rm's primary reports and Microsoft's naming page were not opened directly; Sekoia and Team Cymru details come from press and vendor coverage [S3][S4].
Source disagreement on the SOCKS5 port (11288 versus 11228) appears in press coverage; Microsoft states 11288 [S1][S3].
Overlap with other Microsoft or vendor actor names (for example any MITRE group) is unverified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Cloud identity tenants (Microsoft 365/Entra) used by DoD-adjacent contractors, think tanks and law firms are key terrain, as is any internet-facing edge application [S1]. STEP 2: The adversary hides spray traffic in residential and small-office router IPs, so source-IP reputation and per-account lockouts are weak defenses [S1]. STEP 3: The template is router-proxied low-and-slow spray, then same-day valid-credential logon, then scanning, credential dumping, proxy/RAT persistence and exfiltration attempts [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued spraying against government, defense industrial base and policy organizations in North America and Europe, using refreshed router infrastructure [S1]. MDCOA is use of the same shared credential pool by several Chinese actors against a single DIB tenant during a crisis; Microsoft says multiple actors use these credentials [S1]. Candidate indicators: sign-ins using the user-agent strings and app ID in Microsoft's hunting guidance, one-attempt-per-account failures spread across many accounts and source ISPs, logons from consumer ISP addresses inconsistent with user geography [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: feed identity-provider sign-in telemetry, including failed-attempt patterns across many accounts, into the common operational picture; single-IP thresholds will miss this activity [S1]. (2) Authorities: blocking or lockout actions on contractor tenants rest with the tenant owner; coordinate through DC3 and DIB cybersecurity channels rather than assuming DoD authority. (3) Mission assurance: enforce MFA with no exclusions, disable legacy authentication and move to phishing-resistant methods, as Microsoft recommends, for mission-critical accounts [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with Microsoft and partners; because multiple actors reuse the credentials, prioritize containment and password resets over attribution [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: Storm-0940 is a Chinese threat actor active since at least 2021, known for gaining initial access through password spray and brute-force attacks, as well as exploiting network edge applications. Microsoft has observed Storm-0940 utilizing valid credentials obtained from CovertNetwork-1658's password spray operations, indicating a close operational relationship between the two.
