identification.summary: Microsoft describes Storm-0978 (also DEV-0978; called RomCom by other vendors, after its backdoor) as a Russia-based cybercriminal group that runs opportunistic ransomware and extortion-only operations plus targeted credential-gathering campaigns that likely support intelligence operations [S1]. Microsoft links it to prior management of the Industrial Spy ransomware market and crypter [S1]. Cisco Talos tracks related activity as UAT-5647, a Russian-speaking cluster also known as RomCom [S2]. ESET calls the group Russia-aligned and assessed a 2025 operation as espionage [S4].
identification.firstObserved: RomCom backdoor activity against Ukrainian military targets and spoofed-software sites was reported by BlackBerry in late 2022 [S5]. Microsoft dates Industrial Spy ransomware to May 2022 and fake-installer phishing to October 2022 [S1]. Talos reports UAT-5647 activity since at least late 2023 [S2].
identification.notes: Aliases stated by sources: DEV-0978, RomCom [S1]; UAT-5647 [S2]; Void Rabisu, Tropical Scorpius, UNC2596 [S5][S6]; Underground Team (ransom-note name for the Underground ransomware) [S1]. Cluster boundaries differ by vendor: Microsoft's description centres on ransomware plus credential theft, Talos on a Ukraine/Poland espionage cluster, Trend Micro on a possibly Cuba-linked criminal group [S1][S2][S6]. Treat vendor aliases as overlapping, not identical, until vendors publish mapping evidence.

attribution.sponsor: No government sponsor is named in the sources gathered. Microsoft characterises Storm-0978 as a Russia-based cybercriminal group [S1]. ESET describes RomCom as Russia-aligned [S3][S4]. Reporting on Trend Micro's assessment says there is no evidence of state sponsorship and that the group may be a financially motivated criminal group drawn into espionage by the war in Ukraine [S6].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft's assessment is that the group is cybercriminal with espionage-supporting credential campaigns [S1]. Talos describes UAT-5647 as Russian-speaking [S2]. ESET assesses espionage motive for the 2025 WinRAR operation [S4]. No vendor in these sources attributes the group to a named Russian state organization.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and malware analysis, including Industrial Spy and Underground ransomware code overlap and the CERT-UA-reported compromise of a Ukrainian MoD email account [S1]; Talos analysis of malware variants and keyboard-language checks [S2]; ESET zero-day discovery [S3][S4]; BlackBerry and Trend Micro infrastructure and tooling reporting [S5][S6].

actors.objectives: Mixed financial and intelligence objectives: opportunistic ransomware and extortion, plus credential gathering likely supporting intelligence operations against Ukrainian government and military targets and entities with Ukraine ties [S1]. Talos assesses a staged strategy of long-term access and data exfiltration for espionage, then potential pivot to ransomware [S2]. ESET assessed espionage as the motive for the July 2025 WinRAR operation [S4].

regions: Poland (assessed by Talos from malware keyboard-language checks) [S2]
targeting.notes: Microsoft: espionage-style targeting hit government and military organizations mainly in Ukraine and defense/government entities in Europe and North America with possible Ukraine ties; ransomware victims were largely opportunistic and included telecommunications and finance [S1]. ESET observed Firefox/Windows exploit victims mostly in Europe and North America [S3]. ESET reported no successful compromises from the July 2025 WinRAR phishing, per search coverage of its research [S4].

capabilities.summary: Initial access: trojanized or look-alike installer sites for software such as Adobe products, Advanced IP Scanner, SolarWinds, KeePass and Signal [S1][S5]; phishing with lure documents including a compromised Ukrainian MoD email account (CERT-UA, December 2022) [S1]; spear-phishing with downloaders [S2]. Zero-day use: CVE-2023-36884 Microsoft Office/Word RCE in June 2023 with NATO and Ukrainian World Congress lures [S1]; chained Firefox CVE-2024-9680 and Windows Task Scheduler CVE-2024-49039 in 2024, reported by ESET as RomCom's second in-the-wild zero-day [S3]; WinRAR path-traversal CVE-2025-8088 in July 2025 [S4]. Malware: RomCom backdoor/RAT [S1], SingleCamper RAT variant, RustyClaw and MeltingClaw downloaders, DustyHammock and ShadyHammock backdoors [S2]; SnipBot variant, RustyClaw and a Mythic agent in the 2025 WinRAR chain (per search coverage) [S4]. Post-exploitation: Impacket SMBExec/WMIExec for lateral movement and SAM hive dumping for credentials [S1]. Ransomware: Industrial Spy, Underground (assessed by Microsoft as possibly an Industrial Spy rebrand) and Trigona in at least one attack [S1]. Microsoft says the actor reportedly acquired zero-day exploits [S1].

campaigns.name: Industrial Spy ransomware and marketplace
campaigns.summary: Microsoft dates first sightings of Industrial Spy ransomware to May 2022 and links Storm-0978 to management of its market and crypter. A US advisory reports third-party reporting that Cuba ransomware actors began selling stolen data on the Industrial Spy marketplace around May 2022.

campaigns.name: Fake installer sites and spoofed software
campaigns.summary: Look-alike sites for SolarWinds NPM, KeePass, PDF Reader Pro and others delivered the RomCom RAT; BlackBerry linked related artifacts to attacks on Ukrainian military institutions and noted some English-speaking countries including the UK were targeted.

campaigns.name: Compromised Ukrainian MoD email account
campaigns.summary: Per CERT-UA as cited by Microsoft, a Ukrainian Ministry of Defense email account was compromised and used to send phishing; information-stealing malware was hosted on an actor-controlled site.

campaigns.name: CVE-2023-36884 Office zero-day phishing
campaigns.summary: Phishing with NATO and Ukrainian World Congress lures against defense and government entities in Europe and North America exploited an Office RCE before disclosure; Microsoft patched on 2023-08-08. Ransomware ran concurrently against an unrelated target.

campaigns.name: Underground ransomware
campaigns.summary: Microsoft observed Underground ransomware (ransom notes signed Underground team) with code similarity to Industrial Spy, and assesses it may be a rebrand.

campaigns.name: Targeting of female political leaders (Void Rabisu)
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reported a new RomCom variant used against women political leaders; coverage notes Trend's view that the group is possibly financially motivated and drawn into espionage by the war in Ukraine. Details come from secondary coverage; the Trend Micro report was not opened.

campaigns.name: UAT-5647 campaigns against Ukraine and Poland
campaigns.summary: Talos reported activity since at least late 2023 against Ukrainian government entities and unidentified Polish entities using SingleCamper, RustyClaw, MeltingClaw, DustyHammock and ShadyHammock, and assessed a staged espionage-then-possible-ransomware strategy.

campaigns.name: Firefox and Windows zero-day chain
campaigns.summary: ESET found CVE-2024-9680 (Firefox, found 2024-10-08, patched next day) chained with CVE-2024-49039 (Windows Task Scheduler, patched 2024-11-12; also found independently by Google TAG) for code execution after visiting a malicious page; victims mostly in Europe and North America; RomCom backdoor delivered.

campaigns.name: WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 spear-phishing
campaigns.summary: Per coverage of ESET research, job-application-themed spear-phishing from 2025-07-18 to 2025-07-21 used a WinRAR zero-day to deliver SnipBot variant, RustyClaw and Mythic agent against companies in Europe and Canada; ESET reported no successful compromises. WinRAR 7.13 fixed the flaw on 2025-07-30.

diamond.adversary: Russia-based or Russia-aligned group with mixed criminal and espionage activity; no state sponsor named in sources [S1][S3][S6].
diamond.capability: RomCom family backdoors and downloaders, zero-day exploits (CVE-2023-36884, CVE-2024-9680/49039, CVE-2025-8088), Impacket, and Industrial Spy/Underground ransomware [S1][S2][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Look-alike software download domains (for example advanced-ip-scaner[.]com), actor-controlled sites hosting stealers, a Tor leak site for Underground, and a compromised Ukrainian MoD mailbox for phishing [S1][S5].
diamond.victim: Ukrainian government and military, defense and government bodies in Europe and North America with Ukraine ties, Polish entities, political leaders, and opportunistic ransomware victims in telecommunications and finance [S1][S2][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Russia's war in Ukraine and NATO support for it drive the espionage lures and targets; Trend Micro suggests the war pulled a criminal group toward espionage [S1][S6].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints, Office, WinRAR, Firefox/Thunderbird/Tor Browser, and users who download admin tools from search results [S1][S3][S4].

gaps: No source gathered ties the group to a named Russian state organization; sponsor attribution is open.

Cluster mapping is unsettled: Microsoft Storm-0978, Talos UAT-5647, Trend Micro Void Rabisu, Unit 42 Tropical Scorpius and UNC2596 overlap, but the vendor evidence for equating them, and the claimed Cuba ransomware link, was not verified here (Trend Micro treats the Cuba link as inference per secondary coverage) [S5][S6].

Primary documents not opened: Cisco Talos, ESET WeLiveSecurity, BlackBerry, Trend Micro and Unit 42 blogs failed to load or were unavailable; those findings rely on search-result summaries and secondary coverage.
No reporting after August 2025 was found in this research; current activity is unknown.
The ESET WinRAR report also names other actors exploiting the same flaw; that detail was not verified.
MITRE ATT&CK group ID not present in the record; ATT&CK mapping not attempted.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the user endpoint and the software supply path: admin-tool download sites, mail gateways, archive utilities, browsers and Office, plus allied government mailboxes that can be abused as trusted senders [S1][S3][S4]. STEP 2: The actor reuses public lures (NATO, Ukraine, job applications) and has repeatedly fielded zero-days, so defenders face short patch windows [S1][S3][S4]. STEP 3: Template is lure or fake installer, then RomCom-family backdoor, then Impacket lateral movement and credential theft, with ransomware possible [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued spear-phishing and trojanized-software campaigns against Ukraine-supporting government, defense and telecom entities in Europe and North America. MDCOA is a fresh zero-day used against coalition personnel with a ransomware pivot that disrupts mission systems [S1][S2]. Candidate indicators: look-alike domains for admin tools, Office or archive tools spawning child processes, SAM hive export, Impacket SMBExec/WMIExec activity, and WinRAR versions at or below 7.12 [S1][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor zero-day disclosures for Office, browsers and archive tools and push patch status to operators quickly [S1][S3][S4]. (2) Authorities: coordinate any response beyond owned networks through the appropriate cyber authorities; the sources give no state sponsor to justify escalation. (3) Mission assurance: ransomware pivot risk argues for offline backups and segmentation of mission networks [S1][S2]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with allied and DIB partners, since targeting spans Europe, Canada and North America [S3][S4].

provenance.importedSummary: ROMCOM is an evolving and sophisticated threat actor group that has been using the malware tool ROMCOM for espionage and financially motivated attacks. They have targeted organizations in Ukraine and NATO countries, including military personnel, government agencies, and political leaders. The ROMCOM backdoor is capable of stealing sensitive information and deploying other malware, showcasing the group's adaptability and growing sophistication.

identification.summary: Storm-1084 is a threat actor that has been observed collaborating with the MuddyWater group. They have used the DarkBit persona to mask their involvement in targeted attacks. Storm-1084 has been linked to destructive actions, including the encryption of on-premise devices and deletion of cloud resources. They have been observed using tools such as Rport, Ligolo, and a customized PowerShell backdoor. The extent of their autonomy or collaboration with other Iranian threat actors is currently unclear.

Storm-1099 is a sophisticated Russia-affiliated influence actor that has been conducting pro-Russia influence operations targeting international supporters of Ukraine since Spring 2022. They are known for their website forgery operation called "Doppelganger" and have been actively spreading false information. They have been involved in pushing the claim that Hamas acquired Ukrainian weapons for an attack on Israel. Storm-1099 has also been implicated in amplifying images of graffiti in Paris, suggesting possible Russian involvement and aligning with Russia's Active Measures playbook.

identification.summary: Microsoft describes Storm-1175 as a financially motivated cybercriminal actor that runs high-velocity ransomware campaigns by weaponizing N-day (and occasionally zero-day) vulnerabilities in web-facing systems, then deploying Medusa ransomware [S1]. On 2026-08-02 Microsoft says it began deploying a new ransomware strain, StormEncryptor, its first activity seen by Microsoft since April 2026 [S4].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft reports exploitation of web-facing assets by this actor since 2023 [S1]. The earliest dated indicator in Microsoft's IOC table is 2024-02-23 (SimpleHelp C2 IP) [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Storm-1175 (a Storm-#### designation for a developing cluster) [S1]. No other vendor aliases are stated in the sources gathered. Secondary reporting describes the actor as a former Medusa affiliate [S4]; Medusa itself runs a leak site for double extortion [S1]. Medusa ransomware as a family is distinct from this cluster, which is one actor that deploys it [S1].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor is stated. Microsoft characterizes the actor as a financially motivated cybercriminal actor [S1]. Secondary press (BleepingComputer, The Hacker News, Cloud Security Alliance) describes it as China-based or China-linked [S4][S5][S6].
attribution.confidence: The Microsoft April 2026 blog text retrieved does not state a country of origin [S1]. The China label appears in secondary coverage of Microsoft's reporting [S4][S6]; one CSA summary states the China label rests on operational and behavioral indicators rather than a confirmed link to the PLA or MSS [S5]. Treat geography as reported, not independently verified, and state nexus as unassessed.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and incident observations of exploitation, tooling and ransomware deployment [S1]. The basis for the China-based label is not shown in the sources retrieved.

actors.objectives: Financial gain through data theft, double-extortion and encryption of victim networks with Medusa ransomware and, from August 2026, StormEncryptor [S1][S4].

targeting.notes: Microsoft says recent intrusions heavily affected healthcare organizations, plus education, professional services and finance in Australia, the UK and the US [S1]. Targeting is driven by exposed vulnerable internet-facing products rather than a named sector, so any organization running them is a candidate [S1]. The August 2026 N-able N-central exploitation implies managed-service and RMM-hosting environments are in scope [S4].

capabilities.summary: Rapid weaponization of recently disclosed flaws in internet-facing software; Microsoft lists more than 16 vulnerabilities exploited since 2023 across Exchange, PaperCut, Ivanti, ConnectWise ScreenConnect, JetBrains TeamCity, SimpleHelp, CrushFTP, GoAnywhere MFT, SmarterMail, BeyondTrust and SAP NetWeaver [S1]. Microsoft has seen at least three zero-days, two named: GoAnywhere MFT CVE-2025-10035 and SmarterMail CVE-2026-23760, exploited about a week before public disclosure [S1]. Time from access to exfiltration and ransomware is often a few days and sometimes within 24 hours [S1]. Persistence is by web shell or remote access payload and by creating a new administrator account [S1]. Lateral movement uses PowerShell, PsExec, RDP (enabling it via Windows Firewall changes if blocked), Impacket, renamed Cloudflare tunnels, PDQ Deployer and many RMM tools (Atera, Level, N-able, DWAgent, MeshAgent, ScreenConnect, AnyDesk, SimpleHelp) [S1]. Credential theft uses Impacket-based LSASS dumping, Mimikatz, WDigest enablement, a Veeam credential-recovery script, and NTDS.dit and SAM access [S1]. Defense evasion includes Microsoft Defender registry tampering and AV exclusions [S1]. Exfiltration uses Bandizip and Rclone [S1]. Medusa is typically launched through PDQ Deployer with a script named RunFileCopy.cmd, sometimes by Group Policy update [S1]. In August 2026 the actor deployed StormEncryptor, a C++ ransomware that appends .encrypted and drops a ransom note, detected by Microsoft as Ransom:Win64/StormEncryptor, alongside AnyDesk, SimpleHelp, Advanced IP Scanner and Mimikatz [S4].

campaigns.summary: Exploitation of Ivanti, ScreenConnect, TeamCity and SimpleHelp flaws is listed, with Oracle WebLogic exploitation in late 2024 (specific CVE not identified). Earliest dated IOCs are SimpleHelp C2 IPs from 2024-02-23 [S1].

campaigns.summary: Microsoft publishes a profile on 2026-04-06 including SmarterMail CVE-2026-23760 zero-day exploitation, BeyondTrust CVE-2026-1731, and heavy impact on healthcare in Australia, the UK and US [S1].

campaigns.name: StormEncryptor and suspected N-central exploitation
campaigns.summary: On 2026-08-02 Microsoft says the actor began deploying StormEncryptor, first activity since April 2026 and a shift from Medusa. Initial access likely involved N-able N-central CVE-2026-18577, though the exact vulnerability is unconfirmed [S4].

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated ransomware operator tracked by Microsoft as Storm-1175; reported by secondary sources as China-based [S1][S4][S6].
diamond.capability: N-day and occasional zero-day exploitation of web-facing products, RMM tooling abuse, Impacket/Mimikatz credential theft, Rclone exfiltration, Medusa then StormEncryptor ransomware [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Web shells on exploited servers, SimpleHelp C2 servers (three IPs listed by Microsoft), Cloudflare tunnels, attacker-controlled cloud storage for Rclone sync [S1].
diamond.victim: Healthcare, education, professional services and finance organizations in Australia, UK and US running exposed vulnerable products [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Criminal extortion for profit; no state tasking is stated in Microsoft's text [S1]. Whether the actor has any link to the PRC state is unassessed in the sources [S5].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing file transfer, remote support, email, collaboration and RMM platforms, and Windows domain environments including Defender and PDQ Deployer [S1].

gaps: Microsoft's retrieved April 2026 blog text does not state a country of origin; the China-based label comes from secondary coverage and I could not open Microsoft's August 2026 post or the X thread in full [S1][S4].

Whether Storm-1175 is a Medusa affiliate or a separate operator that left Medusa is stated only in secondary press (BleepingComputer headline 'former Medusa affiliate'); I could not open the full articles [S4].
The third zero-day Microsoft mentions is not named in the retrieved text [S1].
Exact N-central vulnerability used in August 2026 is unconfirmed by Microsoft [S4].
Third-party names such as 'Spearwing' were not found in any source reviewed; no alias is added.
No government attribution, indictment, sanctions or MITRE ATT&CK group entry was found; the mitreGroupId field is empty.
Victim counts, ransom amounts and operator identities are not public in the sources gathered.
Could not open The Hacker News, Security Affairs or BleepingComputer pages directly (host unreachable); their content is taken from search summaries only.

Microsoft's October 2025 GoAnywhere blog and the Microsoft X post on StormEncryptor were not confirmed in search results and were removed as sources; their detail claims were removed or re-pointed to S1/S4.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is internet-facing file transfer, remote support, email and RMM platforms (GoAnywhere, SmarterMail, SimpleHelp, ScreenConnect, N-central) and the domain controllers and backup servers behind them [S1]. STEP 2: The actor is a criminal operator, not a state service, per Microsoft, so defense-sector exposure comes from contractor, healthcare (military health system partners) and managed-service dependencies rather than targeting of DoD by design [S1]. STEP 3: Template is exploit of a fresh vulnerability, often within days or before disclosure, then web shell or RMM install, new admin account, credential dumping, Rclone exfiltration, and Medusa or StormEncryptor via PDQ Deployer or Group Policy [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued opportunistic ransomware against organizations running newly disclosed vulnerable products, with 1-6 day dwell [S1]. MDCOA is exploitation of an RMM or MSP platform to reach many downstream customers, including defense contractors and base-supporting services, at once [S4]. Candidate indicators: unexpected RMM agents (SimpleHelp, MeshAgent, AnyDesk, Atera) on servers, renamed Cloudflare tunnel binaries, new local admin accounts, Defender exclusion or WDigest registry changes, Rclone use, RunFileCopy.cmd, .encrypted files [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor advisories and CISA-style exploited-vulnerability notices for the products listed and treat the patch window as hours, since Microsoft saw next-day and pre-disclosure exploitation [S1]. (2) Authorities: patching, isolation of web-facing systems and RMM hunting on contractor or partner networks depend on owner authorities and DIB reporting channels; coordinate rather than assume control [S1]. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize backups, offline recovery and segmentation of file-transfer and RMM servers from mission systems, given 24-hour to 6-day time to ransomware [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3 and the DIB CS program and with healthcare and MSP partners; because attribution to a state is unestablished, route as criminal ransomware incidents [S1][S5].

identification.summary: Storm-1982 is a Microsoft Threat Intelligence designation with origin listed as China; Microsoft's public naming mapping lists 'SneakyCheff' and 'UNK_SweetSpecter' as other names for it [S1]. No Microsoft narrative report on Storm-1982 was found in open search. The two other names resemble Cisco Talos's 'SneakyChef' (a Chinese-speaking actor using the SugarGh0st and SpiceRAT remote access trojans against government entities) [S3][S4] and Proofpoint's 'UNK_SweetSpecter' (SugarGh0st phishing of people tied to a US AI organization) [S5]. The mapping entry does not explain how Microsoft derived the overlap, so the profile below describes the vendor activity that the aliases point to, not Microsoft-confirmed findings [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Talos: SugarGh0st campaign likely began as early as August 2023 [S2][S3]. Palo Alto Unit 42 reported the overlapping Operation Diplomatic Specter activity as underway since at least late 2022 (as relayed by Talos coverage) [S4].
identification.notes: Vendor cluster boundaries differ and are kept separate here. (1) Talos SneakyChef: government-targeting campaign, SugarGh0st then SpiceRAT [S3]; Talos told press it is linked to Unit 42's Operation Diplomatic Specter [S4]. (2) Proofpoint UNK_SweetSpecter: May 2024 SugarGh0st campaign against fewer than ten individuals connected to one US AI organization; Proofpoint did not tie it to a known nation-state actor [S5]. (3) OpenAI 'SweetSpecter': suspected China-based adversary whose accounts OpenAI banned in October 2024; its spear-phishing carried SugarGh0st [S6]. Whether (2) and (3) are the same cluster as (1), and whether Microsoft's Storm-1982 covers all three, is not stated in the sources reviewed. Microsoft's spelling 'SneakyCheff' differs from Talos's 'SneakyChef' [S1][S3].

attribution.confidence: Microsoft's mapping lists China as the origin of Storm-1982 but gives no confidence statement or sponsor [S1]. Talos assessed with low confidence in November 2023 that the SugarGh0st operator was Chinese-speaking [S2], and with medium confidence in June 2024 that SneakyChef operators are likely Chinese-speaking [S3]. Talos has not attributed SneakyChef to a specific government [S4]. Proofpoint did not attribute UNK_SweetSpecter to a known nation-state actor [S5]. OpenAI stated its banned accounts likely belonged to a suspected China-based adversary, based on a credible source's assessment [S6].
attribution.basis: Talos cited language preferences in the code, use of Gh0st RAT variants, and target selection for the Chinese-speaking assessment [S3]. OpenAI's attribution rested on a credible source and its account-level observations [S6]. No government attribution (indictment, advisory or sanction) was found for this cluster.

actors.objectives: Talos describes SneakyChef as an espionage campaign against government entities, mostly foreign ministries and embassies, using remote access trojans [S3][S4]. Proofpoint's UNK_SweetSpecter activity targeted people connected to a US AI organization; Proofpoint did not state a goal beyond the targeting pattern and noted the timing coincided with US-China tension over AI [S5]. Sponsor-level objectives are not established.

sectors: Government (foreign ministries and embassies, per decoy content) [S3][S4]
Artificial intelligence organizations and associated academia/industry/government personnel (US) [S5][S6]
regions: Uzbekistan and South Korea (initial SugarGh0st campaign) [S2]
EMEA and Asia, widened scope; Talos named Angola, India, Latvia, Saudi Arabia, Turkmenistan, and others per coverage [S3][S4]
targeting.notes: Talos's country list derives partly from decoy-document content, so it indicates lure themes and is provisional [S3][S4]. Proofpoint saw fewer than ten targeted individuals tied to a single US AI organization [S5]. OpenAI reported spear-phishing of its own staff and said earlier SweetSpecter activity focused on political entities in the Middle East, Africa and Asia [S6][S7].

capabilities.summary: SugarGh0st is a customized variant of Gh0st RAT that Talos assessed with high confidence [S2]. Delivery in the Talos-observed campaign used LNK files inside RAR/self-extracting archives that launch VBS or JavaScript stages [S3]. In June 2024 Talos reported a second RAT, SpiceRAT, delivered by two chains, one starting from an LNK in a RAR archive and one from an HTA file; SpiceRAT is sideloaded through a legitimate Samsung RunHelp executable and a malicious DLL [S3][S4]. Proofpoint's May 2024 campaign used AI-themed emails from a free email account with a zip archive containing an LNK that launched a JavaScript dropper and SugarGh0st, and the command-and-control moved to a new domain during the campaign [S5]. OpenAI reported the SweetSpecter actor used its models for vulnerability research, scripting and phishing support, and said this gave no new capability beyond public resources; phishing emails posed as ChatGPT users and carried a zip with an LNK delivering SugarGh0st [S6][S7].

campaigns.name: SugarGh0st campaign against Uzbekistan and South Korea
campaigns.summary: Talos reported on 2023-11-30 a campaign likely started as early as August 2023 delivering the new SugarGh0st RAT, with evidence suggesting targeting of the Uzbekistan Ministry of Foreign Affairs and users in South Korea; Talos assessed low confidence that the operator was Chinese-speaking [S2].

campaigns.name: SugarGh0st phishing of US AI organization personnel (UNK_SweetSpecter)
campaigns.summary: Proofpoint reported a small campaign aimed at fewer than ten individuals connected to a single leading US AI organization, using AI-themed lures, a zip/LNK/JavaScript chain and SugarGh0st; no nation-state attribution was made [S5].

campaigns.name: SneakyChef expansion and SpiceRAT
campaigns.summary: Talos named the actor SneakyChef, reported a wider target set across EMEA and Asia using scanned government documents as lures, introduced SpiceRAT, and confirmed linkage to Unit 42's Operation Diplomatic Specter; Talos assessed medium confidence that the operators are likely Chinese-speaking [S3][S4].

campaigns.name: SweetSpecter spear-phishing of OpenAI staff (reported with account bans, 2024-10)
campaigns.summary: OpenAI's report of 2024-10-01 said it banned accounts likely belonging to a suspected China-based adversary it tracks as SweetSpecter, which used its models for research and scripting. OpenAI said it learned in May 2024, from a credible source, that the adversary was sending spear-phishing emails with a SugarGh0st-bearing attachment to its employees; its security systems blocked the emails. The date field marks the report, not the phishing activity [S6][S7].

diamond.adversary: Storm-1982 per Microsoft, origin China, no sponsor stated [S1]. Related vendor clusters assessed as likely Chinese-speaking at low to medium confidence [S2][S3]; OpenAI says suspected China-based [S6].
diamond.capability: SugarGh0st (customized Gh0st RAT) and SpiceRAT; LNK/RAR/HTA/VBS/JavaScript delivery; DLL sideloading via a legitimate Samsung executable; AI-assisted research and scripting reported by OpenAI [S2][S3][S5][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Proofpoint cited a command-and-control domain change to account.gommask[.]online during its campaign [S5]. Phishing used a free email account [S5]. Wider infrastructure detail was not retrieved.
diamond.victim: Foreign ministries and embassies themes and government entities in EMEA and Asia [S2][S3][S4]; personnel connected to a US AI organization, including OpenAI staff [S5][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Proofpoint noted the AI-organization targeting coincided with US-China tensions over AI access [S5]. Government-targeting lures follow foreign-ministry and embassy themes [S3].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints reached by email attachments (zip/RAR archives with LNK or HTA files); Gh0st-derived RATs [S3][S5].

gaps: No Microsoft report on Storm-1982 was found; the basis for Microsoft's mapping of SneakyCheff and UNK_SweetSpecter to it is unknown [S1].
Whether Talos SneakyChef, Proofpoint UNK_SweetSpecter and OpenAI SweetSpecter are one cluster is unconfirmed; Microsoft's mapping lists two of the names only [S1].
No government attribution or sponsor (MSS, PLA, contractor) identified.

Talos's original blog posts, the Proofpoint report and the OpenAI report could not be opened directly (fetch failed); details come from search-result summaries and press coverage, so verify against primaries.
Unit 42 Operation Diplomatic Specter details were not reviewed; the link is relayed through Talos coverage [S4].
Activity after October 2024 was not found.
Full infrastructure and indicator set not collected.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: relevant battlespace is email-reachable Windows endpoints of foreign ministries, embassies and AI-sector personnel; civilian and allied government networks are the observed environment, not DoD networks [S3][S5]. Step 3 (adversary): a likely Chinese-speaking espionage actor using Gh0st-derived RATs and archive/LNK/HTA delivery [S2][S3]. Step 4, MLCOA: continued phishing with diplomatic or technology-themed lures delivering SugarGh0st/SpiceRAT-style RATs to government and AI-sector users [S3][S5][S6]. MDCOA: broader targeting of defense-adjacent research or contractor staff using AI-themed lures, with AI tools aiding scripting and phishing; this is inference from the OpenAI report [S6]. Candidate indicators: LNK-in-archive attachments, HTA droppers, Samsung RunHelp sideloading of an unsigned DLL, and AI-service-themed lures from free email accounts [S3][S5][S6]. Cluster identity is unresolved, so treat as a hypothesis set.
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track Microsoft, Talos, Proofpoint and OpenAI reporting separately and note the unresolved cluster mapping [S1][S3][S5][S6]. Authorities: observed targets are foreign and civilian entities; any defensive support to partners or defense-industrial-base owners follows existing DCO and information-sharing authorities, which the sources do not address. Mission assurance: prioritize email attachment filtering (archive, LNK, HTA), endpoint detection for DLL sideloading, and user awareness for personnel who work with AI or foreign-ministry counterparts [S3][S5]. Coordination: share indicators with partner CERTs and industry via established channels; the cited material is open vendor reporting and indicators should be re-validated before action.

identification.summary: Storm-2035 is the Microsoft designation for an Iran-linked network that ran websites posing as local US news outlets and posted divisive content aimed at both Democratic and Republican audiences [S1][S2][S6]. Microsoft described it in August 2024 as separate from the IRGC-linked cyber actors (Mint Sandstorm, Peach Sandstorm) named in the same reporting [S1][S6]. OpenAI later banned ChatGPT accounts it tied to Storm-2035 that were generating articles and social media comments [S3][S4]. A later Meta report attributed a separate cluster to Storm-2035 [S7].
identification.firstObserved: Publicly described by Microsoft in August 2024 [S1][S6]. Earlier activity dates are not stated in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: Named sites in press coverage of Microsoft's report include EvenPolitics, Savannah Time and Nio Thinker (four sites in total) [S2][S6]. Microsoft's separate cyber-enabled influence actor Cotton Sandstorm (Emennet Pasargad) is a different Microsoft cluster and is not merged here [S8]. This is an influence-operation designation, not an intrusion set.

attribution.sponsor: Microsoft describes Storm-2035 as Iranian [S1][S2]. A specific Iranian government organization is not named in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Confidence level is not stated in the secondary coverage reviewed. Iran's UN mission denied interfering in the US election [S1][S6].
attribution.basis: Microsoft Threat Analysis Center reporting (read via secondary coverage) [S1][S2][S6]; OpenAI account-level findings [S3][S4]; Meta cluster attribution to Storm-2035 [S7].

actors.objectives: Inflame partisan tensions in the US by engaging voter groups at both ends of the political spectrum with polarizing messaging on the presidential candidates, LGBTQ rights and the Israel-Hamas conflict [S1][S2][S3].

sectors: US voters and political audiences (Democratic- and Republican-leaning)
regions: Azeri-speaking audiences in Azerbaijan and Turkey (Meta cluster attributed to Storm-2035, per secondary coverage) [S7]
targeting.notes: Sites were tailored by audience, for example Nio Thinker aimed at liberal readers and Savannah Time presented as conservative [S2][S5]. OpenAI saw content in English and Spanish [S3][S4].

capabilities.summary: Fake local-news websites posting politically divisive content [S1][S2]. Use of ChatGPT to write long-form articles and short social media comments, posted by more than a dozen personas on X and one on Instagram, with articles on five websites [S3][S4]. OpenAI assessed the operation did not gain meaningful audience engagement; most posts received few or no likes, shares or comments [S3][S5]. Meta tied the Instagram account to an Iranian network it disrupted in December 2022 [S3][S5].

campaigns.summary: Microsoft Threat Analysis Center reported Storm-2035 running four websites posing as news outlets with divisive content targeting both US political camps, in a report that also covered IRGC-linked Mint Sandstorm and Peach Sandstorm [S1][S2][S6].

campaigns.name: OpenAI bans ChatGPT accounts
campaigns.summary: OpenAI banned accounts used to generate long-form articles and social media comments in English and Spanish for Storm-2035; it found little audience engagement [S3][S4][S5].

campaigns.name: OpenAI links an account to IUVM and Storm-2035
campaigns.summary: Per search-result summary of an OpenAI report (not opened), one banned account generated content for both IUVM and Storm-2035, suggesting an operator-level relationship [S9].

campaigns.name: Meta Q1 2025 disruption
campaigns.summary: Meta's Q1 2025 adversarial threat report disrupted an Iranian network attributed to the Storm-2035 cluster, reported as targeting Azeri-speaking audiences with fake personas across Facebook, Instagram and other sites [S7].

diamond.adversary: Iran-linked influence network designated Storm-2035; specific sponsor unnamed in gathered sources [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Fake news sites, fake personas on X and Instagram, AI-generated text [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Websites such as EvenPolitics, Savannah Time and Nio Thinker; social accounts on X and Instagram [S2][S3][S6]. Hosting details are not in the sources gathered.
diamond.victim: US voters of both political leanings [S1][S2]; Azeri-speaking audiences in a Meta-attributed cluster [S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Exploiting US election-season polarization and issues such as the Israel-Hamas conflict and LGBTQ rights [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Social media platforms, web publishing and a commercial generative-AI service whose providers could detect and ban accounts [S3][S4].

gaps: Microsoft's original August 2024 report could not be fetched (host unreachable); details rely on secondary coverage [S1][S2][S6].
OpenAI's own case study (dated 2024-10-01 per search summary) and its Feb 2025 report could not be opened; the IUVM link rests on a search summary [S5][S9].
Sponsoring Iranian organization, confidence level and actor-to-state tasking are not stated in gathered sources.

Whether the Meta Storm-2035 cluster (Azeri-speaking targeting) is the same operators as the 2024 US-focused network is unverified; Meta's report was not opened and the Hacker News summary is ambiguous on targeting [S7].
Relationship to Cotton Sandstorm/Emennet Pasargad is not established; Microsoft reports them as separate [S8].
No post-2025 activity found; a Scotland-related claim could not be verified and is excluded.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The operational environment is the US information environment, including news-like websites and social platforms. STEP 2: The network used low-cost tools with limited engagement, so impact on audiences was low [S3][S5]. STEP 3: Template is fake local-news sites, personas on X and Instagram, and AI-generated English and Spanish text [S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued polarizing content aimed at US audiences around elections and the Israel-Hamas conflict [S1]. MDCOA is better-concealed, more tailored personas or amplification by other Iranian actors that gain traction. Candidate indicators: new local-news-style sites with unclear ownership, repeated persona accounts posting near-identical text, and takedown notices from platforms or AI providers [S3][S7].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track platform and AI-provider disclosures (Microsoft, OpenAI, Meta) as the main source of detection [S1][S3][S7]. (2) Authorities: influence operations against US audiences are outside most DoD network-defense authorities; route findings to appropriate interagency partners. (3) Mission assurance: personnel should be aware that fake news sites may target service members as voters. (4) Coordination: keep this cluster separate from IRGC cyber actors in reporting [S1][S6].

identification.summary: Storm-2077 is Microsoft's name for a China-based threat actor that Microsoft assesses has been active since at least January 2024 [S1]. Microsoft states Storm-2077 overlaps with activity other vendors track as TAG-100 [S1]. Recorded Future's Insikt Group first reported TAG-100 in July 2024, then re-designated it RedNovember in September 2025 and noted the overlap with Microsoft's Storm-2077 [S2][S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: active since at least January 2024 [S1]. Recorded Future: report on TAG-100 published July 2024; RedNovember activity window June 2024 to July 2025 [S2][S6].
identification.notes: Aliases: TAG-100 (Recorded Future, July 2024) and RedNovember (Recorded Future, September 2025) [S2][S6]. The overlap between Microsoft and Recorded Future clusters is stated as an overlap, not an identity, by Microsoft [S1]. Microsoft says Storm-2077 also shared some victimology and techniques with other actors it was already tracking, without naming them [S1].

attribution.sponsor: Microsoft assesses Storm-2077 is a China state threat actor [S1]. Recorded Future assesses RedNovember (formerly TAG-100) as highly likely Chinese state-sponsored, per coverage of its report [S6][S7].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft uses the wording 'assesses' for China state actor status and 'likely' for the intelligence-collection objective [S1]. In July 2024 Recorded Future could not attribute TAG-100 to a specific country but said the victim profile aligned with historical Chinese state-sponsored targeting [S2][S3]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Microsoft cites its own telemetry and analysis of activity affecting a handful of customers [S1]. Recorded Future cites victimology consistent with Chinese state-sponsored groups, later upgraded after further review [S2][S6].

actors.objectives: Microsoft assesses Storm-2077 likely operates with the objective of intelligence collection [S1]. Email theft is a stated focus, since mailboxes can be analyzed later without immediate loss of access [S1].

sectors: Semiconductor supply chain and high-technology manufacturing
regions: Global, including at least ten countries in TAG-100 reporting [S2][S3]
Asia-Pacific intergovernmental organizations; Southeast Asia trade-focused body [S2][S6]
targeting.notes: Microsoft says Storm-2077 initially hit US government agencies and NGOs, then broadened to the defense industrial base, aviation, telecommunications, and financial and legal services, describing targeting as 'all sectors appear to be on the table' [S1]. Recorded Future's TAG-100 report listed two Asia-Pacific intergovernmental organization secretariats, diplomatic entities, ministries of foreign affairs, trade associations, and semiconductor supply-chain, non-profit and religious organizations [S2][S3]. The Record also reported religious organizations in the US and Taiwan and a political party supporting an investigation into the Chinese government [S4]. RedNovember coverage reports at least two US defense contractors and a European engine manufacturer [S6].

capabilities.summary: Microsoft describes credential-phishing for initial access, in some cases likely exploitation of edge-facing devices, reuse of valid credentials, and use of stolen credentials to reach legitimate cloud applications including eDiscovery applications to exfiltrate email; after gaining administrative access the actor created its own application with mail-read rights [S1]. Microsoft's page names no malware or CVEs [S1]. Recorded Future reports exploitation of internet-facing products including Citrix NetScaler, F5 BIG-IP, Zimbra, Microsoft Exchange, SonicWall, Cisco ASA, Palo Alto GlobalProtect and Fortinet FortiGate, with reconnaissance and attempted exploitation of dozens of US organizations after a proof-of-concept for CVE-2024-3400 was released [S2][S3]. Post-access tooling is open source: Pantegana and SparkRAT in TAG-100 reporting, and Pantegana, Cobalt Strike and SparkRAT in RedNovember reporting [S2][S3][S6][S7]. Later reporting adds Ivanti Connect Secure, Sophos and Outlook Web Access as targeted access points [S6]. Recorded Future argues open-source tooling complicates attribution and lets state actors outsource to proxy groups or contractors [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: Earliest Microsoft-observed Storm-2077 activity
campaigns.summary: Microsoft assesses the actor has been active since at least January 2024, initially targeting US government agencies and NGOs [S1].

campaigns.name: TAG-100 / RedNovember edge-device exploitation window opens
campaigns.summary: Recorded Future's later RedNovember reporting dates the activity window from June 2024 to July 2025 [S6][S7].

campaigns.name: Recorded Future publishes TAG-100 report
campaigns.summary: Insikt Group reports likely compromise of two Asia-Pacific intergovernmental organization secretariats with Pantegana, plus victims in over ten countries, using internet-facing appliance exploitation and open-source Go backdoors. Reconnaissance and exploitation attempts against dozens of US organizations followed the CVE-2024-3400 proof-of-concept release [S2][S3][S4].

campaigns.summary: Microsoft describes Storm-2077 phishing, eDiscovery cloud-app credential abuse, and creation of a mail-read application for email exfiltration, and notes TAG-100 overlap [S1].

campaigns.name: Recorded Future re-designates activity as RedNovember
campaigns.summary: Insikt Group assesses the cluster as highly likely Chinese state-sponsored and reports broadened targeting of US defense contractors, aerospace, semiconductors and government networks through firewalls, VPNs and OWA, with an analysis cut-off of 25 July 2025 [S5][S6][S7].

diamond.adversary: China-based state threat actor per Microsoft; highly likely Chinese state-sponsored per Recorded Future [S1][S6]. Operator identities, organization and tasking authority are not public in the sources gathered.
diamond.capability: Credential phishing, edge-device exploitation, cloud application abuse for mail access, and open-source implants (Pantegana, SparkRAT, Cobalt Strike) [S1][S2][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Recorded Future reporting describes C2 for open-source tooling; specific IPs, domains and hosting details were not obtainable from the sources opened here [S2].
diamond.victim: Government, NGO, defense industrial base, aviation, telecommunications, finance, legal, semiconductor and intergovernmental organizations [S1][S2][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection for a PRC state objective as assessed by Microsoft; victim set includes entities tied to Asia-Pacific diplomacy and Taiwan-related religious groups [S1][S4].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing VPN, firewall and mail gateways; cloud email and eDiscovery applications; weak control of application registrations with mail-read permissions [S1][S2][S6].

gaps: Recorded Future's RedNovember report (PDF) and original TAG-100 report could not be opened directly; details come from search excerpts and secondary coverage (The Hacker News, The Record, The Register) [S2][S5][S6][S7].
WebFetch failed for recordedfuture.com, thehackernews.com and theregister.com (host not resolved), so those pages were not read in full.
Microsoft's page names no tools, CVEs, indicators or victims for Storm-2077; the overlap with TAG-100/RedNovember is stated by Microsoft as an overlap only [S1].

Microsoft does not name the other actors whose victimology and techniques Storm-2077 overlapped; one secondary summary claims overlap with Silk Typhoon (HAFNIUM) but this was not verified in a primary source.
A CyCraft report on RedNovember expansion (mentioning a LESLIELOADER loader) appeared in search but could not be searched or opened; its claims are unverified.
Infrastructure indicators, exact CVE list exploited, and the full victim count are not verified here.
No government attribution or sanctions/indictments were found; sponsoring organization (MSS, PLA, contractor) is unknown.
Activity after the 25 July 2025 report cut-off is not covered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes internet-facing VPNs, firewalls and mail gateways, and cloud email tenants including eDiscovery applications [S1][S2][S6]. STEP 2: The actor has expanded from US government and NGOs to the defense industrial base, aviation and semiconductors, so DoD contractors are within the target set [S1][S6]. STEP 3: The observed template is edge-device exploitation or credential phishing, then open-source implants (Pantegana, SparkRAT, Cobalt Strike) or cloud-app abuse, then mailbox collection [S1][S2][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued intelligence collection against DIB, aerospace and allied government email. MDCOA is rapid exploitation of a newly disclosed edge-device vulnerability across DoD-adjacent organizations soon after proof-of-concept release, as seen with CVE-2024-3400 [S2][S3]. Candidate indicators: new application registrations with mail-read permissions, unusual eDiscovery application sign-ins, Pantegana or SparkRAT artifacts on hosts behind edge devices, and exploitation attempts against VPN and firewall appliances [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track edge-device advisories and cloud tenant audit logs for application consent and mail-read grants, since these are the observed collection mechanisms [S1][S2]. (2) Authorities: cloud tenant and perimeter device hardening and hunt actions fall to the system owner; coordinate approvals before remediation on contractor systems. (3) Mission assurance: email holds credentials, financial and intellectual-property data, so assess exposure of mission planning traffic to mailbox compromise [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DIB partners and DC3, and note that vendor names differ (Storm-2077, RedNovember, TAG-100) so reporting should be deconflicted [S1][S6].

provenance.importedSummary: TAG-100 is a cyber-espionage APT that targets government and private sector organizations globally, exploiting vulnerabilities in internet-facing devices such as Citrix NetScaler and F5 BIG-IP for initial access. The group employs open-source tools like Pantegana and SparkRAT for persistence and post-exploitation activities, including credential theft and email data exfiltration. TAG-100 has compromised entities in at least ten countries, including two Asia-Pacific intergovernmental organizations, and focuses on sectors like education, finance, and local government. Their operations highlight the challenges of attribution due to the use of off-the-shelf tools and techniques that overlap with other state-sponsored groups.

identification.summary: Storm-2372 is Microsoft's name for a device code phishing cluster active since August 2024 [S1]. Microsoft initially assessed with moderate confidence that it aligns with Russian interests, victimology and tradecraft, and described it as a suspected nation-state actor [S1]. A 31 July 2026 update on the Microsoft blog says Microsoft has further assessed Storm-2372 to be an initial access operations sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard, based on technical and operational overlaps [S1]. The actor poses as a prominent person relevant to the target on WhatsApp, Signal or Microsoft Teams, then sends invitations to online events or meetings that lead the victim to enter an actor-generated device code on the legitimate Microsoft sign-in page [S1].
identification.firstObserved: August 2024 (Microsoft) [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft uses 'Storm' for temporary, developing clusters; this one has now been folded into Midnight Blizzard as a sub-cluster per the July 2026 update [S1]. The update text was read through a fetch summary of the Microsoft page; confirm wording on the live page. Microsoft says it tracks other groups using similar techniques, including those documented by Volexity [S1]. Volexity separately reported several Russian actors (UTA0304, UTA0307, and CozyLarch assessed with medium confidence to overlap Midnight Blizzard/APT29) using device code phishing from about January 2025 [S2]. Do not merge Volexity clusters into Storm-2372 without a source stating the link.

attribution.sponsor: Russia (suspected). Microsoft: aligned with Russian interests; July 2026 update: sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard [S1]. No government attribution located.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft: moderate confidence in the original February 2025 assessment of Russian alignment [S1]. The 2026 sub-cluster assessment is stated without a confidence level in the text seen [S1].
attribution.basis: Microsoft cites Russian interests, victimology and tradecraft [S1] and, in 2026, technical and operational overlaps with broader Midnight Blizzard operations [S1]. Details of the overlaps are not given in the text seen.

actors.objectives: Initial access to accounts at government, NGO and other organizations, followed by Graph API collection of email, including searches for credentials and government-related terms such as 'ministry' and 'gov' [S1]. Strategic intent is not stated by Microsoft beyond alignment with Russian interests [S1].

targeting.notes: Sectors and regions from Microsoft [S1]. Victim counts and named victims are not public in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: Social engineering of rapport via WhatsApp, Signal or Teams impersonating a relevant prominent person, then Teams-style meeting invitations where the device code is presented as the meeting ID [S1]. The actor generates legitimate device code requests, captures access and refresh tokens and so bypasses passwords [S1]. It then uses Microsoft Graph to search mailboxes for keywords (for example username, password, admin, teamviewer, anydesk, credentials, secret, ministry, gov) and exfiltrate email [S1]. It sends further device code phishing links from compromised internal accounts for lateral spread [S1]. By 14 February 2025 it used the Microsoft Authentication Broker client ID, obtained a refresh token, requested a device registration service token, registered an actor-controlled device in Entra ID, obtained a Primary Refresh Token and collected email from the connected device [S1]. It also began using proxies regionally matched to targets [S1]. Microsoft published no malware, domain, IP or hash indicators [S1].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the cloud identity plane (Entra ID, Microsoft 365 mail, Teams, Graph API) and personal messaging apps used by staff to reach contacts [S1]. STEP 2: The actor needs no malware or password; defender exposure is whether the device code flow is allowed and whether users can be rapport-baited [S1]. STEP 3: Template is impersonation on WhatsApp/Signal/Teams, then fake meeting invite with device code, token capture, Graph keyword search for credentials and government terms, internal re-phishing, then device registration and PRT theft [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued email collection against government, defense, NGO and telecom targets in allied regions. MDCOA is use of captured PRTs and credentials found in mail to pivot to privileged cloud accounts and maintain access after token revocation, which is plausible given the device registration step [S1]. Candidate indicators: device code sign-ins (error 50199 followed by success), new devices registered through the Device Registration Service shortly after, sign-ins from anonymized or target-region proxies, Graph mailbox access with keyword searches, and clicks on device login URLs [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: cloud identity telemetry (Entra sign-in logs, device registration events) must reach cyber defenders; no malware indicators exist to hunt [S1]. (2) Authorities: blocking device code flow and Conditional Access changes sit with tenant owners; confirm who may order them across mission partners [S1]. (3) Mission assurance: prefer phishing-resistant MFA and device enrollment restrictions; revoke refresh tokens when compromise is suspected [S1]. (4) Coordination: personnel contacted via personal messaging apps are outside enterprise monitoring, so reporting channels for suspicious outreach and sharing with coalition and DIB partners should be set up in advance [S1].

identification.summary: Storm-2603 is Microsoft's name for a threat actor first publicly described in July 2025 in connection with exploitation of on-premises SharePoint vulnerabilities (the 'ToolShell' chain), where Microsoft observed it stealing MachineKeys and, from 18 July 2025, deploying Warlock ransomware [S1][S2]. Microsoft says it has also seen the actor deploy LockBit ransomware in the past and that it cannot yet confidently assess the actor's objectives [S1]. Check Point traced related infrastructure to campaigns from March 2025 that delivered LockBit Black and Warlock/x2anylock ransomware [S3]. Other vendors track overlapping activity as GOLD SALEM (Sophos), CL-CRI-1040 (Palo Alto Unit 42) and Longlegs (Symantec) [S3][S4][S5].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft reports exploitation of the SharePoint flaws by actors as early as 7 July 2025 (all three named actors together; no Storm-2603-specific date) and Storm-2603 ransomware deployment from 18 July 2025 [S1]. Check Point links Storm-2603 infrastructure to campaigns dating back to March 2025 [S3]. Sophos lists related incidents from April 2025 [S4].
identification.notes: Vendor cluster boundaries differ and are not proven identical: Sophos GOLD SALEM, Unit 42 CL-CRI-1040 and Symantec Longlegs are described by secondary reporting as the same or overlapping activity [S3][S4][S5]. Microsoft states it found no links between Storm-2603 and other known Chinese threat actors, and distinguishes it from Linen Typhoon and Violet Typhoon, which exploited the same vulnerabilities [S1][S2]. Warlock is the ransomware name; Trend Micro has suggested it may be a rebrand of Anylock (.x2anylock extension) [S6].

attribution.confidence: Microsoft assesses with moderate confidence that Storm-2603 is a China-based threat actor and says it cannot confidently assess its objectives [S1]. Sophos reportedly said it lacks sufficient evidence to confirm the China-based attribution [S4]. Symantec, as reported by BleepingComputer, describes the actor (Longlegs) as China-linked [S5]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry on SharePoint exploitation and ransomware deployment [S1]. Check Point notes custom tooling (ak47c2 C2 framework, DLL sideloading) and earlier LockBit Black/Warlock activity [S3]. The basis for Microsoft's moderate-confidence China assessment is not detailed in the sources reviewed.

actors.objectives: Unconfirmed. Microsoft says it cannot confidently assess objectives; it observed MachineKey theft and ransomware deployment (Warlock, previously LockBit) [S1]. Ransomware use and a leak site (about 60 victims published by September 2025 per Sophos) point to financial extortion [S4], but whether espionage or state tasking is involved is unverified.

sectors: Agriculture, finance and local government, business services, energy (nuclear) and industrial (Sophos incident table, April-August 2025) [S4]
regions: Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking countries in Europe, Africa and Latin America (Symantec, as reported October 2026) [S5]
North America, Europe and South America (Sophos leak-site observations) [S4]
targeting.notes: Initial access depends on unpatched on-premises SharePoint servers, so targeting follows exposure rather than a stated sector priority [S1][S5]. SharePoint Online in Microsoft 365 was reported as not affected [S2]. Victim names were not disclosed in the Symantec reporting [S5].

capabilities.summary: Initial access via CVE-2025-49706 and CVE-2025-49704 (ToolShell chain) against on-premises SharePoint, then the spinstall0.aspx web shell and theft of MachineKeys [S1]. Post-exploitation per Microsoft: whoami discovery, abuse of services.exe to disable Microsoft Defender, PsExec for SYSTEM and lateral movement, Impacket over WMI, Mimikatz against LSASS, scheduled tasks and IIS components loading malicious .NET assemblies for persistence, and Group Policy modification to push Warlock ransomware [S1]. Microsoft also lists an IIS backdoor (IIS_Server_dll.dll), SharpHostInfo and a fast reverse proxy (xd.exe) [S1]. Check Point describes a custom C2 framework the actor called ak47c2 with HTTP and DNS clients and reports multiple ransomware families, including LockBit Black and Warlock/x2anylock [S3]. Sophos reports Velociraptor misuse as ransomware precursor activity from mid-August 2025, VS Code tunnel C2 attempts and a vulnerable-driver (BYOVD) defense-evasion tool [S4]. Symantec, as reported, observed security tools disabled on at least 40 hosts in about two hours and Warlock launched on at least 33 hosts in one intrusion, plus DLL sideloading [S5].

campaigns.summary: Microsoft reported that Storm-2603 exploited on-premises SharePoint CVE-2025-49706 and CVE-2025-49704, deployed the spinstall0.aspx web shell, stole MachineKeys, and from 18 July 2025 deployed Warlock ransomware via Group Policy. Exploitation by the three named actors began as early as 7 July 2025. Microsoft's blog was published 22 July and updated 23 July 2025.

campaigns.name: Continued SharePoint exploitation against critical infrastructure
campaigns.summary: BleepingComputer (2 October 2026, reporting Symantec and Carbon Black) described Warlock/Longlegs intrusions at a water utility, telecom provider, regional government body and university in Europe, Africa and Latin America via SharePoint flaws, with web shells, DLL sideloading and ransomware on at least 33 hosts in one case.

diamond.adversary: Storm-2603, assessed by Microsoft with moderate confidence as China-based, with unassessed objectives; ransomware operator behavior with a Warlock leak site [S1][S4].
diamond.capability: ToolShell SharePoint exploitation, spinstall0.aspx web shell, MachineKey theft, ak47c2 C2, IIS backdoor, PsExec, Impacket, Mimikatz, GPO-based ransomware deployment, Velociraptor, BYOVD [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Microsoft lists C2 domains (update.updatemicfosoft.com, msupdate.updatemicfosoft.com), post-exploitation C2 IPs and an ngrok-hosted PowerShell delivery URL [S1]. Sophos reports a Cloudflare workers.dev domain for Velociraptor download [S4].
diamond.victim: Organizations with internet-facing on-premises SharePoint, including water, telecom, government, education, energy and industrial entities [S4][S5].
diamond.technology: On-premises SharePoint servers (ASP.NET machine keys, IIS), Windows domain environments using Group Policy, and security tooling that can be disabled via registry or vulnerable drivers [S1][S4].

gaps: Objectives and any state tasking are unconfirmed; Microsoft says it cannot confidently assess them [S1].
Basis for Microsoft's moderate-confidence China-based assessment is not public in the sources reviewed; Sophos reportedly lacks evidence to confirm it [S1][S4].

Cluster mapping among Storm-2603, GOLD SALEM, CL-CRI-1040 and Longlegs rests on vendor and press statements; primary Symantec, Unit 42 and Sophos reports could not be opened (hosts blocked from this environment) and were read only via search summaries.
The Check Point primary post could not be fetched; details come from search result summaries.
Warlock-Anylock rebrand claim (Trend Micro) and any Black Basta link are reported secondhand and unverified; the Security.com/Symantec article date (about August 2025) is approximate.
Victim names and counts are not public or are inconsistent across sources (leak-site count about 60 by September 2025; one aggregator cites 396 SharePoint servers across 145 organizations).
No government (CISA, DOJ) attribution or advisory specific to Storm-2603 was located.
Microsoft naming mapping and learn.microsoft.com naming page listed in the actor record were not opened in this pass.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing on-premises SharePoint servers and the Active Directory/Group Policy plane behind them are key terrain; ASP.NET machine keys let an intruder persist after patching [S1][S5]. STEP 2: The actor operates on exposure rather than sector, opportunistically hitting unpatched servers within days of disclosure; Microsoft saw ransomware begin on 18 July 2025 within about 11 days of first exploitation [S1]. STEP 3: Template is ToolShell exploit, web shell, MachineKey theft, Defender disablement, credential dumping, PsExec/Impacket lateral movement, then GPO-pushed ransomware, with DLL sideloading and tunnels for persistence [S1][S3][S4][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued extortion-style ransomware against organizations with unpatched or un-rotated SharePoint, including utilities and telecom [S5]. MDCOA, an assessment not stated in sources, is use of the same access against DoD-adjacent or critical-infrastructure hosts for disruption or espionage if objectives are state-directed, which is unconfirmed [S1]. Candidate indicators: spinstall*.aspx files, debug_dev.js, IIS_Server_dll.dll, xd.exe, unexpected GPO changes, Velociraptor or VS Code tunnel use, and Defender disabled through services.exe registry edits [S1][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track SharePoint exposure and patch/key-rotation status across mission-relevant enclaves, since patching alone does not remove stolen MachineKeys or persistence [S1][S5]. (2) Authorities: because attribution (state versus criminal) is unresolved, determine early whether response falls under defensive cyber operations, law-enforcement or DIB reporting channels; do not assume a state nexus [S1][S4]. (3) Mission assurance: ransomware deployed through Group Policy can reach many hosts in hours, so prepare offline backups and manual fallbacks for dependent mission systems [S1][S5]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3, the DIB CS program and sector partners, and note that Microsoft, Sophos, Symantec and Unit 42 use different names for overlapping activity [S3][S4][S5].

identification.summary: Suckfly is the Symantec name for a China-based cyber-espionage group. Symantec's May 2016 reporting attributes a series of attacks beginning in April 2014 to it [S3][S5]. Symantec believes the group developed the custom Backdoor.Nidiran specifically for espionage and delivered it via strategic web compromise [S1]. The group first came to public attention in March 2016 through its use of stolen code-signing certificates [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: Attacks attributed to Suckfly by Symantec begin April 2014 [S3][S5]; certificate-signed tools in use from early 2014 [S1][S2]. Symantec found the activity in late 2015 [S2].
identification.notes: Suckfly is Symantec's name. The imported record lists APT22 (Mandiant), BRONZE OLIVE (Secureworks) and Group 46 as aliases, and MITRE tracks the group as G0039; I could not open those vendor pages and no cited source here states the mappings, so they are not added or independently confirmed. A MISP galaxy commit discovered in search results shows Suckfly was at one point confused with APT41 and later corrected; do not merge facts across those clusters. Microsoft has no record of a Typhoon/Sleet name for this group in the imported record (msName empty).

attribution.confidence: Symantec states the group is China-based and traced activity to three IP addresses in Chengdu, China [S1]. No source gathered attributes Suckfly to a named PRC government organization.
attribution.basis: Symantec infrastructure observation: activity originated from three separate IP addresses, all in Chengdu, China [S1]. This is a vendor assessment, not government attribution.

actors.objectives: Espionage is the stated purpose of the Nidiran backdoor per Symantec [S1]; the end objective is not established in the sources gathered.

sectors: Healthcare (Indian business unit of a US provider)
regions: South Korea (Seoul companies whose code-signing certificates were stolen) [S1][S2]
targeting.notes: Symantec's May 2016 report lists one of India's largest financial organizations, a large e-commerce company and its shipping vendor, one of India's top five IT firms, two government organizations and the Indian business unit of a US healthcare provider [S3][S4]. Victim names are not public. A secondary blog claims defense and energy targeting and six government victims; that conflicts with the Symantec-based coverage and is not used.

capabilities.summary: Symantec reports the group stole code-signing certificates from nine companies in central Seoul and used them to sign hacking tools and malware [S1][S2]. The exact theft method is unknown; Symantec's most likely scenario is malware inside the victim companies that searched for and extracted certificates [S2]. Tools included a Windows brute-force SMB scanner signed with a certificate belonging to a South Korean mobile software developer, which led to discovery in late 2015 [S2][S6]. The custom Backdoor.Nidiran was delivered via strategic web compromise [S1]. The stolen certificates were still valid when found [S2].

identification.summary: Sunglow Blizzard is the current Microsoft name listed for the former designation DEV-0665 in Microsoft's public threat actor naming mapping [S4]. DEV-0665 was the Microsoft cluster associated with the destructive FoxBlade (HermeticWiper) attacks on Ukraine that began on 2022-02-23 [S1]. The mapping gives no origin or description for the entry [S4].
identification.firstObserved: 2022-02-23 (FoxBlade/HermeticWiper destructive attack first discovered, per Microsoft) [S1]
identification.notes: NAMING CONFLICT. Microsoft's February 2022 post says FoxBlade events were attributed with medium confidence to 'IRIDIUM (previously tracked as DEV-0665)' [S1]. The current mapping file instead lists DEV-0665 as an alias of Sunglow Blizzard and lists IRIDIUM as an alias of Seashell Blizzard (with Sandworm, APT44, VOODOO BEAR and others) [S4]. The two sources do not agree on whether DEV-0665 belongs to Sunglow Blizzard or to the IRIDIUM/Seashell Blizzard cluster, so no facts from the Seashell Blizzard cluster are merged into this record. Microsoft tracks the separate January 2022 WhisperGate actor as DEV-0586 [S1]. Microsoft calls IsaacWiper 'Lasainraw' and says it had not linked it to an attributed actor [S1].

attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributed FoxBlade-associated events with medium confidence to the cluster it then named IRIDIUM (previously DEV-0665) [S1]. ESET stated it had found no tangible connection to a known threat actor and no significant code similarity to other samples in its collection [S2]. No source gathered attributes the Sunglow Blizzard name to a state sponsor.
attribution.basis: Microsoft MSTIC assessment in its February 2022 Ukraine post [S1]. The mapping file gives no origin for Sunglow Blizzard [S4].

actors.objectives: Microsoft assessed a continued risk of destructive activity from the group based on follow-on intrusions observed since 2022-02-23 [S1].

targeting.notes: Microsoft describes the FoxBlade attack as affecting hundreds of systems across government, IT, financial and energy organizations, mainly in or linked to Ukraine [S1]. ESET observed HermeticWiper on hundreds of systems in at least five Ukrainian organizations [S2]. Whether these victims are all attributable to Sunglow Blizzard specifically is not established given the naming conflict.

capabilities.summary: Microsoft's FoxBlade is the same family as ESET's HermeticWiper and HermeticWizard, with SonicVote corresponding to HermeticRansom [S1]. ESET describes HermeticWiper as the wiper, HermeticWizard as a worm that spreads over local networks via WMI and SMB, and HermeticRansom as Go-based ransomware acting as a decoy [S2]. The malware was signed with a certificate issued to Hermetica Digital Ltd, which DigiCert revoked on 2022-02-24 at ESET's request [S2]. Microsoft notes use of a renamed SysInternals sdelete (cdel.exe) for targeted secure deletion in the associated cluster [S1].

campaigns.name: FoxBlade / HermeticWiper attacks on Ukraine

diamond.adversary: Microsoft cluster DEV-0665, now listed as Sunglow Blizzard; sponsor not stated in gathered sources [S4].
diamond.capability: FoxBlade/HermeticWiper, HermeticWizard worm (WMI/SMB), HermeticRansom decoy, renamed sdelete [S1][S2].
diamond.victim: Ukrainian government, IT, financial and energy organizations [S1][S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Destructive activity timed hours before the 2022-02-24 invasion of Ukraine [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints and domain networks reachable by SMB/WMI lateral movement [S2].

gaps: Microsoft's 2022 post names IRIDIUM (previously DEV-0665) while the current mapping lists DEV-0665 under Sunglow Blizzard and IRIDIUM under Seashell Blizzard [S1][S4]. The reason for the divergence (rename, split or correction) was not found in gathered sources.

No state sponsor is stated for Sunglow Blizzard in gathered sources; the mapping file leaves origin blank [S4]. Other vendors' views on HermeticWiper attribution (for example Recorded Future, Virus Bulletin slides) were seen only as search snippets and are not cited.
Initial access, dwell time and C2 infrastructure for the HermeticWiper intrusions were not obtained.
No activity attributed to Sunglow Blizzard after 2022 was found.

Primary documents not opened: ESET original blog (host unreachable by fetch, content taken from search summary), CISA AR22-115B, Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2022 chapter, MISP galaxy and Malpedia entries.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Windows domain networks of government, IT, financial and energy organizations are key terrain; wipers target availability of endpoints [S1][S2]. STEP 2: The actor-cluster pattern shows destructive payloads staged and executed within hours of a kinetic escalation [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Observed template is a signed wiper plus a worm for SMB/WMI spread and a decoy ransomware [S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is destructive wiper attacks against a state's government and critical-sector networks timed to kinetic or political escalation. MDCOA is the same worm-enabled spread across a coalition partner's networks whose boundary is shared with the target state [S2]. Candidate indicators: renamed sdelete use against C:, newly signed binaries from unfamiliar publishers, and anomalous WMI/SMB lateral movement [S1][S2]. Attribution of this cluster is unresolved (see gaps).
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor naming changes, since DEV-0665 maps differently across Microsoft sources [S1][S4]. (2) Authorities: destructive response on partner networks requires coordination with the host nation and supported command; this record gives no authority guidance. (3) Mission assurance: validated offline backups, tamper protection and current endpoint detections are the Microsoft-recommended mitigations [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators and certificate-revocation requests with industry and partners, as ESET did with DigiCert [S2].

identification.summary: China-based cyber-espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Swirl Typhoon and maps to TELLURIUM, STALKER PANDA, Tick, Bronze Butler and REDBALDKNIGHT [S1]. Unit 42 describes Tick as primarily targeting organizations in Japan and the Republic of Korea [S8]. Recent reporting covers a 2021-2022 supply-chain compromise of an East Asian data-loss-prevention (DLP) vendor [S5] and mid-2025 zero-day exploitation of Motex LANSCOPE Endpoint Manager (CVE-2025-61932) [S3][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro says it has tracked the group since 2008 [S9].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Swirl Typhoon; Microsoft's mapping lists TELLURIUM, STALKER PANDA, Tick, Bronze Butler and REDBALDKNIGHT as other names [S1]. Stalker Taurus (Unit 42) appears in this record's imported aliases but was not confirmed in sources gathered here. MITRE tracks the group as BRONZE BUTLER (G0060) [S12]. 'PLA Unit 61419' is a Japanese government attribution of sponsorship, not a vendor cluster name [S10][S11].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China. In April 2021, Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Katsunobu Kato said one of the suspected attackers worked for People's Liberation Army Unit 61419, which is sometimes called Tick [S10]. The National Police Agency's Mitsuhiro Matsumoto said it was highly likely that PLA Unit 61419, a strategic support unit operating from Qingdao, Shandong, was involved [S11].
attribution.confidence: Japanese government officials named PLA Unit 61419 as highly likely involved [S10][S11]. Recorded Future's Insikt Group told The Record the unit-level attribution was most likely based on older Chinese military intelligence collected before recent PLA reforms [S11]. ESET attributed the DLP-vendor compromise to Tick with high confidence [S5]. China rejected the Japanese allegations [S11].
attribution.basis: Japanese police investigation of the 2016 JAXA intrusions, including a case filed against a Chinese national who allegedly rented servers used in the attacks while living in Japan [S10]; vendor malware and infrastructure analysis by Sophos, Unit 42, Trend Micro and ESET [S3][S5][S8][S9].

actors.objectives: Long-term espionage. Trend Micro reported attempts to steal military-related documents from defense firms [S9]. ESET judged cyberespionage the most likely aim of the DLP-vendor compromise, whose customers include government and military bodies [S5]. Sophos said the 2025 LANSCOPE targeting appeared limited to sectors aligned with the group's intelligence objectives [S3][S4].

sectors: Defense, aerospace, chemical and satellite firms [S9]
Government and military customers of a DLP software vendor (supply chain) [S5]
Air-gapped critical systems via South Korean secure USB drives [S8]
regions: East Asia (DLP vendor and its customers) [S5]
Japanese firms with subsidiaries in China [S9]
targeting.notes: Japanese investigators linked the campaign to roughly 200 Japanese companies and research bodies, but JAXA was the only victim publicly named [S10][S11]. Imported actor summary also lists Taiwan, Hong Kong and the United States; no source gathered here confirmed those regions.

capabilities.summary: Zero-day exploitation, including a 2016 zero-day in the Japanese asset-management product SKYSEA Client View [S3] and mid-2025 zero-day exploitation of LANSCOPE Endpoint Manager CVE-2025-61932, which lets unauthenticated attackers run code with SYSTEM privileges [S3][S4][S13]. Supply-chain operations: compromise of a DLP vendor's internal update servers and trojanized third-party tool installers (Q-Dir) passed to customers [S5]. Weaponized secure USB drives aimed at air-gapped systems [S8]. Use of hijacked legitimate email accounts and credentials to deliver malware [S9]. Custom malware families include Daserf [S12], Minzen, Datper, Nioupale and HomamDownloader [S8], ShadowPy, Netboy and Ghostdown [S5], and the Gokcpdoor proxy backdoor, with the Havoc C2 framework used in some 2025 intrusions [S4].
